aberration-abber.title: Aberration (ABBER)
aberration-abber.summary: A moving average with bands set a multiple of the average absolute deviation away, so the channel widens with typical distance from the mean.
aberration-abber.descriptionHtml:
Aberration draws a channel around a moving average of the source. The width of the channel comes from the average absolute deviation: on each bar the study takes the distance between the source and the average, ignoring its sign, and then takes a simple average of those distances over the same period. The upper band is the average plus a multiple of that figure and the lower band is the average minus it.

The centre line can be a simple, exponential, weighted, running (RMA) or low-lag HMA average, chosen from a menu. The exponential choice starts from the first value rather than from a simple average, so it answers from the first bar. During the warmup of the average, the distance is measured against zero, exactly as the calculation reads a missing value as zero.

Because absolute deviation weighs every distance equally rather than squaring it, a single large bar moves these bands less than it moves a band built on standard deviation.
aberration-abber.howToReadHtml:
Price that holds near the centre line is trading inside its usual range. A close beyond the upper or lower band means price has moved further from the average than it typically does over the period, which some traders read as a breakout and others as stretched. Widening bands show dispersion growing; narrowing bands show it shrinking.

The bands follow the average, so they lag a sharp turn by roughly the period. A move outside them says the move is unusual for the recent past, not that it will continue or reverse.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average and the deviations are measured on, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the moving average and in the average of the absolute deviations. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Moving Average Type
settings.html: The kind of average used as the centre line: simple, exponential, weighted, running (RMA) or low-lag HMA.

settings.label: Deviation Multiplier
settings.html: How many average absolute deviations the bands sit from the centre line. A larger value gives a wider channel.

settings.label: Show Moving Average Line
settings.html: Draw the centre line between the bands, or hide it and keep only the two bands.

faq.q: How is this different from a standard deviation band?
faq.html: It measures spread with the average absolute distance from the mean rather than the root of the squared distances. Large outliers count for less, so the bands react less to one extreme bar.

faq.q: Why are the bands missing on the first bars?
faq.html: The bands need both the moving average and a full window of deviations. They appear once the average of the deviations has a full period behind it.

faq.q: Does changing the average type change the width?
faq.html: Yes. The deviations are measured from whichever average is selected, so a faster average sits closer to price and usually gives narrower bands.

related.title: Acceleration Bands (ACCBANDS)
related.summary: An average of the close with bands pushed beyond the averaged high and low by a multiple of the average bar spread.

related.title: Andrews' Pitchfork (AP)
related.summary: Three parallel lines projected from three pivot points read a fixed number of bars back, recomputed on every bar.

related.title: Adaptive Price Zone
related.summary: A double smoothed average of price with a zone around it sized by the double smoothed bar range.

accelerator-oscillator-ac.title: Accelerator Oscillator (AC)
accelerator-oscillator-ac.summary: Measures whether momentum is speeding up or slowing down: the midpoint momentum oscillator less its own five-bar average.
accelerator-oscillator-ac.descriptionHtml:
The Accelerator Oscillator looks one step beyond momentum. It first builds a momentum line from the midpoint of each bar, high plus low over two: a fast simple average of the midpoint minus a slow one. It then subtracts a five-bar simple average of that momentum line from the line itself.

What is left is the change in momentum, so the oscillator tends to turn before the momentum line does. Every average here covers the bars seen so far until its window fills, so the study draws from the first bar. The slow window is always kept at least one bar longer than the fast one. The line is green when it is at or above zero and red when it is below.
accelerator-oscillator-ac.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, momentum is running ahead of its recent average, which means it is accelerating; below zero it is decelerating. A move from red to green says the driving force behind the trend has started to pick up, often before price or the momentum line turns.

The oscillator is sensitive and changes sign often, so a single bar of one colour says little; a run of bars in the same colour is a firmer reading. The values are in price units, and the first bars average fewer than a full window, so they are less reliable than the rest.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: Number of bars in the fast average of the midpoint. Shorter values make the oscillator react sooner.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: Number of bars in the slow average of the midpoint. It is raised to one bar more than the fast length if set lower.

faq.q: How is it different from the momentum line it is built on?
faq.html: The momentum line is a fast minus a slow average of the midpoint. This oscillator subtracts a five-bar average of that line, so it shows how fast momentum is changing rather than its level.

faq.q: Can I change the five-bar smoothing?
faq.html: No. The smoothing window is fixed at five bars; only the fast and slow lengths of the underlying momentum line are settings.

faq.q: What do the colours mean?
faq.html: Green is a reading at or above zero, red is a reading below zero.

related.title: Awesome Oscillator (AO)
related.summary: Plots the fast simple average of the bar midpoint minus the slow one, coloured green while it is rising or flat and red while it is falling.

related.title: Absolute Price Oscillator (APO)
related.summary: Plots the gap between a fast and a slow exponential average in price units, with a correction that removes the starting bias on early bars.

related.title: Bollinger %B
related.summary: Shows where price sits inside its own Bollinger Bands, with 0 at the lower band, 1 at the upper band and readings beyond them outside the bands.

acceleration-bands-accbands.title: Acceleration Bands (ACCBANDS)
acceleration-bands-accbands.summary: An average of the close with bands pushed beyond the averaged high and low by a multiple of the average bar spread.
acceleration-bands-accbands.descriptionHtml:
Acceleration Bands build a channel from the typical shape of recent bars. Over the last period bars the study takes the simple average of the highs, of the lows and of the closes. The middle line is the average close.

The band width is the averaged high minus the averaged low, multiplied by the factor. The upper band adds that width on top of the averaged high, and the lower band subtracts it from the averaged low. Because the bands start from the averaged extremes rather than from the middle line, they are always wider than the typical bar.

The averages are running sums. Until a full period of bars exists they average every bar so far, so the bands are drawn from the first bar and settle into a true rolling average once the window fills.
acceleration-bands-accbands.howToReadHtml:
A close above the upper band means price has moved beyond the recent typical range by more than the usual spread, a sign of an accelerating move up; a close below the lower band is the same on the downside. While price stays between the bands the move is ordinary for the period.

The bands widen when bars get larger and narrow when they get smaller. The first bars use fewer than period bars, so treat the opening stretch with care.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the averages of the high, low and close. Longer gives smoother, slower bands.

settings.label: Factor
settings.html: The multiple of the averaged high to low spread added beyond the averaged high and low. Larger values widen the channel.

faq.q: Why are the bands drawn from the very first bar?
faq.html: The averages divide by however many bars exist until the window is full, so the first bars carry an expanding average instead of a gap.

faq.q: What makes the bands widen?
faq.html: Larger bars. The width is the average high minus the average low times the factor, so a stretch of wide bars pushes the bands apart.

faq.q: Is the middle line an average of the close?
faq.html: Yes. It is the simple average of the close over the same period as the two bands.

related.title: Andrews' Pitchfork (AP)
related.summary: Three parallel lines projected from three pivot points read a fixed number of bars back, recomputed on every bar.

related.title: Aberration (ABBER)
related.summary: A moving average with bands set a multiple of the average absolute deviation away, so the channel widens with typical distance from the mean.

related.title: Adaptive Price Zone
related.summary: A double smoothed average of price with a zone around it sized by the double smoothed bar range.

acceleration-slope-of-slope-accel.title: Acceleration (Slope of Slope) (ACCEL)
acceleration-slope-of-slope-accel.summary: The slope of a rolling regression slope: how fast the trend of the source is itself speeding up or slowing down, bar by bar.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-accel.descriptionHtml:
Acceleration measures the change in a trend rather than the trend itself. It fits a straight line to the source over the last Period bars and takes the slope of that line, which is the trend's speed in price per bar. It then fits a second line, over the same number of bars, to that slope series and plots its slope.

Each fit is a rolling least squares line over the last Period bars, where the x value is the bar number. The sums behind it are kept as running totals: each bar adds the newest point and removes the one that left the window. A bar whose value is absent still takes its place in the window but adds nothing to the sums, and a slope needs at least two valid points.

The second fit cannot start until the first has produced two slopes, so the acceleration line begins one bar after the slope would.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-accel.howToReadHtml:
Above zero the trend's slope is rising: an uptrend is getting steeper or a downtrend is flattening. Below zero the slope is falling: an uptrend is losing speed or a downtrend is getting steeper. A cross of zero marks where the trend's speed stopped increasing and started decreasing, or the other way round, which often comes before the trend itself turns.

The values are in price per bar per bar, so they scale with the instrument's price and are not comparable across symbols. A second derivative is noisier than the first, so use a longer period on fast charts.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars each of the two regression lines is fitted over. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the first regression is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is acceleration not just the change in momentum?
faq.html: Momentum compares two single bars. Here both stages are least squares fits over a window, so every bar in the window counts and a single outlier moves the reading much less.

faq.q: Does a positive value mean price is going up?
faq.html: Not necessarily. It means the slope is rising. A downtrend that is slowing down also has positive acceleration while price is still falling.

faq.q: Why does it start later than the source?
faq.html: The first fit needs two bars to give a slope, and the second fit needs two of those slopes, so the first value appears on the third bar of the chart.

related.title: Two-Argument Arctangent (ATAN2)
related.summary: Plots the angle, in radians from -pi to pi, of the point formed by two chosen bar values, keeping the sign of each in all four quadrants.

related.title: Beta Distribution CDF (BETADIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative Beta distribution, giving a shaped 0 to 1 oscillator.

related.title: Binomial Distribution CDF (BINOMDIST)
related.summary: Treats the source's position in its recent range as a success rate p and plots the probability of at most k successes in n trials.

accumulation-distribution-line-adl.title: Accumulation/Distribution Line (ADL)
accumulation-distribution-line-adl.summary: A running total of volume weighted by where each bar closes within its range, tracking buying and selling pressure over time.
accumulation-distribution-line-adl.descriptionHtml:
The Accumulation/Distribution Line adds up volume, but it weights each bar's volume by where the bar closed inside its own range. A close at the high counts the full volume as buying, a close at the low counts it as selling, and a close in the middle counts nothing.

On every bar the study computes a money flow multiplier: the close minus the low, less the high minus the close, divided by the bar's range. It runs from +1 at the high to -1 at the low, and is 0 on a bar with no range. That multiplier times the bar's volume is the bar's money flow, and the line is the running total of money flow from the first bar. A bar without volume, or with a missing price, adds nothing, so the line stays flat there.
accumulation-distribution-line-adl.howToReadHtml:
Read the direction of the line rather than its level, which depends only on where the chart starts. A rising line says volume has been arriving on closes near the highs, which is read as accumulation; a falling line says closes near the lows, read as distribution.

A common use is to look for disagreement with price: price making a new high while the line fails to, or price falling while the line rises. The line ignores gaps between bars, so a market that gaps up and closes near its low still counts as selling.

faq.q: Why does the line start at a different level on different charts?
faq.html: It is a running total from the first loaded bar, so its absolute value depends on how much history is loaded. Only its direction and its turns carry meaning.

faq.q: What does a bar with no range add?
faq.html: Nothing. When the high equals the low the multiplier is set to 0, so the bar's volume does not move the line.

faq.q: How is it different from on-balance volume?
faq.html: On-balance volume adds or subtracts the whole bar's volume depending on whether the close rose or fell. This line scales the volume by where the close sits within the bar's own range.

related.title: Chaikin A/D Oscillator (ADOSC)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average of the accumulation/distribution line, showing shifts in money flow momentum.

related.title: AOBV - Archer On-Balance Volume (AOBV)
related.summary: Two smoothed lines of on-balance volume, a fast and a slow, that read accumulation and distribution from the first bar.

related.title: Chaikin Money Flow (CMF)
related.summary: The share of recent volume that traded on the buying side, from money flow volume summed over a window and divided by total volume.

chaikin-a-d-oscillator-adosc.title: Chaikin A/D Oscillator (ADOSC)
chaikin-a-d-oscillator-adosc.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average of the accumulation/distribution line, showing shifts in money flow momentum.
chaikin-a-d-oscillator-adosc.descriptionHtml:
The Chaikin A/D Oscillator measures the momentum of the accumulation/distribution line. That line is a running total of volume weighted by where each bar closes inside its range: the close times two, less the high and the low, divided by the range, times the volume. A bar without volume, without range or with a missing price adds nothing.

The study takes two exponential averages of the line, a fast one over the short period and a slow one over the long period, each started from zero. While a compensating weight, which starts at 1 and shrinks by the slow average's factor on every bar, is above a tiny threshold, both averages are divided by one minus that weight. The correction follows the slow average, so it is exact for the slow one and only approximate for the fast one in the first bars. The oscillator is the fast average minus the slow one. On the first bar the correction is not defined, so the line begins on the second bar.
chaikin-a-d-oscillator-adosc.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the fast average of the accumulation/distribution line is above the slow one, meaning the line has been rising recently, read as money flowing in; below zero, the reverse, read as money flowing out. A cross of zero marks a change in that balance, and the oscillator often turns before the line itself does.

Disagreement with price is the common use: price at a new high while the oscillator makes a lower peak suggests buying is fading. The scale is in volume units and depends on the instrument, so compare peaks on the same chart only.

settings.label: Short Period
settings.html: The length of the fast exponential average of the accumulation/distribution line.

settings.label: Long Period
settings.html: The length of the slow exponential average. It also sets how quickly the start-up correction fades.

faq.q: Why is the first bar empty?
faq.html: The start-up correction divides by a number that is exactly zero on the first bar, so there is no reading until the second bar.

faq.q: Why are the values so large?
faq.html: The oscillator is built from a running total of volume, so its scale follows the instrument's volume. Only its sign, its turns and its peaks relative to each other matter.

faq.q: What is the difference from the accumulation/distribution line?
faq.html: The line shows the running total. The oscillator shows whether a short average of that total sits above or below a longer one, that is, whether the total has recently been rising or falling.

related.title: AOBV - Archer On-Balance Volume (AOBV)
related.summary: Two smoothed lines of on-balance volume, a fast and a slow, that read accumulation and distribution from the first bar.

related.title: Accumulation/Distribution Line (ADL)
related.summary: A running total of volume weighted by where each bar closes within its range, tracking buying and selling pressure over time.

related.title: Chaikin Money Flow (CMF)
related.summary: The share of recent volume that traded on the buying side, from money flow volume summed over a window and divided by total volume.

average-daily-range-adr.title: Average Daily Range (ADR)
average-daily-range-adr.summary: Averages the plain high-minus-low range of each bar, with a choice of simple, exponential or weighted smoothing, to show how far price travels in a bar.
average-daily-range-adr.descriptionHtml:
Average Daily Range measures how far price moves within a bar, without the gap component that true range adds. Each bar's range is simply its high minus its low, and a missing range is read as zero. The study then averages that range by one of three methods, chosen with the Method setting.

Method 1 is a simple mean of the last length ranges; while fewer bars exist it averages every bar so far, so it answers from the first bar. Method 2 is a running average with weight 1 / length, started from zero and divided by 1 - e (the weight the zero start still holds), which removes the bias of the zero start. Method 3 is a weighted mean with weight length on the newest bar down to 1 on the oldest, divided by the full sum of weights; bars before the start of the chart count as zero, so its first values ramp up from below.
average-daily-range-adr.howToReadHtml:
Read ADR as the typical size of a bar in price units. On a daily chart that is the typical day's range, which traders compare with the range the current day has covered so far. On an intraday chart it is the typical bar's range.

A rising line means bars are widening, a falling line that they are narrowing. Unlike ATR it ignores gaps, so after a large gap the ADR can understate how far price actually moved. It has no direction.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars of range are averaged. A shorter length follows changes in range faster, a longer one is steadier.

settings.label: Method
settings.html: The smoothing: 1 for a simple mean, 2 for a bias-corrected running average with weight 1 / length, 3 for a linearly weighted mean that favours the newest bars.

faq.q: How is ADR different from ATR?
faq.html: ADR uses only the high minus the low of each bar. ATR also measures from the previous close, so it counts gaps. On instruments that trade around the clock the two are close; where gaps are common, ATR reads higher.

faq.q: Which method should I choose?
faq.html: The simple mean weighs every bar in the window equally. The running average responds faster to a change and never fully forgets older bars. The weighted mean favours the newest bars but still drops a bar once it leaves the window.

faq.q: Why does method 3 start low?
faq.html: The weighted mean always divides by the full sum of weights, and bars before the first one on the chart count as zero, so for the first length bars it is pulled down and climbs to its true level.

related.title: Average True Range (ATR)
related.summary: Measures how far price typically travels in one bar, counting any gap from the previous close, as a smoothed average of the true range.

related.title: Average True Range Normalized (ATRN)
related.summary: Places the current average true range inside its own range over the last ten lengths of bars, from 0 at the lowest to 1 at the highest.

related.title: Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
related.summary: The average true range divided by the close and shown as a percentage, so volatility can be compared across instruments and price levels.

average-directional-movement-index-adx.title: Average Directional Movement Index (ADX)
average-directional-movement-index-adx.summary: Plots ADX with the +DI and -DI lines from running totals that subtract their own earlier value, a recursion that leaves the usual ranges soon after the first period.
average-directional-movement-index-adx.descriptionHtml:
ADX is meant to separate how strongly a market is trending from which way it is trending. Each bar contributes three numbers. The true range is the bar's range, stretched to include any gap from the previous close (on the first bar it is simply high minus low). Plus directional movement is how far the high rose above the previous high, counted only when that rise is larger than the drop of the low and is positive. Minus directional movement is the mirror image for the low.

Each of the three is kept in a running total that, on every bar, adds the new value and subtracts the total itself as it stood period bars earlier, not the value that entered period bars earlier. +DI is 100 times the plus total over the true range total and -DI is the same for the minus total, each capped at 50 but with no floor. DX is the gap between the two as a percentage of their sum, and ADX is a running total of DX built the same way, divided by the period.

That recursion is not a moving sum. For the first period bars it is an ordinary cumulative total, but once it starts subtracting earlier totals it no longer stays bounded: on hourly BTCUSD with the default period of 14, ADX leaves the 0 to 100 range on bar 19, the DI lines turn negative a bar later, and ADX grows to values of the order of 1e76 by the end of 1463 bars. With a period of 1 the totals reduce to the single bar's values and stay in range.
average-directional-movement-index-adx.howToReadHtml:
Only the first period bars or so follow the textbook reading: a rising ADX for a one-sided market, +DI above -DI when upward movement dominates and -DI above +DI when downward movement does. After that the running totals swing negative and grow without limit, so the lines no longer measure trend strength or direction and should not be read as such.

Treat this study as a record of this particular calculation rather than as a trading tool. If you need a usable directional reading, the Directional Movement Index (DX) and ADXR entries in this library use smoothed averages that stay within 0 to 100.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in each running total. A longer period gives smoother, slower lines; a shorter one reacts sooner and is noisier.

faq.q: Why does ADX reach huge negative and positive numbers?
faq.html: Each running total subtracts its own value from period bars earlier instead of the term that entered then. That recursion feeds back on itself, so after the first period the totals oscillate with growing size, and every line built from them follows.

faq.q: Why are the DI lines never above 50?
faq.html: This calculation caps each directional index at 50 before the DX ratio is taken. There is no lower cap, which is why the DI lines can go far below zero once the totals turn negative.

faq.q: Is any setting stable?
faq.html: A period of 1 is: each total then holds only the current bar's value, so +DI and -DI stay between 0 and 50 and ADX between 0 and 100. Every longer period becomes unstable a few bars after the first full period.

related.title: Average Directional Movement Index Rating (ADXR)
related.summary: Averages today's ADX with the ADX from a set number of bars earlier, a steadier read of trend strength drawn with ADX, +DI and -DI.

related.title: Williams Alligator
related.summary: Three smoothed averages of different lengths, each shifted forward by its own number of bars, whose spacing shows trend or rest.

related.title: Archer Moving Averages Trends (AMAT)
related.summary: Flags a bar as trending only when a fast and a slow exponential average agree on both their order and their direction, and measures their spread.

average-directional-movement-index-ratin.title: Average Directional Movement Index Rating (ADXR)
average-directional-movement-index-ratin.summary: Averages today's ADX with the ADX from a set number of bars earlier, a steadier read of trend strength drawn with ADX, +DI and -DI.
average-directional-movement-index-ratin.descriptionHtml:
ADXR smooths trend strength by averaging the current ADX with an older one. It starts from the same building blocks as ADX: the true range of each bar, and the plus and minus directional movement, which is how far the high rose above the previous high or the low fell below the previous low, counted on one side only.

The three are smoothed with Wilder's recursion, each seeded with its first value. While the smoothing is young, each running value is divided by 1 - e, where e is (1 - 1 / period) raised to the bar index, which removes the bias of the seed. +DI and -DI are the smoothed directional movements as a percentage of the smoothed true range, each capped at 50. DX is their gap as a percentage of their sum, and ADX is DX smoothed the same way from a zero start.

ADXR is the average of this bar's ADX and the ADX ratingPeriod bars earlier. Until that many bars exist the earlier value is taken from the first bar, where ADX has no value and counts as zero, so the earliest ADXR readings are about half the ADX.
average-directional-movement-index-ratin.howToReadHtml:
Read ADXR as a slower ADX. Because it mixes in an older reading, it turns later than ADX but moves less on a single burst of activity, which makes it useful for judging whether a market has been trending over a span of bars rather than just now. A rising ADXR says trend strength is building, a falling one that it is fading.

Use the +DI and -DI lines for direction: the higher one shows which side owns the movement. The first stretch of bars is held down by the zero substitution described above, so wait for at least the rating period before trusting the level of the ADXR line.

settings.label: ADX Period
settings.html: The smoothing length for the true range, the directional movement and ADX itself. Longer gives slower, smoother lines.

settings.label: Rating Period
settings.html: How many bars back the older ADX is taken from. A longer gap makes ADXR lag ADX more and smooth it further.

faq.q: How is ADXR different from ADX?
faq.html: ADXR is the average of the current ADX and the ADX from the rating period earlier, so it is smoother and slower to turn than ADX alone.

faq.q: Why is ADXR about half of ADX at the start?
faq.html: Until the rating period has passed, the older reading is taken from the first bar, where ADX has no value and is counted as zero. The average is therefore roughly half the current ADX.

faq.q: Why are the DI lines capped at 50?
faq.html: This calculation limits each directional index to 50 before the DX ratio is taken, so very one-sided movement reads as 50 rather than higher.

related.title: Williams Alligator
related.summary: Three smoothed averages of different lengths, each shifted forward by its own number of bars, whose spacing shows trend or rest.

related.title: Average Directional Movement Index (ADX)
related.summary: Plots ADX with the +DI and -DI lines from running totals that subtract their own earlier value, a recursion that leaves the usual ranges soon after the first period.

related.title: Archer Moving Averages Trends (AMAT)
related.summary: Flags a bar as trending only when a fast and a slow exponential average agree on both their order and their direction, and measures their spread.

adx-variable-moving-average-adxvma.title: ADX Variable Moving Average (ADXVMA)
adx-variable-moving-average-adxvma.summary: An adaptive average that uses the ADX as its smoothing factor, following price closely in a strong trend and flattening in a range.
adx-variable-moving-average-adxvma.descriptionHtml:
The ADX Variable Moving Average is an exponential-style average whose step size changes every bar. On each bar it moves from its previous value toward the source by a fraction of the distance, and that fraction is the ADX divided by 100.

The ADX is built in the usual way. The true range and the upward and downward directional moves are each smoothed with a weight of 1 / Period, giving the plus and minus directional indicators. Their normalised difference, the directional index, is smoothed the same way to give the ADX. Every smoothed value starts from zero and is divided by 1 - beta^n over the early bars, where beta is 1 - 1 / Period, so the ADX is usable from the first bars. The average itself starts at the first source value.
adx-variable-moving-average-adxvma.howToReadHtml:
When the ADX is high the market is trending and the line moves a large share of the way toward price each bar, so it hugs the trend. When the ADX is low the market is directionless and the line barely moves, so it goes flat through a range. A flat ADXVMA is itself a sign of a trendless market, and a line that starts to slope again shows a trend gathering strength.

The ADX measures strength, not direction, so the line can still lag at a sharp reversal: the ADX often stays high for a few bars after a trend ends. It is a trend filter more than a timing tool.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the true range, directional moves and ADX. Longer makes the ADX, and so the line, react more slowly.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default. The ADX itself always uses the high, low and close.

faq.q: Why does the line go flat in a range?
faq.html: A low ADX means a small step size, so each bar the line moves only a little toward price and stays almost level.

faq.q: Does a rising line mean the ADX is rising?
faq.html: No. The ADX only sets how fast the line moves; the direction comes from where price is relative to the line.

related.title: Ahrens Moving Average (AHRENS)
related.summary: A recursive average that steps toward price from the midpoint of its previous value and its value one period ago.

related.title: Arnaud Legoux Moving Average (ALMA)
related.summary: A Gaussian-weighted moving average whose peak weight can slide from the middle of the window toward the newest bar.

related.title: Blackman Moving Average (BLMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Blackman window, a three-term cosine taper that falls to zero at both ends of the lookback.

autoregressive-fir-moving-average-afirma.title: Autoregressive FIR Moving Average (AFIRMA)
autoregressive-fir-moving-average-afirma.summary: A cosine-windowed moving average of recent prices; with the least squares option on, it becomes a plain simple average of the window.
autoregressive-fir-moving-average-afirma.descriptionHtml:
AFIRMA is a finite impulse response average: a weighted mean of the last Period prices whose weights come from a cosine window. The weight of the price k bars back is a0 + a1 * cos(x) + a2 * cos(2x) + a3 * cos(3x), where x = 2 * pi * k / p and p is the window length. The Window Function setting chooses the leading terms: 1 (Hanning) uses 0.5 and -0.5, 2 (Hamming) uses 0.54 and -0.46, 3 (Blackman) uses 0.42, -0.5 and 0.08, and 4 (Blackman-Harris) uses 0.35875, -0.48829 and 0.14128. The two higher terms keep the Blackman-Harris values for every choice, exactly as the calculation is defined, so windows 1 to 3 are not the textbook shapes. Every window gives its largest weight to the middle of the window and small weights to the newest and oldest prices.

The window grows with the chart: on bar i it spans min(i + 1, Period) bars, so the line answers from the first bar.

With Least Squares Method switched on, a straight line is fitted by least squares through the newest n prices, where n is floor((p - 1) / 2) (at most 50). Those newest prices are replaced by their fitted values, the older prices are kept, and the result is the plain, unweighted average of that blended window. A least squares line always has the same total as the prices it fits, so the replacement changes nothing and the result equals the simple moving average of the last p prices; the cosine weights are not used at all in this mode.
autoregressive-fir-moving-average-afirma.howToReadHtml:
Read AFIRMA as a smooth trend line on the price chart. Its slope gives the direction, and price crossing it marks a change in the short-term balance. Because the weights peak in the middle of the window and the newest price gets very little weight, the line lags price by about half the Period.

With the least squares option on, the line is the simple moving average of the window, which is a little less smooth than the cosine-weighted version and has about the same lag. Either way the line is built from bars that have closed; it smooths the past rather than forecasting the next bar.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window spans once the chart is long enough. Larger values smooth more and lag more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken over, the close by default.

settings.label: Window Function
settings.html: Which cosine window shapes the weights: 1 Hanning, 2 Hamming, 3 Blackman, 4 Blackman-Harris. Each sets the leading terms of the weight formula.

settings.label: Least Squares Method
settings.html: Replaces the newest part of the window with a fitted straight line and takes a plain average. Since the fitted values sum to the prices they replace, this gives the simple moving average of the window.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The window grows from one bar up to the Period setting, so an average exists from the start. The earliest values use only a few bars and move more.

faq.q: Which window function should I use?
faq.html: All four put the most weight on the middle of the window and differ only in how the weights taper toward the ends, so the lines are close to each other. The default, window 4, tapers the newest and oldest prices almost to zero weight.

faq.q: What does the least squares option change?
faq.html: It fits a straight line through the newest prices of the window, uses the fitted values in place of those prices, and takes a plain average. A least squares line has the same total as the points it fits, so the result is exactly the simple moving average of the window.

related.title: Ehlers Correlation Cycle (CCOR)
related.summary: Correlates the last Period prices with one cycle of a cosine and of a negative sine, drawn as two lines scaled to -100 and +100.

related.title: Ehlers Cyber Cycle (CCYC)
related.summary: A two-pole high-pass filter over a lightly smoothed price that strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle, with a one-bar trigger line.

related.title: Center of Gravity (CG)
related.summary: Where the weighted balance point of the last N prices sits relative to the middle of the window, an oscillator that turns at cycle highs and lows.

ehlers-automatic-gain-control-agc.title: Ehlers Automatic Gain Control (AGC)
ehlers-automatic-gain-control-agc.summary: A roofing filter that isolates the price cycle, scaled by its own decaying peak so the oscillator always swings between -1 and +1.
ehlers-automatic-gain-control-agc.descriptionHtml:
Automatic Gain Control turns price into a cycle oscillator with a constant height. It first runs a roofing filter: a two-pole highpass with cutoff HP Length removes trends longer than that period, and a Super Smoother with cutoff SS Length removes noise shorter than its period. What is left is a zero-centred wave, plotted as the grey Filter line.

The study then tracks the peak size of that wave. On every bar the peak shrinks by the Decay factor, and if the wave's current magnitude is larger the peak jumps up to it. The AGC line is the wave divided by that peak. Because the divisor is never smaller than the current magnitude of the wave, the result stays between -1 and +1 whatever the price level or volatility.

The highpass starts at zero on the first bar, and its first missing history is read as zero, so the oscillator settles over the first stretch of bars.
ehlers-automatic-gain-control-agc.howToReadHtml:
Read the blue AGC line as a normalised cycle. Readings near +1 mean the cycle is at a peak as large as anything recently seen, readings near -1 mean a matching trough, and crossings of zero are the turns of the cycle from one side to the other. The grey Filter line shows the same wave in price units, so you can see whether a full-height AGC swing came from a big move or a small one.

The scaling hides absolute size: after a quiet spell the peak has decayed, and even a small wiggle can reach +1 or -1. A slower Decay (closer to 1) remembers big swings for longer. The oscillator removes the trend by design, so it says nothing about direction over periods longer than HP Length.

settings.label: Decay
settings.html: The factor the tracked peak is multiplied by on each bar. Values closer to 1 keep large past swings in memory longer.

settings.label: HP Length
settings.html: The highpass cutoff in bars. Cycles and trends longer than this are removed before scaling.

settings.label: SS Length
settings.html: The Super Smoother cutoff in bars. Noise faster than this is removed before scaling.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filters run on, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the AGC line stay between -1 and +1?
faq.html: It is the filtered wave divided by a peak that is never smaller than the wave's current magnitude, so the ratio cannot exceed one in size.

faq.q: What is the grey Filter line?
faq.html: The roofing filter output before scaling: the price cycle in price units, with long trends and short noise removed.

faq.q: Why can a small move read near +1?
faq.html: The peak decays every bar. After a quiet stretch it has shrunk, so a modest swing is large compared with it and fills the whole range.

related.title: Ehlers Adaptive Laguerre Filter (ALAGUERRE)
related.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother whose speed adapts bar by bar to how far it has fallen behind price, speeding up in moves and slowing in ranges.

related.title: Baxter-King Band-Pass Filter (BAXTERKING)
related.summary: A centred, zero-sum band-pass filter on the close that keeps only cycles between two periods and oscillates around zero.

related.title: Bessel 2nd Order Filter (BESSEL)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass smoother with Bessel-style coefficients, giving a smooth price line with a steady, predictable lag.

ahrens-moving-average-ahrens.title: Ahrens Moving Average (AHRENS)
ahrens-moving-average-ahrens.summary: A recursive average that steps toward price from the midpoint of its previous value and its value one period ago.
ahrens-moving-average-ahrens.descriptionHtml:
The Ahrens Moving Average updates itself from its own history. On each bar it takes the midpoint of its previous value and its value Period bars ago, measures how far the source sits from that midpoint, and moves its previous value by that distance divided by Period.

Using the midpoint of two of its own past values, rather than the previous value alone, corrects some of the lag a plain recursive average builds up. On the first bar the line starts at the source, and until it has a value Period bars back the source stands in for that older value.
ahrens-moving-average-ahrens.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend and price below a falling line a downtrend; the slope of the line shows the direction of the trend and how firmly it is holding.

The line moves only 1 / Period of the gap each bar, so it is slow to respond to a sudden move and can trail price for some time after a sharp break. A shorter period makes it follow more closely at the cost of more noise.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How far back the older value is taken and how small each step is. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it use its own value from a period ago?
faq.html: The midpoint of the previous value and the value a period back sits closer to the centre of recent movement, which offsets some of the lag of stepping from the previous value alone.

faq.q: Does it need a warmup?
faq.html: No. It starts at the source on the first bar, but the first Period bars use the source in place of the older value, so they settle in over that stretch.

related.title: Arnaud Legoux Moving Average (ALMA)
related.summary: A Gaussian-weighted moving average whose peak weight can slide from the middle of the window toward the newest bar.

related.title: ADX Variable Moving Average (ADXVMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that uses the ADX as its smoothing factor, following price closely in a strong trend and flattening in a range.

related.title: Blackman Moving Average (BLMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Blackman window, a three-term cosine taper that falls to zero at both ends of the lookback.

ehlers-adaptive-laguerre-filter-alaguerr.title: Ehlers Adaptive Laguerre Filter (ALAGUERRE)
ehlers-adaptive-laguerre-filter-alaguerr.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother whose speed adapts bar by bar to how far it has fallen behind price, speeding up in moves and slowing in ranges.
ehlers-adaptive-laguerre-filter-alaguerr.descriptionHtml:
The Adaptive Laguerre Filter is a cascade of four Laguerre stages, each one a short recursive filter fed by the stage before it. The output is a weighted mix of the four stages, (L0 + 2 * L1 + 2 * L2 + L3) / 6. What makes it adaptive is the smoothing factor: instead of a fixed value it is recomputed on every bar.

On each bar the study measures the tracking error, the distance between the price and the filter's previous value. It finds where that error sits between the highest and lowest errors of the last Length bars, as a number from 0 to 1, and takes the median of that position over the last Median Length bars. That median is the smoothing factor. A large error relative to recent ones gives a factor near 1 and a fast filter; a small one gives a factor near 0 and a slow, smooth filter. When the error range is flat the position is 0.5.

The first bar seeds all four stages with the price, with an error of 0 and a position of 0.5, and those seed values stay in the windows until they age out.
ehlers-adaptive-laguerre-filter-alaguerr.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as an adaptive trend line. In a strong move the filter falls behind, the error grows, and the line speeds up to catch price; in a quiet range the error is small and the line flattens out and ignores noise. A turn in the line after a long flat stretch is therefore more meaningful than a wiggle during a fast move.

The adaptation is relative: the error is judged only against the last Length bars, so after a long quiet spell even a modest move can make the filter fast. The median step keeps one outlier bar from jerking the speed around, at the cost of reacting a few bars later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars of tracking error set the high and low that the current error is compared against.

settings.label: Median Length
settings.html: How many bars of the normalised error the median is taken over. Larger values make the speed change more slowly.

faq.q: What does the filter adapt to?
faq.html: Its own tracking error: how far price is from the filter's previous value, compared with the errors of recent bars. Large errors make it faster, small ones make it slower.

faq.q: Why take a median of the factor?
faq.html: A single wild bar would otherwise swing the smoothing factor to an extreme. The median over a few bars keeps the speed stable while still following real changes.

faq.q: How does it differ from the fixed Laguerre filter?
faq.html: The fixed version uses one damping factor on every bar. This one recomputes the factor on each bar from the tracking error.

related.title: Baxter-King Band-Pass Filter (BAXTERKING)
related.summary: A centred, zero-sum band-pass filter on the close that keeps only cycles between two periods and oscillates around zero.

related.title: Ehlers Automatic Gain Control (AGC)
related.summary: A roofing filter that isolates the price cycle, scaled by its own decaying peak so the oscillator always swings between -1 and +1.

related.title: Bessel 2nd Order Filter (BESSEL)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass smoother with Bessel-style coefficients, giving a smooth price line with a steady, predictable lag.

williams-alligator.title: Williams Alligator
williams-alligator.summary: Three smoothed averages of different lengths, each shifted forward by its own number of bars, whose spacing shows trend or rest.
williams-alligator.descriptionHtml:
The Alligator draws three smoothed averages of the source, the typical price by default. The Jaw is the slowest, the Teeth sit in the middle and the Lips are the fastest. Each is a Wilder average, which weights the newest value by one over its period, and each is displaced to the right by its own offset: the value drawn on a bar is the one computed that many bars earlier.

The averages start from zero and are scaled up by the factor that zero start leaves out, until that factor has decayed away. That way each line reads as the source from the very first bar rather than climbing up from zero, and only the offsets delay where the lines begin.

With the defaults the Jaw uses 13 bars shifted 8, the Teeth 8 bars shifted 5 and the Lips 5 bars shifted 3.
williams-alligator.howToReadHtml:
When the three lines are tangled together, the averages agree and price has no clear direction. When they spread apart in order, Lips above Teeth above Jaw, the market is trending up; Lips below Teeth below Jaw is a downtrend. The wider the spacing, the stronger the move.

A trend is often read as ending when the Lips cross back through the Teeth and the lines start to close up again. Because every line is smoothed and then shifted forward, the picture lags price, so it describes trends after they are under way rather than calling turns.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series all three averages are computed from.

settings.label: Jaw Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the slowest line. A longer period makes it steadier and slower to turn.

settings.label: Jaw Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Jaw is shifted to the right. Zero draws it on the bar it was computed.

settings.label: Teeth Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the middle line.

settings.label: Teeth Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Teeth are shifted to the right.

settings.label: Lips Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the fastest line, the one that reacts first to price.

settings.label: Lips Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Lips are shifted to the right.

faq.q: Why are the lines shifted forward?
faq.html: Each line is drawn its offset number of bars after the bar it was computed on, so the value under a bar reflects price from that many bars earlier. The offsets differ, so in a trend the three lines spread apart by their shift as well as by their smoothing.

faq.q: Why do the lines start a few bars into the chart?
faq.html: The averages answer from the first bar, but each is drawn its offset number of bars later, so the Jaw starts eight bars in by default.

faq.q: Which average does it use?
faq.html: A Wilder average, which is an exponential average with a weight of one over the period, started from zero and scaled so the early values are not pulled toward zero.

related.title: Archer Moving Averages Trends (AMAT)
related.summary: Flags a bar as trending only when a fast and a slow exponential average agree on both their order and their direction, and measures their spread.

related.title: Average Directional Movement Index Rating (ADXR)
related.summary: Averages today's ADX with the ADX from a set number of bars earlier, a steadier read of trend strength drawn with ADX, +DI and -DI.

related.title: Aroon (AROON)
related.summary: Two lines from 0 to 100 that show how recently the window's highest high and lowest low were set, to judge whether a trend is fresh or fading.

arnaud-legoux-moving-average-alma.title: Arnaud Legoux Moving Average (ALMA)
arnaud-legoux-moving-average-alma.summary: A Gaussian-weighted moving average whose peak weight can slide from the middle of the window toward the newest bar.
arnaud-legoux-moving-average-alma.descriptionHtml:
ALMA weights the bars in its window with a Gaussian bell curve. Counting bars back from the current one, the peak of the curve sits at (1 - offset) * (p - 1) bars back, and its width is the window length divided by sigma. Each price is multiplied by its weight, and the sum is divided by the total weight.

The offset moves the peak: at 0.85, the default, most of the weight sits on recent bars and the line follows price closely; at 0.5 the peak is in the middle and the line is smoother but lags more; at 1 the newest bar carries the most weight. Sigma sets how sharp the bell is: a larger sigma concentrates the weight near the peak, a smaller one spreads it across the window. The window grows from the first bar up to the period, so the line is drawn from the start of the chart.
arnaud-legoux-moving-average-alma.howToReadHtml:
Read ALMA as a moving average whose balance between smoothness and lag is set by the offset and sigma. Price above a rising ALMA points to an uptrend and price below a falling one to a downtrend; the slope and its turns carry the signal. With the default offset most of the weight sits on recent bars, so the line stays close to price and turns early.

Tune the offset first: raise it for a faster line, lower it for a smoother one. The first bars use a short window and simply follow price.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Offset
settings.html: Where the peak of the Gaussian weights sits, from 0 (the oldest bar) to 1 (the newest bar). Higher values respond faster.

settings.label: Sigma
settings.html: Sharpness of the bell curve. A larger sigma narrows the weights around the peak; a smaller one spreads them over the window.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being averaged, usually the close.

faq.q: What does the offset do?
faq.html: It slides the heaviest weight along the window. At 0.85 the weight is mostly on recent bars and the line reacts quickly; at 0.5 it is centred and the line is smoother but later.

faq.q: How does sigma change the line?
faq.html: Sigma controls the width of the bell. A high sigma puts nearly all the weight on a few bars around the peak; a low sigma spreads it out, which makes the average closer to a simple one.

faq.q: Why does it draw from the first bar?
faq.html: The window grows from one bar up to the period, and the weights are recomputed for each shorter window, so there is no warmup gap.

related.title: Blackman Moving Average (BLMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Blackman window, a three-term cosine taper that falls to zero at both ends of the lookback.

related.title: Ahrens Moving Average (AHRENS)
related.summary: A recursive average that steps toward price from the midpoint of its previous value and its value one period ago.

related.title: Bessel-Weighted Moving Average (BWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a Bessel-style window, zero at both ends and heaviest in the middle, with an adjustable taper.

archer-moving-averages-trends-amat.title: Archer Moving Averages Trends (AMAT)
archer-moving-averages-trends-amat.summary: Flags a bar as trending only when a fast and a slow exponential average agree on both their order and their direction, and measures their spread.
archer-moving-averages-trends-amat.descriptionHtml:
AMAT asks two exponential moving averages, a fast one and a slow one, whether they agree. Both start from the first value of the source and follow the usual exponential recursion with a weight of 2 / (period + 1).

A bar is an uptrend bar, drawn as a column of +1, when the fast average is above the slow one and both averages rose on this bar. It is a downtrend bar, a column of -1, when the fast average is below the slow one and both fell. Every other bar is 0: the averages are in one order but at least one of them is moving the other way, so the trend is not confirmed.

The second line, Trend Strength %, is the distance between the two averages as a percentage of the slow average. It grows as the averages pull apart and shrinks as they converge, whichever side is on top.
archer-moving-averages-trends-amat.howToReadHtml:
Green columns at +1 mark bars where the uptrend is confirmed by both order and slope, red columns at -1 mark confirmed downtrend bars, and a flat zero means the averages disagree. A long unbroken run of one colour is a clean trend; a mix of zeros and short runs is a market without direction.

Use the strength line to judge how established a trend is. A rising strength line with steady columns shows the averages separating, while a falling one warns that they are converging and a crossing may follow. Both readings come from moving averages, so they confirm a move after it starts rather than predicting it.

settings.label: Fast Period
settings.html: Length of the fast exponential average. A shorter length reacts sooner and breaks the trend state more often.

settings.label: Slow Period
settings.html: Length of the slow exponential average. A longer length makes the trend state steadier and the strength readings larger.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages follow, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the value zero when the fast average is clearly above the slow one?
faq.html: A trend bar also needs both averages to be moving in the trend's direction on that bar. If either one ticked the other way, the bar is reported as 0 until they agree again.

faq.q: Does the strength line show direction?
faq.html: No. It is the absolute spread as a percentage of the slow average, so it never drops below zero while the slow average is above zero. Read the direction from the columns.

faq.q: Why does the first bar show no trend?
faq.html: Both averages and their previous values start at the first source value, so on that bar they are equal and neither the order nor the slope test can pass.

related.title: Aroon (AROON)
related.summary: Two lines from 0 to 100 that show how recently the window's highest high and lowest low were set, to judge whether a trend is fresh or fading.

related.title: Williams Alligator
related.summary: Three smoothed averages of different lengths, each shifted forward by its own number of bars, whose spacing shows trend or rest.

related.title: Aroon Oscillator
related.summary: Aroon Up minus Aroon Down in one line between -100 and +100, with the pane shaded green above zero and red below to show which extreme is fresher.

awesome-oscillator-ao.title: Awesome Oscillator (AO)
awesome-oscillator-ao.summary: Plots the fast simple average of the bar midpoint minus the slow one, coloured green while it is rising or flat and red while it is falling.
awesome-oscillator-ao.descriptionHtml:
The Awesome Oscillator compares short-term and longer-term momentum using the midpoint of each bar, high plus low over two. It takes a fast simple average and a slow simple average of that midpoint and plots the fast one minus the slow one.

Both averages cover the bars seen so far until their windows fill, so the line starts on the first bar instead of after a warmup gap. The slow window is always kept at least one bar longer than the fast one. The line is green on bars where it is at or above its previous value and red where it is lower, and red on the first bar, which has no previous value.
awesome-oscillator-ao.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the recent midpoints are higher than the longer average and momentum is upward; below zero it is downward. A cross of the zero line marks the point where the two averages cross. The colour shows whether the reading is rising or falling from one bar to the next, so a run of green below zero means downward momentum is easing.

The values are in price units, so they scale with the instrument's price. The first bars are averages of fewer than a full window and are less reliable than the rest of the line.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: Number of bars in the fast average of the midpoint. Shorter values react sooner.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: Number of bars in the slow average of the midpoint. It is raised to one bar more than the fast length if set lower.

faq.q: Why does it use the midpoint instead of the close?
faq.html: The midpoint, high plus low over two, reflects where the whole bar traded rather than one closing moment, which makes the averages a little less sensitive to the close alone.

faq.q: What do the colours mean?
faq.html: Green means the oscillator is at or above its value on the previous bar, red means it is lower. The colour describes the change, not whether the value is above or below zero.

faq.q: What if the fast length is not shorter than the slow one?
faq.html: The study keeps the slow window one bar longer than the fast one, so the two averages always differ in length.

related.title: Absolute Price Oscillator (APO)
related.summary: Plots the gap between a fast and a slow exponential average in price units, with a correction that removes the starting bias on early bars.

related.title: Accelerator Oscillator (AC)
related.summary: Measures whether momentum is speeding up or slowing down: the midpoint momentum oscillator less its own five-bar average.

related.title: Bollinger %B
related.summary: Shows where price sits inside its own Bollinger Bands, with 0 at the lower band, 1 at the upper band and readings beyond them outside the bands.

aobv-archer-on-balance-volume-aobv.title: AOBV - Archer On-Balance Volume (AOBV)
aobv-archer-on-balance-volume-aobv.summary: Two smoothed lines of on-balance volume, a fast and a slow, that read accumulation and distribution from the first bar.
aobv-archer-on-balance-volume-aobv.descriptionHtml:
This study smooths on-balance volume with two exponential averages. On-balance volume is a running total: the bar's volume is added when the source is higher than on the previous bar, subtracted when it is lower, and ignored when it is unchanged. A missing volume reads as zero, and a missing source holds the last known one.

The fast line averages that total over 4 bars and the slow line over 14, each with a weight of 2 divided by the period. Each average starts from zero and, while the weight of that zero start is still above a tiny threshold, is divided by one minus that weight, so neither line has a long dead start. On the first bar both lines show the raw on-balance volume.
aobv-archer-on-balance-volume-aobv.howToReadHtml:
When the fast line is above the slow one, on-balance volume has been rising recently, read as accumulation; when it is below, falling, read as distribution. Crossings of the two lines mark changes in that balance. With periods of 4 and 14 bars both lines react quickly, so crossings are frequent on a choppy chart.

Compare the lines with price: price rising while both lines fall means more volume has been trading on down bars than on up bars during the rise. The level of the lines depends on where the chart starts, so read their direction and their crossings, not their value.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose rise or fall decides whether a bar's volume is added or subtracted.

settings.label: Volume
settings.html: The series used as each bar's volume in the running total.

faq.q: Can I change the 4 and 14 bar periods?
faq.html: No. The two smoothing lengths are fixed at 4 and 14 bars; only the source and the volume series can be changed.

faq.q: Why do both lines start at the same value?
faq.html: On the first bar each average has no history, so both show the raw on-balance volume.

faq.q: What does a crossing mean?
faq.html: The fast line crossing above the slow one says on-balance volume has turned up recently; crossing below says it has turned down.

related.title: Chaikin Money Flow (CMF)
related.summary: The share of recent volume that traded on the buying side, from money flow volume summed over a window and divided by total volume.

related.title: Chaikin A/D Oscillator (ADOSC)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average of the accumulation/distribution line, showing shifts in money flow momentum.

related.title: Elder's Force Index (EFI)
related.summary: Multiplies each bar's change in close by its volume and smooths the result, sizing the force behind every move in one line.

andrews-pitchfork-ap.title: Andrews' Pitchfork (AP)
andrews-pitchfork-ap.summary: Three parallel lines projected from three pivot points read a fixed number of bars back, recomputed on every bar.
andrews-pitchfork-ap.descriptionHtml:
A pitchfork is three parallel lines. This study picks its three points by distance rather than by hand: point 1 is the close a set number of bars back, point 2 is the high a set number of bars back, and point 3 is the low a set number of bars back. By default the three distances are 45, 30 and 15 bars. While there is not yet enough history, each point is clamped to the first bar.

The median line starts at point 1 and passes through the midpoint of points 2 and 3. The upper line starts at point 2 and the lower line at point 3, both with the same slope as the median line. The value plotted on each bar is where those three lines reach on that bar.

Because the points move forward with every bar, the fork is redrawn each bar, so the plotted lines trace the projected values over time rather than one fixed drawing. A projection that runs far off the price scale is left out.
andrews-pitchfork-ap.howToReadHtml:
The median line is the path price would follow if it kept the slope set by the three points. Price above the median line is running ahead of that slope and price below it is lagging. The upper and lower lines mark the outer edges of the projected channel, and a close beyond either one is a move outside the channel the three points describe.

The slope changes as the points slide forward, so the lines can bend. Read it as a rolling estimate of trend direction and channel edges, and choose point distances that match the swings you trade.

settings.label: Point 1 (Leftmost)
settings.html: How many bars back the close for the first point is read. It anchors the start of the median line.

settings.label: Point 2 (Second)
settings.html: How many bars back the high for the second point is read. It anchors the upper line.

settings.label: Point 3 (Third)
settings.html: How many bars back the low for the third point is read. It anchors the lower line.

faq.q: Why do the lines bend?
faq.html: The three points move forward one bar at a time, so the slope is recomputed on every bar. The plot joins those per-bar values.

faq.q: Does it find swing highs and lows itself?
faq.html: No. It reads the close, high and low at fixed distances back. Set the distances to suit the swings you want the fork to follow.

faq.q: Why are the lines flat on the first bars?
faq.html: Until there is more history than the shortest point distance, all three points sit on the first bar, the slope is zero and the lines hold that bar's close, high and low. As each point starts to slide forward the slope is measured over a short time base, so the lines can jump before they settle.

related.title: Adaptive Price Zone
related.summary: A double smoothed average of price with a zone around it sized by the double smoothed bar range.

related.title: Acceleration Bands (ACCBANDS)
related.summary: An average of the close with bands pushed beyond the averaged high and low by a multiple of the average bar spread.

related.title: ATR Bands (ATRBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below it.

absolute-price-oscillator-apo.title: Absolute Price Oscillator (APO)
absolute-price-oscillator-apo.summary: Plots the gap between a fast and a slow exponential average in price units, with a correction that removes the starting bias on early bars.
absolute-price-oscillator-apo.descriptionHtml:
The Absolute Price Oscillator measures momentum as the distance between two exponential moving averages of the source, a fast one and a slow one, expressed in the instrument's own price units. When the fast average is above the slow one the reading is positive, and when it is below the reading is negative.

Both averages start from the first value of the source, so the line begins on the first bar at zero. Because an average started this way leans towards its starting value, the study divides both averages by 1 - e, where e is (1 minus the slow weight) raised to the number of bars after the first. As the slow average fills, e shrinks towards zero and the divisor approaches 1. Once e falls below 1e-10 the correction stops and the plain difference is plotted.
absolute-price-oscillator-apo.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the short-term average is running ahead of the long-term one and momentum is upward; below zero it is downward. A cross of the zero line is the point where the two averages cross. The slope of the line shows whether that momentum is building or fading.

Because the values are in price units, readings are not comparable between instruments at very different prices, and the same move reads larger on a higher-priced market. For a comparison across instruments, a percentage version of the same gap is the better tool.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages are computed from, the close by default.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: Length of the fast exponential average. Shorter values make the oscillator react sooner to price changes.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: Length of the slow exponential average, which also sets how long the early bias correction lasts.

faq.q: How is it different from MACD?
faq.html: The main line is the same idea, a fast minus a slow exponential average. This study plots only that line, with no signal line or histogram, and corrects the early bars for the starting bias.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: Both averages begin at the first value of the source, so on the first bar they are equal and their gap is zero.

faq.q: Can I compare readings across instruments?
faq.html: Not directly. The output is in price units, so a 100-point gap means something different on an instrument priced at 1,000 than on one priced at 60,000.

related.title: Bollinger %B
related.summary: Shows where price sits inside its own Bollinger Bands, with 0 at the lower band, 1 at the upper band and readings beyond them outside the bands.

related.title: Awesome Oscillator (AO)
related.summary: Plots the fast simple average of the bar midpoint minus the slow one, coloured green while it is rising or flat and red while it is falling.

related.title: Bulls Bears Index (BBI)
related.summary: One line on the price chart that averages four simple moving averages of different lengths, blending very short, short, medium and long trend.

adaptive-price-zone.title: Adaptive Price Zone
adaptive-price-zone.summary: A double smoothed average of price with a zone around it sized by the double smoothed bar range.
adaptive-price-zone.descriptionHtml:
The Adaptive Price Zone is a centre line with a band on each side. The centre line is price passed through two exponential averages in a row. The band width is the bar range, high minus low, passed through the same two averages and multiplied by the band multiplier.

The smoothing length is the square root of the period, so a period of 20 smooths with a length of about 4.5. That keeps the zone close to price while the double pass smooths out much of the bar to bar noise.

All four averages start at zero. During the opening bars every value is scaled up by a compensator, one divided by one minus the square of the decay factor raised to the bar count, and the compensator switches off once that remainder falls below one in ten billion. This compensator is sized for a single average, so it does not fully undo the zero start of two averages in a row: on the first bar the centre line sits at roughly a fifth of price at the default period, and it climbs to the price scale over the next fifteen or so bars.
adaptive-price-zone.howToReadHtml:
Price inside the zone is trading in its normal range. A close beyond the upper or lower edge is a move larger than the recent bar ranges would suggest. In a sideways market some traders treat the edges as the limits of the range; in a trend price often stays near one edge.

The zone widens as bars grow and narrows as they shrink, which makes a tightening zone a sign of quieter trade. Because the smoothing is short, the zone turns quickly and gives more signals than a slower channel. Ignore the opening bars of the chart, where the zone is still rising from zero toward price.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The smoothing length is the square root of this period. A longer period gives a smoother, slower zone.

settings.label: Band Multiplier
settings.html: How many double smoothed bar ranges the edges sit from the centre line. Larger values widen the zone.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the centre line smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the zone start far below price?
faq.html: The averages start at zero. A compensator scales the opening values up, but it only allows for one level of smoothing, so the double smoothed line still starts well below price and reaches it after roughly fifteen bars at the default period. Read the zone only after that stretch.

faq.q: Why the square root of the period?
faq.html: It keeps the two smoothing passes short enough to follow price closely. Two passes at the full period would lag far behind.

faq.q: What does a narrowing zone mean?
faq.html: The bar ranges are shrinking, so trade is getting quieter. It says nothing about direction.

related.title: ATR Bands (ATRBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below it.

related.title: Andrews' Pitchfork (AP)
related.summary: Three parallel lines projected from three pivot points read a fixed number of bars back, recomputed on every bar.

related.title: Bollinger Bands (BBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average with bands a multiple of the population standard deviation away, drawn from the first bar on an expanding window.

aroon-aroon.title: Aroon (AROON)
aroon-aroon.summary: Two lines from 0 to 100 that show how recently the window's highest high and lowest low were set, to judge whether a trend is fresh or fading.
aroon-aroon.descriptionHtml:
Aroon measures time rather than price. Over a window of period bars it finds the bar that set the highest high and the bar that set the lowest low, and counts how many bars ago each one was.

Aroon Up is 100 * (period - bars since the high) / period, so it reads 100 on the bar that makes a new high for the window and falls steadily toward 0 as that high ages. Aroon Down is the same calculation for the lowest low. Both lines appear once the window has filled.

The study draws reference levels at 70, 50 and 30, and declares four alerts: Aroon Up crossing above Aroon Down, Aroon Down crossing above Aroon Up, a strong uptrend (Up above 70 while Down is below 30) and a strong downtrend (the reverse).
aroon-aroon.howToReadHtml:
When Aroon Up stays near 100 and Aroon Down stays low, the market keeps printing new highs and has not made a new low for a while: an uptrend. The reverse picture is a downtrend. When both lines sit low together, neither extreme has been renewed recently and price is drifting in a range.

A crossing of the two lines shows that the more recent extreme has switched sides, an early hint that control is changing. Aroon only knows when the extremes happened, not by how much price moved, so a fresh high by a single tick counts the same as a large breakout.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the look-back window. A longer window changes the lines more slowly and needs a more lasting move to reach 100.

faq.q: Why does Aroon Up drop in a straight line?
faq.html: Between new highs, the bars-since count rises by one each bar, so Aroon Up falls by 100 divided by the period on every bar. It jumps back up when a new high resets it to 100, or when the old high leaves the window and a more recent high takes its place.

faq.q: What does it mean when both lines are below 50?
faq.html: Neither the high nor the low of the window has been set in the more recent half of it. Price is moving sideways inside an older range.

faq.q: Which alerts does it provide?
faq.html: Aroon Up crossing above Aroon Down, Aroon Down crossing above Aroon Up, a strong uptrend with Up above 70 and Down below 30, and a strong downtrend with Down above 70 and Up below 30.

related.title: Aroon Oscillator
related.summary: Aroon Up minus Aroon Down in one line between -100 and +100, with the pane shaded green above zero and red below to show which extreme is fresher.

related.title: Archer Moving Averages Trends (AMAT)
related.summary: Flags a bar as trending only when a fast and a slow exponential average agree on both their order and their direction, and measures their spread.

related.title: Choppiness Index
related.summary: A 0 to 100 reading of whether recent bars trended or chopped, comparing the summed true range with the window's overall high to low range.

aroon-oscillator.title: Aroon Oscillator
aroon-oscillator.summary: Aroon Up minus Aroon Down in one line between -100 and +100, with the pane shaded green above zero and red below to show which extreme is fresher.
aroon-oscillator.descriptionHtml:
The Aroon Oscillator folds the two Aroon lines into one. Over a window of period bars it finds how many bars ago the highest high and the lowest low were set. Aroon Up is 100 * (period - bars since the high) / period and Aroon Down is the same for the low, so each reads 100 on the bar that sets a new extreme and falls toward 0 as that extreme ages.

The oscillator is Aroon Up minus Aroon Down. Its highest possible reading is 100 * (period - 1) / period, just under +100, when the window's high was set on this bar and its low on the oldest bar of the window; its lowest is the mirror image, just above -100. Zero means the high and the low are the same age.

The pane background is shaded faint green while the oscillator is above zero and faint red while it is at or below zero; the warmup bars before the window fills are left unshaded. Reference lines sit at 0, +50 and -50, and four alerts are declared: crossing above zero, crossing below zero, above +70 and below -70.
aroon-oscillator.howToReadHtml:
A reading above zero says the most recent new high is fresher than the most recent new low, which is how an uptrend looks; below zero says the reverse. Readings beyond +50 or -50 show one side clearly in control, and the alert levels at +70 and -70 mark a strong, one-sided move.

A crossing of zero is the point where the fresher extreme switches sides, and the background colour flips with it. In a sideways market the oscillator swings back and forth through zero often, so treat a single crossing with caution. It measures how recently extremes were set, not how far price moved.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the look-back window. A longer window makes the oscillator smoother and slower to cross zero.

faq.q: Why does the oscillator move in straight steps?
faq.html: Between new extremes each Aroon line changes by exactly 100 divided by the period per bar, so their difference moves in fixed steps until a new high or low resets one of them.

faq.q: What does the background colour show?
faq.html: Green while the oscillator is above zero and red while it is at or below zero. It only starts once the window has filled and the oscillator has a value.

faq.q: Which alerts does it provide?
faq.html: A crossing above zero, a crossing below zero, a reading above +70 for a strong uptrend and a reading below -70 for a strong downtrend.

related.title: Choppiness Index
related.summary: A 0 to 100 reading of whether recent bars trended or chopped, comparing the summed true range with the window's overall high to low range.

related.title: Aroon (AROON)
related.summary: Two lines from 0 to 100 that show how recently the window's highest high and lowest low were set, to judge whether a trend is fresh or fading.

related.title: Jurik Directional Movement Index (DMX)
related.summary: The normalised difference between plus and minus directional movement, smoothed by an adaptive average, from -1 to +1.

accumulation-swing-index-asi.title: Accumulation Swing Index (ASI)
accumulation-swing-index-asi.summary: A running total of each bar's swing index, a score of how strongly the close moved against the previous bar, scaled by the bar's range.
accumulation-swing-index-asi.descriptionHtml:
