The Accumulation Swing Index adds up a swing index computed on every bar. The swing of a bar is (close - prevClose) + 0.5 * (close - open) + 0.25 * (prevClose - prevOpen): mostly the change in close, with smaller shares of this bar's body and the previous bar's body.

The swing is divided by a range R built from three distances: high to previous close, low to previous close, and high to low. Whichever is widest sets the formula. If high to previous close is widest, R = absHC - 0.5 * absLC + 0.25 * absC1O1; if low to previous close is widest, the two swap; otherwise R = absHL + 0.25 * absC1O1, where absC1O1 is the previous bar's body. The result is scaled by 50 * K / T, where K is the larger of the two distances from the previous close and T is the Limit Move setting.

The first bar has no previous bar and contributes zero, and so does any bar whose R works out to zero. The plotted line is the sum of every bar's swing index from the first bar.
accumulation-swing-index-asi.howToReadHtml:
Read the ASI like a cumulative price line that weighs each bar's conviction. A rising ASI means closes have been pushing up against the prior bars; a falling ASI means they have been pushing down. Breaks of the ASI's own highs and lows, or a divergence between the ASI and price, are the usual ways it is used to confirm or question a breakout.

The zero line is the starting value, not a balance point, so the level of the line depends on where the chart begins. The Limit Move setting scales every value equally and changes the size of the numbers, not the shape of the line.

settings.label: Limit Move
settings.html: The scaling constant T. Every swing index is multiplied by K divided by this value, so a larger value shrinks the whole line without changing its shape.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: It is a running total that begins on the first bar of the chart, and the first bar contributes nothing because it has no previous bar.

faq.q: Does the Limit Move setting change the signals?
faq.html: No. It scales every bar's contribution by the same factor, so the line keeps its shape and only its numbers change.

faq.q: What does a divergence mean here?
faq.html: If price makes a new high but the ASI does not, the closes behind that high were weaker than before, which questions the strength of the move.

related.title: Bias (BIAS)
related.summary: The distance of price from its own simple moving average, expressed as a fraction of that average, so stretched moves stand out.

related.title: Balance of Power (BOP)
related.summary: Measures where each bar closed relative to its open, as a share of its range, and smooths it with a warmup-corrected exponential average.

related.title: Commodity Channel Index (CCI)
related.summary: How far the typical price sits from its own average, in units of mean absolute deviation, so readings beyond plus or minus 100 mark stretched moves.

two-argument-arctangent-atan2.title: Two-Argument Arctangent (ATAN2)
two-argument-arctangent-atan2.summary: Plots the angle, in radians from -pi to pi, of the point formed by two chosen bar values, keeping the sign of each in all four quadrants.
two-argument-arctangent-atan2.descriptionHtml:
This study treats two values from each bar as the coordinates of a point and plots the angle from the positive x-axis to that point, in radians. By default the y value is the bar's range (high minus low) and the x value is its midpoint (high plus low, over two), but either can be switched to any price series, the range or volume.

Unlike a plain arctangent of y divided by x, the two-argument form keeps both signs, so it can tell a point in one quadrant from the point opposite it and returns a value anywhere from -pi to pi. The study always divides the smaller magnitude by the larger one before taking the arctangent, so the ratio never grows without bound, and then places the angle in its quadrant from the signs of x and y. A bar where both values are zero has no angle and is left blank.
two-argument-arctangent-atan2.howToReadHtml:
With the default settings both values are positive, so the angle stays between 0 and pi/2 and works as a smooth, bounded version of the range as a fraction of price: a wider bar relative to its price gives a larger angle. Readings near zero mean the bar was narrow compared with where it traded.

With other choices the line can move into other quadrants, and the reference lines at plus and minus pi/2 and pi mark the quadrant boundaries. The study is a numeric building block: it describes a relationship between two values and does not give trading signals by itself.

settings.label: Y (Numerator)
settings.html: The value used as the vertical coordinate: the bar's range, any price series or volume.

settings.label: X (Denominator)
settings.html: The value used as the horizontal coordinate: the bar's range, any price series or volume.

faq.q: Why is the default reading so close to zero?
faq.html: The default angle compares the bar's range with its midpoint price. On most instruments the range is a tiny fraction of the price, so the angle is small, and it rises on wide bars.

faq.q: Why are some bars blank?
faq.html: When both chosen values are exactly zero the angle is undefined, so the study leaves that bar empty rather than inventing a value.

faq.q: Is the output in degrees?
faq.html: No, it is in radians, from -pi to pi. Multiply by 180 and divide by pi to read it in degrees.

related.title: Beta Distribution CDF (BETADIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative Beta distribution, giving a shaped 0 to 1 oscillator.

related.title: Acceleration (Slope of Slope) (ACCEL)
related.summary: The slope of a rolling regression slope: how fast the trend of the source is itself speeding up or slowing down, bar by bar.

related.title: Binomial Distribution CDF (BINOMDIST)
related.summary: Treats the source's position in its recent range as a success rate p and plots the probability of at most k successes in n trials.

average-true-range-atr.title: Average True Range (ATR)
average-true-range-atr.summary: Measures how far price typically travels in one bar, counting any gap from the previous close, as a smoothed average of the true range.
average-true-range-atr.descriptionHtml:
Average True Range measures volatility in price units. Each bar's true range is the largest of three distances: high to low, high to the previous close, and low to the previous close. Taking the previous close into account means a gap between bars counts as movement, which a plain high minus low would miss. On the first bar there is no previous close, so its true range is simply high minus low.

The true range is then smoothed with a running average that gives the newest bar a weight of 1 / length and keeps the rest from the previous value. That average is started from zero, and on each bar it is divided by 1 - e, where e is the weight the zero start still holds. This removes the drag of the zero start, so the line is usable from the very first bar instead of creeping up to its true level over the first length bars.
average-true-range-atr.howToReadHtml:
Read ATR as the size of a typical bar on this chart, in the instrument's own price units. A rising line means bars are getting wider and the market is moving more; a falling line means it is quietening down. Traders use it to size stops and targets, for example a stop placed two ATRs from entry, and to size positions so that each trade risks a similar amount.

ATR says nothing about direction: a strong rally and a sharp fall can show the same reading. Because it is in price units, it cannot be compared across instruments trading at very different prices; use the percent form for that.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the average effectively covers. A shorter length reacts faster to a change in volatility, a longer one is smoother.

faq.q: Why does the line have a value from the first bar?
faq.html: The average starts from zero and is divided by the share of weight it has built up so far, which removes the bias of the zero start. The early values are therefore averages of the bars seen so far rather than numbers dragged toward zero.

faq.q: Why is a gap counted?
faq.html: True range measures from the previous close when that is further away than the bar's own high or low. A market that gaps and then trades in a narrow range has still moved, and the true range records that move.

faq.q: Can I compare ATR between two instruments?
faq.html: Only if they trade at similar prices. ATR is in price units, so a higher priced instrument shows a larger ATR for the same relative movement. The Average True Range Percent study divides by the close for that comparison.

related.title: Average True Range Normalized (ATRN)
related.summary: Places the current average true range inside its own range over the last ten lengths of bars, from 0 at the lowest to 1 at the highest.

related.title: Average Daily Range (ADR)
related.summary: Averages the plain high-minus-low range of each bar, with a choice of simple, exponential or weighted smoothing, to show how far price travels in a bar.

related.title: Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
related.summary: The average true range divided by the close and shown as a percentage, so volatility can be compared across instruments and price levels.

atr-bands-atrbands.title: ATR Bands (ATRBANDS)
atr-bands-atrbands.summary: A simple average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below it.
atr-bands-atrbands.descriptionHtml:
ATR Bands place a band on each side of a simple moving average, at a distance set by the average true range. The middle line is the mean of the source over the last length bars. Until that many bars exist it averages every bar so far, so it is drawn from the first bar.

The true range of a bar is the largest of its high minus its low, the distance from its high to the previous close and the distance from its low to the previous close. The study smooths it with a running average whose weight is one over the length, starting from zero, and divides out the weight that zero start still holds, so the average true range is unbiased from the first bar.

The upper band is the middle line plus the multiplier times the average true range, and the lower band is the middle line minus it.
atr-bands-atrbands.howToReadHtml:
Because the width comes from true range, the bands reflect how far the instrument actually moves per bar, gaps included. A close beyond a band is a move larger than the recent typical range would suggest. Many traders also use the band distance as a stop distance, since it scales with volatility.

The middle line lags price by about half the length, so in a strong trend price can ride one band for a long time. Wider bands mean larger bars, not a direction.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the middle line averages, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars in the middle average and the smoothing length of the average true range.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges the bands sit from the middle line. Larger values give a wider channel.

faq.q: Why are the bands drawn from the first bar?
faq.html: The middle line averages every bar so far until the window fills, and the true range average removes the bias of its zero start, so both have a value from bar one.

faq.q: How is this different from a deviation band?
faq.html: The width comes from bar ranges and gaps, not from how far closes stray from the mean. A quiet trend with large bars still gets wide bands.

faq.q: What is the first bar's true range?
faq.html: The first bar has no previous close, so it compares against its own close and its true range is its high minus its low.

related.title: Bollinger Bands (BBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average with bands a multiple of the population standard deviation away, drawn from the first bar on an expanding window.

related.title: Adaptive Price Zone
related.summary: A double smoothed average of price with a zone around it sized by the double smoothed bar range.

related.title: Donchian Channels (DCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the last period bars, with the midpoint between them, drawn from the first bar.

average-true-range-normalized-atrn.title: Average True Range Normalized (ATRN)
average-true-range-normalized-atrn.summary: Places the current average true range inside its own range over the last ten lengths of bars, from 0 at the lowest to 1 at the highest.
average-true-range-normalized-atrn.descriptionHtml:
Average True Range Normalized answers one question: is volatility high or low compared with its own recent history? It first computes the average true range. Each bar's true range is the largest of high minus low and the distances from the high and the low to the previous close, and on the first bar it is high minus low. That is smoothed with a running average of weight 1 / length, started from zero and divided by 1 - e so it is usable from the first bar.

The study then looks back over the last 10 * length bars, or every bar so far while fewer exist, finds the highest and lowest values of that average, and reports where the current value sits between them: (ATR - lowest) / (highest - lowest). When the highest and lowest are equal the reading is 0.5.
average-true-range-normalized-atrn.howToReadHtml:
A reading near 1 means volatility is at or near the top of its range for the lookback, and a reading near 0 means it is as quiet as it has been. Because the scale is fixed between 0 and 1, the same thresholds work on any instrument. Some traders read very low values as compression and very high values as an already stretched move; the study itself only reports where volatility sits in its range.

The lookback is ten times the length, so with the default of 14 it compares against the last 140 bars. Early in the chart the window is shorter, and the first readings swing widely because there is little history to compare with.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The smoothing length of the average true range. The comparison window is ten times this, so it also sets how far back the high and low are found.

faq.q: What does 0.5 mean?
faq.html: Either the average true range is halfway between its highest and lowest values in the window, or the window is flat, with the highest and lowest equal, in which case the study reports the midpoint rather than dividing by zero.

faq.q: How far back does it compare?
faq.html: Ten times the length, so 140 bars at the default length of 14. While fewer bars exist it uses every bar so far.

faq.q: Why is it useful when ATR already measures volatility?
faq.html: ATR is in price units and has no fixed scale. Normalizing it inside its own range turns it into a 0 to 1 reading of whether volatility is high or low for this instrument at the latest bar, which reads the same way on any chart.

related.title: Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
related.summary: The average true range divided by the close and shown as a percentage, so volatility can be compared across instruments and price levels.

related.title: Average True Range (ATR)
related.summary: Measures how far price typically travels in one bar, counting any gap from the previous close, as a smoothed average of the true range.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width (BBW)
related.summary: The distance between upper and lower deviation bands around a moving mean, in price units, a direct measure of how spread out recent prices are.

average-true-range-percent-atrp.title: Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
average-true-range-percent-atrp.summary: The average true range divided by the close and shown as a percentage, so volatility can be compared across instruments and price levels.
average-true-range-percent-atrp.descriptionHtml:
Average True Range Percent expresses the average true range as a share of the current price. Each bar's true range is the largest of high minus low and the distances from the high and the low to the previous close, so gaps count as movement. On the first bar there is no previous close and the true range is just high minus low.

The true range is smoothed with a running average of weight 1 / length, started from zero and divided by 1 - e on each bar, where e is the weight the zero start still holds, so the average is usable from the first bar. The result is divided by this bar's close and multiplied by 100. A bar with a zero close has no reading.
average-true-range-percent-atrp.howToReadHtml:
Read ATRP as the typical size of one bar as a percentage of price. A reading of 1.5 means a typical bar moves about one and a half percent. Because it is relative to price, it lets you compare how lively two instruments are, or how volatile one instrument is now against years ago when it traded at a very different level.

Rising values mean wider bars relative to price; falling values mean a calmer market. Like ATR it carries no direction, and a falling price on its own raises the reading slightly even when the bars stay the same size.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the average of the true range effectively covers. Shorter reacts faster, longer is smoother.

faq.q: How is this different from ATR?
faq.html: It is the same average true range divided by the close and multiplied by 100. ATR is in price units; ATRP is a percentage, so it compares across instruments and price levels.

faq.q: Why can ATRP rise when the bars do not get bigger?
faq.html: The close is the divisor. If price falls while the size of the bars stays the same, each bar becomes a larger share of the price and the reading rises.

faq.q: Does it have a value from the first bar?
faq.html: Yes. The running average is corrected for its zero start, so it answers from the first bar rather than waiting for a full window.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width (BBW)
related.summary: The distance between upper and lower deviation bands around a moving mean, in price units, a direct measure of how spread out recent prices are.

related.title: Average True Range Normalized (ATRN)
related.summary: Places the current average true range inside its own range over the last ten lengths of bars, from 0 at the lowest to 1 at the highest.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Normalized (BBWN)
related.summary: Rescales the current band width inside its own range over a lookback window, from 0 at the narrowest to 1 at the widest.

avgprice-average-price.title: AVGPRICE: Average Price
avgprice-average-price.summary: The plain mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, drawn on the price chart as one number for where the bar traded.
avgprice-average-price.descriptionHtml:
Average Price reduces each bar to a single value: the sum of its open, high, low and close, divided by four. Every one of the four prices carries the same weight, so the line reflects the whole bar rather than only its last print.

The study draws that value as a line over the price chart. There is no lookback window and no smoothing between bars, so it answers from the very first bar and each point depends on its own bar alone. On a wide bar it sits near the middle of the candle; on a bar that opened and closed near one extreme it leans toward that end.
avgprice-average-price.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the centre of gravity of each bar. When the close sits above the average price, the bar closed above its own average level; when it sits below, the bar closed below it.

Because it is not smoothed, the line moves as much as the bars do. It is most useful as a source series for other studies, such as a moving average or a band, that want a value representing the whole bar instead of the close alone.

faq.q: How is this different from the close?
faq.html: The close is one print at the end of the bar. Average Price weighs the open, the high, the low and the close equally, so a late move that sets no new high or low shifts it by a quarter of what it shifts the close.

faq.q: Does it have a warmup period?
faq.html: No. Each value uses only its own bar, so the line starts on the first bar of the chart.

faq.q: Why is there nothing to configure?
faq.html: The calculation is fixed: four prices, each weighted a quarter. There is no window length or source to choose.

related.title: HA: Heikin-Ashi
related.summary: Smoothed candles drawn over the chart: each closes at the bar's average price and opens at the midpoint of the previous smoothed candle.

related.title: MEDPRICE: Median Price
related.summary: The midpoint of each bar's range, halfway between its high and its low, drawn on the price chart with no smoothing.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

baxter-king-band-pass-filter-baxterking.title: Baxter-King Band-Pass Filter (BAXTERKING)
baxter-king-band-pass-filter-baxterking.summary: A centred, zero-sum band-pass filter on the close that keeps only cycles between two periods and oscillates around zero.
baxter-king-band-pass-filter-baxterking.descriptionHtml:
The Baxter-King Band-Pass Filter extracts the cyclical part of the close whose period lies between Min Period and Max Period. It is a symmetric moving filter with K leads and K lags around a centre bar, so it uses 2K + 1 closes for each value.

The weights start from the ideal band-pass weights: B0 = (b - a) / pi for the centre bar and Bj = (sin(jb) - sin(ja)) / (pi j) for a bar j steps away, where a and b are the angular frequencies of the longest and shortest periods. The same amount is then subtracted from every weight so that all 2K + 1 of them add up to zero. That makes the filter remove any constant level and any straight-line trend, so the output swings around zero.

Because the window is centred, each value describes the bar K bars back, and the first 2K bars of the chart are left blank until a full window exists.
baxter-king-band-pass-filter-baxterking.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the close is in the upper part of a cycle within the chosen band; below zero, it is in the lower part. Turns in the line mark the peaks and troughs of those cycles, and the height of the swings shows how strong the cycle is compared with the rest of the price movement.

The filter is centred, so the newest value reflects the bar K bars ago, not the current bar. That lag is built in: it gives a clean, symmetric picture of past cycles but is late for timing a turn as it happens. A larger K sharpens the band at the cost of more lag and more blank bars at the start.

settings.label: Min Period (pLow)
settings.html: The shortest cycle, in bars, that passes through. Faster swings are filtered out.

settings.label: Max Period (pHigh)
settings.html: The longest cycle, in bars, that passes through. Slower swings and the trend are filtered out. It is kept at least one bar above the minimum.

settings.label: Filter Half-Length (K)
settings.html: The number of bars on each side of the centre bar. Larger values give a sharper band but lag by K bars and leave the first 2K bars blank.

faq.q: Why does the line start 2K bars into the chart?
faq.html: Each value needs K bars on both sides of its centre bar, so the first full window is complete only after 2K bars. Those bars are left blank rather than drawn from a partial window.

faq.q: Why does it oscillate around zero?
faq.html: Its weights are adjusted to add up to zero, so any steady level or straight-line trend in the close cancels out and only the cycles inside the band remain.

faq.q: Is the newest value about the current bar?
faq.html: No. The window is centred, so the latest value describes the bar K bars back. This is the price of a symmetric filter that does not shift cycle timing.

related.title: Bessel 2nd Order Filter (BESSEL)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass smoother with Bessel-style coefficients, giving a smooth price line with a steady, predictable lag.

related.title: Ehlers Adaptive Laguerre Filter (ALAGUERRE)
related.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother whose speed adapts bar by bar to how far it has fallen behind price, speeding up in moves and slowing in ranges.

related.title: Bilateral Filter (BILATERAL)
related.summary: An edge-preserving smoother that weights each recent bar by how far back it is and how close its price is to the current one.

bollinger-bands-bbands.title: Bollinger Bands (BBANDS)
bollinger-bands-bbands.summary: A simple average with bands a multiple of the population standard deviation away, drawn from the first bar on an expanding window.
bollinger-bands-bbands.descriptionHtml:
This study draws a basis line and two bands. The basis is the simple average of the source over the last period bars. The bands sit a multiple of the standard deviation of the same values above and below it, using the population form of the deviation.

The study keeps a running sum of the source and of its square. The variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean, floored at zero because the subtraction can dip just below it on a flat series. Until a full period of bars exists, the sums cover every bar so far, so the first bar plots the source itself with a band of zero width, and the window grows to its full length after period bars.

Because the deviation is squared before it is averaged, large moves widen the bands more than small ones.
bollinger-bands-bbands.howToReadHtml:
Price near the upper band is high relative to its recent average and spread, and price near the lower band is low. A close outside a band is a move of more than the chosen number of deviations. Narrow bands mark a quiet stretch, which some traders watch for a larger move to follow; wide bands mark an active one.

In a strong trend price can walk along one band for many bars, so touching a band is not a reversal signal on its own. The first period bars use a shorter window and should be read with care.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the average and in the standard deviation. Longer gives a smoother, slower channel.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average and deviation are measured on, the close by default.

settings.label: StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many standard deviations the bands sit from the basis. Larger values give a wider channel.

faq.q: Why do the bands start with zero width?
faq.html: With one value there is no spread to measure, so the deviation is zero and both bands sit on the basis. They open up as more bars join the window.

faq.q: Is the deviation the sample or the population form?
faq.html: The population form: the squared distances are divided by the number of values, not by one less.

faq.q: What does a squeeze mean?
faq.html: Narrow bands mean the source has moved little around its average. A squeeze says volatility is low, not which way the next move will go.

related.title: Donchian Channels (DCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the last period bars, with the midpoint between them, drawn from the first bar.

related.title: ATR Bands (ATRBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below it.

related.title: Decay Min-Max Channel (DECAYCHANNEL)
related.summary: A high and low channel whose edges are pulled toward the middle harder the longer they go without a new extreme.

bollinger-b.title: Bollinger %B
bollinger-b.summary: Shows where price sits inside its own Bollinger Bands, with 0 at the lower band, 1 at the upper band and readings beyond them outside the bands.
bollinger-b.descriptionHtml:
Bollinger %B turns the position of price inside its bands into a single number. The bands are a simple average of the source plus and minus a multiple of its standard deviation. %B is the source minus the lower band, divided by the width between the bands, so 0 is the lower band, 0.5 the middle and 1 the upper band.

The study keeps a running sum and sum of squares over the last Period values and divides by the number of values seen so far, so the bands and %B exist from the first bar rather than after a warmup. The standard deviation is the population form. A window with no spread gives bands of zero width, and %B then reads 0.5.
bollinger-b.howToReadHtml:
A reading above 1 means price closed above the upper band, and a reading below 0 means it closed below the lower band. Readings above 0.8 and below 0.2 mark the upper and lower parts of the band, and 0.5 is the moving average. In a strong uptrend %B can stay above 0.8 for many bars, so a high reading is a description of strength, not automatically a sell signal.

Comparing %B highs with price highs is a common use: a new price high with a lower %B high says price is less stretched relative to its volatility than it was before.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the average and the standard deviation. Longer periods give smoother bands that react more slowly.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series placed within the bands, the close by default.

settings.label: StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many standard deviations the bands sit from the average. A larger value widens the bands and keeps %B nearer 0.5.

faq.q: Can %B go above 1 or below 0?
faq.html: Yes. Above 1 means price is above the upper band, below 0 means it is below the lower band. The scale is not capped.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the window fills, the average and the deviation use the bars seen so far, so there is a value from the start. The first few bars rest on very little data.

faq.q: What does a reading of exactly 0.5 on a flat market mean?
faq.html: When every value in the window is the same, the bands have no width. The study reports the midpoint, 0.5, in that case.

related.title: Bulls Bears Index (BBI)
related.summary: One line on the price chart that averages four simple moving averages of different lengths, blending very short, short, medium and long trend.

related.title: Absolute Price Oscillator (APO)
related.summary: Plots the gap between a fast and a slow exponential average in price units, with a correction that removes the starting bias on early bars.

related.title: Bollinger Band Squeeze (BBS)
related.summary: Draws Bollinger Bands and Keltner Channels on price and marks every bar where the bands sit entirely inside the channels, the low-volatility squeeze.

bulls-bears-index-bbi.title: Bulls Bears Index (BBI)
bulls-bears-index-bbi.summary: One line on the price chart that averages four simple moving averages of different lengths, blending very short, short, medium and long trend.
bulls-bears-index-bbi.descriptionHtml:
The Bulls Bears Index takes four simple moving averages of the source, by default over 3, 6, 12 and 24 bars, and plots their plain average as a single line on the price chart. Because the four lengths are spread out, the line reacts faster than a 24-bar average on its own but is steadier than a 3-bar one.

Each average is a rolling mean of the last N values. Until N bars exist it averages the bars it has seen so far, so the line starts on the first bar instead of waiting for the longest window to fill. A missing source value counts as zero in the averages.
bulls-bears-index-bbi.howToReadHtml:
Read it like a single moving average with a balanced lag. Price closing above the line suggests the blended trend favours buyers, and closing below it suggests sellers have the upper hand. The slope of the line shows the direction of that blended trend.

The first 24 bars or so use shortened windows, so treat the earliest part of the line with care. Like any average it lags turning points and gives many crossings in a sideways market.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period 1 (Ultra-Short)
settings.html: Length of the shortest of the four averages. A smaller value makes the line hug price more closely.

settings.label: Period 2 (Short)
settings.html: Length of the second average, the short-term component of the blend.

settings.label: Period 3 (Medium)
settings.html: Length of the third average, the medium-term component of the blend.

settings.label: Period 4 (Long)
settings.html: Length of the longest average. A larger value makes the line smoother and slower.

faq.q: Why is it drawn on the price chart and not in its own pane?
faq.html: It is an average of prices, so it is in the same units as the candles and is easiest to read laid over them.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the very first bar?
faq.html: Each of the four averages uses the bars available while its window is still filling, so there is always a value. The early readings rest on fewer bars than the settings ask for.

faq.q: How is it different from a single moving average?
faq.html: It mixes four lengths with equal weight, so short-term moves shift it a little without letting it whip around as much as a short average would.

related.title: Bollinger Band Squeeze (BBS)
related.summary: Draws Bollinger Bands and Keltner Channels on price and marks every bar where the bands sit entirely inside the channels, the low-volatility squeeze.

related.title: Bollinger %B
related.summary: Shows where price sits inside its own Bollinger Bands, with 0 at the lower band, 1 at the upper band and readings beyond them outside the bands.

related.title: Bull-Bear Power Ratio (BRAR)
related.summary: Two sentiment ratios scaled to 100: BR weighs each bar's reach above and below the previous close, AR the same against the bar's own open.

bollinger-band-squeeze-bbs.title: Bollinger Band Squeeze (BBS)
bollinger-band-squeeze-bbs.summary: Draws Bollinger Bands and Keltner Channels on price and marks every bar where the bands sit entirely inside the channels, the low-volatility squeeze.
bollinger-band-squeeze-bbs.descriptionHtml:
The Bollinger Band Squeeze compares two volatility envelopes around price. The Bollinger Bands are a simple average of the source plus and minus a multiple of its standard deviation. The Keltner Channels are the same kind of average plus and minus a multiple of an average true range. A squeeze is a bar where the upper band is below the upper channel and the lower band is above the lower channel.

Both averages cover the bars seen so far until their windows fill, so everything is drawn from the first bar. The true range uses the previous close, which counts as 0 on the first bar, so that bar's range is the whole price level. The range average is an exponential one started at zero and divided by 1 minus its decay raised to the bars seen, until that correction falls below 1e-10.
bollinger-band-squeeze-bbs.howToReadHtml:
Each bar carries a small dot below it: red during a squeeze and green otherwise, and squeeze bars also get a faint red background. A squeeze means price has been quiet relative to its own typical range, a coil that can come before a larger move. The squeeze does not say which way the move will go; traders usually wait for the bands to expand back outside the channels and for price to leave the range.

The first bars rest on short windows and a large first true range, so early squeeze readings are unreliable. Squeezes can also last a long time on quiet markets without a breakout following.

settings.label: Bollinger Band Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the Bollinger average and standard deviation.

settings.label: BB StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many standard deviations the Bollinger Bands sit from their average. Smaller values make squeezes more frequent.

settings.label: Keltner Channel Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the Keltner average and in the true range average.

settings.label: KC ATR Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges the channels sit from their average. Larger values make squeezes more frequent.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages and the deviation are computed from, the close by default.

settings.label: Show Bands
settings.html: Draw the three Bollinger lines. The squeeze is still computed when they are hidden.

settings.label: Show Channels
settings.html: Draw the three Keltner lines. The squeeze is still computed when they are hidden.

faq.q: What exactly counts as a squeeze?
faq.html: A bar where the upper Bollinger Band is below the upper Keltner Channel and the lower band is above the lower channel, so the bands sit fully inside the channels.

faq.q: Does a squeeze tell me the breakout direction?
faq.html: No. It only says volatility is low compared with the typical range. The direction has to come from price itself or from another study.

faq.q: Why are the first bars often marked as a squeeze?
faq.html: The first true range is measured against a previous close of zero, so it equals the whole price level and makes the early channels very wide, wide enough to hold the bands. That effect fades as the true range average moves on.

related.title: Bull-Bear Power Ratio (BRAR)
related.summary: Two sentiment ratios scaled to 100: BR weighs each bar's reach above and below the previous close, AR the same against the bar's own open.

related.title: Bulls Bears Index (BBI)
related.summary: One line on the price chart that averages four simple moving averages of different lengths, blending very short, short, medium and long trend.

related.title: Chande Forecast Oscillator
related.summary: The percentage gap between price and the value a straight-line fit over the last N bars forecasts for the current bar.

bollinger-band-width-bbw.title: Bollinger Band Width (BBW)
bollinger-band-width-bbw.summary: The distance between upper and lower deviation bands around a moving mean, in price units, a direct measure of how spread out recent prices are.
bollinger-band-width-bbw.descriptionHtml:
Bollinger Band Width measures the gap between the upper and lower bands of a standard deviation channel. Over the last period bars the study keeps a running sum of the source and of its square, and from those computes the mean and the population standard deviation, sqrt(E[x^2] - E[x]^2). A missing source value counts as zero.

The band sits multiplier deviations above and below the mean, so the width between them is 2 * multiplier * deviation. While fewer than period bars exist the window covers every bar so far. The first bar, with a single value, has no width and is left empty.
bollinger-band-width-bbw.howToReadHtml:
A low and falling width means prices have been packed tightly together, the condition often called a squeeze, which traders watch because a larger move can follow. A high and rising width means prices are spreading out, usually during a strong trend or a sharp reversal. The width says nothing about which way the next move will go.

The width is in price units, so its level depends on the price of the instrument. Compare it with its own history on the same chart rather than with another instrument, or use the normalized or percentile versions for a fixed scale.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the mean and deviation are measured over. A longer period gives a smoother, slower width.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the bands are built around, the close by default.

settings.label: StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many deviations each band sits from the mean. The width scales directly with it.

faq.q: Is this the same as the band width divided by the mean?
faq.html: No. This study reports the raw distance between the bands in price units. It is not divided by the middle line.

faq.q: Why is the first bar empty?
faq.html: A deviation needs more than one value. With a single bar the width would be zero, which is not a measurement, so the study leaves it blank.

faq.q: What deviation does it use?
faq.html: The population deviation, which divides by the number of values in the window rather than one fewer.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Normalized (BBWN)
related.summary: Rescales the current band width inside its own range over a lookback window, from 0 at the narrowest to 1 at the widest.

related.title: Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
related.summary: The average true range divided by the close and shown as a percentage, so volatility can be compared across instruments and price levels.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Percentile (BBWP)
related.summary: The share of recent band widths that are narrower than the current one, a 0 to 1 rank of how expanded the bands are now.

bollinger-band-width-normalized-bbwn.title: Bollinger Band Width Normalized (BBWN)
bollinger-band-width-normalized-bbwn.summary: Rescales the current band width inside its own range over a lookback window, from 0 at the narrowest to 1 at the widest.
bollinger-band-width-normalized-bbwn.descriptionHtml:
Bollinger Band Width Normalized takes the distance between deviation bands and places it on a 0 to 1 scale. The width is computed first: over the last period bars the study keeps running sums of the source and its square, takes the mean and the population standard deviation, and the width is 2 * multiplier * deviation. A missing source counts as zero, and the width is zero while the window holds a single value.

It then finds the narrowest and widest band width over the last lookback bars, or every bar so far while fewer exist, and reports (width - narrowest) / (widest - narrowest). When every width in the window is the same, the reading is 0.5.
bollinger-band-width-normalized-bbwn.howToReadHtml:
A reading near 0 means the bands are as narrow as they have been over the lookback, a squeeze, which traders watch because a larger move can follow. A reading near 1 means they are as wide as they have been, usually during a strong move. Because the scale is fixed, the same thresholds, such as below 0.1 or above 0.9, work on any instrument.

The reading is relative to the lookback only: a value of 0 says the bands are the narrowest in that window, not that they are narrow in any absolute sense. The first readings, with little history behind them, swing between the extremes.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the mean and deviation behind each band width are measured over.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the bands are built around, the close by default.

settings.label: StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many deviations each band sits from the mean. It scales every width equally, so it does not change the normalized reading.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many past band widths the current one is compared with. A longer lookback makes extremes rarer.

faq.q: How is this different from the percentile version?
faq.html: This one measures where the width sits between the narrowest and widest values in the window. The percentile version counts how many past widths are narrower. A single extreme value stretches this scale but affects the percentile only by one count.

faq.q: Why does the multiplier not change the reading?
faq.html: Multiplying every width by the same number moves the narrowest, the widest and the current value together, so their ratio is unchanged.

faq.q: What does 0.5 on the first bar mean?
faq.html: With one width there is no range to measure against, so the study reports the midpoint.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Percentile (BBWP)
related.summary: The share of recent band widths that are narrower than the current one, a 0 to 1 rank of how expanded the bands are now.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width (BBW)
related.summary: The distance between upper and lower deviation bands around a moving mean, in price units, a direct measure of how spread out recent prices are.

related.title: Close-to-Close Volatility (CCV)
related.summary: Annualised dispersion of the log returns from one close to the next over a window, ignoring the intrabar range entirely.

bollinger-band-width-percentile-bbwp.title: Bollinger Band Width Percentile (BBWP)
bollinger-band-width-percentile-bbwp.summary: The share of recent band widths that are narrower than the current one, a 0 to 1 rank of how expanded the bands are now.
bollinger-band-width-percentile-bbwp.descriptionHtml:
Bollinger Band Width Percentile ranks the current band width against its own recent history. The width is computed first: over the last period bars the study keeps running sums of the source and of its square, takes the mean and the population standard deviation, and the width is 2 * multiplier * deviation. A missing source counts as zero, and the width is zero while the window holds a single value.

It then looks at the last lookback widths, this one included, or every width so far while fewer exist, and counts how many are narrower than the current width. The count divided by the number of widths in the window is the reading, a fraction between 0 and 1. With only one width there is nothing to rank against, and the reading is 0.5.
bollinger-band-width-percentile-bbwp.howToReadHtml:
A reading near 0 means the bands are narrower now than almost any time in the lookback, a squeeze, which traders watch because a larger move can follow. A reading near 1 means they are wider than almost any time in the lookback, which usually happens during a strong move and can mark a point where volatility is stretched. The value is a fraction, so 0.9 means 90 percent of recent widths were narrower.

Because the current width is part of its own window and never narrower than itself, the reading can approach 1 but cannot reach it. The first readings are based on very few widths and are noisy.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the mean and deviation behind each band width are measured over.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the bands are built around, the close by default.

settings.label: StdDev Multiplier
settings.html: How many deviations each band sits from the mean. It scales every width equally, so it does not change the rank.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many band widths the current one is ranked against. A longer lookback makes extreme readings rarer.

faq.q: Why does the reading never reach 1?
faq.html: The current width is counted in the window but is never narrower than itself, so at most all the other widths are narrower. With a lookback of 252 the highest reading is 251 / 252.

faq.q: Is the scale 0 to 100?
faq.html: No. The study reports a fraction from 0 to 1. Multiply by 100 to read it as a percentage.

faq.q: How is it different from the normalized width?
faq.html: The normalized width measures where the value sits between the narrowest and widest in the window. The percentile counts how many widths are narrower, so a single extreme width does not squash the rest of the scale.

related.title: Close-to-Close Volatility (CCV)
related.summary: Annualised dispersion of the log returns from one close to the next over a window, ignoring the intrabar range entirely.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Normalized (BBWN)
related.summary: Rescales the current band width inside its own range over a lookback window, from 0 at the narrowest to 1 at the widest.

related.title: Conditional Volatility (CV)
related.summary: A GARCH(1,1) volatility estimate that blends a long run level, the latest squared return and the previous variance, shown annualised in percent.

bessel-2nd-order-filter-bessel.title: Bessel 2nd Order Filter (BESSEL)
bessel-2nd-order-filter-bessel.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass smoother with Bessel-style coefficients, giving a smooth price line with a steady, predictable lag.
bessel-2nd-order-filter-bessel.descriptionHtml:
The Bessel 2nd Order Filter is a recursive smoother: each new value blends the current price with the filter's own two previous outputs. Its coefficients come from a Bessel prototype, which keeps the delay through the filter nearly the same for slow and fast price swings, so the shape of a move is preserved rather than distorted.

From the length it computes a = exp(-pi / length), c2 = 2a cos(1.738 pi / length), c3 = -a squared and c1 = 1 - c2 - c3. On each bar the output is c1 times the price plus c2 times the previous output plus c3 times the output before that. The first two bars take the price itself as the seed, and a missing price borrows the previous bar's value.
bessel-2nd-order-filter-bessel.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a moving average with a smooth, even lag. When price is above a rising line the short-term direction is up, and when it is below a falling line it is down. Crossings of price and the line, or turns in the line itself, mark changes in direction.

Because the coefficients add up to one, the line follows the price level closely. A longer length removes more noise but turns later. Like any smoother it lags, so it confirms a move rather than predicting one.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. A longer length smooths more and turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from a simple moving average?
faq.html: It is recursive, so every past bar still has some influence, and its coefficients keep the delay nearly constant across swing lengths. A simple average weighs a fixed window equally and drops older bars abruptly.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The first two bars are seeded with the price itself, so there is no blank warmup. The line needs a few lengths of bars to settle away from that seed.

related.title: Bilateral Filter (BILATERAL)
related.summary: An edge-preserving smoother that weights each recent bar by how far back it is and how close its price is to the current one.

related.title: Baxter-King Band-Pass Filter (BAXTERKING)
related.summary: A centred, zero-sum band-pass filter on the close that keeps only cycles between two periods and oscillates around zero.

related.title: Bandpass Filter (BPF)
related.summary: Runs price through a two-pole highpass and a two-pole lowpass, then plots the price with the band that survives both stages taken out.

beta-distribution-cdf-betadist.title: Beta Distribution CDF (BETADIST)
beta-distribution-cdf-betadist.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative Beta distribution, giving a shaped 0 to 1 oscillator.
beta-distribution-cdf-betadist.descriptionHtml:
This study turns the position of price in its recent range into a probability. First the source is placed in its own recent range: the lowest value of the last Lookback Period bars maps to 0, the highest to 1, and the current value falls somewhere between. When every value in the window is the same the position is taken as 0.5. Near the start of the chart the window is simply the bars that exist, so the line begins on the first bar.

That position x is then passed through the cumulative distribution function of a Beta(alpha, beta) variable, the regularized incomplete beta function I_x(alpha, beta). It is evaluated with a continued fraction (the modified Lentz method), using log-gamma values from the Lanczos approximation, and switches to the mirrored form 1 - I_(1-x)(beta, alpha) past the distribution's mean so the fraction converges quickly.

The two shape settings decide how the raw range position is bent. With both at 1 the output equals the position itself. Larger equal values make the curve steep around the middle of the range and flat toward the ends, so a position away from the centre is pushed toward 0 or 1 and the line spends more time near the extremes; unequal values tilt the curve toward one end.
beta-distribution-cdf-betadist.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a range oscillator from 0 to 1. Near 1 the source is close to the top of its recent range, near 0 close to the bottom, and 0.5 is the middle. The dashed lines at 0.95 and 0.05 mark the extremes where price is pressing against the edge of its window, and the dotted line at 0.5 the midpoint.

The reading is relative to the window only: a strong trend can hold the line near 1 for a long time, and a new high always reads at the top whatever its size. The shape settings change how quickly the line moves into the extreme zones, not where the range itself is.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars, the current one included, set the highest and lowest values the source is scaled against. A longer window changes the reading more slowly.

settings.label: alpha
settings.html: The left shape of the distribution. Below 1 the curve rises quickly near the bottom of the range; above 1 it weights the reading toward the centre.

settings.label: Beta
settings.html: The right shape of the distribution. Below 1 the curve rises sharply near the top of the range; above 1 it weights the reading toward the centre.

faq.q: What do alpha and beta of 1 give?
faq.html: A straight line: the cumulative Beta(1, 1) distribution is the uniform one, so the output equals the plain range position from 0 to 1.

faq.q: Why does the line sit at 0 or 1 for long stretches?
faq.html: Every new high in the window places the source at exactly the top of its range, and every new low at the bottom. In a steady trend that happens bar after bar, so the line stays pinned at the edge.

faq.q: Does a reading of 0.95 mean a 95 percent chance of anything?
faq.html: No. It is the value of a distribution function applied to the range position. It says where price sits in its window after reshaping, not a forecast.

related.title: Binomial Distribution CDF (BINOMDIST)
related.summary: Treats the source's position in its recent range as a success rate p and plots the probability of at most k successes in n trials.

related.title: Two-Argument Arctangent (ATAN2)
related.summary: Plots the angle, in radians from -pi to pi, of the point formed by two chosen bar values, keeping the sign of each in all four quadrants.

related.title: Percentage Change (CHANGE)
related.summary: Plots the fractional change of the source over a set number of bars, so an unchanged series reads zero and a doubling reads one.

bias-bias.title: Bias (BIAS)
bias-bias.summary: The distance of price from its own simple moving average, expressed as a fraction of that average, so stretched moves stand out.
bias-bias.descriptionHtml:
BIAS measures how far price has stretched away from its average. It computes a simple moving average of the source over Length bars and returns (price - average) / average. A reading of 0.02 means price is 2 percent above its average; -0.02 means 2 percent below.

The average is kept as a running sum over the window: each bar adds the new value and removes the one that left the window. Before a full window exists, the average is taken over the bars seen so far, so the line starts on the first bar rather than after a warmup.

Because the result is a fraction of the average, the readings compare across instruments at very different prices.
bias-bias.howToReadHtml:
Positive values mean price is above its average and negative values mean below. Large readings in either direction show a stretched market; traders often watch for extremes that have reversed before on the same instrument, and for the line crossing zero as price crosses its average.

What counts as extreme depends on the instrument and the length, so judge it against the line's own history. In a strong trend the BIAS can stay stretched for a long time, so an extreme reading is not a signal to fade the move by itself.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own average, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the moving average spans. A longer average gives larger, slower readings.

faq.q: Why is the value so small?
faq.html: It is a fraction, not a percentage. Multiply by 100 to read it as a percentage: 0.015 is 1.5 percent above the average.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Before the window is full, the average uses the bars seen so far. The first bar compares price with itself and reads 0.

faq.q: Can I compare it across instruments?
faq.html: Yes. Because it is divided by the average, an instrument at 100 and one at 50,000 give readings on the same scale.

related.title: Balance of Power (BOP)
related.summary: Measures where each bar closed relative to its open, as a share of its range, and smooths it with a warmup-corrected exponential average.

related.title: Accumulation Swing Index (ASI)
related.summary: A running total of each bar's swing index, a score of how strongly the close moved against the previous bar, scaled by the bar's range.

related.title: Commodity Channel Index (CCI)
related.summary: How far the typical price sits from its own average, in units of mean absolute deviation, so readings beyond plus or minus 100 mark stretched moves.

bilateral-filter-bilateral.title: Bilateral Filter (BILATERAL)
bilateral-filter-bilateral.summary: An edge-preserving smoother that weights each recent bar by how far back it is and how close its price is to the current one.
bilateral-filter-bilateral.descriptionHtml:
The Bilateral Filter smooths price inside a range while keeping the edge of a sharp move. It averages the last length prices, but each one gets a weight made of two parts multiplied together.

The spatial weight falls off with distance in bars: exp(-i squared / (2 sigmaS squared)), where sigmaS is the length times the Spatial Sigma Ratio. The range weight falls off with distance in price: exp(-d squared / (2 sigmaR squared)), where d is the gap between that bar's price and the current price and sigmaR is the rolling population standard deviation over the same length times the Range Sigma Multiplier. Bars that are both recent and close in price dominate the average; bars far away in price barely count, which is what stops the filter from smearing a breakout. The line starts once the standard deviation has a full window.
bilateral-filter-bilateral.howToReadHtml:
In a quiet range the line behaves like an ordinary smooth average. When price jumps, the bars from before the jump sit far from the new price and lose their weight, so the line moves with price instead of trailing behind it. That makes it useful for spotting a real change in level without the slow catch-up of a plain average.

The trade-off is that it is less smooth on large single-bar moves, which it treats as edges rather than noise. Raising the range multiplier makes it act more like a normal average; lowering it makes it hug price more tightly.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars are averaged and the window for the standard deviation. Longer smooths more.

settings.label: Spatial Sigma Ratio
settings.html: The spread of the distance-in-bars weight as a fraction of the length. Larger keeps more weight on older bars.

settings.label: Range Sigma Multiplier
settings.html: The spread of the distance-in-price weight as a multiple of the rolling standard deviation. Larger means a move must be bigger before it is treated as an edge.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: Why does it react faster to a breakout than a moving average?
faq.html: Bars whose price is far from the current price get very little weight, so after a jump the old prices hardly pull the line back. A simple moving average weights them the same as every other bar in its window.

faq.q: Why is the start of the chart blank?
faq.html: The range weight depends on the rolling standard deviation, which needs a full window of length bars. Until then there is no value.

faq.q: What happens in a perfectly flat window?
faq.html: The standard deviation is floored at a tiny positive number, so the weights stay defined and the line equals the flat price.

related.title: Bandpass Filter (BPF)
related.summary: Runs price through a two-pole highpass and a two-pole lowpass, then plots the price with the band that survives both stages taken out.

related.title: Bessel 2nd Order Filter (BESSEL)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass smoother with Bessel-style coefficients, giving a smooth price line with a steady, predictable lag.

related.title: Butterworth 2nd Order Filter (BUTTER)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass with a maximally flat passband that smooths away price swings shorter than the length.

binomial-distribution-cdf-binomdist.title: Binomial Distribution CDF (BINOMDIST)
binomial-distribution-cdf-binomdist.summary: Treats the source's position in its recent range as a success rate p and plots the probability of at most k successes in n trials.
binomial-distribution-cdf-binomdist.descriptionHtml:
This study reads the position of price in its recent range as a probability and runs it through the binomial distribution. First the source is placed in its own recent range: the lowest value of the last Lookback Period bars maps to 0, the highest to 1, and the current value falls somewhere between. When every value in the window is the same the position is taken as 0.5. Near the start of the chart the window is simply the bars that exist, so the line begins on the first bar.

That position is used as the success probability p of a single trial. The plot is the cumulative binomial probability P(X <= k): the chance of at most Threshold (k) successes in Trials (n) independent trials, the sum of C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i) for i from 0 to k. Each term is built in logarithms, with the binomial coefficients from the Lanczos log-gamma approximation, so large trial counts stay accurate. When p is exactly 0 the answer is 1, and when p is exactly 1 it is 1 only if k is at least n.

Because a higher p makes many successes more likely, the probability of few successes falls as price rises in its range, so the line moves opposite to the range position.
binomial-distribution-cdf-binomdist.howToReadHtml:
With the default settings, n of 20 and k of 10, the line is near 1 while price sits low in its range and falls toward 0 as price climbs to the top. It crosses 0.5 a little above the middle of the range, since at p = 0.5 the reading is about 0.59. The dashed lines at 0.95 and 0.05 mark where the reading is all but certain either way, so a value below 0.05 means price is near the top of its window and above 0.95 near the bottom.

Raising n makes the change from 1 to 0 sharper, so the line behaves more like a switch; moving k shifts the point in the range where that change happens. The reading is relative to the window only and carries no forecast.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars, the current one included, set the highest and lowest values the source is scaled against. A longer window changes the reading more slowly.

settings.label: Trials (n)
settings.html: The number of trials n. More trials make the line change more abruptly from 1 to 0 as price moves through its range.

settings.label: Threshold (k)
settings.html: The success count k the probability is taken up to. A higher k moves the point where the line falls toward the top of the range.

faq.q: Why does the line fall when price rises?
faq.html: It is the probability of at most k successes. As price moves up its range, p rises, many successes become likely and few successes become unlikely, so P(X <= k) drops.

faq.q: What happens if the threshold is above the number of trials?
faq.html: The sum stops at n, every possible outcome is counted and the line sits at 1 on every bar.

faq.q: Why are the values so close to 0 and 1 most of the time?
faq.html: With 20 trials the binomial distribution is fairly narrow, so the cumulative probability changes quickly around the middle of the range and is near one extreme elsewhere. Fewer trials give a gentler curve.

related.title: Percentage Change (CHANGE)
related.summary: Plots the fractional change of the source over a set number of bars, so an unchanged series reads zero and a doubling reads one.

related.title: Beta Distribution CDF (BETADIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative Beta distribution, giving a shaped 0 to 1 oscillator.

related.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
related.summary: Convolves the source with a Morlet wavelet at one scale and plots the size of the response, showing how strongly that cycle length is present.

blackman-moving-average-blma.title: Blackman Moving Average (BLMA)
blackman-moving-average-blma.summary: A moving average weighted by the Blackman window, a three-term cosine taper that falls to zero at both ends of the lookback.
blackman-moving-average-blma.descriptionHtml:
BLMA weights the bars in its window with the Blackman window. For bar k of a window of p bars, with r = k / (p - 1), the weight is 0.42 - 0.5 cos(2 pi r) + 0.08 cos(4 pi r). The weight is zero at the newest and the oldest bar and peaks in the middle. The weights are normalised to sum to 1, and the average is the weighted sum of the prices.

The smooth taper removes the ringing a flat-weighted average leaves when a large price leaves the window. The window grows from the first bar up to the period, so the line is drawn from the start of the chart. On the first bar, where the window holds one price, the line is that price.
blackman-moving-average-blma.howToReadHtml:
Read BLMA as a very smooth moving average. Because the bars at both ends of the window carry almost no weight, a single bar entering or leaving barely moves the line, and it changes direction cleanly. The heaviest weight is in the middle of the window, so the line lags price by about half the period.

Use it to judge the direction and turns of the trend. For a faster line, shorten the period.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being averaged, usually the close.

faq.q: How does it compare with a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple average weighs every bar equally, so a big bar leaving the window makes the line jump. The Blackman weights fade to zero at the ends, so the line moves smoothly instead.

faq.q: Why does it lag more than an exponential average?
faq.html: Its heaviest weight is in the middle of the window, not on the newest bar, so it follows price about half a period behind.

related.title: Bessel-Weighted Moving Average (BWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a Bessel-style window, zero at both ends and heaviest in the middle, with an adjustable taper.

related.title: Arnaud Legoux Moving Average (ALMA)
related.summary: A Gaussian-weighted moving average whose peak weight can slide from the middle of the window toward the newest bar.

related.title: Convolution Moving Average (CONV)
related.summary: Weights the last few prices by a kernel of numbers you type in, so any smoother or filter can be written as a list of weights.

balance-of-power-bop.title: Balance of Power (BOP)
balance-of-power-bop.summary: Measures where each bar closed relative to its open, as a share of its range, and smooths it with a warmup-corrected exponential average.
balance-of-power-bop.descriptionHtml:
Balance of Power reads each bar as a contest between buyers and sellers. The raw value is (close - open) / (high - low): +1 when the bar opened at its low and closed at its high, -1 for the reverse, and 0 for a bar that closed where it opened. A bar with no range at all reads 0.

The raw value is then smoothed with an exponential average of weight 2 / (length + 1), seeded with the first bar's raw value. While the average is young it is multiplied by a warmup factor 1 / (1 - e), where e is the product of 1 - weight over the bars so far. The factor is large on the first bars and shrinks toward 1 as history builds, and once e falls below 1e-10 it is no longer applied.

A Smoothing Length of 0 turns the smoothing off and plots the raw value of each bar.
balance-of-power-bop.howToReadHtml:
Values above zero mean closes have tended to finish above their opens, a sign buyers controlled the bars; values below zero mean sellers did. The further from zero, the more one-sided the bars. Many traders watch for the smoothed line crossing zero, or for it fading while price keeps rising, as a sign the move is losing support.

The raw reading is noisy from bar to bar, which is why it is smoothed by default. It ignores gaps between bars and volume, so it describes the shape of the bars, not the size of the trade behind them.

settings.label: Smoothing Length
settings.html: The length of the exponential average applied to the raw value. 0 plots the raw value with no smoothing.

faq.q: What range can it take?
faq.html: The raw value lies between -1 and +1, and the smoothed line normally stays inside that range too. On the first few bars the warmup factor is large and can push the line beyond it.

faq.q: Why does the line move a lot on the first bars?
faq.html: The early average has few bars behind it and is multiplied by a warmup factor that starts large. The factor shrinks as bars accumulate, and the line settles.

faq.q: How is a bar with the same high and low handled?
faq.html: It has no range, so its raw value is 0 rather than a division by zero.

related.title: Commodity Channel Index (CCI)
related.summary: How far the typical price sits from its own average, in units of mean absolute deviation, so readings beyond plus or minus 100 mark stretched moves.

related.title: Bias (BIAS)
related.summary: The distance of price from its own simple moving average, expressed as a fraction of that average, so stretched moves stand out.

related.title: Composite Fractal Behavior (CFB)
related.summary: Scores how cleanly price has moved over a ladder of lookbacks and blends the ladder into one length in bars, smoothed twice by an adaptive average.

bandpass-filter-bpf.title: Bandpass Filter (BPF)
bandpass-filter-bpf.summary: Runs price through a two-pole highpass and a two-pole lowpass, then plots the price with the band that survives both stages taken out.
bandpass-filter-bpf.descriptionHtml:
The Bandpass Filter chains two recursive two-pole stages and draws the price minus their output on the price chart.

The first stage is a highpass filter whose period is the Lower Cutoff: it damps swings slower than that period and keeps the faster movement, starting from zero on the first bar. The second stage is a lowpass filter whose period is the Higher Cutoff: it damps swings faster than that period, starting from the first highpass value. Whatever gets through both stages is the band, and the plotted line is the source minus that band.

The two cutoffs decide how much passes. With the lower cutoff below the higher one, as in the defaults of 10 and 20, the two stages overlap in what they damp, so the band is narrow and weak: it peaks for swings of about 14 bars (the geometric mean of the two cutoffs) at roughly a fifth of their size, and the line stays close to price. With the lower cutoff above the higher one, for example 48 and 10, swings between the two periods pass almost in full, and the line keeps only the slow trend and the fastest bar to bar noise.
bandpass-filter-bpf.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as price with one band of swings taken out. Where price oscillates at a period inside the band, the line is calmer than price; slow trends and very fast spikes sit outside the band, so there the line follows price closely.

The gap between price and the line is the band itself, so a wider gap shows a stronger swing of that length. At the default settings the band is small and the line rarely strays far from price. The first bars are a settling period while both recursive stages warm up, so give the line a few cutoff lengths before relying on its shape.

settings.label: Lower Cutoff
settings.html: The period, in bars, of the highpass stage. Swings slower than this are damped before the lowpass stage.

settings.label: Higher Cutoff
settings.html: The period, in bars, of the lowpass stage. Swings faster than this are damped out of the band.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter runs on. The close by default.

faq.q: Why is the line on the price chart instead of a separate pane?
faq.html: It plots the source minus the filtered band, which keeps it at the price level. The band on its own would oscillate around zero.

faq.q: Why does the line barely differ from price at the default settings?
faq.html: With a lower cutoff of 10 and a higher cutoff of 20, each stage damps much of what the other keeps, so at most about a fifth of a 14-bar swing gets through to be removed. Set the lower cutoff above the higher one to pass a wide band between the two periods.

faq.q: Does a missing price break the line?
faq.html: A missing price borrows the previous bar's value. Only when both are missing is that bar left blank, and the highpass picks up again from zero on the next bar.

related.title: Butterworth 2nd Order Filter (BUTTER)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass with a maximally flat passband that smooths away price swings shorter than the length.

related.title: Bilateral Filter (BILATERAL)
related.summary: An edge-preserving smoother that weights each recent bar by how far back it is and how close its price is to the current one.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER2)
related.summary: A second order Butterworth lowpass that smooths price with a maximally flat passband, damping cycles shorter than the length.

bull-bear-power-ratio-brar.title: Bull-Bear Power Ratio (BRAR)
bull-bear-power-ratio-brar.summary: Two sentiment ratios scaled to 100: BR weighs each bar's reach above and below the previous close, AR the same against the bar's own open.
bull-bear-power-ratio-brar.descriptionHtml:
BRAR is a pair of ratios that compare buying strength with selling strength. AR adds up, over the window, how far each bar's high rose above its open and how far its low fell below its open, and divides the first total by the second. BR does the same against the previous bar's close: how far the high reached above it against how far the low fell below it. Negative distances count as zero. Both ratios are multiplied by 100.

The sums cover the bars seen so far until the window fills, so both lines start on the first bar, where the open stands in for the missing previous close. When the lower total is zero, the ratio reads 100.
bull-bear-power-ratio-brar.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 100, the equilibrium line, means buyers and sellers pushed equally far. Above 100, prices reached further up than down over the window; below it, sellers had the larger reach. AR reflects the strength within each bar from its own open, while BR also includes any gap from the previous close, so BR often swings more.

Very high readings mean the market has been one-sided for some time, and some traders read them as stretched. The ratios describe the balance of past bars, not a turning point, and BR in particular can stay extreme through a strong trend.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars summed for both ratios. Longer windows give smoother, slower lines.

faq.q: What is the difference between BR and AR?
faq.html: AR measures each bar's reach from its own open, so it ignores gaps. BR measures from the previous close, so a gap up or down counts towards one side.

faq.q: Why does a ratio sometimes sit at exactly 100?
faq.html: When the lower total in the window is zero there is nothing to divide by, and the study reports 100, the equilibrium value.

faq.q: What is a high reading?
faq.html: Anything well above 100 means the upside reach dominated the window. How high is unusual depends on the instrument, so compare with its own history rather than a fixed number.

related.title: Chande Forecast Oscillator
related.summary: The percentage gap between price and the value a straight-line fit over the last N bars forecasts for the current bar.

related.title: Bollinger Band Squeeze (BBS)
related.summary: Draws Bollinger Bands and Keltner Channels on price and marks every bar where the bands sit entirely inside the channels, the low-volatility squeeze.

related.title: Coppock Curve (COPPOCK)
related.summary: A weighted average of two rates of change added together, a slow momentum line that tends to turn up after a decline runs out.

butterworth-2nd-order-filter-butter.title: Butterworth 2nd Order Filter (BUTTER)
butterworth-2nd-order-filter-butter.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass with a maximally flat passband that smooths away price swings shorter than the length.
butterworth-2nd-order-filter-butter.descriptionHtml:
The Butterworth 2nd Order Filter is a recursive biquad lowpass. It keeps price movement slower than its cutoff period almost untouched and damps faster wiggles, without the ripple that sharper filters add near the cutoff.

From the length it sets omega = 2 pi / length and alpha = sin(omega) / sqrt(2), then builds the coefficients a0 = 1 + alpha, a1 = -2 cos(omega), a2 = 1 - alpha and b0 = b2 = (1 - cos(omega)) / 2, b1 = 1 - cos(omega). Each bar's output is (b0 times the price + b1 times the previous price + b2 times the price two bars back - a1 times the previous output - a2 times the output before that) divided by a0. The first two bars take the price itself as the seed.
butterworth-2nd-order-filter-butter.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth moving average. Price above a rising line shows an upward short-term direction, and below a falling line a downward one. Turns in the line mark where the smoothed direction changes.

A longer length removes more noise and turns later. Because it is recursive, a large spike keeps a small influence for a while after it passes. It confirms direction rather than forecasting it.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Swings shorter than this are damped; a longer length smooths more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: What does maximally flat passband mean for a trader?
faq.html: Moves slower than the cutoff come through at almost their full size, with no bumps or dips added by the filter itself, so the line does not invent small swings of its own.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The first two bars are seeded with the price, so the recursion has something to build on immediately. It settles over the next few lengths of bars.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER2)
related.summary: A second order Butterworth lowpass that smooths price with a maximally flat passband, damping cycles shorter than the length.

related.title: Bandpass Filter (BPF)
related.summary: Runs price through a two-pole highpass and a two-pole lowpass, then plots the price with the band that survives both stages taken out.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER3)
related.summary: A third-order Butterworth lowpass filter on price that removes swings shorter than the chosen period with a steep roll-off and a flat passband.

ehlers-2-pole-butterworth-filter-butter2.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER2)
ehlers-2-pole-butterworth-filter-butter2.summary: A second order Butterworth lowpass that smooths price with a maximally flat passband, damping cycles shorter than the length.
ehlers-2-pole-butterworth-filter-butter2.descriptionHtml:
