This filter is a two-pole recursive lowpass with a maximally flat passband. Price movement slower than the cutoff period passes almost unchanged, and faster cycles are damped without the ripple a simple average leaves behind.

From the length it sets omega = 2 pi / length and alpha = sin(omega) / sqrt(2), giving a0 = 1 + alpha, a1 = -2 cos(omega), a2 = 1 - alpha and b0 = b2 = (1 - cos(omega)) / 2, b1 = 1 - cos(omega). Each bar's value is (b0 times the price + b1 times the previous price + b2 times the price two bars back - a1 times the previous output - a2 times the output before that) divided by a0. The first two bars take the price itself, and a missing price falls back to the previous one, or to zero when both are missing.
ehlers-2-pole-butterworth-filter-butter2.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line with modest lag. Price above a rising line shows upward short-term direction and below a falling line downward direction; a turn in the line marks a change in the smoothed direction.

A longer length smooths more and turns later, a shorter one follows price more closely but lets more noise through. Like every lowpass filter it reports a move after it has begun.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Cycles shorter than this are damped; a longer length smooths more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: Why use this instead of a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple average weighs every bar in its window equally, and its response to fast cycles rises and falls in ripples, so some short swings leak through. This filter's response falls off smoothly past the cutoff, so faster swings are damped more the faster they are.

faq.q: Is there a warmup gap?
faq.html: No. The first two bars are seeded with the price, so the line starts at once and settles over the next few lengths of bars.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER3)
related.summary: A third-order Butterworth lowpass filter on price that removes swings shorter than the chosen period with a steep roll-off and a flat passband.

related.title: Butterworth 2nd Order Filter (BUTTER)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass with a maximally flat passband that smooths away price swings shorter than the length.

related.title: Christiano-Fitzgerald Band-Pass Filter (CFITZ)
related.summary: An asymmetric band-pass filter on the close that weights past bars so the weights sum to zero, giving a cycle line that swings around zero.

ehlers-3-pole-butterworth-filter-butter3.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER3)
ehlers-3-pole-butterworth-filter-butter3.summary: A third-order Butterworth lowpass filter on price that removes swings shorter than the chosen period with a steep roll-off and a flat passband.
ehlers-3-pole-butterworth-filter-butter3.descriptionHtml:
The 3-Pole Butterworth Filter is a recursive lowpass filter. Each new value is a weighted mix of the last four prices and the filter's own last three outputs, with weights set by the cutoff period in Length. Price cycles longer than the cutoff pass through almost untouched, while cycles shorter than it are cut away sharply, so the line keeps the shape of the trend and drops most of the bar-to-bar noise.

The input side uses the binomial weights 1, 3, 3, 1 on the current and three previous prices, scaled so the filter has a gain of exactly one on a flat price. The feedback side uses three coefficients derived from a pole radius of exp(-pi / Length) and an angle of sqrt(3) * pi / Length, which is what gives three poles instead of two.

On the first four bars the study simply plots the price, which seeds the recursion, and from the fifth bar on it runs the full formula. Compared with a two-pole version of the same length, the line is smoother but turns slightly later.
ehlers-3-pole-butterworth-filter-butter3.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a cleaned-up price. When it slopes up the smoothed trend is rising, when it slopes down it is falling, and a turn in the line is a turn in the swing at the scale set by Length. Price crossing the line is a weaker signal than the line itself turning, because the filter is designed to ignore the short swings that cause most crossings.

All lowpass filters lag. A longer Length gives a smoother line that turns later; a shorter one follows price closely but lets more noise through. The first few bars after the start of the chart are a warm-up and should not be read.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Swings shorter than this are filtered out; a larger value gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: How is this different from the two-pole version?
faq.html: The third pole makes the roll-off past the cutoff steeper, so short swings are removed more completely. The price is a little more lag for the same length.

faq.q: Why does the line equal the price on the first bars?
faq.html: The recursion needs four earlier values to start. The first four bars plot the price itself and serve as the seed for the formula from the fifth bar on.

faq.q: Does the line ever overshoot price?
faq.html: It can. A flat passband does not rule out overshoot: after a sharp move the line can briefly run past price before it settles.

related.title: Christiano-Fitzgerald Band-Pass Filter (CFITZ)
related.summary: An asymmetric band-pass filter on the close that weights past bars so the weights sum to zero, giving a cycle line that swings around zero.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER2)
related.summary: A second order Butterworth lowpass that smooths price with a maximally flat passband, damping cycles shorter than the length.

related.title: Chebyshev Type I Filter (CHEBY1)
related.summary: A second order Chebyshev Type I lowpass that trades a controlled bump near the cutoff period for a steeper cut of faster price swings.

bessel-weighted-moving-average-bwma.title: Bessel-Weighted Moving Average (BWMA)
bessel-weighted-moving-average-bwma.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a Bessel-style window, zero at both ends and heaviest in the middle, with an adjustable taper.
bessel-weighted-moving-average-bwma.descriptionHtml:
BWMA weights the bars in its window with a smooth hump. Across the window, a position x runs from -1 at the newest bar to 1 at the oldest, and each bar's weight is 1 - x^2 raised to the power order / 2 + 0.5. The weight is zero at both ends of the window and largest in the middle. The weights are normalised to sum to 1, and the average is the weighted sum of the prices.

The order sets the taper: order 0 uses 1 - x^2 itself, order 1 its 1.5 power, and orders 2 and 3 higher powers that concentrate the weight more sharply on the centre of the window. The window grows from the first bar up to the period, so the line is drawn from the start of the chart; on the first two bars, where every weight comes out as zero, the line is the price itself, and with a period of 1 or 2 it stays the price on every bar.
bessel-weighted-moving-average-bwma.howToReadHtml:
Read BWMA as a smooth moving average. Because the newest and oldest bars carry zero weight and their neighbours very little, the line is less jumpy than a simple average of the same length, and a single bar entering or leaving the window barely moves it. The trade-off is lag: the weights are symmetric around the middle of the window, so the line trails price by about half the period.

Use it to read the direction of the trend and its turns rather than for tight entries. A higher order concentrates the weight on fewer central bars; because the weights stay symmetric, the lag stays at about half the period whatever the order.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Bessel Order
settings.html: How sharply the weights taper toward the ends of the window, from 0 to 3. Higher orders put more of the weight on the centre.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being averaged, usually the close.

faq.q: Why does the newest bar carry no weight?
faq.html: The window is symmetric and falls to zero at both ends, which is what keeps the line smooth. The cost is that the line responds to a move only as it reaches the middle of the window.

faq.q: What does raising the order change?
faq.html: It raises the power applied to the weights, which narrows the hump. The line then depends more on the bars around the centre of the window.

related.title: Convolution Moving Average (CONV)
related.summary: Weights the last few prices by a kernel of numbers you type in, so any smoother or filter can be written as a list of weights.

related.title: Blackman Moving Average (BLMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Blackman window, a three-term cosine taper that falls to zero at both ends of the lookback.

related.title: Coral Filter (CORAL)
related.summary: Six chained exponential smoothings recombined with polynomial weights into a smooth trend line that lags less than a plain average.

commodity-channel-index-cci.title: Commodity Channel Index (CCI)
commodity-channel-index-cci.summary: How far the typical price sits from its own average, in units of mean absolute deviation, so readings beyond plus or minus 100 mark stretched moves.
commodity-channel-index-cci.descriptionHtml:
The CCI works on the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3. It takes the average of the typical price over the last Length bars, then the mean absolute deviation: the average distance of each typical price in the window from that average. The reading is (typical price - average) / (0.015 * mean deviation).

The constant 0.015 is chosen so that most readings fall between -100 and +100. The average is kept as a running sum, and before a full window exists both the average and the deviation use the bars seen so far, so the line starts on the first bar. When every typical price in the window is the same, the deviation is zero and the reading is 0.
commodity-channel-index-cci.howToReadHtml:
Readings above +100 mean the typical price is unusually far above its recent average, and below -100 unusually far below. Traders use moves beyond those levels as signs of strength or weakness, a return inside them as a sign the move is fading, and crossings of zero as a change in which side of the average price is on.

The CCI has no upper or lower bound, so a strong trend can hold it beyond 100 for a long time. Read extremes against the instrument's own history and the trend, not as a fixed signal to reverse.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the average and the mean deviation span. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line with fewer extreme readings.

faq.html: It scales the reading so that most values land between -100 and +100, which makes those two levels a convenient guide.

faq.q: Is the CCI bounded?
faq.html: No. A strong move can push it well past 200 or -200. The plus and minus 100 levels are a guide, not limits.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Before the window is full, the average and the deviation use the bars seen so far. The first bar has no deviation and reads 0.

related.title: Composite Fractal Behavior (CFB)
related.summary: Scores how cleanly price has moved over a ladder of lookbacks and blends the ladder into one length in bars, smoothed twice by an adaptive average.

related.title: Balance of Power (BOP)
related.summary: Measures where each bar closed relative to its open, as a share of its range, and smooths it with a warmup-corrected exponential average.

related.title: Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO)
related.summary: Compares the sum of up moves with the sum of down moves over the window and scales the difference from -100 to +100.

ehlers-correlation-cycle-ccor.title: Ehlers Correlation Cycle (CCOR)
ehlers-correlation-cycle-ccor.summary: Correlates the last Period prices with one cycle of a cosine and of a negative sine, drawn as two lines scaled to -100 and +100.
ehlers-correlation-cycle-ccor.descriptionHtml:
The Correlation Cycle asks how closely recent price resembles a pure wave of a given length. Over the last Period bars it computes the Pearson correlation of price with one full cycle of a cosine (the Real line) and with one full cycle of a negative sine (the Imag line). Each correlation runs from -1 to +1 and is drawn multiplied by 100. Before enough history exists, missing bars in the window are filled with the current price.

The two correlations form a phasor, and the study also tracks its angle in degrees, not allowed to step backward, and a market state from how fast that angle changes. A change smaller than the State Threshold reads as a trend, up when the angle is at or above zero and down when it is at or below zero. As in the indicator this study reproduces, the angle and the state are computed but not drawn. On the very first bar the window holds one price repeated, the correlation is zero over zero, and the study leaves that bar blank.
ehlers-correlation-cycle-ccor.howToReadHtml:
When the market cycles at roughly the chosen period, Real is near +100 around swing highs and near -100 around swing lows, and Imag runs a quarter cycle ahead of it. Real crosses above Imag while price is rising toward a high and below it while price is falling toward a low. The Real line is green while it is above Imag and red otherwise, so a colour change marks a crossing.

When the lines flatten and stop crossing, price no longer looks like a wave of that length, which usually means a trend. The correlations measure shape, not size, so a tiny range can still produce full-scale readings.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length in bars of the reference cosine and sine waves, the cycle length the study looks for.

settings.label: State Threshold (degrees)
settings.html: The angle change per bar below which the market state reads as trending. It feeds the computed state, which is not drawn.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is correlated with the reference waves. The default is the close.

faq.q: Why is the first bar blank?
faq.html: On the first bar every price in the window is the same, so the correlation divides zero by zero. Any number there would be rounding noise, so the study draws nothing on that bar.

faq.q: Why are there no state or angle lines?
faq.html: The calculation tracks the phasor angle and a trend or cycle state, but neither is drawn, matching the indicator this study reproduces. The State Threshold only affects that hidden state.

faq.q: What period should I use?
faq.html: Use the cycle length you expect on your chart. If the lines cross cleanly and regularly, the period is close to the market's own rhythm; if they drift and rarely cross, try another length.

related.title: Ehlers Cyber Cycle (CCYC)
related.summary: A two-pole high-pass filter over a lightly smoothed price that strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle, with a one-bar trigger line.

related.title: Autoregressive FIR Moving Average (AFIRMA)
related.summary: A cosine-windowed moving average of recent prices; with the least squares option on, it becomes a plain simple average of the window.

related.title: Center of Gravity (CG)
related.summary: Where the weighted balance point of the last N prices sits relative to the middle of the window, an oscillator that turns at cycle highs and lows.

close-to-close-volatility-ccv.title: Close-to-Close Volatility (CCV)
close-to-close-volatility-ccv.summary: Annualised dispersion of the log returns from one close to the next over a window, ignoring the intrabar range entirely.
close-to-close-volatility-ccv.descriptionHtml:
Close-to-Close Volatility reads only how far each close travelled from the one before it. For every bar it takes the log return, the natural logarithm of this close over the previous close, and keeps the returns of the last Length bars.

The squared returns in the window are added up and divided by a count of slots, and the square root of that is multiplied by the square root of 252 to put the reading on an annual scale. Two details of the calculation are worth knowing. The returns are measured about zero rather than about their own average, which on short bars makes almost no difference because the average return is tiny. And the count runs one past the window once the window is full, because the first bar, which has no return, is counted as a slot; the reading is therefore slightly smaller than a textbook standard deviation of the same returns.

The Method setting chooses what is plotted. Method 1 plots the reading as it is. Method 2 passes it through a smoothed average with weight 1 / Length, divided by the weight that average has gathered so far so it answers from the first bars. Method 3 plots the same value as method 1.
close-to-close-volatility-ccv.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means closes are jumping further from one bar to the next, a falling line means they are bunching together. Compare the line with its own recent range rather than with a fixed number: a reading near the bottom of that range marks a quiet market, and a spike marks a burst of large moves between closes.

The 252 scale assumes daily bars. On an hourly chart the number is not an annual volatility in the usual sense, but its rises and falls still read the same way. Because only closes are used, a bar with a wide range that closes where it opened adds nothing, so this reading can understate how much price moved inside each bar.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many recent returns go into the window. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Method
settings.html: 1 plots the reading as computed, 2 smooths it with an average of weight 1 / Length, and 3 plots the same value as 1.

faq.q: Why is the first bar empty?
faq.html: The first bar has no previous close, so it has no return to measure and the study leaves it blank.

faq.q: Why does method 3 look exactly like method 1?
faq.html: Method 3 applies every weight to the current reading rather than to past readings, so the weights cancel and the result equals the unsmoothed value.

faq.q: Is the reading an annual percentage?
faq.html: It is a fraction, not a percentage, scaled by the square root of 252. Multiply by 100 for a percentage, and remember the 252 scale is meant for daily bars.

related.title: Conditional Volatility (CV)
related.summary: A GARCH(1,1) volatility estimate that blends a long run level, the latest squared return and the previous variance, shown annualised in percent.

related.title: Bollinger Band Width Percentile (BBWP)
related.summary: The share of recent band widths that are narrower than the current one, a 0 to 1 rank of how expanded the bands are now.

related.title: Chaikin's Volatility (CVI)
related.summary: The percentage change of a smoothed high-low range over a set number of bars, showing whether bar ranges are widening or narrowing.

ehlers-cyber-cycle-ccyc.title: Ehlers Cyber Cycle (CCYC)
ehlers-cyber-cycle-ccyc.summary: A two-pole high-pass filter over a lightly smoothed price that strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle, with a one-bar trigger line.
ehlers-cyber-cycle-ccyc.descriptionHtml:
The Cyber Cycle removes the trend from price and keeps the swing. Price is first smoothed with a four-tap filter, weights 1, 2, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, which kills two-bar and three-bar noise. A two-pole high-pass filter then runs over that smoothed price. The alpha setting sets the filter's cutoff: the filter passes the short oscillations and rejects the slow drift, so what is left swings around zero.

On the first six bars the recursion has no history, so the cycle starts from the second difference of raw price divided by four, which gives it something to converge from instead of a flat start. From the seventh bar on, each value is the high-pass of the smoothed price plus two feedback terms from the previous two cycle values. The trigger line is the cycle delayed by one bar, zero on the first bar.
ehlers-cyber-cycle-ccyc.howToReadHtml:
Read the cycle as the market's swing with the trend taken out. Above zero the short-term swing is up, below zero it is down. Crossings of the cycle and its trigger date the turns: the cycle crossing above the trigger marks a swing low turning up, and crossing below marks a swing high rolling over.

In a strong, steady trend the high-pass filter removes most of the move, so the cycle can turn against the trend often. Use the crossings to time entries in the direction of a trend you have judged by other means, not as stand-alone reversals.

settings.label: alpha
settings.html: The damping of the high-pass filter, from 0.01 to 0.99. Lower values give a smoother, slower cycle; higher values let faster swings through.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is computed from. The default is the bar's midpoint, (high + low) / 2.

faq.q: Why does the trigger line look like the cycle shifted right?
faq.html: It is exactly that: the trigger is the cycle value from one bar earlier. Their crossings are the bars where the cycle changed direction.

faq.q: Why do the first few bars look different?
faq.html: The filter needs two bars of its own history. For the first six bars the study uses the second difference of price instead, and the recursion takes over from the seventh bar.

faq.q: What does changing alpha do?
faq.html: Alpha is the cutoff of the high-pass filter. At 0.07 the cycle is smooth and slow; raising it lets shorter swings through and makes the line busier.

related.title: Center of Gravity (CG)
related.summary: Where the weighted balance point of the last N prices sits relative to the middle of the window, an oscillator that turns at cycle highs and lows.

related.title: Ehlers Correlation Cycle (CCOR)
related.summary: Correlates the last Period prices with one cycle of a cosine and of a negative sine, drawn as two lines scaled to -100 and +100.

related.title: Detrended Synthetic Price (DSP)
related.summary: The gap between a quarter-cycle and a half-cycle exponential average, which strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle swinging around zero.

composite-fractal-behavior-cfb.title: Composite Fractal Behavior (CFB)
composite-fractal-behavior-cfb.summary: Scores how cleanly price has moved over a ladder of lookbacks and blends the ladder into one length in bars, smoothed twice by an adaptive average.
composite-fractal-behavior-cfb.descriptionHtml:
Composite Fractal Behavior looks at a ladder of lookbacks, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 bars and so on, two rungs for each step of depth, so the default depth of 10 has 20 rungs and its longest is 1,536 bars. For each rung it sets how far the current value sits from the earlier values in the window against the path between them, with each step's absolute change weighted by its distance from the newest bar. A straight run scores higher than a window price chops back and forth across. Each rung's score is scaled by how much of its window exists yet and smoothed by an exponential average of length length.

The rungs are then blended. Working outward on each of two interleaved sides, every rung takes the share the shorter rungs before it left over, and the rung lengths are averaged with the squares of those shares as weights. The result, at least 1, is smoothed twice by an adaptive moving average set by jmaPeriod and jmaPhase, then rounded up to a whole number of bars, never below 1.

One detail of the calculation dominates its output. The study keeps the last 2 + 2^(depth - 1) * depth * 2 values, 10,242 at the default depth. The last pair in every window joins the current value with the oldest of them, and until the chart has that many bars it joins it with zero instead. Paired with zero, the whole price level enters every score, the two shortest rungs take nearly all of the weight, and the reading settles at 3. On an hourly chart of about 1,500 bars it read 3 on nearly every bar at depths 7 to 10, and moved between 3 and 8 at depths 2 to 6.
composite-fractal-behavior-cfb.howToReadHtml:
The reading is a number of bars, rounded up. It rises above its usual value only when the longer rungs keep a share of the weight, which needs a clean, one-directional stretch inside their windows; a choppy market leaves it at the shortest rungs. It says nothing about direction: a clean fall scores like a clean rise.

Because the zero pairing described above holds the score of every rung near the same value, the line is flat at 3 on most charts at the default depth, and it varies only at shallower depths, where the oldest kept value is a recent price rather than zero or a price from far back. Treat a change in the reading as a sign that the short-window structure has changed, not as a measured trend length.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price each bar contributes. hlcc4, the default, averages the high, the low and the close counted twice. A missing value counts as zero.

settings.label: CFB Depth
settings.html: How many steps the ladder of lookbacks has, two rungs per step. It also sets how far back the oldest kept value lies, which decides whether the last pair of each window reads a real price or zero.

settings.label: Smooth Length
settings.html: The length of the exponential average applied to each rung's score before the rungs are blended.

settings.label: JMA Period
settings.html: The period of the adaptive average used for both final smoothings. Larger values give a steadier, slower line.

settings.label: JMA Phase
settings.html: Shifts the adaptive average between lag and overshoot, from -100 to 100. Positive values react faster and can overshoot turns.

faq.q: Why does the line sit at 3 most of the time?
faq.html: Until the chart has as many bars as the study keeps (10,242 at the default depth), the last pair in every window compares the current price with zero. That brings the whole price level into each rung's score, so the two shortest rungs, 2 and 3 bars, take almost all of the weight and the rounded result is 3.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is going up?
faq.html: No. The scores measure how cleanly price has moved, in either direction. A steady fall scores the same as a steady rise.

faq.q: Why is the value a whole number?
faq.html: It is a length in bars, so the smoothed result is rounded up to the next whole bar, and it is never below 1.

related.title: Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO)
related.summary: Compares the sum of up moves with the sum of down moves over the window and scales the difference from -100 to +100.

related.title: Commodity Channel Index (CCI)
related.summary: How far the typical price sits from its own average, in units of mean absolute deviation, so readings beyond plus or minus 100 mark stretched moves.

related.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average, a smoothed signal line of that gap, and their difference as a coloured histogram.

christiano-fitzgerald-band-pass-filter-c.title: Christiano-Fitzgerald Band-Pass Filter (CFITZ)
christiano-fitzgerald-band-pass-filter-c.summary: An asymmetric band-pass filter on the close that weights past bars so the weights sum to zero, giving a cycle line that swings around zero.
christiano-fitzgerald-band-pass-filter-c.descriptionHtml:
The Christiano-Fitzgerald Band-Pass Filter extracts the part of the close whose cycles fall between Min Period and Max Period. Unlike a centred filter it looks only backwards from the current bar, so it gives a value on every bar.

The newest close gets half the centre weight B0 = (wh - wl) / pi, where wl and wh are the angular frequencies of the longest and shortest periods. Each earlier close j bars back gets the ideal band-pass weight Bj = (sin(j wh) - sin(j wl)) / (pi j), going back as far as the Max Lookback or the start of the chart. The oldest close used then takes whatever weight makes the total exactly zero. That endpoint correction removes any constant level, so the output oscillates around zero. On the first bar the value is zero, and on the second it is half of B0 times the change in the close.
christiano-fitzgerald-band-pass-filter-c.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the close sits in the upper half of a cycle within the band; below zero, in the lower half. Peaks and troughs of the line mark the turns of those cycles, and the size of the swings shows how strong the cycle is.

Because it uses only past bars, the latest value is available on the current bar, unlike a centred filter, but it rests on a one-sided window and can be noisier than a centred filter. A longer lookback sharpens the band at the cost of more calculation per bar.

settings.label: Min Period (pLow)
settings.html: The shortest cycle, in bars, that passes through. Faster swings are filtered out.

settings.label: Max Period (pHigh)
settings.html: The longest cycle, in bars, that passes through. Slower swings and the trend are filtered out. It is kept at least one bar above the minimum.

settings.label: Max Lookback
settings.html: The most bars of history used for each value. Larger gives a sharper band but costs more work per bar.

faq.q: How is it different from the Baxter-King filter?
faq.html: Baxter-King uses a symmetric window centred K bars back, so its newest value is K bars old. This filter uses only past bars with an endpoint correction, so it has a value on the current bar.

faq.q: Why does it oscillate around zero?
faq.html: The weight on the oldest bar is set so all the weights add up to zero. A constant price level then contributes nothing, leaving only the cycles.

faq.q: Does a longer lookback change early bars?
faq.html: No. Early in the chart the filter can only reach back to the first bar, so the lookback only matters once there is more history than it allows.

related.title: Chebyshev Type I Filter (CHEBY1)
related.summary: A second order Chebyshev Type I lowpass that trades a controlled bump near the cutoff period for a steeper cut of faster price swings.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Butterworth Filter (BUTTER3)
related.summary: A third-order Butterworth lowpass filter on price that removes swings shorter than the chosen period with a steep roll-off and a flat passband.

related.title: Chebyshev Type II Filter (CHEBY2)
related.summary: A second order recursive lowpass with zeros placed among fast swings, rescaled so a flat price passes unchanged; the attenuation setting shapes how it treats the fastest noise.

chande-forecast-oscillator.title: Chande Forecast Oscillator
chande-forecast-oscillator.summary: The percentage gap between price and the value a straight-line fit over the last N bars forecasts for the current bar.
chande-forecast-oscillator.descriptionHtml:
The Chande Forecast Oscillator (CFO) fits a least squares straight line through the last N values of the source and reads that line at the current bar, which is the price the recent trend predicts for now. The oscillator is the difference between the actual price and that forecast, written as a percentage of price.

The fit is kept with running sums over the window, so each bar costs the same no matter how long the period is. Nothing is drawn until the window holds N values, and nothing is drawn on a bar whose price is zero.
chande-forecast-oscillator.howToReadHtml:
A reading near zero means price is sitting on its own recent trend line. A positive reading means price is above where the trend says it should be, and a negative reading means it is below. Large readings mark a move that is pulling away from the recent path, and a return toward zero shows price settling back onto it.

The forecast is only a straight line through recent bars, so it says nothing about where price goes next; it describes how far the latest bar strays from the recent slope.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the straight-line fit covers. A longer period gives a slower trend line and larger swings around it.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: What does a value of 2 mean?
faq.html: Price is 2 percent above the value the straight-line fit through the last N bars gives for the current bar.

faq.q: Why is the first part of the pane empty?
faq.html: The fit needs a full window of N values, so the line starts on bar N minus one.

faq.q: Can the period be 1?
faq.html: A one-bar fit has no slope, so the oscillator draws nothing at that setting.

related.title: Coppock Curve (COPPOCK)
related.summary: A weighted average of two rates of change added together, a slow momentum line that tends to turn up after a decline runs out.

related.title: Bull-Bear Power Ratio (BRAR)
related.summary: Two sentiment ratios scaled to 100: BR weighs each bar's reach above and below the previous close, AR the same against the bar's own open.

related.title: Connors RSI (CRSI)
related.summary: A 0 to 100 oscillator that averages a short price RSI, an RSI of the up or down streak, and the percent rank of the one-bar change.

center-of-gravity-cg.title: Center of Gravity (CG)
center-of-gravity-cg.summary: Where the weighted balance point of the last N prices sits relative to the middle of the window, an oscillator that turns at cycle highs and lows.
center-of-gravity-cg.descriptionHtml:
Center of Gravity treats the last Length prices like weights placed along a ruler. The current bar sits at position 1, the bar before it at position 2, and so on back to the oldest at position Length. Each price is multiplied by its position, the products are added, and the total is divided by the plain sum of the prices. The result is the balance point of the window, a position somewhere between 1 and Length.

The study plots that balance point minus the middle of the window, (Length + 1) / 2, so the line swings around zero. When recent prices are higher than older ones the weight shifts toward position 1 and the value drops below zero; when older prices are higher it rises above zero. Bars before the start of the chart count as zero, so the line answers from the first bar, and a window whose prices add up to zero reads as exactly zero.
center-of-gravity-cg.howToReadHtml:
Read the turns rather than the level. Because the balance point shifts as soon as the newest prices change, the line turns near swing highs and lows with very little lag, and a turn from an extreme often coincides with a turn in price. The values are small and depend on Length and on the price level, so compare a reading with the line's own recent range rather than with a fixed threshold.

On the first Length bars the missing history counts as zero, which distorts the line; ignore that stretch. The study is most useful when price is cycling, and gives repeated small swings in a strong trend.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Period for the Center of Gravity calculation. A longer length smooths the line and shifts it toward longer cycles.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the balance point is computed from.

faq.q: Why are the values so small?
faq.html: The line is a position within the window measured from its middle, and with prices far from zero the balance point moves only slightly from the centre. Its turns matter more than its size.

faq.q: Does a value below zero mean the market is weak?
faq.html: It means the newer prices in the window are higher than the older ones, which pulls the balance point toward the current bar. It describes the shape of the window, not a bullish or bearish verdict.

faq.q: Why is the start of the line strange?
faq.html: Until Length bars exist, the missing bars count as zero, which shifts the balance point. The line is reliable once the window is full.

related.title: Detrended Synthetic Price (DSP)
related.summary: The gap between a quarter-cycle and a half-cycle exponential average, which strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle swinging around zero.

related.title: Ehlers Cyber Cycle (CCYC)
related.summary: A two-pole high-pass filter over a lightly smoothed price that strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle, with a one-bar trigger line.

related.title: EACP: Ehlers Autocorrelation Periodogram
related.summary: The dominant cycle length found by autocorrelating filtered price at every lag and taking the centre of gravity of the resulting power spectrum.

percentage-change-change.title: Percentage Change (CHANGE)
percentage-change-change.summary: Plots the fractional change of the source over a set number of bars, so an unchanged series reads zero and a doubling reads one.
percentage-change-change.descriptionHtml:
Percentage Change (CHANGE) compares the source with its own value a fixed number of bars back. It divides the current value by the value length bars ago and subtracts one, so the result is a fraction: 0.01 is a one percent rise, -0.02 a two percent fall, and 1 a doubling.

The first length bars have no earlier value to compare with and are left blank. A bar whose earlier value is zero is also left blank rather than dividing by zero. With the default length of one, the line is the bar-to-bar return of the source.
percentage-change-change.howToReadHtml:
Read the line around zero. Above zero the source is higher than it was length bars ago, below zero it is lower, and the distance from zero is the size of the move as a fraction. Spikes show the largest moves over the chosen span, and a line that stays near zero shows a market that has gone nowhere over that span.

The value is a ratio, so it compares fairly across price levels: a one percent move reads the same whether price is high or low. It measures only the start and end of the span and says nothing about the path in between.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series to measure, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars back the comparison reaches. One gives the bar-to-bar change; a larger value gives the change over a longer span.

faq.q: Why is the value 0.01 and not 1 for a one percent rise?
faq.html: The line is the raw ratio minus one, a fraction rather than a number of percent. Multiply by 100 to read it in percent.

faq.q: Why are the first bars blank?
faq.html: Each value needs the source from length bars earlier. Until that many bars exist there is nothing to compare with, so the study draws nothing.

faq.q: How is it different from momentum?
faq.html: Momentum is usually the difference between the two prices, in price units. This is their ratio minus one, so it is independent of the price level.

related.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
related.summary: Convolves the source with a Morlet wavelet at one scale and plots the size of the response, showing how strongly that cycle length is present.

related.title: Binomial Distribution CDF (BINOMDIST)
related.summary: Treats the source's position in its recent range as a success rate p and plots the probability of at most k successes in n trials.

related.title: Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)
related.summary: An a trous Haar wavelet decomposition that plots either the smooth trend at the deepest level or the detail removed at one chosen level.

chebyshev-type-i-filter-cheby1.title: Chebyshev Type I Filter (CHEBY1)
chebyshev-type-i-filter-cheby1.summary: A second order Chebyshev Type I lowpass that trades a controlled bump near the cutoff period for a steeper cut of faster price swings.
chebyshev-type-i-filter-cheby1.descriptionHtml:
The Chebyshev Type I Filter is a recursive second order lowpass. Compared with a maximally flat design it allows a ripple in the passband, and in return its response falls away more steeply past the cutoff.

The cutoff is wc = 2 pi / length, pre-warped with tan(wc / 2). The ripple in decibels sets epsilon = sqrt(10 ^ (ripple / 10) - 1), and from it the analogue pole is placed using the hyperbolic sine and cosine of half of asinh(1 / epsilon). The pole is mapped to a digital biquad with the bilinear transform, and each bar's output combines the current and two previous prices with the two previous outputs. The coefficients add up so that a flat price passes unchanged. The first two bars are seeded with the price, and a missing price borrows the previous one.

In this design the ripple shows up as a single bump: swings with a period equal to the length are passed at 10 ^ (ripple / 20) times their size (about 12 percent larger at the default 1 dB), and below that period the response drops quickly. At the defaults, half of a swing's power is gone at a period of about 11 bars.
chebyshev-type-i-filter-cheby1.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a smoothing line. Price above a rising line points to an upward short-term direction, and below a falling line to a downward one. Turns in the line mark changes in the smoothed direction.

The ripple setting changes both the shape and the reach of the filter. A larger ripple enlarges swings near the length period and makes the line overshoot after a sudden jump (by about 15 percent of the jump at 1 dB, and more at higher values). A very small ripple removes the bump but moves the cutoff to much shorter periods, so the line smooths far less: at 0.01 dB and the default length of 20 it passes most swings down to about 6 bars.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Swings at this period are passed with the ripple bump; much shorter swings are cut.

settings.label: Passband Ripple (dB)
settings.html: The size of the bump near the cutoff, in decibels. More ripple gives a steeper cut and more overshoot; less ripple gives a flatter but much weaker filter.

faq.q: What does the ripple setting change?
faq.html: It sets how much swings near the length period are enlarged, 10 ^ (ripple / 20) times at that period. A larger ripple buys a steeper drop for faster swings; a smaller one flattens the response but shifts the cutoff toward much shorter periods.

faq.q: Why can the line overshoot after a sharp move?
faq.html: The bump in the response comes with ringing. After a sudden jump the line goes past the new level before settling: about 15 percent of the jump at 1 dB, and more as the ripple grows.

faq.q: Is there a warmup gap?
faq.html: No. The first two bars are seeded with the price, so the line starts on the first bar and settles over the next few lengths.

related.title: Chebyshev Type II Filter (CHEBY2)
related.summary: A second order recursive lowpass with zeros placed among fast swings, rescaled so a flat price passes unchanged; the attenuation setting shapes how it treats the fastest noise.

related.title: Christiano-Fitzgerald Band-Pass Filter (CFITZ)
related.summary: An asymmetric band-pass filter on the close that weights past bars so the weights sum to zero, giving a cycle line that swings around zero.

related.title: EDCF: Ehlers Distance Coefficient Filter
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights are each bar's summed squared distance from the bars before it, so it turns quickly on sharp moves.

chebyshev-type-ii-filter-cheby2.title: Chebyshev Type II Filter (CHEBY2)
chebyshev-type-ii-filter-cheby2.summary: A second order recursive lowpass with zeros placed among fast swings, rescaled so a flat price passes unchanged; the attenuation setting shapes how it treats the fastest noise.
chebyshev-type-ii-filter-cheby2.descriptionHtml:
The Chebyshev Type II Filter is a recursive second order lowpass built from a Type II analogue design: two poles that set the smoothing and a pair of zeros that remove one band of fast swings almost completely.

The cutoff is wc = 2 pi / length, pre-warped to 2 tan(wc / 2). The Stopband Attenuation in decibels sets epsilon = 1 / sqrt(10 ^ (attenuation / 10) - 1), which places the poles, and the zeros sit at sqrt(2) times the pre-warped cutoff. The design is mapped to a digital biquad with the bilinear transform, and the numerator is then rescaled so the filter has a gain of exactly one for a flat price. Each bar's output combines the current and two previous prices with the two previous outputs. The first two bars are seeded with the price, and a missing price counts as zero.

As computed here, the filter passes swings longer than about 0.8 times the length almost unchanged, halves the power of swings near 0.6 times the length, and wipes out swings near 0.4 times the length (about 4 bars at the default length of 10). The very fastest swings, two bars long, come through at 10 ^ (attenuation / 20) / 4 times their size: about 0.45 at the default 5 dB, one at about 12 dB, and larger than one above that.
chebyshev-type-ii-filter-cheby2.howToReadHtml:
At the default settings, use it as a smooth line that tracks the price level closely. Price above a rising line shows an upward short-term direction and below a falling line a downward one; turns in the line mark changes in the smoothed direction. A longer length smooths more and turns later.

Treat the attenuation setting with care, because it does not behave like a simple strength dial. Raising it above about 12 dB makes the line amplify the fastest bar to bar zigzags, so it becomes noisier than price itself (at 20 dB it is already rougher than the close, and at very high values it swings wildly). Lowering it below about 3 dB adds a bump that enlarges swings a little shorter than the length, by up to about 68 percent at 1 dB. Values around the default of 5 dB keep the line both smooth and flat.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Every feature of the response scales with it: a longer length smooths more and reacts later.

settings.label: Stopband Attenuation (dB)
settings.html: Places the poles of the design. Around 5 dB the line is smooth and flat; well above 12 dB the fastest two-bar swings are amplified, and below about 3 dB swings near the cutoff are enlarged.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: Why does a high attenuation make the line noisier?
faq.html: After the numerator is rescaled for a flat price, the gain for the fastest two-bar swings works out to 10 ^ (attenuation / 20) / 4. That is below one only up to about 12 dB; above it those swings are enlarged rather than removed.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Type I filter?
faq.html: Type I has a bump at the cutoff and puts both its zeros at the fastest two-bar swing, so its cut keeps deepening toward the fastest swings. This filter places its zeros at a band of fast swings near 0.4 times the length and removes that band almost completely, and at moderate attenuation its response for slower swings stays nearly flat.

faq.q: Why is the numerator rescaled?
faq.html: After the transform the filter's gain for a flat price is not exactly one. Rescaling makes a flat price come out unchanged, so the line sits on the price level rather than above or below it.

related.title: EDCF: Ehlers Distance Coefficient Filter
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights are each bar's summed squared distance from the bars before it, so it turns quickly on sharp moves.

related.title: Chebyshev Type I Filter (CHEBY1)
related.summary: A second order Chebyshev Type I lowpass that trades a controlled bump near the cutoff period for a steeper cut of faster price swings.

related.title: Elliptic 2nd Order Filter (ELLIPTIC)
related.summary: A two-pole, two-zero elliptic lowpass on price with a notch just past the cutoff, removing fast noise sharply for a second-order filter.

choppiness-index.title: Choppiness Index
choppiness-index.summary: A 0 to 100 reading of whether recent bars trended or chopped, comparing the summed true range with the window's overall high to low range.
choppiness-index.descriptionHtml:
The Choppiness Index compares how much ground price covered bar by bar with how far it actually travelled. Over a window of length bars it adds up the true range of every bar (each bar's range, stretched to include any gap from the previous close) and divides that total by the window's full range, its highest high minus its lowest low.

The ratio is taken as a base ten logarithm and divided by the logarithm of the number of bars in the window, then multiplied by 100 and held between 0 and 100. When the bars all push the same way, their ranges add up to little more than the window's range and the reading is low. When the bars overlap and go back and forth, their ranges add up to far more than the window's range and the reading is high.

While fewer than length bars exist, the window is every bar so far, so the line starts on the second bar. Dashed reference lines sit at 61.8, 50 and 38.2.
choppiness-index.howToReadHtml:
High readings, above about 61.8, describe a choppy, sideways market where bars overlap a lot; low readings, below about 38.2, describe a market moving steadily in one direction. The index says nothing about which direction, only how directional the movement has been.

Traders often use it as a filter: favour trend-following methods while the index is low or falling, and range methods while it is high. A long stay at high values says only that price has been going back and forth; it does not tell you when that will end or in which direction. The early bars use a shorter window and are less reliable.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars in the window. A longer window gives a smoother reading that changes regime less often.

faq.q: Does a low Choppiness Index mean the market is rising?
faq.html: No. It means the market has been moving in one direction, which could be up or down. Use price or another study to tell which.

faq.q: Where do the 61.8 and 38.2 lines come from?
faq.html: They are customary thresholds for a choppy and a trending market. They are guides drawn on the pane, not part of the calculation.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the second bar?
faq.html: With only one bar the window has no meaningful length to normalise by. From the second bar the window is every bar so far, until it reaches the full length.

related.title: Jurik Directional Movement Index (DMX)
related.summary: The normalised difference between plus and minus directional movement, smoothed by an adaptive average, from -1 to +1.

related.title: Aroon Oscillator
related.summary: Aroon Up minus Aroon Down in one line between -100 and +100, with the pane shaded green above zero and red below to show which extreme is fresher.

related.title: Directional Movement Index (DX)
related.summary: Plots DX, the gap between +DI and -DI as a share of their sum, beside both directional lines, to show how one-sided the movement is.

cumulative-moving-average.title: Cumulative Moving Average
cumulative-moving-average.summary: The running average of every price on the chart so far, from the first bar to the current one, with no lookback window at all.
cumulative-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The Cumulative Moving Average is the plain arithmetic mean of every source value from the first bar on the chart up to the current bar. There is no period to choose: each new bar is added to the sample and nothing ever leaves it.

The study keeps the mean as a running figure and updates it in place on each bar: the new mean is the old mean plus the difference between the new value and the old mean, divided by the number of bars seen. This gives the same answer as summing every value and dividing by the count, without holding the whole history. A bar with no source value is counted with the current mean in its place, so it leaves the line unchanged.

Because every bar carries the same weight, the line moves quickly over the first few bars and then flattens as the sample grows. Late in a long chart a single new bar barely moves it.
cumulative-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the average price of everything loaded on the chart to date, not as a trend follower. Price above the line means the market is trading above its average for the whole sample, and price below it means the opposite. The distance between price and the line shows how far the market has travelled from that long-run centre.

The value depends on where the chart starts. Loading more history, or a different start date, gives a different line, so compare readings only on charts that begin at the same bar. On a long chart the line reacts very little to recent moves.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: Why does the line hardly move late in the chart?
faq.html: Every bar has equal weight, so after a thousand bars a new bar changes the mean by about a thousandth of its distance from the line. The longer the sample, the flatter the line.

faq.q: Why does the line change when I load more history?
faq.html: The average starts at the first bar on the chart. A different first bar means a different sample, so the whole line shifts.

faq.q: How is this different from a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple moving average drops old bars once its window is full. The cumulative average never drops anything, so it measures the whole chart rather than the recent past.

related.title: Cointegration (COINTEGRATION)
related.summary: A rolling unit-root test statistic on the spread between two price series, showing whether that spread has tended to pull back toward its mean.

related.title: Pearson's Correlation (CORRELATION)
related.summary: The Pearson correlation between two series of the chart's symbol over a rolling window, from -1 for opposite moves to +1 for moves in step.

related.title: Covariance (COVARIANCE)
related.summary: The rolling population covariance of two price series over a window, showing whether they have moved together, apart or independently.

chaikin-money-flow-cmf.title: Chaikin Money Flow (CMF)
chaikin-money-flow-cmf.summary: The share of recent volume that traded on the buying side, from money flow volume summed over a window and divided by total volume.
chaikin-money-flow-cmf.descriptionHtml:
Chaikin Money Flow measures whether volume over a recent window has been arriving on closes near the bars' highs or near their lows. Each bar gets a money flow multiplier from where it closed inside its range: +1 at the high, -1 at the low, 0 in the middle and 0 on a bar with no range. The multiplier times the bar's volume is that bar's money flow volume.

The study sums the money flow volume over the last length bars and divides by the total volume of the same bars. The result runs between -1 and +1. While fewer than length bars exist, the window covers every bar so far, so the line reads from the first bar. A window with no volume at all reads 0.
chaikin-money-flow-cmf.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, recent volume has traded mostly on closes in the upper part of each bar, which is read as buying pressure; below zero, the lower part, read as selling pressure. Readings far from zero show a one-sided market, and a cross of the zero line marks a change in which side is in control.

Watch for disagreement with price, such as price rising while the line slips below zero. The reading looks only inside each bar, so a gap between bars does not count, and the first few bars rest on a short window.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the money flow and the volume are summed over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: What range can the value take?
faq.html: Between -1 and +1. It reaches +1 only if every bar with volume in the window closed at its high, and -1 only if every such bar closed at its low.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the very first bar?
faq.html: The sums start from the first bar and cover every bar so far until the window is full, so the line reads from the start on a shorter window.

faq.q: What happens when the window has no volume?
faq.html: The division has no meaning, so the study reads 0 for that bar.

related.title: Elder's Force Index (EFI)
related.summary: Multiplies each bar's change in close by its volume and smooths the result, sizing the force behind every move in one line.

related.title: AOBV - Archer On-Balance Volume (AOBV)
related.summary: Two smoothed lines of on-balance volume, a fast and a slow, that read accumulation and distribution from the first bar.

related.title: Ease of Movement (EOM)
related.summary: Measures how far the midpoint of each bar travelled per unit of volume, averaged over a window, so easy moves on light volume read high.

chande-momentum-oscillator-cmo.title: Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO)
chande-momentum-oscillator-cmo.summary: Compares the sum of up moves with the sum of down moves over the window and scales the difference from -100 to +100.
chande-momentum-oscillator-cmo.descriptionHtml:
The CMO splits each bar's change in the source into an up part and a down part. A rise adds to the up side, a fall adds its size to the down side, and an unchanged bar adds nothing. Over the last Length bars it sums each side and computes 100 * (sumUp - sumDown) / (sumUp + sumDown).

The sums are kept as running totals: each bar adds its own up and down parts and removes those of the bar that left the window. The first bar has no change and adds zero, and before a full window exists the sums cover the bars seen so far, so the line starts on the first bar. When both sums are zero the reading is 0.

Unlike an oscillator that smooths its inputs, the CMO uses the raw sums, so it reacts directly to the moves inside the window.
chande-momentum-oscillator-cmo.howToReadHtml:
A reading of +100 means every move in the window was up; -100 means every move was down; 0 means the up and down moves balanced. Readings beyond +50 or -50 are often treated as stretched, and the line crossing zero shows the window's moves switching from mostly down to mostly up, or the reverse.

Because it uses unsmoothed sums, the CMO can jump when a large bar enters or leaves the window. A longer length steadies it. Stretched readings can last through a strong trend, so they describe one-sided momentum rather than a guaranteed turn.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars of changes are summed. Longer windows give a steadier, slower oscillator.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose changes are measured, the close by default.

faq.q: How is this different from RSI?
faq.html: Both compare up moves with down moves. The CMO uses plain sums over the window and centres on 0 from -100 to +100, while RSI smooths the moves and runs from 0 to 100.

faq.q: Why does the line jump on some bars?
faq.html: When a large move enters or leaves the window, the sums change sharply. There is no smoothing to absorb it.

faq.q: What does a reading of 0 mean?
faq.html: The total of the up moves equals the total of the down moves over the window, or there were no moves at all.

related.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average, a smoothed signal line of that gap, and their difference as a coloured histogram.

related.title: Composite Fractal Behavior (CFB)
related.summary: Scores how cleanly price has moved over a ladder of lookbacks and blends the ladder into one length in bars, smoothed twice by an adaptive average.

related.title: Momentum (MOM)
related.summary: The plain price difference between this bar and the bar a fixed number of bars back, drawn as a line around zero.

cointegration-cointegration.title: Cointegration (COINTEGRATION)
cointegration-cointegration.summary: A rolling unit-root test statistic on the spread between two price series, showing whether that spread has tended to pull back toward its mean.
cointegration-cointegration.descriptionHtml:
Cointegration asks whether two series that wander on their own keep a stable relationship, so that the spread between them keeps returning to an average. This study measures that over a rolling window. It first fits series A against series B: the hedge ratio is their correlation times the ratio of their standard deviations, the intercept lines up their means, and the residual is what is left of A once that fit is taken away.

It then runs a simple regression of the change in the residual on its previous value over one bar fewer than Period. The slope of that regression, divided by its standard error, is the plotted statistic, the same form as the standard unit-root test for mean reversion. The rolling statistics answer from the first bars over however many values the window holds so far, instead of waiting for it to fill, so the line starts early and settles once the window is full.

Both series are read from the same instrument, by default the close as series A and the open as series B.
cointegration-cointegration.howToReadHtml:
A strongly negative value means the spread has tended to snap back after moving away, which is the behaviour of a cointegrated pair. A value near zero means the spread has drifted with no pull back to its mean. As a rough guide, unit-root tests treat values below about -3 as strong evidence of mean reversion, but this rolling version has no exact critical values.

The statistic is noisy over short windows and on an hourly chart. Read it as a description of the recent window, not as a forecast, and look for it to stay negative for a while before trusting a mean-reversion reading.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: Series A, the series regressed on series B. The residual is measured in its units.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: Series B, the second price series of the pair, read from the same instrument.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the rolling fit. The residual regression runs over one bar fewer. A longer period gives a steadier statistic.

faq.q: Can I compare two different instruments?
faq.html: Not in this study: both series are read from the chart's own instrument, so it compares two price series of the same instrument, by default the close and the open.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bars instead of after a full window?
faq.html: The rolling means, deviations and correlation answer over however many bars the window holds so far. The early values rest on very few bars and should be ignored until the window has filled.

faq.q: What value counts as cointegrated?
faq.html: More negative is stronger. Values below about -3 are commonly read as strong mean reversion, but the threshold is a guide rather than an exact test level for this rolling form.

related.title: Pearson's Correlation (CORRELATION)
related.summary: The Pearson correlation between two series of the chart's symbol over a rolling window, from -1 for opposite moves to +1 for moves in step.

related.title: Cumulative Moving Average
related.summary: The running average of every price on the chart so far, from the first bar to the current one, with no lookback window at all.

related.title: Covariance (COVARIANCE)
related.summary: The rolling population covariance of two price series over a window, showing whether they have moved together, apart or independently.

convolution-moving-average-conv.title: Convolution Moving Average (CONV)
convolution-moving-average-conv.summary: Weights the last few prices by a kernel of numbers you type in, so any smoother or filter can be written as a list of weights.
convolution-moving-average-conv.descriptionHtml:
CONV is a general finite filter. The kernel is a list of weights, newest bar first: the first weight multiplies this bar's price, the second the bar before, and so on. The kernel is first normalised by its own sum when that sum is not zero, and the result on each bar is the weighted sum of the prices divided by the weights that were used.

The default kernel is 1, 2.5, -3.14, 0, 1. Weights can be separated by commas, semicolons or any whitespace, and each is a decimal number (such as 2.5 or 1e-2) or an unsigned whole number in hexadecimal, octal or binary (0x1f, 0o17, 0b101). If any entry is not a number, or the field is empty, the default kernel is used. On the opening bars, before the kernel fits, only the weights that land on real prices are used. If the weights used add up to zero the line falls back to this bar's price.
convolution-moving-average-conv.howToReadHtml:
What the line means depends on the kernel. Positive weights that fall off with age make a smoother that lags a little; equal weights make a simple average; a kernel with negative entries, like the default, emphasises some bars against others and can overshoot price. Read the line against price as you would any moving average, and check the shape of your kernel before trusting a crossing.

The filter is short, as long as the kernel, so it reacts quickly but smooths only a few bars.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being filtered, usually the close.

settings.label: Kernel Weights
settings.html: The weights, newest bar first, separated by commas, semicolons or any whitespace. Anything that does not parse falls back to the default kernel.

faq.q: How do I make a simple average?
faq.html: Enter equal weights, for example 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 for a five-bar simple average. The kernel is normalised, so the size of the numbers does not matter, only their ratio.

faq.q: Why can the line move outside the price range?
faq.html: A kernel with negative weights, such as the default, is not an average in the usual sense: it can extrapolate beyond recent prices. Use only positive weights for a line that stays among the prices it averages.

faq.q: What happens if I type something invalid?
faq.html: If any entry is not a number, the whole kernel falls back to the default 1, 2.5, -3.14, 0, 1.

related.title: Coral Filter (CORAL)
related.summary: Six chained exponential smoothings recombined with polynomial weights into a smooth trend line that lags less than a plain average.

related.title: Bessel-Weighted Moving Average (BWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a Bessel-style window, zero at both ends and heaviest in the middle, with an adjustable taper.

related.title: Cubic Regression Moving Average (CRMA)
related.summary: Fits a cubic curve to the lookback window by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar.

coppock-curve-coppock.title: Coppock Curve (COPPOCK)
coppock-curve-coppock.summary: A weighted average of two rates of change added together, a slow momentum line that tends to turn up after a decline runs out.
coppock-curve-coppock.descriptionHtml:
The Coppock Curve adds two percentage rates of change of the source, one over a longer lookback (14 bars by default) and one over a shorter lookback (11 bars), and smooths the sum with a linearly weighted moving average (10 bars), in which the newest value carries the most weight.

Each rate of change counts as zero until its lookback exists. The weighted average uses the values it has while its window fills, weighting them 1 for the oldest up to the count for the newest, so the curve starts on the first bar. A missing source value reads as zero.
coppock-curve-coppock.howToReadHtml:
The curve swings around zero. It was designed as a slow momentum gauge: the classic reading is a turn upward while the curve is below zero, which suggests a decline is losing force. A turn down from above zero suggests an advance is fading. Crossings of the zero line show the combined momentum changing sign.

Because both rates of change and the smoothing are long, it reacts late and is best used to confirm a change in direction rather than to time an entry.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Long ROC Period
settings.html: Lookback of the longer rate of change. A larger value makes the curve slower.

settings.label: Short ROC Period
settings.html: Lookback of the shorter rate of change added to the longer one.

settings.label: WMA Period
settings.html: Length of the weighted average that smooths the summed rates of change.

faq.q: What is the signal people watch for?
faq.html: A turn upward while the curve is below zero. It suggests downside momentum is easing, though it does not say how soon price will follow.

faq.q: Why are the first readings small?
faq.html: Each rate of change counts as zero until its lookback exists, so the early sum is missing one or both parts.

faq.q: Does it work on intraday bars?
faq.html: The calculation counts bars, so it runs on any timeframe. On short bars it becomes a medium-term momentum line rather than the slow gauge it was built as.

related.title: Connors RSI (CRSI)
related.summary: A 0 to 100 oscillator that averages a short price RSI, an RSI of the up or down streak, and the percent rank of the one-bar change.

related.title: Chande Forecast Oscillator
related.summary: The percentage gap between price and the value a straight-line fit over the last N bars forecasts for the current bar.

related.title: Correlation Trend Indicator (CTI)
related.summary: How closely the last N prices line up with a straight rising line, from -1 for a clean decline to +1 for a clean advance.

coral-filter-coral.title: Coral Filter (CORAL)
coral-filter-coral.summary: Six chained exponential smoothings recombined with polynomial weights into a smooth trend line that lags less than a plain average.
coral-filter-coral.descriptionHtml:
The Coral Filter runs the source through six exponential smoothing stages in a row, each one smoothing the output of the stage before it. The smoothing constant comes from the period: an effective length of (Period - 1) / 2 + 1, and a weight of 2 / (length + 1).

The result is not the last stage. It is a weighted sum of stages three to six, with weights that are polynomials in the Constant D setting: -d^3 on stage six, 3(d^2 + d^3) on stage five, -3(2d^2 + d + d^3) on stage four and 3d + 1 + d^3 + 3d^2 on stage three. The weights add up to 1, and they cancel much of the lag that six stages of smoothing would otherwise build up. Every stage starts at zero, so the line rises from zero on the first bars and settles onto price over the first few periods.
coral-filter-coral.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a trend line. Price above a rising Coral line describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend, and a change in the slope of the line is a sign the trend is turning. Because the line is very smooth, its slope gives a cleaner read of direction than price itself.

A higher Constant D makes the line follow price more closely, with more wiggle; a lower one makes it smoother and slower. Ignore the first stretch of bars, where the line is still climbing from its zero start.

settings.label: Smoothing Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing constant of all six stages. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Constant D
settings.html: Weights the stages against each other, from 0 to 1. Higher follows price more closely at the cost of smoothness.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line start near zero?
faq.html: All six stages are set to zero before the first bar, so the line needs a few periods to climb onto price. Read it once it has settled.

faq.q: What does Constant D do?
faq.html: It sets how the four outer stages are mixed. Larger values give more weight to the faster stages and less lag; smaller values give a smoother, slower line.

related.title: Cubic Regression Moving Average (CRMA)
related.summary: Fits a cubic curve to the lookback window by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar.

related.title: Convolution Moving Average (CONV)
related.summary: Weights the last few prices by a kernel of numbers you type in, so any smoother or filter can be written as a list of weights.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler (DECYCLER)
related.summary: Removes the cycles shorter than a cutoff period from price, leaving a trend line with very little lag.

pearson-s-correlation-correlation.title: Pearson's Correlation (CORRELATION)
pearson-s-correlation-correlation.summary: The Pearson correlation between two series of the chart's symbol over a rolling window, from -1 for opposite moves to +1 for moves in step.
pearson-s-correlation-correlation.descriptionHtml:
The study measures how closely two series move together in a straight-line relationship. It keeps running sums of each series, their squares and their product over the last Period bars, then divides the covariance of the two by the product of their standard deviations. The result is +1 when the series rise and fall together in fixed proportion, -1 when one rises exactly as the other falls, and near 0 when their moves are unrelated.

Both series come from the chart's own symbol: by default the close and the volume. A bar enters the window only when both values are present. The coefficient appears as soon as two pairs are held and grows to the full window from there. When either series is flat over the window there is no defined correlation and the bar is left blank.
pearson-s-correlation-correlation.howToReadHtml:
With the default inputs, a positive reading means bars with a higher close have also tended to carry higher volume over the window, and a negative reading means the heavier volume came with the lower closes. Readings near zero mean no consistent link.

Correlation measures a straight-line relationship only, and over a short window it swings widely. It says nothing about which series leads, and a strong reading over a few bars can be chance. Use a longer period for a steadier picture.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: The first series of the pair, the close by default.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: The second series of the pair, taken from the same symbol, volume by default. The menu lists only price series, so volume is available only as this default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars the correlation is measured over. A longer period gives a steadier reading.

faq.q: Can it compare two different instruments?
faq.html: No. Both series come from the symbol on the chart, so it compares two series of one instrument, such as its close and its volume.

faq.q: Why is the line blank on some bars?
faq.html: When one of the series did not change at all over the window, its standard deviation is zero and the correlation is undefined, so nothing is drawn.

faq.q: What counts as a strong correlation?
faq.html: Readings beyond about plus or minus 0.7 are usually called strong and readings inside plus or minus 0.3 weak, but over a short window even a strong reading can be chance.

related.title: Covariance (COVARIANCE)
related.summary: The rolling population covariance of two price series over a window, showing whether they have moved together, apart or independently.

related.title: Cointegration (COINTEGRATION)
related.summary: A rolling unit-root test statistic on the spread between two price series, showing whether that spread has tended to pull back toward its mean.

related.title: Cumulative Mean (CUMMEAN)
related.summary: The running average of a price series over every bar from the start of the chart, a slow baseline that steadies as history grows.

covariance-covariance.title: Covariance (COVARIANCE)
covariance-covariance.summary: The rolling population covariance of two price series over a window, showing whether they have moved together, apart or independently.
covariance-covariance.descriptionHtml:
Covariance measures how two series move together. Over the last Period bars the study keeps running totals of each series and of their product, counting only the bars where both have a value. The covariance is the mean of the products less the product of the two means, the population form.

The window is allowed to be partly filled, so the study answers from the second bar over however many bars it holds so far, and once the window is full the oldest pair leaves as each new one arrives. Both series are read from the same instrument, by default the close as Source 1 and the open as Source 2.
covariance-covariance.howToReadHtml:
A positive value means the two series have tended to sit above their averages together and below them together; a negative value means one has tended to be high when the other is low. A value near zero means no consistent linear relationship over the window.

Covariance is in the units of the two series multiplied together, so its size grows with price and volatility and cannot be compared across instruments. For a scale-free reading of the same relationship, use correlation, which divides covariance by both standard deviations.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: The first price series of the pair, the close by default.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: The second price series of the pair, read from the same instrument, the open by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the rolling window. A longer period gives a smoother line that reacts more slowly.

faq.q: Why is the value so large?
faq.html: Covariance is measured in price times price. On an instrument quoted in the tens of thousands, even a modest joint move gives a large number. Watch its sign and changes rather than its size.

faq.q: Why does it start on the second bar?
faq.html: The window may be partly filled, and the study answers as soon as it holds two pairs. The earliest values rest on few bars and settle once the window is full.

related.title: Cumulative Mean (CUMMEAN)
related.summary: The running average of a price series over every bar from the start of the chart, a slow baseline that steadies as history grows.

related.title: Pearson's Correlation (CORRELATION)
related.summary: The Pearson correlation between two series of the chart's symbol over a rolling window, from -1 for opposite moves to +1 for moves in step.

related.title: Entropy (ENTROPY)
related.summary: Normalised Shannon entropy of the recent window, from 0 when the values crowd into one slice of the range to 1 when they spread evenly.

cubic-regression-moving-average-crma.title: Cubic Regression Moving Average (CRMA)
cubic-regression-moving-average-crma.summary: Fits a cubic curve to the lookback window by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar.
cubic-regression-moving-average-crma.descriptionHtml:
CRMA fits a third-degree polynomial to the prices in the window by least squares, with x counting bars back from the newest (x = 0 is this bar). The fit is found by solving the four normal equations with Gaussian elimination and partial pivoting, and the line is the curve's value at x = 0.

A straight-line fit lags when a trend is speeding up or slowing down. A cubic can bend, so it follows acceleration and deceleration more closely. The window grows from the first bar up to the period; with fewer than four bars a cubic cannot be fitted, and the line is the price itself. If the equations are singular the line also falls back to the price. A missing source value reads as zero.
cubic-regression-moving-average-crma.howToReadHtml:
Read CRMA as a fast, low-lag moving average. Compared with a linear regression or a simple average of the same length, it usually sits closer to price and turns sooner. The price of that speed is overshoot: at a sharp reversal a cubic can swing past price before settling.

Use a longer period to calm it down. A crossing of price and CRMA comes earlier than with slower averages, so confirm it with the slope of the line.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the regression window, at least 4. A longer window gives a steadier fit.

settings.label: Source
