settings.html: The series being fitted, usually the close.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot price at turns?
faq.html: A cubic can bend sharply, so near a reversal the fitted curve can extend beyond the latest price. A longer period reduces the effect.

faq.q: Why does it need at least four bars?
faq.html: A cubic has four coefficients, so it needs at least four points to fit. Before four bars exist the line is the price itself.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler (DECYCLER)
related.summary: Removes the cycles shorter than a cutoff period from price, leaving a trend line with very little lag.

related.title: Coral Filter (CORAL)
related.summary: Six chained exponential smoothings recombined with polynomial weights into a smooth trend line that lags less than a plain average.

related.title: Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA)
related.summary: Two chained exponential averages combined as twice the first minus the second, which removes much of the lag of a single EMA.

connors-rsi-crsi.title: Connors RSI (CRSI)
connors-rsi-crsi.summary: A 0 to 100 oscillator that averages a short price RSI, an RSI of the up or down streak, and the percent rank of the one-bar change.
connors-rsi-crsi.descriptionHtml:
Connors RSI (CRSI) is the average of three readings, each on a 0 to 100 scale. The first is a short RSI of the source, 3 bars by default. The second counts the current run of consecutive higher or lower closes, positive while rising and negative while falling, and takes a short RSI of that run. The third is the percent rank of this bar's one-bar percentage change against the previous changes in the rank window, 100 bars by default.

Both RSI readings use averages that start at zero and are scaled up while that starting bias decays, so they give a value from the second bar onward. The final average is held between 0 and 100.
connors-rsi-crsi.howToReadHtml:
High readings mean price has risen quickly, has been rising for several bars in a row, and has just made one of its larger one-bar gains of the recent past. Low readings mean the opposite. Many traders use the 70 and 30 lines, or more extreme levels such as 90 and 10, to spot short-term stretches that may snap back.

It is a short-term measure. In a strong trend it can stay at an extreme for a long time, so a high reading on its own is not a reason to expect a reversal.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: RSI Period
settings.html: Length of the RSI taken on price. A shorter length makes this component swing harder.

settings.label: Streak RSI Period
settings.html: Length of the RSI taken on the run of consecutive up or down closes.

settings.label: Percent Rank Period
settings.html: How many earlier one-bar changes the current change is ranked against.

faq.q: What is the streak component?
faq.html: It counts consecutive bars in one direction: 3 after three higher closes, -2 after two lower closes, and 0 when the close is unchanged. An RSI of that count rises as a run lengthens.

faq.q: Why does the line start straight away instead of after 100 bars?
faq.html: The percent rank uses whatever earlier changes exist while its window fills, and both RSI parts give a value from the second bar, so the average is drawn from the start.

faq.q: Which levels should I watch?
faq.html: The pane marks 70 and 30. Readings beyond 90 or below 10 are rarer and point to a sharper short-term stretch.

related.title: Correlation Trend Indicator (CTI)
related.summary: How closely the last N prices line up with a straight rising line, from -1 for a clean decline to +1 for a clean advance.

related.title: Coppock Curve (COPPOCK)
related.summary: A weighted average of two rates of change added together, a slow momentum line that tends to turn up after a decline runs out.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler Oscillator (DECO)
related.summary: The difference between two high-pass filters, so only the price cycles between a short and a long cutoff period remain.

correlation-trend-indicator-cti.title: Correlation Trend Indicator (CTI)
correlation-trend-indicator-cti.summary: How closely the last N prices line up with a straight rising line, from -1 for a clean decline to +1 for a clean advance.
correlation-trend-indicator-cti.descriptionHtml:
The Correlation Trend Indicator (CTI) measures the correlation between the last N values of the source and a straight line that rises by one each bar. When price has climbed steadily the correlation is close to +1, when it has fallen steadily it is close to -1, and when it has moved without a clear direction it sits near zero.

The sums the correlation needs are kept running over the window. While the window is still filling it uses the bars available, starting from the second bar. A window in which price did not move at all has nothing to correlate and reads zero. The result is held between -1 and +1.
correlation-trend-indicator-cti.howToReadHtml:
Readings above +0.5 describe a fairly orderly uptrend over the window and readings below -0.5 an orderly downtrend. Values between the two dashed lines mean the recent bars have not followed a straight path. A move from near zero toward one side is a sign a trend is forming, and a fall back toward zero is a sign it is losing its shape.

It measures how straight the path was, not how far price travelled, so a slow, steady drift can score higher than a large but jagged move.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the correlation covers. A longer period looks for a longer, steadier trend.

faq.q: What does a reading of 0.9 mean?
faq.html: The last N prices lie very close to a straight rising line, so the window has been a steady advance.

faq.q: Why does it start on the second bar?
faq.html: A correlation needs at least two points. Until the window is full it uses the bars it has.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean a big move?
faq.html: No. It measures how straight the path was, not its size. A small steady rise can score as high as a large one.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler Oscillator (DECO)
related.summary: The difference between two high-pass filters, so only the price cycles between a short and a long cutoff period remain.

related.title: Connors RSI (CRSI)
related.summary: A 0 to 100 oscillator that averages a short price RSI, an RSI of the up or down streak, and the percent rank of the one-bar change.

related.title: DeMarker Oscillator (DEM)
related.summary: A 0 to 1 oscillator comparing how far highs pushed above the previous high with how far lows pushed below the previous low.

cumulative-mean-cummean.title: Cumulative Mean (CUMMEAN)
cumulative-mean-cummean.summary: The running average of a price series over every bar from the start of the chart, a slow baseline that steadies as history grows.
cumulative-mean-cummean.descriptionHtml:
The cumulative mean is the plain average of every value of the source seen so far. On each bar the study adds the value to a running total, counts it, and plots the total divided by the count. A bar with no value is skipped rather than counted as zero, and the line starts on the first bar that has a value.

Unlike a moving average, nothing ever leaves the window: the first bar of the chart weighs exactly as much as the latest. Each new bar moves the mean by its difference from the mean divided by the number of bars seen, so the line moves less and less as the chart grows.
cumulative-mean-cummean.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the average price across the whole loaded history. Price above it has been trading above that long-run average, and price below it below. Early in the chart the line follows price closely; later it flattens into a baseline.

Because it depends on where the chart starts, the value changes when more or less history is loaded, and it reacts very slowly to a new trend. Use it as a reference level, not as a signal line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line hardly move late in the chart?
faq.html: Each new bar shifts the mean by its distance from the mean divided by the number of bars so far. After a thousand bars, a new bar moves it only a thousandth of that distance.

faq.q: Why does the value change when I load more history?
faq.html: The average covers every loaded bar from the first one. Starting the chart earlier adds older prices to the average, so the whole line shifts.

related.title: Entropy (ENTROPY)
related.summary: Normalised Shannon entropy of the recent window, from 0 when the values crowd into one slice of the range to 1 when they spread evenly.

related.title: Covariance (COVARIANCE)
related.summary: The rolling population covariance of two price series over a window, showing whether they have moved together, apart or independently.

related.title: Geometric Mean (GEOMEAN)
related.summary: The geometric mean of the last N positive prices: the exponential of their average logarithm, a centre line that compounds rather than adds.

conditional-volatility-cv.title: Conditional Volatility (CV)
conditional-volatility-cv.summary: A GARCH(1,1) volatility estimate that blends a long run level, the latest squared return and the previous variance, shown annualised in percent.
conditional-volatility-cv.descriptionHtml:
Conditional Volatility models how volatility clusters: a large move tends to be followed by more large moves, and a calm stretch by more calm. Each bar's variance is built from three parts: a constant term, alpha times the squared log return of this bar, and Beta times the previous bar's variance.

The log return is the natural logarithm of this close over the previous close, held within 20 percent either way so a single gap cannot swamp the model. During the first Length bars the study averages the squared returns to estimate a long run variance. On bar Length that level fixes the constant term as (1 - alpha - beta) times the long run variance, which is what pulls the estimate back towards its usual level over time.

The model stays stable only while alpha plus beta is below 1, so when the two settings add up to 1 or more the study holds beta just under that line. The plotted value is the square root of 252 times the variance, times 100.
conditional-volatility-cv.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the market's current volatility regime. It jumps after a large return, then decays towards its long run level at a pace set by beta: a high beta lets a shock linger for many bars, a low beta lets it fade quickly. A line that keeps climbing means large moves are arriving one after another.

The first bars use only a short running average, so the line settles once the first Length bars have passed. The 252 scale assumes daily bars; on an intraday chart treat the number as a relative reading, not an annual figure.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many opening bars are averaged to estimate the long run variance that anchors the model.

settings.label: alpha
settings.html: Weight on the latest squared return. Higher values make the line react more sharply to each new move.

settings.label: Beta
settings.html: Weight on the previous variance. Higher values make a shock fade more slowly. It is held so that alpha plus beta stays below 1.

faq.q: What happens if alpha plus beta reaches 1?
faq.html: The model would no longer return to a long run level, so the study lowers beta to just under 1 minus alpha before using it.

faq.q: Why are returns capped at 20 percent?
faq.html: A single very large gap would dominate the variance for many bars. Holding each return within 20 percent either way keeps one bar from overwhelming the estimate.

faq.q: How is the line computed during the first Length bars?
faq.html: Until bar Length the constant term is zero. Each bar's variance is alpha times its squared return plus beta times the running average of the squared returns so far. On bar Length that average becomes the long run level, the constant term is fixed from it, and the full model runs from then on.

related.title: Chaikin's Volatility (CVI)
related.summary: The percentage change of a smoothed high-low range over a set number of bars, showing whether bar ranges are widening or narrowing.

related.title: Close-to-Close Volatility (CCV)
related.summary: Annualised dispersion of the log returns from one close to the next over a window, ignoring the intrabar range entirely.

related.title: Elder's Thermometer (ETHERM)
related.summary: Measures how far each bar reaches beyond the previous bar's high or low, with an exponential signal line and a colour for hot and explosive bars.

chaikin-s-volatility-cvi.title: Chaikin's Volatility (CVI)
chaikin-s-volatility-cvi.summary: The percentage change of a smoothed high-low range over a set number of bars, showing whether bar ranges are widening or narrowing.
chaikin-s-volatility-cvi.descriptionHtml:
Chaikin's Volatility tracks how quickly the size of bars is changing. Each bar's range is its high minus its low, with a missing range read as zero. That range is smoothed with an exponential average of weight 2 / (smoothLength + 1). On the first bar the average starts from that bar's range divided by the smoothing length, as if the bars before the chart had no range, so the first stretch of values climbs from below.

The reading is the percentage change of the smoothed range over rocLength bars: (average - average rocLength bars ago) / average rocLength bars ago * 100. It is empty for the first rocLength bars, while there is no older average to compare with. A grey zero line is drawn for reference.
chaikin-s-volatility-cvi.howToReadHtml:
A positive reading means the smoothed range is wider than it was rocLength bars ago, so bars are expanding; a negative reading means they are contracting. Sharp rises often appear as a market accelerates into a move or a sell-off, and long stretches below zero describe a market that is quietening down.

The study measures change in range, not its level, and not direction: a strong rally and a sharp fall both push it up. Ignore the first stretch of readings after the start of the chart, where the average is still climbing from its low starting value and the reading is inflated.

settings.label: ROC Length
settings.html: How many bars back the smoothed range is compared with. A longer length measures a slower change in volatility.

settings.label: Smoothing Length
settings.html: How heavily the high-low range is smoothed before its change is measured. A longer length gives a steadier, slower reading.

faq.q: Why are the first readings so large?
faq.html: The average starts from the first bar's range divided by the smoothing length, which is far below a normal range, and climbs from there. Comparing the climbing average with its own earlier, lower values gives large positive changes until it settles.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is rising?
faq.html: No. It means bar ranges are widening. That happens in fast falls as often as in fast rallies.

faq.q: What is the grey line?
faq.html: A fixed zero reference. Above it the smoothed range is wider than it was rocLength bars ago; below it the range is narrower.

related.title: Elder's Thermometer (ETHERM)
related.summary: Measures how far each bar reaches beyond the previous bar's high or low, with an exponential signal line and a colour for hot and explosive bars.

related.title: Conditional Volatility (CV)
related.summary: A GARCH(1,1) volatility estimate that blends a long run level, the latest squared return and the previous variance, shown annualised in percent.

related.title: Exponential Weighted MA Volatility
related.summary: Volatility from an exponentially weighted average of squared log returns, corrected for start-up bias and optionally annualised.

continuous-wavelet-transform-cwt.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
continuous-wavelet-transform-cwt.summary: Convolves the source with a Morlet wavelet at one scale and plots the size of the response, showing how strongly that cycle length is present.
continuous-wavelet-transform-cwt.descriptionHtml:
This study measures how much of one particular cycle length is present in the recent price history. It slides a Morlet wavelet, a cosine and sine wave wrapped in a bell-shaped Gaussian envelope, across the most recent bars and adds up the products, which is a convolution at a single scale.

The wavelet spans three scales on each side of its centre, so it reads the last 2 x round(3 x Scale) + 1 bars. At each tap the Gaussian weight is e^(-t^2 / 2), with t the tap's offset divided by the scale, and the wave turns at Omega radians per unit of t. The real and imaginary sums are combined into a magnitude and divided by the square root of the scale, so readings at different scales are comparable. History before the first bar counts as zero.

Because the wavelet is centred halfway back in its window, the reading describes the price action around that point rather than the newest bar alone.
continuous-wavelet-transform-cwt.howToReadHtml:
A high value means the price history carries a strong oscillation near the cycle length the scale and omega pick out, or a large move that the wavelet responds to; a low value means that rhythm is weak. Rising readings show a cycle or swing of that size building, falling readings show it fading.

The output is a magnitude in price units, so it is always positive and has no zero line to cross. It also responds to the price level itself, more so at long scales and low omega, and the first bars of the chart are lower because the missing history counts as zero. Compare it within one chart and one setting rather than across instruments.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the wavelet is run over, the close by default.

settings.label: Scale
settings.html: The width of the wavelet. Higher values reach further back and respond to longer, slower cycles.

settings.label: Omega (Central Frequency)
settings.html: How many waves fit inside the envelope. The standard value is 6; higher values give finer frequency detail and a less precise position in time.

faq.q: Which cycle length does a scale pick out?
faq.html: For the Morlet wavelet the period it responds to most is roughly 2 x pi x Scale / Omega bars. With the defaults, scale 10 and omega 6, that is about 10 bars.

faq.q: Why is the line low at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The wavelet reads bars before the first one as zero, so until the whole window has real history the sum is incomplete.

faq.q: Why is the value never negative?
faq.html: It is the magnitude of a complex response, the square root of the real part squared plus the imaginary part squared, so it measures strength and not direction.

related.title: Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)
related.summary: An a trous Haar wavelet decomposition that plots either the smooth trend at the deepest level or the detail removed at one chosen level.

related.title: Percentage Change (CHANGE)
related.summary: Plots the fractional change of the source over a set number of bars, so an unchanged series reads zero and a doubling reads one.

related.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
related.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.

donchian-channels-dchannel.title: Donchian Channels (DCHANNEL)
donchian-channels-dchannel.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the last period bars, with the midpoint between them, drawn from the first bar.
donchian-channels-dchannel.descriptionHtml:
This channel marks the outright range of recent trade. The upper line is the highest value of the high source over the last period bars, the lower line is the lowest value of the low source over the same bars, and the basis is the midpoint between them.

While fewer than period bars exist, the lines use the extremes of every bar so far, so the channel is drawn from the first bar. Both sources can be changed, for example to read the channel off closes or off the bar midpoint instead of the highs and lows.

There is no smoothing. The upper line only moves up when a new high enters the window and only moves down when the old high leaves it, which gives the channel its flat, stepped look.
donchian-channels-dchannel.howToReadHtml:
A bar that pushes the upper line higher is making a new high for the period, the classic breakout condition, and a bar that pushes the lower line lower is making a new low. A flat line means no new extreme on that side for a while. The basis line shows the middle of the range and is often used as a trailing reference.

The channel includes the current bar, so a high equal to the upper line is the new high itself. To test for a break of the previous range, compare against the line from one bar earlier.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars the highest and lowest values are taken over. Longer periods give a wider, slower channel.

settings.label: High Source
settings.html: The series the upper line takes its highest value from, the bar high by default.

settings.label: Low Source
settings.html: The series the lower line takes its lowest value from, the bar low by default.

faq.q: Why does the channel move in steps?
faq.html: Each line is an outright extreme, not an average. It changes only when a new extreme enters the window or the old one drops out.

faq.q: Does the channel include the current bar?
faq.html: Yes. A new high on this bar lifts the upper line on this bar, so compare with the previous bar's line to test a breakout.

faq.q: What is the basis line?
faq.html: The midpoint of the upper and lower lines, halfway between the highest high and the lowest low of the window.

related.title: Decay Min-Max Channel (DECAYCHANNEL)
related.summary: A high and low channel whose edges are pulled toward the middle harder the longer they go without a new extreme.

related.title: Bollinger Bands (BBANDS)
related.summary: A simple average with bands a multiple of the population standard deviation away, drawn from the first bar on an expanding window.

related.title: Fractal Chaos Bands (FCB)
related.summary: Bands at the highest recent three-bar fractal high and the lowest recent fractal low, with optional marks on the fractal bars.

decay-min-max-channel-decaychannel.title: Decay Min-Max Channel (DECAYCHANNEL)
decay-min-max-channel-decaychannel.summary: A high and low channel whose edges are pulled toward the middle harder the longer they go without a new extreme.
decay-min-max-channel-decaychannel.descriptionHtml:
The Decay Min-Max Channel starts from the highest high and lowest low of recent bars, but its edges do not wait for the window to drop an old extreme. Each edge keeps a clock of how many bars have passed since price set a new extreme on that side. A new high resets the upper clock and moves the upper edge to that high; a new low does the same below.

On every bar each edge moves toward the channel midpoint by a share of its distance from it. That share is one minus the exponential of minus the decay rate times the clock, and the decay rate is the natural log of two divided by the period. On the bar right after a new extreme the share is small; once an edge has gone period bars without a new extreme it closes half its gap to the midpoint on every bar. Because the pull repeats bar after bar, a quiet edge comes in well before period bars have passed.

The edges are then held inside the highest high and lowest low of the last period bars, or of every bar so far while that window is still filling.
decay-min-max-channel-decaychannel.howToReadHtml:
A fresh extreme snaps the edge outward, so an edge that sits on price marks a side that is still making new highs or lows. An edge that has drifted inward shows a side that has gone quiet. When both edges converge, the market has stopped making new extremes in either direction and the range is tightening.

A break of a decayed edge is a smaller move than a break of the full range, so this channel reacts sooner than a plain high and low channel, at the cost of more false breaks.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window for the high and low limits, and the number of bars without a new extreme after which an edge closes half its gap to the midpoint on each bar. Longer periods decay more slowly and give a wider channel.

faq.q: How fast do the edges decay?
faq.html: The share of the gap to the midpoint that an edge closes on a bar grows with the bars since its last new extreme: it is one minus two to the power of minus that count over the period. It reaches one half after period quiet bars, and because the pull compounds, the edge is already well inside the range by then.

faq.q: Can an edge move past the window's high or low?
faq.html: No. After decaying, the upper edge is capped at the window's highest high and the lower edge is floored at its lowest low.

faq.q: Why does an edge jump outward?
faq.html: A bar that reaches or passes the current edge resets that side's clock and moves the edge to the bar's extreme.

related.title: Fractal Chaos Bands (FCB)
related.summary: Bands at the highest recent three-bar fractal high and the lowest recent fractal low, with optional marks on the fractal bars.

related.title: Donchian Channels (DCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the last period bars, with the midpoint between them, drawn from the first bar.

related.title: Jurik Volatility Bands (JBANDS)
related.summary: Upper and lower bands that snap to a bar's extreme when price pushes through and otherwise fall back at a rate set by relative volatility.

ehlers-decycler-oscillator-deco.title: Ehlers Decycler Oscillator (DECO)
ehlers-decycler-oscillator-deco.summary: The difference between two high-pass filters, so only the price cycles between a short and a long cutoff period remain.
ehlers-decycler-oscillator-deco.descriptionHtml:
The Ehlers Decycler Oscillator (DECO) runs two 2-pole high-pass filters over the source. A high-pass filter removes cycles longer than its cutoff, so the long filter (60 bars by default) keeps everything shorter than 60 bars and the short filter (30 bars) keeps everything shorter than 30. Subtracting the short filter from the long one leaves the band of cycles between the two cutoffs, with the trend removed.

Both filters start at zero on the first two bars, and a missing source value reads as zero. Nothing is drawn unless the short period is below the long period.
ehlers-decycler-oscillator-deco.howToReadHtml:
The line swings around zero as the mid-length cycles move price up and down. Turns at a peak or trough mark the turning points of those cycles, and crossings of the zero line show the cycle changing phase. Because the trend is filtered out, the oscillator stays centred on zero even during a long advance or decline.

The filters need some bars to settle, so the opening stretch of the line is not reliable. It describes cycles in the past data and does not predict that they will continue.

settings.label: Short Period
settings.html: The short cutoff: cycles shorter than this are removed from the result.

settings.label: Long Period
settings.html: The long cutoff: cycles longer than this, including the trend, are removed. It must be above the short period.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: Why is the pane empty?
faq.html: The short period must be below the long period. When it is not, there is no band of cycles to keep, so nothing is drawn.

faq.q: What does a zero crossing mean?
faq.html: The cycles between the two cutoffs have changed phase, from pushing price up to pushing it down or the reverse.

faq.q: Why does it ignore the trend?
faq.html: Both filters remove cycles longer than their cutoff, and the long cutoff removes the trend, so what remains is the swing around it.

related.title: DeMarker Oscillator (DEM)
related.summary: A 0 to 1 oscillator comparing how far highs pushed above the previous high with how far lows pushed below the previous low.

related.title: Correlation Trend Indicator (CTI)
related.summary: How closely the last N prices line up with a straight rising line, from -1 for a clean decline to +1 for a clean advance.

related.title: Derivative Oscillator (DOSC)
related.summary: A double-smoothed RSI minus its own moving average, a momentum line that crosses zero as the smoothed RSI moves through its average.

ehlers-decycler-decycler.title: Ehlers Decycler (DECYCLER)
ehlers-decycler-decycler.summary: Removes the cycles shorter than a cutoff period from price, leaving a trend line with very little lag.
ehlers-decycler-decycler.descriptionHtml:
The Decycler subtracts a high-pass filter from price. A two-pole high-pass filter keeps only the swings shorter than the cutoff Period and blocks the slower movement. Taking that output away from price leaves the slower part: the trend, with the short cycles removed.

The filter works on the second difference of price, the change in the bar-to-bar change, and feeds back its own previous two values. Its coefficients come from the cutoff period through a cosine and a sine of 0.707 * 2 * pi / Period. The filter is held at zero for the first two bars, and a price before the first bar is read as zero.
ehlers-decycler-decycler.howToReadHtml:
Read the Decycler as a trend line that lags far less than a moving average of a similar length. Price above a rising Decycler describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend, and a change in its slope marks a change in the trend.

The cutoff period sets what counts as noise: a cycle shorter than it is removed, a longer one passes through into the line. A short period leaves a line close to price; a long one gives a smoother line that turns later. Over the first stretch of bars the filter is still settling.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The cutoff period of the high-pass filter. Swings shorter than this are removed; longer values give a smoother trend line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it lag less than a moving average?
faq.html: Instead of averaging a window of bars, it subtracts a high-pass filter from price. Only the swings shorter than the cutoff are removed, so the slower movement of price passes through almost unchanged.

faq.q: What does the period mean here?
faq.html: It is the cycle length in bars at which the filter starts to remove movement. Shorter cycles are taken out, longer ones remain in the line.

related.title: Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA)
related.summary: Two chained exponential averages combined as twice the first minus the second, which removes much of the lag of a single EMA.

related.title: Cubic Regression Moving Average (CRMA)
related.summary: Fits a cubic curve to the lookback window by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar.

related.title: Deviation-Scaled Moving Average (DSMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that speeds up when its tracking error is large against its recent size and slows down when it is small.

demarker-oscillator-dem.title: DeMarker Oscillator (DEM)
demarker-oscillator-dem.summary: A 0 to 1 oscillator comparing how far highs pushed above the previous high with how far lows pushed below the previous low.
demarker-oscillator-dem.descriptionHtml:
The DeMarker Oscillator (DEM) looks at each bar's extension beyond the previous bar. The up extension is how far the high rose above the previous high, or zero if it did not. The down extension is how far the low fell below the previous low, or zero if it did not. Both are summed over the last N bars, and the oscillator is the up total divided by the sum of both totals.

Bars before the first count as zero in the totals, so the line starts on the first bar with partial totals. When neither side extended at all in the window the reading is 0.5.
demarker-oscillator-dem.howToReadHtml:
Readings near 1 mean recent bars have mostly been pushing to new highs, and readings near 0 mean they have mostly been pushing to new lows. The dashed lines at 0.7 and 0.3 are the usual overbought and oversold zones, with 0.5 as the balance point. A turn back from beyond 0.7 or 0.3 is often read as momentum fading on that side.

It uses only highs and lows, not closes, so it reflects how far bars reached rather than where they settled. In a strong trend it can stay in an extreme zone for many bars.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the up and down extensions are summed over. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: Why is it 0.5 on some bars?
faq.html: When no bar in the window extended beyond its predecessor on either side, both totals are zero and the oscillator reads the neutral 0.5.

faq.q: How is it different from the RSI?
faq.html: The RSI compares closes; this compares how far highs and lows extended past the previous bar, so it reacts to how far each bar reached.

faq.q: Why are the first readings different from later ones?
faq.html: Until N bars exist the totals cover fewer bars, so the early values rest on a shorter window.

related.title: Derivative Oscillator (DOSC)
related.summary: A double-smoothed RSI minus its own moving average, a momentum line that crosses zero as the smoothed RSI moves through its average.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler Oscillator (DECO)
related.summary: The difference between two high-pass filters, so only the price cycles between a short and a long cutoff period remain.

related.title: Detrended Price Oscillator (DPO)
related.summary: Price minus a simple moving average taken from about half a period earlier, so the trend drops out and shorter cycles stand out.

double-exponential-moving-average-dema.title: Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA)
double-exponential-moving-average-dema.summary: Two chained exponential averages combined as twice the first minus the second, which removes much of the lag of a single EMA.
double-exponential-moving-average-dema.descriptionHtml:
The DEMA computes an exponential average of the source, then an exponential average of that average, both with the weight 2 / (Period + 1). The plotted value is twice the first average minus the second. The gap between the two averages estimates how far the first one trails price, and adding that gap to the first average takes much of the lag out.

Both averages start from zero. Over the early bars each is divided by 1 - beta^n, where beta is 1 - 2 / (Period + 1) and n is the number of bars so far, which removes the bias of the zero start. Once beta^n falls below 1e-10 the correction stops, because it no longer changes anything. The line is drawn from the first bar.
double-exponential-moving-average-dema.howToReadHtml:
The DEMA follows price more closely than an EMA of the same period and turns sooner after a reversal. Price above a rising DEMA describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend; crossings of a short DEMA through a long one are a common trend-change trigger.

The lag correction can overshoot: after a sharp move the DEMA may run past price for a bar or two before settling. In a choppy market its speed also gives more false turns than a plain EMA.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of both exponential averages. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Is this the same as an EMA of an EMA?
faq.html: No. It uses an EMA of an EMA as a measure of lag, and plots twice the first EMA minus that, which sits closer to price than either.

faq.q: Why is the line usable from the first bar?
faq.html: Each average is divided by 1 - beta^n while that term is still meaningful, which removes the drag of starting from zero.

related.title: Deviation-Scaled Moving Average (DSMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that speeds up when its tracking error is large against its recent size and slows down when it is small.

related.title: Ehlers Decycler (DECYCLER)
related.summary: Removes the cycles shorter than a cutoff period from price, leaving a trend line with very little lag.

related.title: Double Weighted Moving Average (DWMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average applied twice over the same period, smoother than one pass while still leaning on recent bars.

dirty-data-injection-dirty.title: Dirty Data Injection (DIRTY)
dirty-data-injection-dirty.summary: Echoes a price series with regular gaps cut into it, so you can see how other studies cope with missing bars.
dirty-data-injection-dirty.descriptionHtml:
Dirty Data Injection is a test tool rather than a market study. It copies the chosen source series bar for bar, but blanks it on a fixed schedule: the very first bar is always empty, and after that the first few bars of every cycle are left empty too.

The cycle length is the NA Injection Interval and the number of blank bars at the start of each cycle is the NA Gap Size. A bar is blank when its position in the run, divided by the interval, leaves a remainder smaller than the gap size. With the defaults of 10 and 5, bars 0 to 4 are blank, bars 5 to 9 carry the source, bars 10 to 14 are blank again, and so on.

Nothing is smoothed or averaged. Every value that is drawn is exactly the source value on that bar.
dirty-data-injection-dirty.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a picture of a broken data feed. The line is the source where data is present and a gap where it has been removed, so it shows at a glance which bars an indicator would have to handle without a value.

It carries no trading signal. Its use is in building and checking other scripts: feed the same gap pattern into a calculation and confirm that its warmup, its running sums and its markers behave sensibly when bars are missing, rather than treating a gap as zero.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is copied onto the chart where it is not blanked.

settings.label: NA Injection Interval
settings.html: The length of one cycle in bars. A larger value spaces the gaps further apart.

settings.label: NA Gap Size
settings.html: How many bars at the start of each cycle are left empty. A value equal to or above the interval blanks every bar.

faq.q: Why is the first bar always empty?
faq.html: The first bar is blanked unconditionally, in addition to the gap at the start of every cycle, so every run begins with a missing value.

faq.q: Is this meant to be traded?
faq.html: No. It reproduces the source with holes in it. Its only job is to give other calculations a series with known gaps to test against.

faq.q: What happens if the gap size is larger than the interval?
faq.html: Every bar falls inside a gap, so nothing is drawn at all.

related.title: Huber Loss (HUBER)
related.summary: The average Huber penalty of the gap between price and its own exponential average: squared for small gaps, linear for large ones.

related.title: Log-Cosh Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of log(cosh(actual minus predicted)), an error measure that acts squared for small misses and linear for large ones.

related.title: Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the arctangent of the absolute percentage error between two series, bounded between zero and pi/2.

jurik-directional-movement-index-dmx.title: Jurik Directional Movement Index (DMX)
jurik-directional-movement-index-dmx.summary: The normalised difference between plus and minus directional movement, smoothed by an adaptive average, from -1 to +1.
jurik-directional-movement-index-dmx.descriptionHtml:
DMX starts from the directional movement of each bar. Upward movement is the rise in the high from the previous bar, counted only when it is positive and larger than the fall in the low; downward movement is the fall in the low, counted under the mirror condition. Each is smoothed with a Wilder average that starts from zero and is scaled up by the factor that zero start leaves out, giving a plus and a minus directional value.

The raw reading is their difference divided by their sum, so it runs from -1 when all movement is downward to +1 when all of it is upward, and it is zero when there is no movement at all.

That raw reading is then passed through an adaptive average instead of the usual second Wilder smoothing. The average tracks its own volatility over the last ten bars and against a longer running mean of it, and speeds up when the input jumps and slows down when it is quiet, which keeps the line smooth with less delay than a fixed average of similar smoothness.
jurik-directional-movement-index-dmx.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, upward directional movement has dominated; below zero, downward. The further from zero, the more one-sided the movement. A cross of zero marks the point where the balance of directional movement changes side, and it tends to come earlier and with fewer false crossings than a line smoothed the usual way.

The line measures direction, not strength of trend in the usual sense: a slow, steady climb and a sharp rally can read alike. The first bars are shaped by the zero-started averages and settle after a few periods.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the directional movement smoothing, which also sets the constants of the adaptive average. A longer period gives a slower, smoother line.

faq.q: Why does the line stay between -1 and +1?
faq.html: The raw value is the difference of the two directional values divided by their sum, which can never exceed one in size. The adaptive average stays close to that range.

faq.q: How is it different from the usual directional index?
faq.html: The usual index smooths the directional difference with another Wilder average and drops the sign. This one keeps the sign and uses an adaptive average that reacts faster with less whipsaw.

faq.q: What does a reading of zero mean?
faq.html: Upward and downward movement have been in balance over the smoothing window, or there has been no directional movement at all.

related.title: Directional Movement Index (DX)
related.summary: Plots DX, the gap between +DI and -DI as a share of their sum, beside both directional lines, to show how one-sided the movement is.

related.title: Choppiness Index
related.summary: A 0 to 100 reading of whether recent bars trended or chopped, comparing the summed true range with the window's overall high to low range.

related.title: Gann High-Low Activator
related.summary: A trailing line built from short averages of the highs and lows that flips sides when price closes beyond it, with BUY and SELL marks on each flip.

derivative-oscillator-dosc.title: Derivative Oscillator (DOSC)
derivative-oscillator-dosc.summary: A double-smoothed RSI minus its own moving average, a momentum line that crosses zero as the smoothed RSI moves through its average.
derivative-oscillator-dosc.descriptionHtml:
The Derivative Oscillator (DOSC) starts from an RSI of the source (14 bars by default). It smooths that RSI twice with exponential averages (5 and then 3 bars), each starting from its first input, and then subtracts a simple average of the double-smoothed line (9 bars) used as a signal line. The plotted value is the gap between the smoothed RSI and that signal line.

The RSI here treats the bar before the first as a price of zero, and until the RSI period has passed its averages are simply the current bar's gain and loss; after that they are smoothed with weight one over the period. The signal average uses the bars it has while its window fills, so the oscillator is drawn from the first bar.
derivative-oscillator-dosc.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the double-smoothed RSI sits above its own recent average, so momentum has been improving. Below zero it sits under that average, so momentum has been weakening. Crossings of the zero line are the main event: a cross up suggests momentum has turned higher and a cross down that it has turned lower. A shrinking distance from zero shows the current swing in momentum losing strength.

The opening bars are dominated by the warmup and should be ignored. Like any momentum measure it can cross back and forth in a flat market.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: RSI Period
settings.html: Length of the RSI the oscillator is built from.

settings.label: EMA1 Period
settings.html: Length of the first exponential smoothing applied to the RSI.

settings.label: EMA2 Period
settings.html: Length of the second exponential smoothing, applied to the first.

settings.label: Signal Period
settings.html: Length of the simple average used as the signal line that is subtracted.

faq.q: What does a cross above zero mean?
faq.html: The double-smoothed RSI has moved above its own recent average, which means RSI momentum has turned upward.

faq.q: Why are the first bars so extreme?
faq.html: The bar before the first counts as a price of zero, so the first change is a full-size gain and the RSI starts at 100. The smoothing works that start out over the following bars.

faq.q: Is it the same as an RSI?
faq.html: No. It is built from an RSI but shows how far the smoothed RSI sits from its own average, so it centres on zero rather than 50 and its sign shows whether that smoothed RSI is above or below its recent mean.

related.title: Detrended Price Oscillator (DPO)
related.summary: Price minus a simple moving average taken from about half a period earlier, so the trend drops out and shorter cycles stand out.

related.title: DeMarker Oscillator (DEM)
related.summary: A 0 to 1 oscillator comparing how far highs pushed above the previous high with how far lows pushed below the previous low.

related.title: Dynamic Momentum Index (DYMOI)
related.summary: An RSI whose lookback shortens when recent volatility rises and lengthens when it falls, kept between a minimum and a maximum period.

detrended-price-oscillator-dpo.title: Detrended Price Oscillator (DPO)
detrended-price-oscillator-dpo.summary: Price minus a simple moving average taken from about half a period earlier, so the trend drops out and shorter cycles stand out.
detrended-price-oscillator-dpo.descriptionHtml:
The Detrended Price Oscillator (DPO) compares the current price with a simple moving average of the source that is shifted back in time. The average covers N bars (20 by default) and is read as it stood half the period plus one bars ago. Subtracting it from price removes the longer trend and leaves the shorter swings.

Where the average's window reaches back before the first bar, the missing slots are filled with the bar's own value, so the average exists from the first bar. The oscillator itself starts once the shift has bars to read.
detrended-price-oscillator-dpo.howToReadHtml:
Peaks and troughs in the oscillator show the timing of price swings that are shorter than the period. Measuring the bars between successive peaks, or between successive troughs, gives a rough length for the cycle the market has been moving in. Readings above zero mean price is above its displaced average and readings below zero mean it is below.

Because the average is displaced, the oscillator is not meant to signal the current trend. It is a tool for spotting cycle length and overbought or oversold swings relative to recent history.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of the moving average. It also sets the shift, which is half the period plus one bar.

faq.q: Which average is subtracted?
faq.html: The simple average of the last N values as it stood half the period plus one bars ago (11 bars ago at the default 20). Price is compared with that older baseline, not with the current average.

faq.q: Can I use it to follow the trend?
faq.html: Not well. It deliberately removes the trend, so it is better suited to timing swings inside a range or measuring cycle length.

faq.q: Why is the first part empty?
faq.html: The value is price minus the average from half the period plus one bars earlier, so it needs that many bars before it can be drawn.

related.title: Dynamic Momentum Index (DYMOI)
related.summary: An RSI whose lookback shortens when recent volatility rises and lengthens when it falls, kept between a minimum and a maximum period.

related.title: Derivative Oscillator (DOSC)
related.summary: A double-smoothed RSI minus its own moving average, a momentum line that crosses zero as the smoothed RSI moves through its average.

related.title: Efficiency Ratio (ER)
related.summary: The net price move over N bars divided by the sum of every bar-to-bar move, from 0 for pure chop to 1 for a straight trend.

deviation-scaled-moving-average-dsma.title: Deviation-Scaled Moving Average (DSMA)
deviation-scaled-moving-average-dsma.summary: An adaptive average that speeds up when its tracking error is large against its recent size and slows down when it is small.
deviation-scaled-moving-average-dsma.descriptionHtml:
The DSMA is an exponential-style average whose smoothing factor is set fresh on every bar. It first measures the tracking error, the source minus the previous value of the average. That error is passed through a two-pole smoothing filter tuned to half the period, which removes bar-to-bar noise.

The smoothed error is then divided by its own root mean square over the last Period bars, which says how unusual the current error is. That ratio, made positive and multiplied by 5 * Scale Factor / Period, is the share of the distance to the source the average moves this bar, capped at 1. On the first bar the average starts at the source.
deviation-scaled-moving-average-dsma.howToReadHtml:
In a quiet market the error is small compared with its recent size and the line moves slowly, staying smooth. When price breaks away and the error grows well beyond its usual size, the line accelerates to catch up. So the DSMA keeps out of the way in a range and responds quickly to a genuine move.

Read it as a trend line: price above a rising DSMA describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend. A sudden spike can still pull the line sharply, and a higher Scale Factor makes it react to smaller deviations.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing filter and the window of the root mean square. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Scale Factor
settings.html: Scales how far the average moves for a given deviation. Higher reacts faster to the deviation-scaled error.

faq.q: Why does it speed up after a breakout?
faq.html: The tracking error grows much larger than its recent root mean square, so the ratio, and with it the step size, rises.

faq.q: Can the step size exceed 1?
faq.html: No. It is capped at 1, at which point the average jumps all the way to the source on that bar.

related.title: Double Weighted Moving Average (DWMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average applied twice over the same period, smoother than one pass while still leaning on recent bars.

related.title: Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA)
related.summary: Two chained exponential averages combined as twice the first minus the second, which removes much of the lag of a single EMA.

related.title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
related.summary: An exponential average with a warmup correction, so it is accurate from the first bar rather than crawling up from a zero start.

detrended-synthetic-price-dsp.title: Detrended Synthetic Price (DSP)
detrended-synthetic-price-dsp.summary: The gap between a quarter-cycle and a half-cycle exponential average, which strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle swinging around zero.
detrended-synthetic-price-dsp.descriptionHtml:
Detrended Synthetic Price takes the dominant cycle period as its input and builds two exponential averages of the source from it: a fast one over a quarter of the period, at least 2 bars, and a slow one over half the period, at least 3 bars, each rounded to a whole number. The study plots the fast average minus the slow one.

Both averages start at zero. While their starting weight is still decaying, each is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, which removes the pull toward zero on the early bars, and once that weight is negligible the plain averages are used. Subtracting a slower average from a faster one cancels the trend that both share, so what remains oscillates around the zero line at roughly the cycle period.
detrended-synthetic-price-dsp.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means the short-term average is gaining on the longer one, and a falling line the opposite. Crossings of zero mark the points where the two averages meet, which tend to fall near the middle of each swing, and the peaks and troughs of the line mark the cycle's turning points. The size of the swings is in price units, so it grows with price and with volatility.

The study assumes a steady dominant cycle. When the market trends hard or the cycle length changes, the line drifts and its turns become less regular; set the period to the cycle you actually see on the chart.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages are taken from. The typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, by default.

settings.label: Dominant Cycle Period
settings.html: The cycle length in bars. The fast average covers a quarter of it and the slow average half of it.

faq.q: What should the period be set to?
faq.html: The length in bars of the cycle you see on the chart, peak to peak. The default is 40; a shorter period follows faster swings.

faq.q: Why does it start without a warmup gap?
faq.html: Both averages divide out the weight they have not gathered yet, so their early values are not dragged toward zero and the line is usable from the first bars.

faq.q: Is this the same as MACD?
faq.html: It is built the same way, a fast exponential average minus a slow one, but the two lengths are tied to a quarter and a half of one cycle period and there is no signal line.

related.title: EACP: Ehlers Autocorrelation Periodogram
related.summary: The dominant cycle length found by autocorrelating filtered price at every lag and taking the centre of gravity of the resulting power spectrum.

related.title: Center of Gravity (CG)
related.summary: Where the weighted balance point of the last N prices sits relative to the middle of the window, an oscillator that turns at cycle highs and lows.

related.title: Ehlers Even Better Sinewave (EBSW)
related.summary: A detrended, smoothed price cycle normalised by its own recent power into a wave that runs between -1 and +1.

double-weighted-moving-average-dwma.title: Double Weighted Moving Average (DWMA)
double-weighted-moving-average-dwma.summary: A linearly weighted moving average applied twice over the same period, smoother than one pass while still leaning on recent bars.
double-weighted-moving-average-dwma.descriptionHtml:
DWMA runs a linearly weighted moving average over the source, then runs a second one over that result, both with the same period. In each pass the newest bar carries weight equal to the window fill and the oldest weight 1, and the sum is divided by the total weight.

Each pass is kept with running sums. While the window is still filling it averages the values so far, so both passes, and the line, answer from the first bar. Once the window is full, each new bar removes the window sum from the weighted sum and adds the new value at the top weight. A missing source value counts as zero.
double-weighted-moving-average-dwma.howToReadHtml:
Read DWMA as a smooth trend line. The second pass removes most of the jitter one weighted average leaves, at the cost of more lag than a single pass. Price above a rising DWMA points to an uptrend and price below a falling one to a downtrend; turns in the line are cleaner than in a single weighted average.

Because it is smoothed twice, DWMA turns later than the price it follows. Pair it with a faster average if you want an early warning.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window for both weighted passes. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being averaged, usually the close.

faq.q: How is it different from a single weighted average?
faq.html: It applies the weighted average twice. The second pass smooths the first, so the line is steadier but lags more.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the first bar?
faq.html: Each pass averages the values that have arrived so far while its window fills, rather than waiting for a full period.

related.title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
related.summary: An exponential average with a warmup correction, so it is accurate from the first bar rather than crawling up from a zero start.

related.title: Deviation-Scaled Moving Average (DSMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that speeds up when its tracking error is large against its recent size and slows down when it is small.

related.title: Endpoint Moving Average (EPMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average whose weights fall from the newest bar to the oldest, plotted from the first bar.

discrete-wavelet-transform-dwt.title: Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)
discrete-wavelet-transform-dwt.summary: An a trous Haar wavelet decomposition that plots either the smooth trend at the deepest level or the detail removed at one chosen level.
discrete-wavelet-transform-dwt.descriptionHtml:
This study splits the source into a smooth trend and a set of detail layers with a stationary, a trous Haar wavelet. Each level averages the previous approximation with itself a fixed number of bars back, and the lag doubles from level to level: 1 bar at level 1, 2 at level 2, 4 at level 3, up to 128 at level 8. The detail at a level is what that averaging removed, the previous approximation minus the new one.

With Output Component at 0 the plot is the approximation at the deepest level, a smoothed trend whose lookback is about 2 to the power of the level count. With a value from 1 to 8 it is the detail at that level instead, the part of price movement in that band of cycle lengths. A component above the level count is read as the deepest detail available. Where a lagged value does not exist yet, near the start of the chart, the current one is used instead.

Adding all the detail layers to the deepest approximation gives back the source exactly, which is what makes the decomposition useful for separating trend from noise.
discrete-wavelet-transform-dwt.howToReadHtml:
At component 0 read the line as a trend filter on the price chart's own scale: more levels make it smoother and slower. At a detail component the line oscillates around the dotted zero line: above zero the finer approximation one level up (the source itself at level 1) is above the smoother one at that level, below zero it is beneath it. Low levels hold bar to bar noise, higher levels hold slower swings.

The approximation lags price, roughly by half its lookback, and the detail layers only describe movement that has already happened. Use the trend for direction and a detail layer to see the swings of one size on their own.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is decomposed, the close by default.

settings.label: Decomposition Levels
settings.html: How many times the series is halved into a smoother approximation. Each extra level doubles the lookback, so the trend becomes smoother and slower.

settings.label: Output Component
settings.html: Which layer to plot: 0 for the smooth approximation, or 1 to 8 for the detail at that level. A value above the level count shows the deepest detail.

faq.q: Why is it called stationary or a trous?
faq.html: The series is never downsampled. Instead of dropping every other bar, each level spreads its average over a wider gap, so every level has a value on every bar and nothing shifts when a new bar arrives.

faq.q: What does component 1 show?
faq.html: The finest detail: half the difference between each bar and the one before it. It is mostly bar to bar noise.

faq.q: How long is the lookback?
faq.html: About 2 to the power of the level count, so 16 bars at the default of 4 levels and 256 at 8.

related.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
related.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.

related.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
related.summary: Convolves the source with a Morlet wavelet at one scale and plots the size of the response, showing how strongly that cycle length is present.

related.title: Exponential Distribution CDF (EXPDIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through an exponential distribution, so it rises quickly off the lows.

directional-movement-index-dx.title: Directional Movement Index (DX)
directional-movement-index-dx.summary: Plots DX, the gap between +DI and -DI as a share of their sum, beside both directional lines, to show how one-sided the movement is.
directional-movement-index-dx.descriptionHtml:
DX is the raw reading behind ADX. Each bar contributes its true range (the bar's range, stretched to include any gap from the previous close) and its plus and minus directional movement: how far the high rose above the previous high or the low fell below the previous low, counted on one side only and only when that side's move is the larger and positive.

The three are smoothed with Wilder's weight of 1 / period, starting from zero. Early on, a zero start pulls the values down, so while its weight is still visible each smoothed value is divided by 1 - e, where e is (1 - 1 / period) raised to the number of bars seen. That correction lets the lines carry usable values from the first bar.

+DI and -DI are the smoothed plus and minus movement as a percentage of the smoothed true range. DX is 100 * |+DI - -DI| / (+DI + -DI): 0 when the two sides are balanced and 100 when only one side is moving. A dashed line at 25 marks a common threshold for a strong trend.
directional-movement-index-dx.howToReadHtml:
Read DX for how one-sided the movement is and the DI lines for which side it favours. DX above 25 suggests a trending market; DX below it suggests the two sides are roughly balanced. When +DI (green) is above -DI (red), upward movement dominates, and the reverse for downward movement.

DX is not smoothed a second time, so it jumps around more than ADX. It can give an earlier hint that a trend is gaining or losing strength, while ADX, its smoothed form, is steadier. A spike in DX on its own can come from a single large bar.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The Wilder smoothing length for true range and directional movement. Longer gives steadier lines; shorter reacts faster.

faq.q: How is DX different from ADX?
faq.html: ADX is a smoothed average of DX. DX itself is the unsmoothed reading on each bar, so it is faster and noisier.

faq.q: Why does the line have values from the first bar?
faq.html: The smoothing starts from zero and each value is divided by a correction factor that removes the weight of that zero start, so the early values are already on the right scale.

faq.q: What does a DX of 0 mean?
faq.html: The smoothed plus and minus directional movement are equal, so neither buyers nor sellers are pushing the range further than the other.

related.title: Gann High-Low Activator
related.summary: A trailing line built from short averages of the highs and lows that flips sides when price closes beyond it, with BUY and SELL marks on each flip.

related.title: Jurik Directional Movement Index (DMX)
related.summary: The normalised difference between plus and minus directional movement, smoothed by an adaptive average, from -1 to +1.

related.title: HT_TRENDMODE: Hilbert Transform Trend Mode
related.summary: A step line that reads 1 when a Hilbert transform cycle measurement says the market is trending and 0 when it says the market is cycling.

dynamic-momentum-index-dymoi.title: Dynamic Momentum Index (DYMOI)
dynamic-momentum-index-dymoi.summary: An RSI whose lookback shortens when recent volatility rises and lengthens when it falls, kept between a minimum and a maximum period.
dynamic-momentum-index-dymoi.descriptionHtml:
The Dynamic Momentum Index (DYMOI) is an RSI that changes its length bar by bar. It compares a short standard deviation of the source (5 bars by default) with a longer one (10 bars). The base period (14) is divided by that ratio and rounded, so a burst of recent volatility shortens the lookback and a quiet spell lengthens it, and the result is kept between the minimum and maximum periods.

The RSI is then smoothed with weight one over that changing period. Its averages start at zero and are scaled up while that starting bias decays, so it gives a value from the second bar. Both standard deviations use the bars available while their windows fill, and the result is held between 0 and 100.
dynamic-momentum-index-dymoi.howToReadHtml:
Read it like an RSI: 70 and above is the usual overbought zone, 30 and below oversold, and 50 the balance point. The difference is in its speed. When the market turns volatile it shortens its lookback and reacts faster, and when the market calms it lengthens and steadies.

The adaptive length helps it keep up in fast markets, but it also means a single volatile stretch can push it to an extreme quickly. It can stay overbought or oversold for long periods in a strong trend.

settings.label: Base RSI Period
settings.html: The RSI length used when short and long volatility are equal; it is divided by their ratio.

settings.label: Short StdDev Period
settings.html: Length of the short standard deviation that measures recent volatility.

settings.label: Long StdDev Period
settings.html: Length of the long standard deviation used as the baseline; it is kept longer than the short one.

settings.label: Min Period
settings.html: The shortest RSI length the adaptive period may reach.

settings.label: Max Period
settings.html: The longest RSI length the adaptive period may reach.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: When does the lookback get shorter?
faq.html: When the short standard deviation rises relative to the long one, which is what happens when the latest bars are more volatile than the recent norm.

faq.q: How is it different from a fixed RSI?
faq.html: A fixed RSI uses the same length on every bar. This one varies between the minimum and maximum period, so it reacts faster in volatile spells.

faq.q: Why does it read 50 on the first bar?
faq.html: There is no earlier price to compare with, so there is no gain or loss yet and the reading is the neutral 50.

related.title: Efficiency Ratio (ER)
related.summary: The net price move over N bars divided by the sum of every bar-to-bar move, from 0 for pure chop to 1 for a straight trend.

related.title: Detrended Price Oscillator (DPO)
related.summary: Price minus a simple moving average taken from about half a period earlier, so the trend drops out and shorter cycles stand out.

related.title: Elder Ray Index (ERI)
related.summary: Bull Power and Bear Power: how far each bar's high and low reached away from an exponential average of the close.

eacp-ehlers-autocorrelation-periodogram.title: EACP: Ehlers Autocorrelation Periodogram
eacp-ehlers-autocorrelation-periodogram.summary: The dominant cycle length found by autocorrelating filtered price at every lag and taking the centre of gravity of the resulting power spectrum.
eacp-ehlers-autocorrelation-periodogram.descriptionHtml:
The Autocorrelation Periodogram estimates the market's dominant cycle length from a spectrum. Price first goes through a two-pole high-pass filter set by Max Period, which removes the trend, and a super smoother set by Min Period, which removes the fastest noise. The filtered series is then correlated with itself at every lag from 2 to Max Period, using a Pearson correlation over Autocorrelation Length bars, or over the lag itself when that length is zero.

A discrete Fourier transform turns that set of correlations into power at each period from Min Period to Max Period. Each bin is smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against its previous bar and normalised by a running peak that decays slowly unless a new peak arrives; Enhance Resolution cubes the normalised power to sharpen the peaks. The Dominant Cycle is the power-weighted average of the periods holding at least half the peak, smoothed with a weight of 0.2. Normalized Power is the normalised power of the bin at that period.
eacp-ehlers-autocorrelation-periodogram.howToReadHtml:
Read Dominant Cycle as the market's current rhythm in bars, and use it to set the length of oscillators and averages from the data. Normalized Power near 1 means that cycle stands out clearly in the spectrum; a low value means the reading is weak and the market is not cycling cleanly.

The opening stretch of the chart shows a large transient while the smoothing warms up, and the scaling that removes the seed feeds back into the state, so ignore the first few dozen bars. The estimate cannot report cycles outside the range you set.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the spectrum is computed from. The default is the close.

settings.label: Min Period
settings.html: The shortest cycle considered, in bars. It also sets the super smoother that removes faster noise.

settings.label: Max Period
settings.html: The longest cycle considered, in bars. It also sets the high-pass filter that removes the trend.

settings.label: Autocorrelation Length
settings.html: How many bars each correlation is averaged over. Zero uses the lag itself, which weighs long lags more evenly.

settings.label: Enhance Resolution
settings.html: Cube the normalised power so the strongest periods dominate and the dominant cycle reading is sharper.

faq.q: Why is the first part of the line so wild?
faq.html: During warmup the smoothed dominant cycle is scaled to cancel its starting seed, and that scaled value feeds back into the next bar. The result is a large transient on the opening bars that settles once the warmup ends.

faq.q: What does Normalized Power tell me?
faq.html: How strong the reported cycle is relative to the strongest power seen recently. Near 1 the cycle is clear; a low value means the dominant cycle reading is weak.

faq.q: Is it slow to compute?
faq.html: It does more work per bar than most studies: a correlation at every lag and a transform at every period. With the default 8 to 48 bar range that is a few thousand steps per bar.

related.title: Ehlers Even Better Sinewave (EBSW)
related.summary: A detrended, smoothed price cycle normalised by its own recent power into a wave that runs between -1 and +1.

related.title: Detrended Synthetic Price (DSP)
related.summary: The gap between a quarter-cycle and a half-cycle exponential average, which strips out the trend and leaves the dominant cycle swinging around zero.

related.title: HOMOD: Homodyne Discriminator Dominant Cycle
related.summary: The dominant cycle length in bars from a homodyne discriminator on a Hilbert transform of price, held to your period range and smoothed.

ehlers-even-better-sinewave-ebsw.title: Ehlers Even Better Sinewave (EBSW)
ehlers-even-better-sinewave-ebsw.summary: A detrended, smoothed price cycle normalised by its own recent power into a wave that runs between -1 and +1.
ehlers-even-better-sinewave-ebsw.descriptionHtml:
The Even Better Sinewave turns price into a bounded wave. A one-pole high-pass filter removes cycles longer than the High-Pass Filter Length, so the trend drops out. A two-pole super smoother, set by the Super Smoother Filter Length, then removes the fast noise from the two-bar average of that high-pass output.

The last step is an automatic gain control. The study takes the mean of the last three filtered values and divides it by the square root of their mean square, the wave's recent power. That ratio is held to the range -1 to +1. Because the result is divided by its own size, a quiet market and a volatile one both produce a wave of the same height, and the line reads as a position in the cycle rather than as a price distance.
ehlers-even-better-sinewave-ebsw.howToReadHtml:
Values near +1 mean the cycle is at or near a top, values near -1 mean it is at or near a bottom, and the zero line is the midpoint of the swing. In a market that is cycling, the line moves smoothly between the extremes and its turns from +1 and -1 mark swing highs and lows.

In a trend the wave tends to stick near one extreme for many bars. That flat stretch says the market is trending rather than cycling, so it is not a reversal reading.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the wave is computed from. The default is the close.

settings.label: High-Pass Filter Length
settings.html: Cycles longer than this many bars are removed as trend. A larger value keeps slower swings in the wave.

settings.label: Super Smoother Filter Length
settings.html: The smoothing applied after detrending. A larger value gives a smoother wave that turns later.

faq.q: Why does the wave stay pinned at +1 or -1?
faq.html: The gain control divides the wave by its own power, so a steady one-way move keeps the ratio at an extreme. A wave that stays pinned means the market is trending, not cycling.

faq.q: Is the value a price?
faq.html: No. It is a ratio between -1 and +1, so it compares across instruments and timeframes, but it says nothing about how far price moved.

faq.q: How do the two lengths interact?
faq.html: The high-pass length sets the longest cycle kept and the smoother length sets the shortest. Keep the high-pass length well above the smoother length, or the band in between gets too narrow to hold a cycle.

related.title: HOMOD: Homodyne Discriminator Dominant Cycle
related.summary: The dominant cycle length in bars from a homodyne discriminator on a Hilbert transform of price, held to your period range and smoothed.

related.title: EACP: Ehlers Autocorrelation Periodogram
related.summary: The dominant cycle length found by autocorrelating filtered price at every lag and taking the centre of gravity of the resulting power spectrum.

related.title: HT_DCPERIOD: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Period
related.summary: The length in bars of the market's dominant cycle, measured by a Hilbert transform of smoothed price, held to 6 to 50 bars and smoothed.

edcf-ehlers-distance-coefficient-filter.title: EDCF: Ehlers Distance Coefficient Filter
edcf-ehlers-distance-coefficient-filter.summary: A weighted average whose weights are each bar's summed squared distance from the bars before it, so it turns quickly on sharp moves.
edcf-ehlers-distance-coefficient-filter.descriptionHtml:
The Distance Coefficient Filter is a finite window average with weights that adapt to price. For each of the last length prices it adds up the squared differences between that price and each of the length - 1 prices before it. That sum is the bar's weight.

The filter is the sum of weight times price divided by the sum of the weights. In a flat stretch the weights are nearly equal and the filter behaves like a simple average. When price moves sharply, the bars around the move are far from their neighbours, get much larger weights and pull the filter toward them, so it turns quickly and then settles. The weights reach back 2 x (length - 1) bars, so until that much history exists the line shows the price itself, and a perfectly flat window, where every weight is zero, also falls back to the price.
edcf-ehlers-distance-coefficient-filter.howToReadHtml:
Use it like an adaptive moving average. In quiet conditions it is smooth and close to a simple average; when price breaks out it moves to the new level faster than a fixed average would. Price holding above a rising line shows upward pressure, and below a falling line downward pressure.

Its speed comes from weighting outlier bars heavily, so a single sharp spike can tug the line noticeably until it leaves the window. The first bars of the chart show the raw price rather than a filtered value.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of prices averaged and the distance window for each weight. Larger is smoother with more lag.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter runs on. The bar midpoint, high plus low over two, by default.

faq.q: Why does the line equal price at the start of the chart?
faq.html: Each value needs 2 x (length - 1) bars of history to compute every distance. Until then the line shows the price itself rather than a partial average.

faq.q: Why does it react quickly to breakouts?
faq.html: Bars that sit far from their neighbours get large weights, so the prices right after a sharp move dominate the average and the line jumps toward them.

faq.q: What happens in a perfectly flat market?
faq.html: Every distance is zero, so every weight is zero and there is no average to take. The line falls back to the current price.

related.title: Elliptic 2nd Order Filter (ELLIPTIC)
related.summary: A two-pole, two-zero elliptic lowpass on price with a notch just past the cutoff, removing fast noise sharply for a second-order filter.

related.title: Chebyshev Type II Filter (CHEBY2)
related.summary: A second order recursive lowpass with zeros placed among fast swings, rescaled so a flat price passes unchanged; the attenuation setting shapes how it treats the fastest noise.

related.title: Gaussian Filter (GAUSS)
related.summary: A weighted average of recent prices using a bell-shaped Gaussian kernel whose width is set by sigma, answering from the first bar.

elder-s-force-index-efi.title: Elder's Force Index (EFI)
elder-s-force-index-efi.summary: Multiplies each bar's change in close by its volume and smooths the result, sizing the force behind every move in one line.
elder-s-force-index-efi.descriptionHtml:
The Force Index combines the direction and size of a price move with the volume behind it. On each bar the raw force is the change in close from the previous bar times this bar's volume. A large move on heavy volume gives a large raw force; a small move or a quiet bar gives a small one. The first bar compares with itself, so its force is zero.

The raw force is smoothed with an exponential mean of Length bars, weighted 2 / (Length + 1). The mean starts from zero, and while that zero start still matters it is divided by one minus the decayed seed weight, which removes the pull toward zero. The line therefore reads true from the first bars instead of creeping up from nothing. Once the seed weight has decayed below 1e-10 the correction stops.
elder-s-force-index-efi.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, buyers have had the stronger hand over the smoothing period: closes have been rising on volume. Below zero, sellers have. A cross of the zero line marks a change in which side is pushing, and a spike shows a single forceful move.

The values are in price times volume, so they are only comparable with the indicator's own history on the same symbol. A short Length reacts to each bar and suits timing entries; a longer Length shows the broader balance. A falling peak while price makes a new high suggests the move is running on less force.

settings.label: Length
