settings.html: The length of the exponential mean that smooths the raw force. A shorter length follows each bar closely; a longer one shows the broader balance of force.

faq.q: Why is the first value exactly zero?
faq.html: The first bar has no earlier close, so it compares with its own close and the change is zero.

faq.q: Why does the line not start near zero and climb?
faq.html: The exponential mean is corrected for its zero start during the early bars, so the first readings already reflect the raw force rather than a mean dragged toward zero.

faq.q: Can I compare the reading across symbols?
faq.html: Not directly. The value is a price change times volume, so its size depends on the symbol's price level and volume. Compare it with its own history instead.

related.title: Ease of Movement (EOM)
related.summary: Measures how far the midpoint of each bar travelled per unit of volume, averaged over a window, so easy moves on light volume read high.

related.title: Chaikin Money Flow (CMF)
related.summary: The share of recent volume that traded on the buying side, from money flow volume summed over a window and divided by total volume.

related.title: Elastic Volume Weighted Moving Average (EVWMA)
related.summary: A moving average that steps toward price by each bar's share of recent volume, so heavy bars move it far and quiet bars barely move it.

elliptic-2nd-order-filter-elliptic.title: Elliptic 2nd Order Filter (ELLIPTIC)
elliptic-2nd-order-filter-elliptic.summary: A two-pole, two-zero elliptic lowpass on price with a notch just past the cutoff, removing fast noise sharply for a second-order filter.
elliptic-2nd-order-filter-elliptic.descriptionHtml:
The Elliptic 2nd Order Filter is a biquad lowpass: each value combines the current and two previous prices with the filter's own two previous values. Its design allows 1 dB of ripple in the passband and requires 40 dB of rejection in the stopband. In exchange for that small ripple, its two zeros put a notch just above the cutoff frequency, so the line drops fast noise more steeply than a Butterworth filter of the same order.

The cutoff is set by Length. The study pre-warps the cutoff with tan(pi / Length), scales a fixed normalised prototype to it and converts the result into the five coefficients of the difference equation. The input coefficients are normalised so a flat price passes through unchanged.

The first two bars plot the price itself and seed the recursion.
elliptic-2nd-order-filter-elliptic.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed price. Its slope shows the direction of the trend at the scale of Length, and a turn in the line marks a turn in the swing. The notch removes most of the short wiggles just past the cutoff, so the line shows fewer small false turns than a simple average of similar lag.

The price of the sharp cutoff is a little passband ripple: after a sudden move the line can wobble slightly or overshoot before settling. Like any lowpass filter it lags; a larger Length smooths more and turns later.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Swings shorter than this are removed; larger values smooth more and lag more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: What do Rp=1 and Rs=40 in the line title mean?
faq.html: The design allows 1 dB of ripple in the passband and gives at least 40 dB of rejection in the stopband.

faq.q: Why choose an elliptic filter over a Butterworth?
faq.html: For the same order it cuts off more steeply, thanks to the notch past the cutoff. The trade-off is slight ripple and overshoot.

faq.q: Why does the line equal price on the first two bars?
faq.html: The recursion needs two previous outputs. The first two bars use the price as those seeds.

related.title: Gaussian Filter (GAUSS)
related.summary: A weighted average of recent prices using a bell-shaped Gaussian kernel whose width is set by sigma, answering from the first bar.

related.title: EDCF: Ehlers Distance Coefficient Filter
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights are each bar's summed squared distance from the bars before it, so it turns quickly on sharp moves.

related.title: Hann FIR Filter (HANN)
related.summary: A finite-window weighted average of price with raised-cosine weights, smoother and less ringing than a flat moving average of the same length.

exponential-moving-average-ema.title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
exponential-moving-average-ema.summary: An exponential average with a warmup correction, so it is accurate from the first bar rather than crawling up from a zero start.
exponential-moving-average-ema.descriptionHtml:
The EMA moves from its previous value toward the source by a fixed share of the distance each bar. The share is 2 / (Period + 1), so recent bars count most and the weight of older bars fades away geometrically.

The average starts from zero. Over the early bars it is divided by 1 - beta^n, where beta is 1 - 2 / (Period + 1) and n is the number of bars so far. That correction removes the bias of the zero start exactly, so the first value equals the first source value and the line is unbiased from there on. Once beta^n falls below 1e-10 the correction is switched off, because it no longer changes anything.
exponential-moving-average-ema.howToReadHtml:
The EMA is the standard smooth trend line. Price above a rising EMA describes an uptrend, price below a falling one a downtrend, and the slope shows the direction. Two EMAs of different periods crossing each other is one of the most common trend signals.

It reacts faster than a simple average of the same period because it weights recent bars more, but it still lags price and gives false crossings in a sideways market. A longer period filters more noise and turns later.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the share of the distance the average moves each bar. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: How does the warmup differ from a usual EMA?
faq.html: A usual EMA starts from a simple average or the first value. This one starts from zero and divides by 1 - beta^n, which makes every early value an exactly weighted average of the bars seen so far.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the first bar?
faq.html: With the warmup correction, the first value is the first source value, so nothing needs to be left blank.

related.title: Endpoint Moving Average (EPMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average whose weights fall from the newest bar to the oldest, plotted from the first bar.

related.title: Double Weighted Moving Average (DWMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average applied twice over the same period, smoother than one pass while still leaning on recent bars.

related.title: Fractal Adaptive Moving Average (FRAMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose smoothing follows the fractal dimension of price: fast in a clean trend, nearly still in a choppy range.

entropy-entropy.title: Entropy (ENTROPY)
entropy-entropy.summary: Normalised Shannon entropy of the recent window, from 0 when the values crowd into one slice of the range to 1 when they spread evenly.
entropy-entropy.descriptionHtml:
Entropy measures how evenly the values in the lookback window are spread. The study divides a price range into equal slices, called bins, drops each value of the window into its bin, and counts the bins. From those counts it computes the Shannon entropy, the sum of minus p times the natural log of p over every bin that holds a share p of the values. It then divides by the log of the number of bins, the entropy of a perfectly flat spread, so the reading sits between 0 and 1.

The range and the number of bins are not reset for each window. The lowest and highest values are kept from every value seen so far, so the range is the range of the whole chart to date. The count that sets the number of bins also grows with every value scanned, which takes it to its ceiling of 100 bins within the first few dozen bars. The reading is therefore the spread of the recent window measured against the whole range seen so far.

The line needs at least two values before it draws, and reads 0 if every value seen so far is the same.
entropy-entropy.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means the values in the recent window fall into only a few slices of the chart's range: price has been sitting in a narrow band. A higher reading means the window has travelled across more of the range. Because the range keeps growing with the chart, a window of the same width reads lower late in a long chart than early in it.

Use it to compare quiet and active stretches on the same chart rather than as an absolute number. It says nothing about direction.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose spread is measured, such as the close.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many recent bars are dropped into the bins. A longer window covers more of the range and usually reads higher.

faq.q: Why is the reading low even when price moves?
faq.html: The bins divide the whole range seen so far, often into 100 slices. A window of a few bars only reaches a handful of them unless it covers a large part of that range.

faq.q: Why does the same move read differently later in the chart?
faq.html: The range used for the bins grows as new highs and lows arrive, so each bin gets wider and the same window lands in fewer of them.

faq.q: What does a reading of 1 mean?
faq.html: Every bin holds the same share of the window's values, a perfectly even spread. With 100 bins and a short window that cannot happen, so readings stay well below 1.

related.title: Geometric Mean (GEOMEAN)
related.summary: The geometric mean of the last N positive prices: the exponential of their average logarithm, a centre line that compounds rather than adds.

related.title: Cumulative Mean (CUMMEAN)
related.summary: The running average of a price series over every bar from the start of the chart, a slow baseline that steadies as history grows.

related.title: Granger Causality Test (GRANGER)
related.summary: An F-statistic asking whether the previous value of a second series improves the prediction of the first beyond its own previous value.

ease-of-movement-eom.title: Ease of Movement (EOM)
ease-of-movement-eom.summary: Measures how far the midpoint of each bar travelled per unit of volume, averaged over a window, so easy moves on light volume read high.
ease-of-movement-eom.descriptionHtml:
Ease of Movement asks how much volume it took to move price. For each bar it takes the change in the bar's midpoint, the average of high and low, against the previous bar's midpoint. It then builds a box ratio: the bar's volume divided by the Smoothing setting, divided by the bar's range. The raw value is the midpoint change divided by that box ratio, so a wide move on light volume gives a large reading and a small move on heavy volume gives one near zero.

A bar with no range or no volume contributes zero, and the first bar compares with itself, so its change is zero. The raw values are averaged with a simple mean over the Period window. During the first bars the mean covers however many bars have arrived, so the line starts on the first bar instead of waiting for the window to fill.

Note that the two settings do different jobs than their names suggest: Period is the averaging window and Smoothing is the divisor applied to volume.
ease-of-movement-eom.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the midpoint has been rising with relatively little volume behind it, which reads as price moving up easily. Below zero, it has been falling easily. Readings close to zero mean price is moving little for the volume traded, a sign of effort without progress.

The scale depends on the instrument's volume and on the Smoothing divisor, so compare readings on the same chart rather than across symbols. A cross of the zero line is the usual signal, and it lags the price turn by part of the averaging window.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the simple mean of the raw values. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Smoothing
settings.html: The divisor applied to volume in the box ratio. A larger value shrinks the box ratio and scales every reading up by the same factor; the shape of the line does not change.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar instead of after the window fills?
faq.html: The mean divides by the number of bars seen until the window is full, so the first readings are averages of fewer bars rather than blanks.

faq.q: What happens on a bar with zero range?
faq.html: The box ratio cannot be formed, so that bar adds zero to the average rather than a division by zero.

faq.q: Why are the values so small or so large on some symbols?
faq.html: The reading is a price change divided by volume per unit of range, so its size follows the symbol's volume. Change the Smoothing divisor to rescale it, or compare it only with its own history.

related.title: Elastic Volume Weighted Moving Average (EVWMA)
related.summary: A moving average that steps toward price by each bar's share of recent volume, so heavy bars move it far and quiet bars barely move it.

related.title: Elder's Force Index (EFI)
related.summary: Multiplies each bar's change in close by its volume and smooths the result, sizing the force behind every move in one line.

related.title: Intraday Intensity Index (III)
related.summary: Signs each bar's volume by where the close sits in the bar's range, then averages it over a window or adds it into a running total.

endpoint-moving-average-epma.title: Endpoint Moving Average (EPMA)
endpoint-moving-average-epma.summary: A linearly weighted average whose weights fall from the newest bar to the oldest, plotted from the first bar.
endpoint-moving-average-epma.descriptionHtml:
The Endpoint Moving Average weights the bars of its window in a straight line: the newest bar takes a weight equal to the window length, the bar before it one less, and so on down to a weight of one on the oldest bar. The weighted prices are added up and divided by the sum of the weights, so the newest price carries the most of the line.

The window grows with the chart. On the first bar it holds one price, on the second bar two, and it keeps growing until it holds period bars, after which it rolls forward one bar at a time. That is why the line is drawn from the very first bar rather than after a warmup. A missing price adds neither value nor weight, so the remaining bars keep their relative weighting.
endpoint-moving-average-epma.howToReadHtml:
Read the EPMA as a moving average that leans toward the most recent price. It follows price more closely than a simple average of the same length and turns sooner, so a close above a rising EPMA describes a market holding its recent gains, and a close below a falling one the opposite.

Its first few values rest on fewer bars than the period, so they track price almost exactly. Like every average it trails a sharp move, and on a short period it reacts to noise as well as trend.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the full window. A longer period smooths more and reacts later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: How does the EPMA weight its bars?
faq.html: In a straight line: the newest bar gets a weight equal to the window length and each older bar one less, down to one on the oldest bar.

faq.q: Why is there no warmup?
faq.html: The window grows with the chart until it holds the full period, so every bar has a value. Early values use fewer bars and sit very close to price.

faq.q: How is it different from a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple average gives every bar in the window the same weight. The EPMA gives the newest bars more, so it lags less and turns sooner.

related.title: Fractal Adaptive Moving Average (FRAMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose smoothing follows the fractal dimension of price: fast in a clean trend, nearly still in a choppy range.

related.title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
related.summary: An exponential average with a warmup correction, so it is accurate from the first bar rather than crawling up from a zero start.

related.title: Fibonacci Weighted Moving Average (FWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Fibonacci sequence, so the newest bars dominate and the line hugs price closely.

efficiency-ratio-er.title: Efficiency Ratio (ER)
efficiency-ratio-er.summary: The net price move over N bars divided by the sum of every bar-to-bar move, from 0 for pure chop to 1 for a straight trend.
efficiency-ratio-er.descriptionHtml:
The Efficiency Ratio (ER) compares how far price has travelled in a straight line with how far it moved in total. The net move is the absolute difference between the source now and N bars ago (10 by default). The total, or noise, is the sum of the absolute bar-to-bar changes over the same N bars. The ratio of the two lies between 0 and 1.

The noise total is kept running from the first bar, while the net move is zero until N bars exist, so the line starts at zero. A missing source value reads as zero, and the result is held between 0 and 1.
efficiency-ratio-er.howToReadHtml:
A reading near 1 means almost every bar moved in the same direction, so the market is trending efficiently. A reading near 0 means price went back and forth and ended near where it started, which is a choppy, range-bound market. The 0.5 line is a rough divider between the two.

It says nothing about direction, only about how clean the move was. Many traders use it to decide when a trend-following method is likely to work and when to stand aside.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the net move and the noise are measured over. A longer period gives a slower, steadier reading.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is rising?
faq.html: No. It means the move was efficient in either direction. A steady fall also reads close to 1.

faq.q: Why is it zero at the start?
faq.html: The net move is only measured once N bars exist, so until then the ratio is zero.

faq.q: Where is it used besides on its own?
faq.html: The same ratio is the building block of adaptive moving averages, which speed up when it is high and slow down when it is low.

related.title: Elder Ray Index (ERI)
related.summary: Bull Power and Bear Power: how far each bar's high and low reached away from an exponential average of the close.

related.title: Dynamic Momentum Index (DYMOI)
related.summary: An RSI whose lookback shortens when recent volatility rises and lengthens when it falls, kept between a minimum and a maximum period.

related.title: Force Index (FI)
related.summary: The change in close multiplied by volume and smoothed with an exponential average, showing who won each stretch of bars and with how much weight.

elder-ray-index-eri.title: Elder Ray Index (ERI)
elder-ray-index-eri.summary: Bull Power and Bear Power: how far each bar's high and low reached away from an exponential average of the close.
elder-ray-index-eri.descriptionHtml:
The study draws two lines around a centerline, an exponential moving average of the close with weight 2 / (period + 1). Bull Power is the bar's high minus the centerline, the distance buyers managed to push price above the average. Bear Power is the bar's low minus the centerline, the distance sellers pushed it below.

The centerline starts from the first close and, while it is filling, is still divided by the weight it has gathered so far. That correction is meant for an average that starts from zero, so on these bars it lifts the centerline well above price, and both lines open with a large negative excursion before they settle. On the first bar the centerline is the close divided by the weight, seven times the price at the default period of 13, so treat the first stretch of bars, a few times the period, as warmup.

A missing close enters the average as zero.
elder-ray-index-eri.howToReadHtml:
Bull Power above zero means the bar traded above the average, and Bear Power below zero means it traded below it. In a healthy uptrend Bull Power stays positive while Bear Power stays shallow or rises toward zero; in a downtrend the reverse. A common reading is to look for Bear Power climbing while still negative in an uptrend, as sellers tire, or Bull Power falling while still positive in a downtrend.

The values are in price units, so compare them with their own history. Ignore the opening stretch of bars, where the centerline correction distorts both lines.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average used as the centerline. Longer periods give a slower centerline and wider readings.

faq.q: Why do both lines start with a big drop?
faq.html: The centerline starts from the first close and is still divided by the weight it has gathered while it fills, which lifts it above price on the first bars. Both lines are measured from that centerline, so they open strongly negative until the correction fades.

faq.q: Can Bull Power be negative?
faq.html: Yes. If a bar's high stays below the average, as in a firm downtrend, Bull Power is negative. Likewise Bear Power is positive when a bar's low stays above the average.

faq.q: What units are the lines in?
faq.html: Price units: each line is a high or a low minus the average. A move of the same size reads larger on a high-priced instrument.

related.title: Force Index (FI)
related.summary: The change in close multiplied by volume and smoothed with an exponential average, showing who won each stretch of bars and with how much weight.

related.title: Efficiency Ratio (ER)
related.summary: The net price move over N bars divided by the sum of every bar-to-bar move, from 0 for pure chop to 1 for a straight trend.

related.title: Fisher Transform
related.summary: Places price inside its recent range, smooths it, and stretches it with the inverse hyperbolic tangent so turning points read as sharp peaks.

elder-s-thermometer-etherm.title: Elder's Thermometer (ETHERM)
elder-s-thermometer-etherm.summary: Measures how far each bar reaches beyond the previous bar's high or low, with an exponential signal line and a colour for hot and explosive bars.
elder-s-thermometer-etherm.descriptionHtml:
Elder's Thermometer measures how far a bar pushes outside the bar before it. For each bar it takes the distance between this high and the previous high, and between the previous low and this low, and keeps the larger of the two. An inside bar, one whose high is below the previous high and whose low is above the previous low, reads zero. The first bar compares against itself and reads zero as well.

The signal line is an exponential mean of the reading with weight 2 / (EMA Period + 1). It starts from zero and is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, so it gives a usable value from the first bar instead of rising slowly from zero.

The histogram is coloured bar by bar: red when the reading is at least Explosive Threshold times the signal line, orange when it is at or above the signal line, and blue otherwise.
elder-s-thermometer-etherm.howToReadHtml:
Blue bars are bars whose reach beyond the previous bar is below its recent average, as in a quiet market where bars stay mostly inside each other. Orange bars reach at least as far as that average. Red bars reach at least Explosive Threshold times the average: an unusually large push in one bar, which a trader may read as a sign that a quiet stretch has ended or that a move is stretched.

A run of low readings means the bars are overlapping and the range is compressing. The reading is in price units, so its size depends on the instrument and is best compared with the signal line rather than with a fixed number. It shows the size of a push, not its direction, and it says nothing about what the next bar will do.

settings.label: EMA Period
settings.html: Length of the exponential signal line. A longer period gives a steadier baseline that reacts more slowly.

settings.label: Explosive Threshold
settings.html: How many times the signal line a bar must reach to be coloured red. Lower values mark more bars as explosive.

faq.q: Why do some bars read exactly zero?
faq.html: An inside bar, whose high is below the previous high and whose low is above the previous low, reads zero by definition, and so does the first bar.

faq.q: What do the three colours mean?
faq.html: Blue is below the signal line, orange is at or above it, and red is at least the Explosive Threshold times the signal line.

faq.q: Does it show direction?
faq.html: No. It uses the larger of the upward and downward reach, so an explosive bar can be a jump up or a drop down. Read direction from the price bars.

related.title: Exponential Weighted MA Volatility
related.summary: Volatility from an exponentially weighted average of squared log returns, corrected for start-up bias and optionally annualised.

related.title: Chaikin's Volatility (CVI)
related.summary: The percentage change of a smoothed high-low range over a set number of bars, showing whether bar ranges are widening or narrowing.

related.title: Garman-Klass Volatility (GKV)
related.summary: Volatility estimated from each bar's open, high, low and close, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

elastic-volume-weighted-moving-average-e.title: Elastic Volume Weighted Moving Average (EVWMA)
elastic-volume-weighted-moving-average-e.summary: A moving average that steps toward price by each bar's share of recent volume, so heavy bars move it far and quiet bars barely move it.
elastic-volume-weighted-moving-average-e.descriptionHtml:
The Elastic Volume Weighted Moving Average is drawn on the price chart. It keeps a running total of the volume traded over the last Period bars. On each bar the previous average is weighted by the window's volume minus this bar's volume, the current price is weighted by this bar's volume, and the sum is divided by the window's volume.

The effect is that the line moves toward price by the fraction of recent volume that this bar carries. A bar with a large share of the window's volume pulls the average most of the way to price; a bar with little volume leaves it almost where it was. The average starts at the first bar's price, and while the window is still filling it uses the volume of the bars seen so far. A window with no volume at all holds the line flat.
elastic-volume-weighted-moving-average-e.howToReadHtml:
Read it like any moving average: price above a rising line is an uptrend, price below a falling line a downtrend. The difference is in how it reacts. It jumps on high-volume bars and stalls on quiet ones, so a breakout on heavy volume pulls it along quickly while a drift on thin volume hardly moves it.

Because the speed comes from volume rather than from a fixed weight, the line can sit still for a while and then catch up in a few bars. It needs real volume; on a series without volume it simply holds its first value.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars whose volume forms the window. A longer window makes each bar's share smaller, so the line moves more slowly.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

faq.q: How is this different from a volume weighted moving average?
faq.html: A volume weighted moving average recomputes a weighted mean of the window every bar. This line carries its previous value forward and only steps toward price by this bar's share of the window's volume.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes stay flat?
faq.html: A bar with no volume has no share of the window, so it does not move the average. On a series without volume the line holds its starting value.

related.title: Intraday Intensity Index (III)
related.summary: Signs each bar's volume by where the close sits in the bar's range, then averages it over a window or adds it into a running total.

related.title: Ease of Movement (EOM)
related.summary: Measures how far the midpoint of each bar travelled per unit of volume, averaged over a window, so easy moves on light volume read high.

related.title: Klinger Volume Oscillator (KVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of trend-signed volume force, with a signal line and a coloured histogram.

exponential-weighted-ma-volatility.title: Exponential Weighted MA Volatility
exponential-weighted-ma-volatility.summary: Volatility from an exponentially weighted average of squared log returns, corrected for start-up bias and optionally annualised.
exponential-weighted-ma-volatility.descriptionHtml:
Exponential Weighted MA Volatility estimates volatility by giving every past return a weight that decays smoothly, rather than counting the returns in a fixed window equally and then dropping them. For each bar it takes the log return of the source, the natural logarithm of this value over the previous one, and squares it. The first bar has no previous value and reads a return of zero.

The squared returns are smoothed with an average of weight 1 / Length, seeded with the first squared return. Early on that average still carries much of its seed, so the study divides it by the weight it has gathered so far, which offsets most of the start-up bias and makes the reading usable from the first bars. The square root of the result is the volatility per bar, and with Annualize Volatility on it is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.
exponential-weighted-ma-volatility.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means returns are getting larger, a falling line means the market is calming down. Because old returns fade gradually rather than dropping out of a window all at once, the line has none of the sudden steps a rolling standard deviation shows when a large return leaves its window.

Compare the line with its own history rather than with a fixed number. A spike after a shock decays at a pace set by Length. Set Annual Periods to the number of bars in a year on your chart if you want a true annual figure; the default of 252 suits daily bars.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose returns are measured, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Sets the smoothing weight 1 / Length. A longer length remembers returns for more bars and gives a steadier line.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, the per-bar volatility is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: Bars in a year used for annualising: 252 for daily bars, 52 for weekly bars.

faq.q: How is this different from a rolling standard deviation?
faq.html: Every past return keeps a weight that shrinks over time instead of counting fully and then vanishing, so the line reacts quickly to new moves and has no steps when an old return leaves the window.

faq.q: Why is the line usable from the first bars?
faq.html: The smoothed average is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, which removes the bias of the start and gives a fair reading early on.

faq.q: Is the average return subtracted?
faq.html: No. The squared returns are averaged about zero, which is the usual choice for short bars where the average return is tiny.

related.title: Garman-Klass Volatility (GKV)
related.summary: Volatility estimated from each bar's open, high, low and close, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

related.title: Elder's Thermometer (ETHERM)
related.summary: Measures how far each bar reaches beyond the previous bar's high or low, with an exponential signal line and a colour for hot and explosive bars.

related.title: High-Low Volatility (HLV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log range of each bar, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

exponential-transformation-exp.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
exponential-transformation-exp.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.
exponential-transformation-exp.descriptionHtml:
This study raises e, about 2.718, to the power of the source on every bar: y = e^x. It has no lookback and no state, so each bar's value depends only on that bar's source.

The transform turns a series measured on an additive scale into one on a multiplicative scale. It undoes a natural logarithm, so a log price becomes a price again and a log return becomes a growth factor, where 0 maps to 1, 0.1 to about 1.105 and -0.1 to about 0.905.

The result grows very fast. Above a source value of about 709 it is too large to represent, and those bars are left empty rather than drawn as an infinite value. On a price above about 709 the line is empty, and on a lower price the values it does draw are astronomically large, so the transform is only useful on a source that is already close to zero.
exponential-transformation-exp.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the source re-expressed as a multiplier: a value of 1 means the source was 0, above 1 means it was positive and below 1 means it was negative, never reaching zero. Equal steps in the source become equal percentage steps in the output, so large positive readings are stretched and negative ones compressed.

Applied to an ordinary price the study shows nothing useful: e to the power of a price above about 709 overflows and leaves the bar empty, and a lower price gives an astronomically large number. It is meant for a source scaled near zero, such as a log return, a z-score or another oscillator centred on zero.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series that is exponentiated. It should already be close to zero, since e to the power of any value above about 709 cannot be represented.

faq.q: Why is my pane empty on a price chart?
faq.html: e to the power of a price above about 709 is too large to represent, so every such bar is left empty. Use a source that is already scaled near zero.

faq.q: Can the output be negative?
faq.html: No. e to any power is positive. A negative source gives a value between 0 and 1.

faq.q: How does it relate to the logarithm?
faq.html: It is the inverse of the natural logarithm: applying it to the log of a series gives the series back.

related.title: Exponential Distribution CDF (EXPDIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through an exponential distribution, so it rises quickly off the lows.

related.title: Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)
related.summary: An a trous Haar wavelet decomposition that plots either the smooth trend at the deepest level or the detail removed at one chosen level.

related.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
related.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.

exponential-distribution-cdf-expdist.title: Exponential Distribution CDF (EXPDIST)
exponential-distribution-cdf-expdist.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through an exponential distribution, so it rises quickly off the lows.
exponential-distribution-cdf-expdist.descriptionHtml:
This study maps the position of price in its recent range onto the cumulative exponential distribution. First the source is placed in its own recent range: the lowest value of the last Lookback Period bars maps to 0, the highest to 1, and the current value falls somewhere between. When every value in the window is the same the position is taken as 0.5. Near the start of the chart the window is simply the bars that exist, so the line begins on the first bar.

That position x is passed through 1 - e^(-lambda x). At the bottom of the range the result is 0, and it climbs toward 1 as price moves up, quickly at first and then more slowly. A position at or below zero reads as exactly 0. Because x never exceeds 1, the top of the range reads 1 - e^(-lambda), which is about 0.95 at the default lambda of 3.

Lambda is the rate of the distribution. A larger value makes the curve rise faster, so even a modest lift off the lows reads close to 1.
exponential-distribution-cdf-expdist.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a range oscillator that is sensitive near the bottom and compressed near the top. A value near 0 means price is at the low of its window; with the default lambda, half the range is about 0.78 and the top of the range about 0.95, near the upper level. The levels at 0.95, 0.5 and 0.05 mark the upper zone, the midline and the lower zone.

Because of the curve's shape, the line is most useful for spotting price lifting off its lows; moves near the top barely change it. With a high lambda it saturates near 1 for most of the range, and with a lambda below 1 it is close to a straight line in the range position but tops out well below 1, about 0.39 at a lambda of 0.5.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars, the current one included, set the highest and lowest values the source is scaled against. A longer window changes the reading more slowly.

settings.label: Lambda
settings.html: The rate of the exponential curve. Higher values make the line rise toward 1 faster as price leaves the bottom of its range.

faq.q: Why does the line never quite reach 1?
faq.html: The range position is at most 1, so the highest possible value is 1 - e^(-lambda). At the default lambda of 3 that is about 0.95.

faq.q: What happens in a flat market?
faq.html: If every value in the window is the same, the position is taken as 0.5 and the reading is 1 - e^(-lambda / 2), about 0.78 with the defaults.

exptrans.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
exptrans.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.
exptrans.descriptionHtml:
This study raises e, about 2.718, to the power of the source on every bar: y = e^x. It has no lookback and no state, so each bar's value depends only on that bar's source.

The transform turns a series measured on an additive scale into one on a multiplicative scale. It undoes a natural logarithm, so a log price becomes a price again and a log return becomes a growth factor, where 0 maps to 1, 0.1 to about 1.105 and -0.1 to about 0.905.

The result grows very fast. Above a source value of about 709 it is too large to represent, and those bars are left empty rather than drawn as an infinite value. On a price above about 709 the line is empty, and on a lower price the values it does draw are astronomically large, so the transform is only useful on a source that is already close to zero.
exptrans.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the source re-expressed as a multiplier: a value of 1 means the source was 0, above 1 means it was positive and below 1 means it was negative, never reaching zero. Equal steps in the source become equal percentage steps in the output, so large positive readings are stretched and negative ones compressed.

Applied to an ordinary price the study shows nothing useful: e to the power of a price above about 709 overflows and leaves the bar empty, and a lower price gives an astronomically large number. It is meant for a source scaled near zero, such as a log return, a z-score or another oscillator centred on zero.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series that is exponentiated. It should already be close to zero, since e to the power of any value above about 709 cannot be represented.

faq.q: Why is my pane empty on a price chart?
faq.html: e to the power of a price above about 709 is too large to represent, so every such bar is left empty. Use a source that is already scaled near zero.

faq.q: Can the output be negative?
faq.html: No. e to any power is positive. A negative source gives a value between 0 and 1.

faq.q: How does it relate to the logarithm?
faq.html: It is the inverse of the natural logarithm: applying it to the log of a series gives the series back.

related.title: F-Distribution CDF (FDIST)

related.title: Exponential Distribution CDF (EXPDIST)

fractal-chaos-bands-fcb.title: Fractal Chaos Bands (FCB)
fractal-chaos-bands-fcb.summary: Bands at the highest recent three-bar fractal high and the lowest recent fractal low, with optional marks on the fractal bars.
fractal-chaos-bands-fcb.descriptionHtml:
Fractal Chaos Bands build a channel from swing points rather than from every bar. A fractal high is a bar whose high is above the highs of the bars on either side, and a fractal low is a bar whose low is below both neighbours. A fractal is known one bar after it forms.

The study carries the latest fractal high and the latest fractal low forward, starting from the first bar's own high and low. The upper band is the highest of those carried fractal highs over the last period bars, and the lower band is the lowest of the carried fractal lows, using every bar so far while the window fills.

With Show Fractal Points switched on, each fractal is marked on the bar that printed it, one bar back from the bar that confirmed it.
fractal-chaos-bands-fcb.howToReadHtml:
The bands mark the most extreme swing points of the period, so they step rather than slide. A close above the upper band breaks the highest recent swing high, and a close below the lower band breaks the lowest recent swing low. While price stays inside, the market is trading within its recent swing structure.

Flat bands for a long stretch mean no new swing has exceeded the old extremes. The fractal marks show where each swing was set; some traders place a stop just beyond the latest one.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars the highest fractal high and lowest fractal low are taken over. Longer periods hold old swings longer.

settings.label: Show Fractal Points
settings.html: Mark each fractal high and fractal low on the bar that printed it.

faq.q: Why are the fractal marks one bar behind?
faq.html: A three-bar fractal needs the bar after the middle bar to confirm it. The test runs on that confirming bar, and the mark is drawn one bar back, on the middle bar, at its high or low.

faq.q: Why do the bands stay flat?
faq.html: They follow the most extreme swing in the window. Until a new fractal exceeds it or it leaves the window, the band does not move.

faq.q: How is this different from a plain high and low channel?
faq.html: Only swing points count. A single tall bar that is not higher than its neighbours on both sides does not move the band.

related.title: Jurik Volatility Bands (JBANDS)
related.summary: Upper and lower bands that snap to a bar's extreme when price pushes through and otherwise fall back at a rate set by relative volatility.

related.title: Decay Min-Max Channel (DECAYCHANNEL)
related.summary: A high and low channel whose edges are pulled toward the middle harder the longer they go without a new extreme.

related.title: Keltner Channel (KCHANNEL)
related.summary: An exponential average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below, drawn from the first bar.

f-distribution-cdf-fdist.title: F-Distribution CDF (FDIST)
f-distribution-cdf-fdist.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative F distribution, a bounded 0 to 1 oscillator.
f-distribution-cdf-fdist.descriptionHtml:
This study reads the position of price in its recent range through the cumulative distribution of an F variable. First the source is placed in its own recent range: the lowest value of the last Lookback Period bars maps to 0, the highest to 1, and the current value falls somewhere between. When every value in the window is the same the position is taken as 0.5. Near the start of the chart the window is simply the bars that exist, so the line begins on the first bar.

That position is used as the F value x. Its cumulative probability with d1 and d2 degrees of freedom equals the regularized incomplete beta function I_t(d1 / 2, d2 / 2) at t = d1 x / (d1 x + d2). The study evaluates it with a continued fraction (Lentz's method), using log-gamma values from the Lanczos approximation, and switches to the mirrored form past the mean so the fraction converges quickly.

Since x only runs from 0 to 1, the line uses the lower part of the F distribution: at the top of the range, with the default 5 and 5 degrees of freedom, the reading is 0.5. The two degrees of freedom change how quickly the line rises off the bottom of the range and how high it can go.
f-distribution-cdf-fdist.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a range oscillator that starts at 0 when price is at the bottom of its window and rises as price climbs. With d1 and d2 equal the top of the range reads exactly 0.5, the midline, so with the defaults the line never reaches the upper level at 0.95. A d2 larger than d1 lifts that ceiling a little (about 0.53 at d1 5 and d2 8, about 0.68 at d1 1 and d2 100) and a d1 larger than d2 lowers it. The lower level at 0.05 marks price pressing on the bottom of its window.

The reading is relative to the window only and its scale depends on the two settings, so compare values within one setup. It is a reshaped range position, not a statistical test of anything on the chart.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars, the current one included, set the highest and lowest values the source is scaled against. A longer window changes the reading more slowly.

settings.label: d1 (numerator df)
settings.html: The numerator degrees of freedom. Raising it makes the line climb more slowly from the bottom of the range and lowers the reading at the top.

settings.label: d2 (denominator df)
settings.html: The denominator degrees of freedom. Raising it lets the line climb a little higher, so the top of the range reads above 0.5.

faq.q: Why does the line stop at 0.5 with the default settings?
faq.html: The range position is at most 1. For an F distribution with equal degrees of freedom the probability of a value at or below 1 is exactly one half, so the top of the range reads 0.5.

faq.q: Can it reach the upper level at 0.95?
faq.html: No. The highest reading is the F probability at 1. With both degrees of freedom at 1 or more it stays between about 0.32 and 0.68: raising d2 relative to d1 moves it up, raising d1 moves it down. Even the smallest allowed d1 of 0.1 with a large d2 only reaches about 0.88.

faq.q: Is it a test of whether two variances differ?
faq.html: No. The F distribution only supplies the shape of the curve. The input is where price sits in its own range, not a ratio of variances.

related.title: FFT Dominant Cycle (Radix-2 FFT)
related.summary: Estimates the length of the strongest price cycle, in bars, from a Hann-windowed fast Fourier transform of the last N bars.

related.title: Exponential Transformation (EXP)
related.summary: Applies y = e^x to the source bar by bar, a numeric transform meant for series already scaled near zero, such as a log return.

related.title: Gamma Distribution CDF (GAMMADIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range through the gamma cumulative distribution, giving an oscillator from 0 to 1.

fft-dominant-cycle-radix-2-fft.title: FFT Dominant Cycle (Radix-2 FFT)
fft-dominant-cycle-radix-2-fft.summary: Estimates the length of the strongest price cycle, in bars, from a Hann-windowed fast Fourier transform of the last N bars.
fft-dominant-cycle-radix-2-fft.descriptionHtml:
This study looks for the cycle that carries the most energy in recent price. On each bar it takes the last N bars of the source, oldest to newest, tapers them with a Hann window, and runs a radix-2 fast Fourier transform over them. Each frequency bin k of the result corresponds to a cycle of N / k bars.

The study searches only the bins whose periods lie between the minimum and maximum period, and picks the one with the largest power. A parabola through that bin and its two neighbours refines the peak between bins, and the dominant period is N divided by the refined bin, clamped into the period band. The maximum period is capped at half the window, the longest cycle the transform can resolve. The line starts once N bars of history exist.
fft-dominant-cycle-radix-2-fft.howToReadHtml:
Read the value as the length, in bars, of the cycle that currently dominates price. A low reading means short, choppy swings dominate, and a high reading means price is moving in longer waves. The reference lines at 8 and 20 bars split the pane into fast, middle and slow cycles.

The estimate is often used to tune other studies, for example setting an oscillator's length to half the dominant cycle. It works best when price is actually cycling. In a strong trend the power piles up at the longest periods and the reading sits at the top of the band, which says more about the trend than about a cycle.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose dominant cycle is measured.

settings.label: Window Size
settings.html: How many bars enter the transform: 32, 64 or 128. Any other value is read as 64. The longest period the transform can resolve is half the window.

settings.label: Min Period
settings.html: The shortest cycle, in bars, that the search considers. Raising it ignores faster swings.

settings.label: Max Period
settings.html: The longest cycle, in bars, that the search considers. It is capped at half the window size.

faq.q: Why is the reading stuck at the maximum period?
faq.html: The strongest power is at the slowest cycle in the band, which usually means price is trending rather than cycling. Widen the window or treat the reading as a sign of trend.

faq.q: Why is the value not a whole number?
faq.html: The peak bin is refined with a parabola through its neighbours, which places the peak between bins and gives a fractional period.

faq.q: When does the line start?
faq.html: It needs one full window of history, so it starts once N bars exist: after 64 bars with the default window.

related.title: Gamma Distribution CDF (GAMMADIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range through the gamma cumulative distribution, giving an oscillator from 0 to 1.

related.title: F-Distribution CDF (FDIST)
related.summary: Scales the source to 0 to 1 within its recent range and reads that position through the cumulative F distribution, a bounded 0 to 1 oscillator.

related.title: Highest Value (HIGHEST)
related.summary: Traces the highest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the highest value seen so far.

force-index-fi.title: Force Index (FI)
force-index-fi.summary: The change in close multiplied by volume and smoothed with an exponential average, showing who won each stretch of bars and with how much weight.
force-index-fi.descriptionHtml:
The Force Index combines three things a bar says about the market: the direction of the move, its size, and the volume behind it. On each bar the raw force is the close minus the previous close, multiplied by the bar's volume. On the first bar there is no previous close, and the raw force is zero.

The raw force is then smoothed with an exponential average of weight 2 / (period + 1), seeded with the first raw value. While the average is filling, it is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, which lifts the early values. A missing close or a missing volume reads as zero.
force-index-fi.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, buyers have had the upper hand over the period, and below zero sellers have. The height of the line reflects both how far price moved and how much volume traded, so a large reading is a move with conviction behind it. Crossings of zero mark a change in who is in control, and a new price high made with a lower Force Index peak shows the move is running on less weight.

The scale depends on the instrument's price and volume, so compare the line with its own history only. On a series with no volume the line stays at zero.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average applied to the raw force. Short periods follow each push; long periods show the underlying balance.

faq.q: Why is the line zero on a symbol with no volume?
faq.html: The raw force is the price change times volume, and missing volume reads as zero, so every raw value is zero.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: The first bar has no previous close, so its raw force is zero and the average is seeded with that zero. From the second bar the average is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, which scales the early values up toward the raw force until the correction fades.

faq.q: What period should I use?
faq.html: The default is 13. A period of 2 follows the force of each push closely and turns often, while a longer one shows which side has dominated over a longer stretch.

related.title: Fisher Transform
related.summary: Places price inside its recent range, smooths it, and stretches it with the inverse hyperbolic tangent so turning points read as sharp peaks.

related.title: Elder Ray Index (ERI)
related.summary: Bull Power and Bear Power: how far each bar's high and low reached away from an exponential average of the close.

related.title: Fisher04 - Ehlers 2004 Cybernetic Analysis
related.summary: A Fisher transform of the bar midpoint within its recent range, with a signal line that is simply the previous bar's value.

fisher-transform.title: Fisher Transform
fisher-transform.summary: Places price inside its recent range, smooths it, and stretches it with the inverse hyperbolic tangent so turning points read as sharp peaks.
fisher-transform.descriptionHtml:
The Fisher Transform turns the position of price within its recent range into a line with sharp, well-defined turns. On each bar it takes the source (the bar midpoint by default) and finds where it sits between the highest and lowest values of the source over the period, scaled to run from -1 at the low to +1 at the high. While the window is still filling, or when the range is flat, the position reads as the middle, zero.

That position is smoothed with an exponential weight of 0.33 and held just inside -0.999 to 0.999. The study then applies the inverse hyperbolic tangent, half the natural logarithm of (1 + value) / (1 - value), which stretches values near the edges far out. The Signal line is the same exponential smoothing, weight 0.33, applied to the Fisher line.
fisher-transform.howToReadHtml:
Readings beyond +2 and -2 mark price pressing against the top or bottom of its recent range for several bars, and the stretch of the transform makes those extremes stand out. A turn of the Fisher line from an extreme, and especially its cross of the Signal line, is the usual cue that the move is losing steam.

In a strong trend the line can stay pinned near an extreme for a long time, so a high reading alone is not a reason to fade the move. Shorter periods give more frequent and sharper turns.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars the highest and lowest values are taken over. A shorter window makes the line swing to its extremes more often.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series placed inside its range. The default is the bar midpoint, the average of high and low.

faq.q: Why is the value clamped at 0.999?
faq.html: The inverse hyperbolic tangent grows without bound as its input approaches 1. Holding the smoothed value just inside the bounds keeps the line finite.

faq.q: What is the Signal line?
faq.html: An exponential average of the Fisher line with the same 0.33 weight. It lags the Fisher line slightly, so their crossings mark turns.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: Until the period has passed, the range is not yet known, so the position reads as the middle and the smoothed value builds up from zero.

related.title: Fisher04 - Ehlers 2004 Cybernetic Analysis
related.summary: A Fisher transform of the bar midpoint within its recent range, with a signal line that is simply the previous bar's value.

related.title: Force Index (FI)
related.summary: The change in close multiplied by volume and smoothed with an exponential average, showing who won each stretch of bars and with how much weight.

related.title: Williams Gator Oscillator
related.summary: Two histograms that show how far apart the three displaced alligator lines have moved: wide bars for a trending market, bars near zero for a quiet one.

fisher04-ehlers-2004-cybernetic-analysis.title: Fisher04 - Ehlers 2004 Cybernetic Analysis
fisher04-ehlers-2004-cybernetic-analysis.summary: A Fisher transform of the bar midpoint within its recent range, with a signal line that is simply the previous bar's value.
fisher04-ehlers-2004-cybernetic-analysis.descriptionHtml:
This variant of the Fisher transform reads the bar midpoint, the average of high and low, and finds where it sits between the highest and lowest midpoint over the length. That position is centred on zero (it runs from -0.5 at the low to +0.5 at the high) and half of the previous bar's value is added to it, which smooths it. While the window is filling, or when it is flat, the value resets to zero. It is then held inside -0.9999 to 0.9999.

The Fisher line is a quarter of the natural logarithm of (1 + value) / (1 - value), plus half of its own previous value, so the transform itself is also smoothed. The Signal line is the Fisher line's value on the previous bar, so the two cross whenever the Fisher line changes direction.
fisher04-ehlers-2004-cybernetic-analysis.howToReadHtml:
The Fisher04 line swings between sharp peaks and troughs. A turn of the line, which is the same thing as a cross of the Signal line, is the basic event: crossing down from a high reading suggests the upswing is ending, and crossing up from a low reading the reverse. Readings far from zero show price pressed hard against the edge of its recent range.

Because the signal is only a one-bar delay, crossings are frequent in choppy markets. Crossings that happen well away from zero mark turns from a stretched reading; crossings near zero are mostly noise.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars the highest and lowest midpoint are taken over. A shorter length gives faster, more frequent turns.

faq.q: Why is the signal line the previous bar's value?
faq.html: That is how this version defines it. A cross of the two lines is then exactly a change of direction of the Fisher line.

faq.q: Can I change the price it reads?
faq.html: No. It always reads the bar midpoint, the average of high and low, as the calculation is defined.

faq.q: How does it differ from the other Fisher Transform in the library?
faq.html: This one centres the position on zero and smooths with half of the previous value, applies a quarter-log transform with its own smoothing, and uses a one-bar delay as the signal. The other smooths with a 0.33 weight and uses an exponential average as its signal.

related.title: Williams Gator Oscillator
related.summary: Two histograms that show how far apart the three displaced alligator lines have moved: wide bars for a trending market, bars near zero for a quiet one.

related.title: Fisher Transform
related.summary: Places price inside its recent range, smooths it, and stretches it with the inverse hyperbolic tangent so turning points read as sharp peaks.

related.title: Intraday Momentum Index (IMI)
related.summary: An oscillator from 0 to 100 built from candle bodies: the share of the period's body size that came from bars closing above their open.

williams-fractals.title: Williams Fractals
williams-fractals.summary: Marks every five-bar swing high and swing low, the turning points where price stalled and reversed for at least two bars on each side.
williams-fractals.descriptionHtml:
Williams Fractals picks out the simplest kind of swing point on a chart. An up fractal is a bar whose high is higher than the highs of the two bars before it and the two bars after it. A down fractal is the mirror image: a bar whose low is lower than the lows of the two bars on either side.

Because the test needs two bars after the middle bar, a fractal is only known two bars after it forms. The study runs the test on the bar that confirms it and draws the mark two bars back, on the bar it describes, so nothing on the chart changes once it has been drawn. Up fractals are drawn in red at the high, where a swing topped out, and down fractals in green at the low, where a swing bottomed.
williams-fractals.howToReadHtml:
Read the marks as a map of where the market has recently turned. A cluster of up fractals at a similar price is a ceiling that sellers have defended more than once, and a cluster of down fractals is a floor. Many traders place a stop just beyond the most recent fractal against their position, and treat a close beyond the latest up fractal as a break of the swing structure.

Remember the two-bar delay. The newest two bars can never carry a mark yet, so a fractal is information about the recent past rather than a signal on the bar you are looking at.

settings.label: Show Up Fractals
settings.html: Draw the swing highs, the bars whose high stands above the two bars on each side.

settings.label: Show Down Fractals
settings.html: Draw the swing lows, the bars whose low sits below the two bars on each side.

faq.q: Why does the newest fractal appear two bars late?
faq.html: A fractal needs two bars after the middle bar to confirm it. The study waits for those two bars and then draws the mark back on the bar that formed the swing, so a mark never appears and then disappears.

faq.q: Can a bar be an up fractal and a down fractal at once?
faq.html: Yes. A wide bar whose high is above and whose low is below the two bars on each side carries both marks, which usually means the market swung hard in both directions around it.

faq.q: What timeframe does it work on?
faq.html: Any. The test counts bars, not time, so it reads the same way on an hourly chart and a daily one. On a faster chart there are more fractals and each one matters less.

related.title: Pivot Points (Classic)
related.summary: The classic floor pivot: the previous day, week or month's high, low and close turned into a central pivot with three supports and three resistances.

related.title: Pivot Points (Camarilla)
related.summary: Four supports and four resistances placed tightly around the previous period's close, each a fixed fraction of that period's range away from it.

related.title: Pivot Points (DeMark)
related.summary: A pivot, one resistance and one support from the previous period, weighted by whether that period closed above, below or at its open.

fractal-adaptive-moving-average-frama.title: Fractal Adaptive Moving Average (FRAMA)
fractal-adaptive-moving-average-frama.summary: An adaptive average whose smoothing follows the fractal dimension of price: fast in a clean trend, nearly still in a choppy range.
fractal-adaptive-moving-average-frama.descriptionHtml:
The FRAMA is an exponential-style average whose smoothing factor comes from the shape of recent price. The window is Period bars, rounded up to an even number, and split into a newer half and an older half. The study takes the price range of each half and of the whole window, each divided by its length.

From those three ranges it estimates the fractal dimension: (log(N1 + N2) - log(N3)) / log(2). A clean trend has a dimension near 1, because the two half ranges add up to the full range; a choppy market has a dimension near 2. The smoothing factor is exp(-4.6 * (dimension - 1)), held between 0.01 and 1, and the average moves that share of the way toward the source each bar. The line is drawn once a full window exists.
fractal-adaptive-moving-average-frama.howToReadHtml:
In a trend the dimension is low, the smoothing factor is high, and the FRAMA follows price closely. In a sideways, overlapping market the dimension is high and the factor falls toward 0.01, so the line goes almost flat. A flat FRAMA therefore marks congestion, and a line that starts to move again marks price beginning to trend.

Read price against the line as with any trend average. Because the factor can jump from small to large in a few bars, the line can move abruptly at a breakout; that is the design, not an error. A flat window, where the range is zero, uses a factor of 1 and the line equals the source.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window used to measure the fractal dimension, rounded up to an even number. Longer is steadier but slower to adapt.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged and measured, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is an odd period rounded up?
faq.html: The window is split into two equal halves, so it must have an even length. An odd period gains one bar.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes jump?
faq.html: When price changes from choppy to trending the smoothing factor can rise sharply within a few bars, so the line catches up with price quickly.

faq.q: Why are the first bars blank?
faq.html: The fractal dimension needs a full window of prices, so the line waits until that many bars exist.

related.title: Fibonacci Weighted Moving Average (FWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Fibonacci sequence, so the newest bars dominate and the line hugs price closely.

related.title: Endpoint Moving Average (EPMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average whose weights fall from the newest bar to the oldest, plotted from the first bar.

related.title: Generalized Double Exponential Moving Average (GDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average with an adjustable lag correction, from a plain EMA at v = 0 to a line that removes more lag than it adds above v = 1.

fibonacci-weighted-moving-average-fwma.title: Fibonacci Weighted Moving Average (FWMA)
fibonacci-weighted-moving-average-fwma.summary: A moving average weighted by the Fibonacci sequence, so the newest bars dominate and the line hugs price closely.
fibonacci-weighted-moving-average-fwma.descriptionHtml:
The Fibonacci Weighted Moving Average gives each bar of its window a Fibonacci number as its weight. The oldest bar takes 1, the next 1, then 2, 3, 5, 8 and on, so the newest bar carries the largest number. The weighted prices are summed and divided by the sum of the weights.

Fibonacci numbers grow much faster than the straight-line weights of an ordinary weighted average, so the last few bars account for most of the result and the line tracks price closely. The window grows with the chart until it holds period bars, with the weights rebuilt for each length, so the line is drawn from the first bar. A missing price is skipped along with its weight.
fibonacci-weighted-moving-average-fwma.howToReadHtml:
Read the FWMA as a fast trend line. Because the newest bars dominate, it turns almost as soon as price does, and the distance between price and the line is usually small. A rising line with price above it describes an advancing market; a falling line with price below it a declining one.

The same speed is its limit: it smooths less than most averages of the same length, so in a choppy market it whips back and forth with price. A longer period adds bars to the window, but because their weights are small the extra smoothing is modest.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of Fibonacci weights in the window, one per bar. More weights add older bars with very small weights.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the FWMA react so quickly?
faq.html: Fibonacci weights grow faster than linear ones, so the newest few bars carry most of the weight and older bars contribute very little.

faq.q: Does a longer period make it much smoother?
faq.html: Less than you might expect. Each extra bar joins the oldest end of the window with a weight of 1, which is tiny next to the large weights on recent bars.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The window grows with the chart until it holds the full period, rebuilding the Fibonacci weights for each length, so every bar has a value.

related.title: Generalized Double Exponential Moving Average (GDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average with an adjustable lag correction, from a plain EMA at v = 0 to a line that removes more lag than it adds above v = 1.

related.title: Fractal Adaptive Moving Average (FRAMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose smoothing follows the fractal dimension of price: fast in a clean trend, nearly still in a choppy range.

related.title: Gaussian-Weighted Moving Average (GWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a bell curve centred on the middle of the window, tapering at both ends.

gamma-distribution-cdf-gammadist.title: Gamma Distribution CDF (GAMMADIST)
gamma-distribution-cdf-gammadist.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range through the gamma cumulative distribution, giving an oscillator from 0 to 1.
gamma-distribution-cdf-gammadist.descriptionHtml:
This study turns the position of price inside its recent range into a probability. First it min-max normalises the source over the lookback window: 0 at the lowest value of the window, 1 at the highest, and 0.5 when the window is flat. That position is multiplied by the rate beta, and the result is passed to the cumulative distribution function of a gamma distribution with shape alpha.

The gamma CDF is the regularized lower incomplete gamma function. Below alpha + 1 it is summed as a series, and above it the complement is found with a continued fraction, both to a tolerance of 1e-10, with the gamma function itself from the Lanczos approximation. While fewer than period bars exist, the range is taken over every bar so far, so the line answers from the first bar.
gamma-distribution-cdf-gammadist.howToReadHtml:
Values near 1 mean price is near the top of its recent range and values near 0 mean it is near the bottom. Unlike a plain range position, the gamma curve bends the scale: with the default shape of 2 and rate of 3, the bottom of the range maps to 0, the middle to about 0.44, and the top to about 0.80. Raising the rate pushes more of the range towards 1, and raising the shape pushes it towards 0.

The reference lines at 0.05, 0.5 and 0.95 mark the tails and the middle of the distribution. A reading above 0.95 needs both price near the top of the range and a rate large enough for the curve to reach that far, so check the settings before reading it as an extreme.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose position inside its own high-low range is measured.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars set the high and low used to normalise the source. A longer window gives a wider range and a slower oscillator.

settings.label: Shape (alpha)
settings.html: The shape of the gamma distribution. Below 1 the curve rises steeply from zero, at 1 it is exponential, and above 1 it is S-shaped and shifted to the right.

settings.label: Rate (beta)
settings.html: Multiplies the normalised position before the CDF is applied. A higher rate stretches the range further along the curve, so the top of the range reads closer to 1.

faq.q: Why does the line not reach 1 at the top of the range?
faq.html: The top of the range maps to the CDF at the rate value. With a shape of 2 and a rate of 3 that is about 0.80. Raise the rate to let the top of the range read higher.

faq.q: What happens when the window is flat?
faq.html: A window with no range puts the position at 0.5, which is then scaled by the rate and passed through the curve like any other position.

faq.q: Does the line need a warmup?
faq.html: No. Until period bars exist, the range is taken over every bar seen so far, so the line has a value from the first bar.

related.title: Highest Value (HIGHEST)
related.summary: Traces the highest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the highest value seen so far.

related.title: FFT Dominant Cycle (Radix-2 FFT)
related.summary: Estimates the length of the strongest price cycle, in bars, from a Hann-windowed fast Fourier transform of the last N bars.

related.title: Midprice (HL2)
related.summary: Draws the midpoint of every bar's range, half the sum of its high and its low, as a single line over the price.

williams-gator-oscillator.title: Williams Gator Oscillator
williams-gator-oscillator.summary: Two histograms that show how far apart the three displaced alligator lines have moved: wide bars for a trending market, bars near zero for a quiet one.
williams-gator-oscillator.descriptionHtml:
The Gator Oscillator is built from three smoothed lines, the Jaw, the Teeth and the Lips, each a smoothed moving average of the source (the typical price by default) that moves one period's share of the way toward the source on every bar with its own period and its own forward displacement. Each average starts from zero and is divided by a correction factor while that start still matters, so it reads as the source from the first bar.

The upper histogram is the distance between the Jaw and the Teeth, and the lower histogram is the distance between the Teeth and the Lips, drawn below zero. A bar is green while its gap is widening or holding and red while it narrows. Because each line is displaced, the value on a bar uses the Jaw from jawOffset bars ago, the Teeth from teethOffset bars ago and the Lips from lipsOffset bars ago.
williams-gator-oscillator.howToReadHtml:
When both histograms grow away from zero with green bars, the three lines are spreading apart and the market is trending. When both shrink toward zero with red bars, the lines are converging and the market is resting or ranging.

A common reading splits the cycle into phases: a quiet stretch with both bars small, one histogram turning green as the lines start to separate, both bars green as the trend runs, and red bars returning as it fades. The oscillator shows how strong a move is, not which way it is going; read the direction from price or from the lines themselves.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the three lines smooth. The typical price is the default.

settings.label: Jaw Period
settings.html: The length of the slowest line. A longer Jaw widens the upper histogram during trends.

settings.label: Jaw Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Jaw is displaced forward, so the histogram reads its value from that many bars ago.

settings.label: Teeth Period
settings.html: The length of the middle line, which both histograms are measured against.

settings.label: Teeth Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Teeth line is displaced forward before the gaps are measured.

settings.label: Lips Period
settings.html: The length of the fastest line. A shorter Lips makes the lower histogram react sooner.

settings.label: Lips Offset
settings.html: How many bars the Lips line is displaced forward before the gap to the Teeth is measured.

faq.q: Why is the lower histogram negative?
faq.html: It is drawn below zero only so the two gaps can be read side by side. Its size is the distance between the Teeth and the Lips, which is always positive.

faq.q: What do the colours mean?
faq.html: Green means the gap is at least as wide as on the previous bar, and red means it has narrowed. On the lower histogram a widening gap is a bar that moves further below zero.

faq.q: Does it show the direction of the trend?
faq.html: No. Both gaps are measured as distances, so an up trend and a down trend look the same. Use price or the three lines to tell the direction.

related.title: Intraday Momentum Index (IMI)
related.summary: An oscillator from 0 to 100 built from candle bodies: the share of the period's body size that came from bars closing above their open.

related.title: Fisher04 - Ehlers 2004 Cybernetic Analysis
related.summary: A Fisher transform of the bar midpoint within its recent range, with a signal line that is simply the previous bar's value.

related.title: Inertia
related.summary: The distance between the source and the end of a least-squares line fitted through its recent values, positive when price runs ahead of its trend.

gaussian-filter-gauss.title: Gaussian Filter (GAUSS)
gaussian-filter-gauss.summary: A weighted average of recent prices using a bell-shaped Gaussian kernel whose width is set by sigma, answering from the first bar.
gaussian-filter-gauss.descriptionHtml:
The Gaussian Filter is a convolution: each value is a weighted sum of the current price and the prices before it, with weights taken from a Gaussian bell curve. The kernel has 2 * ceil(3 * Sigma) + 1 taps, the weights fall off as exp(-x^2 / (2 * Sigma^2)) from the centre tap, and they are scaled to add up to one.

The taps are laid against the bars counting back from the current one, so the current bar takes the first tap and the oldest bar in the window takes the last. Because the curve is symmetric, the newest and oldest bars get the smallest weights and the bars in the middle of the window get the most.

On early bars, where the full window is not yet available, only the existing taps are used and the sum is divided by the weight actually used, so the filter answers from the first bar.
gaussian-filter-gauss.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smooth version of price centred some bars in the past. Its slope gives the trend direction and its turns mark swings at the scale of Sigma. Because the heaviest weights sit in the middle of the window, the line lags by about half the window, roughly 3 * Sigma bars.

A small Sigma gives a short window that follows price closely; a large one gives a wide, very smooth line that turns late. The bell shape avoids the jumps a simple moving average shows when a big bar enters or leaves its window.

settings.label: Sigma
settings.html: The width of the Gaussian kernel. Larger values use more bars, smooth harder and lag more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter averages, the close by default.

faq.q: How many bars does the filter use?
faq.html: 2 * ceil(3 * Sigma) + 1. At the default Sigma of 1 that is 7 bars; at 1.5 it is 11.

faq.q: Why does the line lag about half the window?
faq.html: The kernel is a symmetric bell laid over the window, so the most weight falls on the middle bars, not on the newest one.

faq.q: Why does it start on the first bar?
faq.html: Early bars use only the taps that have a bar under them and divide by those weights, so a value exists from the very first bar.

related.title: Hann FIR Filter (HANN)
related.summary: A finite-window weighted average of price with raised-cosine weights, smoother and less ringing than a flat moving average of the same length.

related.title: Elliptic 2nd Order Filter (ELLIPTIC)
related.summary: A two-pole, two-zero elliptic lowpass on price with a notch just past the cutoff, removing fast noise sharply for a second-order filter.

related.title: Hodrick-Prescott Filter (HP)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend drawn on the chart and a cycle drawn in its own pane, with lambda setting how stiff the trend is.

generalized-double-exponential-moving-av.title: Generalized Double Exponential Moving Average (GDEMA)
