generalized-double-exponential-moving-av.summary: A double exponential average with an adjustable lag correction, from a plain EMA at v = 0 to a line that removes more lag than it adds above v = 1.
generalized-double-exponential-moving-av.descriptionHtml:
GDEMA builds on two exponential averages. The first smooths the source with the weight 2 / (period + 1). The second smooths the first with the same weight, so it lags further behind price. The gap between them measures how much lag the smoothing added, and the study subtracts a share of that gap: the line is (1 + v) * EMA1 - v * EMA2.

The factor v sets how much lag is taken out. At 0 the line is the first average alone, at 1 it is the classic double exponential average, and above 1 it removes more lag than the smoothing put in, so the line leads turns and overshoots them.

Both averages start from zero, and on the early bars each is divided by 1 - beta^n, where beta is one minus the weight and n the number of bars seen. That removes the pull toward zero, so the line follows price from the first bar instead of waiting for a warmup.
generalized-double-exponential-moving-av.howToReadHtml:
Read GDEMA like any moving average: price above a rising line is an uptrend, price below a falling line a downtrend, and a cross of price through the line is an early hint that the move is changing. Compared with an exponential average of the same period it turns sooner, because part of its lag has been taken out.

The price of a faster turn is overshoot. With a high v the line runs past price at the end of a sharp move and then snaps back, which can look like a false signal. Keep v near 1 for a balanced line and lower it on choppy charts.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of both exponential averages. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Volume Factor (v)
settings.html: How much of the lag is subtracted: 0 is a plain exponential average, 1 the standard double exponential average, and higher values lead price more and overshoot more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Does the Volume Factor use traded volume?
faq.html: No. The name only describes how much of the lag correction is applied. The calculation reads the source price alone and never touches volume.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the very first bar?
faq.html: Both averages start from zero and are scaled up by 1 / (1 - beta^n) while they are young, which removes the bias toward zero. Once that correction is negligible it is switched off and the averages run unscaled.

faq.q: What does a v above 1 do?
faq.html: It subtracts more lag than the smoothing added, so the line leads price through a turn. That makes it faster but also makes it overshoot after sharp moves.

related.title: Gaussian-Weighted Moving Average (GWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a bell curve centred on the middle of the window, tapering at both ends.

related.title: Fibonacci Weighted Moving Average (FWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Fibonacci sequence, so the newest bars dominate and the line hugs price closely.

related.title: Hamming Moving Average (HAMMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Hamming window, heaviest in the middle of the lookback and lightest at its two ends.

geometric-mean-geomean.title: Geometric Mean (GEOMEAN)
geometric-mean-geomean.summary: The geometric mean of the last N positive prices: the exponential of their average logarithm, a centre line that compounds rather than adds.
geometric-mean-geomean.descriptionHtml:
The Geometric Mean takes the positive source values in the lookback window, averages their natural logarithms, and turns that average back into a price with the exponential function. Averaging logarithms treats equal percentage moves as equal steps, so a doubling and a halving cancel out, which suits a series that grows and shrinks in percentage terms.

The study keeps a running sum of logarithms and a count of the values in the window. Each bar adds the new value and takes out the value that has just left the window. A value that is missing, zero or negative is left out and does not count, so the window simply holds fewer points. The window grows from the first bar, so the line starts on bar 0 with a mean of one value and becomes a full length bar mean once enough bars have passed.

For any set of positive numbers the geometric mean is at or below the arithmetic mean, and a single large spike pulls it up less than it pulls a simple average.
geometric-mean-geomean.howToReadHtml:
Read it like a slow, steady moving average drawn on the price chart. Price above the line means the latest bars are trading above the compounded centre of the window, and price below it means the opposite. Because it gives large values less pull, it sits slightly under a simple moving average of the same length, and the gap between the two widens when the window holds a wide spread of prices.

It lags like any average over a window, and the first length bars are drawn from fewer values than the full window, so the start of the line is noisier.

settings.label: Source (must be positive values)
settings.html: The price series that is averaged. Bars whose value is zero or negative are left out of the window.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window gives a smoother line that reacts more slowly.

faq.q: Why is the line below a simple moving average of the same length?
faq.html: The geometric mean of positive numbers is never larger than their arithmetic mean, and the gap grows with the spread of the values. On a quiet window the two lines almost touch.

faq.q: What happens to a zero or negative value?
faq.html: It is skipped. The window keeps its length in bars, but that bar adds nothing to the sum of logarithms and is not counted, so the mean is taken over the remaining values.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The window grows from the first bar, so the first reading is the value itself and each later bar adds one more value until the window is full.

related.title: Granger Causality Test (GRANGER)
related.summary: An F-statistic asking whether the previous value of a second series improves the prediction of the first beyond its own previous value.

related.title: Entropy (ENTROPY)
related.summary: Normalised Shannon entropy of the recent window, from 0 when the values crowd into one slice of the range to 1 when they spread evenly.

related.title: Harmonic Mean (HARMEAN)
related.summary: The harmonic mean of the last N positive values: the count divided by the sum of their reciprocals, a mean pulled toward the smaller readings.

gann-high-low-activator.title: Gann High-Low Activator
gann-high-low-activator.summary: A trailing line built from short averages of the highs and lows that flips sides when price closes beyond it, with BUY and SELL marks on each flip.
gann-high-low-activator.descriptionHtml:
This high-low activator keeps track of a simple trend state using two short simple moving averages: one of the bar highs and one of the bar lows, both over period bars (3 by default).

The trend turns up on a close above the average of the highs and turns down on a close below the average of the lows. A close between the two averages changes nothing, so the state holds until price clearly breaks the other way. On the first bar the state starts as up, unless that close already sits on or below the average of the lows; with any period above 1 the averages have no value yet, so the start is always up.

The plotted line follows the state. In an uptrend it is the average of the lows, drawn in green under price; in a downtrend it is the average of the highs, drawn in red above price. A BUY mark below the bar and a SELL mark above it show each change of state, and the first bar always carries a mark for the starting state.
gann-high-low-activator.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a trailing stop that moves with the trend. While price stays on the green line's side, the uptrend is intact; a close below the average of the lows flips the line red and above price, and prints a SELL mark. The reverse sequence prints a BUY mark.

With the default short period the line hugs price and flips often, which suits short swings but gives many false turns in a sideways market. A longer period gives fewer, later flips. Each mark is drawn on the bar whose close caused the flip, so it does not move once the bar has closed.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the averages of the highs and lows. A longer period moves the line further from price and makes it flip less often.

faq.q: Why does the line jump from below price to above it?
faq.html: On a flip the line switches from the average of the lows to the average of the highs, or back. The jump is the distance between the two averages.

faq.q: Why is there a mark on the very first bar?
faq.html: The study has no earlier state to compare with, so the first bar's state always counts as a change and is marked.

faq.q: What happens when the close lands between the two averages?
faq.html: Nothing changes. The trend keeps its previous state until a close goes above the average of the highs or below the average of the lows.

related.title: HT_TRENDMODE: Hilbert Transform Trend Mode
related.summary: A step line that reads 1 when a Hilbert transform cycle measurement says the market is trending and 0 when it says the market is cycling.

related.title: Directional Movement Index (DX)
related.summary: Plots DX, the gap between +DI and -DI as a share of their sum, beside both directional lines, to show how one-sided the movement is.

related.title: Ichimoku Cloud
related.summary: Five lines built from range midpoints, with a shaded cloud projected ahead of price that marks trend, support and resistance at a glance.

garman-klass-volatility-gkv.title: Garman-Klass Volatility (GKV)
garman-klass-volatility-gkv.summary: Volatility estimated from each bar's open, high, low and close, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.
garman-klass-volatility-gkv.descriptionHtml:
Garman-Klass Volatility estimates volatility from the whole bar instead of from closes alone. For each bar it takes the log range, the natural logarithm of the high minus that of the low, and the log body, the logarithm of the close minus that of the open. The estimator is half the squared log range minus 0.3862941611 (that is, 2 ln 2 - 1) times the squared log body.

The estimator is smoothed with an average of weight 1 / Length, seeded with the first value, and divided by the weight that average has gathered so far to remove the start-up bias. The square root of the result is the volatility per bar. With Annualize Volatility on it is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

Because a bar's body never exceeds its range and 0.5 is larger than 0.386, the estimator is never negative on consistent prices. The study still leaves a bar empty if the smoothed estimate ever falls below zero, which only inconsistent price data can cause.
garman-klass-volatility-gkv.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means bars are getting wider relative to their price, a falling line means they are narrowing. Because it uses the range of every bar, it reacts to a market that swings widely inside each bar even when the closes barely move, which a close-to-close measure would miss.

Read it against its own history: readings near its lows mark quiet bars, and spikes mark bursts of wide bars. The default 252 periods suits daily bars; on other timeframes set Annual Periods to the bars in a year, or switch annualising off and read it as a per-bar figure. Large overnight gaps are not captured, since only the bar's own prices are used.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Sets the smoothing weight 1 / Length. A longer length gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, the per-bar volatility is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: Bars in a year used for annualising: 252 for daily bars, 52 for weekly bars.

faq.q: Why use the open, high, low and close rather than just the close?
faq.html: The range of each bar carries much more information about how much price moved than a single close, so the estimate settles with fewer bars.

faq.q: Can the estimate be negative?
faq.html: Not on consistent prices. The body of a bar is never wider than its range, and the range term carries a weight of 0.5 against 0.386 for the body, so the estimator stays at zero or above. If bad data ever made the smoothed value negative, the study would leave that bar empty rather than take a square root.

faq.q: Does it include gaps between bars?
faq.html: No. It reads only the prices inside each bar, so a jump from one close to the next open is not measured.

related.title: High-Low Volatility (HLV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log range of each bar, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

related.title: Exponential Weighted MA Volatility
related.summary: Volatility from an exponentially weighted average of squared log returns, corrected for start-up bias and optionally annualised.

related.title: Historical Volatility (HV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of log returns over a rolling window, optionally scaled to an annual figure.

granger-causality-test-granger.title: Granger Causality Test (GRANGER)
granger-causality-test-granger.summary: An F-statistic asking whether the previous value of a second series improves the prediction of the first beyond its own previous value.
granger-causality-test-granger.descriptionHtml:
A Granger causality test asks whether knowing the past of one series helps predict another. This study runs the one-lag version. It fits two regressions over the lookback window: a restricted model that predicts Source 1 from its own previous value, and an unrestricted model that adds the previous value of Source 2. If adding Source 2 shrinks the prediction errors by a lot, the F-statistic is large.

The means, variances and covariances behind both regressions are each kept over a window of the last period bars. Each deviation is measured against the mean as it stood on the bar it entered the window, rather than the current mean. From these the study works out both sets of coefficients, then sums the squared residuals of each model over the window.

The two sums of squared residuals are carried from bar to bar and keep growing rather than being reset on each bar, so the F-statistic, (SSR1 - SSR2) / (SSR2 / (period - 3)), is taken between the two running totals and is floored at zero. Both series come from the instrument on the chart: by default the close and the volume.
granger-causality-test-granger.howToReadHtml:
A higher value means the previous bar of Source 2 has added more explanatory power for Source 1 than Source 1's own previous bar alone. A value near zero means it has added little. Because the residual totals run from the start of the chart, the line reflects the whole history so far and changes slowly late in a long chart.

The test measures predictive association in the data, not real cause and effect. It is a single-lag test with a short window, so treat it as a rough gauge of whether one series leads the other rather than as a formal result.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: The series being predicted, the close by default.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: The series tested as a predictor, the volume by default. Both series come from the instrument on the chart.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The lookback for the regressions, at least 4 bars. A longer window gives steadier coefficients.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean Source 2 causes Source 1?
faq.html: No. It means the previous value of Source 2 helped predict Source 1 in this data. That is a statistical lead, not proof of cause.

faq.q: Why does the line change so slowly late in the chart?
faq.html: The sums of squared residuals keep adding from the first bar instead of being reset, so each new bar is a small part of a growing total.

faq.q: Why is the minimum period 4?
faq.html: The unrestricted model has three parameters, and the F-statistic divides by the period minus 3, so the window needs more than three observations.

related.title: Harmonic Mean (HARMEAN)
related.summary: The harmonic mean of the last N positive values: the count divided by the sum of their reciprocals, a mean pulled toward the smaller readings.

related.title: Geometric Mean (GEOMEAN)
related.summary: The geometric mean of the last N positive prices: the exponential of their average logarithm, a centre line that compounds rather than adds.

related.title: Hurst Exponent (HURST)
related.summary: Rescaled range estimate of the Hurst exponent of recent log returns: above 0.5 reads as trending, below 0.5 as mean reverting.

gaussian-weighted-moving-average-gwma.title: Gaussian-Weighted Moving Average (GWMA)
gaussian-weighted-moving-average-gwma.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a bell curve centred on the middle of the window, tapering at both ends.
gaussian-weighted-moving-average-gwma.descriptionHtml:
The Gaussian-Weighted Moving Average weights the bars of its window with a bell curve. The curve is centred on the middle of the window, so the bars near the centre carry the most weight and the newest and oldest bars the least. The width of the bell is the Sigma setting multiplied by the window length, and the weights are scaled to sum to one before the weighted prices are added up.

The window grows with the chart until it holds period bars, and the bell is rebuilt for each length, so the line is drawn from the first bar. A missing price is skipped along with its weight. The taper at both ends softens the step a flat average shows when a large bar enters or leaves the window.
gaussian-weighted-moving-average-gwma.howToReadHtml:
Read the GWMA as a smooth trend line. Because its weight is centred on the middle of the window, it lags more than an average that favours the newest bar, roughly half a window behind price, but its path is very even. Use it to judge the direction and slope of the trend rather than to time turns.

A smaller Sigma narrows the bell, concentrating weight on fewer central bars; a larger Sigma spreads it toward an equal weighting. In either case the line trails sharp moves, so price crossing it is a late signal.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the full window. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Sigma
settings.html: Width of the bell as a fraction of the window. Lower values narrow it around the centre; higher values flatten it toward equal weights.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the GWMA lag more than an exponential average?
faq.html: Its weights peak at the centre of the window, not at the newest bar, so the line describes where price was about half a window ago.

faq.q: What does Sigma change?
faq.html: The spread of the bell curve. At 0.1 nearly all the weight sits on the central bars; at 1 the curve is broad and the weights are close to equal.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The window grows with the chart until it holds the full period, and the bell weights are rebuilt for each length, so every bar has a value.

related.title: Hamming Moving Average (HAMMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Hamming window, heaviest in the middle of the lookback and lightest at its two ends.

related.title: Generalized Double Exponential Moving Average (GDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average with an adjustable lag correction, from a plain EMA at v = 0 to a line that removes more lag than it adds above v = 1.

related.title: Hanning Moving Average (HANMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a raised cosine window, zero at both ends of the lookback and heaviest in the middle.

ha-heikin-ashi.title: HA: Heikin-Ashi
ha-heikin-ashi.summary: Smoothed candles drawn over the chart: each closes at the bar's average price and opens at the midpoint of the previous smoothed candle.
ha-heikin-ashi.descriptionHtml:
Heikin-Ashi redraws every bar as a synthetic candle. Its close is the average of the bar's open, high, low and close. Its open is the midpoint of the previous synthetic candle's open and close; on the first bar, where there is no previous candle, it is the midpoint of the bar's own open and close.

The high of the synthetic candle is the highest of the bar's high, the synthetic open and the synthetic close, and the low is the lowest of the three. Each candle is drawn green when its synthetic close is at or above its synthetic open and red otherwise, with body, border and wick in the same colour. Because each open carries half of the previous candle, the series is smoothed without being shifted in time.
ha-heikin-ashi.howToReadHtml:
Runs of green candles with little or no lower wick show a steady advance, and runs of red candles with little or no upper wick show a steady decline. Small bodies with wicks on both sides, or a change of colour, show the move losing pace.

The synthetic prices are not prices that traded: the open and close of a smoothed candle usually differ from the real open and close of the bar. Use the candles to read the trend, and read entries, stops and fills from the real bars underneath.

faq.q: Why do the candles differ from the real bars?
faq.html: Each synthetic close is the bar's average price and each synthetic open carries half of the previous candle, so the values are smoothed versions of the bar, not prices that printed.

faq.q: Why are there fewer colour changes than on the real chart?
faq.html: The open of each candle is tied to the previous one, so a single bar against the trend rarely flips the colour. That is the smoothing doing its job.

faq.q: Is it shifted in time?
faq.html: No. Every candle uses only its own bar and the previous synthetic candle, so it sits on the same bar as the price it describes. The smoothing does mean a turn in price can take a bar or more to change the candle colour.

related.title: MEDPRICE: Median Price
related.summary: The midpoint of each bar's range, halfway between its high and its low, drawn on the price chart with no smoothing.

related.title: AVGPRICE: Average Price
related.summary: The plain mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, drawn on the price chart as one number for where the bar traded.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

hamming-moving-average-hamma.title: Hamming Moving Average (HAMMA)
hamming-moving-average-hamma.summary: A moving average weighted by the Hamming window, heaviest in the middle of the lookback and lightest at its two ends.
hamming-moving-average-hamma.descriptionHtml:
The Hamming Moving Average weights the bars of its window with the Hamming taper, 0.54 - 0.46 * cos(2 * pi * k / (N - 1)), where k counts bars back from the newest and N is the window length. The weight is 0.08 at both ends of the window and rises to 1 in the middle, so the central bars dominate. The weighted prices are summed and divided by the sum of the weights.

The window grows with the chart until it holds period bars, with the weights rebuilt for each length. A window of a single bar weights that bar by one, so the line starts on the first bar at the price itself. A missing price is skipped with its weight, and a window with no usable weight falls back to the current price.
hamming-moving-average-hamma.howToReadHtml:
Read the HAMMA as a smooth trend line. Tapering the ends means a large bar entering or leaving the window moves the line gently rather than in a step, so its path is cleaner than a simple average of the same length. Because the weight sits in the middle of the window, the line runs roughly half a window behind price.

Use it for the direction and slope of the trend. It is slow to confirm a reversal, and a cross of price through the line comes after much of the move has happened.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the full window. A longer period smooths more and lags more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Hanning average?
faq.html: Both use a cosine taper. The Hamming taper keeps a small weight of 0.08 at the ends of the window, while the Hanning taper falls all the way to zero.

faq.q: Why is the line smoother than a simple average?
faq.html: Bars enter and leave the window with small weights, so a single large bar shifts the line gradually instead of in one jump.

faq.q: Where does the line start?
faq.html: On the first bar. The window grows with the chart, and a one-bar window simply returns the price.

related.title: Hanning Moving Average (HANMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a raised cosine window, zero at both ends of the lookback and heaviest in the middle.

related.title: Gaussian-Weighted Moving Average (GWMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow a bell curve centred on the middle of the window, tapering at both ends.

related.title: Hull Exponential Moving Average (HEMA)
related.summary: A low-lag average that combines a fast and a slow exponential average with logarithmic weights and smooths the result once more.

hanning-moving-average-hanma.title: Hanning Moving Average (HANMA)
hanning-moving-average-hanma.summary: A moving average weighted by a raised cosine window, zero at both ends of the lookback and heaviest in the middle.
hanning-moving-average-hanma.descriptionHtml:
The Hanning Moving Average weights the bars of its window with a raised cosine, 0.5 * (1 - cos(2 * pi * k / (N - 1))), where k counts bars back from the newest and N is the window length. The weight is zero on the newest and oldest bars and rises to one in the middle, so the centre of the window carries the most. The weighted prices are summed and divided by the sum of the weights.

The window grows with the chart until it holds period bars, with the weights rebuilt for each length. A one-bar window weights that bar by one, and a two-bar window, whose two weights are both zero, falls back to the current price. A missing price is skipped with its weight.
hanning-moving-average-hanma.howToReadHtml:
Read the HANMA as a very smooth trend line. Because both ends of the window carry no weight, bars slide in and out without any step in the line, and it filters out short swings well. The cost is lag: with the weight in the middle of the window, the line runs about half a window behind price.

Note that the newest bar has zero weight, so the latest close does not move the line until the next bar. Use the line for the direction of the trend, not to time entries.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the full window. A longer period smooths more and lags more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the latest close not move the line?
faq.html: The raised cosine gives zero weight to both ends of the window, including the newest bar. That bar starts to count once the next bar arrives.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Hamming average?
faq.html: The Hamming taper keeps a small weight of 0.08 at the ends, while the Hanning taper falls to zero, which smooths a little more.

faq.q: What happens on the second bar of the chart?
faq.html: A two-bar window has zero weight on both bars, so the line falls back to the current price there.

related.title: Hull Exponential Moving Average (HEMA)
related.summary: A low-lag average that combines a fast and a slow exponential average with logarithmic weights and smooths the result once more.

related.title: Hamming Moving Average (HAMMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by the Hamming window, heaviest in the middle of the lookback and lightest at its two ends.

related.title: Henderson Moving Average (HEND)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average with closed-form Henderson weights that pass a cubic trend through without distortion.

hann-fir-filter-hann.title: Hann FIR Filter (HANN)
hann-fir-filter-hann.summary: A finite-window weighted average of price with raised-cosine weights, smoother and less ringing than a flat moving average of the same length.
hann-fir-filter-hann.descriptionHtml:
The Hann FIR Filter averages the last Length prices with weights from a Hann window: tap i weighs 0.5 * (1 - cos(2 * pi * i / (Length - 1))). The weights rise from zero at the oldest bar to a peak in the middle of the window and fall back to zero at the newest bar. The weighted sum is divided by the total weight, so a flat price passes through unchanged.

Tapering both ends of the window means a bar fades in and out of the average gradually instead of jumping in and dropping out, which removes most of the ringing and the sudden steps of a simple moving average.

Before Length bars exist the filter uses the first few taps only, over the bars that are there. On the first bar the single tap weighs zero, so the line starts at the price itself. A Length of 1 has no defined weight and plots the price.
hann-fir-filter-hann.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smooth trend line. Its slope gives the direction and its turns mark swings at the scale of Length. Because the weights peak in the middle of the window, the line lags by about half of Length bars, more than a weighted average that favours recent bars.

The smoothness makes crossings of price and the line fewer and more deliberate, but they come late. Use a shorter Length to follow price more closely, or compare it with a faster average to judge momentum.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars in the window. Larger values smooth more and lag more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter averages, the close by default.

faq.q: Why do the newest and oldest bars count for almost nothing?
faq.html: The Hann window tapers to zero at both ends, so bars enter and leave the average smoothly. The middle of the window carries the most weight.

faq.q: How does it compare with a simple moving average?
faq.html: It is smoother and does not jump when a large bar enters or leaves the window, but it lags about the same, half the length.

faq.q: What happens at a Length of 1?
faq.html: The single weight is undefined, so the line simply plots the price.

related.title: Hodrick-Prescott Filter (HP)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend drawn on the chart and a cycle drawn in its own pane, with lambda setting how stiff the trend is.

related.title: Gaussian Filter (GAUSS)
related.summary: A weighted average of recent prices using a bell-shaped Gaussian kernel whose width is set by sigma, answering from the first bar.

related.title: Highpass Filter (2-Pole) (HPF)
related.summary: Strips out price swings shorter than a chosen cycle length with a two-pole highpass filter and draws the smooth trend that is left behind.

harmonic-mean-harmean.title: Harmonic Mean (HARMEAN)
harmonic-mean-harmean.summary: The harmonic mean of the last N positive values: the count divided by the sum of their reciprocals, a mean pulled toward the smaller readings.
harmonic-mean-harmean.descriptionHtml:
The Harmonic Mean averages the reciprocals of the positive source values in the lookback window and then inverts the result. Put another way, it is the number of values divided by the sum of one over each value. Small values have large reciprocals, so they carry more weight, and the harmonic mean sits at or below both the geometric and the arithmetic mean of the same window.

The study keeps a running sum of reciprocals and a count of the values in the window. Each bar adds the new value and takes out the value that has just left the window. A value that is missing, zero or negative is skipped and does not count. The window grows from the first bar, so the first reading is on bar 0 and the full length bar window is in place once enough bars have passed.

It is drawn in its own pane so the line can be read on its own scale.
harmonic-mean-harmean.howToReadHtml:
Treat it as a centre line that leans toward the low end of the window. When the harmonic mean falls clearly below a simple average of the same length, the window holds a wide spread of values with some low readings pulling it down. When the two are close, the window is tight.

It is an average, so it lags price and carries no signal by itself. Its early bars are computed from fewer values than the full window, and any bar whose source is zero or negative is left out of the mean.

settings.label: Source (must be positive values)
settings.html: The series that is averaged. Bars whose value is zero or negative are left out of the window.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: Why is it lower than a simple moving average?
faq.html: Averaging reciprocals gives the small values more weight, so the result leans toward them. For positive numbers the harmonic mean is never above the arithmetic mean.

faq.q: What does it skip?
faq.html: Any bar whose source value is missing, zero or negative. That bar still occupies a slot in the window but adds nothing to the mean.

faq.q: When is a harmonic mean the right average?
faq.html: When the values are rates or ratios. Averaging the prices paid when the same amount of money is spent on each bar gives the harmonic mean, not the simple one.

related.title: Hurst Exponent (HURST)
related.summary: Rescaled range estimate of the Hurst exponent of recent log returns: above 0.5 reads as trending, below 0.5 as mean reverting.

related.title: Granger Causality Test (GRANGER)
related.summary: An F-statistic asking whether the previous value of a second series improves the prediction of the first beyond its own previous value.

related.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
related.summary: The distance between the 75th and the 25th percentile of the last N values, a measure of spread that ignores the extremes.

hull-exponential-moving-average-hema.title: Hull Exponential Moving Average (HEMA)
hull-exponential-moving-average-hema.summary: A low-lag average that combines a fast and a slow exponential average with logarithmic weights and smooths the result once more.
hull-exponential-moving-average-hema.descriptionHtml:
HEMA applies the lag-cancelling idea of the Hull average to exponential averages instead of weighted windows. A slow average uses the weight 3 / (2 * period - 1), and a fast average gets a weight derived from the slow one through a logarithmic ratio, ln(2) / (1 + ln(2)).

The two are blended so that the slow average's lag is subtracted from the fast one, which gives a de-lagged series. That series is then smoothed by a third exponential average whose weight comes from half the square root of the period, which removes most of the noise the blend introduced.

All three averages start from zero and are scaled by 1 / (1 - decay) on the early bars, so the line follows price from the first bar. A period of 1 makes the slow weight 3, whose logarithm does not exist, so nothing is drawn at that setting.
hull-exponential-moving-average-hema.howToReadHtml:
HEMA is a fast trend line: it turns close to where price turns, with smooth curves rather than the stepped turns of a windowed Hull average. Price holding above a rising HEMA reads as an uptrend, and the line turning down is an early warning that the move is fading.

The lag cancellation that makes it fast also makes it overshoot after sharp moves, so a single bar crossing the line is weak evidence. Raise the period on noisy charts.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the slow, fast and final smoothing weights. A longer period gives a smoother line that turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Why is nothing drawn with a period of 1?
faq.html: The slow weight becomes 3, and the logarithm of 1 - 3 does not exist, so the whole calculation has no value. Use a period of 2 or more.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Hull Moving Average?
faq.html: The Hull average uses weighted moving windows. HEMA uses exponential averages throughout, so it responds from the first bar and turns without the small steps a windowed average shows.

related.title: Henderson Moving Average (HEND)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average with closed-form Henderson weights that pass a cubic trend through without distortion.

related.title: Hanning Moving Average (HANMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a raised cosine window, zero at both ends of the lookback and heaviest in the middle.

related.title: Hull Moving Average (HMA)
related.summary: Twice a half-period weighted average less a full-period one, smoothed again over the square root of the period.

henderson-moving-average-hend.title: Henderson Moving Average (HEND)
henderson-moving-average-hend.summary: A symmetric weighted average with closed-form Henderson weights that pass a cubic trend through without distortion.
henderson-moving-average-hend.descriptionHtml:
The Henderson Moving Average is a symmetric weighted average from the field of seasonal adjustment. Its weights come from a closed formula that depends only on the window length. They are largest at the centre of the window, fall away toward the edges and turn slightly negative at the outermost bars. That shape lets a smooth trend, up to a cubic curve, pass through the filter unchanged while short swings are suppressed.

The window must be odd and at least five bars long; an even period is raised to the next odd number. The weights are computed once, scaled to sum to one and applied to the last period prices. Until the window is full the line sits on the price itself, and a missing price counts as zero.
henderson-moving-average-hend.howToReadHtml:
Read the HEND as a trend line that keeps the shape of curving moves better than a simple or weighted average. Because the weights are symmetric, the value on any bar describes the middle of its window, so the line runs about half a window behind price. The negative edge weights make it hug turning points more tightly than a plain average of the same length.

Use it to see the direction and curvature of the trend. It is not a fast signal line, and the first bars, where it equals price, carry no smoothing.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of the window, odd and at least 5. An even value is raised to the next odd one. Longer windows smooth more and lag more.

faq.q: Why must the period be odd?
faq.html: The Henderson weights are symmetric around a central bar, which needs the same number of bars on each side. An even setting is raised by one.

faq.q: Why are some weights negative?
faq.html: The formula is built to pass a cubic trend through unchanged. Small negative weights at the edges are what let it follow a curving trend instead of flattening it.

faq.q: Why does the line equal price at the start of the chart?
faq.html: Until the window holds the full period, there are not enough bars to apply the weights, so the line simply returns the price.

related.title: Hull Moving Average (HMA)
related.summary: Twice a half-period weighted average less a full-period one, smoothed again over the square root of the period.

related.title: Hull Exponential Moving Average (HEMA)
related.summary: A low-lag average that combines a fast and a slow exponential average with logarithmic weights and smooths the result once more.

related.title: Holt Exponential Moving Average (HOLT)
related.summary: Double exponential smoothing that tracks a level and a trend and plots their sum, so the line lags less than a plain EMA while a move runs.

highest-value-highest.title: Highest Value (HIGHEST)
highest-value-highest.summary: Traces the highest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the highest value seen so far.
highest-value-highest.descriptionHtml:
Highest Value draws the running maximum of a price series over a fixed lookback. On each bar it looks at the last period values of the source and plots the largest of them, so the line steps up the moment a new high enters the window and steps down only when the old high drops out of the back of it.

While fewer than period bars exist, the line is the highest value seen since the first bar, so it starts on the very first bar instead of waiting out a warmup. A missing source value is read as zero and still takes its place in the window. Once the window is full, the line is the plain rolling highest of the last period bars, the current bar included.
highest-value-highest.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the ceiling of recent trading. A flat stretch means no new high has been made inside the window, and the length of the flat stretch shows how long the last high has held. A step up means price has just set a new high for the window. When the line steps down, the old high has aged out, which often follows a quiet or falling market.

The window includes the current bar, so the source can never be above the line. To test for a breakout, compare the source with the line one bar earlier. A short period hugs price closely, while a long period marks the major swing highs.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window holds old highs for longer and changes less often.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose highest value is tracked, for example the close or the high of each bar.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the window holds period bars, the study reports the highest value seen so far. After that it reports the highest value of the last period bars.

faq.q: Can the source ever be above the line?
faq.html: No. The window includes the current bar, so the line is always at or above the source. Compare the source with the previous bar's value of the line to spot a new high.

faq.q: Should I use the high or the close as the source?
faq.html: Use the high to track the true price ceiling, including wicks. Use the close when only settled prices matter, which gives a lower and steadier line.

related.title: Midprice (HL2)
related.summary: Draws the midpoint of every bar's range, half the sum of its high and its low, as a single line over the price.

related.title: Gamma Distribution CDF (GAMMADIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range through the gamma cumulative distribution, giving an oscillator from 0 to 1.

related.title: Typical Price (HLC3)
related.summary: Draws the typical price of each bar, the average of its high, low and close, as one line over the candles.

midprice-hl2.title: Midprice (HL2)
midprice-hl2.summary: Draws the midpoint of every bar's range, half the sum of its high and its low, as a single line over the price.
midprice-hl2.descriptionHtml:
Midprice (HL2) reduces each bar to one number: the point halfway between its high and its low. It is computed as (high + low) * 0.5 on every bar, with no lookback and no smoothing, so each value depends only on the bar it is drawn on.

The open and the close play no part in it. Two bars with the same range but opposite bodies, one closing at its high and one at its low, have exactly the same midprice. That makes the line a neutral reference for where a bar traded rather than where it finished, and it is a common input to other studies that want a price free of the closing tick.
midprice-hl2.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the centre of each bar's range. A close above the line means the bar settled in the upper half of what it traded, and a close below means it settled in the lower half; a run of closes on one side shows which half buyers or sellers kept winning.

Because it has no lookback, the line is as noisy as the bars themselves and does not mark a trend on its own. It is most useful as a reference price, or as the source for an average or an oscillator that needs a value less tied to the close.

faq.q: How is this different from the close?
faq.html: The close is where the bar finished. The midprice is the centre of the bar's whole range and ignores where it finished, so it moves less on a bar that closes at an extreme.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. Each value uses only the high and low of its own bar, so once a bar is complete its midprice never changes. On the newest bar it moves as the high and low extend.

faq.q: Why use it as a source for another indicator?
faq.html: An average or oscillator fed with the midprice reacts to the range a bar traded rather than to its last tick, which can make it steadier on bars with long wicks.

related.title: Typical Price (HLC3)
related.summary: Draws the typical price of each bar, the average of its high, low and close, as one line over the candles.

related.title: Highest Value (HIGHEST)
related.summary: Traces the highest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the highest value seen so far.

related.title: Weighted Close (HLCC4)
related.summary: Draws the weighted close of each bar, the average of high, low and the close counted twice, as one line over the candles.

typical-price-hlc3.title: Typical Price (HLC3)
typical-price-hlc3.summary: Draws the typical price of each bar, the average of its high, low and close, as one line over the candles.
typical-price-hlc3.descriptionHtml:
Typical Price reduces each bar to a single number that stands in for the whole bar. It adds the high, the low and the close and scales the total to a third, so the line sits roughly in the middle of where the bar traded, pulled slightly towards the close.

The study scales by the constant 0.333333 rather than dividing by exactly 3, so its values sit a fraction of a unit below an exact third on high-priced instruments. On a price near 60,000 the line sits about 0.06 below an exact third. There are no settings and no warmup: the line starts on the first bar.
typical-price-hlc3.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoother version of the close. Because it includes the high and the low, a bar with a long wick pulls the line towards that wick even if the close finished elsewhere. Many other studies, such as money flow and commodity channel calculations, use this price as their input, so plotting it shows exactly what they are reading.

It is not a signal on its own. Crossings of price and this line happen constantly and carry little meaning; use it as a reference price or as the input to another calculation.

faq.q: Why is the value slightly below (high + low + close) / 3?
faq.html: The study multiplies by 0.333333 instead of dividing by 3. The gap is one part in a million of the price, which is invisible on a chart but shows up in the last decimals.

faq.q: How is it different from the close?
faq.html: The close is one moment of the bar. The typical price blends the close with the bar's extremes, so it moves less on bars that closed near one end of a wide range.

faq.q: Does it need any history?
faq.html: No. Each bar's value uses only that bar, so the line is drawn from the very first bar and never changes once the bar has closed.

related.title: Weighted Close (HLCC4)
related.summary: Draws the weighted close of each bar, the average of high, low and the close counted twice, as one line over the candles.

related.title: Midprice (HL2)
related.summary: Draws the midpoint of every bar's range, half the sum of its high and its low, as a single line over the price.

related.title: Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT)
related.summary: Rebuilds price from only the slowest frequency components of a Hann-windowed transform, a smooth line that ignores fast swings.

weighted-close-hlcc4.title: Weighted Close (HLCC4)
weighted-close-hlcc4.summary: Draws the weighted close of each bar, the average of high, low and the close counted twice, as one line over the candles.
weighted-close-hlcc4.descriptionHtml:
Weighted Close is a single price for each bar that leans towards where the bar settled. It adds the high, the low and the close twice, then takes a quarter of the total. The close therefore carries half of the weight and the two extremes a quarter each.

Compared with the typical price, which weights high, low and close equally, the weighted close follows the close more closely while still reflecting how far the bar ranged. There are no settings and no warmup: every bar is computed from its own prices alone, so the line starts on the first bar.
weighted-close-hlcc4.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a close that has been nudged towards the middle of the bar. On a bar that closed at its high, the line sits a quarter of the range below the close; on a bar that closed exactly mid-range, it sits on the close.

It is most useful as an input to other studies, such as averages and oscillators, when you want them to favour the closing price without ignoring the bar's range. On its own it gives no signals, and crossings of price and this line carry little meaning.

faq.q: How much weight does the close get?
faq.html: Half. The close is counted twice out of four terms, while the high and the low get a quarter each.

faq.q: When would I use this instead of the typical price?
faq.html: When the close matters more to you than the extremes. The weighted close stays nearer the settlement price, while the typical price gives the high and low a third each.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. Each value uses only its own bar's prices, so once a bar has closed its value never changes.

related.title: Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT)
related.summary: Rebuilds price from only the slowest frequency components of a Hann-windowed transform, a smooth line that ignores fast swings.

related.title: Typical Price (HLC3)
related.summary: Draws the typical price of each bar, the average of its high, low and close, as one line over the candles.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JERK)
related.summary: Three chained rolling regressions, slope then acceleration then jerk, showing how quickly a trend's acceleration is itself changing.

high-low-volatility-hlv.title: High-Low Volatility (HLV)
high-low-volatility-hlv.summary: Volatility from the squared log range of each bar, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.
high-low-volatility-hlv.descriptionHtml:
High-Low Volatility estimates volatility from the distance between each bar's high and low. For each bar it takes the log range, the natural logarithm of the high minus that of the low, squares it and multiplies it by 0.3606737602, which is 1 / (4 ln 2). That constant turns the squared range into an estimate of the variance of returns.

The estimate is smoothed with an average of weight 1 / Length, seeded with the first bar's value. Early on that average still leans on its seed, so the study divides it by the weight it has gathered so far, which removes the start-up bias. The square root of the result is the volatility per bar, and with Annualize Volatility on it is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.
high-low-volatility-hlv.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means bars are getting wider, a falling line means they are tightening. Because it measures the full range of every bar, it responds to a market that swings back and forth inside each bar even when closes hardly change.

Read it against its own past values. A stretch near its lows marks narrow bars, and a spike marks a burst of wide bars. The default 252 periods suits daily bars; set Annual Periods to the bars in a year on your chart, or switch annualising off to read a per-bar figure. Gaps between one close and the next open are not included.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Sets the smoothing weight 1 / Length. A longer length gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, the per-bar volatility is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: Bars in a year used for annualising: 252 for daily bars, 52 for weekly bars.

faq.q: Why the constant 1 / (4 ln 2)?
faq.html: It is the factor that turns the average squared log range into an estimate of the variance of returns when prices move as a random walk without drift, so the result is on the same scale as a close-to-close volatility.

faq.q: How does it differ from Parkinson Volatility in this library?
faq.html: Both use the same squared log range. This one seeds its average with the first bar and corrects the start-up bias, so it answers from the first bar; Parkinson Volatility waits until its window is full.

faq.q: Does it see gaps?
faq.html: No. It only uses each bar's high and low, so a jump between bars does not raise the reading.

related.title: Historical Volatility (HV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of log returns over a rolling window, optionally scaled to an annual figure.

related.title: Garman-Klass Volatility (GKV)
related.summary: Volatility estimated from each bar's open, high, low and close, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

related.title: Jurik Volatility (JVOLTY)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio of an adaptive moving average, shown on its own: current movement over its smoothed average, floored at 1.

hull-moving-average-hma.title: Hull Moving Average (HMA)
hull-moving-average-hma.summary: Twice a half-period weighted average less a full-period one, smoothed again over the square root of the period.
hull-moving-average-hma.descriptionHtml:
The Hull Moving Average is built from linearly weighted averages, in which the newest bar carries the most weight. It takes a weighted average over half the period and another over the full period. Twice the half-period average less the full-period average leans ahead of both and cancels most of their lag. That difference is then smoothed by one more weighted average over the square root of the period.

Half the period and the square root of the period are each rounded to the nearest whole bar and never fall below one. All three averages answer from the first bar: until a window is full they weight the bars seen so far 1, 2 and up and divide by the sum of those weights, so the line is drawn from the start of the chart.
hull-moving-average-hma.howToReadHtml:
Read the HMA as a fast, smooth trend line. It follows price closely and turns quickly, so its slope is the main thing to read: rising describes an uptrend, falling a downtrend, and a change of slope an early sign the move is fading.

The lag reduction comes from extrapolation, so after a sharp reversal the line overshoots price before it settles, and in a range it changes direction often. The first bars use short windows and track price almost exactly.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of the full weighted average. The half-period and square-root windows are derived from it. Longer periods are smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the HMA lag less than a weighted average of the same length?
faq.html: Twice the half-period average less the full-period one extrapolates ahead and cancels most of the lag. The final short smoothing then removes the noise that step adds.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot after a sharp turn?
faq.html: The extrapolation projects the recent difference between the two averages forward. After a sudden reversal that difference is large, so the line briefly runs past price.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the first bar?
faq.html: Each weighted average uses the bars available until its window is full, so the line exists from the start, resting on fewer bars at first.

related.title: Holt Exponential Moving Average (HOLT)
related.summary: Double exponential smoothing that tracks a level and a trend and plots their sum, so the line lags less than a plain EMA while a move runs.

related.title: Henderson Moving Average (HEND)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average with closed-form Henderson weights that pass a cubic trend through without distortion.

related.title: Hilbert Trendline (HTIT)
related.summary: A trendline built from a twice smoothed price plus a small cyclic correction measured with a Hilbert transform.

holt-exponential-moving-average-holt.title: Holt Exponential Moving Average (HOLT)
holt-exponential-moving-average-holt.summary: Double exponential smoothing that tracks a level and a trend and plots their sum, so the line lags less than a plain EMA while a move runs.
holt-exponential-moving-average-holt.descriptionHtml:
HOLT keeps two numbers from bar to bar: a level and a trend. Each bar the level is pulled toward the source by the weight alpha = 2 / (period + 1), starting from where the previous level plus the previous trend said it would be. The trend is then updated from the change in the level, smoothed by its own weight gamma.

The plotted line is the level plus the trend, a one-bar-ahead forecast. Because the trend term carries the line forward in the direction of the move, it keeps up with a steady trend that a plain exponential average would trail.

The first bar sets the level to the source with a zero trend and shows the source unchanged. When Gamma is left at 0, the trend uses the same weight as the level.
holt-exponential-moving-average-holt.howToReadHtml:
Use HOLT as a fast trend line. While price trends steadily, the line sits close to price rather than trailing behind it, and its slope is a direct read of the current trend. A flattening line says the trend term is fading.

The forecast keeps going in the direction it has been moving, so at a sharp reversal the line overshoots for a few bars before turning. A larger Gamma makes the trend react faster and overshoot more; a smaller one gives a steadier but slower trend.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the level weight 2 / (period + 1). A longer period gives a smoother line that reacts more slowly.

settings.label: Gamma (0 = auto)
settings.html: Smoothing weight for the trend term. At 0 it uses the same weight as the level; higher values let the trend change faster.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes run ahead of price?
faq.html: It plots the level plus the trend, which is a forecast of the next bar. After a strong move the trend term keeps pushing the line on for a few bars before it catches the reversal.

faq.q: What does Gamma 0 mean?
faq.html: It is the automatic setting: the trend is smoothed with the same weight as the level, 2 / (period + 1).

faq.q: How is this different from a double exponential average?
faq.html: A double exponential average subtracts the lag of a second smoothing. HOLT instead tracks an explicit trend and adds it to the level, which behaves similarly in a steady trend but responds differently at turns.

related.title: Hilbert Trendline (HTIT)
related.summary: A trendline built from a twice smoothed price plus a small cyclic correction measured with a Hilbert transform.

related.title: Hull Moving Average (HMA)
related.summary: Twice a half-period weighted average less a full-period one, smoothed again over the square root of the period.

related.title: Holt-Winters Moving Average (HWMA)
related.summary: Triple exponential smoothing that tracks level, velocity and acceleration, so the line keeps moving through a turn instead of flattening.

homod-homodyne-discriminator-dominant-cy.title: HOMOD: Homodyne Discriminator Dominant Cycle
homod-homodyne-discriminator-dominant-cy.summary: The dominant cycle length in bars from a homodyne discriminator on a Hilbert transform of price, held to your period range and smoothed.
homod-homodyne-discriminator-dominant-cy.descriptionHtml:
The homodyne discriminator measures the market's dominant cycle length by multiplying the cycle by a delayed copy of itself. Price is smoothed with weights 4, 3, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, then a four-tap Hilbert transform splits it into in-phase and quadrature components, each smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against its previous bar. The width of every Hilbert stage follows the smoothed period from the previous bar, so the transform adapts as it goes.

Multiplying this bar's phasor by the conjugate of the previous one gives the angle the cycle turned through in a bar; a full turn over that angle is the period. The raw period is held between Min Period and Max Period and blended 0.2 / 0.8 into a running period that starts from 15. That is smoothed again with a weight of 0.33, and while the smoother's starting weight is still large the result is divided by one minus that weight, so the opening bars are not pulled toward the seed.
homod-homodyne-discriminator-dominant-cy.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the current rhythm of the market in bars: 20 means a swing from low to low is taking about 20 bars. Use it to set the length of other tools from the data, or to see whether the market's rhythm is speeding up or slowing down.

The measurement only means something while the market is cycling. In a strong trend there is little cycle to measure and the reading is less dependable. Each raw period is clamped to the range you set, so a line that sits near either limit means the estimate is being cut off there.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3.

settings.label: Min Period
settings.html: The shortest cycle, in bars, the discriminator may report. Shorter raw readings are raised to this value.

settings.label: Max Period
settings.html: The longest cycle, in bars, the discriminator may report. It is kept at least half a bar above the minimum.

faq.q: Why is it called a homodyne discriminator?
faq.html: It multiplies the cycle by a one-bar delayed copy of itself, the way a homodyne receiver mixes a signal with itself, and reads the cycle length from the phase difference that product shows.

faq.q: Why does the line move so smoothly?
faq.html: The raw period is smoothed twice, first 0.2 / 0.8 and then with a weight of 0.33, so it follows changes in the market's rhythm over several bars rather than jumping.

faq.q: What range should I set?
faq.html: The defaults of 6 to 50 bars suit most charts. Narrow the range if you know the cycles you care about, which also stops the reading from wandering in a trend.

related.title: HT_DCPERIOD: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Period
related.summary: The length in bars of the market's dominant cycle, measured by a Hilbert transform of smoothed price, held to 6 to 50 bars and smoothed.

related.title: Ehlers Even Better Sinewave (EBSW)
related.summary: A detrended, smoothed price cycle normalised by its own recent power into a wave that runs between -1 and +1.

related.title: HT_DCPHASE: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Phase
related.summary: Where the market sits inside its dominant cycle, as an angle in radians from -pi to pi, from the Hilbert transform's in-phase and quadrature parts.

hodrick-prescott-filter-hp.title: Hodrick-Prescott Filter (HP)
hodrick-prescott-filter-hp.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend drawn on the chart and a cycle drawn in its own pane, with lambda setting how stiff the trend is.
hodrick-prescott-filter-hp.descriptionHtml:
This study divides the source into two parts. The trend is a smooth line drawn on the price chart, and the cycle is whatever is left of price once that trend is removed, drawn around zero in a pane of its own.

The trend is a causal, one-pass approximation of the classic two-sided smoothing filter, so it uses only the bars up to the current one. The Lambda setting is turned into a smoothing factor alpha = (r - 1) / (r + 1), where r is half the square root of lambda, held between 0.0001 and 0.9999. Each bar the trend takes (1 - alpha) of the new price, alpha of the previous trend, and adds half of alpha times the change in the trend over the last bar, a momentum term that helps it keep up with a steady move. The first bar starts the trend at the first price.

The cycle is simply the source minus the trend, so it is positive when price sits above its trend and negative when it sits below.
hodrick-prescott-filter-hp.howToReadHtml:
Use the trend line on the chart as the direction of the market with the noise taken out, and the cycle pane as a measure of how stretched price is from that direction. A cycle far above zero means price has run ahead of its trend; far below zero means it has fallen behind. A cycle that turns back toward zero often marks the end of a swing.

Raising lambda gives a stiffer trend that bends slowly and pushes more of the movement into the cycle; lowering it lets the trend hug price. Because only past bars are used, the trend still lags turning points, and the cycle has no fixed upper or lower bound.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is split into trend and cycle, the close by default.

settings.label: Lambda (Smoothing)
settings.html: How strongly the trend is pulled toward a smooth line. Higher values give a stiffer trend and a larger cycle.

faq.q: Why is the trend on the price chart while the cycle has its own pane?
faq.html: The trend is measured in price and belongs next to the candles. The cycle is a difference from the trend that swings around zero, so it needs its own scale.

faq.q: Does this filter repaint?
faq.html: No. This version runs forward one bar at a time and uses only the current and earlier bars, so a value never changes once its bar has closed.

faq.q: What lambda should I use?
faq.html: The default of 677 gives a smoothing factor of about 0.86, so each bar the trend takes about 14 percent of the new price. Try larger values for a slower trend that captures only the main direction, or smaller values for one that follows price closely. At a lambda of 4 or less the factor is held at its 0.0001 floor and the trend is almost exactly price.

related.title: Highpass Filter (2-Pole) (HPF)
related.summary: Strips out price swings shorter than a chosen cycle length with a two-pole highpass filter and draws the smooth trend that is left behind.

related.title: Hann FIR Filter (HANN)
related.summary: A finite-window weighted average of price with raised-cosine weights, smoother and less ringing than a flat moving average of the same length.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KALMAN)
related.summary: Smooths price with a one-dimensional Kalman filter, where process noise and measurement noise decide how much each new bar moves the line.

highpass-filter-2-pole-hpf.title: Highpass Filter (2-Pole) (HPF)
highpass-filter-2-pole-hpf.summary: Strips out price swings shorter than a chosen cycle length with a two-pole highpass filter and draws the smooth trend that is left behind.
highpass-filter-2-pole-hpf.descriptionHtml:
This study separates price into a fast part and a slow part. A two-pole highpass filter picks out every swing shorter than the Length setting, the cutoff period, and the study draws what remains once that fast part is subtracted from the source. The line on the chart is therefore a trend component: the slow drift of price with the quick oscillations removed.

The highpass is a second-order recursive filter. Its coefficients come from the cutoff angle 2 * pi / Length: a smoothing factor alpha = (cos + sin - 1) / cos and a gain (1 - alpha / 2)^2. Each bar feeds the second difference of the source (this bar, minus twice the previous one, plus the one before that) into the filter together with its own two previous outputs. On the first two bars the missing inputs repeat the newest one, so the filter starts at rest.

Because the drawn line is the source minus a highpass rather than a moving average, it follows the price level directly and carries less lag than an average of similar smoothness.
highpass-filter-2-pole-hpf.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the underlying direction of price once the short cycles are taken away. When it rises, the slow component is rising even if individual bars are noisy; when it flattens or turns, the drift behind the swings has changed. Price crossing the line shows the fast part changing sign, which is often a pullback inside a trend rather than a reversal.

A longer Length removes more of the movement and gives a smoother, slower line. A two-pole filter can overshoot briefly after a sharp jump in price, so a sudden kink in the line after a gap is the filter settling, not a new signal.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Swings shorter than this are removed from the drawn line; a larger value gives a smoother trend.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does a highpass filter draw a smooth line?
faq.html: The highpass captures the fast oscillations. The study draws the source minus that highpass, so what you see is the slow part of price that the highpass did not take.

faq.q: How is this different from a moving average?
faq.html: A moving average smooths by averaging past bars and lags by about half its window. Subtracting a two-pole highpass keeps the current price level in the result, so the trend line lags less for the same smoothness.

faq.q: What does the Length setting mean in practice?
faq.html: It is the shortest cycle, in bars, that survives into the line. With the default of 40 on an hourly chart, swings that complete in less than about 40 hours are filtered out.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KALMAN)
related.summary: Smooths price with a one-dimensional Kalman filter, where process noise and measurement noise decide how much each new bar moves the line.

related.title: Hodrick-Prescott Filter (HP)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend drawn on the chart and a cycle drawn in its own pane, with lambda setting how stiff the trend is.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KF)
related.summary: Treats price as a noisy reading of a hidden level and tracks that level, with the balance of process noise and measurement noise setting its speed.

ht-dcperiod-hilbert-transform-dominant-c.title: HT_DCPERIOD: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Period
ht-dcperiod-hilbert-transform-dominant-c.summary: The length in bars of the market's dominant cycle, measured by a Hilbert transform of smoothed price, held to 6 to 50 bars and smoothed.
ht-dcperiod-hilbert-transform-dominant-c.descriptionHtml:
This study estimates how many bars one full cycle of the market currently takes. Price is smoothed with weights 4, 3, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, then a four-tap Hilbert transform splits it into an in-phase component and a quadrature component a quarter cycle apart. The width of every Hilbert stage follows the smoothed period from the previous bar, so the filter adapts to the cycle it is measuring.

The in-phase and quadrature parts form a phasor, each leg smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against its previous bar. Multiplying this bar's phasor by the conjugate of the previous one, and smoothing that product the same way, gives the angle the cycle turned through in one bar. A full turn over that angle is the period. It is held between 6 and 50 bars, starts from 15, and is smoothed 0.33 / 0.67 into the plotted value.
ht-dcperiod-hilbert-transform-dominant-c.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the current rhythm of the market in bars. A value of 20 means swings are taking about 20 bars from low to low. Many cycle tools take a length setting, and this reading is a way to set it from the data instead of guessing; the dashed levels at 15 and 30 bars mark short and long cycles.

The estimate is only meaningful while the market is actually cycling. In a strong trend there is little cycle to measure, and the period wanders or presses against the 6 and 50 bar limits.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3.

faq.q: Why is the period never below 6 or above 50?
faq.html: Each bar's raw period is clamped to 6 to 50 bars before it is smoothed, so the smoothed line also stays inside that range.

faq.q: Why does the line start at 15?
faq.html: Both the raw and the smoothed period start at 15 bars, and the first bars of data move them away from that seed gradually.

faq.q: Can I use the reading as a length for another indicator?
faq.html: Yes. Read the current value and set an oscillator or average to about that length, so its length follows the market's measured rhythm instead of a fixed guess.

related.title: HT_DCPHASE: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Phase
related.summary: Where the market sits inside its dominant cycle, as an angle in radians from -pi to pi, from the Hilbert transform's in-phase and quadrature parts.

related.title: HOMOD: Homodyne Discriminator Dominant Cycle
related.summary: The dominant cycle length in bars from a homodyne discriminator on a Hilbert transform of price, held to your period range and smoothed.

related.title: HT_PHASOR: Hilbert Transform Phasor Components
related.summary: The in-phase and quadrature components of the dominant cycle from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price, drawn as two lines.

ht-dcphase-hilbert-transform-dominant-cy.title: HT_DCPHASE: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Phase
ht-dcphase-hilbert-transform-dominant-cy.summary: Where the market sits inside its dominant cycle, as an angle in radians from -pi to pi, from the Hilbert transform's in-phase and quadrature parts.
ht-dcphase-hilbert-transform-dominant-cy.descriptionHtml:
This study reports the phase of the market's dominant cycle. Price is smoothed with weights 4, 3, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, then a four-tap Hilbert transform splits it into an in-phase component and a quadrature component a quarter cycle apart. The width of every Hilbert stage follows the smoothed dominant cycle period, which the study measures from how far the phasor turns each bar, holds between 6 and 50 bars and smooths, so the transform adapts to the cycle it is measuring.

The in-phase and quadrature parts are each smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against their previous bar. The plotted phase is the angle of that smoothed pair, the quadrature over the in-phase, computed with a quadrant-aware arctangent so it covers the whole circle from -pi to pi. On a bar where both parts are zero the previous phase is kept.
ht-dcphase-hilbert-transform-dominant-cy.howToReadHtml:
In this calculation the phase falls as a cycle unfolds and wraps from -pi back up to +pi once per cycle. The dashed levels at zero and at plus and minus pi/2, about 1.57, split the circle into quarters, so you can see which quarter of its cycle the market is in.

A phase that falls at a steady rate means a clean cycle. A phase that stalls, jumps or runs the other way means the market is not cycling at the moment, and any timing read from it is unreliable.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3.

faq.q: Why does the line jump from bottom to top?
faq.html: The phase is an angle. It falls through each cycle and wraps from -pi to +pi when it completes a full turn. The jump is the start of a new turn, not a sudden move in price.

faq.q: Is the phase in degrees?
faq.html: No, in radians. Pi radians is 180 degrees, so the pane runs from about -3.14 to +3.14.

faq.q: Why is there no period setting?
faq.html: The study measures the cycle period itself from the data and uses it to tune the transform, so there is nothing to set beyond the source.

related.title: HT_PHASOR: Hilbert Transform Phasor Components
related.summary: The in-phase and quadrature components of the dominant cycle from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price, drawn as two lines.

related.title: HT_DCPERIOD: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Period
related.summary: The length in bars of the market's dominant cycle, measured by a Hilbert transform of smoothed price, held to 6 to 50 bars and smoothed.

related.title: HT_SINE: Hilbert Transform - SineWave
related.summary: The sine of the dominant cycle's phase, and the sine of that phase plus 45 degrees, from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price.

ht-phasor-hilbert-transform-phasor-compo.title: HT_PHASOR: Hilbert Transform Phasor Components
ht-phasor-hilbert-transform-phasor-compo.summary: The in-phase and quadrature components of the dominant cycle from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price, drawn as two lines.
ht-phasor-hilbert-transform-phasor-compo.descriptionHtml:
This study splits the market's dominant cycle into two parts a quarter cycle apart. Price is smoothed with weights 4, 3, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, then a four-tap Hilbert transform produces a detrended series, an in-phase component (the detrended value three bars back) and a quadrature component. Two further Hilbert stages advance each part, and the in-phase and quadrature lines are combined from them and smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against their previous bar.

The width of every Hilbert stage follows the smoothed dominant cycle period. That period is measured each bar from how far the phasor turned, held between 6 and 50 bars, starts from 15, and is smoothed, so the transform adapts to the cycle it is measuring. The two plotted lines are the smoothed InPhase and Quadrature components, in price units.
ht-phasor-hilbert-transform-phasor-compo.howToReadHtml:
In a cycling market the two lines oscillate around zero with the Quadrature line a quarter cycle ahead of or behind InPhase, so their crossings come at regular spacing. The angle of the pair is the cycle phase and its length is the cycle amplitude, which other Hilbert studies build on.

The lines are in price units, so their size grows with volatility and with the price level. When they shrink toward zero and stop alternating, there is no clear cycle to read.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3.

faq.q: What are in-phase and quadrature?
faq.html: Two views of the same cycle a quarter turn apart, like the cosine and sine of one angle. Together they give the cycle's phase and amplitude.

faq.q: Why are the values so small compared with price?
faq.html: They measure the detrended swing, not price itself, so they hover around zero and scale with how far price oscillates.

faq.q: How is this related to the phase and period studies?
faq.html: The phase study plots the angle of these two lines, and the period study plots how fast that angle turns. All three share the same adaptive transform.

related.title: HT_SINE: Hilbert Transform - SineWave
related.summary: The sine of the dominant cycle's phase, and the sine of that phase plus 45 degrees, from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price.

related.title: HT_DCPHASE: Hilbert Transform Dominant Cycle Phase
related.summary: Where the market sits inside its dominant cycle, as an angle in radians from -pi to pi, from the Hilbert transform's in-phase and quadrature parts.

related.title: Lunar Phase (LUNAR)
