related.summary: The illuminated fraction of the moon at each bar's opening time, from 0 at new moon to 1 at full moon, with markers at the four main phases.

ht-sine-hilbert-transform-sinewave.title: HT_SINE: Hilbert Transform - SineWave
ht-sine-hilbert-transform-sinewave.summary: The sine of the dominant cycle's phase, and the sine of that phase plus 45 degrees, from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price.
ht-sine-hilbert-transform-sinewave.descriptionHtml:
This study draws the market's dominant cycle as a clean sine wave. Price is smoothed with weights 4, 3, 2 and 1 over the last four bars, then a four-tap Hilbert transform splits it into an in-phase and a quadrature component, each smoothed 0.2 / 0.8 against its previous bar. The width of every Hilbert stage follows the smoothed dominant cycle period, measured each bar from how far the phasor turned and held between 6 and 50 bars, so the transform adapts to the cycle it is measuring.

The phase is the angle of the quadrature over the in-phase part, from a quadrant-aware arctangent, and is kept from the previous bar when both parts are zero. The Sine line is the sine of that phase, and the LeadSine line is the sine of the phase plus 45 degrees. In this calculation the phase falls as a cycle unfolds, so LeadSine repeats the Sine line about an eighth of a cycle later rather than ahead of it.
ht-sine-hilbert-transform-sinewave.howToReadHtml:
Both lines run between -1 and +1. While the market cycles they swing together, with LeadSine an eighth of a cycle behind Sine, and they cross twice per cycle: just after each crest and just after each trough of the Sine line. Read the pair for where the market is in its cycle and how regular that cycle is; the crossings confirm a turn of the Sine line rather than anticipate it.

When the market trends, the phase stalls and the two lines flatten, drift apart or cross repeatedly without a clean wave. Check that the lines are swinging in a regular rhythm before reading anything into them.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3.

faq.q: Why are there two lines?
faq.html: LeadSine is the sine of the phase plus 45 degrees. It traces the same wave as Sine, offset by an eighth of a cycle, and the two cross just after each crest and trough of the Sine line.

faq.q: Why does LeadSine not turn first?
faq.html: Adding 45 degrees puts a line ahead only when the phase rises. Here the phase is the angle of the quadrature part over the in-phase part, and that angle falls as a cycle unfolds, so LeadSine reaches each value an eighth of a cycle after Sine. The line keeps the name LeadSine.

faq.q: Why do the lines stay flat for long stretches?
faq.html: A flat stretch means the measured phase stopped advancing, which happens when price trends instead of cycling. The wave only swings while there is a cycle to follow.

faq.q: Does the value say how far price will move?
faq.html: No. The lines are sines of an angle, always between -1 and +1, so they show timing within the cycle and nothing about its size.

related.title: Lunar Phase (LUNAR)
related.summary: The illuminated fraction of the moon at each bar's opening time, from 0 at new moon to 1 at full moon, with markers at the four main phases.

related.title: HT_PHASOR: Hilbert Transform Phasor Components
related.summary: The in-phase and quadrature components of the dominant cycle from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price, drawn as two lines.

related.title: Multilayer Perceptron Predictor
related.summary: A small neural network trained bar by bar on six price features, drawing its five-bar price prediction back on the bar it was made from.

ht-trendmode-hilbert-transform-trend-mod.title: HT_TRENDMODE: Hilbert Transform Trend Mode
ht-trendmode-hilbert-transform-trend-mod.summary: A step line that reads 1 when a Hilbert transform cycle measurement says the market is trending and 0 when it says the market is cycling.
ht-trendmode-hilbert-transform-trend-mod.descriptionHtml:
HT_TRENDMODE uses a Hilbert transform to measure the market's dominant cycle and then asks whether price is behaving like a cycle or like a trend.

The source (the typical price by default) is first smoothed with a four-bar weighted average and detrended with a short Hilbert filter whose bandwidth follows the current smoothed period. The same filter splits the result into an in-phase and a quadrature part, and advances each by 90 degrees. Those parts form a phasor, smoothed from bar to bar, and a homodyne discriminator turns the phase change between bars into a cycle period, held between 6 and 50 bars and smoothed again into the smoothed period.

Separately, the study tracks the phase of the cycle and how fast it is turning. A phase change smaller than 0.1 is ignored, and the last real change is kept instead. Two pi divided by that change, smoothed, is the instantaneous period. When the instantaneous period is more than 1.5 times the smoothed period, the phase is barely turning, which is how a trend looks, and the study reads 1. Otherwise it reads 0. All earlier values before the first bar count as zero, and the cycle state starts at a 15 bar period.
ht-trendmode-hilbert-transform-trend-mod.howToReadHtml:
Read the step line as a regime switch. A green 1 says the cycle measurement has stalled and price is trending, which suits trend-following tools. A red 0 says price is moving in measurable cycles, which suits oscillators and range methods.

The line is binary and can flip often when the market sits between the two regimes, so it works best as a filter for other tools rather than as a trade signal by itself. The first few dozen bars are spent filling the filters and settling the period estimate, so ignore the readings there.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the cycle is measured on. The default is the typical price, the average of high, low and close.

faq.q: What do 1 and 0 mean?
faq.html: 1 means the measured cycle has slowed so much that price is treated as trending. 0 means price is cycling at a measurable period.

faq.q: Why does the line flip back and forth sometimes?
faq.html: When the instantaneous period sits close to 1.5 times the smoothed period, small changes push it over and back. Those stretches are a market between regimes, not a clean trend or a clean cycle.

faq.q: Why should I ignore the first bars?
faq.html: The filters reach six bars back several times over and the period estimate starts from a fixed 15 bars, so it takes a while for the measurement to reflect the real data.

related.title: Ichimoku Cloud
related.summary: Five lines built from range midpoints, with a shaded cloud projected ahead of price that marks trend, support and resistance at a glance.

related.title: Gann High-Low Activator
related.summary: A trailing line built from short averages of the highs and lows that flips sides when price closes beyond it, with BUY and SELL marks on each flip.

related.title: PFE: Polarized Fractal Efficiency
related.summary: How directly price travelled over a lookback, from -100 to +100: the straight-line distance over the path actually walked, signed by direction.

hilbert-trendline-htit.title: Hilbert Trendline (HTIT)
hilbert-trendline-htit.summary: A trendline built from a twice smoothed price plus a small cyclic correction measured with a Hilbert transform.
hilbert-trendline-htit.descriptionHtml:
HTIT starts by smoothing the source twice with a four-bar weighted average. It then runs the smoothed price through a Hilbert transform, a set of four-tap filters that split it into an in-phase component and a quadrature component, ninety degrees apart. Comparing those components bar to bar gives an estimate of the dominant cycle period, smoothed and held between 6 and 50 bars, which scales the gain of every filter stage.

The phase of the in-phase and quadrature pair and their combined strength add a small cyclic correction to the smoothed price. The trendline then mixes that corrected value with its own previous value, so it follows the trend while the cycle swings around it.

The first bars are empty while the filters fill: the transform needs several bars of smoothed history before it answers.
hilbert-trendline-htit.howToReadHtml:
Use HTIT as the trend underneath the cycles. When price oscillates around a flat or gently sloping HTIT, the market is cycling; when price moves away and the line follows with a steady slope, it is trending. Crosses of price and the line mark shifts between the two.

Each bar the line is 0.9 of the corrected smoothed price plus 0.1 of its own previous value, so it stays close to the double smoothed price and turns with it rather than behaving like a long, slow average. The cycle estimate needs a stretch of bars to settle, so the earliest part of the line is less reliable.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Why is the start of the chart empty?
faq.html: The double smoothing and the Hilbert filters read several bars of history. Until those exist the values are absent and nothing is drawn.

faq.q: Does it have a length setting?
faq.html: No. The smoothing is fixed: two four-bar weighted averages, then a blend of 0.9 of the new value with 0.1 of the previous trendline. The measured cycle period, kept between 6 and 50 bars, only scales the gain of the Hilbert filters that size the cyclic correction.

faq.q: What does the cycle correction do?
faq.html: It adds a small amount, scaled by the cycle's strength and the sine of its phase, to the smoothed price before the trendline is updated, so the line accounts for where price is within the cycle.

related.title: Holt-Winters Moving Average (HWMA)
related.summary: Triple exponential smoothing that tracks level, velocity and acceleration, so the line keeps moving through a turn instead of flattening.

related.title: Holt Exponential Moving Average (HOLT)
related.summary: Double exponential smoothing that tracks a level and a trend and plots their sum, so the line lags less than a plain EMA while a move runs.

related.title: Integral of Linear Regression Slope (ILRS)
related.summary: Adds up the rolling least squares slope bar by bar, giving a price follower built from the speed of the trend.

huber-loss-huber.title: Huber Loss (HUBER)
huber-loss-huber.summary: The average Huber penalty of the gap between price and its own exponential average: squared for small gaps, linear for large ones.
huber-loss-huber.descriptionHtml:
Huber Loss measures how far the source has strayed from its exponential moving average, using a penalty that treats small and large gaps differently. On each bar the error is the source minus the average. While the size of that error is at or below Delta, the penalty is half the error squared. Beyond Delta the penalty grows only in proportion to the error: Delta times the size of the error, minus half of Delta squared.

The average is an exponential mean of the period, seeded with the simple average of its first period values, and it is drawn on the price chart. The penalties are then averaged over the last period bars, counting only bars that have a penalty, so the pane line starts on the same bar as the average.

Because large errors are penalised linearly, a single violent bar moves the reading far less than it would move a mean squared error.
huber-loss-huber.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means price has been hugging its average; a rising reading means it has been pulling away from it, either in a trend or in a burst of volatility. Spikes in the pane mark stretches where price ran far from the average line drawn on the chart.

Delta is in price units, so its meaning depends on the instrument. On an instrument that trades in the thousands, almost every gap is larger than the default Delta and the reading behaves like a scaled average absolute error. Raise Delta toward a typical bar range to bring the squared part into play.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window the penalties are averaged over. A longer period gives a slower reference and a smoother reading.

settings.label: Delta
settings.html: The error size, in price units, where the penalty switches from squared to linear. A larger value treats more gaps as small ones.

faq.q: Why use Huber loss instead of squared error?
faq.html: Squared error lets one very large gap dominate the average. The Huber penalty grows only linearly past Delta, so the reading reflects typical behaviour more than single outliers.

faq.q: What is the line on the price chart?
faq.html: It is the exponential average the errors are measured from, drawn on the price pane so you can see the gaps the pane is measuring.

faq.q: Why does the reading look like an absolute error on my chart?
faq.html: Delta is in price units. When nearly every gap is bigger than Delta, every penalty is on the linear side, so the result is close to Delta times the average absolute gap.

related.title: Log-Cosh Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of log(cosh(actual minus predicted)), an error measure that acts squared for small misses and linear for large ones.

related.title: Dirty Data Injection (DIRTY)
related.summary: Echoes a price series with regular gaps cut into it, so you can see how other studies cope with missing bars.

related.title: Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the arctangent of the absolute percentage error between two series, bounded between zero and pi/2.

hurst-exponent-hurst.title: Hurst Exponent (HURST)
hurst-exponent-hurst.summary: Rescaled range estimate of the Hurst exponent of recent log returns: above 0.5 reads as trending, below 0.5 as mean reverting.
hurst-exponent-hurst.descriptionHtml:
The Hurst exponent describes how a series wanders. A value of 0.5 is what a random walk gives, a value above 0.5 means moves tend to be followed by moves the same way, and a value below 0.5 means moves tend to be reversed.

The study estimates it by rescaled range analysis of the log returns, the natural log of each price over the one before. For every sub-period size n from 10 up to half the lookback, it cuts the lookback into as many sub-periods of n returns as fit, counted back from the current bar. For each sub-period it takes the running sum of the returns' deviations from their own mean, measures the range of that running sum, and divides by the standard deviation. The average of these rescaled ranges is paired with n. The exponent is the least squares slope of the log of the average rescaled range against the log of n.

A sub-period that reaches back before the first bar, that holds a missing return, or whose returns are all equal adds nothing but still counts in the average. The line therefore starts well before the lookback is full, from only the sub-periods that fit, and those early readings rest on few data points.
hurst-exponent-hurst.howToReadHtml:
Readings above 0.5 suggest the recent returns have been persistent, the behaviour a trend-following approach relies on. Readings below 0.5 suggest anti-persistence, where moves have tended to reverse. Readings near 0.5 suggest no memory either way.

The estimate is noisy, especially with a short lookback, and rescaled range analysis tends to read somewhat above 0.5 even on random data, so watch how the line changes rather than reading one value against 0.5 exactly. Long lookbacks are slow, because the work per bar grows with the square of the length.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose log returns are analysed. It must be positive.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The lookback, from 20 to 500 bars. Sub-periods run from 10 bars up to half of it. A longer lookback gives a steadier estimate but costs more work per bar.

faq.q: What does a value of 0.5 mean?
faq.html: That the returns behave like a random walk, with no tendency to continue or reverse. Above 0.5 they tend to continue, below 0.5 they tend to reverse.

faq.q: Why does the line start before the lookback is full?
faq.html: Sub-periods that reach before the first bar are skipped while still counting in each average, so a reading appears as soon as two sub-period sizes find at least one complete sub-period.

faq.q: Why is the minimum length 20?
faq.html: The smallest sub-period is 10 returns and the largest is half the lookback, so at least two sizes need a lookback of 20 or more.

related.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
related.summary: The distance between the 75th and the 25th percentile of the last N values, a measure of spread that ignores the extremes.

related.title: Harmonic Mean (HARMEAN)
related.summary: The harmonic mean of the last N positive values: the count divided by the sum of their reciprocals, a mean pulled toward the smaller readings.

related.title: Jarque-Bera Test (JB)
related.summary: A statistic that tests whether the last N values look normally distributed, built from their skewness and excess kurtosis.

historical-volatility-hv.title: Historical Volatility (HV)
historical-volatility-hv.summary: The population standard deviation of log returns over a rolling window, optionally scaled to an annual figure.
historical-volatility-hv.descriptionHtml:
Historical Volatility is the classic realised volatility measure. For each bar it takes the log return of the source, the natural logarithm of this value over the previous one, and keeps the last Length returns.

It then takes the population standard deviation of those returns: the average of the squared returns minus the square of their average, floored at zero, and the square root of that. Until the window is full it uses the returns available, so the line starts on the second bar, reading zero while there is only one return. With Annualize Volatility on, the result is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.
historical-volatility-hv.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means returns are becoming more spread out, a falling line means the market is calming. Compare the reading with its own history: a stretch near the bottom of its range marks a calm market, and a spike follows a burst of large returns.

Every return in the window counts equally and drops out all at once when it leaves, so a single large bar lifts the line for exactly Length bars and then lets it fall in one step. The default 252 periods suits daily bars; on other timeframes set Annual Periods to the bars in a year or switch annualising off.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose returns are measured, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many recent returns go into the standard deviation. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, the standard deviation is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: Bars in a year used for annualising: 252 for daily bars, 52 for weekly bars.

faq.q: Why does the line drop suddenly sometimes?
faq.html: A large return leaves the window all at once after Length bars, so the standard deviation falls in a single step on that bar.

faq.q: Is it a sample or a population standard deviation?
faq.html: Population: the squared deviations are divided by the number of returns, not by one less.

faq.q: Why is it zero on the second bar?
faq.html: With a single return there is nothing to spread around, so the standard deviation is zero until a second return arrives.

related.title: Jurik Volatility (JVOLTY)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio of an adaptive moving average, shown on its own: current movement over its smoothed average, floored at 1.

related.title: High-Low Volatility (HLV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log range of each bar, smoothed with a bias-corrected average and optionally annualised.

related.title: Normalized Jurik Volatility (JVOLTYN)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio passed through a logistic curve, so it reads 0.5 at normal pace and climbs towards 1 as movement grows.

holt-winters-moving-average-hwma.title: Holt-Winters Moving Average (HWMA)
holt-winters-moving-average-hwma.summary: Triple exponential smoothing that tracks level, velocity and acceleration, so the line keeps moving through a turn instead of flattening.
holt-winters-moving-average-hwma.descriptionHtml:
HWMA carries three numbers from bar to bar. The level is pulled toward the source with the weight 2 / (period + 1), starting from where the previous level, velocity and half the acceleration said it would be. The velocity is updated from the change in the level, and the acceleration from the change in the velocity, both with the weight 1 / period.

The plotted value is level plus velocity plus half the acceleration: a projection one bar ahead from the current level, velocity and acceleration. Modelling the acceleration lets the line bend with a curving move rather than lagging behind it.

The first bar sets the level to the source with zero velocity and acceleration, and shows the source unchanged.
holt-winters-moving-average-hwma.howToReadHtml:
Read HWMA as a trend line that projects its own motion forward. In a smooth trend it hugs price, and when a move starts to curve the acceleration term bends the line with it earlier than a simple average would.

Because it projects velocity and acceleration forward, it overshoots at abrupt reversals and can swing past price in a choppy range. A longer period damps all three terms and gives a calmer line; a short period makes it very responsive and noisy.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets all three smoothing weights. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line with less overshoot.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: What do velocity and acceleration mean here?
faq.html: Velocity is the smoothed change in the level per bar, and acceleration is the smoothed change in the velocity. Both are carried forward and added to the level to form the plotted value.

faq.q: Why does HWMA overshoot at reversals?
faq.html: It projects the current velocity and acceleration forward, so for a few bars after a sharp turn it still points in the old direction until the terms adjust.

related.title: Integral of Linear Regression Slope (ILRS)
related.summary: Adds up the rolling least squares slope bar by bar, giving a price follower built from the speed of the trend.

related.title: Hilbert Trendline (HTIT)
related.summary: A trendline built from a twice smoothed price plus a small cyclic correction measured with a Hilbert transform.

related.title: Jurik Moving Average (JMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that smooths harder in quiet markets and follows faster in volatile ones, with a phase control for lag versus overshoot.

ichimoku-cloud.title: Ichimoku Cloud
ichimoku-cloud.summary: Five lines built from range midpoints, with a shaded cloud projected ahead of price that marks trend, support and resistance at a glance.
ichimoku-cloud.descriptionHtml:
Ichimoku Cloud reads the market from the midpoints of recent ranges. Each of its averages is not a mean of closes but the average of the highest high and the lowest low over a window, so it follows where price has traded rather than where it closed.

The Conversion Line is the midpoint of the last 9 bars and the Base Line the midpoint of the last 26. Leading Span A is the average of those two lines, and Leading Span B is the midpoint of the last 52 bars. Both leading spans are drawn 25 bars ahead of the bar that computed them, so the cloud between them extends past the newest candle into the space on the right. The Lagging Span is the close drawn 25 bars back.

The cloud is shaded green where Leading Span A is above Leading Span B and red where it is below. With the default offsets the projection matches the classic displacement of 26, counting the current bar as the first.
ichimoku-cloud.howToReadHtml:
Price above the cloud is usually read as an uptrend and price below it as a downtrend; price inside the cloud is a market without a clear side. The cloud's edges act as support and resistance, and a thick cloud is a stronger barrier than a thin one.

A green cloud ahead of price means the shorter midpoint leads the longer one, a red cloud the reverse, and a change of colour in the projected part is an early sign that the balance is shifting. Many traders also watch the Conversion Line crossing the Base Line, and check that the Lagging Span sits clear of the candles from 25 bars ago before trusting a move. Like every trend tool it lags in a sideways market, where the lines tangle and the cloud flips often.

settings.label: Conversion Line Length
settings.html: Bars in the window for the Conversion Line, the fastest midpoint. Shorter lengths react to price sooner.

settings.label: Base Line Length
settings.html: Bars in the window for the Base Line. It also feeds Leading Span A, which averages the Conversion and Base lines.

settings.label: Leading Span B Length
settings.html: Bars in the window for Leading Span B, the slowest midpoint and the cloud's longer edge.

settings.label: Cloud Offset
settings.html: How many bars ahead the leading spans and the cloud are drawn. 25 matches a displacement of 26.

settings.label: Lagging Span Offset
settings.html: How many bars back the close is drawn, written as a negative number. -25 matches a displacement of 26.

faq.q: Why are there two offset settings instead of one displacement?
faq.html: In OpenScript a plot's offset is fixed before the first bar and can take a setting only as its whole value, not a calculation on it. Projecting the cloud forward and the Lagging Span back needs two different numbers, so each is its own setting. The defaults, 25 and -25, give the classic displacement of 26.

faq.q: Why does the cloud continue past the last candle?
faq.html: The leading spans are drawn 25 bars after the bar that computed them, so the most recent values land in the space to the right of the newest candle. That projected part of the cloud is known now and does not change as new bars arrive.

faq.q: Why is the Lagging Span missing on the most recent bars?
faq.html: It is the close drawn 25 bars back, so the last 25 bars have no close yet to show there.

faq.q: What do the colours of the cloud mean?
faq.html: Green where Leading Span A is above Leading Span B, red where it is below. The colour says which midpoint leads, not where price is.

related.title: PFE: Polarized Fractal Efficiency
related.summary: How directly price travelled over a lookback, from -100 to +100: the straight-line distance over the path actually walked, signed by direction.

related.title: HT_TRENDMODE: Hilbert Transform Trend Mode
related.summary: A step line that reads 1 when a Hilbert transform cycle measurement says the market is trending and 0 when it says the market is cycling.

related.title: Qstick Indicator
related.summary: A moving average of the candle body, close minus open, that reads whether bars have been closing above or below where they opened.

inverse-fast-fourier-transform-ifft.title: Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT)
inverse-fast-fourier-transform-ifft.summary: Rebuilds price from only the slowest frequency components of a Hann-windowed transform, a smooth line that ignores fast swings.
inverse-fast-fourier-transform-ifft.descriptionHtml:
This study takes the last N bars of the source, tapers them with a Hann window, and splits them into frequency components with a Fourier transform. It keeps only the constant (DC) term and the lowest harmonics components, throws the faster ones away, and sums what is left back into a single value for the current bar. The result is a low-pass filtered version of price drawn on the chart.

Because both the forward transform and the rebuild run over the same windowed samples, the whole calculation reduces to one weighted sum of the last N bars, with a fixed weight per lag: the Hann taper times 1 + 2 * sum(cos(2 * pi * k * n / N)) over the kept harmonics, divided by N. The study builds those weights once and applies them on every bar. Bars before the first one count as zero, so the line answers from the first bar but only settles once N bars of history exist.
inverse-fast-fourier-transform-ifft.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the slow shape of price. Fewer harmonics give a smoother line that follows only the broad swings, while more harmonics let it follow shorter cycles more closely. A larger window gives finer frequency resolution, so each kept harmonic describes a longer cycle.

The Hann taper weights the middle of the window most and gives the current bar a weight of zero, so the line describes the window as a whole rather than the newest bar, and it lags turns in price. During the first N bars the window is padded with zeros, so the line starts near zero and climbs towards price; ignore that stretch.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series that is transformed and rebuilt.

settings.label: Window Size
settings.html: How many bars enter the transform: 32, 64 or 128. Any other value is read as 64. A larger window resolves longer cycles and gives a smoother line.

settings.label: Harmonics
settings.html: How many of the lowest-frequency components are kept, up to half the window. Fewer harmonics give a smoother line.

faq.q: Why does the line start near zero?
faq.html: Bars before the first one count as zero, so for the first N bars the window is partly empty and the weighted sum is too small. The line is meaningful once N bars of history exist.

faq.q: Why does the window accept only 32, 64 or 128?
faq.html: The transform is set up for those three sizes. Any other value falls back to 64.

faq.q: Is this a forecast?
faq.html: No. Every value is built from the current and past bars only, and a value never changes once its bar has closed.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JERK)
related.summary: Three chained rolling regressions, slope then acceleration then jerk, showing how quickly a trend's acceleration is itself changing.

related.title: Weighted Close (HLCC4)
related.summary: Draws the weighted close of each bar, the average of high, low and the close counted twice, as one line over the candles.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JOLT)
related.summary: The slope of acceleration from three nested rolling least squares fits, measuring how fast a trend's curvature is changing.

intraday-intensity-index-iii.title: Intraday Intensity Index (III)
intraday-intensity-index-iii.summary: Signs each bar's volume by where the close sits in the bar's range, then averages it over a window or adds it into a running total.
intraday-intensity-index-iii.descriptionHtml:
The Intraday Intensity Index reads where each bar closed inside its own range. The position multiplier is (2 x close - high - low) / (high - low): +1 when the bar closes on its high, -1 when it closes on its low, and 0 when it closes exactly in the middle. That multiplier is applied to the bar's volume, floored at 1, so every bar contributes a share of its volume with the sign of its close. A bar with no range contributes zero.

In the default mode the values are summed over the last Period bars and divided by the full period from the first bar, so the early readings are damped rather than absent. With Cumulative Mode on, the values are instead added into a running total from the first bar, which turns the study into an accumulation line.
intraday-intensity-index-iii.howToReadHtml:
In the default mode, a reading above zero means bars have tended to close in the upper part of their range on their volume, a sign of buying pressure; below zero means closes near the lows. The size of the reading tells you how much volume sat behind that pressure.

In Cumulative Mode, read the slope rather than the level. A rising line means volume keeps closing near the highs; a line that falls while price rises suggests the advance is not being supported. The first Period bars of the default mode are smaller than they would be later, because the sum is divided by the full period before the window has filled.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars summed and divided in the default mode. A longer period gives a smoother line; it has no effect in Cumulative Mode.

settings.label: Cumulative Mode
settings.html: Off: plot the windowed average. On: plot the running total of every bar's signed volume from the first bar.

faq.q: Why are the first readings smaller than the rest?
faq.html: The window sum is always divided by the full period, so until the window has filled it is divided by more bars than it holds and the values are damped.

faq.q: What does a bar that closes mid-range add?
faq.html: Nothing. A close exactly halfway between the high and the low has a multiplier of zero, whatever the volume.

faq.q: Why is volume floored at 1?
faq.html: So the study still draws on a series that carries no volume: each bar then counts its close position with a weight of one.

related.title: Klinger Volume Oscillator (KVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of trend-signed volume force, with a signal line and a coloured histogram.

related.title: Elastic Volume Weighted Moving Average (EVWMA)
related.summary: A moving average that steps toward price by each bar's share of recent volume, so heavy bars move it far and quiet bars barely move it.

related.title: Money Flow Index (MFI)
related.summary: A volume-weighted strength oscillator from 0 to 100 that compares money flowing in on rising bars with money flowing out on falling bars.

integral-of-linear-regression-slope-ilrs.title: Integral of Linear Regression Slope (ILRS)
integral-of-linear-regression-slope-ilrs.summary: Adds up the rolling least squares slope bar by bar, giving a price follower built from the speed of the trend.
integral-of-linear-regression-slope-ilrs.descriptionHtml:
The Integral of Linear Regression Slope fits a least squares straight line to the last period prices on every bar and keeps only its slope, the average change per bar over the window. It then adds that slope to a running total that starts at the first price. The line is the running sum, or integral, of trend speed.

When price rises steadily the slope is positive and the line climbs at the same rate; when price falls it declines. Until the window is full the slope is fitted to the bars seen so far, and on the first bar the line equals the price. A missing price counts as zero in the fit.
integral-of-linear-regression-slope-ilrs.howToReadHtml:
Read the ILRS as a smooth price follower. Its direction is the sign of the regression slope, so a rising line means the fitted trend over the window points up and a falling line means it points down. It turns as soon as the slope changes sign, which is earlier than most averages of the same length.

Because it is a running total of slopes rather than an average of prices, it can drift away from price over a long chart, so judge it by its direction and turns rather than by its level relative to the close.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the regression is fitted to, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the regression window. A longer window gives a steadier slope that changes direction later.

faq.q: Why does the line not always sit near price?
faq.html: It is built by adding up slopes from the first price, not by averaging prices, so small differences accumulate and the line can drift apart from the close over a long chart.

faq.q: How does it relate to a least squares moving average?
faq.html: Both fit a straight line to the window. The least squares average plots the fitted value at the newest bar; this line adds up the fitted slope from bar to bar.

faq.q: What does a flat line mean?
faq.html: The regression slope is near zero, so prices across the window show no clear rising or falling trend.

related.title: Jurik Moving Average (JMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that smooths harder in quiet markets and follows faster in volatile ones, with a phase control for lag versus overshoot.

related.title: Holt-Winters Moving Average (HWMA)
related.summary: Triple exponential smoothing that tracks level, velocity and acceleration, so the line keeps moving through a turn instead of flattening.

related.title: Kaiser Window Moving Average (KAISER)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by the Kaiser window, with a beta setting that shapes how fast the weights taper.

intraday-momentum-index-imi.title: Intraday Momentum Index (IMI)
intraday-momentum-index-imi.summary: An oscillator from 0 to 100 built from candle bodies: the share of the period's body size that came from bars closing above their open.
intraday-momentum-index-imi.descriptionHtml:
The Intraday Momentum Index works like a relative strength reading, but it compares each bar's close with its own open rather than with the previous close. A bar that closed above its open adds its body (close minus open) to the gains; a bar that closed below its open adds its body (open minus close) to the losses. A bar that closed exactly at its open adds nothing.

The study keeps running totals of the gains and losses over the last period bars. Bars before the first count as zero, so the line starts on the first bar with a shorter window. The plotted value is 100 times the gains divided by the gains plus the losses. When there are no bodies at all in the window, it reads 50.
intraday-momentum-index-imi.howToReadHtml:
Readings above 50 mean more of the period's body size came from up bars, buying inside the bars; readings below 50 mean selling did. Values near 70 and above are often treated as overbought and values near 30 and below as oversold, and turns from those zones as the signal.

Because it ignores gaps between bars, the IMI can disagree with a close-to-close oscillator when price gaps and then drifts the other way within the bars. That disagreement is the information it adds. Short periods make it swing hard.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars whose bodies are added up. A shorter period makes the oscillator react faster and reach its extremes more often.

faq.q: How is it different from RSI?
faq.html: RSI measures changes from one close to the next. IMI measures each bar's close against its own open, so moves that happen as gaps between bars do not count.

faq.q: Why does it read exactly 50 sometimes?
faq.html: When every bar in the window closed at its open there are no bodies to compare, and the study reads that as neutral, 50.

faq.q: Does it need intraday bars?
faq.html: No. It works on any interval; each bar's open and close are what it reads, whatever length of time the bar covers.

related.title: Inertia
related.summary: The distance between the source and the end of a least-squares line fitted through its recent values, positive when price runs ahead of its trend.

related.title: Williams Gator Oscillator
related.summary: Two histograms that show how far apart the three displaced alligator lines have moved: wide bars for a trending market, bars near zero for a quiet one.

related.title: KDJ
related.summary: A stochastic oscillator with three lines: K smooths the raw stochastic, D smooths K, and J leads both by extrapolating their gap.

inertia.title: Inertia
inertia.summary: The distance between the source and the end of a least-squares line fitted through its recent values, positive when price runs ahead of its trend.
inertia.descriptionHtml:
Inertia fits a straight line by least squares through the last values of the source, one value per bar, and takes the value of that line on the current bar. The plotted figure is the source minus that value: how far price sits above or below its own recent trend line.

The window is the length, or every bar so far when fewer bars exist, so the line starts on the first bar rather than after a warmup. A one-bar window has no slope, and the study reads it as 0. A missing value inside the window counts as zero in the fit, and a missing value on the current bar leaves the plot blank.
inertia.howToReadHtml:
Positive values mean price has run ahead of the straight line through the recent bars, and negative values mean it has lagged behind. A value near zero means price is sitting on its trend line, whichever way that line slopes. Large readings show price stretched away from its trend, which often precedes either an acceleration or a pull back toward the line.

The value is in price units, so compare it with its own history. A short length tracks small swings and turns often, while a long length measures the stretch away from a broader trend.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars the regression line is fitted through. On the opening bars the window is shorter, limited to the bars available.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the line is fitted to and compared with.

faq.q: Does a positive value mean the trend is up?
faq.html: No. It means price is above its own trend line, which can slope up or down. A falling market that bounces can read positive while the line still slopes down.

faq.q: Why does the first bar read zero?
faq.html: On the first bar the window holds a single value, and a one-value fit has no slope, so the study reads it as zero.

faq.q: What units is it in?
faq.html: The units of the source, usually price. The same reading means a bigger stretch on a low-priced instrument than on a high-priced one.

related.title: KDJ
related.summary: A stochastic oscillator with three lines: K smooths the raw stochastic, D smooths K, and J leads both by extrapolating their gap.

related.title: Intraday Momentum Index (IMI)
related.summary: An oscillator from 0 to 100 built from candle bodies: the share of the period's body size that came from bars closing above their open.

related.title: Kairi Relative Index (KRI)
related.summary: The percentage distance of price from its own simple moving average, so zero is the average and the extremes show how stretched price has become.

interquartile-range-iqr.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
interquartile-range-iqr.summary: The distance between the 75th and the 25th percentile of the last N values, a measure of spread that ignores the extremes.
interquartile-range-iqr.descriptionHtml:
The Interquartile Range is the width of the middle half of the values in the lookback window. The study collects the source values from the last length bars, sorts them, and finds the first quartile (the 25th percentile) and the third quartile (the 75th percentile). The plotted value is the third quartile minus the first.

Each percentile is found by linear interpolation: its rank is the percentage times one less than the number of values, and when that rank falls between two sorted values the answer is taken that fraction of the way from the lower to the upper one.

Missing values are skipped, and on the first bars the window simply holds every value so far, so the line has a reading from the first bar. Because the top and bottom quarters of the window are ignored, one extreme bar moves the IQR far less than it moves a standard deviation.
interquartile-range-iqr.howToReadHtml:
A wider IQR means the bulk of recent prices is spread over a larger range, and a narrower one means the market has been trading in a tight band. Because the extremes are left out, a single spike barely changes it, so a rising IQR points to a broad widening of the range rather than one outlier.

The value is in price units, so compare it with its own history on the same instrument. It measures spread only and says nothing about direction.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose spread is measured, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window gives a steadier reading that reacts more slowly.

faq.q: Why use the IQR instead of a standard deviation?
faq.html: The IQR looks only at the middle half of the window, so a single extreme bar has little effect. A standard deviation squares every distance, so one outlier can dominate it.

faq.q: How are the quartiles found when they fall between two values?
faq.html: By linear interpolation between the two neighbouring sorted values, in proportion to how far the rank falls between them.

faq.q: Why does it read zero on the first bar?
faq.html: The window holds a single value, so both quartiles are that value and the range between them is zero.

related.title: Jarque-Bera Test (JB)
related.summary: A statistic that tests whether the last N values look normally distributed, built from their skewness and excess kurtosis.

related.title: Hurst Exponent (HURST)
related.summary: Rescaled range estimate of the Hurst exponent of recent log returns: above 0.5 reads as trending, below 0.5 as mean reverting.

related.title: Kendall Rank Correlation (KENDALL)
related.summary: Kendall's tau between two series over the last N bars: +1 when they always move the same way, -1 when they always move apart.

jarque-bera-test-jb.title: Jarque-Bera Test (JB)
jarque-bera-test-jb.summary: A statistic that tests whether the last N values look normally distributed, built from their skewness and excess kurtosis.
jarque-bera-test-jb.descriptionHtml:
The Jarque-Bera statistic measures how far the shape of a sample departs from a normal distribution. It combines two numbers: the skewness, which says whether the values lean to one side, and the excess kurtosis, which says whether the tails are fatter or thinner than normal. Both are zero for a normal distribution.

The study takes the last length values, finds their mean, and computes the second, third and fourth central moments. The skewness is the third moment over the standard deviation cubed, and the excess kurtosis is the fourth moment over the standard deviation to the fourth power, minus 3. The statistic is the sample size over 6, times the squared skewness plus a quarter of the squared excess kurtosis.

The line starts once the window is full. A window with a missing value, or with almost no spread, gives no reading. Three reference lines mark the critical values of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom: 4.605 for the 10% level, 5.991 for 5% and 9.21 for 1%.
jarque-bera-test-jb.howToReadHtml:
A reading below 4.605 means the test does not reject normality for the window even at the 10% level. A reading above 5.991 means the window departs from normal at the 5% level, and above 9.21 at the 1% level, usually because of a sharp move that skewed the window or fattened its tails. Spikes often mark the bars where a large move entered the window.

The test is built for independent samples, and consecutive prices are not independent, so treat the levels as a guide to unusual shape rather than a formal test. The test is applied to the source values as they are, not to their returns, so on a price source it describes the shape of the recent prices in the window.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose distribution is tested, such as the close.

settings.label: Lookback Period (Sample Size)
settings.html: How many bars form the sample, from 10 to 200. A larger sample gives a steadier statistic that reacts more slowly.

faq.q: What do the three horizontal lines mean?
faq.html: They are the chi-squared critical values with two degrees of freedom at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels. A reading above a line rejects normality at that level.

faq.q: Why are there gaps in the line?
faq.html: A window that contains a missing value, or whose values barely vary, has no meaningful skewness or kurtosis, so the study draws nothing on that bar.

faq.q: Does a high reading predict direction?
faq.html: No. It says the window's shape is unusual, not which way price will move next.

related.title: Kendall Rank Correlation (KENDALL)
related.summary: Kendall's tau between two series over the last N bars: +1 when they always move the same way, -1 when they always move apart.

related.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
related.summary: The distance between the 75th and the 25th percentile of the last N values, a measure of spread that ignores the extremes.

related.title: Kurtosis, tailedness (KURTOSIS)
related.summary: Excess kurtosis of the last N values: above zero when the window has fatter tails and a sharper peak than a normal distribution.

jurik-volatility-bands-jbands.title: Jurik Volatility Bands (JBANDS)
jurik-volatility-bands-jbands.summary: Upper and lower bands that snap to a bar's extreme when price pushes through and otherwise fall back at a rate set by relative volatility.
jurik-volatility-bands-jbands.descriptionHtml:
These bands follow the bar midpoint with an asymmetric rule. When the midpoint rises above the previous upper band, the upper band jumps to the bar's high. Otherwise the upper band is set above the bar's high by a share of the gap between the previous upper band and the midpoint, so it eases down toward price. The lower band does the mirror image with the low. Both bands start at the first source value.

Volatility on a bar is the larger of the two distances from the midpoint to the previous bands. The study keeps a ten-bar running sum of that volatility, scaled by a constant from the period (one tenth at a period of 10 or less, which makes it a ten-bar average), and a slow exponential average of that sum. Relative volatility, this bar's volatility over that average, held between one and a cap set by the period, sets the share of the gap a band keeps: higher relative volatility shrinks the share, so the band falls back toward price faster.

The constants that shape the response come only from the period, so a longer period keeps a larger share of the gap and gives bands that hold their level longer.
jurik-volatility-bands-jbands.howToReadHtml:
The upper band hugs the highs in a rally and the lower band hugs the lows in a decline, while the opposite band lags behind. The gap between them is a measure of recent range. A band that suddenly closes in on price after a quiet spell shows volatility picking up.

When price pushes through a band it snaps to the bar's extreme, so a series of snaps on one side marks a persistent move. The bands are adaptive and can change shape quickly, so read them alongside the price structure.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the constants that shape how quickly the bands fall back and the cap on relative volatility. Longer periods give slower, steadier bands.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose first value seeds both bands, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the upper band sometimes jump straight to the high?
faq.html: When the bar midpoint rises above the upper band, the rule sets the band to that bar's high instead of easing toward it.

faq.q: What does relative volatility do?
faq.html: It compares this bar's distance from the bands with its recent average. Higher values let the bands close the gap to price faster, up to a cap set by the period.

faq.q: Where does the source setting come in?
faq.html: Only in the starting value of both bands. After the first bar the bands follow the bar's high, low and midpoint.

related.title: Keltner Channel (KCHANNEL)
related.summary: An exponential average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below, drawn from the first bar.

related.title: Fractal Chaos Bands (FCB)
related.summary: Bands at the highest recent three-bar fractal high and the lowest recent fractal low, with optional marks on the fractal bars.

related.title: MA Envelope (MAE)
related.summary: A moving average with two bands set a fixed percentage above and below it, so the channel scales with price rather than with volatility.

acceleration-slope-of-slope-jerk.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JERK)
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jerk.summary: Three chained rolling regressions, slope then acceleration then jerk, showing how quickly a trend's acceleration is itself changing.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jerk.descriptionHtml:
Jerk is the third step in a chain of rolling regressions. The first fits a straight line to the source over the last Period bars and takes its slope, the trend's speed. The second fits a line to that slope series, giving acceleration. The third fits a line to the acceleration series, and its slope is the plotted jerk.

Each fit is a rolling least squares line over the last Period bars, where the x value is the bar number. The sums behind it are kept as running totals: each bar adds the newest point and removes the one that left the window. A bar whose value is absent still takes its place in the window but adds nothing to the sums, and a slope needs at least two valid points.

Each stage starts once the stage before it has produced two values, so the jerk line begins on the fourth bar of the chart.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jerk.howToReadHtml:
Jerk above zero means acceleration is rising; below zero it is falling. Its zero crossings mark the turning points of acceleration, which tend to come ahead of the turning points of the slope, which in turn come ahead of the trend. That makes it an early but noisy warning that the character of a move is shifting.

Each derivative amplifies noise, so expect a busy line on short periods and fast charts. The values are in price units per bar cubed and scale with the instrument, so compare readings only within one chart.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars each of the three regression lines is fitted over. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the first regression is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: What does jerk add over acceleration?
faq.html: Acceleration tells you whether the trend is speeding up. Jerk tells you whether that speeding up is itself increasing or fading, so it turns before acceleration does, at the cost of more noise.

faq.q: Why is the line so noisy?
faq.html: Every regression stage measures a rate of change of the stage before it, and each one magnifies small wiggles. A longer period calms all three stages at once.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JOLT)
related.summary: The slope of acceleration from three nested rolling least squares fits, measuring how fast a trend's curvature is changing.

related.title: Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT)
related.summary: Rebuilds price from only the slowest frequency components of a Hann-windowed transform, a smooth line that ignores fast swings.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Rescales the source around its own moving average with a scale and an offset, stretching or damping every excursion from the mean.

jurik-moving-average-jma.title: Jurik Moving Average (JMA)
jurik-moving-average-jma.summary: An adaptive average that smooths harder in quiet markets and follows faster in volatile ones, with a phase control for lag versus overshoot.
jurik-moving-average-jma.descriptionHtml:
JMA measures volatility as how far price sits outside a pair of adaptive bands from the previous bar. That volatility is summed over ten bars and then given its own slow exponential average, and the ratio of the current volatility to that average is the relative volatility, held between 1 and a cap set by the period.

Relative volatility sets the smoothing for the bar: the base weight from the period and Power is raised to a power of the relative volatility, so a quiet bar is smoothed heavily and a volatile bar lets price through. The bands themselves are tightened toward price by the same measure.

The line passes through three stages: an adaptive average, a lead added from the difference between price and that average scaled by the phase, and a final adaptive filter that settles the result.
jurik-moving-average-jma.howToReadHtml:
JMA is a smooth trend line that stays flat in a quiet range and moves quickly once a real move starts. Its slope is the trend; price crossing it with the line turning is a change of direction.

Phase trades lag against overshoot. A negative phase holds the line back and smooths it, a positive phase pushes it toward price and makes it overshoot at turns. Power sets the overall smoothness: lower values give a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars the smoothing is built around. A longer period gives a smoother line and allows a larger volatility range.

settings.label: Phase
settings.html: From -100 to 100. Negative values reduce overshoot and add lag, positive values cut lag and add overshoot.

settings.label: Power
settings.html: From 0.1 to 1. Lower values make the base smoothing heavier and the curve smoother.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Why does JMA stay flat in some stretches?
faq.html: When volatility is low relative to its own average, the smoothing weight becomes very heavy and the line barely moves. That is the intended behaviour in a quiet range.

faq.q: What does Phase do?
faq.html: It scales a lead term added between the first and last stages. Raising it brings the line closer to price at the cost of overshoot at turns; lowering it does the opposite. The input tooltip says negative values reduce lag, but in the calculation it is a higher Phase that adds more of the lead term and brings the line closer to price.

faq.q: Does it need a warmup?
faq.html: No. Every stage starts from the first price, so the line is drawn from the first bar. The volatility average takes a while to settle, so the early adaptivity is rougher.

related.title: Kaiser Window Moving Average (KAISER)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by the Kaiser window, with a beta setting that shapes how fast the weights taper.

related.title: Integral of Linear Regression Slope (ILRS)
related.summary: Adds up the rolling least squares slope bar by bar, giving a price follower built from the speed of the trend.

related.title: Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA)
related.summary: An average whose speed follows the efficiency ratio: it tracks a clean trend closely and flattens out when price chops back and forth.

acceleration-slope-of-slope-jolt.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JOLT)
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jolt.summary: The slope of acceleration from three nested rolling least squares fits, measuring how fast a trend's curvature is changing.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jolt.descriptionHtml:
Jolt is built from three nested rolling regressions over the same lookback. The first fits a straight line to the source over the last Period bars and takes its slope. The second fits a line to that slope series to give acceleration, the curvature of the trend. The third fits a line to the acceleration and plots its slope, the rate at which the curvature changes.

Each fit is a rolling least squares line over the last Period bars, where the x value is the bar number. The sums behind it are kept as running totals: each bar adds the newest point and removes the one that left the window. A bar whose value is absent still takes its place in the window but adds nothing to the sums, and a slope needs at least two valid points.

Each stage needs two values from the stage before it, so the jolt line begins on the fourth bar of the chart.
acceleration-slope-of-slope-jolt.howToReadHtml:
Positive jolt means the trend's acceleration is increasing, negative means it is decreasing. A swing of jolt through zero marks a peak or trough in acceleration, which usually comes before the slope and then the price turn. Use it as an early hint that a move is changing character, and confirm it with the slope or with price.

Because it is a third difference, jolt is noisy and its values scale with the instrument's price. Longer periods give a steadier line; very short ones mostly show noise.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The lookback used by each of the three least squares slope passes. A longer period smooths every stage.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the first slope is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: Is jolt the same as jerk?
faq.html: It is the same calculation: three chained least squares slopes over one lookback. The two names describe the third derivative of price with respect to time.

faq.q: Where does the line start?
faq.html: On the fourth bar. The first fit needs two bars, the second needs two slopes and the third needs two acceleration values.

faq.q: Should I trade its zero crossings alone?
faq.html: No. A third derivative turns often and early. Its crossings are best used as a warning that the trend's curvature is changing, read together with the trend itself.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Rescales the source around its own moving average with a scale and an offset, stretching or damping every excursion from the mean.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JERK)
related.summary: Three chained rolling regressions, slope then acceleration then jerk, showing how quickly a trend's acceleration is itself changing.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Applies y = a * (x - SMA) + SMA + b to the source, so the scale reshapes swings around the average and the offset shifts the line.

jurik-volatility-jvolty.title: Jurik Volatility (JVOLTY)
jurik-volatility-jvolty.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio of an adaptive moving average, shown on its own: current movement over its smoothed average, floored at 1.
jurik-volatility-jvolty.descriptionHtml:
This study shows the volatility term that drives an adaptive moving average. It keeps two bands that follow the source: on each bar it measures how far the source sits from the upper band and from the lower band, and the larger distance is that bar's raw volatility.

The raw volatility is summed over a ten bar window, scaled by a factor that depends on Period, and then smoothed by a slow exponential mean whose weight is 2 / (max(4 times Period, 65) + 1). The plotted value is the raw volatility divided by that smoothed average, floored at 1 and capped at a ceiling that also depends on Period.

The ratio feeds back into the bands: when it is high the bands are pulled towards the source faster, so the next bar's distances are measured from a tighter reference. A bar that sets a new extreme moves the band to the source outright.
jurik-volatility-jvolty.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 1 means price is moving at or below its usual pace. Readings above 1 mean the latest move is larger than the recent average, and the higher the line, the more unusual the move. The line cannot rise above its cap, which is about 2.8 at the default period, so sustained readings near the top mark strong expansion.

Use it to tell quiet stretches from active ones. It does not show direction. Because the smoothing is slow, the line can stay at 1 for long periods and then jump when activity returns.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the band adaptation speed, the slow smoothing weight and the cap on the ratio. Larger periods give a slower average and a lower cap: about 6.3 at a period of 5, 2.8 at 10 and 2.2 at 20.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the bands follow, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line sit at exactly 1 so often?
faq.html: The ratio is floored at 1, so any bar that moves no more than the smoothed average reads 1. The one exception is a Period of 1, where the cap works out to zero and the line reads 0 from the second bar on.

faq.q: What sets the upper limit?
faq.html: The cap is computed from Period. At the default of 10 it is about 2.8; shorter periods allow a higher ceiling and longer periods a lower one.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is going up?
faq.html: No. It measures how far price moved from its adaptive bands in either direction, so a sharp drop reads as high as a sharp rise.

related.title: Normalized Jurik Volatility (JVOLTYN)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio passed through a logistic curve, so it reads 0.5 at normal pace and climbs towards 1 as movement grows.

related.title: Historical Volatility (HV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of log returns over a rolling window, optionally scaled to an annual figure.

related.title: Mass Index (MASSI)
related.summary: Sums the ratio of a single to a double exponential average of the bar range, so a widening range shows as a bulge in the line.

normalized-jurik-volatility-jvoltyn.title: Normalized Jurik Volatility (JVOLTYN)
normalized-jurik-volatility-jvoltyn.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio passed through a logistic curve, so it reads 0.5 at normal pace and climbs towards 1 as movement grows.
normalized-jurik-volatility-jvoltyn.descriptionHtml:
This study takes the adaptive volatility ratio of an adaptive moving average and squashes it into a bounded range. The ratio is built from two bands that follow the source: on each bar the larger distance from the source to either band is the raw volatility. That raw value is summed over ten bars, scaled by a factor that depends on Period, and smoothed by a slow exponential mean. The ratio is the raw volatility over that average, floored at 1 and capped at a ceiling set by Period.

The plotted value is 1 / (1 + e^(-1.5 (ratio - 1))). A ratio of 1 gives exactly 0.5, and larger ratios rise towards 1 along a smooth curve. As with the unbounded version, the ratio feeds back into the bands, pulling them towards the source faster when movement is high.
normalized-jurik-volatility-jvoltyn.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 0.5 means price is moving at or below its usual pace, which is where the line spends most of its time. Rises above 0.5 mark bars that moved further than the recent average, and readings near 0.94 mark the strongest expansion the cap allows at the default period.

The bounded scale makes it easy to set fixed thresholds or to compare instruments. It does not show direction, and because the underlying average is slow the line can rest at 0.5 for long stretches before jumping when activity returns.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the band adaptation speed, the slow smoothing weight and the cap on the ratio before it is squashed.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the bands follow, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line never fall below 0.5?
faq.html: The underlying ratio is floored at 1, and the logistic curve maps a ratio of 1 to exactly 0.5. At a Period of 1 the cap on the ratio works out to zero, so from the second bar on the ratio is 0 and the line reads about 0.18.

faq.q: How high can it go?
faq.html: It is limited by the cap on the ratio. At the default period of 10 the ratio stops near 2.8, which maps to roughly 0.94.

faq.q: How is this different from Jurik Volatility (JVOLTY)?
faq.html: The calculation is the same; this version passes the ratio through a logistic curve so it stays between 0.5 and 1 instead of running from 1 up to its cap.

related.title: Mass Index (MASSI)
related.summary: Sums the ratio of a single to a double exponential average of the bar range, so a widening range shows as a bulge in the line.

related.title: Jurik Volatility (JVOLTY)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio of an adaptive moving average, shown on its own: current movement over its smoothed average, floored at 1.

related.title: Normalized Average True Range
related.summary: The average true range expressed as a percentage of the close, so volatility compares across instruments and price levels.

kaiser-window-moving-average-kaiser.title: Kaiser Window Moving Average (KAISER)
kaiser-window-moving-average-kaiser.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by the Kaiser window, with a beta setting that shapes how fast the weights taper.
kaiser-window-moving-average-kaiser.descriptionHtml:
The Kaiser Window Moving Average weights the bars of its window with the Kaiser window, a symmetric bell built from the modified Bessel function of order zero. Each weight is I0(beta * sqrt(1 - t^2)) / I0(beta), where t runs from -1 on the oldest bar to 1 on the newest, and I0 is summed as a 25-term power series. The weights are computed once and scaled to sum to one.

The beta setting shapes the window. At 0 every weight is equal and the line is a simple moving average; as beta rises the weights concentrate on the centre of the window and the edges fade, so bars entering or leaving the window move the line less. Until the window holds period bars the line sits on the price, and a missing price counts as zero.
kaiser-window-moving-average-kaiser.howToReadHtml:
Read the KAISER line as a smooth trend line whose character you choose with beta. A low beta behaves like a simple average, with a step in the line whenever a large bar leaves the window. A higher beta fades the edges so those steps disappear, and puts more of the weight on fewer central bars. Whatever the beta, the weights are symmetric, so the line describes the middle of its window and runs about half a window behind price.

Use it for the direction and slope of the trend. The first bars, where the line equals price, carry no smoothing.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window. A longer window smooths more and lags more.

settings.label: Beta (shape)
settings.html: How sharply the weights taper from the centre. 0 gives equal weights; higher values concentrate weight on the middle bars.

faq.q: What does beta 0 give?
faq.html: Equal weights on every bar of the window, which is a simple moving average.

faq.q: Which beta should I use?
faq.html: The default of 3 is a general setting. Around 5.65 the taper resembles a Blackman window and around 8.6 a Hamming-like shape. Higher values concentrate the weight on the middle bars; the delay stays about half a window at every setting.

faq.q: Why does the line equal price at the start?
faq.html: Until the window holds the full period the weights cannot be applied, so the line returns the price itself.

related.title: Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA)
related.summary: An average whose speed follows the efficiency ratio: it tracks a clean trend closely and flattens out when price chops back and forth.

related.title: Jurik Moving Average (JMA)
related.summary: An adaptive average that smooths harder in quiet markets and follows faster in volatile ones, with a phase control for lag versus overshoot.

related.title: Lanczos (Sinc) Window Moving Average (LANCZOS)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by one lobe of the sinc function, peaking at the centre of the window.

kalman-filter-kalman.title: Kalman Filter (KALMAN)
kalman-filter-kalman.summary: Smooths price with a one-dimensional Kalman filter, where process noise and measurement noise decide how much each new bar moves the line.
kalman-filter-kalman.descriptionHtml:
This study treats price as a noisy reading of a hidden level and keeps a running estimate of that level. Each bar it predicts that the level has not moved, adds the process noise Q to the uncertainty of that prediction, and then corrects the estimate toward the new price by a gain.

The gain is p / (p + R), where p is the uncertainty after the prediction and R is the measurement noise. A large gain means the new price is trusted and the line moves most of the way to it; a small gain means the price is treated as noise and the line barely moves. After the correction the uncertainty shrinks by the share the gain used. The estimate starts at the first price with an uncertainty of 1, and a missing price reading counts as zero.

After a few bars the uncertainty settles to a steady value set only by Q and R, so the filter behaves like a smoothing average whose speed you set through those two numbers.
kalman-filter-kalman.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the filtered price level. When price stays above it and it slopes up, the hidden level is rising; when price stays below it and it slopes down, the level is falling. The distance between price and the line shows how much of the latest move the filter has dismissed as noise.

Raise Q or lower R and the line follows price closely with little lag but more wiggle. Lower Q or raise R and it becomes smoother and slower. The filter assumes a level that does not trend, so in a strong steady move it will lag behind price.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

settings.label: Process Noise (Q)
settings.html: How much the hidden level is assumed to move by itself each bar. Larger values make the line track price more closely.

settings.label: Measurement Noise (R)
settings.html: How noisy each price reading is assumed to be. Larger values trust each bar less and smooth the line more.

faq.q: What matters more, Q or R?
faq.html: Their balance. Raising Q relative to R speeds the line up; raising R relative to Q slows it down. Moving both together in the same direction changes the line much less.

faq.q: Why does the line start exactly on the first price?
faq.html: The estimate is seeded with the first price and an uncertainty of 1, then corrected on every later bar.

faq.q: Is this a prediction of the next bar?
faq.html: No. It is an estimate of the current underlying level using the bars so far. The prediction step inside the filter only assumes the level stays where it was.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KF)
related.summary: Treats price as a noisy reading of a hidden level and tracks that level, with the balance of process noise and measurement noise setting its speed.

related.title: Highpass Filter (2-Pole) (HPF)
related.summary: Strips out price swings shorter than a chosen cycle length with a two-pole highpass filter and draws the smooth trend that is left behind.

related.title: Ehlers Laguerre Filter (LAGUERRE)
related.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother on price with one damping setting, giving a smooth trend line from very few bars of history.

kaufman-s-adaptive-moving-average-kama.title: Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA)
kaufman-s-adaptive-moving-average-kama.summary: An average whose speed follows the efficiency ratio: it tracks a clean trend closely and flattens out when price chops back and forth.
kaufman-s-adaptive-moving-average-kama.descriptionHtml:
KAMA adapts its smoothing to how directional price has been. The efficiency ratio divides the net move over the period, the distance from the source period bars ago to now, by the total distance travelled bar by bar over the same bars. A straight run gives a ratio near 1; a choppy stretch that goes nowhere gives a ratio near 0.

The ratio slides the smoothing constant between a slow weight 2 / (slow + 1) and a fast weight 2 / (fast + 1), and the result is squared. Each bar the line moves toward price by that constant times the gap. Until enough bars exist to measure the ratio it reads as 0, so the line starts at the first price and moves at the slow rate.

The fast period must give a larger weight than the slow period. If it does not, the settings are refused and the line is left empty.
kaufman-s-adaptive-moving-average-kama.howToReadHtml:
In a clean trend KAMA follows price closely, and in a sideways market it goes nearly flat. That makes a flat KAMA a sign of a range and a KAMA that starts to slope a sign that a directional move has begun.

Price can cross a flat KAMA many times inside a range, so a cross means more once the line itself has started to slope. The line can also be slow to react at the very start of a trend, while the efficiency ratio is still low.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars over which the efficiency ratio is measured. A longer period reacts more slowly to changes in directionality.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

settings.label: Fast EMA Period
settings.html: The length whose weight the line uses in a perfectly efficient trend. Smaller values let it chase price harder.

settings.label: Slow EMA Period
settings.html: The length whose weight the line uses in pure noise. Larger values make it flatter in a range.

faq.q: Why does KAMA go flat?
faq.html: When price moves back and forth without net progress, the efficiency ratio is near 0 and the smoothing constant falls to the slow weight squared, which is very small, so the line hardly moves.

faq.q: Why is the line empty with some settings?
faq.html: The fast period has to produce a larger weight than the slow period. If the fast period is not shorter than the slow period the settings are refused and nothing is drawn.

faq.q: Why is the smoothing constant squared?
faq.html: Squaring makes the line react far more to efficiency than a straight blend would. With the default fast and slow periods of 2 and 30, the constant is about 0.004 at an efficiency ratio of 0, about 0.13 at 0.5 and about 0.44 at 1, so the line barely moves in noise.

related.title: Lanczos (Sinc) Window Moving Average (LANCZOS)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by one lobe of the sinc function, peaking at the centre of the window.

related.title: Kaiser Window Moving Average (KAISER)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by the Kaiser window, with a beta setting that shapes how fast the weights taper.

related.title: Leader EMA (LEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average plus a smoothed copy of its own tracking error, so it leans ahead of a plain EMA of the same period.

keltner-channel-kchannel.title: Keltner Channel (KCHANNEL)
keltner-channel-kchannel.summary: An exponential average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below, drawn from the first bar.
keltner-channel-kchannel.descriptionHtml:
This channel places bands around an exponential moving average at a distance set by the average true range. The middle line keeps a running sum and a running weight that both decay by the exponential factor, and divides one by the other, so on the first bar it equals the source and it needs no seed window.

The true range of a bar is the largest of its high minus its low, the distance from its high to the previous close and the distance from its low to the previous close. The study smooths it with a running average whose weight is one over the length, starting from zero, and divides out the weight that zero start still holds, so the average true range is unbiased from the first bar.

The upper band is the middle line plus the multiplier times the average true range, and the lower band is the middle line minus it.
keltner-channel-kchannel.howToReadHtml:
In a steady trend price tends to stay on one side of the middle line and lean on one band. A close outside the channel is a move larger than the typical bar range would suggest, which trend traders read as strength and range traders as stretch. Some traders treat a pullback to the middle line inside a trend as an entry area.
