Because the width comes from true range rather than closing deviation, the channel does not widen just because closes drift away from the average, and it does widen on gaps. It still lags a sharp turn by roughly the length.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the middle exponential average follows, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the true range smoothing. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges the bands sit from the middle line. Larger values give a wider channel.

faq.q: Why is the channel present from the first bar?
faq.html: Both the average and the true range smoothing correct for their zero start, so they have usable values from bar one.

faq.q: How is this different from a standard deviation band?
faq.html: The width comes from bar ranges and gaps instead of from how far closes stray from the mean, so a steady drift in closes does not widen it, while gaps and large bars do.

faq.q: What is the first bar's true range?
faq.html: With no previous close, the first bar compares against its own close, so its true range is its high minus its low.

related.title: MA Envelope (MAE)
related.summary: A moving average with two bands set a fixed percentage above and below it, so the channel scales with price rather than with volatility.

related.title: Jurik Volatility Bands (JBANDS)
related.summary: Upper and lower bands that snap to a bar's extreme when price pushes through and otherwise fall back at a rate set by relative volatility.

related.title: Min-Max Channel (MMCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and the lowest low of the lookback window drawn as a channel, marking the levels a breakout has to clear.

kdj.title: KDJ
kdj.summary: A stochastic oscillator with three lines: K smooths the raw stochastic, D smooths K, and J leads both by extrapolating their gap.
kdj.descriptionHtml:
KDJ starts from the raw stochastic value: where the close sits between the lowest low and the highest high of the last length bars, scaled from 0 to 100. On the opening bars the window holds every bar so far, so the lines start on the first bar. When the window has no range, the raw value reads 50.

K is a running average of the raw value with weight 1 / signal, and D is the same running average applied to that K average before its correction. Both averages start from zero, and while each is filling it is divided by the weight it has gathered so far. For K that removes the bias of the zero start. D, however, smooths the uncorrected K, which is itself still biased toward zero, so on the opening bars D sits well below K (at the default settings D opens at a third of K). Both plotted lines are held inside 0 to 100.

J is three times K minus twice D. It moves further and faster than either, and it can travel outside 0 to 100. Because D starts low, J opens far above 100 and only settles once D has caught up, after a few multiples of the signal setting.
kdj.howToReadHtml:
K above D is the bullish order and K below D the bearish one, and their crossings are the usual signal. The dashed lines at 80 and 20 mark the overbought and oversold zones for K, and 70 and 30 those for D. J reaching above 100 or below 0 shows a stretched move, and because it extends the gap between K and D it is the first of the three lines to turn.

Like any stochastic, KDJ can stay overbought through a strong uptrend and oversold through a strong downtrend, so read its extremes together with the trend. Ignore the opening bars, where D is still catching up with K.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars for the highest high and lowest low. A shorter length makes the raw stochastic swing more.

settings.label: signal
settings.html: The smoothing for K and D: each uses a running average with weight one divided by this number. Larger values give smoother, slower lines.

faq.q: Why can J go above 100 or below 0?
faq.html: J is three times K minus twice D. When K moves away from D, J extends the gap, so it can leave the range that K and D are held inside.

faq.q: Why does D start so far below K, and J so far above 100?
faq.html: D is a running average of the uncorrected K, and that K is still pulled toward its zero start on the opening bars. The correction applied to D removes only D's own start-up bias, not the one it inherits, so D opens low and J, which subtracts twice D, opens high. Both settle after a few multiples of the signal setting.

faq.q: How is K different from a plain stochastic %K?
faq.html: K is the raw stochastic smoothed by a running average with weight one divided by the signal setting, so each new raw value moves it by that fraction of the gap. With the default of 3 it moves a third of the way toward each new raw value.

kdj.deviation: The smoothing setting is labelled signal in lower case rather than Signal, because signal is a built-in name in OpenScript, so the setting cannot be assigned to a name of its own and is keyed by its label instead.

related.title: Kairi Relative Index (KRI)
related.summary: The percentage distance of price from its own simple moving average, so zero is the average and the extremes show how stretched price has become.

related.title: Inertia
related.summary: The distance between the source and the end of a least-squares line fitted through its recent values, positive when price runs ahead of its trend.

related.title: KST Oscillator (KST)
related.summary: Four rates of change over increasing lookbacks, each smoothed and summed with weights 1 to 4, plus a smoothed signal line.

kendall-rank-correlation-kendall.title: Kendall Rank Correlation (KENDALL)
kendall-rank-correlation-kendall.summary: Kendall's tau between two series over the last N bars: +1 when they always move the same way, -1 when they always move apart.
kendall-rank-correlation-kendall.descriptionHtml:
Kendall rank correlation measures whether two series tend to rise and fall together, using only the order of their values, not their size. The study takes the last period bars of both series and compares every pair of bars in that window. A pair is concordant when both series changed in the same direction between the two bars, and discordant when they changed in opposite directions. A pair where either series did not change counts as neither.

The reading, tau, is the number of concordant pairs minus the number of discordant pairs, divided by the total number of pairs, period * (period - 1) / 2. It runs from -1 to +1.

Both series come from the instrument on the chart, by default the close and the volume. A missing value in either series anywhere in the window gives no reading on that bar, and the line starts once the window is full.
kendall-rank-correlation-kendall.howToReadHtml:
A reading near +1 means the two series have been ranked the same way across the window: when one was higher, so was the other. A reading near -1 means they have moved in opposite directions, and a reading near 0 means there is no consistent relationship. Because only the order of the values counts, one extreme bar cannot dominate the result the way it can in an ordinary correlation.

With the default inputs the study asks whether price and volume have tended to rise together over the window. It measures association, not cause.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: The first series compared, the close by default.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: The second series compared, the volume by default. Both series come from the instrument on the chart.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars form the window, from 2 to 60. Every pair is compared, so the work grows with the square of this number.

faq.q: How is it different from an ordinary correlation?
faq.html: An ordinary correlation uses the values themselves, so one large move can swing it. Kendall's tau looks only at whether each pair of bars moved the same way, so it is steadier when the window contains outliers.

faq.q: Why can it not reach exactly +1 when the series look aligned?
faq.html: Pairs where either series did not change count as neither concordant nor discordant but still count in the total, which pulls the reading toward zero.

faq.q: Why is the period capped at 60?
faq.html: Every pair of bars in the window is compared on every bar, so the work grows with the square of the period. The cap keeps the study quick.

related.title: Kurtosis, tailedness (KURTOSIS)
related.summary: Excess kurtosis of the last N values: above zero when the window has fatter tails and a sharper peak than a normal distribution.

related.title: Jarque-Bera Test (JB)
related.summary: A statistic that tests whether the last N values look normally distributed, built from their skewness and excess kurtosis.

related.title: Linear Regression (LINREG)
related.summary: The end point of a least squares line fitted through the last N values, the price the recent trend says this bar should have.

kalman-filter-kf.title: Kalman Filter (KF)
kalman-filter-kf.summary: Treats price as a noisy reading of a hidden level and tracks that level, with the balance of process noise and measurement noise setting its speed.
kalman-filter-kf.descriptionHtml:
This study keeps an estimate of a hidden price level and its uncertainty, and updates both on every bar. First it predicts: the level is assumed unchanged, and the uncertainty grows by the process noise Q. Then it corrects: the estimate moves toward the new price by a gain of p / (p + R), where p is the predicted uncertainty and R the measurement noise, and the uncertainty shrinks by the same share.

The estimate is seeded on the first bar with that bar's price and an uncertainty of 1, and seeded again if it ever goes missing. A missing price reading counts as zero.

After the first few bars the uncertainty reaches a steady value fixed by Q and R, and from then on the line moves a constant share of the way toward each new price. In that state it behaves like an exponential average whose speed comes from the two noise settings rather than from a bar count.
kalman-filter-kf.howToReadHtml:
Treat the line as the price level once noise is filtered out. Its slope shows the direction of that level, and the gap between price and the line shows how much of the newest move the filter has not yet believed. Price holding on one side of the line for several bars is a sign that the level itself is moving.

A larger Q follows price more closely, and a larger R smooths it more. Because the model assumes a level with no built-in trend, the line lags a strong steady move and catches up once the move slows.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series treated as the noisy measurement, the close by default.

settings.label: Process Noise (Q)
settings.html: How much the hidden level is assumed to move on its own each bar. Larger values track price more closely.

settings.label: Measurement Noise (R)
settings.html: How noisy each price reading is assumed to be. Larger values smooth the output more.

faq.q: How do I make the line smoother?
faq.html: Lower Q or raise R. Either change tells the filter to trust each new bar less, so it moves a smaller share of the way toward each price.

faq.q: Why does it behave like an exponential average after a while?
faq.html: The uncertainty settles to a fixed value set by Q and R, so the gain becomes constant. A constant gain applied to each new price is exactly an exponential average.

faq.q: Does the line change once a bar has closed?
faq.html: No. Each value depends only on the current and earlier bars.

related.title: Ehlers Laguerre Filter (LAGUERRE)
related.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother on price with one damping setting, giving a smooth trend line from very few bars of history.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KALMAN)
related.summary: Smooths price with a one-dimensional Kalman filter, where process noise and measurement noise decide how much each new bar moves the line.

related.title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter (LMS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that predicts each bar from the bars before it and keeps adjusting its own weights toward whatever would have been right.

kairi-relative-index-kri.title: Kairi Relative Index (KRI)
kairi-relative-index-kri.summary: The percentage distance of price from its own simple moving average, so zero is the average and the extremes show how stretched price has become.
kairi-relative-index-kri.descriptionHtml:
The Kairi Relative Index answers one question: how far, in percent, is price from its average? On each bar it takes a simple moving average of the source over the period and plots 100 times (source minus average) divided by the average.

The average starts on the first bar. Until the period has filled, it is the average of every value so far, so the line has no warmup gap. A missing source value enters the average as zero. If the average is exactly zero, the study reads 0.
kairi-relative-index-kri.howToReadHtml:
Zero means price sits on its average. Positive values show price above the average by that many percent, and negative values below it. Large readings mark price stretched far from its mean, which traders often read as a setup for a pull back toward the average, especially when the reading turns back.

There are no fixed overbought or oversold levels: how far is far depends on the instrument and the period. Look at the extremes the line has reached on the same chart before, and remember that in a strong trend price can stay stretched for a long time.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the simple moving average. A longer period gives a slower average and larger percentage readings.

faq.q: Why are percentages used instead of price?
faq.html: A percentage distance means the same thing at any price level, so readings can be compared across instruments and across years of one chart.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The average uses every value so far until a full period is available, so there is always an average to compare with.

faq.q: What counts as an extreme reading?
faq.html: It depends on the market's volatility and the period. Mark the levels where the line has turned before on the same chart and interval, and use those.

related.title: KST Oscillator (KST)
related.summary: Four rates of change over increasing lookbacks, each smoothed and summed with weights 1 to 4, plus a smoothed signal line.

related.title: KDJ
related.summary: A stochastic oscillator with three lines: K smooths the raw stochastic, D smooths K, and J leads both by extrapolating their gap.

related.title: LRSI: Laguerre RSI
related.summary: An RSI built from four cascaded Laguerre filter stages instead of a lookback window, reading 0 to 1 and turning within a couple of bars.

kst-oscillator-kst.title: KST Oscillator (KST)
kst-oscillator-kst.summary: Four rates of change over increasing lookbacks, each smoothed and summed with weights 1 to 4, plus a smoothed signal line.
kst-oscillator-kst.descriptionHtml:
The KST Oscillator blends momentum over four horizons into one line. It takes four rates of change of the source, in percent, over the ROC periods (10, 15, 20 and 30 bars by default). Until a lookback exists, the earlier value reads as zero and that rate of change reads zero.

Each rate of change is smoothed by its own simple average (10, 10, 10 and 15 bars by default), and the four smoothed rates are added with weights 1, 2, 3 and 4, so the longer horizons count for more. The Signal line is a simple average of KST over the signal period.

Every simple average here starts on the first bar: until its window has filled, it averages every value so far. A missing source value counts as zero.
kst-oscillator-kst.howToReadHtml:
KST above zero means momentum across the four horizons is positive overall, and below zero negative. A cross of KST above its Signal line is read as momentum turning up and a cross below as momentum turning down; crossings of zero show a change in the broader momentum. Divergence between KST and price, such as a new price high with a lower KST peak, warns that the move is weakening.

Because it is built from long lookbacks and heavy smoothing, KST is slow, and its signals suit swings rather than single bars. The opening stretch of bars, before the longest lookback and smoothing have filled, is a warmup.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the rates of change are measured on.

settings.label: ROC Period 1
settings.html: Lookback of the shortest rate of change, which carries weight 1.

settings.label: ROC Period 2
settings.html: Lookback of the second rate of change, which carries weight 2.

settings.label: ROC Period 3
settings.html: Lookback of the third rate of change, which carries weight 3.

settings.label: ROC Period 4
settings.html: Lookback of the longest rate of change, which carries weight 4.

settings.label: SMA Smooth 1
settings.html: Length of the simple average applied to the first rate of change.

settings.label: SMA Smooth 2
settings.html: Length of the simple average applied to the second rate of change.

settings.label: SMA Smooth 3
settings.html: Length of the simple average applied to the third rate of change.

settings.label: SMA Smooth 4
settings.html: Length of the simple average applied to the fourth rate of change.

settings.label: Signal Period
settings.html: Length of the simple average of KST that forms the Signal line.

faq.q: Why are the longer rates weighted more?
faq.html: The weights 1, 2, 3 and 4 make the slower horizons dominate, so the line follows the broader swing while the shorter rates help it turn sooner.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Each average uses every value so far until its window fills, and a rate of change without its lookback reads zero, so there is always a value. The first stretch of bars is still a warmup.

faq.q: Is KST bounded?
faq.html: No. It is a weighted sum of percentages, so its range depends on how volatile the instrument is. Read its crossings and turns rather than a fixed level.

related.title: LRSI: Laguerre RSI
related.summary: An RSI built from four cascaded Laguerre filter stages instead of a lookback window, reading 0 to 1 and turning within a couple of bars.

related.title: Kairi Relative Index (KRI)
related.summary: The percentage distance of price from its own simple moving average, so zero is the average and the extremes show how stretched price has become.

related.title: MARKETFI: Market Facilitation Index
related.summary: The bar's high-to-low range divided by its volume: how much price movement each traded unit bought on that bar.

kurtosis-tailedness-kurtosis.title: Kurtosis, tailedness (KURTOSIS)
kurtosis-tailedness-kurtosis.summary: Excess kurtosis of the last N values: above zero when the window has fatter tails and a sharper peak than a normal distribution.
kurtosis-tailedness-kurtosis.descriptionHtml:
Kurtosis measures how much of a window's spread comes from a few values far from the mean rather than from many values near it. This study reports excess kurtosis, which is the fourth central moment divided by the squared variance, minus 3. A normal distribution reads 0, a window with fatter tails reads above 0, and a flatter, more even window reads below 0.

The study keeps running sums of the values and of their squares, cubes and fourth powers over the last period bars, adding the value entering and removing the value leaving. From those sums it forms the mean, the variance and the fourth central moment. It waits until the window holds at least four values, and a window with no spread at all reads 0.

Missing values are left out of the sums, so the window holds fewer points rather than breaking.
kurtosis-tailedness-kurtosis.howToReadHtml:
A reading well above zero means the window has had a few unusually large moves relative to its typical spread, which is what traders call fat tails. A reading near or below zero means the values are spread more evenly, with no outliers standing out. A spike often marks the bar where a sudden jump entered the window, and it drops again when that bar leaves.

The measure is noisy on short windows, because a single value can dominate the fourth power. It describes the shape of the window, not the direction of the trend.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. At least four are needed. A longer window gives a steadier reading.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose distribution is measured, such as the close.

faq.q: Why can the value be negative?
faq.html: This is excess kurtosis, with 3 subtracted so that a normal distribution reads 0. A window flatter than normal, with no outliers, reads below 0.

faq.q: Why does it jump and then fall back?
faq.html: A single large value raises the fourth moment sharply while it is in the window. Once it slides out of the window, the reading drops.

faq.q: Why are the first few bars empty?
faq.html: A kurtosis needs at least four values. The study waits for four before it draws.

related.title: Linear Regression (LINREG)
related.summary: The end point of a least squares line fitted through the last N values, the price the recent trend says this bar should have.

related.title: Kendall Rank Correlation (KENDALL)
related.summary: Kendall's tau between two series over the last N bars: +1 when they always move the same way, -1 when they always move apart.

related.title: Mean Deviation (MEANDEV)
related.summary: The average absolute distance of the last N values from their own mean, a measure of spread that does not square the outliers.

klinger-volume-oscillator-kvo.title: Klinger Volume Oscillator (KVO)
klinger-volume-oscillator-kvo.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of trend-signed volume force, with a signal line and a coloured histogram.
klinger-volume-oscillator-kvo.descriptionHtml:
The Klinger Volume Oscillator turns volume into a signed force and compares its short-term and long-term flow. The trend is +1 while the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, is rising against the previous bar and -1 while it is falling; an unchanged bar keeps the previous trend. The bar's volume is multiplied by that trend and by a weight taken from where the close sits in the bar's range (0 when the close is exactly mid-range, 1 when it is on the high or the low), giving the volume force. A bar with no range carries no force.

The force is smoothed by a fast and a slow exponential mean, and the KVO line is the fast mean minus the slow one. A signal line is an exponential mean of the KVO line, and the histogram is the KVO line minus the signal, drawn green at or above zero and red below. Each mean starts from zero and is divided by one minus its decayed seed weight during the early bars, so the lines read true from the first bar.
klinger-volume-oscillator-kvo.howToReadHtml:
A KVO line above zero means the short-term flow of volume force is stronger than the long-term flow in the up direction; below zero, in the down direction. The usual signals are the KVO line crossing its signal line, shown by the histogram changing colour, and the KVO line crossing the zero line.

Divergence is the other common reading: price making a new high while the KVO line makes a lower one suggests the volume behind the move is fading. The values are in units of volume, so compare them only with the oscillator's own history on the same symbol.

settings.label: Fast EMA Period
settings.html: The length of the fast exponential mean of volume force. A shorter value makes the KVO line react faster.

settings.label: Slow EMA Period
settings.html: The length of the slow exponential mean that the fast one is measured against. A longer value sets a steadier baseline.

settings.label: Signal Line Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential mean of the KVO line that forms the signal line and, with it, the histogram.

faq.q: What does the histogram colour mean?
faq.html: Green when the KVO line is at or above its signal line, red when it is below. A change of colour is a crossing of the two lines.

faq.q: Why does the trend not change on a flat bar?
faq.html: The trend only flips when the typical price rises or falls. A bar with the same typical price as the one before keeps the previous direction.

faq.q: Why are the early values not pulled toward zero?
faq.html: Each exponential mean starts at zero, and during the early bars it is divided by a correction that removes the effect of that start.

related.title: Money Flow Index (MFI)
related.summary: A volume-weighted strength oscillator from 0 to 100 that compares money flowing in on rising bars with money flowing out on falling bars.

related.title: Intraday Intensity Index (III)
related.summary: Signs each bar's volume by where the close sits in the bar's range, then averages it over a window or adds it into a running total.

related.title: Negative Volume Index (NVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume fell against the bar before.

ehlers-laguerre-filter-laguerre.title: Ehlers Laguerre Filter (LAGUERRE)
ehlers-laguerre-filter-laguerre.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother on price with one damping setting, giving a smooth trend line from very few bars of history.
ehlers-laguerre-filter-laguerre.descriptionHtml:
The Laguerre Filter passes price through four stages. The first stage is an exponential smoothing with factor 1 - Gamma. Each later stage is an all-pass section that takes the stage above it and its own previous value, delaying the signal a little more without smoothing it away. The plotted value is a weighted mix of the four, (L0 + 2 * L1 + 2 * L2 + L3) / 6.

The single setting, Gamma, controls how much each stage leans on its past. At 0 the filter is a plain weighted average of the last four prices. As Gamma rises toward 1 each stage holds on to its history more, so the line gets smoother and slower.

All four stages start at the first price, so the line begins on the first bar at the price itself.
ehlers-laguerre-filter-laguerre.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed price whose speed you set with one number. Its slope gives the direction of the trend, and a turn in the line marks a turn in the swing at the scale Gamma implies. Price holding above a rising line fits an uptrend; price holding below a falling line fits a downtrend.

Because the filter reaches a smooth result from only four stages, it reacts faster than a long moving average of similar smoothness, but it still lags. High values of Gamma lag a lot and can miss quick reversals; low values follow price closely and show more noise.

settings.label: Gamma
settings.html: The damping factor from 0 to 0.99. 0 gives a short weighted average; higher values smooth more and lag more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: What happens at a Gamma of 0?
faq.html: Each stage simply passes on the previous stage's last value, so the line becomes a fixed weighted average of the last four prices with weights 1, 2, 2 and 1.

faq.q: Why does it need so little history?
faq.html: The smoothing comes from the four recursive stages rather than from a long window, so it answers from the first bar.

faq.q: How is it different from the adaptive version?
faq.html: Here the damping factor is fixed by Gamma. The adaptive version recomputes it every bar from how far the filter has fallen behind price.

related.title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter (LMS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that predicts each bar from the bars before it and keeps adjusting its own weights toward whatever would have been right.

related.title: Kalman Filter (KF)
related.summary: Treats price as a noisy reading of a hidden level and tracks that level, with the balance of process noise and measurement noise setting its speed.

related.title: LOESS Filter
related.summary: Fits a tricube-weighted straight line through a short window of recent prices and draws the value of that line at the centre of the window.

lanczos-sinc-window-moving-average-lancz.title: Lanczos (Sinc) Window Moving Average (LANCZOS)
lanczos-sinc-window-moving-average-lancz.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by one lobe of the sinc function, peaking at the centre of the window.
lanczos-sinc-window-moving-average-lancz.descriptionHtml:
The Lanczos Window Moving Average weights the bars of its window with one lobe of the sinc function, sin(pi * x) / (pi * x). The position x runs from -1 on the oldest bar to 1 on the newest, so the weight is 1 at the centre of the window and falls smoothly to zero at both ends. The weights are computed once and scaled to sum to one. With a period of 2 both weights fall at the ends of the lobe and are effectively zero, so they are left unscaled and the line sits near zero once the window fills; use a period of 3 or more.

On every bar the last period prices are multiplied by their weights and added up. Until the window is full the line sits on the price itself, and a missing price counts as zero. The smooth roll-off at the edges keeps the line free of the steps a flat average shows when a large bar enters or leaves the window.
lanczos-sinc-window-moving-average-lancz.howToReadHtml:
Read the LANCZOS line as a smooth trend line. Its weights peak in the middle of the window, so it runs roughly half a window behind price and turns well after price does. In exchange its path is clean, with little reaction to single large bars.

Use it for the direction and slope of the trend rather than for timing. Because the newest and oldest bars carry almost no weight, the latest close barely moves the line until later bars arrive.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window. A longer window smooths more and lags more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: What shape are the weights?
faq.html: One lobe of the sinc function: 1 at the centre of the window, falling smoothly to zero at the oldest and newest bars.

faq.q: Why does the newest close barely move the line?
faq.html: The sinc lobe gives almost no weight to the ends of the window, and the newest bar is at one end. Its effect grows as it moves toward the centre.

faq.q: Why does the line equal price at the start?
faq.html: Until the window holds the full period the weights cannot be applied, so the line returns the price itself.

related.title: Leader EMA (LEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average plus a smoothed copy of its own tracking error, so it leans ahead of a plain EMA of the same period.

related.title: Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA)
related.summary: An average whose speed follows the efficiency ratio: it tracks a clean trend closely and flattens out when price chops back and forth.

related.title: Least Squares Moving Average (LSMA)
related.summary: Fits a least squares straight line to the last N prices and plots its value at the current bar.

leader-ema-lema.title: Leader EMA (LEMA)
leader-ema-lema.summary: An exponential average plus a smoothed copy of its own tracking error, so it leans ahead of a plain EMA of the same period.
leader-ema-lema.descriptionHtml:
LEMA starts with an exponential average of the source using the weight 2 / (period + 1). It then measures that average's tracking error, the source minus the average, and smooths the error with a second exponential average of the same weight. The line is the first average plus the smoothed error.

Adding the error back pulls the line toward price in the direction it has been lagging, so it leans ahead of a plain exponential average without losing its smoothness.

Both averages start from zero and on the early bars are divided by 1 - beta^n, where beta is one minus the weight. That removes the pull toward zero, so the line follows price from the first bar. An absent source reads as zero.
leader-ema-lema.howToReadHtml:
Use LEMA as a quicker exponential average. It sits closer to price during a trend and turns earlier when the trend ends, so a cross of price through LEMA or of LEMA through a slower average comes sooner than it would with a plain one.

The lead comes from adding the smoothed error back, so after a sudden spike LEMA can briefly run ahead of price before settling. On very noisy charts use a longer period.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of both exponential averages. A longer period gives a smoother line with a smaller lead.

faq.q: How is LEMA different from a double exponential average?
faq.html: Once the early-bar correction has faded they give the same line. Smoothing the error source - EMA with an exponential average equals the EMA of the source minus the EMA of the EMA, so the sum is 2 * EMA - EMA(EMA), the double exponential formula. LEMA reaches it by smoothing the tracking error, and only the first bars differ, because each stage is corrected for its zero start separately.

faq.q: Why is the line drawn from the first bar?
faq.html: Both averages are scaled by 1 / (1 - beta^n) while they are young, which removes the bias of starting at zero, so no warmup gap is needed.

related.title: Least Squares Moving Average (LSMA)
related.summary: Fits a least squares straight line to the last N prices and plots its value at the current bar.

related.title: Lanczos (Sinc) Window Moving Average (LANCZOS)
related.summary: A symmetric moving average weighted by one lobe of the sinc function, peaking at the centre of the window.

related.title: Linear Time Moving Average (LTMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average over the period: the newest bar counts the full period, the oldest counts one, and older bars fade out evenly.

linear-transformation-linear.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
linear-transformation-linear.summary: Rescales the source around its own moving average with a scale and an offset, stretching or damping every excursion from the mean.
linear-transformation-linear.descriptionHtml:
The Linear Transformation applies y = a * (x - average) + average + b to the source on every bar. The average is a simple moving average of the source over smaPeriod bars. The scale a multiplies the distance between the source and that average, and the offset b moves the whole result up or down.

With a above 1 every swing away from the average is exaggerated, with a between 0 and 1 it is damped, and with a negative a the series is mirrored about its average. The average itself is never moved except by the offset. While fewer than smaPeriod bars exist, the average is taken over every bar so far, so the line answers from the first bar.
linear-transformation-linear.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the source with its deviations from the mean scaled by a and then shifted by b. Where the source crosses its average the transformed line passes through the average plus b. Where the source is far from its average, the transformed line is a times as far.

The study adds no new information about direction; it reshapes the series so that small departures from the mean are easier or harder to see. During the first smaPeriod bars the average is built from a shorter history, so values there are less settled than later ones.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series that is rescaled about its own moving average.

settings.label: SMA Period
settings.html: How many bars the moving average covers. A longer average is smoother, so more of the price movement counts as deviation.

settings.label: Scale (a)
settings.html: Multiplies the distance between the source and its average. Above 1 stretches swings, between 0 and 1 damps them, and below 0 mirrors them.

settings.label: Offset (b)
settings.html: A constant added to every value, which moves the whole line up or down without changing its shape.

faq.q: What happens with a scale of 1 and an offset of 0?
faq.html: The output equals the source exactly, because the distance from the average is added back unchanged.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until smaPeriod bars exist, the average is taken over every bar seen so far, so there is always an average to scale around.

faq.q: What does a negative scale do?
faq.html: It mirrors the series about its moving average: a bar above the average is plotted the same distance below it, times the size of the scale.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Applies y = a * (x - SMA) + SMA + b to the source, so the scale reshapes swings around the average and the offset shifts the line.

related.title: Acceleration, Slope of Slope (JOLT)
related.summary: The slope of acceleration from three nested rolling least squares fits, measuring how fast a trend's curvature is changing.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Plots the natural logarithm of the source in its own pane, so equal percentage moves take up equal vertical distance.

lineartrans.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
lineartrans.summary: Applies y = a * (x - SMA) + SMA + b to the source, so the scale reshapes swings around the average and the offset shifts the line.
lineartrans.descriptionHtml:
This Linear Transformation rescales a series about its own simple moving average. On every bar it computes the average of the source over period bars, takes the distance between the source and that average, multiplies the distance by the scale a, adds the average back and finally adds the offset b.

The result changes how large the swings around the average look: a scale above 1 exaggerates them, a scale between 0 and 1 shrinks them towards the average, and a negative scale flips them to the other side. While fewer than period bars exist, the average is taken over every bar so far, so the line has a value from the first bar.
lineartrans.howToReadHtml:
Treat the line as a reshaped copy of the source. Its distance from the average plus b is always a times the source's distance from the average. Because the average moves too, a peak or trough of the line can fall on a different bar from the matching turn in the source when a is not 1. A large scale makes small departures from the mean easy to see, and a small scale keeps the line close to the trend.

The offset is useful for placing the line where it does not overlap another study in the same pane. The first period bars use a shorter average, so those values settle as more history arrives.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series that is rescaled about its own moving average.

settings.label: SMA Period
settings.html: How many bars the moving average covers. A longer period gives a slower average and larger deviations to scale.

settings.label: Scale (a)
settings.html: Multiplies the distance from the average. Values above 1 stretch the swings, values between 0 and 1 damp them, and negative values mirror them.

settings.label: Offset (b)
settings.html: A constant added to every bar, shifting the whole line up or down without changing its shape.

faq.q: What happens with a scale of 1 and an offset of 0?
faq.html: The output equals the source exactly, because the distance from the average is added back unchanged. With a scale of 0 the output is the average plus the offset.

faq.q: How is the average built during the first bars?
faq.html: Until period bars exist, it is the mean of every bar seen so far. After that it is the ordinary simple moving average of the last period bars.

faq.q: What is the offset for?
faq.html: It shifts the line by a fixed amount, which keeps it apart from other lines in the same pane or lets it sit on a chosen reference level.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Plots the natural logarithm of the source in its own pane, so equal percentage moves take up equal vertical distance.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Rescales the source around its own moving average with a scale and an offset, stretching or damping every excursion from the mean.

related.title: Log-Normal Distribution CDF (LOGNORMDIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range off a log-normal cumulative curve, an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

linear-regression-linreg.title: Linear Regression (LINREG)
linear-regression-linreg.summary: The end point of a least squares line fitted through the last N values, the price the recent trend says this bar should have.
linear-regression-linreg.descriptionHtml:
Linear Regression fits a straight line through the last period source values by least squares and plots the point where that line ends, on the current bar. The x axis is the position in the window, 0 for the oldest value up to period - 1 for the newest, and the y axis is the source.

The study keeps the window as a list of values, oldest first. On each bar it sums the values and the values weighted by their position, works out the slope and the intercept from those sums, and reads the line at the newest position. A missing source value is replaced by the last value that was present.

The window grows from two values, so the first reading is on the second bar, where the line simply runs through both points and ends at the newest value. Once the window is full it slides one bar at a time.
linear-regression-linreg.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed version of the source that follows the trend more closely than a simple moving average of the same length, because a straight-line fit has less lag than a flat average. When price is above the line it is running ahead of the recent trend, and when it is below it is falling behind.

The slope of the plotted line shows the direction of the fit, but a straight line cannot follow a turn, so after a reversal the line keeps extending the old trend for part of the window before it catches up. A short period hugs price closely and is noisy.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the line is fitted through. A longer period gives a smoother line that is slower to turn.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series the line is fitted to, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: Why does it lag less than a simple moving average?
faq.html: A moving average reports the centre of the window, which sits half a window in the past. The regression line is read at its newest end, so it projects the window's trend up to the current bar.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot after a reversal?
faq.html: The fit is a straight line through the whole window. Until enough bars of the new direction are in the window, the line still leans the old way.

faq.q: Why is it drawn in its own pane?
faq.html: That is how this study is laid out. The values are in the same units as the source, so they can be compared with price directly.

related.title: Mean Deviation (MEANDEV)
related.summary: The average absolute distance of the last N values from their own mean, a measure of spread that does not square the outliers.

related.title: Kurtosis, tailedness (KURTOSIS)
related.summary: Excess kurtosis of the last N values: above zero when the window has fatter tails and a sharper peak than a normal distribution.

related.title: Median
related.summary: The middle value of the source over a rolling window, a centre line that a single outlier bar cannot drag around the way it drags a mean.

least-mean-squares-adaptive-filter-lms.title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter (LMS)
least-mean-squares-adaptive-filter-lms.summary: An adaptive filter that predicts each bar from the bars before it and keeps adjusting its own weights toward whatever would have been right.
least-mean-squares-adaptive-filter-lms.descriptionHtml:
This study is a filter that learns. It holds one weight for each of the previous Filter Order bars, and on every bar it predicts the current price as the weighted sum of those earlier prices. The line on the chart is that prediction, made before the current bar is seen.

Once the bar is known, the error between price and the prediction is used to adjust every weight. Each weight moves by mu / (tiny + sum of squared inputs) * error * input, a normalised least mean squares step: dividing by the energy of the inputs keeps the speed of learning the same whatever the price level. The weights start at zero and are kept for the whole run, so the filter keeps refining itself as more bars arrive.

History before the first bar reads as zero, so the first Filter Order predictions rest on padded inputs. They still train the weights, but they are not drawn.
least-mean-squares-adaptive-filter-lms.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the filter's best estimate of price built only from the bars before it. While the market behaves the way it has recently, the line sits close to price; when price breaks away sharply, the gap widens until the weights adapt. A persistent gap in one direction shows a move the recent pattern did not anticipate.

A higher learning rate makes the weights react faster, so the line follows price more tightly but with more noise. More taps let the filter use a longer stretch of history and adapt more slowly. The prediction is not a forecast of the next bar on the chart; it is an estimate of the current bar from the ones before it.

settings.label: Filter Order (taps)
settings.html: How many previous bars the filter weighs. More taps capture longer structure but adapt more slowly, and the line starts later.

settings.label: Learning Rate (mu)
settings.html: The size of each weight update. Higher values follow price faster with more noise; lower values give a calmer, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter predicts and learns from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line start a few bars into the chart?
faq.html: The first predictions use history padded with zeros, because the earlier bars do not exist. Those bars still train the weights, but the line is only drawn once a full set of real bars is available.

faq.q: Why is the step normalised?
faq.html: Without normalisation a high-priced instrument would make the weights jump far more than a low-priced one. Dividing by the sum of squared inputs makes the learning rate mean the same thing on any price level.

faq.q: Does the filter forget old behaviour?
faq.html: Gradually. Every new error pulls the weights toward the latest pattern, so recent bars dominate, but there is no explicit forgetting factor.

related.title: LOESS Filter
related.summary: Fits a tricube-weighted straight line through a short window of recent prices and draws the value of that line at the centre of the window.

related.title: Ehlers Laguerre Filter (LAGUERRE)
related.summary: A four-stage Laguerre smoother on price with one damping setting, giving a smooth trend line from very few bars of history.

related.title: Modular Filter (MODF)
related.summary: Blends two exponential bands, one that snaps up to price and one that snaps down, into a filter that ranges from smooth average to trailing stop.

loess-filter.title: LOESS Filter
loess-filter.summary: Fits a tricube-weighted straight line through a short window of recent prices and draws the value of that line at the centre of the window.
loess-filter.descriptionHtml:
This study smooths price with local regression. On each bar it takes a window of recent values, fits a straight line through them by weighted least squares, and draws one point of that line. The window size is the Length setting, rounded down to an odd number so the window has a centre.

Tap i of the window is the value i bars back, placed at the position x = i - half, where half is half the window rounded down. Each tap is weighted with the tricube kernel (1 - |x / half|^3)^3, which is largest at the centre of the window and falls to exactly zero at both ends. The fitted line is then read at x = 0, the centre bar of the window, which is half bars back. Because the weights are the same on both sides of the centre, once the window is full the fitted slope adds nothing at that point, and the value drawn equals the tricube-weighted average of the window: with the default Length of 7, the centre bar weighs 1, its neighbours about 0.89, the next pair about 0.35 and the two ends 0.

On the first bars, taps before the start of the chart are skipped, so the window is lopsided and the slope does shift the result. When no tap carries weight the bar keeps its own price, and when the remaining taps cannot define a line the bar has no value.
loess-filter.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed price centred on a bar in the middle of the window. The value drawn on the newest bar describes price about half a window ago, so the line lags price by roughly half the Length, much like a simple average of the same length, but its bell-shaped weights give a smoother curve with fewer steps when bars enter and leave the window. A rising line shows that the weighted centre of the recent window is moving up; a flattening line shows the window turning.

A longer window gives a smoother, slower line. The newest bar and the oldest bar of the window carry zero weight, so a sharp move on the latest bar does not show at all until the next bar, and takes several bars to show fully.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The number of bars in the fitting window, rounded down to an odd number. Larger windows smooth more and react later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is smoothed, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the window always odd?
faq.html: An odd window has a single centre bar, which is where the fitted line is read. An even length is reduced by one to get there.

faq.q: Why do the outermost bars not count?
faq.html: The tricube weight is zero at the edge of the window, so the oldest and newest taps contribute nothing. This makes the fit change smoothly as bars enter and leave the window.

faq.q: How is this different from a moving average?
faq.html: Once the window is full it is a centred weighted moving average: the symmetric tricube weights cancel the slope of the fit at the centre, so the result is the weighted mean of the window. Compared with a simple average of the same length it lags about as much but weights the centre most and the ends not at all, which gives a smoother line.

related.title: Modular Filter (MODF)
related.summary: Blends two exponential bands, one that snaps up to price and one that snaps down, into a filter that ranges from smooth average to trailing stop.

related.title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter (LMS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that predicts each bar from the bars before it and keeps adjusting its own weights toward whatever would have been right.

related.title: Notch Filter (NOTCH)
related.summary: Removes one chosen cycle length from price with a second-order notch filter and leaves the rest of the movement close to untouched.

logarithmic-transformation-log.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
logarithmic-transformation-log.summary: Plots the natural logarithm of the source in its own pane, so equal percentage moves take up equal vertical distance.
logarithmic-transformation-log.descriptionHtml:
The Logarithmic Transformation takes the natural logarithm of the chosen source on every bar and plots it in a separate pane. On a log scale a move from 100 to 110 covers the same height as a move from 1,000 to 1,100, because both are ten percent. A series that compounds at a steady rate becomes a straight line.

The calculation is a single step: ln(source). The logarithm only exists for values above zero, so a bar whose source is zero or negative is left blank rather than plotted. Nothing is averaged or smoothed, so the line has no warmup and answers from the first bar.
logarithmic-transformation-log.howToReadHtml:
Read the slope of the line as the rate of growth. A straight rising stretch means price is compounding at a steady percentage rate, a steepening curve means growth is speeding up, and a flattening curve means it is slowing. The difference between two values on the line is the log return between those bars, which is close to the percentage change for small moves.

The transformation changes the scale, not the shape of individual bars, so it adds no new information about turning points. It is most useful over long histories, where large price ranges would otherwise squash the early part of the chart.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series to transform, for example the close. Values at or below zero have no logarithm and leave a gap.

faq.q: Why are some bars blank?
faq.html: The natural logarithm is defined only for values above zero. A source of zero or below has no logarithm, so that bar is left empty.

faq.q: How do I read a change on the line?
faq.html: A difference of 0.01 between two bars is a log return of 1 percent, which is about a 1 percent price change. Larger differences are continuously compounded returns, so 0.1 is about 10.5 percent.

faq.q: Is this the same as a log price axis?
faq.html: It shows the same picture, but as a plotted series in its own pane, so its values can be read directly and compared with other studies.

related.title: Log-Normal Distribution CDF (LOGNORMDIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range off a log-normal cumulative curve, an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

related.title: Linear Transformation (LINEAR)
related.summary: Applies y = a * (x - SMA) + SMA + b to the source, so the scale reshapes swings around the average and the offset shifts the line.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Turns the source into its natural logarithm, compressing a multiplicative price scale into an additive one in a separate pane.

log-cosh-loss.title: Log-Cosh Loss
log-cosh-loss.summary: A rolling average of log(cosh(actual minus predicted)), an error measure that acts squared for small misses and linear for large ones.
log-cosh-loss.descriptionHtml:
Log-Cosh Loss measures how far one price series sits from another, treated as a forecast. On every bar it takes the gap between the actual series (the close by default) and the predicted series (the open by default) and passes it through log(cosh(x)), the natural logarithm of the hyperbolic cosine of the gap. The study then plots the simple average of that loss over the last Length bars.

The shape of log(cosh(x)) is what makes it useful. For a small gap it is close to half the squared gap, so it behaves like a squared error and rewards small, steady misses. For a large gap it grows like the absolute gap minus log(2), so a single outlier adds to the average in proportion to its size rather than to its square. Beyond a gap of 20 the study uses that straight-line form directly, so a very large gap cannot overflow the exponential.

An absent value on either series is read as zero, and the line has no value until the window has filled.
log-cosh-loss.howToReadHtml:
The line is never negative, and zero means the two series agreed on every bar of the window. A rising line means the gap between actual and predicted has been widening; a falling one means they have been converging. With the default inputs the gap is the bar body. Where bodies are many price units wide, the line reads close to the average body less about 0.69; where they are a fraction of a unit, it reads closer to half the average squared body.

The value is in squared price units for small gaps and price units for large ones, so it is not comparable across instruments with very different prices. Compare it with its own history rather than with a fixed threshold.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the loss is averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the outcome. The close by default.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast of the actual series. The open by default.

faq.q: Why use log-cosh instead of a squared error?
faq.html: A squared error lets one large miss dominate the average. Log-cosh behaves like a squared error for small misses but grows only linearly for large ones, so the average reflects the typical miss more than the worst one.

faq.q: What does it measure with the default inputs?
faq.html: With close as actual and open as predicted, the gap is the bar's body, so the line is a smoothed measure of how far price travels from open to close.

faq.q: Why is the line empty at the start of the chart?
faq.html: It is a simple average over the last Length bars, so it has no value until that many bars have passed.

related.title: Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the arctangent of the absolute percentage error between two series, bounded between zero and pi/2.

related.title: Huber Loss (HUBER)
related.summary: The average Huber penalty of the gap between price and its own exponential average: squared for small gaps, linear for large ones.

related.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
related.summary: The average absolute distance between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, read as the typical error of that average.

log-normal-distribution-cdf-lognormdist.title: Log-Normal Distribution CDF (LOGNORMDIST)
log-normal-distribution-cdf-lognormdist.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range off a log-normal cumulative curve, an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.
log-normal-distribution-cdf-lognormdist.descriptionHtml:
This study first normalises the source to its recent range: over the lookback window it finds the lowest and highest values and expresses the current value as a position from 0 at the low to 1 at the high. A flat window, with no range, puts the position at 0.5, and the position is floored at 1e-10 so its logarithm always exists.

The position is then read off the cumulative distribution of a log-normal distribution: the study takes (ln(position) - mu) / sigma and passes it through the standard normal CDF, computed with the five-term polynomial approximation 26.2.17 of Abramowitz and Stegun, whose error is below 7.5e-8. While fewer than period bars exist, the range is taken over every bar so far, so the line answers from the first bar.
log-normal-distribution-cdf-lognormdist.howToReadHtml:
Readings near 1 mean price is at the top of its recent range and readings near 0 mean it is at the bottom, but the scale is bent by the log-normal curve. With the default mu of 0 and sigma of 1, the top of the range reads 0.5, the middle about 0.24, and the bottom close to 0, so most of the oscillator's movement happens in the lower half of the pane.

Lower sigma to make the S-curve steeper, so small changes in position move the line more. Negative values of mu move the curve left, letting the top of the range read above 0.5 and reach the 0.95 reference line. The lines at 0.05, 0.5 and 0.95 mark the tails and the middle of the distribution.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose position inside its own high-low range is measured.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars set the high and low used to normalise the source. A longer window gives a wider range and a slower oscillator.

settings.label: Mu
settings.html: The location of the curve, the mean of ln of the position. Lower values shift the curve left so a given position reads higher.

settings.label: Sigma
settings.html: The spread of the curve, the standard deviation of ln of the position. Lower values make the S-curve steeper.

faq.q: Why does the line top out at 0.5 with the default settings?
faq.html: At the top of the range the position is 1 and ln(1) is 0, which equals the default mu, so the CDF reads exactly 0.5. Set mu below zero to let the top of the range read higher.

faq.q: Why is the position floored at 1e-10?
faq.html: At the bottom of the range the position is 0, and the logarithm of 0 does not exist. The floor keeps the value finite, so the line reads very close to 0 there instead of leaving a gap.

faq.q: Does the line need a warmup?
faq.html: No. Until period bars exist, the range is taken over every bar seen so far, so the line has a value from the first bar.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Turns the source into its natural logarithm, compressing a multiplicative price scale into an additive one in a separate pane.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Plots the natural logarithm of the source in its own pane, so equal percentage moves take up equal vertical distance.

related.title: Lowest Value (LOWEST)
related.summary: Traces the lowest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the lowest value seen so far.

logtrans.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
logtrans.summary: Turns the source into its natural logarithm, compressing a multiplicative price scale into an additive one in a separate pane.
logtrans.descriptionHtml:
This study applies the natural logarithm to the chosen source on every bar. Prices grow multiplicatively: a stock that doubles from 50 to 100 and then from 100 to 200 has made the same move twice. On a log scale those two moves are the same height, so the chart shows proportional change rather than absolute change.

The calculation is ln(source) and nothing else. There is no window and no smoothing, so the line answers from the first bar. Zero and negative values have no logarithm, and any bar whose source falls there is left as a gap instead of being plotted.
logtrans.howToReadHtml:
Use the line to judge growth in percentage terms. A straight rising line is steady compound growth, a curve bending upward is accelerating growth, and a curve bending flat is slowing growth. The vertical gap between any two points is the log return over that stretch, which is easy to compare across different price levels.

The study does not smooth or signal anything by itself. It is a change of scale, most helpful on long histories or on instruments whose price has moved through several multiples, where a plain price pane hides the early moves.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series to transform. Any bar whose value is zero or negative is left blank because it has no logarithm.

faq.q: Does the line need a warmup?
faq.html: No. Each bar is transformed on its own, so the first bar already has a value.

faq.q: What does a difference of 0.05 on the line mean?
faq.html: It is a log return of 0.05, which is a price change of about 5.1 percent. For small moves the log return and the percentage change are almost the same.

faq.q: Why would I use this instead of the price itself?
faq.html: Equal percentage moves look equal on the log line, so a trend that compounds steadily shows as a straight line and moves at different price levels can be compared fairly.

related.title: Lowest Value (LOWEST)
related.summary: Traces the lowest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the lowest value seen so far.

related.title: Log-Normal Distribution CDF (LOGNORMDIST)
related.summary: Reads the source's position inside its recent high-low range off a log-normal cumulative curve, an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

related.title: Min-Max Normalization (NORMALIZE)
related.summary: Rescales the source to a 0 to 1 range by its own lowest and highest readings over a lookback window.

lowest-value-lowest.title: Lowest Value (LOWEST)
lowest-value-lowest.summary: Traces the lowest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the lowest value seen so far.
lowest-value-lowest.descriptionHtml:
Lowest Value draws the running minimum of a price series over a fixed lookback. On each bar it looks at the last period values of the source and plots the smallest of them, so the line steps down the moment a new low enters the window and steps up only when the old low drops out of the back of it.

While fewer than period bars exist, the line is the lowest value seen since the first bar, so it starts on the very first bar instead of leaving a warmup gap. A missing source value is read as zero and still takes its place in the window. Once the window is full, the line is the plain rolling lowest of the last period bars, the current bar included.
lowest-value-lowest.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the floor of recent trading. A flat stretch means no new low has been made inside the window, and its length shows how long the last low has held. A step down means price has just set a new low for the window. When the line steps up, the old low has aged out, which often follows a quiet or rising market.

The window includes the current bar, so the source can never be below the line. To test for a breakdown, compare the source with the line one bar earlier. With the low as the source, the line has the shape of a simple channel stop for a long position.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window holds old lows for longer and changes less often.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose lowest value is tracked, for example the close or the low of each bar.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the window holds period bars, the study reports the lowest value seen so far. After that it reports the lowest value of the last period bars.

faq.q: Can the source ever be below the line?
faq.html: No. The window includes the current bar, so the line is always at or below the source. Compare the source with the previous bar's value of the line to spot a new low.

faq.q: Can I use it as a trailing stop?
faq.html: Yes. With the low as the source, the line rises as old lows drop out and never falls unless price makes a new low, which is the shape of a simple channel stop for a long position.

related.title: Min-Max Normalization (NORMALIZE)
related.summary: Rescales the source to a 0 to 1 range by its own lowest and highest readings over a lookback window.

related.title: Logarithmic Transformation (LOG)
related.summary: Turns the source into its natural logarithm, compressing a multiplicative price scale into an additive one in a separate pane.

related.title: Normal Distribution CDF (NORMDIST)
related.summary: Turns the source's z-score over a rolling window into a normal cumulative probability, read as a percentile from 0 to 1.

lrsi-laguerre-rsi.title: LRSI: Laguerre RSI
lrsi-laguerre-rsi.summary: An RSI built from four cascaded Laguerre filter stages instead of a lookback window, reading 0 to 1 and turning within a couple of bars.
lrsi-laguerre-rsi.descriptionHtml:
The Laguerre RSI replaces the fixed lookback of an ordinary RSI with four filter stages chained one after another. The first stage is an exponential smoothing of the close with weight 1 - gamma. Each later stage takes the stage above it, its own previous value and the upper stage's previous value, so every stage is a slightly more delayed copy of the price. All four stages start at zero.

On each bar the study compares neighbouring stages. Where a faster stage sits above the slower one below it, the gap counts as a rise; where it sits below, the gap counts as a fall. The rises are added into cu and the falls into cd, and the line is cu / (cu + cd), so it runs from 0 to 1. When all four stages agree exactly, as on a perfectly flat market, the study reads 0.5.

Gamma is the only setting. A low gamma lets each stage follow price closely, so the line reacts within a bar or two and swings hard between the extremes. A high gamma makes every stage slower and the line smoother.
lrsi-laguerre-rsi.howToReadHtml:
Read it like a fast RSI on a 0 to 1 scale. Above 0.8 the recent bars have been almost all rises, below 0.2 almost all falls, and 0.5 is balance. Because it reacts so quickly, the line often pins at 1 or 0 during a strong run; many traders treat a move back down through 0.8, or back up through 0.2, as the first sign the run is tiring.

The speed that makes it useful also makes it noisy on a low gamma, and an extreme reading in a trend can last for many bars. Treat a cross of the reference lines as a prompt to look at the price chart, not as a signal on its own.

settings.label: Gamma
settings.html: The damping factor from 0 to 1. Lower values make the line react faster and swing harder; higher values make it smoother and slower.

faq.q: Why is the scale 0 to 1 rather than 0 to 100?
faq.html: The line is the share of the stage-to-stage movement that was upward, a fraction from 0 to 1. Multiply by 100 to read it as a percentage; the levels at 0.8, 0.5 and 0.2 are the usual 80, 50 and 20.

faq.q: What does a reading of exactly 0.5 mean?
faq.html: Either the rises and falls between the stages balance, or all four stages hold the same value, which happens on a flat market. The study reads 0.5 instead of dividing by zero.

faq.q: What gamma should I use?
faq.html: The default 0.5 is a middle ground. Drop toward 0.2 for a faster, choppier line on short trades, or raise toward 0.8 for a smoother line that ignores small swings.

related.title: MARKETFI: Market Facilitation Index
related.summary: The bar's high-to-low range divided by its volume: how much price movement each traded unit bought on that bar.

related.title: KST Oscillator (KST)
related.summary: Four rates of change over increasing lookbacks, each smoothed and summed with weights 1 to 4, plus a smoothed signal line.

related.title: Ehlers MESA Stochastic (MSTOCH)
related.summary: A stochastic taken on filtered price, with trend and noise removed first, then smoothed into an oscillator between 0 and 1.

least-squares-moving-average-lsma.title: Least Squares Moving Average (LSMA)
least-squares-moving-average-lsma.summary: Fits a least squares straight line to the last N prices and plots its value at the current bar.
least-squares-moving-average-lsma.descriptionHtml:
The Least Squares Moving Average fits a straight line through the last period prices by least squares, the line that minimises the sum of squared distances to the prices in the window. It then plots the value of that line on the current bar rather than the average of the window. Because the fitted line follows the trend, its endpoint sits close to the latest price and lags far less than a simple average.

The window grows with the chart until it holds period bars, and the very first bar of the chart never enters it. Wherever a line cannot yet be fitted, on the first two bars or with a period of one, the value is the source itself.
least-squares-moving-average-lsma.howToReadHtml:
Read the LSMA as a trend line that projects the recent trend to the present bar. In a steady trend it runs right alongside price; when the trend bends, it overshoots for a few bars because the fitted line still points the old way.

A close above a rising LSMA describes a market keeping pace with its trend, and a cross of price through the line can mark a change in the short-term direction. On a short period it is noisy, since a straight line through a few bars swings with every bar.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars the straight line is fitted to. A longer window gives a steadier line that reacts later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the line is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it lag less than a simple average?
faq.html: A simple average sits at the middle of its window. The LSMA reads the fitted trend line at the newest bar, which is where the trend has carried price.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot at turns?
faq.html: The straight line is fitted to the whole window. Right after a reversal most of the window still slopes the old way, so the endpoint keeps moving in that direction for a few bars.

faq.q: What happens at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The first bar never enters the window, so the line equals price until there are at least two bars after it to fit.

related.title: Linear Time Moving Average (LTMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average over the period: the newest bar counts the full period, the oldest counts one, and older bars fade out evenly.

related.title: Leader EMA (LEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average plus a smoothed copy of its own tracking error, so it leans ahead of a plain EMA of the same period.

related.title: MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA)
related.summary: Two adaptive averages whose smoothing is set by how far the measured cycle phase steps each bar; FAMA follows MAMA at half the rate.

linear-time-moving-average-ltma.title: Linear Time Moving Average (LTMA)
linear-time-moving-average-ltma.summary: A linearly weighted average over the period: the newest bar counts the full period, the oldest counts one, and older bars fade out evenly.
linear-time-moving-average-ltma.descriptionHtml:
LTMA weights each bar in the window by how recent it is. The newest bar gets a weight equal to the period, the bar before it one less, and so on down to a weight of one for the oldest bar. The line is the weighted sum divided by the sum of the weights.

The weighted sum is rolled forward each bar: the new bar is added at the full weight, and the previous window's plain sum is subtracted, which lowers every older bar by exactly one step. That gives the same result as summing the window from scratch.

Before the window fills, the same weights apply to the bars that exist, starting from the period for the newest bar, and the divisor is the sum of those weights. So the line is drawn from the first bar.
linear-time-moving-average-ltma.howToReadHtml:
Read LTMA like a weighted moving average. It responds faster than a simple average of the same length because recent bars count more, but it still uses the whole window, so it is smoother than a short average.

Price above a rising LTMA is an uptrend, below a falling one a downtrend. Its first bars use a partial window, so treat the early part of the line as rough.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in the window and the weight given to the newest bar. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Is this the same as a weighted moving average?
faq.html: Once the window is full it gives the same linear weights, newest bar weighted by the period. It differs on the first bars, where it averages the bars that exist rather than waiting for a full window.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Before the window fills, the weights run from the period downward over the bars there are, and the divisor uses only those weights, so there is always a value.

related.title: MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA)
related.summary: Two adaptive averages whose smoothing is set by how far the measured cycle phase steps each bar; FAMA follows MAMA at half the rate.

related.title: Least Squares Moving Average (LSMA)
related.summary: Fits a least squares straight line to the last N prices and plots its value at the current bar.

related.title: Moving Average Variable Period (MAVP)
related.summary: An exponential average whose period is clamped between a floor and a ceiling, with a warmup correction so it draws from the first bar.

lunar-phase-lunar.title: Lunar Phase (LUNAR)
lunar-phase-lunar.summary: The illuminated fraction of the moon at each bar's opening time, from 0 at new moon to 1 at full moon, with markers at the four main phases.
lunar-phase-lunar.descriptionHtml:
This study computes the moon's phase from the calendar alone; it reads no price at all. From each bar's opening time in UTC it works out the Julian date and the centuries since the J2000.0 epoch, then the mean longitude of the moon, the mean elongation, the sun's and the moon's mean anomaly and the moon's argument of latitude, each as a polynomial in time.

The six largest periodic terms correct the moon's longitude, and the sun's mean longitude is subtracted to give the phase angle between them. The plotted value is one minus the cosine of that angle, halved: 0 at new moon, 0.5 at the quarters and 1 at full moon. Markers label new moon (New) and full moon (Full) where the phase turns at its low and high ends, and the first quarter (FQ) and last quarter (LQ) where it crosses one half rising and falling.
lunar-phase-lunar.howToReadHtml:
The line rises from new moon to full moon over about two weeks and falls back over the next two. The markers show where each phase begins, so you can line up price behaviour against the lunar calendar and judge for yourself whether any pattern holds on your instrument.

The value depends only on time, so it is the same on every instrument and the newest bar is never revised. It is an approximation good to a fraction of a day, which is plenty at hourly and daily resolution. Nothing in the calculation looks at the market.

faq.q: Does it use price at all?
faq.html: No. The phase comes only from the bar's opening time, so every instrument on the same timeframe shows the same line and the same markers.

faq.q: Why might a marker be a bar away from a published new moon time?
faq.html: The study uses the six largest correction terms of the moon's longitude, not the full theory, and it samples once per bar. The phase is accurate to a fraction of a day, and the marker lands on the bar where the turn is first visible.

faq.q: What time zone does it use?
faq.html: UTC. The phase is computed from the bar's opening instant, which does not depend on the chart's time zone.

related.title: Multilayer Perceptron Predictor
related.summary: A small neural network trained bar by bar on six price features, drawing its five-bar price prediction back on the bar it was made from.

related.title: HT_SINE: Hilbert Transform - SineWave
related.summary: The sine of the dominant cycle's phase, and the sine of that phase plus 45 degrees, from an adaptive Hilbert transform of smoothed price.

related.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
related.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.

mean-arctangent-absolute-percentage-erro.title: Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error
mean-arctangent-absolute-percentage-erro.summary: A rolling average of the arctangent of the absolute percentage error between two series, bounded between zero and pi/2.
mean-arctangent-absolute-percentage-erro.descriptionHtml:
Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error compares an actual series (the close by default) with a predicted series (the open by default). On every bar it divides the absolute gap between them by the absolute actual value, then takes the arctangent of that ratio. The study plots the simple average of those values over the last Length bars.

The arctangent is what sets it apart from a plain percentage error. A ratio near zero passes through almost unchanged, but a very large ratio is squeezed towards pi/2, about 1.571, so no single bar can push the average without limit. When the actual value is effectively zero the bar counts as the largest possible error, pi/2. An absent value on either series is read as zero.

The pane shows a dashed zero line and a dashed line at pi/2, the ceiling of the reading. The axis carries a percent sign, but the values are radians, not scaled by 100.
mean-arctangent-absolute-percentage-erro.howToReadHtml:
