The line sits between zero and pi/2. Zero means the predicted series matched the actual one on every bar of the window. For small errors the value is close to the plain ratio, so a reading of 0.002 means the two series were typically about 0.2 percent apart.

With the default inputs it measures how large the bar body is relative to price, smoothed over the window. Rising readings mean bars have been opening further from where they close. The line has no value until Length bars have passed.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the arctangent errors are averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the outcome and used as the base of the percentage. The close by default.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast of the actual series. The open by default.

faq.q: Why use the arctangent?
faq.html: A plain percentage error explodes when the actual value is near zero. The arctangent bounds each bar's error at pi/2, so the average stays finite and readable.

faq.q: Is the value a percentage?
faq.html: The axis shows a percent sign, but the numbers are not multiplied by 100. For small errors the value is the error as a fraction, so 0.01 means about one percent.

faq.q: What is the upper dashed line?
faq.html: It marks pi/2, the largest value any bar can contribute. A bar reaches it only when its actual value is effectively zero; a very large error brings a bar close to it without reaching it. The average touches the line only if every bar in the window did so.

related.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
related.summary: The average absolute distance between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, read as the typical error of that average.

related.title: Log-Cosh Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of log(cosh(actual minus predicted)), an error measure that acts squared for small misses and linear for large ones.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Deviation (MAPD)
related.summary: The average distance between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of the EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

moving-average-convergence-divergence-ma.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
moving-average-convergence-divergence-ma.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average, a smoothed signal line of that gap, and their difference as a coloured histogram.
moving-average-convergence-divergence-ma.descriptionHtml:
MACD measures trend and momentum as the distance between two exponential moving averages of the source. The MACD line is the fast average minus the slow one. The signal line is an exponential average of the MACD line over signalLength bars, and the histogram is the MACD line minus the signal line, green when it is zero or above and red when it is below.

The averages here start from zero and correct for that start. While the starting value still carries weight, each average is divided by (1 - e), where e is (1 - weight) raised to the number of bars seen, and weight is 2 / (length + 1). This removes the pull of the zero seed, so all three lines answer from the first bar instead of after a long warmup. Once every correction has decayed below 1e-10 the averages run as plain exponential averages.
moving-average-convergence-divergence-ma.howToReadHtml:
When the MACD line is above zero the fast average is above the slow one, which is the shape of an uptrend; below zero is the shape of a downtrend. The histogram shows whether that gap is widening or narrowing: bars growing away from zero mean momentum is building, bars shrinking toward zero mean it is fading.

A MACD line crossing above its signal line flips the histogram from red to green, and many traders read it as momentum turning up; the opposite cross reads as momentum turning down. Crosses come late in fast markets and often whipsaw in sideways ones, so they read best alongside the direction of the larger trend.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: The length of the fast exponential average. A shorter fast length makes the MACD line react sooner.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: The length of the slow exponential average that the fast one is measured against.

settings.label: Signal Length
settings.html: The length of the exponential average of the MACD line that forms the signal line and sets the histogram.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages are taken over. Close is the default.

faq.q: Why does it draw from the first bar?
faq.html: The averages start at zero and divide out the weight of that start while it still matters, so they give a usable value from the first bar instead of waiting for a seed window.

faq.q: What do the histogram colours mean?
faq.html: Green bars are zero or above, where the MACD line is at or above its signal line. Red bars are below zero, where it is under the signal line.

faq.q: Is the reading comparable between instruments?
faq.html: No. The MACD line is in price units, so its size scales with the instrument's price. The Percentage Price Oscillator gives the same gap as a percentage of the slow average.

related.title: Momentum (MOM)
related.summary: The plain price difference between this bar and the bar a fixed number of bars back, drawn as a line around zero.

related.title: Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO)
related.summary: Compares the sum of up moves with the sum of down moves over the window and scales the difference from -100 to +100.

related.title: Price Momentum Oscillator (PMO)
related.summary: A percentage rate of change smoothed twice by exponential averages, with a third average as its signal line.

mean-absolute-error-mae.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
mean-absolute-error-mae.summary: The average absolute distance between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, read as the typical error of that average.
mean-absolute-error-mae.descriptionHtml:
Mean Absolute Error treats an exponential moving average as a forecast of price and measures how wrong it has been. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through the warmup. On every bar the study takes the absolute gap between the source and the average.

Those gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry a gap, so the reading begins on the first bar where the average exists and its window widens until it is full. The result is in the same units as price.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-absolute-error-mae.howToReadHtml:
Read the value as the typical distance, in price units, between price and its average over the recent past. A rising reading means price has been moving further from its average, which happens in strong trends and in volatile stretches. A falling reading means price has settled close to its average.

Because it is measured in price units, the reading grows with the price level and is not comparable between instruments at very different prices. For a scale-free version, use the percentage forms such as MAPE.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the window the error is averaged over.

faq.q: What does the EMA on the price chart have to do with the pane?
faq.html: It is the forecast being scored. The pane shows the average distance between price and that line over the last Period bars.

faq.q: How is MAE different from MSE?
faq.html: MAE averages the absolute gaps, so it is in price units and treats every miss in proportion to its size. MSE squares the gaps first, so large misses count far more.

faq.q: Why is there nothing for the first bars?
faq.html: The EMA is seeded from a simple average of its first Period values, so neither the average nor the error exists before the chart has Period bars.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Deviation (MAPD)
related.summary: The average distance between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of the EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Mean Arctangent Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the arctangent of the absolute percentage error between two series, bounded between zero and pi/2.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Error (MAPE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of price, over a rolling window of bars.

ma-envelope-mae.title: MA Envelope (MAE)
ma-envelope-mae.summary: A moving average with two bands set a fixed percentage above and below it, so the channel scales with price rather than with volatility.
ma-envelope-mae.descriptionHtml:
MA Envelope draws a moving average of the source and two bands a fixed percentage of that average away from it. With the default 1 percent, the upper band is the average times 1.01 and the lower band the average times 0.99, so the channel is always the same proportional width whatever the market is doing.

The average can be an exponential, simple or weighted mean, chosen in the menu. Each one answers from the first bar. The exponential mean divides out the weight of the history that does not exist yet, so its early values are not pulled toward zero. The simple mean averages however many bars exist until the window holds Length of them. The weighted mean gives the newest bar weight Length and the oldest weight 1, and counts bars before the start of the chart as zero, so its first values sit below price until the window fills.
ma-envelope-mae.howToReadHtml:
Read the bands as a fixed-distance stretch from the average. A close outside the upper band means price has run more than the chosen percentage above its mean, and a close below the lower band the same on the downside. In a range these are places where price has often reverted; in a strong trend price can ride along one band for many bars.

Because the width does not follow volatility, one percentage will not suit every instrument or timeframe. Set it so that the bands contain most of the recent price action, and widen it for a more volatile market.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average and its bands are built from.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the average covers. A longer length gives a smoother, slower centre line.

settings.label: Percentage
settings.html: The distance of each band from the average, as a percentage of the average. A larger value widens the envelope.

settings.label: MA Type
settings.html: The average the envelope is built around: SMA (simple), EMA (exponential, the default) or WMA (linearly weighted).

faq.q: How is this different from standard deviation bands?
faq.html: Standard deviation bands widen and narrow with the scatter of price around the average. An envelope stays a fixed percentage of the average, so its width only changes when the price level changes.

faq.q: Why does the WMA line start well below price?
faq.html: The weighted mean counts bars before the start of the chart as zero while keeping the full window's total weight, so until Length bars exist its value is pulled down. It settles once the window is full.

faq.q: What percentage should I use?
faq.html: Pick one that contains most of the recent bars. On an hourly chart of a quiet instrument that may be well under 1 percent; on a volatile one or a daily chart, several percent.

related.title: Min-Max Channel (MMCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and the lowest low of the lookback window drawn as a channel, marking the levels a breakout has to clear.

related.title: Keltner Channel (KCHANNEL)
related.summary: An exponential average of the source with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below, drawn from the first bar.

related.title: Price Channel (PCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the lookback window with their midpoint, showing the extremes a new move has to break.

mesa-adaptive-moving-average-mama.title: MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA)
mesa-adaptive-moving-average-mama.summary: Two adaptive averages whose smoothing is set by how far the measured cycle phase steps each bar; FAMA follows MAMA at half the rate.
mesa-adaptive-moving-average-mama.descriptionHtml:
MAMA begins with a four-bar weighted price and smooths it again. A Hilbert transform then splits the smoothed price into an in-phase and a quadrature component, and from those the study measures the phase of the dominant cycle and estimates its period, which in turn scales the filters.

The key quantity is the phase step: the previous bar's phase minus this bar's. A step of one radian or more is treated as zero, and a negative step has a full turn of 2 * pi added. The smoothing constant is fastLimit / (deltaPhase / 0.5) ^ 2, held between the slow and fast limits, so a step of half a radian or less gives the fast limit, a larger step gives a smaller constant, and a step that ran backwards and was wrapped gives a very small constant, the slow limit itself at the default settings. MAMA moves toward price by that constant each bar. FAMA, the following average, moves toward MAMA at half the constant.

The first bar starts both lines at the price, and if the calculation ever loses its value they restart from price on the next bar. The slow limit is never allowed above the fast limit.
mesa-adaptive-moving-average-mama.howToReadHtml:
Read the two lines together. In a move MAMA pulls away from FAMA in the direction of price, and when the move turns MAMA crosses FAMA. That cross is the usual signal, and the gap between the lines shows how far MAMA has run ahead of its follower.

When the measured phase steps are large or run backwards, the smoothing constant falls toward the slow limit and both lines flatten and sit close together, so crosses become rare. A higher fast limit makes MAMA react sooner; a lower slow limit makes both lines flatter while the constant sits at that floor.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

settings.label: Fast Limit
settings.html: The largest smoothing constant allowed. Higher values let MAMA follow price more closely during fast moves.

settings.label: Slow Limit
settings.html: The smallest smoothing constant allowed. Lower values make the lines flatter in quiet markets.

faq.q: What is FAMA?
faq.html: The following average. It moves toward MAMA with half of MAMA's smoothing constant each bar, so it trails MAMA and the two cross when the trend turns.

faq.q: Why do the lines go flat at times?
faq.html: When the phase step is between half a radian and one radian, or runs backwards, the smoothing constant drops, down to the slow limit, and both lines barely move until the phase steps shrink again.

faq.q: What happens if the slow limit is set above the fast limit?
faq.html: It is held at the fast limit, so the smoothing constant is fixed at that value and the line stops adapting.

related.title: Moving Average Variable Period (MAVP)
related.summary: An exponential average whose period is clamped between a floor and a ceiling, with a warmup correction so it draws from the first bar.

related.title: Linear Time Moving Average (LTMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average over the period: the newest bar counts the full period, the oldest counts one, and older bars fade out evenly.

related.title: MCNMA - McNicholl EMA
related.summary: A low-lag average: twice a triple exponential average minus the triple exponential average of it, built from six cascaded stages.

mean-absolute-deviation-mapd.title: Mean Absolute %Deviation (MAPD)
mean-absolute-deviation-mapd.summary: The average distance between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of the EMA, over a rolling window of bars.
mean-absolute-deviation-mapd.descriptionHtml:
Mean Absolute %Deviation measures how far price typically strays from its own trend, in percent. The trend is an exponential moving average of the source over Period bars, seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study takes the absolute gap between the source and that average and divides it by the average, then multiplies by 100.

Those percentage deviations are averaged over the last Period bars, with the window held to at most 4000 bars, and only bars that carry a deviation are counted. The reading therefore starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full. A bar where the average is exactly zero carries no deviation.

The study plots the deviation as a shaded area in its own pane and draws the reference average on the price chart, so you can see the trend line the deviation is measured from.
mean-absolute-deviation-mapd.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means price has been hugging its average; a high one means it has been swinging well away from it. Because the deviation is a percentage of the average, the reading can be compared across instruments and across long stretches of history where the price level changed a lot.

The reading has no sign, so it says how wide the departures have been, not whether price is above or below the average. Use the EMA on the price chart for direction. A long period makes both the average and the window slow, so the reading responds late to a change in behaviour.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the averaging window. The averaging window is held to at most 4000 bars.

faq.q: How is this different from MAPE?
faq.html: Both average an absolute percentage gap between price and its EMA. This study divides by the average, while MAPE divides by price, so the two differ slightly when price is far from its average.

faq.q: Why does the line start so late?
faq.html: The reference EMA needs Period bars before it has a value, and the deviation cannot be measured before then. With the default of 100 the first reading is on the hundredth bar of the chart.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is about to revert?
faq.html: No. It says price has recently been far from its average. Trends can keep price away from its average for a long time.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Error (MAPE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of price, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
related.summary: The average absolute distance between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, read as the typical error of that average.

related.title: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, divided by a naive-forecast scale, over a rolling window of bars.

mean-absolute-error-mape.title: Mean Absolute %Error (MAPE)
mean-absolute-error-mape.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of price, over a rolling window of bars.
mean-absolute-error-mape.descriptionHtml:
Mean Absolute %Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price, in percent. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study divides the absolute gap between the source and the average by the source and multiplies by 100. A bar where the source is exactly zero carries no error.

The percentage errors are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry an error. The reading starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-absolute-error-mape.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 2 means price has typically been 2 percent away from its average over the window. Because it is a percentage, it can be compared between instruments and across periods where the price level changed. A rising line means price is pulling away from its average; a falling one means it is settling back near it.

The reading has no sign, so it does not say which side of the average price is on. Look at the EMA on the price chart for that.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the window the percentage error is averaged over.

faq.q: Why divide by price rather than by the average?
faq.html: That is the usual definition of a percentage error, where the actual value is the base. The MAPD study divides by the average instead; the two readings are close unless price is far from its average.

faq.q: Can the reading be negative?
faq.html: No. It averages absolute percentage gaps, so it is zero or above. Use MPE for a signed version that shows bias.

faq.q: When does the first value appear?
faq.html: On the first bar where the EMA has a value, which is bar number Period counting from one. With the default of 100 that is the hundredth bar of the chart.

related.title: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, divided by a naive-forecast scale, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Deviation (MAPD)
related.summary: The average distance between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of the EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Median Absolute Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the absolute gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a typical error that ignores outliers.

marketfi-market-facilitation-index.title: MARKETFI: Market Facilitation Index
marketfi-market-facilitation-index.summary: The bar's high-to-low range divided by its volume: how much price movement each traded unit bought on that bar.
marketfi-market-facilitation-index.descriptionHtml:
The Market Facilitation Index measures how efficiently volume moves price. For each bar it takes the distance from the high to the low and divides it by the bar's volume. A large reading means price travelled a long way on little trade; a small reading means a lot of trade moved price very little.

The calculation looks at one bar only, so there is no warmup and no setting. A bar that reports no volume, or a volume of zero, reads 0, which the study treats as no market activity rather than a gap in the line.

Because the value is a price distance per unit of volume, its size depends entirely on the instrument. On an instrument with large volume numbers the readings are tiny fractions, so compare the line with its own recent history rather than with a fixed threshold.
marketfi-market-facilitation-index.howToReadHtml:
Read the line together with volume. A rising index on rising volume is an efficient move: more trade and more price change per unit of it, the shape of a trend with conviction. A falling index on rising volume is a squat bar, heavy trade that moved price very little, which often appears where buyers and sellers are fighting before a turn. A rising index on falling volume is a move with little participation behind it.

The index on its own says nothing about direction; a wide down bar and a wide up bar read the same. Use it to judge the quality of a move you can see on the price chart.

faq.q: Why are the values so small?
faq.html: The index is a price range divided by volume. When volume runs into hundreds or thousands of units per bar the result is a small fraction. Its shape over time matters, not its absolute size.

faq.q: Why does the line drop to 0 on some bars?
faq.html: A bar with no reported volume, or a volume of zero, cannot be divided by, so the study reads 0 there to mark no market activity.

faq.q: Does it show whether price is going up or down?
faq.html: No. It uses the bar's range, which is the same size for an up bar and a down bar. Pair it with the price chart or a trend tool for direction.

related.title: Ehlers MESA Stochastic (MSTOCH)
related.summary: A stochastic taken on filtered price, with trend and noise removed first, then smoothed into an oscillator between 0 and 1.

related.title: LRSI: Laguerre RSI
related.summary: An RSI built from four cascaded Laguerre filter stages instead of a lookback window, reading 0 to 1 and turning within a couple of bars.

related.title: Pretty Good Oscillator
related.summary: How far price sits from its simple average, measured in units of average true range, so a reading beyond plus or minus 3 marks a stretched move.

mean-absolute-scaled-error-mase.title: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
mean-absolute-scaled-error-mase.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, divided by a naive-forecast scale, over a rolling window of bars.
mean-absolute-scaled-error-mase.descriptionHtml:
Mean Absolute Scaled Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price, divided by a scale meant to come from a naive forecast. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study takes the absolute gap between the source and the average and divides it by the scale.

The scale is measured once, on the first bar of the chart, as the mean absolute one-bar change of the source over the window. On the first bar there is no earlier bar to compare with, so no change is counted and the scale is set to 1 for the whole chart. In practice the reading therefore equals the plain mean absolute error, in price units.

The scaled errors are averaged over the last Period bars, at most 4000, counting only the bars that carry an error. The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-absolute-scaled-error-mase.howToReadHtml:
Read the value as the typical distance between price and its average over the recent past. A rising reading means price is pulling away from its average faster than before, which is common in a strong trend or a volatile stretch. A falling reading means price has settled near its average.

Because the scale settles at 1, the reading is in price units and grows with the price level, so compare it with its own history rather than with another instrument.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the error averaging window, which is held to at most 4000 bars.

faq.q: Why does it read the same as MAE?
faq.html: The scale is measured only on the first bar, where no earlier bar exists to compare against, so it settles at 1 and the division leaves the error unchanged. The study keeps that calculation exactly as written.

faq.q: What is the EMA on the price chart?
faq.html: It is the forecast being scored. The pane shows how far price has been from that line on average.

faq.q: Why does the line start late?
faq.html: The EMA has no value until the chart has Period bars, so the error cannot be measured before then.

related.title: Median Absolute Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the absolute gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a typical error that ignores outliers.

related.title: Mean Absolute %Error (MAPE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, as a percentage of price, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Median Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the percentage gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a forecast error score that one outlier bar barely moves.

mass-index-massi.title: Mass Index (MASSI)
mass-index-massi.summary: Sums the ratio of a single to a double exponential average of the bar range, so a widening range shows as a bulge in the line.
mass-index-massi.descriptionHtml:
The Mass Index watches the width of each bar, the high minus the low, for signs that the range is expanding. It smooths the range with an exponential mean of weight 2 / (EMA Length + 1), then smooths that mean again with the same weight. Both means start from zero, so during the first bars each is divided by the weight it has gathered so far; once that start-up weight falls below a tiny threshold the correction is dropped.

The ratio of the single mean to the double mean is above 1 when the range is widening, because the single mean responds first, and below 1 when it is narrowing. The study adds up that ratio over the last Sum Length bars. With the defaults the line hovers near 25, the value it would read if the range were steady, and the line is empty until Sum Length bars have passed.
mass-index-massi.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means bar ranges are widening, a falling line means they are contracting. A common reading watches for a bulge: the line rising through a high level and then falling back, which suggests the range expansion is ending and the current trend may be about to reverse.

The line says nothing about direction. Use a trend tool or price itself to decide which way a possible reversal would go. Levels depend on Sum Length, since the line is centred near that number.

settings.label: EMA Length
settings.html: Length of both exponential means of the range. A longer length reacts more slowly to changes in bar width.

settings.label: Sum Length
settings.html: How many bars of the ratio are added up. It also sets the level the line hovers around, which equals this number.

faq.q: Why does the line hover near 25?
faq.html: When the range is steady the single and double means are equal and the ratio is 1, so the sum over 25 bars is 25.

faq.q: Does it tell me which way price will turn?
faq.html: No. It measures only the width of the bars, so you need price or a trend tool to judge direction.

faq.q: Why is the line empty at the start?
faq.html: The sum needs Sum Length bars of the ratio before it has a full window to add up.

related.title: Normalized Average True Range
related.summary: The average true range expressed as a percentage of the close, so volatility compares across instruments and price levels.

related.title: Normalized Jurik Volatility (JVOLTYN)
related.summary: The adaptive volatility ratio passed through a logistic curve, so it reads 0.5 at normal pace and climbs towards 1 as movement grows.

related.title: Parkinson Volatility (PV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log ratio of each bar's high to its low, smoothed over a window and optionally annualised.

moving-average-variable-period-mavp.title: Moving Average Variable Period (MAVP)
moving-average-variable-period-mavp.summary: An exponential average whose period is clamped between a floor and a ceiling, with a warmup correction so it draws from the first bar.
moving-average-variable-period-mavp.descriptionHtml:
The MAVP is an exponential moving average built around a period that is held between a minimum and a maximum. The base period is clamped into that range, and the smoothing factor is two divided by the clamped period plus one. In this study the period is the same on every bar, so the line is an exponential average of the clamped length.

The running average starts at zero. During warmup it is divided by one minus (1 - alpha) raised to the number of bars seen, which removes the pull toward zero and makes the first bar equal the source. Once (1 - alpha) raised to the bars seen falls below 1e-10, the correction is dropped and the line is the plain recursion. A missing source value is read as zero so the recursion never breaks. If the maximum is set below the minimum, the maximum is lifted to the minimum so the line still draws.
moving-average-variable-period-mavp.howToReadHtml:
Read it like any exponential average. A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend, a falling line with price below it a downtrend, and the distance between price and the line shows how stretched the move is.

The minimum and maximum period only matter when the base period falls outside them: a base period below the minimum is raised to it and one above the maximum is lowered to it. With the defaults the line is a 10-bar exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The base period of the exponential average before it is clamped.

settings.label: Min Period
settings.html: The shortest period allowed. A base period below it is raised to this value.

settings.label: Max Period
settings.html: The longest period allowed. A base period above it is lowered to this value.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Does the period change from bar to bar?
faq.html: Not in this study. The per-bar period is the base period on every bar, clamped between the minimum and the maximum, so the line is an exponential average of one fixed length.

faq.q: What happens if the maximum is below the minimum?
faq.html: The maximum is raised to the minimum, so the period becomes the minimum and the line keeps drawing instead of failing.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The average starts at zero and is divided by a warmup correction that removes that zero start. The first value equals the source and the correction fades out as bars arrive.

related.title: MCNMA - McNicholl EMA
related.summary: A low-lag average: twice a triple exponential average minus the triple exponential average of it, built from six cascaded stages.

related.title: MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA)
related.summary: Two adaptive averages whose smoothing is set by how far the measured cycle phase steps each bar; FAMA follows MAMA at half the rate.

related.title: McGinley Dynamic Indicator (MGDI)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose step toward price is divided by the fourth power of the price to line ratio, so it follows falls faster than rallies.

mcnma-mcnicholl-ema.title: MCNMA - McNicholl EMA
mcnma-mcnicholl-ema.summary: A low-lag average: twice a triple exponential average minus the triple exponential average of it, built from six cascaded stages.
mcnma-mcnicholl-ema.descriptionHtml:
MCNMA chains six exponential averages that all use the weight 2 / (period + 1). The first three form a triple exponential average of the source, 3 * e1 - 3 * e2 + e3. That result feeds the next three, which form a triple exponential average of the first one.

The line is twice the first triple average minus the second. The second is a smoothed copy of the first, so the difference between them estimates the lag the smoothing adds, and subtracting it pushes the line back toward price.

All six stages are seeded with the first source value, so the line answers from the first bar. An absent source reads as zero.
mcnma-mcnicholl-ema.howToReadHtml:
MCNMA is a very responsive trend line. It turns close to where price turns and stays close to price in a steady trend, so it suits faster crossover systems and trailing references.

The lag removal also amplifies noise and makes the line overshoot after sharp moves. On noisy charts a longer period helps, and a cross of price through the line is stronger evidence when the line itself has turned.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Length of every exponential stage. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line that overshoots less.

faq.q: How does it remove lag?
faq.html: It subtracts a smoothed copy of a triple exponential average from twice that average. The difference between the two is an estimate of the lag, so taking it out brings the line back toward price.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot?
faq.html: Removing lag means projecting recent movement forward. After a sharp move that reverses, the projection runs past price for a few bars.

related.title: McGinley Dynamic Indicator (MGDI)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose step toward price is divided by the fourth power of the price to line ratio, so it follows falls faster than rallies.

related.title: Moving Average Variable Period (MAVP)
related.summary: An exponential average whose period is clamped between a floor and a ceiling, with a warmup correction so it draws from the first bar.

related.title: Modified Moving Average (MMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average plus a linear end-point correction from the same window, which removes most of the lag of the plain mean.

median-absolute-error.title: Median Absolute Error
median-absolute-error.summary: The rolling median of the absolute gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a typical error that ignores outliers.
median-absolute-error.descriptionHtml:
Median Absolute Error compares an actual series (the close by default) with a predicted series (the open by default). On every bar it takes the absolute gap between them, and then reports the median of the last Length gaps instead of their average. An absent value on either series is read as zero.

The median here is the nearest-rank middle value: the gaps in the window are sorted and the value at rank ceil(Length / 2) is taken. For an odd window that is the exact middle; for an even window it is the lower of the two middle values rather than their average. The line has no value until the window has filled.

The pane shows a dashed zero line for reference.
median-absolute-error.howToReadHtml:
Read the value as the size of a typical gap, in price units, over the recent window. With the default inputs it is the typical bar body, the distance from open to close. Half the bars in the window had a smaller gap and half a larger one.

Because it is a median, one very wide bar barely moves it, which makes it steadier than a mean absolute error. The flip side is that it is slow to admit a real change: the line only shifts once about half the window has changed character. It is in price units, so compare it with its own history rather than across instruments.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the median is taken over. A longer window gives a steadier, slower line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the outcome. The close by default.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast of the actual series. The open by default.

faq.q: Why use a median rather than a mean?
faq.html: A mean is pulled up by a single large miss. The median reports the middle gap in the window, so occasional outliers have almost no effect.

faq.q: What happens with an even Length?
faq.html: The study takes the lower of the two middle values rather than averaging them, so the reading is always one of the actual gaps in the window.

faq.q: Why does the line move in steps?
faq.html: The median is always one of the gaps in the window, so it holds its value while the gaps entering and leaving the window fall on the same side of the middle, and jumps to a neighbouring gap when they do not.

related.title: Median Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the percentage gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a forecast error score that one outlier bar barely moves.

related.title: Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)
related.summary: The average absolute gap between price and its own EMA, divided by a naive-forecast scale, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Mean Error (ME)
related.summary: The average signed gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, showing whether price has been sitting above or below it.

median-absolute-percentage-error.title: Median Absolute Percentage Error
median-absolute-percentage-error.summary: The rolling median of the percentage gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a forecast error score that one outlier bar barely moves.
median-absolute-percentage-error.descriptionHtml:
Median Absolute Percentage Error (MdAPE) scores how far a predicted series sits from an actual series, in percent of the actual. On every bar it takes the absolute gap between the two, divides it by the absolute actual value and multiplies by 100. If the actual value is too close to zero to divide by, the bar scores 0.

The study then takes the median of the last Length of those percentage errors. The median is found by nearest rank: the window is sorted and the value at position ceil(Length / 2) is returned, so an even window answers one of its own members rather than the average of the two middle values. With the default settings the actual series is the close and the predicted series is the open, so the reading is the typical size of the open to close move as a percentage of the close.
median-absolute-percentage-error.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means the predicted series usually lands close to the actual one; a high reading means the typical miss is large. Because it is a median, a single bar with a huge error barely changes it, which makes it a steadier score than an average of the same errors. Compare it with a mean based error: if the mean jumps while the median stays flat, the error came from a few extreme bars.

The line has no value until Length bars have passed. It measures the size of the miss only, not its direction, and a percentage scale says little when the actual series sits near zero.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars of percentage error the median is taken over. A longer window moves more slowly.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth. The error is measured as a percentage of this series.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: Why use a median instead of the mean?
faq.html: The median ignores how large the extreme errors are, so one bar with a very large miss changes the reading by at most one rank. The mean of the same errors can jump a long way on that one bar.

faq.q: What happens with an even Length?
faq.html: The window is sorted and the value at position Length divided by two is returned, so with 14 bars it is the 7th smallest error. It is always one of the errors in the window, never an average of two.

faq.q: What does it measure with the default settings?
faq.html: The actual series is the close and the predicted series is the open, so it reports the median size of each bar's open to close move as a percentage of the close.

related.title: Mean Error (ME)
related.summary: The average signed gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, showing whether price has been sitting above or below it.

related.title: Median Absolute Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the absolute gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a typical error that ignores outliers.

related.title: Mean %Error (MPE)
related.summary: The average signed percentage by which price sits above or below its own EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

mean-error-me.title: Mean Error (ME)
mean-error-me.summary: The average signed gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, showing whether price has been sitting above or below it.
mean-error-me.descriptionHtml:
Mean Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price, keeping the sign of every miss. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study subtracts the average from the source, so the gap is positive when price is above the average and negative when it is below.

Those signed gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, at most 4000, counting only the bars that carry a gap. The reading starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full. Because positive and negative gaps cancel, the result is a measure of bias rather than of size.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-error-me.howToReadHtml:
A reading above zero means price has, on balance, been above its average over the window, which is what an uptrend looks like. A reading below zero means price has been below it. A reading near zero means the misses have balanced out: either price has been hugging the average, or it has swung evenly on both sides.

Because cancellation hides size, a near-zero reading is not proof that price has been close to the average. Pair it with MAE to see how large the misses were. The value is in price units.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the averaging window, which is held to at most 4000 bars.

faq.q: What does a positive value mean?
faq.html: Price has been above its EMA more, or by more, than it has been below it over the window. It is a sign of upward bias.

faq.q: Why can the reading be close to zero in a volatile market?
faq.html: Positive and negative gaps cancel. A market that swings widely around its average can still average out near zero.

faq.q: How is this different from MPE?
faq.html: Mean Error is in price units. MPE divides each gap by price first, so it is in percent and comparable across instruments.

related.title: Mean %Error (MPE)
related.summary: The average signed percentage by which price sits above or below its own EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Median Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: The rolling median of the percentage gap between an actual series and a predicted one, a forecast error score that one outlier bar barely moves.

related.title: Mean Relative Absolute Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the absolute gap between two series as a fraction of the actual value, where 0 is a perfect match.

mean-deviation-meandev.title: Mean Deviation (MEANDEV)
mean-deviation-meandev.summary: The average absolute distance of the last N values from their own mean, a measure of spread that does not square the outliers.
mean-deviation-meandev.descriptionHtml:
Mean Deviation measures how far the values in the lookback window sit from their own average. The study takes the mean of the last period values, then averages the absolute distance of each of those values from that mean. The answer is in price units, like the source.

The window grows from the first bar: until period bars have passed, the mean and the deviation are taken over every bar so far, so the line has a reading from bar 0. A missing source value is counted as zero.

Unlike a standard deviation, which squares each distance before averaging, mean deviation adds the distances as they are. A single large move therefore raises it less, and it reads closer to the typical distance from the mean.
mean-deviation-meandev.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means the values in the window are spreading out from their average, which usually comes with a larger move or a breakout. A falling line means the window is tightening around its average, as in a quiet range. Compare the reading with its own history on the same chart rather than with a fixed number, because it is in price units.

It says nothing about direction: a sharp rise and a sharp fall both push it up. The first period bars use a shorter window and read less reliably.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer window gives a smoother measure of spread that reacts more slowly.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose spread is measured, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: How is it different from standard deviation?
faq.html: Standard deviation squares each distance before averaging and takes the square root at the end, so large distances count for more. Mean deviation averages the plain distances, so it is less sensitive to a single outlier and is usually a little smaller.

faq.q: Why does it have a value on the first bars?
faq.html: The window grows from the first bar, so early readings are taken over however many bars exist. A window of one bar has no spread and reads zero.

faq.q: Is a high value bullish or bearish?
faq.html: Neither. It measures how scattered the window is, not which way price moved.

related.title: Median
related.summary: The middle value of the source over a rolling window, a centre line that a single outlier bar cannot drag around the way it drags a mean.

related.title: Linear Regression (LINREG)
related.summary: The end point of a least squares line fitted through the last N values, the price the recent trend says this bar should have.

related.title: Mode
related.summary: The value that repeats most often in the recent window, drawn only when some value actually repeats, marking prices the market keeps returning to.

median.title: Median
median.summary: The middle value of the source over a rolling window, a centre line that a single outlier bar cannot drag around the way it drags a mean.
median.descriptionHtml:
The Median study sorts the last Period values of the source and plots the one in the middle. When the window holds an odd number of values that is the single middle value; when it holds an even number it is the average of the two middle values.

Unlike a simple moving average, the median ignores how far the extreme values sit from the centre. One bar with a huge wick or a bad print moves a mean by its full size divided by the window, but it moves the median by at most one rank. That makes the line a steadier estimate of where price has typically been.

The study answers from the first bar. Before the window has filled it takes the median of the bars that exist so far, and any absent value in the window is skipped rather than counted.
median.howToReadHtml:
Read the median as the typical price of the recent window. A current value above the line is higher than at least half of the recent values, and a value below it is lower than at least half of them. Because it moves in steps rather than smoothly, it often stays flat for several bars and then jumps, which is normal for a rank statistic.

It lags in a strong trend just as an average does, and after a sudden jump it moves to the new level only once more than half of the window's values sit there.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the median is taken from, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars are ranked. A longer period gives a steadier line that responds later.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes stay flat and then jump?
faq.html: The median is one of the window's own values, or the average of two of them, so it only changes when the middle rank changes. A new bar that lands well away from the centre may not move it at all.

faq.q: How is it different from a simple moving average?
faq.html: An average adds up every value, so a single extreme bar pulls it by its full size. The median only looks at order, so the same bar moves it by at most one position in the sorted window.

faq.q: Does it have a warmup period?
faq.html: No. On early bars it takes the median of however many bars exist, so the first value is simply the first bar's source.

related.title: Mode
related.summary: The value that repeats most often in the recent window, drawn only when some value actually repeats, marking prices the market keeps returning to.

related.title: Mean Deviation (MEANDEV)
related.summary: The average absolute distance of the last N values from their own mean, a measure of spread that does not square the outliers.

related.title: Percentile
related.summary: The value at a chosen percentile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart, interpolated between the two nearest ranks.

medprice-median-price.title: MEDPRICE: Median Price
medprice-median-price.summary: The midpoint of each bar's range, halfway between its high and its low, drawn on the price chart with no smoothing.
medprice-median-price.descriptionHtml:
Median Price is the middle of each bar's range: its high plus its low, divided by two. It ignores where the bar opened and closed and looks only at the two extremes it reached.

The study draws that midpoint as a line over the price chart. It has no lookback window and no smoothing, so it starts on the first bar and each point depends only on its own bar. The name refers to the middle of the range, not to a statistical median taken over many bars.
medprice-median-price.howToReadHtml:
Compare the close with the median price to see which half of its range a bar finished in. A close above the line means buyers held the bar in its upper half; a close below means it settled in the lower half.

The line follows each bar's range closely and is not a trend filter on its own. It is often used as the input to other studies, such as moving averages or oscillators, that want a value less sensitive to the closing print.

faq.q: Is this a median over several bars?
faq.html: No. It is the midpoint of a single bar, (high + low) / 2. Each bar has its own value and there is no window.

faq.q: Why use it instead of the close?
faq.html: It depends only on how far the bar travelled in each direction, so a late spike into the close does not move it unless that spike also set a new high or low.

faq.q: Does it need any warmup?
faq.html: No. It answers from the first bar, because it never looks back at earlier bars.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

related.title: HA: Heikin-Ashi
related.summary: Smoothed candles drawn over the chart: each closes at the bar's average price and opens at the midpoint of the previous smoothed candle.

related.title: MIDPRICE: Midpoint Price over Period
related.summary: The centre of the recent trading range: the highest high and the lowest low of the last N bars, averaged into one line.

money-flow-index-mfi.title: Money Flow Index (MFI)
money-flow-index-mfi.summary: A volume-weighted strength oscillator from 0 to 100 that compares money flowing in on rising bars with money flowing out on falling bars.
money-flow-index-mfi.descriptionHtml:
The Money Flow Index measures buying and selling pressure with both price and volume. Each bar's raw money flow is its typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, times its volume. When the typical price is higher than on the previous bar the flow counts as positive, when it is lower it counts as negative, and when it is unchanged it counts as neither. The first bar compares with itself and counts as neither.

The positive and negative flows are summed over the last MFI Period bars, using however many bars have arrived until the window fills. The money ratio is positive flow divided by negative flow, and the index is 100 - 100 / (1 + ratio). When the window holds no negative flow at all, the ratio is taken as zero, so the index reads 0 on those bars rather than 100.
money-flow-index-mfi.howToReadHtml:
High readings mean most of the recent money flow came on rising bars; low readings mean it came on falling bars. Many traders treat readings above 80 as stretched to the upside and below 20 as stretched to the downside, and watch for the index to turn back from those zones.

Divergence is the other use: price making a new high while the index makes a lower one suggests the volume behind the advance is fading. Keep in mind the special case: a window with no falling bars reads 0, not 100, which can happen early in the series or with a very short period.

settings.label: MFI Period
settings.html: The number of bars over which positive and negative money flow are summed. A shorter period reacts faster and reaches the extremes more often.

faq.q: Why does the index sometimes drop to 0 during a strong rise?
faq.html: When every bar in the window rose, there is no negative flow and the ratio is taken as zero, so the index reads 0 rather than 100. Watch for this with short periods.

faq.q: How is this different from an RSI?
faq.html: An RSI compares the size of up and down price changes. This index weights each bar by typical price times volume, so a move on heavy volume counts for more.

faq.q: Does the index wait for the window to fill?
faq.html: No. The sums cover however many bars have arrived, so it answers from the first bar.

related.title: Negative Volume Index (NVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume fell against the bar before.

related.title: Klinger Volume Oscillator (KVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of trend-signed volume force, with a signal line and a coloured histogram.

related.title: On Balance Volume (OBV)
related.summary: A running total that adds each bar's volume on a higher close and subtracts it on a lower close, tracking where volume is flowing.

mcginley-dynamic-indicator-mgdi.title: McGinley Dynamic Indicator (MGDI)
mcginley-dynamic-indicator-mgdi.summary: An adaptive average whose step toward price is divided by the fourth power of the price to line ratio, so it follows falls faster than rallies.
mcginley-dynamic-indicator-mgdi.descriptionHtml:
MGDI starts at the first price. Each later bar it moves toward the source by the gap between them divided by factor * period * (price / line) ^ 4. When price is above the line in a rally, the ratio is greater than 1 and the line moves more slowly; when price drops below the line, the ratio falls under 1 and the line follows more quickly.

The divisor is kept at least 0.001 in size so the step can never blow up. If the line ever sits at zero, it resets to the current price.

The Factor scales the whole divisor. A smaller factor makes the line follow price more tightly, and a larger one makes it smoother.
mcginley-dynamic-indicator-mgdi.howToReadHtml:
Use MGDI as a trend line that adjusts its own speed. While price stays near the line the divisor is close to factor * period, so it moves like a short exponential average; a price well below the line shrinks the divisor and pulls the line down quickly, and a price well above it enlarges the divisor and slows the line.

Price crossing the line with the line turning is the usual reading of a change in direction. Because the speed depends on the ratio of price to the line, it reacts faster to falls than to rises of the same size, and on a strong rally it can lag noticeably.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The base length in the divisor. A longer period makes the line move more slowly toward price.

settings.label: Factor
settings.html: Multiplies the divisor. Lower values make the line track price more closely; higher values smooth it.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows. Close is the usual choice; hl2 or another blend smooths out closes that jump around.

faq.q: Why does MGDI react faster to drops than to rallies?
faq.html: The divisor uses (price / line) ^ 4. Below the line that ratio is under 1, the divisor shrinks and the step grows; above the line the divisor grows and the step shrinks.

faq.q: What does the Factor do?
faq.html: It scales the divisor directly. At 0.6 the line moves toward price faster than at 1.0, which gives a tighter fit at the cost of more noise.

related.title: Modified Moving Average (MMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average plus a linear end-point correction from the same window, which removes most of the lag of the plain mean.

related.title: MCNMA - McNicholl EMA
related.summary: A low-lag average: twice a triple exponential average minus the triple exponential average of it, built from six cascaded stages.

related.title: Non-Lag Moving Average (NLMA)
related.summary: A long weighted average whose cosine kernel adds negative weights to older bars, cutting lag while still smoothing short noise.

midpoint-midpoint.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
midpoint-midpoint.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.
midpoint-midpoint.descriptionHtml:
Midpoint finds the highest and the lowest value of one source series, the close by default, over the last length bars, and draws the point halfway between them. It describes the centre of the range the source has covered recently, not an average of every value in the window.

Because only the two extremes matter, the line holds flat for as long as no new high or low enters or leaves the window, then steps when one does. The line is absent until the window has filled, so the first length - 1 bars carry no value.
midpoint-midpoint.howToReadHtml:
Price above the midpoint is trading in the upper half of its recent range, and price below it in the lower half. A rising midpoint shows the range itself moving up, which happens only when new highs are set or old lows drop out of the window.

The flat stretches are a feature of the calculation, not a sign that nothing is happening. Pair it with the range itself or with a trend study, since the midpoint alone says where the centre is, not how wide the range is.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose highest and lowest values are measured. The close is the default; a median or typical price gives a smoother range.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the range covers. A longer window gives a steadier line that steps less often and starts later.

faq.q: How is this different from Midpoint Price over Period?
faq.html: Midpoint uses one source series, so its range runs from the lowest close to the highest close by default. Midpoint Price over Period uses the highest high and the lowest low, so its range includes the wicks.

faq.q: Why does the line move in steps?
faq.html: It changes only when the highest or lowest value in the window changes. Between those moments it stays flat, unlike a moving average that shifts on every bar.

faq.q: When does the first value appear?
faq.html: On bar length - 1, the first bar where the window holds a full length bars.

related.title: MIDPRICE: Midpoint Price over Period
related.summary: The centre of the recent trading range: the highest high and the lowest low of the last N bars, averaged into one line.

related.title: MEDPRICE: Median Price
related.summary: The midpoint of each bar's range, halfway between its high and its low, drawn on the price chart with no smoothing.

related.title: TYPPRICE: Typical Price
related.summary: The plain average of each bar's high, low and close, a single price for where the bar traded, drawn on the price chart.

midprice-midpoint-price-over-period.title: MIDPRICE: Midpoint Price over Period
midprice-midpoint-price-over-period.summary: The centre of the recent trading range: the highest high and the lowest low of the last N bars, averaged into one line.
midprice-midpoint-price-over-period.descriptionHtml:
Midpoint Price over Period takes the highest high and the lowest low of the last period bars and draws the point halfway between them. It marks the centre of the range the market has traded over the window, wicks included, rather than the centre of the latest bar.

Only the two extremes enter the calculation, so the line stays flat while no new high or low arrives and no old one leaves the window, and it steps when one does. It is absent until the window has filled, which means the first period - 1 bars carry no value. It is the same centre line that a price channel built on highs and lows draws between its two edges.
midprice-midpoint-price-over-period.howToReadHtml:
Price trading above the line is in the upper half of its recent range, and price below it is in the lower half. A move back to the line after a run means price has returned to the middle of its recent range.

The line only shifts when the range itself shifts, so a long flat stretch means the range has been stable, not that price has been still. It says nothing about how wide the range is; read it beside the high and low it is built from.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the range covers. A longer period gives a steadier line that steps less often and starts later.

faq.q: How does it differ from Median Price?
faq.html: Median Price is the midpoint of a single bar. Midpoint Price over Period is the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low across many bars, so it describes the recent range rather than the latest candle.

faq.q: Why does it ignore the close?
faq.html: It is a range measure. The highest high and lowest low define the edges of the range, and the line sits halfway between them whatever the closes did.

faq.q: When does the first value appear?
faq.html: On bar period - 1, once the window holds a full set of bars.

related.title: TYPPRICE: Typical Price
related.summary: The plain average of each bar's high, low and close, a single price for where the bar traded, drawn on the price chart.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

related.title: WCLPRICE: Weighted Close Price
related.summary: A single-bar average that counts the close twice, so the close carries half the weight and the high and the low a quarter each.

multilayer-perceptron-predictor.title: Multilayer Perceptron Predictor
multilayer-perceptron-predictor.summary: A small neural network trained bar by bar on six price features, drawing its five-bar price prediction back on the bar it was made from.
multilayer-perceptron-predictor.descriptionHtml:
This study runs a small feed-forward neural network with six inputs, hidden layers of 8 and 4 nodes, and one output. The six inputs are price features, each squeezed into the range -1 to 1 with a hyperbolic tangent: a 20-bar weighted trend line against its 100-bar average, the 14-bar RSI divided by 100, the 14-bar ATR against its own 14-bar average, the close against its 20-bar average, the 10-bar momentum as a share of the close, and a 5-bar exponential average against a 20-bar one.

The weights start from a fixed, repeatable pattern and are trained on every bar by gradient descent, with a learning rate of 0.0025 that decays slowly over the run, a Huber loss and gradients capped at 5. The network reads the features as they stood five bars earlier and predicts a squeezed log return over the next five bars. That return is turned back into a price from the close five bars earlier, and the line is drawn on that earlier bar, so each point sits on the bar it was a prediction for.

The training target is the log return measured once, over the first five bars the network sees, and it stays fixed for the rest of the run. Nothing is drawn until every feature has warmed up, which takes about 120 bars. On the newest bar a label shows the network's projection five bars ahead, run on the current features.
multilayer-perceptron-predictor.howToReadHtml:
Treat the line as an experiment rather than a signal. Because each point is drawn on the bar it predicted from, you can see directly how far the network's guesses sat from the price that followed. The label on the newest bar shows the price the trained network projects five bars ahead.

The network is tiny, its training target is fixed after the first bars, and it learns only from this chart, so its output mostly follows recent price with a bias. Do not read the projection as a forecast to trade on; use it to study how a simple learning model behaves on this instrument.

faq.q: Why does the line start so late?
faq.html: The slowest feature compares a 20-bar weighted trend line with its 100-bar average, so it needs about 120 bars. The network makes no prediction until all six features exist.

faq.q: Why is the line drawn five bars back?
faq.html: Each prediction is made from the features five bars earlier and is drawn on that bar, so the line can be compared against the price that actually arrived.

faq.q: Can I change the network or its learning rate?
faq.html: No. The layer sizes, learning rate, loss and feature set are fixed constants, so the study has no settings.

related.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
related.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.

related.title: Lunar Phase (LUNAR)
related.summary: The illuminated fraction of the moon at each bar's opening time, from 0 at new moon to 1 at full moon, with markers at the four main phases.

related.title: Ehlers Sine Wave (SINE)
related.summary: The phase of the detrended price cycle as a wave between -1 and +1, from the in-phase value over its length with a quadrature partner.

modified-moving-average-mma.title: Modified Moving Average (MMA)
modified-moving-average-mma.summary: A simple moving average plus a linear end-point correction from the same window, which removes most of the lag of the plain mean.
modified-moving-average-mma.descriptionHtml:
MMA starts from the simple average of the last period values. It then adds a correction that estimates where the line would be at the newest bar if the values in the window lay on a straight line. Walking the window from the newest value to the oldest, each value is weighted by (n - (2k + 1)) / 2, where n is the number of values and k is its position, so recent values get positive weight and older ones negative weight. The weighted sum times six, divided by n x (n + 1), is added to the mean.

The result is the end point of a least-squares straight line fitted through the window: it keeps the smoothness of the mean but sits much nearer the latest price. On the first bars the window holds fewer values and both parts use only those, so the line starts on the first bar.
modified-moving-average-mma.howToReadHtml:
Read MMA as a low-lag trend line. In a steady trend it rides close to price instead of trailing behind it as a simple average does, so a turn in MMA appears sooner after a turn in price.

The correction projects the recent slope, so after a sharp move the line can overshoot price, and in a choppy market it changes direction more often than a simple average of the same length. Compare it with the plain SMA of the same period to see how much of the gap the correction closes.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the window, from 2 to 4000. A longer window gives a smoother line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: How is MMA related to a linear regression line?
faq.html: The correction added to the mean is the slope of the window times half its span, so MMA equals the newest point of a least-squares straight line fitted through the window, just computed as a mean plus a correction.

faq.q: Why can MMA move beyond price?
faq.html: It extends the recent slope to the newest bar. After a fast move that then stalls, the projected slope carries the line past the latest price for a few bars.

faq.q: Why does it draw from the first bar?
faq.html: The mean and the correction both use however many values the window holds so far, so the first bar equals the source and the window grows to its full length.

related.title: Non-Lag Moving Average (NLMA)
related.summary: A long weighted average whose cosine kernel adds negative weights to older bars, cutting lag while still smoothing short noise.

related.title: McGinley Dynamic Indicator (MGDI)
related.summary: An adaptive average whose step toward price is divided by the fourth power of the price to line ratio, so it follows falls faster than rallies.

related.title: NMA - Natural Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average whose speed is set by where in the window the movement of log price happened: recent movement makes it fast.

min-max-channel-mmchannel.title: Min-Max Channel (MMCHANNEL)
min-max-channel-mmchannel.summary: The highest high and the lowest low of the lookback window drawn as a channel, marking the levels a breakout has to clear.
min-max-channel-mmchannel.descriptionHtml:
Min-Max Channel tracks the two extremes of the recent past. The upper line is the highest value of the high source over the last Period bars, and the lower line is the lowest value of the low source over the same bars. The space between them is shaded.

The channel answers from the very first bar. Until Period bars exist it uses every bar so far, so the early lines are the running high and low of the chart rather than a blank warmup. After that each line is the extreme of a fixed window, so it steps down or up as an old extreme drops out of the window and holds flat while no new extreme forms.

By default the edges are built from the bar highs and lows, and either can be switched to another source such as the close.
min-max-channel-mmchannel.howToReadHtml:
The upper line is the price that a move has to exceed to set a new Period high, and the lower line the price a move has to break to set a new Period low. A bar that pushes the upper line up is a fresh breakout, and a long flat stretch of both lines is a range.

The channel says nothing about direction by itself and it never leads price: an edge only moves when price makes a new extreme or an old one leaves the window. Use a longer period for the larger swing structure and a shorter one for tight breakouts.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer period gives a wider channel whose edges move less often.

settings.label: High Source
settings.html: The series whose highest value forms the upper edge. The bar high by default.

settings.label: Low Source
settings.html: The series whose lowest value forms the lower edge. The bar low by default.

faq.q: Why do the lines start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until Period bars exist the channel uses every bar it has, so the first values are the running high and low of the chart so far rather than nothing.

faq.q: How does it differ from Price Channel?
faq.html: Price Channel uses the same windowed highest high and lowest low of the bar highs and lows and adds their midpoint. Min-Max Channel draws only the two edges, and lets either edge be built from another source such as the close.

faq.q: Why would I change the sources?
faq.html: Using the close for both edges gives a channel of closing extremes, which ignores intrabar spikes and is often used to confirm a breakout on a close.

related.title: Price Channel (PCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the lookback window with their midpoint, showing the extremes a new move has to break.

related.title: MA Envelope (MAE)
related.summary: A moving average with two bands set a fixed percentage above and below it, so the channel scales with price rather than with volatility.

related.title: Regression Channels (REGCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares trend line through the last N prices, with bands set a multiple of the fit's own residual spread above and below it.

mode.title: Mode
mode.summary: The value that repeats most often in the recent window, drawn only when some value actually repeats, marking prices the market keeps returning to.
mode.descriptionHtml:
The Mode study counts how many times each distinct value of the source appears in the last Period bars and plots the one that appears most often. Values are compared exactly, so two closes count as the same only when they are equal to the last decimal.

When two or more values share the highest count, the winner is the one met first while walking back from the current bar, which is the most recent of the tied values. When every value in the window is different there is no mode, and the study draws nothing on that bar.

Early bars use as many bars as exist rather than waiting for a full window, and absent values are skipped.
mode.howToReadHtml:
A mode that appears and holds the same value over many bars shows a price the instrument keeps settling at, often a round number or a level where orders cluster. Gaps in the line are bars where no value repeated in the window, which is the usual case for a finely priced instrument with a short period.

The study is most useful on a coarse source or a longer period, where repeats are common. On a source with many decimals it may draw very little, which is an honest answer rather than a fault.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose repeated values are counted. A coarser series repeats more often.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars are counted. A longer period finds more repeats and changes less often.

faq.q: Why are there gaps in the line?
faq.html: On those bars every value in the window was different, so no value is more common than another and there is no mode to draw.

faq.q: Which value wins a tie?
faq.html: The one met first walking back from the current bar, which is the most recent of the tied values. A later value has to repeat strictly more often to replace it.

faq.q: What period suits it?
faq.html: A longer period gives repeats more chance to appear. With a short period on a finely priced instrument the line will be mostly empty.

related.title: Percentile
related.summary: The value at a chosen percentile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart, interpolated between the two nearest ranks.

related.title: Median
related.summary: The middle value of the source over a rolling window, a centre line that a single outlier bar cannot drag around the way it drags a mean.

related.title: Polynomial Fitting (POLYFIT)
related.summary: Fits a least-squares polynomial of the chosen degree to the recent window and plots the fitted curve's value at the current bar.

modular-filter-modf.title: Modular Filter (MODF)
modular-filter-modf.summary: Blends two exponential bands, one that snaps up to price and one that snaps down, into a filter that ranges from smooth average to trailing stop.
modular-filter-modf.descriptionHtml:
This study builds two exponential bands from the source with a smoothing factor of 2 / (Period + 1). The upper band is an exponential average that jumps straight to price whenever price rises above it; the lower band does the same whenever price falls below it. Both bands start at zero. On the first bar the upper band snaps straight to price, while the lower band climbs up from zero over the following bars.

A side flag records which band price last touched: it becomes 1 on a bar where price equals the upper band, 0 on a bar where it equals the lower band, and otherwise keeps its previous value. The output then mixes the bands with Beta. On the up side it is beta * upper + (1 - beta) * lower, on the down side beta * lower + (1 - beta) * upper. With Beta at 1 the line follows the band on the side price last touched; with Beta at 0 it sits on the opposite band, like a trailing stop.

With Feedback switched on, the input to both bands is a blend of the source and the previous output, weighted by Feedback Weight, which smooths the line further.
modular-filter-modf.howToReadHtml:
With a high Beta, read the line as a smooth filter that follows price closely after each new touch of a band. With a low Beta, read it as a trailing stop: the line stays on the far side of price and only flips when price reaches the other band. A change of side is a change in which band price last touched, which marks a new swing direction.

A longer Period widens the bands and slows the line. Feedback adds smoothing at the cost of more lag. Because the lower band starts at zero, the line begins well below price and needs some bars at the start of the chart to catch up before it can be read.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential bands. Longer periods give slower bands and a smoother line.
