settings.label: Beta
settings.html: The blend between the bands. 1.0 behaves as a smooth filter that follows price, 0.0 as a trailing stop on the far band.

settings.label: Feedback
settings.html: When on, the bands are fed a blend of price and the previous output instead of price alone, which smooths the line.

settings.label: Feedback Weight
settings.html: The share of price in the feedback blend. Lower values lean more on the previous output and give a smoother line. Used only with Feedback on.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

faq.q: What does Beta actually change?
faq.html: It decides how much of each band goes into the line. Near 1 the line hugs the band price last touched; near 0 it stays on the opposite band, so it trails price like a stop.

faq.q: Why does the line start below price and climb?
faq.html: Both bands start at zero. The upper band jumps to price on the first bar, but the lower band rises from zero at the exponential rate, so the blend starts at roughly Beta times price (about 83 percent of it at the defaults) and closes the gap over the first couple of Period lengths.

faq.q: When should I turn Feedback on?
faq.html: When the line is too jumpy for your timeframe. Feedback feeds part of the previous output back in, which damps quick reversals but adds lag.

related.title: Notch Filter (NOTCH)
related.summary: Removes one chosen cycle length from price with a second-order notch filter and leaves the rest of the movement close to untouched.

related.title: LOESS Filter
related.summary: Fits a tricube-weighted straight line through a short window of recent prices and draws the value of that line at the centre of the window.

related.title: NW - Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression
related.summary: A backward-looking kernel regression: each bar is a Gaussian weighted average of recent prices, with the bandwidth setting how fast older bars fade.

momentum-mom.title: Momentum (MOM)
momentum-mom.summary: The plain price difference between this bar and the bar a fixed number of bars back, drawn as a line around zero.
momentum-mom.descriptionHtml:
Momentum is the simplest measure of how fast price is moving. On every bar it takes the chosen source and subtracts the value of the same source length bars earlier. The answer is in price units: on a market trading near 60,000 a reading of 500 means price is 500 higher than it was length bars ago.

There is no smoothing and no scaling, so the line reacts as soon as price does and carries all of its noise. The first length bars have no reading, because there is no bar that far back to compare with, and the line starts once there is.
momentum-mom.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, price is higher than it was length bars ago; below zero, it is lower. The further the line is from zero, the faster the move. A line that keeps rising while price rises says the advance is speeding up, and a line that turns down while price is still climbing says the advance is slowing, which often comes before a pause or a turn.

Because the reading is in price units, its size depends on the instrument's price level, so compare it only with its own history on the same chart. A single large bar entering or leaving the window can jump the line, which is the cost of having no smoothing.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars back the comparison reaches. A short length follows every swing; a long one shows the broader trend of the move.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own earlier value. Close is the default; hl2 and the other blends soften bars with long wicks.

faq.q: Why is the start of the chart blank?
faq.html: The first reading needs a bar length bars back. Until the chart has that many bars there is nothing to subtract, so the line starts on bar length.

faq.q: How is this different from Rate of Change Percentage?
faq.html: Momentum is the raw difference in price units. A percentage rate of change divides that difference by the older price, so its readings compare across instruments and price levels.

faq.q: Does a zero cross mean anything?
faq.html: A cross above zero means price has just risen above where it was length bars ago, and a cross below means it has fallen under it. It describes the move; it does not forecast the next one.

related.title: Price Momentum Oscillator (PMO)
related.summary: A percentage rate of change smoothed twice by exponential averages, with a third average as its signal line.

related.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average, a smoothed signal line of that gap, and their difference as a coloured histogram.

related.title: Percentage Price Oscillator (PPO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

mean-error-mpe.title: Mean %Error (MPE)
mean-error-mpe.summary: The average signed percentage by which price sits above or below its own EMA, over a rolling window of bars.
mean-error-mpe.descriptionHtml:
Mean %Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price, in percent and with the sign kept. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study subtracts the average from the source, divides by the source and multiplies by 100. A bar where the source is exactly zero carries no error.

The signed percentage errors are averaged over the last Period bars, at most 4000, counting only the bars that carry an error. The reading starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full. Positive and negative errors cancel, so the result shows a persistent bias as a level away from zero.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-error-mpe.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 1.5 means price has, on balance, been about 1.5 percent above its average over the window, the shape of an uptrend. A negative reading means price has been below its average. Because it is a percentage, the reading can be compared between instruments.

A reading near zero does not mean price has been close to the average, only that the misses on each side have balanced. Pair it with MAPE to see how large the misses were.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the averaging window, which is held to at most 4000 bars.

faq.q: How is MPE different from MAPE?
faq.html: MAPE takes the absolute value of each percentage error, so it measures size. MPE keeps the sign, so it measures bias, and errors on opposite sides cancel.

faq.q: What does a reading that stays above zero tell me?
faq.html: Price has spent the window mostly above its EMA, which is typical of a sustained rise. The longer and higher it stays, the stronger the bias.

faq.q: Why does the line start late?
faq.html: The EMA has no value until the chart has Period bars, so the error cannot be measured before then.

related.title: Mean Relative Absolute Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the absolute gap between two series as a fraction of the actual value, where 0 is a perfect match.

related.title: Mean Error (ME)
related.summary: The average signed gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, showing whether price has been sitting above or below it.

related.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, a measure that weighs large misses heavily.

mean-relative-absolute-error.title: Mean Relative Absolute Error
mean-relative-absolute-error.summary: A rolling average of the absolute gap between two series as a fraction of the actual value, where 0 is a perfect match.
mean-relative-absolute-error.descriptionHtml:
Mean Relative Absolute Error compares an actual series (the close by default) with a predicted series (the open by default). On every bar it divides the absolute gap between them by the absolute actual value, giving the error as a fraction of the level. The study plots the simple average of those fractions over the last Length bars.

When the actual value is effectively zero the bar contributes zero rather than an infinite ratio. An absent actual value reads as 1 in the denominator and as 0 in the gap, and an absent predicted value reads as 0.

The pane shows a dotted line at 0, labelled Perfect, and a dotted line at 1, an error as large as the level itself.
mean-relative-absolute-error.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 0.003 means the predicted series was typically 0.3 percent away from the actual one over the window. Zero would mean a perfect match on every bar, and 1 would mean the typical miss was as large as the actual value. With the default inputs the reading is the average bar body as a fraction of the close, a scale-free measure of how much price moves inside each bar.

Because it is a ratio, the reading can be compared between instruments at different price levels. The line has no value until Length bars have passed.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the relative errors are averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the outcome and used as the base of each ratio. The close by default.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast of the actual series. The open by default.

faq.q: What do the two dotted lines mean?
faq.html: The line at 0 marks a perfect forecast. The line at 1 marks an average error as large as the actual value itself, which on a price chart would be an enormous miss.

faq.q: Is this a percentage?
faq.html: It is a fraction. Multiply by 100 to read it as a percentage, so 0.01 is a one percent average error.

faq.q: Why does a zero actual value add nothing?
faq.html: Dividing by zero has no answer, so a bar whose actual value is effectively zero contributes an error of zero instead.

related.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, a measure that weighs large misses heavily.

related.title: Mean %Error (MPE)
related.summary: The average signed percentage by which price sits above or below its own EMA, over a rolling window of bars.

related.title: Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (MSLE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between log(1 + price) and log(1 + its EMA) over a rolling window, a scale-free error measure.

mean-squared-error-mse.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
mean-squared-error-mse.summary: The average squared gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, a measure that weighs large misses heavily.
mean-squared-error-mse.descriptionHtml:
Mean Squared Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through the warmup. On every bar the study subtracts the average from the source and squares the result.

Those squared gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry a gap. The reading starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full. Squaring makes every gap positive and gives large gaps far more weight than small ones, so one wide departure from the average lifts the reading sharply.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-squared-error-mse.howToReadHtml:
A rising reading means price has been moving further from its average, and a spike marks a bar or a short run of bars that broke well away from it. A falling reading means price has settled close to its average.

The value is in squared price units, so it grows with the square of the price level and is not comparable between instruments. Its square root is the root mean squared error, back in price units. Compare the reading with its own history rather than with a fixed level.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the window the squared error is averaged over.

faq.q: Why are the numbers so large?
faq.html: The gaps are squared, so a gap of 100 price units contributes 10,000. The reading is in squared price units.

faq.q: How is MSE different from MAE?
faq.html: MAE averages absolute gaps, treating each miss in proportion to its size. MSE squares them first, so a few large misses dominate the reading.

faq.q: Why is there nothing for the first bars?
faq.html: The EMA is seeded from a simple average of its first Period values, so neither the average nor the error exists before the chart has Period bars.

related.title: Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (MSLE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between log(1 + price) and log(1 + its EMA) over a rolling window, a scale-free error measure.

related.title: Mean Relative Absolute Error
related.summary: A rolling average of the absolute gap between two series as a fraction of the actual value, where 0 is a perfect match.

related.title: Pseudo-Huber Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of the smooth Huber loss between an actual and a predicted series, quadratic for small misses and close to linear for large ones.

mean-squared-logarithmic-error-msle.title: Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (MSLE)
mean-squared-logarithmic-error-msle.summary: The average squared gap between log(1 + price) and log(1 + its EMA) over a rolling window, a scale-free error measure.
mean-squared-logarithmic-error-msle.descriptionHtml:
Mean Squared Logarithmic Error scores an exponential moving average as a forecast of price on a logarithmic scale. The average is taken over Period bars and seeded with the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the study takes the natural logarithm of one plus the source and of one plus the average, subtracts the second from the first and squares the result. When either value is at or below minus one the logarithm has no answer and the bar carries no error.

The squared log gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry an error, so the reading starts on the first bar where the average exists and widens its window until it is full. Working with logarithms turns the gap into something close to a relative change, so the reading stays comparable as the price level moves.

The error is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane, and the reference average is drawn on the price chart.
mean-squared-logarithmic-error-msle.howToReadHtml:
For prices well above one, the log gap is close to the percentage distance from the average, so a reading of 0.0004 corresponds to a typical distance of about 2 percent (the square root of 0.0004 is 0.02). A rising reading means price is pulling away from its average; a falling one means it is settling near it.

Because the gaps are squared, a few wide departures dominate the reading. The values are small, so read the pane with enough decimals, and compare the line with its own history.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series measured against its own average. The close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the reference EMA and of the averaging window, held to between 1 and 4000 bars.

faq.q: Why take logarithms?
faq.html: The log gap measures relative distance rather than distance in price units, so the reading does not grow just because the instrument became more expensive.

faq.q: Why are the values so small?
faq.html: A log gap of 0.02 is roughly a 2 percent distance, and squaring it gives 0.0004. Take the square root of the reading to get back to a rough typical percentage as a fraction.

faq.q: How does it differ from MSE?
faq.html: MSE squares the gap in price units, so it depends on the price level. MSLE squares the gap in logarithms, so it is close to a squared percentage and comparable across instruments.

related.title: Pseudo-Huber Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of the smooth Huber loss between an actual and a predicted series, quadratic for small misses and close to linear for large ones.

related.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between price and its own EMA over a rolling window, a measure that weighs large misses heavily.

related.title: Quantile Loss (Pinball Loss)
related.summary: A rolling average of the pinball loss, an error score that charges misses above and below the forecast at different rates set by a quantile.

ehlers-mesa-stochastic-mstoch.title: Ehlers MESA Stochastic (MSTOCH)
ehlers-mesa-stochastic-mstoch.summary: A stochastic taken on filtered price, with trend and noise removed first, then smoothed into an oscillator between 0 and 1.
ehlers-mesa-stochastic-mstoch.descriptionHtml:
The Ehlers MESA Stochastic (MSTOCH) first passes the source through a roofing filter: a 2-pole high-pass filter (48 bars by default) removes the trend and longer cycles, and a super smoother (10 bars) removes the short noise. It then measures where the filtered value sits between its highest and lowest values over the stochastic length (20 bars), and smooths that reading with the same super smoother.

On the first bars, missing earlier prices fold back onto the nearest price that exists, and bars before the first read the current filtered value in the stochastic window. When the window has no range the raw stochastic is 0.5. The result is held between 0 and 1.
ehlers-mesa-stochastic-mstoch.howToReadHtml:
Readings above 0.8 mean the filtered price is near the top of its recent range and readings below 0.2 mean it is near the bottom, with 0.5 in the middle. Because trend and noise are filtered out before the stochastic is taken, the line follows the swings between the two cutoff periods rather than raw price, and a turn back out of a zone marks a turn in that filtered swing.

The filters need bars to settle, so the opening stretch is not reliable. In a strong trend the filtered series can still cycle through both zones, so the reading describes the swing around the trend rather than the trend itself.

settings.label: Stochastic Length
settings.html: How many bars of filtered price the highest and lowest values are taken over.

settings.label: HP Length
settings.html: High-pass cutoff period: cycles longer than this, including the trend, are removed.

settings.label: SS Length
settings.html: Super smoother cutoff period: cycles shorter than this are removed, and the final line is smoothed with it too.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: How is it different from an ordinary stochastic?
faq.html: An ordinary stochastic works on raw price. This one removes the trend and the short noise first, so it reacts to the swings in between.

faq.q: Which levels matter?
faq.html: The pane marks 0.8 and 0.2 as the upper and lower zones and 0.5 as the midline.

faq.q: Why does it start at 0.5?
faq.html: On the first bar the filtered series has no range yet, so the stochastic reads the neutral 0.5 and the smoother starts from there.

related.title: Pretty Good Oscillator
related.summary: How far price sits from its simple average, measured in units of average true range, so a reading beyond plus or minus 3 marks a stretched move.

related.title: MARKETFI: Market Facilitation Index
related.summary: The bar's high-to-low range divided by its volume: how much price movement each traded unit bought on that bar.

related.title: Psychological Line (PSL)
related.summary: The percentage of up bars among the last N bars, a simple count of how one-sided recent trading has been, from 0 to 100.

normalized-average-true-range.title: Normalized Average True Range
normalized-average-true-range.summary: The average true range expressed as a percentage of the close, so volatility compares across instruments and price levels.
normalized-average-true-range.descriptionHtml:
Normalized Average True Range takes the average true range and divides it by the close, then multiplies by 100. The true range of a bar is the largest of three distances: the high minus the low, the high against the previous close, and the low against the previous close. The first bar measures against its own close.

The true range is smoothed with an average of weight 1 / Length. That average starts from zero and is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, so the first bar already reads its own true range and the line has no empty stretch at the start. Expressing the result as a percentage of the close means a reading of 1 says the instrument typically moves about 1 percent per bar, whatever its price.
normalized-average-true-range.howToReadHtml:
Higher readings mean bigger typical bar-to-bar moves relative to price, lower readings mean a quieter market. Because it is a percentage, you can compare a high priced and a low priced instrument directly, or compare the same instrument years apart when its price was very different.

It can be used to size stops: a stop set at a multiple of the reading is the same distance in percentage terms on any instrument. It does not show direction, and a single large gap raises it for several bars as the average works through it.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Sets the smoothing weight 1 / Length for the true range. A longer length gives a steadier, slower line.

faq.q: Why divide by the close?
faq.html: The raw average true range is in price units, so it is larger for expensive instruments. Dividing by the close turns it into a percentage that compares across instruments.

faq.q: Why does it answer from the first bar?
faq.html: The average starts from zero and is divided by the weight it has gathered, which removes the start-up bias without waiting for a full window.

faq.q: Does it include gaps?
faq.html: Yes. The true range measures the high and low against the previous close, so a gap between bars counts towards the reading.

related.title: Parkinson Volatility (PV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log ratio of each bar's high to its low, smoothed over a window and optionally annualised.

related.title: Mass Index (MASSI)
related.summary: Sums the ratio of a single to a double exponential average of the bar range, so a widening range shows as a bulge in the line.

related.title: Rogers-Satchell Volatility (RSV)
related.summary: A volatility estimate built from each bar's open, high, low and close designed so that a steady trend does not inflate it.

non-lag-moving-average-nlma.title: Non-Lag Moving Average (NLMA)
non-lag-moving-average-nlma.summary: A long weighted average whose cosine kernel adds negative weights to older bars, cutting lag while still smoothing short noise.
non-lag-moving-average-nlma.descriptionHtml:
The Non-Lag Moving Average convolves the source with a fixed kernel that spans 5 * period - 1 bars. The first period - 1 taps form a focus zone where a variable t ramps from 0 to 1; the remaining taps carry t on upward. Each tap weighs cos(pi * t), and once t passes one half that is damped by 1 / (3 pi t + 1). The last tap weighs nothing.

The cosine swings below zero and back, so some older bars get negative weight. Those negative weights subtract part of the old price history, which pulls the line toward the newest bars and reduces lag. The weighted sum is divided by the sum of the weights, so a flat price passes through unchanged. Until the kernel has a full window the line shows the price, and a missing price counts as zero.
non-lag-moving-average-nlma.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a trend line that stays close to price. It turns sooner than a simple or exponential average of a similar smoothness, so a change in its slope arrives earlier. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

The price of low lag is overshoot: after a sharp reversal the negative weights can push the line slightly past price before it settles. The kernel is five times the period long, so the line only starts filtering after that many bars; before then it equals the price.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The conceptual averaging period. The kernel itself spans 5 * period - 1 bars, so a larger value smooths more and needs more history.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the kernel five times longer than the period?
faq.html: That is how the kernel is laid out: the focus zone takes the first period - 1 taps, and the damped cosine carries on over the remaining 4 * period taps, swinging between positive and negative weights several more times as it fades.

faq.q: Why does the line equal the price on early bars?
faq.html: The filter needs a full kernel of history, 5 * period - 1 bars. Before that it shows the price rather than a partial result.

faq.q: Can it overshoot price?
faq.html: Yes. The negative weights that reduce lag also make the line run a little past a sharp turn before it catches up.

related.title: NMA - Natural Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average whose speed is set by where in the window the movement of log price happened: recent movement makes it fast.

related.title: Modified Moving Average (MMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average plus a linear end-point correction from the same window, which removes most of the lag of the plain mean.

related.title: Nyquist Moving Average (NYQMA)
related.summary: A weighted average pushed forward by its distance from a second, smoother average of itself, which takes back most of its lag.

nma-natural-moving-average.title: NMA - Natural Moving Average
nma-natural-moving-average.summary: An adaptive average whose speed is set by where in the window the movement of log price happened: recent movement makes it fast.
nma-natural-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
NMA works on the natural log of price, scaled by 1000. For each of the last period steps it takes the size of the move between neighbouring bars, then weights it with a square-root kernel: the newest step gets weight sqrt(1) - sqrt(0), the next sqrt(2) - sqrt(1), and so on, so weight falls off with age. The smoothing ratio is the weighted total divided by the plain total of the same moves.

When most of the movement in the window happened in the newest bars, the ratio is high and the line moves quickly toward price. When the movement is spread through the window or sits in older bars, the ratio is low and the line smooths hard. The average starts at the first source value and then steps toward the source by the ratio on each bar. Bars before the start of the chart read as zero, so the first few ratios are dominated by that first large step.
nma-natural-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read NMA as a trend line that changes speed on its own. During a fresh breakout, when the latest bars carry the movement, it catches up with price quickly; in a market that has gone quiet after earlier swings, it flattens and ignores small moves.

A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend and a falling line with price below it a downtrend. Give it a period's worth of bars before relying on it, because the earliest ratios are shaped by the start of the chart rather than by price behaviour.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many steps of log price are weighed to set the smoothing ratio. A longer period spreads the kernel and slows the line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it use the log of price?
faq.html: Log price turns moves into percentages, so the ratio responds to the relative size of moves and reads the same at any price level.

faq.q: What makes the ratio high?
faq.html: Movement concentrated in the newest bars. The square-root kernel gives the newest step the largest weight, so a big recent move against a quiet past pushes the ratio toward one.

faq.q: Why do the first bars look different?
faq.html: Bars before the start of the chart read as zero, so the first step is very large and dominates the ratio until enough real bars fill the window.

related.title: Nyquist Moving Average (NYQMA)
related.summary: A weighted average pushed forward by its distance from a second, smoother average of itself, which takes back most of its lag.

related.title: Non-Lag Moving Average (NLMA)
related.summary: A long weighted average whose cosine kernel adds negative weights to older bars, cutting lag while still smoothing short noise.

related.title: Parzen Window Moving Average (PARZEN)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a smooth piecewise cubic bell that falls to zero at both ends of the window, for a quiet line with little ripple.

min-max-normalization-normalize.title: Min-Max Normalization (NORMALIZE)
min-max-normalization-normalize.summary: Rescales the source to a 0 to 1 range by its own lowest and highest readings over a lookback window.
min-max-normalization-normalize.descriptionHtml:
Min-Max Normalization (NORMALIZE) shows where the current value of the source sits inside its recent range. On each bar it finds the lowest and the highest values of the source over the last length bars, this bar included, and computes (source - lowest) / (highest - lowest). The result is 0 when the source is at the bottom of the window, 1 when it is at the top, and in between otherwise.

The search starts from the current bar and takes in every present value before it, so on a chart shorter than the window the range is measured against the bars that exist so far. When every value in the window is the same, the range is zero and the study reads 0.
min-max-normalization-normalize.howToReadHtml:
Readings near 1 mean the source is at or close to the top of its recent range, and readings near 0 mean it is at or close to the bottom. A move from the low end to the high end shows price travelling across its whole recent range. Because the scale is always 0 to 1, the line can be compared across instruments with very different prices.

A reading of 1 is not a sell signal by itself: in a strong trend the source can sit at the top of its window for many bars, because each new high also raises the window's top. A longer length makes the scale steadier and slower to reach its extremes.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series to normalise, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Lookback Length
settings.html: How many bars, this one included, set the lowest and highest values. A longer window gives a steadier scale that reaches 0 and 1 less often.

faq.q: Why does the line stay at 1 during a rally?
faq.html: Each new high becomes the top of the window, so the source sits exactly at the top and reads 1. It drops below 1 only when the source falls back from the highest value in the window.

faq.q: Why is the value 0 on some bars where price did move?
faq.html: If every value in the window is equal, the range is zero and the study reads 0. That happens mostly with a length of 1, where the window holds only the current bar.

faq.q: How is it different from a stochastic oscillator?
faq.html: The stochastic usually measures the close against the highest high and lowest low. This study measures the chosen source against its own lowest and highest values, on a 0 to 1 scale, without smoothing.

related.title: Normal Distribution CDF (NORMDIST)
related.summary: Turns the source's z-score over a rolling window into a normal cumulative probability, read as a percentile from 0 to 1.

related.title: Lowest Value (LOWEST)
related.summary: Traces the lowest value of the source over a rolling window, starting on the first bar with the lowest value seen so far.

related.title: Open-Close Midpoint (OC2)
related.summary: Draws the centre of every candle body, half the sum of its open and its close, ignoring the wicks entirely.

normal-distribution-cdf-normdist.title: Normal Distribution CDF (NORMDIST)
normal-distribution-cdf-normdist.summary: Turns the source's z-score over a rolling window into a normal cumulative probability, read as a percentile from 0 to 1.
normal-distribution-cdf-normdist.descriptionHtml:
Normal Distribution CDF (NORMDIST) asks how unusual the current value is compared with its own recent history. On each bar it takes the last period values of the source, computes their mean and their standard deviation (the population form, the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean), and expresses the current value as a z-score: how many standard deviations it sits from the mean.

The z-score is then shifted by Mu and divided by Sigma, and passed through the cumulative distribution function of the normal distribution. The study evaluates that function with a three-term approximation of the error function whose error is below 1.5e-7. The output runs from 0 to 1: 0.5 means the value is at its recent mean, 0.84 is about one standard deviation above it, and 0.975 about two. Until two values are available the reading is 0.5. On a window where the source has not moved at all, the z-score is taken as zero, so the reading is 0.5 at the default Mu.
normal-distribution-cdf-normdist.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a percentile. Above the 0.975 line, the source is more than about two standard deviations above its recent mean, which would be rare if the values were normally distributed; below 0.025 it is just as far below. The 0.841 and 0.159 lines mark one standard deviation either side, and 0.5 is the mean.

Extreme readings show stretched prices, but price is not normally distributed, and in a trend the source can stay near 0 or 1 for a long time. The window is short-term memory: a long period makes the scale slower to adapt, a short one makes every swing look extreme.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series to score against its own recent mean and spread.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars set the mean and standard deviation. A shorter window adapts faster and reaches the extremes more often.

settings.label: Mu
settings.html: Subtracted from the z-score before the probability is taken. A positive value shifts the whole line down, so the source must be further above its mean to read 0.5.

settings.label: Sigma
settings.html: Divides the z-score before the probability is taken. A value above 1 squeezes the line toward 0.5; a value below 1 pushes it to the extremes sooner.

faq.q: What does a reading of 0.975 mean?
faq.html: With the default Mu and Sigma, the source is about two standard deviations above its mean over the lookback window. Under a normal distribution only about 2.5 percent of readings would be that high.

faq.q: Why can the line sit near 1 for a long time?
faq.html: In a steady trend the latest value keeps landing far from the window's mean. The study measures position, not exhaustion, so it can stay extreme while the trend lasts.

faq.q: Why is the first bar 0.5?
faq.html: A spread needs at least two values. Until the window holds two, the study reports the centre of the scale.

related.title: Open-Close Midpoint (OC2)
related.summary: Draws the centre of every candle body, half the sum of its open and its close, ignoring the wicks entirely.

related.title: Min-Max Normalization (NORMALIZE)
related.summary: Rescales the source to a 0 to 1 range by its own lowest and highest readings over a lookback window.

related.title: Open-High-Low Average (OHL3)
related.summary: Draws the average of each bar's open, high and low, a reference price that leaves out where the bar closed.

notch-filter-notch.title: Notch Filter (NOTCH)
notch-filter-notch.summary: Removes one chosen cycle length from price with a second-order notch filter and leaves the rest of the movement close to untouched.
notch-filter-notch.descriptionHtml:
This study takes one cycle out of price. It is a second-order recursive notch filter centred on the Period to Remove: a swing of exactly that length is cancelled, swings close to it are reduced, and slower and faster movement passes through almost unchanged.

The centre angle is 2 * pi / Period. The width of the notch is the Relative Bandwidth times that angle, and half of it, held between 0.0001 and just under a quarter turn, sets a pole factor (1 - tan) / (1 + tan). From the pole factor and the cosine of the centre angle come the filter coefficients, and each bar's output combines the current price, the two previous prices and the two previous outputs.

On the first bar the delay line is filled with the first price, so the filter starts at rest instead of jumping from zero. A missing price reading counts as zero.
notch-filter-notch.howToReadHtml:
Use the line as price with one rhythm taken out. If a market keeps repeating a swing of a known length, for example a session cycle on intraday bars, setting the period to that length removes it and makes the underlying move easier to see. The line stays close to price otherwise, so it adds very little lag compared with a smoothing average.

A wider bandwidth removes cycles over a broader range around the period, at the cost of a little more distortion nearby. If the period you choose does not match a real cycle in the data, the filter simply has little effect.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

settings.label: Period to Remove
settings.html: The cycle length, in bars, at the centre of the notch. A swing of exactly this length is cancelled.

settings.label: Relative Bandwidth
settings.html: The width of the notch as a fraction of its centre frequency. Larger values remove a broader range of cycles around the period.

faq.q: How is a notch filter different from a moving average?
faq.html: A moving average removes all fast movement and lags. A notch removes only a narrow range of cycle lengths and leaves the rest, so the line stays close to price.

faq.q: How do I choose the period?
faq.html: Pick a cycle you can see repeating in the data, such as the number of bars in a trading session. If you are unsure, compare a few periods and keep the one that removes the most regular wiggle.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first price?
faq.html: The delay line is filled with the first price on the first bar, so the filter begins at rest rather than climbing up from zero.

related.title: NW - Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression
related.summary: A backward-looking kernel regression: each bar is a Gaussian weighted average of recent prices, with the bandwidth setting how fast older bars fade.

related.title: Modular Filter (MODF)
related.summary: Blends two exponential bands, one that snaps up to price and one that snaps down, into a filter that ranges from smooth average to trailing stop.

related.title: One Euro Filter (ONEEURO)
related.summary: An adaptive smoother that filters heavily while price is quiet and lifts its cutoff when price moves fast, trading jitter against lag.

negative-volume-index-nvi.title: Negative Volume Index (NVI)
negative-volume-index-nvi.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume fell against the bar before.
negative-volume-index-nvi.descriptionHtml:
The Negative Volume Index tracks what price does on quieter bars. It starts at 100. On each bar whose volume is lower than the previous bar's volume, the index is multiplied by this bar's price divided by the previous bar's price, so it takes on that bar's percentage change. On every other bar, when volume rose or stayed the same, the index holds flat.

The first bar has no previous bar, so it holds at 100. A bar is skipped as well when the previous price is zero or the previous volume is not above zero, which avoids dividing by nothing. The price followed is the Price Source setting, the close by default.
negative-volume-index-nvi.howToReadHtml:
Because the index only moves on bars where volume fell, it shows the trend made on the quieter bars. A rising index means price has tended to advance on falling volume; a falling one means it has tended to decline on falling volume. Many traders compare the index with a long moving average of itself to judge the trend.

The level is the compounded price change on the quieter bars since the start at 100, not a price, so read the direction and the slope. On a series without volume the index stays flat at 100, since no bar can show falling volume.

settings.label: Price Source
settings.html: The price whose percentage change the index takes on the qualifying bars, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line stay flat for stretches?
faq.html: It only moves on bars whose volume is lower than the bar before. Through a run of rising volume it holds its last value.

faq.q: What does the value 100 mean?
faq.html: It is only the starting point. The index compounds price changes from there, so its level tells you the combined change on the quieter bars since the first bar.

related.title: On Balance Volume (OBV)
related.summary: A running total that adds each bar's volume on a higher close and subtracts it on a lower close, tracking where volume is flowing.

related.title: Money Flow Index (MFI)
related.summary: A volume-weighted strength oscillator from 0 to 100 that compares money flowing in on rising bars with money flowing out on falling bars.

related.title: Price Volume Divergence (PVD)
related.summary: Compares the direction of price change with the direction of volume change and sizes the disagreement, positive when they diverge.

nw-nadaraya-watson-kernel-regression.title: NW - Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression
nw-nadaraya-watson-kernel-regression.summary: A backward-looking kernel regression: each bar is a Gaussian weighted average of recent prices, with the bandwidth setting how fast older bars fade.
nw-nadaraya-watson-kernel-regression.descriptionHtml:
This study smooths price with a kernel regression that looks only backward. On each bar it averages the last Period values, giving the value i bars back the Gaussian weight exp(-i^2 / (2 * h^2)), where h is the Bandwidth. The current bar has weight 1, and the weight of older bars falls away smoothly, quickly for a small bandwidth and slowly for a large one.

The result is the weighted sum of the prices divided by the sum of the weights. At the start of the chart the window simply holds every bar so far, so the line begins on the first bar and widens to its full length as bars arrive. A missing price counts as zero while still carrying its weight.

Because it uses only the current and earlier bars, the line never changes once a bar has closed.
nw-nadaraya-watson-kernel-regression.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed price. Its slope shows the direction of the recent average and the distance from price shows how far price has moved away from that average. Price crossing the line marks the latest move overtaking the weighted recent past.

The bandwidth does most of the work: a small bandwidth concentrates the weight on the last few bars and tracks price closely, while a large one spreads it across the window and gives a slow, smooth line. The Period only needs to be long enough to hold the bars that still carry meaningful weight, roughly three bandwidths.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the average looks back over. Bars beyond about three bandwidths carry almost no weight, so a much longer period changes little.

settings.label: Bandwidth (h)
settings.html: The width of the Gaussian kernel. Small values track price closely; large values smooth heavily.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Does this line repaint?
faq.html: No. It only weights the current and earlier bars, so each value is fixed once its bar closes. Kernel regressions that also look at later bars do repaint; this one does not.

faq.q: Why does the line appear from the very first bar?
faq.html: The window grows with the data: on early bars it uses every bar available, and it reaches the full Period once enough bars exist.

faq.q: Which setting should I adjust first?
faq.html: The bandwidth. It decides how quickly older bars lose weight, which is what sets the smoothness. Adjust the Period only if you raise the bandwidth so far that the window cuts off bars that still carry weight.

related.title: One Euro Filter (ONEEURO)
related.summary: An adaptive smoother that filters heavily while price is quiet and lifts its cutoff when price moves fast, trading jitter against lag.

related.title: Notch Filter (NOTCH)
related.summary: Removes one chosen cycle length from price with a second-order notch filter and leaves the rest of the movement close to untouched.

related.title: Recursive Least Squares Adaptive Filter (RLS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that re-estimates its weights every bar by recursive least squares, with a forgetting factor setting how much history still counts.

nyquist-moving-average-nyqma.title: Nyquist Moving Average (NYQMA)
nyquist-moving-average-nyqma.summary: A weighted average pushed forward by its distance from a second, smoother average of itself, which takes back most of its lag.
nyquist-moving-average-nyqma.descriptionHtml:
The Nyquist Moving Average starts from two linearly weighted averages. The first, MA1, weights the source over period bars with the newest bar weighing most. The second, MA2, applies the same weighting to MA1 over a shorter n2 bars. The second period is held at or below half the first, which is what keeps the second smoothing from folding short cycles back into the result.

The line is (1 + alpha) * MA1 - alpha * MA2, with alpha = n2 / (period - n2). Since MA2 lags MA1, adding back a fraction of their gap moves the line forward and cancels much of MA1's lag. While their windows fill, both averages cover every bar seen so far, so the line starts on the first bar, and a missing price counts as zero.
nyquist-moving-average-nyqma.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line that keeps up with price better than a weighted average of the same period. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend; the slope of the line is the main signal.

The lag correction comes from extrapolation, so after a sharp turn the line can overshoot for a few bars. A larger second period corrects more lag and overshoots more; a smaller one is closer to a plain weighted average.

settings.label: Period (N1)
settings.html: The window of the main weighted average. A longer period gives a smoother line.

settings.label: Nyquist Period (N2)
settings.html: The window of the second average, held at no more than half of Period (N1). A larger value corrects more lag.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the second period capped at half the first?
faq.html: A second smoothing longer than half the first would fold short cycles back into the result. Holding it at or below half keeps the correction clean.

faq.q: Why can the line move past price?
faq.html: It extrapolates the gap between two averages. After a sharp reversal that gap still points the old way for a few bars, so the line overshoots before it turns.

faq.q: What happens if I set N2 above half of N1?
faq.html: It is clamped to half of N1, rounded down, so the line does not change beyond that point.

related.title: Parzen Window Moving Average (PARZEN)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a smooth piecewise cubic bell that falls to zero at both ends of the window, for a quiet line with little ripple.

related.title: NMA - Natural Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average whose speed is set by where in the window the movement of log price happened: recent movement makes it fast.

related.title: Ehlers Predictive Moving Average (PMA)
related.summary: A weighted average with one lag cancelled by extrapolation, plus a faster trigger line that leads it.

on-balance-volume-obv.title: On Balance Volume (OBV)
on-balance-volume-obv.summary: A running total that adds each bar's volume on a higher close and subtracts it on a lower close, tracking where volume is flowing.
on-balance-volume-obv.descriptionHtml:
On Balance Volume keeps one running total from the first bar. When a bar closes above the previous bar's close, its whole volume is added to the total. When it closes below, its volume is subtracted. When the close is unchanged, the total does not move.

The total starts at zero, and the first bar compares with its own close, so it adds nothing. A missing volume reads as zero, and a bar with no close leaves the total as it was. There are no settings: the line depends only on the closes and the volume of the bars on the chart.
on-balance-volume-obv.howToReadHtml:
Read the direction of the line rather than its level, which depends only on where the chart starts. A rising line says volume has been arriving on up closes, a falling one that it has been arriving on down closes. When price and the line move together the trend has volume behind it.

The most watched reading is a divergence: price making a new high while the line fails to, or price making a new low while the line holds up. Because a bar counts its whole volume whatever the size of its move, one heavy bar with a tiny close change can shift the line a long way.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero on my chart?
faq.html: The running total begins on the first loaded bar. Its level depends only on that starting point, so compare slopes and turns, not values between charts.

faq.q: Does the size of the price move matter?
faq.html: No. Only the direction of the close matters. A bar that closes one tick higher adds its full volume, the same as a bar that rallies strongly.

related.title: Price Volume Divergence (PVD)
related.summary: Compares the direction of price change with the direction of volume change and sizes the disagreement, positive when they diverge.

related.title: Negative Volume Index (NVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume fell against the bar before.

related.title: Positive Volume Index (PVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume rose against the bar before.

open-close-midpoint-oc2.title: Open-Close Midpoint (OC2)
open-close-midpoint-oc2.summary: Draws the centre of every candle body, half the sum of its open and its close, ignoring the wicks entirely.
open-close-midpoint-oc2.descriptionHtml:
Open-Close Midpoint (OC2) marks the centre of each candle's body. It is computed as (open + close) * 0.5 on every bar, with no lookback and no smoothing, so each value belongs to the bar it is drawn on.

The high and the low play no part in it. A bar with a long wick and a bar with none, if they open and close at the same prices, get the same value. The line therefore follows where trading started and finished on each bar and leaves out the excursions in between, which makes it a body-centred reference price rather than a range-centred one.
open-close-midpoint-oc2.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the middle of each body. When the line steps up bar after bar, both the opens and the closes are rising; when it steps down, both are falling. Compared with the midprice of the range, it sits closer to where the bar spent its decisive moments and is not pulled by a single spike.

It has no lookback, so it carries every bar's noise and does not define a trend by itself. Use it as a reference level inside the bar or as the source for an average that should ignore the wicks.

faq.q: Why ignore the high and the low?
faq.html: A wick can be one brief print. Using only the open and the close keeps the reference on the prices the bar actually started and finished at.

faq.q: How does it compare with the midprice of the range?
faq.html: The range midprice is half of high plus low and moves with the wicks. The body midpoint moves only with the open and the close, so the two separate most on bars with long wicks on one side.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. Once a bar has closed its value is fixed. On the newest bar it moves with the close until the bar completes.

related.title: Open-High-Low Average (OHL3)
related.summary: Draws the average of each bar's open, high and low, a reference price that leaves out where the bar closed.

related.title: Normal Distribution CDF (NORMDIST)
related.summary: Turns the source's z-score over a rolling window into a normal cumulative probability, read as a percentile from 0 to 1.

related.title: OHLC Average (OHLC4)
related.summary: Draws the mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, one quieter representative price for the whole bar.

open-high-low-average-ohl3.title: Open-High-Low Average (OHL3)
open-high-low-average-ohl3.summary: Draws the average of each bar's open, high and low, a reference price that leaves out where the bar closed.
open-high-low-average-ohl3.descriptionHtml:
Open-High-Low Average (OHL3) takes the open, the high and the low of each bar, adds them and multiplies the sum by the constant 0.333333. That is the average of the three prices to within a millionth of its value, and the study keeps the fixed constant rather than dividing by three so that its values are exactly reproducible.

Leaving out the close is the point of the calculation. The line describes where the bar started and how far it traded in each direction, not where it settled, so it tracks the bar's traded range and opening level rather than its outcome. Each value uses only its own bar, with no lookback and no smoothing.
open-high-low-average-ohl3.howToReadHtml:
Compare the close with the line. A close above the open, high and low average means the bar finished above the centre of what it opened at and traded through, which leans bullish for that bar; a close below it leans bearish. A run of closes on one side shows persistent pressure in that direction.

The line has no memory and is as noisy as the bars. It is most useful as a per-bar reference or as an input for other studies that should not be driven by the close.

faq.q: Why multiply by 0.333333 instead of dividing by three?
faq.html: The calculation is defined with that constant, and the study keeps it so the numbers match the definition exactly. The difference from a true third is one part in a million, too small to see on a chart.

faq.q: Why leave out the close?
faq.html: So the line does not depend on where the bar settled. It then serves as a yardstick to judge the close against, which an average that includes the close cannot do as cleanly.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. A completed bar's value never changes. On the newest bar it moves only when the high or the low extends.

related.title: OHLC Average (OHLC4)
related.summary: Draws the mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, one quieter representative price for the whole bar.

related.title: Open-Close Midpoint (OC2)
related.summary: Draws the centre of every candle body, half the sum of its open and its close, ignoring the wicks entirely.

related.title: Poisson Distribution CDF (POISSONDIST)
related.summary: Reads price's position in its recent range as a Poisson event rate and plots the chance of at most k events at that rate.

ohlc-average-ohlc4.title: OHLC Average (OHLC4)
ohlc-average-ohlc4.summary: Draws the mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, one quieter representative price for the whole bar.
ohlc-average-ohlc4.descriptionHtml:
OHLC Average (OHLC4) adds the open, high, low and close of each bar and multiplies the sum by 0.25. The result is the plain mean of the four prices, computed bar by bar with no lookback and no smoothing.

Because every part of the bar contributes equally, the value moves less than the close alone on a bar that ends at an extreme, and less than the range midpoint on a bar with a long wick on one side. That balance is why the four-price mean is a common input to other studies: it gives one representative price per bar that is less sensitive to any single print.
ohlc-average-ohlc4.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the bar's average price. A close above it means the bar finished above its own average, a sign that the later part of the bar was stronger; a close below it means the opposite. When the line itself rises bar after bar, the whole bar, not just its close, is moving higher.

It carries every bar's noise because it has no lookback. Use it as a reference price on the chart, or as a smoother source for averages and oscillators.

faq.q: Is this the same as the volume weighted average price?
faq.html: No. It uses only the four prices of each bar, weights them equally and ignores volume. A volume weighted average accumulates price times volume over a session.

faq.q: Why would I feed it to another indicator?
faq.html: It is less tied to the closing tick than the close, so an average or oscillator built on it tends to react a little more smoothly to bars with long wicks.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. A completed bar's value is fixed. On the newest bar it moves with the close and with any new high or low.

related.title: Poisson Distribution CDF (POISSONDIST)
related.summary: Reads price's position in its recent range as a Poisson event rate and plots the chance of at most k events at that rate.

related.title: Open-High-Low Average (OHL3)
related.summary: Draws the average of each bar's open, high and low, a reference price that leaves out where the bar closed.

related.title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
related.summary: Splits the gap between price and its 20-bar average into an upper line for strength and a mirrored lower line for weakness.

one-euro-filter-oneeuro.title: One Euro Filter (ONEEURO)
one-euro-filter-oneeuro.summary: An adaptive smoother that filters heavily while price is quiet and lifts its cutoff when price moves fast, trading jitter against lag.
one-euro-filter-oneeuro.descriptionHtml:
This study is an adaptive low-pass filter. Its smoothing changes from bar to bar with the speed of price: when price barely moves it smooths hard to remove jitter, and when price moves quickly it smooths less so the line keeps up.

Each bar it first measures speed. The raw change from the previous price is smoothed with a fixed factor rD / (rD + 1), where rD = 2 * pi * Derivative Cutoff. That smoothed speed sets the cutoff of the main filter: fc = Min Cutoff + beta * |speed|. The cutoff becomes a smoothing factor rC / (rC + 1) with rC = 2 * pi * fc, and the line moves that share of the way from its previous value toward the new price.

The filter starts on the first price with a speed of zero. If a price reading is ever missing, the state is cleared and the next price seeds it again.
one-euro-filter-oneeuro.howToReadHtml:
In a quiet market the line is smooth and sits steadily through small wiggles; in a fast move it tightens onto price. That makes the distance between price and the line a rough measure of how decisive a move is: a move fast enough to drag the line with it is more than noise.

With the default Min Cutoff of 1 the line still moves about 86 percent of the way to each new price on a still bar, so it hugs price closely; lower the Min Cutoff well below 1 for a smoother line when price is calm, and raise the speed coefficient to cut lag in fast moves. The speed term works in price units, so on a high-priced instrument a small beta already has a large effect; tune it on the instrument you trade.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered, the close by default.

settings.label: Min Cutoff Frequency
settings.html: The cutoff used when price is still. Lower values smooth more when the market is quiet.

settings.label: Speed Coefficient (beta)
settings.html: How much the cutoff rises with speed. Higher values reduce lag during rapid moves.

settings.label: Derivative Cutoff
settings.html: The cutoff of the speed estimate itself. Lower values give a steadier speed reading and a more gradual change in smoothing.

faq.q: Why does the smoothing change from bar to bar?
faq.html: The cutoff of the filter is tied to the smoothed speed of price. Slow price gives a low cutoff and heavy smoothing; fast price gives a high cutoff and light smoothing.

faq.q: Why does a tiny beta have a big effect?
faq.html: Beta multiplies the speed in price units. On an instrument that moves hundreds of points per bar, even 0.007 lifts the cutoff a lot, so the line follows price closely.

faq.q: Where does the line start?
faq.html: On the first bar it equals that bar's price, with the speed set to zero, and adapts from there.

related.title: Recursive Least Squares Adaptive Filter (RLS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that re-estimates its weights every bar by recursive least squares, with a forgetting factor setting how much history still counts.

related.title: NW - Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression
related.summary: A backward-looking kernel regression: each bar is a Gaussian weighted average of recent prices, with the bandwidth setting how fast older bars fade.

related.title: Ehlers Recursive Median Filter (RMED)
related.summary: An exponential smoothing of the five-bar median price, which ignores one-bar spikes that would jolt an ordinary moving average.

parzen-window-moving-average-parzen.title: Parzen Window Moving Average (PARZEN)
parzen-window-moving-average-parzen.summary: A moving average weighted by a smooth piecewise cubic bell that falls to zero at both ends of the window, for a quiet line with little ripple.
parzen-window-moving-average-parzen.descriptionHtml:
The Parzen Window Moving Average weights each bar of its window by a piecewise cubic curve. Each position in the window is mapped to u, running from -1 at the oldest bar to 1 at the newest. In the middle half the weight is 1 - 6u^2 + 6|u|^3, and toward the edges it is 2(1 - |u|)^3, which reaches zero smoothly at both ends. The weights are scaled to sum to one and multiplied into the source.

Because the weights fade to zero without a step at either edge, a bar entering or leaving the window barely moves the line. That keeps the average free of the small jumps a plain average shows. Until period bars exist the line shows the price itself, and a missing price counts as zero.
parzen-window-moving-average-parzen.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line. The weights are concentrated in the middle of the window, so the effective smoothing is narrower than the period and the line lags price by about half the window. A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend, and a falling line with price below it a downtrend.

Its strength is how cleanly it turns: short ripples are suppressed hard, so a change in slope is seldom noise. On the first bars, before a full window exists, it simply follows price.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the cubic window spans. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: Why does the window fade to zero at the edges?
faq.html: A weight that drops to zero smoothly means a bar enters and leaves the average gradually. That removes the small steps a plain average makes when an old price drops out.

faq.q: What does it show before the window is full?
faq.html: The price itself. The weighted average begins once period bars exist.

faq.q: How does it compare with a triangular average?
faq.html: Both are symmetric and peak in the middle. The cubic shape here is rounder and fades out more gently, so it suppresses short ripples more strongly.

related.title: Ehlers Predictive Moving Average (PMA)
related.summary: A weighted average with one lag cancelled by extrapolation, plus a faster trigger line that leads it.

related.title: Nyquist Moving Average (NYQMA)
related.summary: A weighted average pushed forward by its distance from a second, smoother average of itself, which takes back most of its lag.

related.title: Pascal Weighted Moving Average (PWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a row of Pascal's triangle, a bell of binomial weights that puts most of the weight on the middle of the window.

price-channel-pchannel.title: Price Channel (PCHANNEL)
price-channel-pchannel.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the lookback window with their midpoint, showing the extremes a new move has to break.
price-channel-pchannel.descriptionHtml:
Price Channel draws three lines from the bar highs and lows of the last Length bars. The upper channel is the highest high in that window, the lower channel is the lowest low, and the middle channel is the point halfway between them. The area between the outer lines is shaded.

The channel answers from the first bar. Until Length bars exist it uses every bar so far, so the early lines are the running high and low of the chart. After that each outer line is the extreme of a fixed window and steps as old extremes drop out. A missing high or low is read as zero.
price-channel-pchannel.howToReadHtml:
A close above the upper channel means price has made a new Length bar high, and a close below the lower channel a new Length bar low; breakout systems act on exactly those events. The middle line is the centre of the recent range, and price holding above it suggests buyers control the range while price below it suggests sellers do.

The edges never anticipate a move. They only follow price, holding flat in a range and stepping when a new extreme is set or an old one leaves the window.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the window covers. A longer length gives a wider channel and fewer breakouts.

faq.q: What does the middle line add?
faq.html: It is the midpoint of the highest high and the lowest low, the centre of the recent range. It is often used as a trailing level or a bias line rather than as a signal on its own.

faq.q: Why does an edge suddenly jump?
faq.html: An edge is the extreme of a fixed window. When the bar that set it falls out of the window, the edge moves to the next most extreme value, which can be some distance away.

faq.q: How does it start before Length bars exist?
faq.html: It uses every bar it has, so the early values are the running high and low of the chart so far.

related.title: Regression Channels (REGCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares trend line through the last N prices, with bands set a multiple of the fit's own residual spread above and below it.

related.title: Min-Max Channel (MMCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and the lowest low of the lookback window drawn as a channel, marking the levels a breakout has to clear.

related.title: Standard Deviation Channel (SDCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares line through the lookback window with a channel a fixed multiple of the residual standard deviation on each side.

percentile.title: Percentile
percentile.summary: The value at a chosen percentile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart, interpolated between the two nearest ranks.
percentile.descriptionHtml:
The Percentile study sorts the last Period values of the source and plots the value at the chosen percentile. The rank is the percentile as a fraction times one less than the number of values, and when that rank falls between two positions the study interpolates linearly between the two neighbouring values.

A percentile of 50 gives the median, 0 gives the lowest value in the window and 100 the highest. The default of 25 traces the lower quartile, a level that about a quarter of the recent source values sit below.

The study answers from the first bar, ranking however many bars exist until the window fills, and it skips absent values.
percentile.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a floor or ceiling drawn from the distribution of recent prices rather than from a single extreme. A low percentile marks where price has rarely traded in the window, and a close below it is unusual for the period. A high percentile does the same for the top.

Two copies of the study, one at a low and one at a high percentile, make a band that ignores single outlier bars, unlike a channel built from the window's highest and lowest values. Like any rolling statistic it trails a fast move.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose values are ranked.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars are ranked. A longer period gives a steadier level.

settings.label: percentile
settings.html: Which percentile to draw, from 0 for the window low to 100 for the window high; 50 is the median.

faq.q: How is it different from the window's lowest value?
faq.html: The lowest value is set by a single bar. A low percentile such as 10 or 25 ignores the few most extreme bars, so one spike does not move it.

faq.q: Why is the setting labelled in lower case?
faq.html: The setting is stored under the name percentile, which is also the name of a built-in function, so its label carries that name directly. It still accepts any value from 0 to 100.

faq.q: What does interpolation change?
faq.html: When the chosen percentile falls between two ranked values, the line sits proportionally between them instead of jumping from one to the other, so it moves more smoothly.

related.title: Polynomial Fitting (POLYFIT)
related.summary: Fits a least-squares polynomial of the chosen degree to the recent window and plots the fitted curve's value at the current bar.

related.title: Mode
related.summary: The value that repeats most often in the recent window, drawn only when some value actually repeats, marking prices the market keeps returning to.

related.title: Quantile (QUANTILE)
related.summary: The requested quantile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart: 0.5 is the rolling median, 0 the low, 1 the high.

pfe-polarized-fractal-efficiency.title: PFE: Polarized Fractal Efficiency
pfe-polarized-fractal-efficiency.summary: How directly price travelled over a lookback, from -100 to +100: the straight-line distance over the path actually walked, signed by direction.
pfe-polarized-fractal-efficiency.descriptionHtml:
Polarized Fractal Efficiency compares two distances. The straight line is the hypotenuse of the change in the close over the period and the period itself counted in bars. The fractal path is the sum of the same kind of step for every bar in between: the square root of each bar-to-bar change squared plus one. Dividing the straight line by the path and multiplying by 100 gives the efficiency, which is then made negative when the close is lower than it was period bars ago.

A move that goes straight in one direction has a path almost as short as the straight line, so it reads close to +100 or -100. A choppy move walks a long path to get nowhere and reads near zero.

The raw value is smoothed by an exponential average of the smooth period. The average is seeded with the first raw value and scaled by a correction that fades away over the first bars. The line starts once period bars of history exist.
pfe-polarized-fractal-efficiency.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, price has been moving up efficiently; below zero, down. Readings beyond the dashed +50 and -50 lines show a strong, direct move, and readings near zero show a market that is busy but going nowhere. A turn back toward zero from an extreme is an early sign that the move is losing its directness.

The step length adds one bar of time to each price change, so the scale depends on how large price changes are compared with one. On an instrument that moves many points per bar the time term matters little and the reading behaves mostly like a ratio of net to total price movement.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the straight line and the path span. A longer period measures efficiency over a longer swing.

settings.label: Smooth Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average applied to the raw efficiency. A longer value gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: What do the dashed lines at 50 and -50 mean?
faq.html: They mark efficient moves. Beyond them, price has taken a fairly direct route over the period, up above +50 and down below -50.

faq.q: Why is the sign sometimes negative?
faq.html: The efficiency itself is always positive. It is made negative when the close is below the close period bars ago, so the sign carries the direction.

faq.q: When does the line start?
faq.html: On the first bar that has a close period bars back, because the straight line needs both ends.

related.title: Qstick Indicator
related.summary: A moving average of the candle body, close minus open, that reads whether bars have been closing above or below where they opened.

related.title: Ichimoku Cloud
related.summary: Five lines built from range midpoints, with a shaded cloud projected ahead of price that marks trend, support and resistance at a glance.

related.title: RAVI: Chande Range Action Verification Index
related.summary: The percentage gap between a fast and a slow simple average of the close, read against a threshold to separate trends from ranges.

pretty-good-oscillator.title: Pretty Good Oscillator
pretty-good-oscillator.summary: How far price sits from its simple average, measured in units of average true range, so a reading beyond plus or minus 3 marks a stretched move.
pretty-good-oscillator.descriptionHtml:
The Pretty Good Oscillator expresses the distance between the source and its moving average in units of volatility. It subtracts a simple average of the source from the source itself and divides the result by the average true range, both over the same period.

The simple average is taken over the bars seen so far until a full period has passed, so it answers from the first bar. The average true range is an exponential mean of true range with weight 1 / period, started at zero and divided by the weight still owed to that start while it matters, which keeps the first bars from reading too low. True range on the first bar is simply the high minus the low.

A reading of 2 means the source is two average bar ranges above its average. Because the scale is in volatility units it reads the same way on a quiet instrument and a volatile one. The pane is shaded red while the oscillator is above 3 and green while it is below minus 3.
pretty-good-oscillator.howToReadHtml:
Around zero, price is close to its average and nothing is stretched. Readings above 3 say price has run unusually far above its average for the volatility it normally shows, and readings below minus 3 the same on the downside; the shading makes these stretches easy to spot. Some traders read a push beyond 3 as the start of a breakout, others as a move that is likely to snap back, and the price chart has to decide which.

The oscillator follows the average with a lag, and in a strong trend it can stay beyond 3 for a long stretch. A return through zero says price has come back to its average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars for both the simple average and the average true range. Longer periods give a slower average and a steadier range.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own average, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the pane shaded on some bars?
faq.html: Red shading marks bars where the oscillator is above 3, and green shading marks bars below minus 3: the two zones where price is stretched by more than three average bar ranges from its average.

faq.q: Why divide by the average true range?
faq.html: A plain price distance means different things on different instruments. Dividing by the average bar range turns it into a count of typical bars, so the same thresholds work across instruments and timeframes.

faq.q: Does it answer from the first bar?
faq.html: Yes. The average uses the bars seen so far until a full period exists, and the range is corrected for its zero start, so the line has no blank warmup.

related.title: Psychological Line (PSL)
related.summary: The percentage of up bars among the last N bars, a simple count of how one-sided recent trading has been, from 0 to 100.

related.title: Ehlers MESA Stochastic (MSTOCH)
related.summary: A stochastic taken on filtered price, with trend and noise removed first, then smoothed into an oscillator between 0 and 1.

related.title: Quantitative Qualitative Estimation (QQE)
related.summary: A smoothed RSI with a trailing band set by the RSI's own volatility; when the line crosses the trailing level, momentum has shifted.

ehlers-phasor-analysis-phasor.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
ehlers-phasor-analysis-phasor.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.
ehlers-phasor-analysis-phasor.descriptionHtml:
Phasor Analysis measures where price sits inside a cycle of a chosen length. Over the last Period bars it correlates price with one cycle of a cosine and one cycle of a negative sine. Bars before the first one count as zero, so the early window is zero padded. The two correlations are the real and imaginary parts of a phasor, and the study turns them into an angle in degrees.

The angle is unwrapped against the previous bar so it runs continuously instead of jumping a full turn, so it is not confined to -180 to +180 degrees. It also ratchets: a backward step is held at the previous value when the new angle is above -135 degrees and the previous one below 135, or when both are below -90. From the step between bars the study derives a cycle period, a full turn of 360 degrees over the step, reusing the previous period whenever the step stalls or runs backward and holding it between 1 and 60 bars. When the angle advances 6 degrees or less in a bar, the trend state reads +1 if the angle is at or beyond plus or minus 90 degrees and -1 if it is between them; otherwise it is 0.
ehlers-phasor-analysis-phasor.howToReadHtml:
In a market that is cycling, the Phasor Angle climbs steadily, and the speed of the climb sets the Derived Period. Because the angle is unwrapped, it can run to several hundred degrees and then drop back by close to a full turn when the unwrapping resets. When the angle stops advancing, the market has stopped cycling and is trending; the Trend State histogram marks those bars. The unwrapped angle usually sits beyond 90 degrees, so most of the marked bars read +1.

The derived period is noisy bar to bar and is clamped to 60 bars, so read it as a rough guide to the current rhythm rather than an exact count. The two optional plots are off by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length in bars of the reference cosine and sine, the cycle length the phasor is measured against.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series correlated with the reference waves. The default is the close.

settings.label: Show Derived Period
settings.html: Draw the cycle period derived from how far the angle moved this bar, between 1 and 60 bars.

settings.label: Show Trend State Variable
settings.html: Draw the trend state histogram: +1 for a stalled angle at the extremes, -1 for a stalled angle in the middle, 0 otherwise.

faq.q: Why does the angle sometimes stay flat?
faq.html: The angle ratchets. A backward step is held at the previous value when the new angle is above -135 degrees and the previous one below 135, or when both are below -90, so a market that is not cycling often shows a flat angle rather than one that wanders back.

faq.q: Why is the derived period capped at 60?
