faq.html: A very small angle step would give an enormous period. The study holds the result between 1 and 60 bars so the plot stays readable.

faq.q: What does a Trend State of -1 mean?
faq.html: The angle advanced 6 degrees or less this bar while sitting between -90 and +90 degrees, which the study reads as a cycle mode rather than a trend. Because the angle is unwrapped and usually sits beyond 90 degrees, this reading is uncommon.

related.title: Ehlers Sine Wave (SINE)
related.summary: The phase of the detrended price cycle as a wave between -1 and +1, from the in-phase value over its length with a quadrature partner.

related.title: Multilayer Perceptron Predictor
related.summary: A small neural network trained bar by bar on six price features, drawing its five-bar price prediction back on the bar it was made from.

related.title: Solar Cycle (SOLAR)
related.summary: Plots the sine of the Sun's position along the ecliptic at each bar's time, a calendar wave from -1 at the winter solstice to +1 at the summer solstice.

pivot-points-classic.title: Pivot Points (Classic)
pivot-points-classic.summary: The classic floor pivot: the previous day, week or month's high, low and close turned into a central pivot with three supports and three resistances.
pivot-points-classic.descriptionHtml:
Classic pivot points turn the last completed period into a set of horizontal levels for the current one. The central pivot is the average of the previous period's high, low and close. The first resistance is twice the pivot less the previous low, and the first support is twice the pivot less the previous high. The second levels sit one full previous range above and below the pivot, and the third levels extend twice the distance between the pivot and the previous low or high beyond the previous high or low.

The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The study folds the chart's own bars into those periods as it goes, keeps the high, low and close of the period being built, and on the first bar of a new period hands them over as the previous period. Every bar of a period therefore shows the same levels, drawn as steps.
pivot-points-classic.howToReadHtml:
The pivot is the balance point of the previous period: price above it leans bullish for the period and price below it leans bearish. R1 to R3 above and S1 to S3 below are the levels traders watch for price to pause or turn, and once price breaks through one, the next level out becomes the following reference.

The levels are computed, not observed: they say where the previous period's range projects, not where orders actually sit. They are most useful on intraday charts with the daily setting, and on daily charts with the weekly or monthly setting.

settings.label: Pivot Timeframe
settings.html: The period the levels are built from: D uses the previous day, W the previous Monday-start week and M the previous calendar month. A longer period gives wider levels that stay in place for longer.

settings.label: Show Pivot Point
settings.html: Draw the central pivot line. Turning it off hides the line without changing any other level.

settings.label: Show R1
settings.html: Draw the first resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show R2
settings.html: Draw the second resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show R3
settings.html: Draw the third resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S1
settings.html: Draw the first support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S2
settings.html: Draw the second support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S3
settings.html: Draw the third support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?
faq.html: No. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, which has already closed, so the lines are fixed for the whole period and step to new values when the next one begins.

faq.q: Why are there no levels at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The levels come from the previous completed period. Until the chart holds one whole day, week or month of bars, there is no completed period to read, so the first period on the chart carries no lines.

faq.q: How are R2 and S2 set?
faq.html: They sit one full range of the previous period above and below the pivot, so a wide previous period spreads them apart and a quiet one pulls them close.

related.title: Pivot Points (Camarilla)
related.summary: Four supports and four resistances placed tightly around the previous period's close, each a fixed fraction of that period's range away from it.

related.title: Williams Fractals
related.summary: Marks every five-bar swing high and swing low, the turning points where price stalled and reversed for at least two bars on each side.

related.title: Pivot Points (DeMark)
related.summary: A pivot, one resistance and one support from the previous period, weighted by whether that period closed above, below or at its open.

pivot-points-camarilla.title: Pivot Points (Camarilla)
pivot-points-camarilla.summary: Four supports and four resistances placed tightly around the previous period's close, each a fixed fraction of that period's range away from it.
pivot-points-camarilla.descriptionHtml:
Camarilla pivots build their levels around the previous period's close rather than around a central pivot. Each level is the previous close plus or minus a fixed fraction of the previous period's range: the range times 1.0833, 1.1666, 1.25 and 1.5, each divided by 12, for levels one to four. That puts R1 and S1 about 9 percent of the range from the close and R4 and S4 one eighth of the range from it, so the levels are much tighter than classic pivots.

The study also draws the classic central pivot, the average of the previous high, low and close. The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The chart's own bars are folded into those periods, and every bar of a period reads the high, low and close of the period before it, so the levels hold steady through each period.
pivot-points-camarilla.howToReadHtml:
Because the levels sit close to the previous close, price reaches several of them in a normal period. A common reading treats R3 and S3 as the edges of the expected range, where traders look for price to turn back, and R4 and S4 as breakout levels, where a move beyond them suggests the range has given way.

The levels describe the previous period's range and close, nothing more. On a day that opens far from the previous close, most levels can be left behind at once, and the reading of turns and breakouts no longer applies.

settings.label: Pivot Timeframe
settings.html: The period the levels are built from: D uses the previous day, W the previous Monday-start week and M the previous calendar month. A longer period gives wider levels that stay in place for longer.

settings.label: Show Pivot Point
settings.html: Draw the central pivot line. Turning it off hides the line without changing any other level.

settings.label: Show R1
settings.html: Draw the first resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show R2
settings.html: Draw the second resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show R3
settings.html: Draw the third resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show R4
settings.html: Draw the fourth resistance level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S1
settings.html: Draw the first support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S2
settings.html: Draw the second support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S3
settings.html: Draw the third support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

settings.label: Show S4
settings.html: Draw the fourth support level. Turning it off hides that line only.

faq.q: Why are the levels centred on the close and not on the pivot?
faq.html: That is how this method is defined: every support and resistance is the previous close plus or minus a fraction of the previous range. The central pivot line is drawn as well for reference, but no level is built from it.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?
faq.html: No. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, which has already closed, so the lines are fixed for the whole period and step to new values when the next one begins.

faq.q: Why are there no levels at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The levels come from the previous completed period. Until the chart holds one whole day, week or month of bars, there is no completed period to read, so the first period on the chart carries no lines.

related.title: Pivot Points (DeMark)
related.summary: A pivot, one resistance and one support from the previous period, weighted by whether that period closed above, below or at its open.

related.title: Pivot Points (Classic)
related.summary: The classic floor pivot: the previous day, week or month's high, low and close turned into a central pivot with three supports and three resistances.

related.title: Pivot Points (Extended)
related.summary: The classic floor pivot carried out to five resistance and five support levels, built from the previous day, week or month's high, low and close.

pivot-points-demark.title: Pivot Points (DeMark)
pivot-points-demark.summary: A pivot, one resistance and one support from the previous period, weighted by whether that period closed above, below or at its open.
pivot-points-demark.descriptionHtml:
This pivot method weighs the previous period by how it closed. It first forms a sum X from the previous period's open, high, low and close. When the period closed below its open, X is the high plus twice the low plus the close. When it closed above its open, X is twice the high plus the low plus the close. When it closed exactly at its open, X is the high plus the low plus twice the close.

The pivot is X divided by 4, the resistance R1 is X divided by 2 less the previous low, and the support S1 is X divided by 2 less the previous high. The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The study folds the chart's own bars into those periods, remembering each period's first open, highest high, lowest low and last close, and every bar of a period reads the period before it.
pivot-points-demark.howToReadHtml:
Read R1 as the expected high and S1 as the expected low of the current period, and the pivot as its centre. Because a down period leans on its low and an up period on its high, the levels shift in the direction the previous period moved, rather than sitting symmetrically around its average.

With only one level on each side, a break beyond R1 or S1 leaves no further reference from this study. The levels are projections from the previous period, so treat them as areas to watch rather than as prices that must hold.

faq.q: Why does this study have only one support and one resistance?
faq.html: The method defines a single projected high and low for the period. There are no second or third levels to draw.

faq.q: What decides the weighting?
faq.html: Only the previous period's close against its open. A close below the open doubles the weight of the low, a close above doubles the high, and an unchanged close doubles the close.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?
faq.html: No. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, which has already closed, so the lines are fixed for the whole period and step to new values when the next one begins.

pivot-points-extended.title: Pivot Points (Extended)
pivot-points-extended.summary: The classic floor pivot carried out to five resistance and five support levels, built from the previous day, week or month's high, low and close.
pivot-points-extended.descriptionHtml:
Extended pivot points start from the classic pivot, the average of the previous period's high, low and close, and carry the levels further out. R1 and S1 are twice the pivot less the previous low or high, and R2 and S2 sit one full previous range above and below the pivot. From the third level on, each step adds another multiple of the distance between the pivot and the previous low (for resistances) or high (for supports): R3 is the previous high plus twice that distance, R4 plus three times and R5 plus four times, and the supports mirror them below the previous low.

The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The study folds the chart's own bars into those periods and starts a new period on the bar whose date, week or month differs from the bar before it. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, so the levels hold steady for the whole period.
pivot-points-extended.howToReadHtml:
Use the inner levels the way classic pivots are used: the pivot as the balance point, R1 and S1 as the first levels to watch for a pause. The outer levels, R4, R5, S4 and S5, are reached only when the current period travels well beyond the previous period's range, so price trading out there marks an exceptional move rather than a normal one.

The outer levels are spaced evenly and grow with the previous range, so after a wide period they can sit far away and rarely matter. Hide the ones you do not use to keep the chart readable.

faq.q: How do the extended levels differ from the classic ones?
faq.html: R1 to R3 and S1 to S3 are the same as the classic pivot levels. R4, R5, S4 and S5 continue the pattern of R3 and S3 by adding one more multiple of the pivot's distance from the previous low or high each time.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?
faq.html: No. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, which has already closed, so the lines are fixed for the whole period and step to new values when the next one begins.

faq.q: Which calendar decides where a day or week starts?

pivot-points-fibonacci.title: Pivot Points (Fibonacci)
pivot-points-fibonacci.summary: Three supports and three resistances placed 38.2, 61.8 and 100 percent of the previous period's range away from the classic pivot.
pivot-points-fibonacci.descriptionHtml:
Fibonacci pivot points share the classic central pivot, the average of the previous period's high, low and close, but place the other levels by fixed fractions of the previous period's range. R1 and S1 sit 0.382 of the range above and below the pivot, R2 and S2 sit 0.618 of the range away, and R3 and S3 sit one full range away.

The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The study folds the chart's own bars into those periods as it goes, and every bar of a period reads the high, low and close of the period before it. The result is a set of step lines that hold steady for each period and move when the next one starts.
pivot-points-fibonacci.howToReadHtml:
The pivot is the reference: trading above it leans bullish and below it bearish for the period. The 38.2 and 61.8 percent levels are the levels traders watch for a pullback or an extension to stall, and the 100 percent levels mark a move as large as the whole previous range.

Because each distance is a fixed share of the previous range, a wide previous period spreads the levels out and a quiet one bunches them up. They describe the previous period only and carry no information about news or events in the current one.

faq.q: What do the percentages in the labels mean?
faq.html: Each level's distance from the pivot as a share of the previous period's range: 38.2 percent, 61.8 percent and the full range.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?
faq.html: No. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, which has already closed, so the lines are fixed for the whole period and step to new values when the next one begins.

faq.q: Why are there no levels at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The levels come from the previous completed period. Until the chart holds one whole day, week or month of bars, there is no completed period to read, so the first period on the chart carries no lines.

pivot-points-woodie.title: Pivot Points (Woodie)
pivot-points-woodie.summary: A pivot that weights the previous close twice, with three supports and three resistances built from the previous day, week or month.
pivot-points-woodie.descriptionHtml:
This pivot variant gives the previous close more weight than the classic method. The pivot is the previous high plus the previous low plus twice the previous close, all divided by 4. The other levels follow the classic formulas from that pivot: R1 and S1 are twice the pivot less the previous low or high, R2 and S2 sit one full previous range above and below the pivot, and R3 and S3 extend twice the pivot's distance from the previous low or high beyond the previous high or low.

The period can be a day, a Monday-start week or a calendar month. The study folds the chart's own bars into those periods and, on the first bar of a new period, hands the completed one over. Every bar of a period reads the period before it, so the levels hold steady as step lines.
pivot-points-woodie.howToReadHtml:
Because the close counts twice, the pivot sits nearer to where the previous period finished than the classic pivot does. Read it as the period's balance point, with R1 and S1 as the first areas of resistance and support and the outer levels as targets for a stronger move.

The weighting toward the close matters most after a period that closed near one end of its range. After a period that closed near its middle, the levels are almost the same as classic pivots.

faq.html: The classic pivot averages high, low and close equally. This one counts the close twice and divides by four, so the pivot and every level built from it lean toward where the previous period closed.

faq.q: Do the levels move during the day?

faq.q: Which calendar decides where a day or week starts?

ehlers-predictive-moving-average-pma.title: Ehlers Predictive Moving Average (PMA)
ehlers-predictive-moving-average-pma.summary: A weighted average with one lag cancelled by extrapolation, plus a faster trigger line that leads it.
ehlers-predictive-moving-average-pma.descriptionHtml:
The Predictive Moving Average starts from a linearly weighted moving average of the source, in which the newest bar carries the most weight and each older bar one step less. It then takes a second weighted average of that first one. Because each smoothing pass adds lag, the gap between the two averages is an estimate of that lag, and the PMA adds it back: the line is twice the first average less the second.

A second line, the trigger, is four times the first average less the second, divided by three. It sits closer to the newest price than the PMA, so it turns first. Both averages answer from the first bar: until the window holds period bars they weight the bars seen so far 1, 2 and up and divide by the sum of those weights.
ehlers-predictive-moving-average-pma.howToReadHtml:
Read the PMA as a low-lag trend line that follows price closely without the jitter of the raw close. The trigger line runs slightly ahead of it, so when the trigger crosses above the PMA the short-term pace has turned up, and when it crosses below the pace has turned down.

The extrapolation that removes lag also makes the line overshoot after a sharp reversal, and in a sideways market the two lines cross often and say little. Use the crossings with a view of the larger trend rather than on their own.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Number of bars in each weighted average. A longer period gives smoother lines that react later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages are taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: What is the difference between the PMA and the trigger line?
faq.html: Both are built from the same two weighted averages. The PMA is twice the first less the second; the trigger is four times the first less the second, divided by three, which places it nearer the newest price so it turns sooner.

faq.q: Why does the line appear from the very first bar?
faq.html: The weighted averages use as many bars as exist until the window is full, weighting them 1, 2 and up. The first few values therefore rest on a shorter window than the period setting.

faq.q: Why does the PMA sometimes move past price after a sharp turn?
faq.html: It cancels lag by extrapolating the difference between two averages. After a sudden reversal that difference is large, so the line briefly runs beyond the turn before settling.

related.title: Pascal Weighted Moving Average (PWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a row of Pascal's triangle, a bell of binomial weights that puts most of the weight on the middle of the window.

related.title: Parzen Window Moving Average (PARZEN)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a smooth piecewise cubic bell that falls to zero at both ends of the window, for a quiet line with little ripple.

related.title: Quadruple EMA (QEMA)
related.summary: Four chained exponential stages with rising smoothing factors, combined 4, -6, 4, -1 to cancel most of the lag of an ordinary EMA.

price-momentum-oscillator-pmo.title: Price Momentum Oscillator (PMO)
price-momentum-oscillator-pmo.summary: A percentage rate of change smoothed twice by exponential averages, with a third average as its signal line.
price-momentum-oscillator-pmo.descriptionHtml:
The Price Momentum Oscillator starts from the percentage rate of change of the source over rocLength bars: the source minus the source that many bars back, divided by the older value, times 100. Until the chart has rocLength bars the lookback reaches back only to the first bar, so the very first reading is zero.

That rate of change is smoothed by an exponential average of length smooth1, and the result is smoothed again by one of length smooth2. The second average is the PMO line. A third exponential average of the PMO over signalLength bars is the signal line. Each average uses the weight 2 / (length + 1) and starts from its first value, so both lines are drawn from the first bar.
price-momentum-oscillator-pmo.howToReadHtml:
The PMO is a smoothed momentum line. Above zero, price has been rising over the rate-of-change lookback; below zero, falling. The double smoothing removes most of the bar-to-bar noise, so a turn in the PMO is usually a real change in momentum rather than one odd bar.

A PMO crossing above its signal line is commonly read as momentum turning up, and a cross below as momentum turning down. Readings far from zero show a stretched move. Because the line is a percentage, its levels can be compared across instruments, though each instrument has its own normal range. The early bars reflect a shorter lookback and settle once the averages have seen enough data.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose rate of change is measured. Close is the default.

settings.label: ROC Length
settings.html: How many bars back the percentage rate of change reaches before smoothing.

settings.label: First Smoothing Length
settings.html: The length of the first exponential average applied to the rate of change. Longer values give a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Second Smoothing Length
settings.html: The length of the second exponential average, whose output is the PMO line.

settings.label: Signal Line Length
settings.html: The length of the exponential average of the PMO that forms the signal line.

faq.q: Why is the first reading zero?
faq.html: On the first bar the lookback can only reach the first bar itself, so the rate of change is zero. The lookback grows with the chart until it reaches rocLength.

faq.q: What does the signal line add?
faq.html: It is a slower average of the PMO. Its crosses with the PMO mark the points where the smoothed momentum turns, and the gap between the two shows how firmly it is turning.

related.title: Percentage Price Oscillator (PPO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

related.title: Momentum (MOM)
related.summary: The plain price difference between this bar and the bar a fixed number of bars back, drawn as a line around zero.

related.title: Rate of Change (ROC)
related.summary: The source now minus the source a number of bars back, in price units, with a lookback that grows from the first bar up to the length.

poisson-distribution-cdf-poissondist.title: Poisson Distribution CDF (POISSONDIST)
poisson-distribution-cdf-poissondist.summary: Reads price's position in its recent range as a Poisson event rate and plots the chance of at most k events at that rate.
poisson-distribution-cdf-poissondist.descriptionHtml:
Poisson Distribution CDF (POISSONDIST) maps price onto a probability in three steps. First it min-max normalises the source over the last period bars, so the current value becomes a number from 0 at the window's low to 1 at its high; a flat window reads 0.5. Second it multiplies that position by Lambda Scale to get an event rate, lambda. Third it plots the Poisson cumulative probability that at most k events occur at that rate.

The probability is computed as one minus the regularized lower incomplete gamma function of k + 1 and lambda. The study evaluates that function with a series expansion for small lambda and a continued fraction for large lambda, using a Lanczos approximation of the log-gamma function. The series and the continued fraction each stop once a step changes the result by less than a relative 1e-10, or after 200 steps. When lambda is zero, all the probability sits at zero events and the result is 1.
poisson-distribution-cdf-poissondist.howToReadHtml:
The scale is inverted relative to price. When the source sits near the top of its range, lambda is high, so seeing at most k events is unlikely and the line falls toward 0. When the source sits near the bottom, lambda is low and the line rises toward 1. The 0.95 and 0.05 lines mark the tails, and 0.5 the middle.

The shape of the response depends on k and Lambda Scale together: the line crosses 0.5 roughly where lambda reaches k, so a larger k or a smaller scale keeps the line high across more of the range. It is a nonlinear lens on the position of price in its range, not a forecast.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose position in its recent range sets the event rate.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars, this one included, set the low and high of the range used for normalising.

settings.label: Threshold (k)
settings.html: The event count in P(X <= k). A larger k keeps the probability high until price is further up its range.

settings.label: Lambda Scale
settings.html: Multiplies the 0 to 1 range position to give lambda. A larger scale spans a wider range of event rates and makes the line fall faster as price rises.

faq.q: Why does the line fall when price rises?
faq.html: A higher position in the range gives a higher event rate, and at a higher rate it is less likely that only k or fewer events occur. So the probability drops as price climbs its range.

faq.q: Where does the line cross 0.5?
faq.html: Roughly where lambda, the range position times Lambda Scale, is close to k. With the defaults of k = 5 and a scale of 10, that is near the middle of the range.

faq.q: Why is the value exactly 1 on some bars?
faq.html: When the source is at the very bottom of its window, lambda is zero, and with a zero rate there are never any events, so P(X <= k) is 1.

related.title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
related.summary: Splits the gap between price and its 20-bar average into an upper line for strength and a mirrored lower line for weakness.

related.title: OHLC Average (OHLC4)
related.summary: Draws the mean of each bar's open, high, low and close, one quieter representative price for the whole bar.

related.title: Logistic Function (SIGMOID)
related.summary: Passes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the logistic curve, giving an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

polynomial-fitting-polyfit.title: Polynomial Fitting (POLYFIT)
polynomial-fitting-polyfit.summary: Fits a least-squares polynomial of the chosen degree to the recent window and plots the fitted curve's value at the current bar.
polynomial-fitting-polyfit.descriptionHtml:
The study takes the last Period values of the source, spreads them evenly over x from 0 at the oldest to 1 at the newest, and fits a polynomial of the chosen degree to them by least squares. It builds the normal equations from summed powers of x and solves them by Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting. The plotted value is the fitted curve evaluated at the newest bar, which on this scale is simply the sum of the coefficients.

Degree 1 is a straight line, so the study then gives the end point of a linear regression. Degree 2 lets the line bend, and higher degrees follow the window more closely. The degree is capped at one less than the period. An absent source value repeats the last value that was present, and the study starts once the window holds at least two more values than the degree.
polynomial-fitting-polyfit.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a smoothed estimate of where price is now, given the shape of the recent window. A low degree gives a calm line that lags turns; a higher degree hugs price more closely and turns sooner, but it also reacts more to noise near the end of the window, where a polynomial fit is least stable.

The value at each bar comes from its own fit, so the curve drawn across the chart joins many separate end points rather than one fitted curve. Degree 2 with a moderate period is a reasonable middle ground.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent values each fit uses. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Degree
settings.html: The polynomial degree: 1 for a straight line, 2 for a curve with one bend, up to 6.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the polynomial is fitted to.

faq.q: Is degree 1 the same as a linear regression line?
faq.html: Yes. With degree 1 the study fits a straight line to the window and plots its value at the newest bar, the end point of a linear regression.

faq.q: Should I use a high degree?
faq.html: Rarely. A high degree follows the window closely but swings at its ends, and the newest bar is an end, so the line becomes jumpy. Degrees 1 to 3 are the usual choices.

faq.q: Why does the line start a few bars in?
faq.html: A fit of degree d needs at least d + 2 values in the window before the study draws it, so the first few bars have no value.

related.title: Quantile (QUANTILE)
related.summary: The requested quantile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart: 0.5 is the rolling median, 0 the low, 1 the high.

related.title: Percentile
related.summary: The value at a chosen percentile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart, interpolated between the two nearest ranks.

related.title: Skewness (SKEW)
related.summary: A rolling measure of how lopsided the recent values are about their mean: positive when the long tail is above, negative when it is below.

percentage-price-oscillator-ppo.title: Percentage Price Oscillator (PPO)
percentage-price-oscillator-ppo.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.
percentage-price-oscillator-ppo.descriptionHtml:
The Percentage Price Oscillator measures the same gap as MACD, the fast average minus the slow average, but divides it by the slow average and multiplies by 100. The result is a percentage, so it reads the same way on any price level. A signal line smooths the PPO, and the histogram is the PPO minus its signal.

The three averages here use a weight of 2 / length. Each starts with its accumulator at zero and returns the first value unchanged; after that the accumulator is divided by (1 - e), where e is (1 - weight) raised to the number of updates, until e drops below 1e-10. That correction removes the pull of the zero start, so every line answers from the first bar. A bar where the slow average is zero gives no PPO reading, and the signal keeps its last value there.
percentage-price-oscillator-ppo.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the fast average is above the slow one by that percentage, which is the shape of an uptrend; below zero, it is the shape of a downtrend. A PPO of 1.5 means the fast average sits 1.5 percent above the slow one. The histogram shows whether the PPO is pulling away from its signal line or closing in on it.

A PPO crossing above its signal line, which turns the histogram positive, is commonly read as momentum turning up, and the opposite cross as momentum turning down. Because the reading is a percentage, it can be compared across instruments and across long stretches of history where price has changed level.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both averages are taken over. Close is the default.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: The length of the fast average. A shorter fast length makes the PPO react sooner and swing further.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: The length of the slow average, which is also the base the percentage is measured against.

settings.label: Signal Length
settings.html: The length of the average of the PPO that forms the signal line and sets the histogram.

faq.q: How is PPO different from MACD?
faq.html: MACD is the gap between the averages in price units. PPO divides that gap by the slow average, so it is a percentage and compares across instruments and price levels.

faq.q: Why do the averages use 2 / length?
faq.html: That is the weight this calculation uses. It makes each average a little faster than one using 2 / (length + 1) at the same length.

faq.q: Why does it answer from the first bar?
faq.html: Each average divides out the weight of its zero start while that start still matters, so no seed window is needed.

related.summary: The source now minus the source a number of bars back, in price units, with a lookback that grows from the first bar up to the length.

related.title: Price Momentum Oscillator (PMO)
related.summary: A percentage rate of change smoothed twice by exponential averages, with a third average as its signal line.

related.title: Rate of Change Percentage (ROCP)
related.summary: The percentage change between the source now and the source a number of bars back, with a lookback that grows from the first bar.

parabolic-sar.title: Parabolic SAR
parabolic-sar.summary: A trailing stop and reverse line that accelerates toward price as a trend makes new extremes, and flips to the other side when price trades through it.
parabolic-sar.descriptionHtml:
Parabolic SAR (stop and reverse) draws a stop level on every bar that trails the trend. In an uptrend it sits below price and climbs; in a downtrend it sits above price and falls. Each bar the stop moves toward the extreme point of the trend, the highest high of an uptrend or the lowest low of a downtrend, by a fraction called the acceleration factor.

The factor starts at Start AF and grows by AF Increment every time the trend sets a new extreme, up to Max AF, so the stop closes in faster the longer a trend runs. A rising stop is never allowed above the lows of the previous two bars, and a falling stop never below their highs. When a bar trades through the stop, the side flips: the stop jumps to the old extreme point and the factor starts again.

The first bar picks the starting side from its own direction (up when it closed above its open) and starts the stop at the far end of its range. The study draws the stop as two lines, PSAR Above in red on bars where it sits above the close and PSAR Below in green where it sits below.
parabolic-sar.howToReadHtml:
The green line under price marks an uptrend and the red line over price marks a downtrend. A switch from one line to the other is a reversal of the system: the previous trend's stop was hit. The line can serve as a trailing stop for an open position, moving the exit to each new stop value.

The study works best in a steady trend. In a sideways market price crosses the stop often, so it flips back and forth and each flip is small and late. Raising the factors makes the stop follow price more closely and flip more often; lowering them gives the trend more room.

settings.label: Start AF
settings.html: The acceleration factor at the start of each trend. A higher value pulls the first stops closer to price.

settings.label: AF Increment
settings.html: How much the factor grows each time the trend makes a new extreme, so how quickly the stop closes in.

settings.label: Max AF
settings.html: The ceiling on the factor. A value at or below Start AF is lifted to Start AF, and the factor then never grows.

faq.q: Why do the lines break on some bars?
faq.html: Each bar's stop goes on the red line when it sits above the close and on the green line when it sits below. On a bar where the stop sits exactly on the close, neither line has a value, so the bar shows nothing. Each flip of side also ends one line and starts the other.

faq.q: Why does the stop jump so far when it flips?
faq.html: On a reversal the stop moves to the extreme point of the trend that just ended, the highest high of an uptrend or the lowest low of a downtrend, which can be some distance from price.

faq.q: What happens if Max AF is set below Start AF?
faq.html: The ceiling is lifted to the start value, so the factor stays at Start AF for the whole trend and the stop approaches price at a constant rate.

related.title: Swing High/Low Detection
related.summary: Finds bars whose high or low is the extreme of the bars on both sides and holds the latest swing high and swing low as two horizontal lines.

related.title: Pivot Points (Woodie)
related.summary: A pivot that weights the previous close twice, with three supports and three resistances built from the previous day, week or month.

related.title: TTM Scalper Alert
related.summary: Marks every three-bar pivot: a bar whose high tops both neighbours, or whose low sits under both, as short-term turning points.

pseudo-huber-loss.title: Pseudo-Huber Loss
pseudo-huber-loss.summary: A rolling average of the smooth Huber loss between an actual and a predicted series, quadratic for small misses and close to linear for large ones.
pseudo-huber-loss.descriptionHtml:
Pseudo-Huber Loss scores the gap between an actual series and a predicted series with a loss that behaves like a squared error for small misses and like an absolute error for large ones. On every bar the error is the actual value minus the predicted value. That error is divided by Delta, and the loss is Delta squared times the square root of one plus that ratio squared, minus one.

For an error much smaller than Delta the loss is close to half the squared error. For an error much larger than Delta it grows almost in a straight line, at about Delta times the absolute error, so a single large miss cannot dominate the reading the way it does in a squared error. The study plots the simple average of this loss over the last Length bars. An absent value on either side is read as zero.
pseudo-huber-loss.howToReadHtml:
A lower line means the predicted series has been tracking the actual one more closely. The line is in squared price units for small errors and in price units times Delta for large ones, so read it against its own history rather than as an absolute number. A rising line says the misses are getting larger; a spike that fades quickly is a short burst of large errors.

Delta sets where the loss changes character. Set it near the size of an ordinary miss on your chart: much smaller and almost every bar is in the linear zone, much larger and the loss acts like a plain squared error. The line has no value for the first Length minus one bars.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the loss is averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Delta (transition scale)
settings.html: The error size where the loss turns from quadratic to roughly linear. Raise it to punish large misses more heavily.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: How is this different from a plain squared error?
faq.html: A squared error grows with the square of every miss, so one large miss can swamp the average. This loss grows only about linearly once the miss is larger than Delta, which keeps a single outlier from taking over.

faq.q: What value of Delta should I use?
faq.html: Pick something near the size of a normal miss in price units. With the default of 1 on an instrument that moves hundreds of points per bar, nearly every bar is in the linear zone and the line sits close to Delta times the mean absolute error.

faq.q: Can the line go below zero?
faq.html: No. The loss is zero only when the two series agree exactly and is positive otherwise, so the average is never negative.

related.title: Quantile Loss (Pinball Loss)
related.summary: A rolling average of the pinball loss, an error score that charges misses above and below the forecast at different rates set by a quantile.

related.title: Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (MSLE)
related.summary: The average squared gap between log(1 + price) and log(1 + its EMA) over a rolling window, a scale-free error measure.

related.title: Relative Absolute Error (RAE)
related.summary: Absolute error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the absolute error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

psychological-line-psl.title: Psychological Line (PSL)
psychological-line-psl.summary: The percentage of up bars among the last N bars, a simple count of how one-sided recent trading has been, from 0 to 100.
psychological-line-psl.descriptionHtml:
The Psychological Line counts how many of the recent bars closed up. A bar counts as up when its source value is higher than the previous bar's; an equal or lower value counts as not up. The study adds up the up bars over the last period bars and expresses the count as a percentage of the bars in the window.

Until a full period of bars has been seen, the percentage is taken over the bars that exist, so the line answers from the first bar. The first bar has no previous bar to compare with and never counts as up.

Because it is a share of a count, the line always sits between 0 and 100. With the default period of 12 it moves in steps of about 8.3, one step for each bar that enters or leaves the window.
psychological-line-psl.howToReadHtml:
A reading above 50 says more of the recent bars closed up than not; below 50, more closed flat or down. The dashed lines at 75 and 25 mark the stretched readings the study is usually watched for: at 75 or more, three quarters of the recent bars rose, which some traders read as a crowd leaning too far one way, and at 25 or less the reverse.

The count ignores how far each bar moved, so a run of small up bars can read high while price has gone nowhere. Use it as a gauge of mood alongside the price chart.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars are counted. A short period makes the line jumpy; a long one makes it slower and closer to 50.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared bar to bar to decide which bars count as up, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line move in steps?
faq.html: It is a count divided by the window length, so it can only take a fixed set of values. With a period of 12 each up bar is worth about 8.3 points.

faq.q: Does a flat bar count as up?
faq.html: No. Only a bar whose source is strictly higher than the previous bar's counts as up; an unchanged bar counts with the down bars.

faq.q: Can it go beyond 0 or 100?
faq.html: No. It is the share of bars that rose, so it is always between 0 and 100.

related.title: Quantitative Qualitative Estimation (QQE)
related.summary: A smoothed RSI with a trailing band set by the RSI's own volatility; when the line crosses the trailing level, momentum has shifted.

related.title: Pretty Good Oscillator
related.summary: How far price sits from its simple average, measured in units of average true range, so a reading beyond plus or minus 3 marks a stretched move.

related.title: Ehlers Reflex Indicator (REFLEX)
related.summary: A zero-centred cycle oscillator that measures how far a smoothed price bends away from a straight line drawn across one period.

parkinson-volatility-pv.title: Parkinson Volatility (PV)
parkinson-volatility-pv.summary: Volatility from the squared log ratio of each bar's high to its low, smoothed over a window and optionally annualised.
parkinson-volatility-pv.descriptionHtml:
Parkinson Volatility estimates volatility from each bar's range instead of from close-to-close returns. For each bar it takes the natural logarithm of the high over the low and squares it; a bar whose high equals its low contributes zero.

The squared values are smoothed with a running average of weight 1 / Length, seeded with the simple average of the first Length values, so the line is empty until a full window has passed. The smoothed value is divided by 4 ln 2, which puts it on the scale of the variance of returns, and the square root gives the volatility per bar. With Annualize Volatility on it is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.
parkinson-volatility-pv.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means bar ranges are widening relative to price, a falling line means they are narrowing. Because every bar's full range is used, it picks up a market that swings within each bar even when the closes barely move, and it settles with fewer bars than a close-to-close measure.

Read it against its own history: readings near its lows mark narrow bars, and spikes mark bursts of wide bars. Gaps between one close and the next open are not measured, so on instruments that gap often it can understate the total movement. The default 252 periods suits daily bars.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Length of the smoothing average. A longer length gives a smoother line and a longer empty stretch at the start.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, the per-bar volatility is multiplied by the square root of Annual Periods.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: Bars in a year used for annualising: 252 for daily bars, 52 for weekly bars.

faq.q: Why is the line empty for the first bars?
faq.html: The smoothing average is seeded with the simple average of the first Length values, so it has no value until that many bars have passed.

faq.q: Why divide by 4 ln 2?
faq.html: That factor converts the average squared log range into an estimate of the variance of returns, so the result is comparable with other volatility measures.

faq.q: How is it different from High-Low Volatility (HLV)?
faq.html: Both use the squared log range. High-Low Volatility answers from the first bar with a bias correction, while this one waits for a full window before its first value.

related.title: Rogers-Satchell Volatility (RSV)
related.summary: A volatility estimate built from each bar's open, high, low and close designed so that a steady trend does not inflate it.

related.title: Normalized Average True Range
related.summary: The average true range expressed as a percentage of the close, so volatility compares across instruments and price levels.

related.title: Realized Volatility (RV)
related.summary: Volatility measured from the size of close-to-close log returns, smoothed with a simple average and optionally scaled to a yearly figure.

price-volume-divergence-pvd.title: Price Volume Divergence (PVD)
price-volume-divergence-pvd.summary: Compares the direction of price change with the direction of volume change and sizes the disagreement, positive when they diverge.
price-volume-divergence-pvd.descriptionHtml:
Price Volume Divergence compares two rates of change. The price rate of change is the percentage move in close over Price Period bars, and the volume rate of change is the percentage move in volume over Volume Period bars. Volume is floored at 1, so the study still draws on a series without volume. Until a period has passed, the change is measured from the first bar, and on the first bar itself it is zero.

Each rate of change is reduced to its direction: +1, -1 or 0. The raw value is the price direction times the opposite of the volume direction, times the sum of the two absolute rates of change. So it is positive when price and volume moved in opposite directions, negative when they moved together, and zero when either was unchanged. The raw value is smoothed with a simple mean over Smoothing Period bars, which covers however many bars have arrived until the window fills.
price-volume-divergence-pvd.howToReadHtml:
A positive reading means price and volume have been pulling apart: price rising on falling volume, or falling on rising volume. A negative reading means they agree. The further from zero, the larger the combined moves behind the reading.

A rise into positive territory during an advance suggests the move is happening on shrinking volume, which some traders read as a weakening trend. The line is noisy with short periods and can swing sharply on a single bar with an unusual volume change; a longer Smoothing Period calms it.

settings.label: Price Period
settings.html: The number of bars over which the percentage change in close is measured.

settings.label: Volume Period
settings.html: The number of bars over which the percentage change in volume is measured.

settings.label: Divergence Threshold
settings.html: Kept for reference only. Changing it does not change the plotted line.

settings.label: Smoothing Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the simple mean applied to the raw divergence. A longer period gives a calmer line.

faq.q: Does a positive reading mean price will fall?
faq.html: No. It means price and volume moved in opposite directions over the chosen periods: price up on falling volume, or price down on rising volume. It describes what happened, not what comes next.

faq.q: What does the Divergence Threshold do?
faq.html: Nothing to the line. The setting is declared but not used in the calculation, so moving it leaves the plot unchanged.

faq.q: Why are the early values measured from the first bar?
faq.html: Until a full period has passed there is no bar that far back, so the rate of change is taken from the first bar instead, and the first bar itself reads zero.

related.title: Positive Volume Index (PVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume rose against the bar before.

related.title: On Balance Volume (OBV)
related.summary: A running total that adds each bar's volume on a higher close and subtracts it on a lower close, tracking where volume is flowing.

related.title: Percentage Volume Oscillator (PVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of volume as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

positive-volume-index-pvi.title: Positive Volume Index (PVI)
positive-volume-index-pvi.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume rose against the bar before.
positive-volume-index-pvi.descriptionHtml:
The Positive Volume Index tracks what price does on busier bars. It starts at 100. On each bar whose volume is higher than the previous bar's volume, the index is multiplied by this bar's price divided by the previous bar's price, so it takes on that bar's percentage change. On every other bar, when volume fell or stayed the same, the index holds flat.

The first bar has no previous bar, so it holds at 100. A bar is skipped as well when the previous price is zero or the previous volume is not above zero, which avoids dividing by nothing. The price followed is the Price Source setting, the close by default.
positive-volume-index-pvi.howToReadHtml:
Because the index only moves on bars where volume rose, it shows the trend made when activity picked up. A rising index means price has tended to advance on rising volume; a falling one means rising volume has come with declines. Many traders compare the index with a long moving average of itself to judge the trend.

The level is the compounded price change on the busier bars since the start at 100, not a price, so read the direction and the slope. Pair it with the Negative Volume Index to compare how price behaves on busy bars against quiet ones.

settings.label: Price Source
settings.html: The price whose percentage change the index takes on the qualifying bars, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line stay flat for stretches?
faq.html: It only moves on bars whose volume is higher than the bar before. Through a run of falling volume it holds its last value.

faq.q: How does it relate to the Negative Volume Index?
faq.html: They split the bars between them: this index moves on bars where volume rose, the negative index on bars where it fell. Bars with unchanged volume move neither.

related.title: Percentage Volume Oscillator (PVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of volume as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

related.title: Price Volume Divergence (PVD)
related.summary: Compares the direction of price change with the direction of volume change and sizes the disagreement, positive when they diverge.

related.title: Price Volume Rank (PVR)
related.summary: Classifies every bar from 0 to 4 by whether price and volume rose or fell together against the bar before.

percentage-volume-oscillator-pvo.title: Percentage Volume Oscillator (PVO)
percentage-volume-oscillator-pvo.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of volume as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.
percentage-volume-oscillator-pvo.descriptionHtml:
The Percentage Volume Oscillator measures whether volume is expanding or contracting. It takes a fast and a slow exponential mean of each bar's volume and expresses their difference as a percentage of the slow mean: (fast - slow) / slow x 100. A signal line is an exponential mean of that percentage, and the histogram is the oscillator minus the signal.

Each mean starts from zero and, while that start still matters, is divided by one minus its decayed seed weight, so the lines read true from the first bar. The correction ends once the slowest of the three seed weights has fallen to 1e-10. The slow period has to be longer than the fast one: when it is set equal to or shorter than the fast period, it is held one bar longer than the fast period instead.
percentage-volume-oscillator-pvo.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, recent volume is running above its longer average, so participation is expanding; below zero, it is contracting. The size of the reading is the percentage gap, so +20 means the fast mean is 20 percent above the slow one.

The oscillator says nothing about price direction on its own. It is usually read alongside price: a breakout with the oscillator rising above zero has volume behind it, while one with the oscillator below zero is happening on thin trade. Crossings of the signal line, where the histogram changes sign, mark turns in the volume trend.

settings.label: Fast Period
settings.html: The length of the fast exponential mean of volume. A shorter value reacts to each surge in volume more quickly.

settings.label: Slow Period
settings.html: The length of the slow exponential mean used as the baseline. If it is not longer than the fast period, it is held one bar longer than the fast period.

settings.label: Signal Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential mean of the oscillator that forms the signal line and the histogram.

faq.q: What happens if I set the slow period below the fast period?
faq.html: The study uses a slow period one bar longer than the fast period instead, so the oscillator is never drawn inverted.

faq.q: Does it show whether buyers or sellers are in control?
faq.html: No. It only measures volume against its own average. Read price to see which side the volume is on.

related.title: Price Volume Rank (PVR)
related.summary: Classifies every bar from 0 to 4 by whether price and volume rose or fell together against the bar before.

related.title: Positive Volume Index (PVI)
related.summary: A cumulative index starting at 100 that follows the price change only on bars whose volume rose against the bar before.

related.title: Price Volume Trend (PVT)
related.summary: A running total of volume weighted by each bar's percentage price change, drawn with a moving average signal line and shaded by which of the two leads.

price-volume-rank-pvr.title: Price Volume Rank (PVR)
price-volume-rank-pvr.summary: Classifies every bar from 0 to 4 by whether price and volume rose or fell together against the bar before.
price-volume-rank-pvr.descriptionHtml:
Price Volume Rank sorts each bar into one of five cases by comparing its price and volume with the previous bar. A rank of 1 means price rose and volume rose. A rank of 2 means price rose while volume fell or stayed the same. A rank of 3 means price fell and volume fell. A rank of 4 means price fell while volume rose or stayed the same. A rank of 0 means price was unchanged, whatever the volume did.

The price compared is the Price Source setting, the close by default, and a missing volume reads as zero. The first bar compares with itself, so it ranks 0. The result is drawn as a step line, so each bar's class shows as a flat segment.
price-volume-rank-pvr.howToReadHtml:
Ranks 1 and 3 are the confirmed cases, where volume moved the same way as price: rising price on rising volume, falling price on falling volume. Ranks 2 and 4 are the divergent cases. A run of 1s suggests a well supported advance, while a run of 2s suggests the advance is happening on thinning volume.

The rank is a single-bar classification with no smoothing, so it changes often. It is most useful read as a pattern over several bars, or smoothed with an average of your own, rather than acting on any one bar.

settings.label: Price Source
settings.html: The price compared with the previous bar to decide whether price rose, fell or was unchanged, the close by default.

faq.q: Which ranks are up bars and which are down bars?
faq.html: Ranks 1 and 2 are bars where price rose, ranks 3 and 4 bars where it fell. Within each pair the rank only tells you whether volume moved the same way as price (1 and 3) or the other way (2 and 4).

faq.q: Why is the first bar ranked 0?
faq.html: There is no earlier bar, so it compares with itself and its price is unchanged.

related.title: Price Volume Trend (PVT)
related.summary: A running total of volume weighted by each bar's percentage price change, drawn with a moving average signal line and shaded by which of the two leads.

related.title: Percentage Volume Oscillator (PVO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential mean of volume as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

related.title: Trade Volume Index (TVI)
related.summary: A running total of volume that adds while price ticks up by more than a minimum move and subtracts while it ticks down, holding direction through smaller moves.

price-volume-trend-pvt.title: Price Volume Trend (PVT)
price-volume-trend-pvt.summary: A running total of volume weighted by each bar's percentage price change, drawn with a moving average signal line and shaded by which of the two leads.
price-volume-trend-pvt.descriptionHtml:
Price Volume Trend adds up volume, but only in proportion to how far price moved. On each bar the study takes the close's percentage change from the previous close and multiplies it by the bar's volume, then adds that to a total that starts at zero on the first bar. A bar that rises 1% on heavy volume adds a lot; a bar that barely moves adds almost nothing, whatever its volume.

This makes it a finer cousin of on-balance volume, which adds or subtracts the whole of each bar's volume by direction alone. The first bar compares its close with itself and adds nothing, and a bar without volume adds nothing.

A signal line, the simple moving average of the total over the chosen period, is drawn beside it. The pane is shaded green while the total is above its signal and red otherwise, including the warmup bars before the signal exists. A dashed zero line marks where the total started.
price-volume-trend-pvt.howToReadHtml:
Read the slope of the PVT line rather than its level, because the level depends entirely on where the chart begins. A rising line says volume has been arriving on up moves, which is accumulation; a falling line says it has been arriving on down moves. When price makes a new high and the PVT line does not, the move is being made on thinner participation.

The green and red shading shows whether the line is above or below its own average, a quick read of whether recent flow is stronger or weaker than usual. Crossings of the signal line come often in a sideways market, so treat them as context rather than as entries on their own.

settings.label: Signal Line Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the simple moving average drawn as the signal line. A longer period gives a slower signal that the PVT line crosses less often.

faq.q: How is it different from on-balance volume?
faq.html: On-balance volume adds or subtracts the whole of a bar's volume according to the direction of the close. PVT scales the volume by the size of the percentage move, so small moves count for little and large moves count for a lot.

faq.q: Why is the background red at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The signal line needs a full window of bars before it exists. Until then the line cannot be above its signal, so those bars are shaded red.

faq.q: Does the absolute value of PVT mean anything?
faq.html: Not on its own. The total starts at zero on the first bar of the chart, so its level shifts with the history loaded. Compare its direction and its swings with those of price instead.

related.title: Trade Volume Index (TVI)
related.summary: A running total of volume that adds while price ticks up by more than a minimum move and subtracts while it ticks down, holding direction through smaller moves.

related.title: Price Volume Rank (PVR)
related.summary: Classifies every bar from 0 to 4 by whether price and volume rose or fell together against the bar before.

related.title: Time Weighted Average Price (TWAP)
related.summary: The plain running average of price since the chosen period began, where every bar counts once regardless of how much traded in it.

pascal-weighted-moving-average-pwma.title: Pascal Weighted Moving Average (PWMA)
pascal-weighted-moving-average-pwma.summary: A moving average weighted by a row of Pascal's triangle, a bell of binomial weights that puts most of the weight on the middle of the window.
pascal-weighted-moving-average-pwma.descriptionHtml:
The Pascal Weighted Moving Average weights each bar of its window by a binomial coefficient. With p bars in the window the weights are one row of Pascal's triangle: the first is 1 and each next one is the previous times (p - k) / k. For a window of five that gives 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. The weighted sum of the source is divided by the sum of the weights.

The binomial weights form a bell centred on the middle of the window, very close to a Gaussian, so bars near the ends count for almost nothing and the middle bars dominate. The window grows with the data until it reaches period, so the line starts on the first bar. A missing price is left out with its weight.
pascal-weighted-moving-average-pwma.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a very smooth trend line. Because the bell is narrow, the effective smoothing is shorter than the period suggests, and the line lags price by about half the window. A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend, and a falling line with price below it a downtrend.

Its slope is the useful part: turns in the line are clean and seldom reverse on a single bar. Until period bars exist the window is shorter, so the earliest values follow price more closely.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the binomial bell spans. A longer period smooths more and lags more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why do the bars at the ends hardly count?
faq.html: Binomial coefficients grow quickly toward the middle of the row. In a 10-bar window the two end bars weigh 1 each while the middle ones weigh 126, so the ends barely move the result.

faq.q: Is there an upper limit on the period?
faq.html: Yes, 1000. The coefficients become too large to hold in a number much beyond that.

faq.q: How is it different from a Gaussian average?
faq.html: A binomial row is the whole-number cousin of a Gaussian bell. The two give very similar lines, but this one needs no width setting: the period fixes the shape.

related.title: Quadruple EMA (QEMA)
related.summary: Four chained exponential stages with rising smoothing factors, combined 4, -6, 4, -1 to cancel most of the lag of an ordinary EMA.

related.title: Ehlers Predictive Moving Average (PMA)
related.summary: A weighted average with one lag cancelled by extrapolation, plus a faster trigger line that leads it.

related.title: Quadratic Regression Moving Average (QRMA)
related.summary: Fits a parabola to the last N prices by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar, so the line follows curvature as well as slope.

quadruple-ema-qema.title: Quadruple EMA (QEMA)
quadruple-ema-qema.summary: Four chained exponential stages with rising smoothing factors, combined 4, -6, 4, -1 to cancel most of the lag of an ordinary EMA.
quadruple-ema-qema.descriptionHtml:
QEMA chains four exponential averages and combines them to remove lag. The first stage uses the usual smoothing factor, two over the period plus one. Each later stage is faster than the one before it by the cube root of one over the first factor, so the fourth factor lands on one and that stage follows its input. The output is four times the first stage, minus six times the second, plus four times the third, minus the fourth.

Every stage starts at zero. During warmup each one is divided by its own correction, one minus its beta raised to the number of bars seen, which removes the pull toward zero and puts the first value on the source. Once the first stage's beta raised to the bars seen falls below 1e-10, all corrections are dropped and the stages run as plain recursions. Bars with a missing source leave a gap and do not move the stages.
quadruple-ema-qema.howToReadHtml:
QEMA is a fast trend line: it follows price more tightly than an EMA of the same period and turns sooner after a reversal. Price above a rising QEMA describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend.

Because the combination extrapolates, QEMA can overshoot price after a sharp move and can whip back and forth in a sideways market. Use a longer period when the line is too nervous for the timeframe, and treat a single turn as a hint rather than a confirmed change of trend.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the first stage's smoothing factor, from which the other three are derived. A larger period gives a smoother line.

faq.q: Why are the four smoothing factors different?
faq.html: Each stage is faster than the one before by the same ratio, the cube root of one over the first factor. That spacing lets the 4, -6, 4, -1 combination cancel most of the lag.

faq.q: How does it compare with TEMA?
faq.html: TEMA combines three stages that share one factor. QEMA adds a fourth stage and spaces the factors, which removes more lag but makes the line more prone to overshoot.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Each stage is divided by a warmup correction that removes the effect of starting at zero, so the first value equals the source.

related.title: Quadratic Regression Moving Average (QRMA)
related.summary: Fits a parabola to the last N prices by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar, so the line follows curvature as well as slope.

related.title: Pascal Weighted Moving Average (PWMA)
related.summary: A moving average weighted by a row of Pascal's triangle, a bell of binomial weights that puts most of the weight on the middle of the window.

related.title: Rainbow Moving Average (RAIN)
related.summary: Ten simple averages stacked on top of each other and blended back into one line, with the faster layers weighted most.

quantitative-qualitative-estimation-qqe.title: Quantitative Qualitative Estimation (QQE)
quantitative-qualitative-estimation-qqe.summary: A smoothed RSI with a trailing band set by the RSI's own volatility; when the line crosses the trailing level, momentum has shifted.
quantitative-qualitative-estimation-qqe.descriptionHtml:
QQE starts with an RSI of the source, its gains and losses smoothed with weight 1 / RSI Period, and smooths it with an exponential mean of length Smooth Factor. That smoothed RSI is the yellow QQE line.

The study then measures how much the QQE line moves from bar to bar. It takes the absolute change of the line and smooths it twice with an exponential mean of length 2 x Smooth Factor - 1, which gives a dynamic average range. Multiplying that range by the QQE Factor sets a band above and below the line.

The trailing level follows the band like a stop. While the line and its previous reading are both above the trailing level, the level can only rise toward the lower band; while both are below, it can only fall toward the upper band. When the line crosses it, the trailing level jumps to the band on the other side. Every smoothing stage starts at zero and is divided by the weight still owed to that start, so both lines answer from the first bar.
quantitative-qualitative-estimation-qqe.howToReadHtml:
Watch the QQE line against the trailing line. A cross of the QQE line above the trailing line says momentum has turned up by more than its usual noise; a cross below says it has turned down. The levels at 70, 50 and 30 give the usual RSI context: a cross up from below 30, or a cross down from above 70, comes from a stretched reading.

The band width adapts to how much the RSI has been moving, so in choppy conditions the trailing line sits further away and crosses are rarer. A larger QQE Factor widens the band and gives fewer, later crosses.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the RSI is computed from, the close by default.

settings.label: RSI Period
settings.html: The length of the RSI. A shorter period makes the RSI and everything built on it faster and noisier.

settings.label: Smooth Factor
settings.html: The length of the exponential mean applied to the RSI; the range smoothing uses twice this minus one. Higher values give smoother lines.

settings.label: QQE Factor
settings.html: The multiple of the dynamic average range used to place the trailing band. Larger values keep the trailing line further away and give fewer crosses.

faq.q: What is the trailing line?
faq.html: A level that follows the QQE line at a distance set by the line's own recent volatility. It only moves toward the line while the line stays on one side, and jumps to the other side when the line crosses it, much like a trailing stop.

faq.q: Why does the trailing line jump?
faq.html: When the QQE line crosses it, the trailing level flips from the band below the line to the band above it, or the reverse. The jump marks the bar where momentum changed side.

faq.q: Is the QQE line the same as an RSI?
faq.html: It is an RSI smoothed with an exponential mean, so it follows the same 0 to 100 scale with less noise and a little more lag.

related.title: Ehlers Reflex Indicator (REFLEX)
related.summary: A zero-centred cycle oscillator that measures how far a smoothed price bends away from a straight line drawn across one period.

related.title: Psychological Line (PSL)
related.summary: The percentage of up bars among the last N bars, a simple count of how one-sided recent trading has been, from 0 to 100.

related.title: Ehlers Reverse EMA (REVERSEEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average minus its own reversed-filter estimate, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that keeps the smoothing but sheds the lag.

quadratic-regression-moving-average-qrma.title: Quadratic Regression Moving Average (QRMA)
quadratic-regression-moving-average-qrma.summary: Fits a parabola to the last N prices by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar, so the line follows curvature as well as slope.
quadratic-regression-moving-average-qrma.descriptionHtml:
The Quadratic Regression Moving Average fits the curve y = a + b x + c x^2 to the source over the last period bars, with x = 0 at the oldest bar of the window and x = period - 1 at the newest. The fit is ordinary least squares: the three normal equations are solved with Cramer's rule, using sums of x up to the fourth power that depend only on the period.

The value plotted is the fitted curve at the newest bar. A straight-line fit can only follow a slope; adding the squared term lets the line bend with a move that is speeding up or slowing down. Until period bars exist the line shows the price itself, and a missing price counts as zero.
quadratic-regression-moving-average-qrma.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a fast trend line. Because it fits curvature, it stays close to price through accelerating moves and turns sooner than a simple or linear average of the same length. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

The same flexibility is its limit: at the end of the window a parabola can overshoot, so after a sharp reversal the line may briefly run past price. Shorter periods make it react faster and more nervously; longer ones steady it.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the parabola is fitted to. At least 3, since a parabola needs three points.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the curve is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from a linear regression average?
faq.html: A linear fit draws a straight line through the window, so it lags whenever the move curves. The quadratic fit adds a bend and keeps up with a move that is accelerating or fading.

faq.q: Why can it overshoot price?
faq.html: The parabola is read at the very end of the window, where a curve fitted to the past is least constrained. After a sharp turn it can extend the old curvature for a few bars.

faq.q: Why must the period be at least 3?
faq.html: A parabola has three unknowns, so it needs at least three bars to be fitted.

related.title: Rainbow Moving Average (RAIN)
related.summary: Ten simple averages stacked on top of each other and blended back into one line, with the faster layers weighted most.

related.title: Quadruple EMA (QEMA)
related.summary: Four chained exponential stages with rising smoothing factors, combined 4, -6, 4, -1 to cancel most of the lag of an ordinary EMA.

related.title: Regularized EMA (REMA)
related.summary: An exponential average blended with a regularization term by a lambda setting, which in this form slows the step by alpha times lambda.

qstick-indicator.title: Qstick Indicator
qstick-indicator.summary: A moving average of the candle body, close minus open, that reads whether bars have been closing above or below where they opened.
qstick-indicator.descriptionHtml:
Qstick averages the body of each candle: the close minus the open. A positive body means the bar closed above its open, a negative body that it closed below. Averaging those bodies shows whether buying or selling has dominated within the bars over the recent past.

Two averages are offered. The simple form starts on the first bar as a mean of every body seen so far and becomes a rolling mean of the last length bars once that many have arrived. The exponential form starts its recursion at zero on the first bar, so its earliest readings are pulled toward zero before they settle.

The pane is shaded green behind bars where the reading is above zero and red where it is at or below zero, and a dashed line marks zero.
qstick-indicator.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, candles have on balance been closing higher than they opened, which points to buying pressure inside the bars. Below zero, the reverse. A cross of the zero line, which flips the background colour, marks a change in which side has controlled the bars.

Qstick looks only at the body of each bar and ignores gaps between bars, so a market that gaps up and then drifts lower within each bar can read negative while price rises. A longer length smooths out single large candles; the exponential form reacts faster than the simple one.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the average covers. A longer length gives a smoother line that crosses zero less often.

settings.label: MA Type
settings.html: Chooses a simple mean of the bodies or an exponential one. The exponential form weights recent bars more and starts from zero.

settings.label: Close Source
settings.html: The series used as the close of each body. Changing it measures a different part of the bar.

settings.label: Open Source
settings.html: The series used as the open of each body, subtracted from the close source on every bar.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The simple form averages however many bodies it has until it holds a full window, and the exponential form starts from zero, so both answer from the first bar.

faq.q: What does the background colour show?
faq.html: Green behind bars where the reading is above zero and red where it is zero or below, so the side in control is visible without reading the scale.

faq.q: Why does Qstick disagree with the price trend sometimes?
faq.html: It measures only close minus open inside each bar. Gaps between bars are left out, so a rising market built on opening gaps can still show a negative reading.

related.title: RAVI: Chande Range Action Verification Index
related.summary: The percentage gap between a fast and a slow simple average of the close, read against a threshold to separate trends from ranges.

related.title: PFE: Polarized Fractal Efficiency
related.summary: How directly price travelled over a lookback, from -100 to +100: the straight-line distance over the path actually walked, signed by direction.

related.title: SuperTrend
related.summary: A trailing line set a multiple of average true range away from the bar midpoint, which flips sides when the close breaks through it.

quantile-quantile.title: Quantile (QUANTILE)
quantile-quantile.summary: The requested quantile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart: 0.5 is the rolling median, 0 the low, 1 the high.
quantile-quantile.descriptionHtml:
The Quantile study sorts the last Period values of the source and plots the value at the requested quantile level. The rank is the level times one less than the number of values, and when it falls between two positions the study interpolates linearly between the neighbouring values.

A level of 0.5 gives the rolling median, 0 the lowest value in the window and 1 the highest. The default of 0.25 is the lower quartile, the level a quarter of the recent bars sit below.

The window at the left edge of the chart is ranked over the bars that exist, so the study answers from the first bar, and absent values are skipped.
quantile-quantile.howToReadHtml:
