Use a low level as a robust floor and a high level as a robust ceiling for the recent range. Unlike the highest and lowest values of the window, a quantile is not set by a single extreme bar, so a one-off spike does not shift it.

Price holding above the lower quartile shows the recent distribution being respected, and a value below it is lower than roughly three quarters of the recent values. The line trails a fast move, as any rolling statistic does.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose values are ranked.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent bars are ranked. A longer period gives a steadier level.

settings.label: Quantile Level (0.0-1.0)
settings.html: Which quantile to draw, from 0 for the window low to 1 for the window high; 0.5 is the median.

faq.q: How does this differ from the Percentile study?
faq.html: They compute the same thing on different scales: a quantile level of 0.25 is the 25th percentile. This study takes the level as a fraction from 0 to 1.

faq.q: Why use a quantile instead of the window low?
faq.html: The window low is set by one bar, so a single spike moves it. A quantile such as 0.1 ignores the most extreme few bars and gives a steadier level.

faq.q: Does it wait for a full window?
faq.html: No. Until the window fills it ranks the bars that exist, so the line starts on the first bar.

related.title: Skewness (SKEW)
related.summary: A rolling measure of how lopsided the recent values are about their mean: positive when the long tail is above, negative when it is below.

related.title: Polynomial Fitting (POLYFIT)
related.summary: Fits a least-squares polynomial of the chosen degree to the recent window and plots the fitted curve's value at the current bar.

related.title: Spearman Rank Correlation (SPEARMAN)
related.summary: Correlation between the ranks of two series of the chart's symbol over a window: whether they move together in order, regardless of size.

quantile-loss-pinball-loss.title: Quantile Loss (Pinball Loss)
quantile-loss-pinball-loss.summary: A rolling average of the pinball loss, an error score that charges misses above and below the forecast at different rates set by a quantile.
quantile-loss-pinball-loss.descriptionHtml:
Quantile Loss, also called pinball loss, scores a predicted series against an actual series while treating the two directions of a miss differently. On every bar the difference is the actual value minus the predicted value. When the actual is at or above the prediction, the loss is Quantile times that difference. When the actual is below the prediction, the loss is one minus Quantile times the size of the miss.

The study plots the simple average of this loss over the last Length bars. At a quantile of 0.5 both directions cost the same and the line is half the mean absolute error. Above 0.5, a prediction that falls short of the actual is charged more; below 0.5, a prediction that overshoots is charged more. An absent value on either side is read as zero.
quantile-loss-pinball-loss.howToReadHtml:
A lower line means the predicted series has been closer to the actual one in the way the quantile cares about. With a high quantile, a rising line says the forecast has been too low too often; with a low quantile, it says the forecast has been too high. Compare the line at two quantiles to see which side the misses fall on.

The loss is in price units, so read it against its own history. It has no value for the first Length minus one bars, and it says how large the weighted miss is, not which bars caused it.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the loss is averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Quantile
settings.html: How the two directions of a miss are weighted. 0.5 weights them equally; higher values charge under-prediction more, lower values charge over-prediction more.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: What does a quantile of 0.9 mean here?
faq.html: A miss where the actual ends above the prediction costs 0.9 per point, and a miss where it ends below costs 0.1 per point. The line then rewards a forecast that sits near the upper edge of where price lands.

faq.q: How does it relate to the mean absolute error?
faq.html: At a quantile of 0.5 every miss costs half its size, so the line is exactly half the mean absolute error over the same window.

faq.q: With the default settings, what is being scored?
faq.html: The open is the prediction and the close is the actual, so the line averages each bar's open to close move, weighted by whether the bar closed up or down.

related.title: Relative Absolute Error (RAE)
related.summary: Absolute error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the absolute error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

related.title: Pseudo-Huber Loss
related.summary: A rolling average of the smooth Huber loss between an actual and a predicted series, quadratic for small misses and close to linear for large ones.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
related.summary: The typical distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, in price units, with the average drawn on the chart.

relative-absolute-error-rae.title: Relative Absolute Error (RAE)
relative-absolute-error-rae.summary: Absolute error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the absolute error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.
relative-absolute-error-rae.descriptionHtml:
Relative Absolute Error (RAE) asks whether an exponential moving average tracks price better than a flat rolling mean does. The exponential average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through that warmup. The baseline is the mean of the source over the last Period bars, including this one; before that many bars have passed it is the mean of every bar so far.

On every bar the study takes the absolute gap between the source and the exponential average, and the absolute gap between the source and the baseline mean. Each is totalled over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry a value. RAE is the first total divided by the second. When the baseline total is zero the reading is 1. The exponential average is drawn on the price chart.
relative-absolute-error-rae.howToReadHtml:
Below 1, the exponential average has been a closer fit to price than the flat mean of the window; above 1, it has been a worse fit. In a steady trend the exponential average follows price while the flat mean lags far behind, so RAE drops well below 1. In a choppy range the flat mean sits in the middle of the noise and is hard to beat, so RAE moves toward or above 1.

The first bar reads 1, and the line then has no value until the exponential average starts on bar Period minus one. The ratio says which fit was better, not how large either error was.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being fitted by both the exponential average and the rolling mean.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window used for the baseline mean and both error totals.

faq.q: What does a reading of 0.5 mean?
faq.html: The exponential average's absolute misses over the window added up to half of the flat mean's misses, so it fitted price about twice as closely.

faq.q: Why does the very first bar show 1?
faq.html: On the first bar the baseline mean is that bar's own value, so the baseline error is zero, and a zero baseline is reported as 1.

faq.q: How is it different from the Relative Squared Error?
faq.html: This one totals absolute gaps, so every point of error counts the same. The squared version gives large gaps much more weight.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
related.summary: The typical distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, in price units, with the average drawn on the chart.

related.title: Quantile Loss (Pinball Loss)
related.summary: A rolling average of the pinball loss, an error score that charges misses above and below the forecast at different rates set by a quantile.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE)
related.summary: The typical log distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, a relative gap that does not depend on price level.

rainbow-moving-average-rain.title: Rainbow Moving Average (RAIN)
rainbow-moving-average-rain.summary: Ten simple averages stacked on top of each other and blended back into one line, with the faster layers weighted most.
rainbow-moving-average-rain.descriptionHtml:
The Rainbow Moving Average smooths the source ten times in a row. Layer one is a simple average of the source over period bars, layer two is the same average of layer one, and so on up to layer ten. Each layer is smoother and slower than the one below it.

The ten layers are then blended into a single line with weights 5, 4, 3 and 2 for the first four layers and 1 for each of the other six, and the total is divided by 20. The faster layers carry most of the weight, so the result is smooth without being as slow as the tenth layer. Every layer averages the bars seen so far until its window is full, so the line starts on the first bar, and a missing price counts as zero.
rainbow-moving-average-rain.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line built from a whole family of averages. With the default period of 2 it sits close to price but filters out single-bar noise; larger periods make each layer slower and the blend much smoother. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

Because it mixes ten layers of different speeds, its lag is longer than one simple average of the same period. Keep the period small unless you want only the broad swing.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window of each of the ten stacked averages. Small values already smooth a lot, because the averaging is repeated ten times.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the first layer averages, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the default period only 2?
faq.html: The averaging is applied ten times, so even a 2-bar window ends up smoothing over many bars. A period of 10 or more makes the blend very slow.

faq.q: Why are the first layers weighted more?
faq.html: The early layers follow price closely and the later ones lag. Weighting the early ones more keeps the line smooth while limiting the lag.

faq.q: Where are the ten layers?
faq.html: This study draws only the blended line. The layers are computed and combined, not plotted.

related.title: Regularized EMA (REMA)
related.summary: An exponential average blended with a regularization term by a lambda setting, which in this form slows the step by alpha times lambda.

related.title: Quadratic Regression Moving Average (QRMA)
related.summary: Fits a parabola to the last N prices by least squares and plots the fitted value at the newest bar, so the line follows curvature as well as slope.

related.title: Recursive Gaussian Moving Average (RGMA)
related.summary: A cascade of identical exponential stages that approximates a Gaussian filter, giving a very smooth line with an even response.

ravi-chande-range-action-verification-in.title: RAVI: Chande Range Action Verification Index
ravi-chande-range-action-verification-in.summary: The percentage gap between a fast and a slow simple average of the close, read against a threshold to separate trends from ranges.
ravi-chande-range-action-verification-in.descriptionHtml:
The Range Action Verification Index measures how far apart a short and a long simple moving average of the close have drifted. It takes the absolute difference between the two averages and expresses it as a percentage of the long average, so the reading is always zero or above and compares across instruments of very different price.

When price trends, the fast average pulls away from the slow one and the reading rises. When price moves sideways, the two averages sit close together and the reading falls toward zero. A fixed threshold line, 3% by default, is drawn as the dividing line between the two states.

The short period must be shorter than the long period; if it is not, the study draws nothing. The line starts once the long average has a full window of closes.
ravi-chande-range-action-verification-in.howToReadHtml:
Read the line against the dashed threshold. Above it, the averages have separated enough to class the market as trending. Below it, they sit close together and the market is classed as ranging.

The index has no direction: a strong fall and a strong rise both push it up. Pair it with the slope of an average or with price itself to know which way the trend runs. The right threshold depends on the instrument and the timeframe: shorter bars usually leave a smaller percentage gap between the two averages, so a level below the default may separate the two states better on them.

settings.label: Short Period
settings.html: The length of the fast simple average. A shorter value reacts sooner and makes the reading noisier.

settings.label: Long Period
settings.html: The length of the slow simple average. It also sets how many bars pass before the line first appears.

settings.label: Threshold
settings.html: Where the dashed dividing line between trending and ranging is drawn, in percent. It does not change the calculation.

faq.q: Why is the line always positive?
faq.html: It uses the absolute gap between the two averages, so it measures how strong the separation is and not which side the fast average is on.

faq.q: Why does nothing appear when I change the periods?
faq.html: The short period must be smaller than the long period. When it is not, the study treats the settings as invalid and draws no line.

faq.q: How is it different from a moving average crossover?
faq.html: A crossover tells you which average is on top. This index tells you how far apart they are as a share of the slow average, which is a measure of whether the market is trending at all.

related.title: SuperTrend
related.summary: A trailing line set a multiple of average true range away from the bar midpoint, which flips sides when the close breaks through it.

related.title: Qstick Indicator
related.summary: A moving average of the candle body, close minus open, that reads whether bars have been closing above or below where they opened.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.

ehlers-reflex-indicator-reflex.title: Ehlers Reflex Indicator (REFLEX)
ehlers-reflex-indicator-reflex.summary: A zero-centred cycle oscillator that measures how far a smoothed price bends away from a straight line drawn across one period.
ehlers-reflex-indicator-reflex.descriptionHtml:
REFLEX looks for the turning points of price cycles. It first smooths the source with a two-pole filter tuned to half the period, which removes most of the bar-to-bar noise while keeping the cycle. It then draws a straight line from the filtered value one period ago to the filtered value now and averages the gap between that line and the filtered series at every bar in between.

When price travels in a straight line the gap is close to zero. When it bends, rising and then falling or the reverse, the filtered series bows away from the line and the average gap grows. That gap is divided by the square root of an exponential mean of its own square (a running root mean square with a weight of 0.04), so the result reads roughly in units of its own recent spread, and the same levels mean the same thing on any instrument.

The filter and the mean square start from zero, and the line reads zero until a full period of filtered values exists. On the first bar with a reading the mean square holds only that one value, so the line opens at plus or minus 5 and then settles, which makes the opening stretch a warmup rather than a reading.
ehlers-reflex-indicator-reflex.howToReadHtml:
Read REFLEX as a cycle gauge around zero. A move above +1 says the smoothed price has bowed upward further than usual compared with its recent behaviour, and a move below -1 says the same downward. Turns of the line from beyond those levels are the moments the cycle is rolling over, and crossings of zero mark the middle of a swing.

It is built to follow cycles, not trends. In a long, steady trend the line drifts back toward zero because a straight move has nothing to reflect, so a quiet reading does not mean the market is quiet. Very short periods make it jumpy, and very long ones make it slow to turn.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The cycle length in bars. The smoothing filter is tuned to half of it, and the straight line and the averaged gap both span this many bars.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the indicator reads. A missing value enters the filter as zero.

faq.q: What do the +1 and -1 levels mean?
faq.html: The output is divided by a running root mean square of itself, so plus and minus one are roughly one unit of its own recent spread. Readings beyond them are larger bends than the line has been showing lately.

faq.q: Why is the line flat at zero and then jumps to 5?
faq.html: The averaged gap needs a full period of filtered values, so until the period has passed it is held at zero. The running mean square also starts from zero, so on the first bar with a gap it equals 0.04 times that gap squared, and the gap divided by its square root is exactly plus or minus 5. The line then settles over the following bars.

faq.q: How is it different from a trend gauge built on the same filter?
faq.html: This one measures the gap to a straight line through the window, which removes the trend and leaves the bend. A trend gauge measures the gap to each past value directly, so it keeps the trend in.

related.title: Ehlers Reverse EMA (REVERSEEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average minus its own reversed-filter estimate, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that keeps the smoothing but sheds the lag.

related.title: Quantitative Qualitative Estimation (QQE)
related.summary: A smoothed RSI with a trailing band set by the RSI's own volatility; when the line crosses the trailing level, momentum has shifted.

related.title: Relative Vigor Index (RVGI)
related.summary: Compares where bars close relative to their open with the size of their range, so it reads the conviction behind a move as a signed ratio.

regression-channels-regchannel.title: Regression Channels (REGCHANNEL)
regression-channels-regchannel.summary: A least-squares trend line through the last N prices, with bands set a multiple of the fit's own residual spread above and below it.
regression-channels-regchannel.descriptionHtml:
Regression Channels fits a straight line through the last Period values of the source by least squares, the line that keeps the squared vertical distances to the prices as small as possible. The regression line on each bar is where that fitted line ends, on the current bar.

The bands measure how closely prices hug the fit. The study takes each price in the window, subtracts the fitted line's value at that bar, squares the result, averages the squares over the window and takes the square root. That root mean square residual, times the multiplier, sets the distance of the upper and lower bands from the regression line. The upper half of the channel is shaded red and the lower half green.

The line needs a full window, so it starts on bar Period - 1.
regression-channels-regchannel.howToReadHtml:
The regression line tracks the trend of the window rather than a flat average, so in a steady move it sits close to price with little lag. The bands widen when prices scatter around the trend and narrow when they follow it closely. A close outside a band is a move that is unusual for the current trend; inside a clean trend, price returning toward the line after touching a band is the common pattern.

Each value is the end of a fresh fit, so a new bar can change the slope noticeably on a short period. Past values never change, but the newest point reacts sharply to large bars near the end of the window.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the line is fitted through. A longer period gives a steadier trend line and wider bands.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the line is fitted to.

settings.label: Standard Deviation Multiplier
settings.html: Band distance as a multiple of the root mean square residual of the fit. A larger value widens the channel.

faq.q: How is the band width calculated?
faq.html: From the residuals of the fit: each price minus the fitted line at that bar, squared, averaged over the window and square rooted. The sum is divided by Period, not Period - 1.

faq.q: Why does the line react to a single large bar?
faq.html: The newest bar sits at the end of the fit, where it has the most leverage on the slope. A big bar can tilt the whole line and move its end point.

faq.q: Why is there nothing on the first bars?
faq.html: A fit needs a full window of Period values, so the first line appears on bar Period - 1.

related.title: Standard Deviation Channel (SDCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares line through the lookback window with a channel a fixed multiple of the residual standard deviation on each side.

related.title: Price Channel (PCHANNEL)
related.summary: The highest high and lowest low of the lookback window with their midpoint, showing the extremes a new move has to break.

related.title: Stoller Average Range Channel (STARCHANNEL)
related.summary: A simple mean of the source as the centre line, with bands a multiple of an average true range above and below it.

rectified-linear-unit-relu.title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
rectified-linear-unit-relu.summary: Splits the gap between price and its 20-bar average into an upper line for strength and a mirrored lower line for weakness.
rectified-linear-unit-relu.descriptionHtml:
Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) applies the rectifier function, which keeps a value when it is positive and replaces it with zero otherwise, to the distance between the source and its 20-bar simple moving average.

Two lines come out of it. ReLU Up is the larger of zero and the source minus the average, so it is positive only while the source is above the average. ReLU Down is the larger of zero and the average minus the source, drawn with its sign flipped, so it is negative only while the source is below the average. At any bar at most one of the two is away from zero. The average length is fixed at 20 bars, so both lines are blank for the first 19 bars.
rectified-linear-unit-relu.howToReadHtml:
The green line above zero shows how far the source sits above its 20-bar average, and the red line below zero shows how far it sits below. Only one side is active at a time, so the pane reads as a split view of the deviation: long stretches of green mean the source has held above its average, and a deepening red line means it is pulling further below.

The values are in price units, so they grow with the price level and with volatility. A switch from one side to the other is the source crossing its average, which is a lagging event like any moving average cross.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with its own 20-bar simple average.

faq.q: Can I change the 20-bar length?
faq.html: No. The average length is fixed at 20 bars in this study, and only the source can be chosen.

faq.q: Why is the lower line negative?
faq.html: The rectified value on the weak side is always zero or positive. The study flips its sign so the weak side is drawn below zero and the two sides read as one picture.

faq.q: What does it mean when both lines are at zero?
faq.html: The source is exactly on its average. Both rectified values are zero at that moment.

related.title: Logistic Function (SIGMOID)
related.summary: Passes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the logistic curve, giving an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

related.title: Poisson Distribution CDF (POISSONDIST)
related.summary: Reads price's position in its recent range as a Poisson event rate and plots the chance of at most k events at that rate.

related.title: Slope, Linear Regression (SLOPE)
related.summary: Plots the slope of the least squares line fitted through the last N values, in price units per bar.

regularized-ema-rema.title: Regularized EMA (REMA)
regularized-ema-rema.summary: An exponential average blended with a regularization term by a lambda setting, which in this form slows the step by alpha times lambda.
regularized-ema-rema.descriptionHtml:
REMA mixes two candidates for the next value. The first is an ordinary exponential step toward the source, with a smoothing factor of two over the period plus one. The second is a regularization term meant to continue the average's own recent movement. The lambda setting blends them: one is the plain exponential average and lower values lean on the regularization term.

In the calculation as written, the previous value is updated to the current value before the regularization term reads it, so that term equals the current value. Each bar therefore moves the average toward the source by the smoothing factor times lambda: lambda acts as a multiplier that slows the average down, and at zero the line stays flat at its first value. The line is seeded with the first source value, and a missing source value carries the previous value forward.
regularized-ema-rema.howToReadHtml:
Read REMA as an exponential average whose speed is set by both the period and lambda. At lambda one it is a standard EMA of the period. At 0.5 it moves half as far each bar, which is close to an EMA of about twice the period, and smaller values make it slower still.

Price above a rising line describes an uptrend and price below a falling line a downtrend. Keep lambda above zero: at zero the line never leaves its first value and says nothing about price.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing factor, two over the period plus one. A larger period gives a slower line.

settings.label: Lambda
settings.html: Blends the exponential step with the regularization term, from 0 to 1. Lower values make the line slower; 1 is a standard EMA.

faq.q: Why does a lower lambda only slow the line down?
faq.html: The regularization term reads the previous value after it has been set to the current one, so it equals the current value. Blending toward it shortens each step to the smoothing factor times lambda.

faq.q: What happens at lambda zero?
faq.html: Every step has zero length, so the line stays at the first source value for the whole chart.

faq.q: What does lambda one give?
faq.html: A standard exponential moving average of the period, seeded with the first source value.

related.title: Recursive Gaussian Moving Average (RGMA)
related.summary: A cascade of identical exponential stages that approximates a Gaussian filter, giving a very smooth line with an even response.

related.title: Rainbow Moving Average (RAIN)
related.summary: Ten simple averages stacked on top of each other and blended back into one line, with the faster layers weighted most.

related.title: Wilder's Moving Average (RMA)
related.summary: A slow exponential average with a smoothing factor of one over the period, corrected during warmup so it draws from the first bar.

ehlers-reverse-ema-reverseema.title: Ehlers Reverse EMA (REVERSEEMA)
ehlers-reverse-ema-reverseema.summary: An exponential average minus its own reversed-filter estimate, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that keeps the smoothing but sheds the lag.
ehlers-reverse-ema-reverseema.descriptionHtml:
This study starts from an ordinary exponential moving average of the source with weight 2 / (period + 1). While the average is filling it is divided by the weight it has gathered so far, so the first values are not dragged toward the zero it starts from.

The average is then passed through eight cascaded reverse stages. Each stage takes the stage below it, multiplies it by the decay factor (1 minus the weight) raised to a doubling power (1, 2, 4 up to 128), and adds the previous bar's value of the stage below. Together the stages approximate the inverse of the exponential filter. The plotted value is the average minus the weight times the last stage, which leaves a line centred on zero.

All eight stages start from zero, and each one reads the stage below it one bar late, so the cascade takes eight bars to fill. Until then the last stage is far too small, and the line opens near the level of the price itself before it drops into its normal range around zero. A missing source value enters the calculation as zero and is blanked on the plot, but the state still moves forward on that bar.
ehlers-reverse-ema-reverseema.howToReadHtml:
Treat the line as a smoothed momentum reading. Above zero, the recent smoothed price is running ahead of what the reversed filter expects; below zero it is falling behind. Crossings of zero and turns from an extreme are the events most traders watch, often together with the trend of the price itself.

The size of the swings depends on the instrument's price, so compare the line with its own history rather than with a fixed number. A short period reacts quickly and turns often; a long period is calmer and slower.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the base exponential average. A longer period gives a smoother, slower oscillator.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is taken over.

faq.q: Why are there eight reverse stages?
faq.html: Each stage doubles the power of the decay factor, so eight stages reach a power of 128, by which point the factor is effectively zero for any usual period and further stages change nothing.

faq.q: Is the value in price units?
faq.html: Yes. It is a difference between two price-based quantities, so its scale follows the instrument's price. Use the zero line and the turns rather than a fixed threshold.

faq.q: Why does the line start near the price and then collapse?
faq.html: The reverse stages start from zero and each one reads the stage below it one bar late, so the last stage is not complete until the ninth bar. Before that, little is subtracted from the average and the line reads close to the price itself. Ignore those opening bars, and with a long period the stretch after them as well, while the stages settle.

related.title: Relative Vigor Index (RVGI)
related.summary: Compares where bars close relative to their open with the size of their range, so it reads the conviction behind a move as a signed ratio.

related.title: Ehlers Reflex Indicator (REFLEX)
related.summary: A zero-centred cycle oscillator that measures how far a smoothed price bends away from a straight line drawn across one period.

related.title: Stochastic Momentum Index (SMI)
related.summary: Where the close sits relative to the midpoint of its recent high-low range, double smoothed and centred on zero, with a smoothed signal line.

recursive-gaussian-moving-average-rgma.title: Recursive Gaussian Moving Average (RGMA)
recursive-gaussian-moving-average-rgma.summary: A cascade of identical exponential stages that approximates a Gaussian filter, giving a very smooth line with an even response.
recursive-gaussian-moving-average-rgma.descriptionHtml:
RGMA passes the source through a chain of exponential averages, one per pass, with each stage smoothing the output of the stage before it on the same bar. Repeating a simple exponential filter several times makes its response approach the bell shape of a Gaussian filter, which smooths noise evenly without the sharp edges of a plain window.

To keep the overall smoothing about the same whatever the number of passes, the period is divided by the square root of the passes before the smoothing factor is computed: alpha = 2 / (period / sqrt(passes) + 1). Every stage is seeded with the first source value and that value is drawn on the first bar, so the line has no warmup gap.
recursive-gaussian-moving-average-rgma.howToReadHtml:
RGMA is a smooth trend line. Its direction describes the trend, and price crossing it marks a move that has outlasted the filter's noise. Because the cascade spreads its weight smoothly over recent bars, the line bends gradually rather than in steps.

More passes make the response more bell shaped and the line smoother, but every extra stage adds some delay, so turns are confirmed late. Fewer passes make it closer to a single exponential average. Choose the period for the swing size you care about and leave the passes at the default unless the line is too jagged.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The base smoothing length. A larger period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Passes
settings.html: How many exponential stages are chained, from 1 to 10. More passes make the smoothing more Gaussian.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the period divided by the square root of the passes?
faq.html: Each extra stage adds smoothing. Shortening the per-stage length by the square root of the passes keeps the total smoothing roughly the same, so changing the passes changes the shape of the response more than its length.

faq.q: What does one pass give?
faq.html: A single exponential average with the smoothing factor two over the period plus one.

faq.q: Is this an exact Gaussian filter?
faq.html: No. It is a recursive approximation: chaining exponential stages approaches a Gaussian response as the passes rise, without computing Gaussian weights.

related.title: Wilder's Moving Average (RMA)
related.summary: A slow exponential average with a smoothing factor of one over the period, corrected during warmup so it draws from the first bar.

related.title: Regularized EMA (REMA)
related.summary: An exponential average blended with a regularization term by a lambda setting, which in this form slows the step by alpha times lambda.

related.title: RWMA: Range Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close where each bar is weighted by its own high to low range, so wide bars pull the line harder than narrow ones.

recursive-least-squares-adaptive-filter-.title: Recursive Least Squares Adaptive Filter (RLS)
recursive-least-squares-adaptive-filter-.summary: An adaptive filter that re-estimates its weights every bar by recursive least squares, with a forgetting factor setting how much history still counts.
recursive-least-squares-adaptive-filter-.descriptionHtml:
This study predicts each bar from the previous Filter Order bars with a set of weights that it re-estimates on every bar. The line on the chart is the prediction made before the current bar updates the weights.

The update is recursive least squares. The filter keeps an inverse correlation matrix P, which starts at 100 times the identity, and the weights, which start at zero. Each bar it forms the gain vector k = P x / (lambda + x' P x) from the input vector x of past prices, moves the weights by k times the prediction error, and updates P to (P - k (P x)') / lambda. Dividing by the Forgetting Factor lambda each bar makes older bars count for less, so the filter can follow a change in behaviour.

History before the first bar reads as zero. While every weight is still zero the prediction is a flat zero, so the line is drawn from the first bar after a weight has moved.
recursive-least-squares-adaptive-filter-.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a fast adaptive estimate of price. Because recursive least squares solves for the best weights over all the history it remembers, it converges far faster than a simple gradient method and usually sits very close to price. Gaps between price and the line show moves the recent pattern did not predict.

A forgetting factor near 1 remembers a long history and gives a steadier line; a lower value adapts quickly to a new regime but reacts more to noise. More taps model a longer memory of past bars. The prediction is an estimate of the current bar from earlier bars, not a forecast of the next one.

settings.label: Filter Order (taps)
settings.html: How many previous bars the filter weighs. More taps model longer structure and cost more to compute.

settings.label: Forgetting Factor (Lambda)
settings.html: How much history is kept. Values close to 1 remember more bars; lower values let the filter adapt faster to a change.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter predicts and learns from, the close by default.

faq.q: How is this different from the least mean squares filter?
faq.html: Both predict price from past bars with adaptive weights. Least mean squares nudges the weights a small step along the error, while recursive least squares solves for the best weights over its remembered history each bar, so it adapts much faster.

faq.q: Why is the first bar or two blank?
faq.html: The weights start at zero, so the very first predictions are an exact zero. Those bars are left empty and the line starts once a weight has moved.

faq.q: What does the forgetting factor do in practice?
faq.html: It sets an effective memory of about 1 / (1 - lambda) bars. At 0.99 that is roughly 100 bars; at 0.95 it is about 20, which reacts faster but is noisier.

related.title: Ehlers Recursive Median Filter (RMED)
related.summary: An exponential smoothing of the five-bar median price, which ignores one-bar spikes that would jolt an ordinary moving average.

related.title: One Euro Filter (ONEEURO)
related.summary: An adaptive smoother that filters heavily while price is quiet and lifts its cutoff when price moves fast, trading jitter against lag.

related.title: Ehlers Roofing Filter (ROOFING)
related.summary: A highpass and a Super Smoother in series that keep only the price cycles between two lengths, plotted as a zero-centred oscillator.

wilder-s-moving-average-rma.title: Wilder's Moving Average (RMA)
wilder-s-moving-average-rma.summary: A slow exponential average with a smoothing factor of one over the period, corrected during warmup so it draws from the first bar.
wilder-s-moving-average-rma.descriptionHtml:
The RMA is an exponential moving average whose smoothing factor is one divided by the period, rather than two divided by the period plus one. That makes it noticeably slower than an EMA of the same length: a 10-bar RMA reacts at roughly the pace of a 19-bar EMA. It is the average used inside the classic ATR and RSI calculations.

This version does not start from a simple average of the first bars. It starts the running average at zero and divides it by one minus (1 - 1/period) raised to the number of bars seen. That division removes the pull toward zero that a zero start would leave, so the very first bar equals the source and every later bar is a properly weighted average of the bars so far. Once (1 - 1/period) raised to the bars seen falls below 1e-10, the correction is dropped and the line is the plain recursion.
wilder-s-moving-average-rma.howToReadHtml:
Read the RMA as a smooth, slow trend line. Price holding above a rising RMA describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend; the slope changes direction only after a sustained move, so it filters out most single-bar noise.

The price of that smoothness is lag. Turns in the line come late, and in a sideways market price crosses it often without any trend following. Because the line is corrected from the first bar, the earliest values are averages of only a few bars and move more than the settled line does.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing factor to one over this number. A larger period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: How is the RMA different from an EMA of the same period?
faq.html: The RMA uses a smoothing factor of one over the period, the EMA two over the period plus one. A 10-bar RMA therefore weights the newest bar at 10 percent against roughly 18 percent for a 10-bar EMA, so it is slower and smoother.

faq.q: Why does the line appear on the very first bar?
faq.html: The running average is divided by a warmup correction that removes the effect of starting at zero. The first bar equals the source, and the correction fades out as more bars arrive.

faq.q: Will it match an RMA seeded with a simple average?
faq.html: Not on the early bars. A simple-average seed waits for a full window and then starts from that mean, while this version weights every bar from the first. After enough bars both settle to the same recursion and the difference shrinks toward zero.

related.title: RWMA: Range Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close where each bar is weighted by its own high to low range, so wide bars pull the line harder than narrow ones.

related.title: Recursive Gaussian Moving Average (RGMA)
related.summary: A cascade of identical exponential stages that approximates a Gaussian filter, giving a very smooth line with an even response.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Moving Average (SGMA)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average over an odd window: a fixed coefficient table for degree 2 on 5, 7 or 9 bars, and a polynomial weight shape otherwise.

ehlers-recursive-median-filter-rmed.title: Ehlers Recursive Median Filter (RMED)
ehlers-recursive-median-filter-rmed.summary: An exponential smoothing of the five-bar median price, which ignores one-bar spikes that would jolt an ordinary moving average.
ehlers-recursive-median-filter-rmed.descriptionHtml:
The Recursive Median Filter combines two ideas. First it takes the median of the last five prices, which throws away the two highest and the two lowest and so is not moved by a single spike bar. Then it smooths that median with an exponential filter whose factor is set by Period.

The factor is (cos(a) + sin(a) - 1) / cos(a), where a is one full cycle divided by Period, held between 0 and 1. This places the cutoff of the exponential stage at a cycle of Period bars. Each new value is that factor times the five-bar median plus the rest times the previous value.

The first value is the first price. Before five bars exist, the missing places in the median window count as zero, which pulls the earliest values down; this start-up effect fades as the recursion moves on.
ehlers-recursive-median-filter-rmed.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a trend line that is hard to fool with one bar. A sudden wick or a single bad print does not move the median, so the line keeps its path; a move that lasts three bars or more does move it. Its slope gives the trend direction, and a turn marks a turn in the swing at the scale of Period.

The median adds a couple of bars of delay on top of the exponential smoothing, so the line turns later than a plain exponential average of the same period. The very first bars are a start-up and should not be read.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The cycle length in bars that sets the smoothing factor. Larger values give a slower, smoother line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the median is taken from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why use a median instead of the price?
faq.html: The median of five bars ignores a single extreme value, so one spike bar does not pull the line. An ordinary average would move with it.

faq.q: Why does the line dip at the very start?
faq.html: Before five bars exist, the empty places in the median window count as zero. The effect fades as the smoothing carries on.

faq.q: What does Period actually control?
faq.html: Only the smoothing factor of the exponential stage. The median window is always five bars.

related.title: Ehlers Roofing Filter (ROOFING)
related.summary: A highpass and a Super Smoother in series that keep only the price cycles between two lengths, plotted as a zero-centred oscillator.

related.title: Recursive Least Squares Adaptive Filter (RLS)
related.summary: An adaptive filter that re-estimates its weights every bar by recursive least squares, with a forgetting factor setting how much history still counts.

related.title: SAK: Swiss Army Knife Indicator
related.summary: One second-order recursive filter whose coefficients switch it between nine filters, from smoothers to highpass, bandpass and bandstop.

root-mean-squared-error-rmse.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
root-mean-squared-error-rmse.summary: The typical distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, in price units, with the average drawn on the chart.
root-mean-squared-error-rmse.descriptionHtml:
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) here measures how far a source series ranges from its own exponential moving average. The average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through that warmup. On every bar where it exists, the gap between the source and the average is squared.

The squared gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry one, and the square root of that mean is plotted as a shaded area in its own pane. Squaring before averaging gives large gaps more weight than small ones, and the square root brings the result back to price units. The exponential average itself is drawn on the price chart.
root-mean-squared-error-rmse.howToReadHtml:
Read the pane as the typical size of the gap between price and its trend line. A rising RMSE means price is swinging further from the average than it has been, which usually comes with a stronger trend or a more volatile market. A falling RMSE means price is hugging the average, often a quiet or ranging spell.

The value is in price units, so compare it with its own history on the same instrument rather than across instruments. Because the gaps are squared, one sharp bar raises it more than several small ones. Nothing is drawn until the average has a value, on bar Period minus one.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series compared with its own exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window the squared gaps are averaged over. A longer period gives a slower average and a smoother error line.

faq.q: What is the forecast being scored here?
faq.html: The exponential moving average of the source, with the same length as the error window. The study treats the average as a forecast of price and reports how far price has strayed from it.

faq.q: Why does the line appear only after a while?
faq.html: The exponential average starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value until that many bars have passed, and there is no gap to measure before then.

faq.q: How is it different from the mean absolute error?
faq.html: Squaring each gap before averaging makes large gaps count for much more, so RMSE rises faster than the mean absolute error when price makes a sudden move away from the average.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE)
related.summary: The typical log distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, a relative gap that does not depend on price level.

related.title: Relative Absolute Error (RAE)
related.summary: Absolute error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the absolute error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

related.title: Relative Squared Error (RSE)
related.summary: Squared error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the squared error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

root-mean-squared-logarithmic-error-rmsl.title: Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE)
root-mean-squared-logarithmic-error-rmsl.summary: The typical log distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, a relative gap that does not depend on price level.
root-mean-squared-logarithmic-error-rmsl.descriptionHtml:
Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE) measures how far a source series ranges from its own exponential moving average, in relative rather than absolute terms. The average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through that warmup.

On every bar where the average exists, the study takes the natural logarithm of one plus the source and of one plus the average, and squares the difference. A bar where either value is at or below minus one has no logarithm and is left out. The squared log gaps are averaged over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry one, and the square root is plotted as a shaded area. The exponential average itself is drawn on the price chart.
root-mean-squared-logarithmic-error-rmsl.howToReadHtml:
For prices well above one, the reading is close to the typical percentage gap between price and its average, written as a fraction: 0.01 is about one percent. A rising line means price is moving further from its trend in relative terms; a falling line means it is staying close.

Because it is a relative measure, the reading is comparable across instruments at very different price levels, which the plain squared error is not. Large gaps still count for more than small ones because they are squared. Nothing is drawn until the average has a value, on bar Period minus one.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series compared with its own exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window the squared log gaps are averaged over. A longer period gives a slower average and a smoother error line.

faq.q: Why add one before taking the logarithm?
faq.html: It keeps the logarithm defined when a value is zero. For prices in the hundreds or thousands the added one makes almost no difference, and the reading is effectively the log ratio of price to its average.

faq.q: How do I turn the reading into a percentage?
faq.html: For small readings, multiply by 100. A value of 0.02 means price has typically been about two percent away from its exponential average over the window.

faq.q: When is a bar left out?
faq.html: Only when the source or the average is at or below minus one, where the logarithm does not exist. On ordinary price series no bar is left out after the warmup.

related.title: Relative Squared Error (RSE)
related.summary: Squared error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the squared error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
related.summary: The typical distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, in price units, with the average drawn on the chart.

related.title: R² Coefficient of Determination (RSQUARED)
related.summary: How much of price's variation around its rolling mean an exponential average explains: 1 is a perfect fit and below 0 is worse than flat.

rate-of-change-roc.title: Rate of Change (ROC)
rate-of-change-roc.summary: The source now minus the source a number of bars back, in price units, with a lookback that grows from the first bar up to the length.
rate-of-change-roc.descriptionHtml:
Rate of Change measures how far price has moved over a lookback, in the instrument's own price units. On each bar it subtracts the source value of an earlier bar from the current one.

The lookback does not start at full length. On the first bar it is zero bars, so the reading is zero; on each bar with a usable reference it grows by one until it reaches length, and then it stays there. The line therefore starts on the first bar, comparing with the first bar of the chart, instead of leaving a gap while the window fills. Once the lookback is full the reading is simply the source minus the source length bars ago.
rate-of-change-roc.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, price is higher than it was over the lookback; below zero, it is lower. The distance from zero is the size of the move in price units, so a larger reading is a faster move. A turn in the line before a turn in price can show a move losing speed.

The first length bars use a shorter lookback, so they are not comparable with the rest of the line. Because the result is in price units rather than a percentage, compare it only with its own history on the same instrument.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose change is measured. Close is the default; hl2 and the other blends soften bars with long wicks.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The full lookback in bars. The lookback grows to this number over the first bars and then stays fixed.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero on the first bar?
faq.html: The lookback starts at zero bars and grows by one bar on each bar, so the first bar is compared with itself. After length bars the lookback is full.

faq.q: Is this a percentage?
faq.html: No. It is the difference in price units. The ROCP study gives the same change as a percentage, and ROCR gives it as a ratio.

related.title: Rate of Change Percentage (ROCP)
related.summary: The percentage change between the source now and the source a number of bars back, with a lookback that grows from the first bar.

related.title: Percentage Price Oscillator (PPO)
related.summary: The gap between a fast and a slow exponential average as a percentage of the slow one, with a signal line and a histogram.

related.title: Rate of Change Ratio (ROCR)
related.summary: The ratio of the source now to the source a number of bars back, so 1 is unchanged, above 1 is a rise and below 1 a fall.

rate-of-change-percentage-rocp.title: Rate of Change Percentage (ROCP)
rate-of-change-percentage-rocp.summary: The percentage change between the source now and the source a number of bars back, with a lookback that grows from the first bar.
rate-of-change-percentage-rocp.descriptionHtml:
Rate of Change Percentage expresses the move over a lookback as a percentage of the older price. On each bar it takes the source, subtracts the reference value, divides by the reference and multiplies by 100.

The lookback starts at zero bars and grows by one on each bar whose reference value is present and not zero, until it reaches length. So the line begins on the first bar at zero instead of after a gap, and the early readings compare against the first bars of the chart. A reference of zero gives no reading on that bar and holds the lookback where it is.
rate-of-change-percentage-rocp.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 2 means price is 2 percent above where it was length bars ago, and a reading of -2 means it is 2 percent below. Because it is a percentage, the line reads the same way on a cheap instrument and an expensive one, and readings from different charts can be compared.

Watch the direction of the line as well as its sign: a falling line above zero means the advance is still there but slowing. The first length bars use a shorter lookback and are not comparable with the rest.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose percentage change is measured. Close is the default; hl2 and the other blends soften bars with long wicks.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The full lookback in bars. Longer lookbacks show larger, slower swings in the percentage.

faq.q: How does it differ from ROC and ROCR?
faq.html: All three compare the same two prices. ROC gives the difference in price units, ROCP gives it as a percentage of the older price, and ROCR gives the ratio of the two.

faq.q: Why are the first readings small?
faq.html: The lookback grows from zero bars to length over the first bars, so the early readings measure a shorter move.

related.title: Rate of Change Ratio (ROCR)
related.summary: The ratio of the source now to the source a number of bars back, so 1 is unchanged, above 1 is a rise and below 1 a fall.

related.title: Rate of Change (ROC)
related.summary: The source now minus the source a number of bars back, in price units, with a lookback that grows from the first bar up to the length.

related.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
related.summary: Average up move against average down move over the lookback, mapped onto a scale from 0 to 100.

rate-of-change-ratio-rocr.title: Rate of Change Ratio (ROCR)
rate-of-change-ratio-rocr.summary: The ratio of the source now to the source a number of bars back, so 1 is unchanged, above 1 is a rise and below 1 a fall.
rate-of-change-ratio-rocr.descriptionHtml:
Rate of Change Ratio divides the current source value by the value from an earlier bar. A result of 1 means price is where it was, 1.05 means it is 5 percent higher and 0.95 means it is 5 percent lower.

The lookback starts at zero bars and grows by one on each bar whose reference value is present and not zero, until it reaches length, then stays there. The line therefore starts on the first bar at exactly 1, and the early readings compare against the first bars of the chart rather than leaving a gap.
rate-of-change-ratio-rocr.howToReadHtml:
Read the line against 1. Above 1, price is higher than it was over the lookback; below 1, it is lower. The distance from 1 is the size of the move as a fraction of the older price, so the reading compares across instruments.

A ratio is lopsided: a fall of 50 percent reads 0.5 while a rise of 50 percent reads 1.5, so large declines look smaller on the chart than large advances of the same percentage. The first length bars use a shorter lookback.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose ratio to its earlier value is measured. Close is the default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The full lookback in bars. The lookback grows to it over the first bars and then stays fixed.

faq.q: Why is the first value exactly 1?
faq.html: The lookback starts at zero bars, so the first bar is divided by itself. The lookback then grows by a bar on each bar until it reaches length.

faq.q: How do I turn the ratio into a percentage?
faq.html: Subtract 1 and multiply by 100. A ratio of 1.03 is a rise of 3 percent. The ROCP study plots that percentage directly.

related.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
related.summary: Average up move against average down move over the lookback, mapped onto a scale from 0 to 100.

related.title: Rate of Change Percentage (ROCP)
related.summary: The percentage change between the source now and the source a number of bars back, with a lookback that grows from the first bar.

related.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.

ehlers-roofing-filter-roofing.title: Ehlers Roofing Filter (ROOFING)
ehlers-roofing-filter-roofing.summary: A highpass and a Super Smoother in series that keep only the price cycles between two lengths, plotted as a zero-centred oscillator.
ehlers-roofing-filter-roofing.descriptionHtml:
The Roofing Filter is a bandpass built from two stages. The first is a two-pole highpass with cutoff HP Length: it removes trends and cycles longer than that many bars, leaving a wave that wanders around zero. The second is a Super Smoother with cutoff SS Length: it removes the fast noise shorter than that many bars.

What remains is the band of cycles between the two lengths, shown as a single line in its own pane around a dashed zero level. The highpass uses the current price and the two before it, and both stages feed back their own last two values.

On the first bars, missing earlier prices are read as the current one, so the highpass starts at zero and the oscillator builds from there.
ehlers-roofing-filter-roofing.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the cycle part of price. Above zero, price is above its long-term path in this cycle band; below zero, it is below. Peaks and troughs of the line are the cycle's highs and lows, and the zero crossings are the turns between them. Because the trend has been removed, the line says nothing about the longer trend; read it alongside a trend measure of your choice.

The values are in price units and are not normalised, so the height of the swings grows with volatility and price level. A cycle longer than HP Length is invisible here, which is the point of the filter but also its limit.

settings.label: HP Length
settings.html: The highpass cutoff in bars. Trends and cycles longer than this are removed.

settings.label: SS Length
settings.html: The Super Smoother cutoff in bars. Noise faster than this is removed.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter runs on, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is it called a roofing filter?
faq.html: It puts a ceiling and a floor on the cycle lengths that get through: the highpass sets the longest and the smoother sets the shortest.

faq.q: What units is the line in?
faq.html: Price units. It is the filtered deviation of price, not a percentage or a normalised score.

faq.q: How should I set the two lengths?
faq.html: Keep HP Length well above SS Length. The band between them is the range of cycle lengths the line shows.

related.title: SAK: Swiss Army Knife Indicator
related.summary: One second-order recursive filter whose coefficients switch it between nine filters, from smoothers to highpass, bandpass and bandstop.

related.title: Ehlers Recursive Median Filter (RMED)
related.summary: An exponential smoothing of the five-bar median price, which ignores one-bar spikes that would jolt an ordinary moving average.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Filter (SGF)
related.summary: A smoothing line built from a polynomial fitting kernel, which at the default order keeps the height of a swing better than a plain moving average of the same length.

relative-squared-error-rse.title: Relative Squared Error (RSE)
relative-squared-error-rse.summary: Squared error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the squared error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.
relative-squared-error-rse.descriptionHtml:
Relative Squared Error (RSE) asks whether an exponential moving average tracks price better than a flat rolling mean does, giving large misses extra weight. The exponential average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through that warmup. The baseline is the mean of the source over the last Period bars, including this one; before that many bars have passed it is the mean of every bar so far.

On every bar the study squares the gap between the source and the exponential average, and squares the gap between the source and the baseline mean. Each is totalled over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry a value. RSE is the first total divided by the second. When the baseline total is zero the reading is 1. The exponential average is drawn on the price chart.
relative-squared-error-rse.howToReadHtml:
Below 1, the exponential average has fitted price more closely than the flat mean of the window; above 1, it has fitted worse. In a clean trend the flat mean falls far behind price and RSE drops close to zero. In a sideways market the flat mean is a good fit and RSE climbs toward or above 1. Because the gaps are squared, one sharp move counts heavily in both totals.

The first bar reads 1, and the line then has no value until the exponential average starts on bar Period minus one. The ratio says which fit was better, not how large either error was. One minus RSE is the same idea as the R squared of the exponential average against the window mean.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being fitted by both the exponential average and the rolling mean.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window used for the baseline mean and both error totals.

faq.q: What does a reading near zero mean?
faq.html: The exponential average's squared misses were tiny compared with those of the flat mean, which happens when price trends steadily: the average follows it and the flat mean does not.

faq.q: Why does the very first bar show 1?
faq.html: On the first bar the baseline mean is that bar's own value, so the baseline error is zero, and a zero baseline is reported as 1.

faq.q: How is it different from the Relative Absolute Error?
faq.html: This one squares each gap before totalling, so large gaps dominate. The absolute version counts every point of error the same.

related.title: R² Coefficient of Determination (RSQUARED)
related.summary: How much of price's variation around its rolling mean an exponential average explains: 1 is a perfect fit and below 0 is worse than flat.

related.title: Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE)
related.summary: The typical log distance between price and its own exponential average over a rolling window, a relative gap that does not depend on price level.

related.title: Symmetric Mean Absolute %Error (SMAPE)
related.summary: The average symmetric percentage gap between price and its own exponential average, a bounded error score that treats overshoot and undershoot alike.

relative-strength-index-rsi.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
relative-strength-index-rsi.summary: Average up move against average down move over the lookback, mapped onto a scale from 0 to 100.
relative-strength-index-rsi.descriptionHtml:
The Relative Strength Index compares the size of recent rises with the size of recent falls. Each bar's change in the source is split into an up move (the rise, or zero) and a down move (the fall, or zero). Each is smoothed with a running average whose weight is 1 / length, and the reading is 100 - 100 / (1 + average up / average down).

This version has its own warmup. For the first length bars each average simply holds that bar's own move, so the early readings swing between the extremes; from bar length on the averages are smoothed. The first bar has no previous bar and so no reading. When the average down move is zero the reading is a full 100.
relative-strength-index-rsi.howToReadHtml:
The line moves between 0 and 100. Readings near 100 mean the rises in the window have far outweighed the falls, and readings near 0 mean the reverse; 50 is balance. Many traders treat readings above 70 as stretched to the upside and below 30 as stretched to the downside, and watch for the line to turn back from those zones.

In a strong trend the line can stay in an extreme zone for a long time, so an extreme reading alone is not a reason to trade against the move. Ignore the first length bars, where each average is a single bar's move rather than a smoothed figure.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The smoothing length for the up and down averages, and the number of warmup bars. Shorter lengths reach the extremes more often.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose bar-to-bar changes are measured. Close is the default.

faq.q: Why do the first bars jump between 0 and 100?
faq.html: Before bar length each average holds only that bar's own move, so a rising bar reads 100 and a falling bar reads 0. Smoothing starts at bar length.

faq.q: What does a reading of exactly 100 mean?
faq.html: The average down move is zero, so no fall is left in the average. The study reports a full 100 in that case.

faq.q: Are the 70 and 30 lines drawn?
faq.html: No. The study draws only the line. The 70 and 30 zones are a common way to read it, and you can judge other thresholds against your own instrument.

related.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.

related.title: Rate of Change Ratio (ROCR)
related.summary: The ratio of the source now to the source a number of bars back, so 1 is unchanged, above 1 is a rise and below 1 a fall.

related.title: SAM: Smoothed Adaptive Momentum
related.summary: Momentum over a lookback set by a measured price cycle, then smoothed by a two-pole filter, with a zero line for reference.

r-coefficient-of-determination-rsquared.title: R² Coefficient of Determination (RSQUARED)
r-coefficient-of-determination-rsquared.summary: How much of price's variation around its rolling mean an exponential average explains: 1 is a perfect fit and below 0 is worse than flat.
r-coefficient-of-determination-rsquared.descriptionHtml:
The R squared coefficient of determination here measures how well an exponential moving average of the source explains the source's own movement. The exponential average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values, so it has no value through that warmup. The reference for comparison is the mean of the source over the last Period bars, including this one; before that many bars have passed it is the mean of every bar so far.

On every bar the study squares the gap between the source and the exponential average (the residual) and squares the gap between the source and the window mean (the total variation). Each is totalled over the last Period bars, counting only the bars that carry a value. The score is one minus the residual total divided by the variation total, and a window with no variation reads 1. The exponential average is drawn on the price chart.
r-coefficient-of-determination-rsquared.howToReadHtml:
A score near 1 means the exponential average follows price closely relative to how much price has moved around its mean, which is typical of a steady trend. A score near 0 means the average explains no more than the flat mean would, and a negative score means it does worse, which happens in choppy markets where the average lags every turn.

The score has no value until the exponential average starts on bar Period minus one. It is a measure of fit, not of direction: a strong downtrend scores as high as a strong uptrend.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being explained by its own exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window used for the mean and both totals.

faq.q: Can the score be negative?
faq.html: Yes. If the exponential average misses price by more, in squared terms, than the flat mean of the window does, the ratio passes 1 and the score drops below zero.

faq.q: How does it relate to the Relative Squared Error?
faq.html: It is one minus that ratio over the same window and the same average, so a high score here is a low reading there.

faq.q: Does a high score mean price will keep trending?
faq.html: No. It describes how well the average has fitted the bars in the window. It says nothing about the next bar.

related.title: Symmetric Mean Absolute %Error (SMAPE)
related.summary: The average symmetric percentage gap between price and its own exponential average, a bounded error score that treats overshoot and undershoot alike.

related.title: Relative Squared Error (RSE)
related.summary: Squared error of an exponential average as a forecast, divided by the squared error of a plain rolling mean: below 1 the average does better.

related.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
related.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.

rogers-satchell-volatility-rsv.title: Rogers-Satchell Volatility (RSV)
rogers-satchell-volatility-rsv.summary: A volatility estimate built from each bar's open, high, low and close designed so that a steady trend does not inflate it.
rogers-satchell-volatility-rsv.descriptionHtml:
Rogers-Satchell volatility estimates how much price is fluctuating using all four prices of each bar rather than only the close. Its useful property is that a steady trend does not inflate it: the formula is built so that a persistent drift up or down cancels out, leaving the fluctuation around it.

For every bar the study takes logarithms of price ratios: the log of high over open times the log of high over close, plus the log of low over open times the log of low over close. That is the bar's variance. Prices are floored at a tiny positive number so the logarithms stay defined. A simple moving average of the variance over length bars is taken, and its square root is the volatility. With annualising switched on the result is multiplied by the square root of the number of periods in a year.
rogers-satchell-volatility-rsv.howToReadHtml:
The value is a volatility per bar, or per year when annualised. A rising line means bars are swinging more widely within themselves; a falling line means the market is calming. Compare it with its own history on the same chart to judge whether volatility is high or low.

The estimate ignores the gap between one bar's close and the next bar's open, so it understates volatility on a market that gaps often. The annualising factor assumes the number you give for periods in a year matches your chart's timeframe.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the per-bar variance is averaged over before the square root is taken.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, multiplies the result by the square root of the annual periods so it reads as a yearly figure.

settings.label: Annual Periods
settings.html: How many bars of this timeframe make a year, used only when annualising, for example 252 on a daily chart.

faq.q: Why use this instead of the standard deviation of closes?
faq.html: It uses the open, high, low and close of each bar, so it draws more information from the same number of bars, and a steady trend does not raise it.

faq.q: What should Annual Periods be on an hourly chart?
faq.html: The number of hourly bars in a year for that market. A market that trades around the clock has 24 times 365, or 8760. A market with seven hourly bars a day on 252 trading days has 1764.

faq.q: Does it include overnight gaps?
faq.html: No. Every term is measured inside a single bar, so the move between one close and the next open is not counted.

related.title: Realized Volatility (RV)
related.summary: Volatility measured from the size of close-to-close log returns, smoothed with a simple average and optionally scaled to a yearly figure.

related.title: Parkinson Volatility (PV)
related.summary: Volatility from the squared log ratio of each bar's high to its low, smoothed over a window and optionally annualised.

related.title: Relative Volatility Index (RVI)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator built on standard deviation, showing whether volatility is arriving on rising or falling bars.

relative-strength-xtra-rsx.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
relative-strength-xtra-rsx.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.
relative-strength-xtra-rsx.descriptionHtml:
RSX asks the same question as the Relative Strength Index, how large recent rises have been next to recent falls, but smooths the moves with an adaptive filter instead of a plain average. Each bar's change in the source is split into an up move and a down move, and each is fed through its own copy of the filter. The reading is 100 - 100 / (1 + smoothed up / smoothed down), and it is 0 when the smoothed down move is zero.

The filter keeps a pair of trailing bands around its input and measures how far each new value jumps outside them. It compares that jump with its own recent average of jumps, kept over the last ten values, and uses the ratio to set how quickly a two-stage smoother follows the input: a large jump makes it follow faster, a quiet stretch makes it follow slowly. All of its constants are set by length. The first bar has no previous value, so neither side moves and there is no reading until the second bar.
relative-strength-xtra-rsx.howToReadHtml:
Read RSX on the same 0 to 100 scale as RSI. High readings mean the smoothed rises have outweighed the smoothed falls, low readings the reverse, and 50 is balance. Because the filter removes most bar-to-bar noise, the line turns less often and more cleanly than RSI at the same length, which makes its turns and its crosses of fixed levels easier to read. Any smoothing adds some delay, so compare its turns with price before relying on them.

The smoother line also means fewer touches of extreme zones, so thresholds that suit RSI may be too wide here. Like any momentum oscillator, it can stay high or low for a long time in a strong trend.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: Sets every constant of the adaptive filter. Longer lengths give a smoother line that turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose bar-to-bar changes are measured. Close is the default.

faq.q: How is RSX different from RSI?
faq.html: Both compare up moves with down moves on a 0 to 100 scale. RSI smooths them with a running average; RSX uses an adaptive filter that follows quickly after large jumps and slowly in quiet stretches, so its line is much smoother.

faq.q: Why does it read 0 when there are no down moves?
faq.html: When the smoothed down move is zero the ratio is taken as zero, so the reading is 0. This is a property of the calculation, not a signal.

related.title: SAM: Smoothed Adaptive Momentum
related.summary: Momentum over a lookback set by a measured price cycle, then smoothed by a two-pole filter, with a zero line for reference.

related.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
related.summary: Average up move against average down move over the lookback, mapped onto a scale from 0 to 100.

related.title: True Strength Index (TSI)
related.summary: Double-smoothed price change over double-smoothed absolute price change, as a percentage from -100 to 100, with a signal line.

realized-volatility-rv.title: Realized Volatility (RV)
realized-volatility-rv.summary: Volatility measured from the size of close-to-close log returns, smoothed with a simple average and optionally scaled to a yearly figure.
realized-volatility-rv.descriptionHtml:
Realized volatility measures how much price has actually moved, as opposed to how much the market expects it to move. On each bar the study takes the log return from the previous close to this close, squares it to get the bar's realized variance, and takes the square root to get the bar's volatility, which is the size of the return without its sign.

Those per-bar values are smoothed with a simple moving average over the smoothing length. With annualising switched on the average is multiplied by the square root of the number of periods in a year. The first bar has no previous close, so the line begins once a full window of returns exists.
realized-volatility-rv.howToReadHtml:
The line shows the typical size of a bar's move over the recent window. A rising line means bars are moving further from close to close; a falling line means the market is settling.

Each bar contributes one close-to-close return, so a single large bar lifts the line for exactly the smoothing length and then drops out. The yearly figure is only as right as the Annual Periods value you give for your timeframe.

settings.label: Smoothing Length
settings.html: How many per-bar volatilities the simple average covers. A longer length gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Annualize Volatility
settings.html: When on, multiplies the result by the square root of the annual periods so it reads as a yearly figure.

settings.label: Annual Periods
