settings.html: How many bars of this timeframe make a year, used only when annualising, for example 252 on a daily chart or 52 on a weekly one.

faq.q: Why do the first bars show nothing?
faq.html: The first bar has no previous close and so no return. The line starts once the smoothing window holds that many returns.

faq.q: Is this the same as a standard deviation of returns?
faq.html: No. It averages the absolute size of each return rather than measuring the spread around the mean return. A steady trend therefore counts in full here, while a standard deviation would subtract it as the mean.

faq.q: What does the annualised number mean?
faq.html: It scales the per-bar figure up to a year by the square root of the number of periods, so it can be compared with yearly volatility figures quoted elsewhere.

related.title: Relative Volatility Index (RVI)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator built on standard deviation, showing whether volatility is arriving on rising or falling bars.

related.title: Rogers-Satchell Volatility (RSV)
related.summary: A volatility estimate built from each bar's open, high, low and close designed so that a steady trend does not inflate it.

related.title: True Range
related.summary: Measures each bar's full movement, the bar's own range widened to include any gap from the previous close.

relative-vigor-index-rvgi.title: Relative Vigor Index (RVGI)
relative-vigor-index-rvgi.summary: Compares where bars close relative to their open with the size of their range, so it reads the conviction behind a move as a signed ratio.
relative-vigor-index-rvgi.descriptionHtml:
The Relative Vigor Index asks how much of each bar's range was covered in the direction of the close. For every bar it takes the close minus the open and the high minus the low. Each series is smoothed with symmetric four-bar weights of 1, 2, 2 and 1, so the newest bar and the bar three back count once and the two in between count twice. A bar before the first one counts as zero.

The smoothed close-minus-open is averaged over the last period bars, and so is the smoothed range, using the bars seen so far until a full period exists. The index is the first average divided by the second, and reads 0 when the range average is zero.

The signal line applies the same 1, 2, 2, 1 weights to the index itself. Both lines answer from the first bar.
relative-vigor-index-rvgi.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, bars have been closing above their opens on average, a sign of buying vigour; below zero, closing below their opens. The further from zero, the more of each bar's range the closes have covered. A cross of the index above its signal line says the vigour is improving, and a cross below says it is fading.

The lines are smoothed and so lag price by a few bars, and in a sideways market they cross often. Many traders look for the crosses that come after a stretched reading, or for a divergence where price makes a new high or low that the index does not confirm.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the smoothed close-minus-open and the smoothed range are averaged over. Longer periods give a smoother, slower index.

faq.q: What do the weights 1, 2, 2, 1 do?
faq.html: They smooth each series over four bars while giving the two middle bars double weight. The result sits one and a half bars behind the newest bar, and it cancels completely a swing that alternates every bar or repeats every three bars.

faq.q: What does a cross of the signal line mean?
faq.html: The signal line is a short weighted average of the index. When the index crosses above it, recent vigour is stronger than over the last few bars; when it crosses below, it is weaker.

faq.q: Why does it answer from the first bar?
faq.html: Missing earlier bars count as zero in the four-bar weights, and the averages use the bars seen so far until a full period exists, so the line has no blank warmup.

related.title: Stochastic Momentum Index (SMI)
related.summary: Where the close sits relative to the midpoint of its recent high-low range, double smoothed and centred on zero, with a smoothed signal line.

related.title: Ehlers Reverse EMA (REVERSEEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average minus its own reversed-filter estimate, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that keeps the smoothing but sheds the lag.

related.title: Squeeze Momentum (SQUEEZE)
related.summary: Flags the quiet stretches where the Bollinger Bands sit inside the Keltner Channel, and draws a momentum histogram for the move that follows.

relative-volatility-index-rvi.title: Relative Volatility Index (RVI)
relative-volatility-index-rvi.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator built on standard deviation, showing whether volatility is arriving on rising or falling bars.
relative-volatility-index-rvi.descriptionHtml:
The Relative Volatility Index applies the logic of the relative strength index to volatility instead of price change. It asks whether the market's volatility is showing up on up bars or on down bars.

On each bar the study computes a population standard deviation of the source over a window that grows to the StdDev length. If the source rose from the previous bar, that deviation is counted as upward volatility; if it fell, as downward volatility; an unchanged bar and the first bar count neither. The two series are each smoothed with a Wilder average started from zero and corrected for that start. The result is 100 times the upward average divided by the sum of both, and 50 when there is nothing to divide.
relative-volatility-index-rvi.howToReadHtml:
Above 50, volatility has come mostly on rising bars; below 50, mostly on falling bars. Readings near the extremes mean almost all the recent volatility arrived in one direction. It can serve as a filter on other signals, for example taking long setups only while it is above 50.

It measures where volatility occurred, not how much there was, so a quiet market can still read near an extreme. The first bars rest on a short window and settle as the averages fill.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose changes and standard deviation are measured.

settings.label: StdDev Length
settings.html: How many bars the standard deviation covers once its window has filled.

settings.label: RMA Length (Wilder's Smoothing)
settings.html: How many bars the Wilder averages of upward and downward volatility span. A longer length gives a smoother line.

faq.q: How is it different from the RSI?
faq.html: The RSI averages the size of each price change. This index averages the standard deviation instead, crediting it to the up or down side by the direction of the bar.

faq.q: Why does it start at 50?
faq.html: On the first bar there is no previous value and no deviation, so neither side has anything and the reading is set to the midpoint.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean high volatility?
faq.html: No. It means the volatility that occurred came mostly on rising bars. The amount of volatility is not shown.

related.title: True Range
related.summary: Measures each bar's full movement, the bar's own range widened to include any gap from the previous close.

related.title: Realized Volatility (RV)
related.summary: Volatility measured from the size of close-to-close log returns, smoothed with a simple average and optionally scaled to a yearly figure.

related.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
related.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.

rwma-range-weighted-moving-average.title: RWMA: Range Weighted Moving Average
rwma-range-weighted-moving-average.summary: A moving average of the close where each bar is weighted by its own high to low range, so wide bars pull the line harder than narrow ones.
rwma-range-weighted-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The Range Weighted Moving Average averages the close over the last period bars, but instead of counting each bar equally it weights each one by its range, high - low (never less than zero). The sum of close times range is divided by the sum of the ranges.

A wide bar, often one with a lot of participation behind it, pulls the average toward its close, while a narrow inside bar barely moves it. Until period bars exist, and on any window where every bar has zero range, the line shows the close itself.
rwma-range-weighted-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read it like any moving average, with one difference: it follows the bars that moved the most. After a large range bar the line jumps toward that bar's close, and a run of quiet bars leaves it almost where it was. Price holding above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

Compare it with a simple average of the same length. When the range weighted line sits above the simple one, the wide bars closed higher than the narrow ones, which suggests the larger moves were up moves.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars are averaged. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: Why weight by range instead of volume?
faq.html: The range needs only the high and the low, so the average works the same on any instrument, with or without volume. It measures how far price travelled within the bar rather than how much traded.

faq.q: What does it show on the first bars?
faq.html: The close itself, until the window holds period bars. After that it is the range weighted average.

faq.q: What happens on a run of bars with no range?
faq.html: If every bar in the window has zero range there is nothing to weight by, so the line shows the close.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Moving Average (SGMA)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average over an odd window: a fixed coefficient table for degree 2 on 5, 7 or 9 bars, and a polynomial weight shape otherwise.

related.title: Wilder's Moving Average (RMA)
related.summary: A slow exponential average with a smoothing factor of one over the period, corrected during warmup so it draws from the first bar.

related.title: Sine-weighted Moving Average (SINEMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow half a sine wave across the window, so the middle bars count most and the line runs smooth.

sak-swiss-army-knife-indicator.title: SAK: Swiss Army Knife Indicator
sak-swiss-army-knife-indicator.summary: One second-order recursive filter whose coefficients switch it between nine filters, from smoothers to highpass, bandpass and bandstop.
sak-swiss-army-knife-indicator.descriptionHtml:
This study runs a single filter equation on the close, out = c0 * (b0 * P + b1 * P[1] + b2 * P[2]) + a1 * out[1] + a2 * out[2], and changes only its coefficients to become different filters. The Filter Type menu picks the set: an exponential average (EMA), a simple average (SMA), a Gaussian, a Butterworth, a smoother, a one-pole highpass (HP), a two-pole highpass (2PHP), a bandpass (BP) or a bandstop (BS).

The coefficients come from the Period. The one-pole types use alpha = (cos + sin - 1) / cos of the angle 2 * pi / Period; the Gaussian, Butterworth and two-pole highpass use a two-pole factor built from 2.415 * (1 - cos); the bandpass and bandstop use the period together with Delta (BW), the bandwidth. The SMA type uses its own running-sum form over SMA Length (N): add the newest close, drop the close N bars back.

Every read of the past counts a missing bar as zero, so the filter answers from the first bar. The default, the bandpass, swings around zero and is drawn in its own pane with a zero line.
sak-swiss-army-knife-indicator.howToReadHtml:
Read the line according to the filter you picked. The bandpass, the default, isolates swings near the chosen period: peaks and troughs in it are the tops and bottoms of that cycle, and crossings of zero mark its turns. The highpass types show fast movement around zero with the trend removed. The bandstop and the EMA, SMA, Gauss and Butter types keep the price level, so in this pane they trace price rather than oscillate. The Smooth type has no feedback terms and its coefficients scale the level down, so its line sits well below price and is best read by its shape.

The early bars start from zero, so give each filter time to settle before reading it, longer for the two-pole types. A narrower Delta makes the bandpass more selective and slower to respond.

settings.label: Filter Type
settings.html: Which filter the shared equation becomes: EMA, SMA, Gauss, Butter, Smooth, HP, 2PHP, BP (bandpass) or BS (bandstop).

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The critical period in bars for every type except SMA. For the bandpass and bandstop it is the centre of the band.

settings.label: SMA Length (N)
settings.html: The number of closes averaged by the SMA type. It has no effect on the other types.

settings.label: Delta (BW)
settings.html: The relative bandwidth of the bandpass and bandstop types. Smaller values pass a narrower range of cycles.

faq.q: Why does the default line swing around zero?
faq.html: The default type is the bandpass, which keeps only cycles near the chosen period and removes the price level, so it oscillates around zero.

faq.q: Why do the smoothing types look like price in this pane?
faq.html: EMA, SMA, Gauss, Butter and the bandstop keep the price level, so their values sit at price, not around zero. Smooth is the exception: its gain on the price level is alpha squared, so its line has the shape of a smoothed price at a fraction of its height.

faq.q: Why does the line start near zero and climb?
faq.html: Every past value before the first bar counts as zero, so the recursive types begin from zero and take some bars to reach price or settle into their cycle.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Filter (SGF)
related.summary: A smoothing line built from a polynomial fitting kernel, which at the default order keeps the height of a swing better than a plain moving average of the same length.

related.title: Ehlers Roofing Filter (ROOFING)
related.summary: A highpass and a Super Smoother in series that keep only the price cycles between two lengths, plotted as a zero-centred oscillator.

related.title: Ehlers Super Passband Filter (SPBF)
related.summary: The difference of two fast exponential smoothings of price, a zero-centred passband line with a root-mean-square envelope above and below.

sam-smoothed-adaptive-momentum.title: SAM: Smoothed Adaptive Momentum
sam-smoothed-adaptive-momentum.summary: Momentum over a lookback set by a measured price cycle, then smoothed by a two-pole filter, with a zero line for reference.
sam-smoothed-adaptive-momentum.descriptionHtml:
Smoothed Adaptive Momentum measures the change in the close over a lookback that is not fixed. The study first estimates the dominant cycle of the market and then takes momentum over one cycle: the close now minus the close that many bars back.

The cycle estimate runs in stages. The close is smoothed with a four-bar weighted average, a detrender and a quadrature filter split it into two components, both are advanced by a quarter turn, and the products of the results are averaged with the weight alpha. The phase angle between them gives a cycle period, held between 6 and 50 bars and then smoothed twice from a start of zero; the lookback is that smoothed period rounded down, at least 1 bar, so it climbs from 1 over the first bars and stays below 50. The momentum is then passed through a two-pole smoothing filter whose cutoff is cutoff bars. Every read of a bar before the start of the chart counts as zero, so the line starts on the first bar.

The cycle estimate depends on the price level. The detrender multiplies by a factor that grows with its own previous value, so on an instrument priced in the tens of thousands its stages grow without limit and run past the largest number the engine holds. Each such value counts as zero on the next bar, the period falls to its 6-bar floor, and the smoothed period settles just under 6, so the lookback is 5 bars for most of the chart. On the same bars scaled to lower prices the lookback instead sat at 49 bars, at 6, or moved between 27 and 49, so the lookback is not a reliable measure of the market's cycle.
sam-smoothed-adaptive-momentum.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, the close is higher than it was one measured cycle ago; below zero, lower. The smoothing filter removes most of the bar-to-bar noise, so a turn in the line reflects a change in the direction of the move over the last cycle. A crossing of the zero line marks the close moving back through its level of one cycle earlier.

The reading is in price units, so its size scales with the instrument's price. The first bars are distorted because the earlier bars are counted as zero, so read the line only once it has settled.

settings.label: alpha
settings.html: The weight used to average the cycle components. Smaller values make the cycle estimate steadier and slower to change.

settings.label: Cutoff
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars of the two-pole filter applied to the momentum. Larger values give a smoother, slower line.

faq.q: What lookback does the momentum use?
faq.html: The twice-smoothed cycle period, rounded down to whole bars, at least 1 and below 50. On a high-priced instrument the cycle stages overflow, the period sits at its 6-bar floor and the lookback is 5 bars; at other price levels it can sit at 49 bars or move between the two.

faq.q: Why does the line start with a large swing?
faq.html: Bars before the start of the chart are counted as zero, so the first momentum values compare the close with zero. The filter carries that start for a few bars before the line settles.

faq.q: Can I change the source?
faq.html: No. The study always measures the close.

related.title: True Strength Index (TSI)
related.summary: Double-smoothed price change over double-smoothed absolute price change, as a percentage from -100 to 100, with a signal line.

related.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.

related.title: Velocity (VEL)
related.summary: The change of price over a lookback, smoothed by an adaptive Jurik-style filter so the momentum reading turns with less lag than raw momentum.

standard-deviation-channel-sdchannel.title: Standard Deviation Channel (SDCHANNEL)
standard-deviation-channel-sdchannel.summary: A least-squares line through the lookback window with a channel a fixed multiple of the residual standard deviation on each side.
standard-deviation-channel-sdchannel.descriptionHtml:
Standard Deviation Channel fits a straight trend line through the last Period values of the source by least squares and plots the value of that line on the current bar as the regression line. It then measures how far the prices in the window sit from the fitted line: each residual is squared, the squares are averaged over the window and the square root is taken.

That standard deviation of the residuals, times the multiplier, is added to and subtracted from the regression line to give the upper and lower channel. The area above the line is shaded red and the area below it green. The residual sum is divided by Period rather than Period - 1, and the line starts once a full window exists, on bar Period - 1.
standard-deviation-channel-sdchannel.howToReadHtml:
The middle line follows the slope of the recent trend, and the channel shows how far price usually strays from it. In an orderly trend the channel is narrow and price tends to return toward the line after touching an edge. A close well outside the channel is unusual for the current fit and often comes as the trend changes pace or direction.

The channel is recomputed from a fresh fit on every bar, so on a short period its slope can swing quickly. Pair it with a longer period to judge the main trend.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the line is fitted through. A longer period gives a smoother line and a wider channel.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the channel is fitted to.

settings.label: Standard Deviation Multiplier
settings.html: Channel distance as a multiple of the standard deviation of the regression residuals. A larger value widens the channel.

faq.q: Is this the standard deviation of price?
faq.html: No. It is the standard deviation of the distances between each price and the fitted trend line, so a clean trend gives a narrow channel even when price has moved a long way.

faq.q: How does it differ from standard deviation bands around a moving average?
faq.html: Those bands sit around a moving average, which lags behind a trend. This channel sits around a sloped regression line, so in a trend it lags less and its width reflects scatter around the trend, not the trend itself.

faq.q: When does the channel first appear?
faq.html: On bar Period - 1, the first bar with a full window to fit.

related.title: Stoller Average Range Channel (STARCHANNEL)
related.summary: A simple mean of the source as the centre line, with bands a multiple of an average true range above and below it.

related.title: Regression Channels (REGCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares trend line through the last N prices, with bands set a multiple of the fit's own residual spread above and below it.

related.title: Super Trend Bands (STBANDS)
related.summary: Ratcheting upper and lower bands built from the bar midpoint plus and minus a multiple of the average true range, tightening until price breaks them.

savitzky-golay-filter-sgf.title: Savitzky-Golay Filter (SGF)
savitzky-golay-filter-sgf.summary: A smoothing line built from a polynomial fitting kernel, which at the default order keeps the height of a swing better than a plain moving average of the same length.
savitzky-golay-filter-sgf.descriptionHtml:
The SGF is a smoother that weights a fixed window of past prices with a kernel taken from a closed-form polynomial weighting. A plain average gives every bar in its window the same weight, which flattens peaks and troughs. At the default order of 2 the kernel gives the middle of the window the most weight and lets the weights fall away, and turn negative, toward both ends, so a swing keeps more of its height.

The window is always an odd number of bars: an even setting is rounded down by one. For a polynomial order of 2 the weight of the tap k places from the centre is 3 * (3 * N * N - 7 - 20 * k * k), where N is the window size; for order 4 it is 15 + k * k * (6 * k * k - 20), which is positive everywhere and grows quickly toward the ends of the window. Any other order uses a simple triangle. The weights are normalised to sum to one and then applied with the newest bar taking the first tap, so the line is computed from past bars only.

On the first bars, before a full window exists, the taps that would reach before the first bar are skipped and the remaining weights are renormalised, so the line answers from the first bar. If the polynomial order is not smaller than the window, the line is not drawn.
savitzky-golay-filter-sgf.howToReadHtml:
At the default order, read the SGF as a smoothed price that keeps peaks and troughs sharper than a simple moving average of the same window. Because the kernel is symmetric and is applied to past bars only, its centre sits about half a window back, so its turns arrive roughly as late as the moving average's. When price crosses it or it changes direction, that is the filter's view of a change in short-term direction. Because the weights at both ends of the window are negative, a sharp move first nudges the line the wrong way for a bar or two and later makes it overshoot before it settles.

A longer window removes more noise and responds later. The line is computed only from bars that have closed, so it never repaints, but it still lags price; it is a picture of where price has been, not a forecast of where it goes next.

settings.label: Window Size
settings.html: How many bars the kernel spans. An even number is rounded down to the odd number below it. Larger windows smooth more and lag more.

settings.label: Polynomial Order
settings.html: The order of the closed-form weighting, 2 or 4. Order 2 favours the middle of the window; order 4 gives its largest weights to the newest and oldest bars of the window. Any other value falls back to a triangular weighting.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does an even window size behave like the odd number below it?
faq.html: The kernel needs a single middle tap, so the window is always odd. A setting of 20 runs as 19.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes dip against a sharp move and then overshoot it?
faq.html: At order 2 the weights at both ends of the window are negative, which is how the filter preserves peaks. A jump first meets the negative weights at the newest end, which pull the line briefly the wrong way; while the oldest taps still hold the earlier price, their negative weights push the line past the new level, until the jump has crossed the whole window.

faq.q: Why is the line missing entirely?
faq.html: If the polynomial order is equal to or larger than the window size, the fit is undefined and nothing is drawn. Raise the window size above the order.

related.title: Ehlers Super Passband Filter (SPBF)
related.summary: The difference of two fast exponential smoothings of price, a zero-centred passband line with a root-mean-square envelope above and below.

related.title: SAK: Swiss Army Knife Indicator
related.summary: One second-order recursive filter whose coefficients switch it between nine filters, from smoothers to highpass, bandpass and bandstop.

related.title: Supersmooth Filter (SSF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass filter that removes short-term chop from price with much less lag than a moving average of the same length.

savitzky-golay-moving-average-sgma.title: Savitzky-Golay Moving Average (SGMA)
savitzky-golay-moving-average-sgma.summary: A symmetric weighted average over an odd window: a fixed coefficient table for degree 2 on 5, 7 or 9 bars, and a polynomial weight shape otherwise.
savitzky-golay-moving-average-sgma.descriptionHtml:
The Savitzky-Golay Moving Average weights each bar of an odd-length window by a symmetric shape. Each position is mapped to x, from -1 at one end of the window to 1 at the other. The degree picks the shape: degree 0 weighs every bar the same, degree 1 is a triangle 1 - |x|, degree 2 is a parabola 1 - x^2, degree 3 is 1 - |x^3| and degree 4 is 1 - x^4. For degree 2 with a window of 5, 7 or 9 bars, a fixed table of coefficients is used instead, with small negative weights at the ends.

The weights are scaled to sum to one and the weighted sum of the source is divided by the total weight. An even period is raised by one so the window has a middle bar, and a degree the window cannot support falls back to 2. The window grows with the data until it reaches the full length, so the line starts on the first bar; a missing price is left out with its weight, and a window with no usable weights shows the source.
savitzky-golay-moving-average-sgma.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line. At the default settings (degree 2, 9 bars) the tabulated coefficients have small negative end weights, which keep more of the height of peaks and troughs than a simple average. With other settings every weight is positive: degree 1 concentrates the weight most in the middle, degree 2 a little less, and degrees 3 and 4 spread it more evenly, closer to the equal weights of degree 0. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

The weights are symmetric, so the line lags price by about half the window whatever the degree. Choose a short period for a responsive line and a longer one for the broad swing.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window length. An even value is raised by one so the window has a middle bar.

settings.label: Polynomial Degree
settings.html: The weight shape, from 0 (equal weights) to 4. Degree 1 is the most peaked; 2, 3 and 4 spread the weight progressively more evenly across the window.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why must the period be odd?
faq.html: A symmetric window needs a middle bar. An even period is raised by one, so 10 behaves like 11.

faq.q: What does the degree change?
faq.html: The shape of the weights. Degree 0 counts every bar equally, degree 1 is a triangle and degree 2 a parabola that peaks in the middle. Degrees 3 and 4 are flatter, closer to equal weights.

faq.q: Why are some weights negative at the default settings?
faq.html: With degree 2 and a 5, 7 or 9-bar window the study uses a fixed table of coefficients whose end weights are slightly negative. That keeps peaks sharper than a purely positive bell would. Any other period or degree uses only positive weights.

related.title: Sine-weighted Moving Average (SINEMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow half a sine wave across the window, so the middle bars count most and the line runs smooth.

related.title: RWMA: Range Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close where each bar is weighted by its own high to low range, so wide bars pull the line harder than narrow ones.

related.title: Simple Moving Average (SMA)
related.summary: The plain average of the last N prices, with every bar in the window counted equally, drawn from the very first bar of the chart.

logistic-function-sigmoid.title: Logistic Function (SIGMOID)
logistic-function-sigmoid.summary: Passes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the logistic curve, giving an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.
logistic-function-sigmoid.descriptionHtml:
The Logistic Function study measures how far the source sits from its 200-bar simple moving average and squashes that distance into the range 0 to 1. The formula is 1 / (1 + exp(-k * (source - SMA200))). When price sits exactly on its average the result is 0.5. Above the average it rises towards 1, and below the average it falls towards 0, but it never quite reaches either end.

The steepness k sets how quickly the curve saturates. The distance is measured in price units, so on a high-priced instrument a small k is needed to keep the line away from its limits. The average needs 200 bars of history, so the line starts on bar 200. Where the exponent is above 700, far below the average, the curve is already below 1e-304 and the result is written as exactly 0.
logistic-function-sigmoid.howToReadHtml:
Read 0.5 as price at its long average, values near 1 as price stretched well above it, and values near 0 as price stretched well below it. Because the curve flattens at both ends, a large excursion and a very large one look almost the same, which keeps extreme bars from dominating the pane.

If the line spends most of its time pinned at 0 or 1, the steepness is too high for the instrument's price level: lower k until the swings in between are visible. The 200-bar midpoint is fixed, so the study describes the position of price against a slow trend, not short-term momentum.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series compared with its own 200-bar simple moving average.

settings.label: Steepness (k)
settings.html: Multiplies the distance from the average before the curve is applied. A higher value makes the curve steeper, so it reaches 0 or 1 closer to the average.

faq.q: Why is the pane blank for the first 199 bars?
faq.html: The midpoint is a 200-bar simple moving average, which has no value until 200 bars exist. The curve needs that midpoint, so it starts on bar 200.

faq.q: Why is my line stuck at 0 or 1?
faq.html: The distance from the average is in price units. On an instrument priced in thousands, a steepness of 0.5 turns even a small move into a large exponent. Lower the steepness until the line moves through the middle of the range.

faq.q: Can I change the 200-bar average?
faq.html: No. The midpoint length is fixed at 200 bars in this study. Only the source and the steepness are settings.

related.title: Slope, Linear Regression (SLOPE)
related.summary: Plots the slope of the least squares line fitted through the last N values, in price units per bar.

related.title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
related.summary: Splits the gap between price and its 20-bar average into an upper line for strength and a mirrored lower line for weakness.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots the square root of the chosen source, which compresses large values and stretches small ones onto a flatter scale.

ehlers-sine-wave-sine.title: Ehlers Sine Wave (SINE)
ehlers-sine-wave-sine.summary: The phase of the detrended price cycle as a wave between -1 and +1, from the in-phase value over its length with a quadrature partner.
ehlers-sine-wave-sine.descriptionHtml:
The Sine Wave reports where price sits inside its current cycle. First a high-pass filter removes cycles longer than the High-Pass Filter Length. A two-pole super smoother, set by the Super-Smoother Filter Length, then cleans the two-bar average of that output, leaving the cycle.

A four-tap Hilbert transform of the smoothed cycle, built from its values one, three, five and seven bars back, gives a quadrature component that runs a quarter cycle apart from it. The study divides the smoothed cycle by the length of the pair, the square root of the sum of both squared, and holds the result to the range -1 to +1. That ratio is the sine of the cycle's phase, so the line traces a wave whatever the size of the move.
ehlers-sine-wave-sine.howToReadHtml:
Near +1 the cycle is at its crest and near -1 it is at its trough, with zero crossings marking the midpoints. In a market that is cycling the line swings smoothly between the extremes, and turns away from them come close to swing highs and lows.

When the market trends, the phase stalls and the line can sit near one extreme or flip abruptly. Treat a line that stops swinging as a sign that there is no clean cycle to trade, rather than as an overbought or oversold reading.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the wave is computed from. The default is the close.

settings.label: High-Pass Filter Length
settings.html: Detrending period: cycles longer than this many bars are removed. A larger value keeps slower swings.

settings.label: Super-Smoother Filter Length
settings.html: The smoothing applied after detrending. A larger value gives a smoother wave that turns later.

faq.q: Why does the line jump from one extreme to the other?
faq.html: The value is a phase, not a price. When the quadrature component crosses zero while the in-phase value is small, the phase moves quickly and the line can swing across the pane in a bar or two.

faq.q: How is this different from the Even Better Sinewave?
faq.html: This study normalises against a Hilbert quadrature partner, so it measures phase. The Even Better Sinewave normalises against the wave's own recent power, so it measures amplitude relative to its recent size.

faq.q: What happens at a high-pass length of 4?
faq.html: At that length the filter coefficient is zero over zero. The study uses the limit, which is 0, so the filter still works.

related.title: Solar Cycle (SOLAR)
related.summary: Plots the sine of the Sun's position along the ecliptic at each bar's time, a calendar wave from -1 at the winter solstice to +1 at the summer solstice.

related.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
related.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.

related.title: SSF-Based Detrended Synthetic Price
related.summary: Subtracts a half-cycle Super Smoother filter from a quarter-cycle one, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that follows the market's dominant cycle.

sine-weighted-moving-average-sinema.title: Sine-weighted Moving Average (SINEMA)
sine-weighted-moving-average-sinema.summary: A moving average whose weights follow half a sine wave across the window, so the middle bars count most and the line runs smooth.
sine-weighted-moving-average-sinema.descriptionHtml:
The Sine-weighted Moving Average spreads half a sine wave across its window. With p bars in the window, the bar k bars back weighs sin(pi * (k + 1) / p): small at the newest bar, largest near the middle, and zero at the oldest, so in effect the average covers the newest p - 1 bars. The weighted sum of the source is divided by the sum of the weights.

The window grows with the data until it reaches period, so the line starts on the first bar. A missing price is left out together with its weight, and a window whose weights add to zero shows the source itself.
sine-weighted-moving-average-sinema.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line. The rounded weights damp single-bar noise more than a simple average while keeping a similar lag of about half the window. A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend, and a falling line with price below it a downtrend; a change in the line's slope is the signal to watch.

Because the newest bar carries little weight, the line reacts to a sudden move a few bars later than a front-weighted average would. Until period bars exist the window is shorter.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the half sine wave spans. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the newest bar weigh so little?
faq.html: The sine wave starts near zero at the newest bar and peaks in the middle of the window. That rounded shape is what makes the line smooth, at the cost of reacting a little later.

faq.q: How does it compare with a simple average?
faq.html: Over the same period it lags about as much but is smoother, because the edges of the window fade in and out instead of switching on and off.

faq.q: What does a period of 1 show?
faq.html: The source itself: a one-bar window averages just the current price. A period of 2 also follows the source, because the older of its two bars weighs zero.

related.title: Simple Moving Average (SMA)
related.summary: The plain average of the last N prices, with every bar in the window counted equally, drawn from the very first bar of the chart.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Moving Average (SGMA)
related.summary: A symmetric weighted average over an odd window: a fixed coefficient table for degree 2 on 5, 7 or 9 bars, and a polynomial weight shape otherwise.

related.title: SP15: Spencer 15-Point Moving Average
related.summary: A fixed 15-bar weighted average of the close, with weights chosen so that cycles four and five bars long are removed rather than only damped.

skewness-skew.title: Skewness (SKEW)
skewness-skew.summary: A rolling measure of how lopsided the recent values are about their mean: positive when the long tail is above, negative when it is below.
skewness-skew.descriptionHtml:
Skewness describes the asymmetry of a distribution. This study estimates it over the last Length bars as the third moment about the mean divided by the cube of the standard deviation.

It does so with a fixed amount of work per bar. It keeps a rolling mean of the source, measures each bar's deviation from the mean as it stood on that bar, and keeps rolling sums of the squared and cubed deviations. The window is never re-centred on the latest mean, so the result is an approximation of the textbook skewness rather than an exact recomputation of the window. Until the window is full, the means are taken over the bars that exist.

When the standard deviation is effectively zero the study reads 0, and an absent value counts as zero.
skewness-skew.howToReadHtml:
A positive reading means the recent values have a longer tail above the mean: most bars sat a little below it, with a few large values above. A negative reading means the reverse, a few sharp drops among many small gains. A reading near zero means the recent values are roughly symmetric.

On raw price, the only kind of series the Source menu offers, the reading mostly reflects the shape of the recent trend; persistent negative skew in a returns series, which needs a small edit to the script, points to occasional large drops. The measure is sensitive to a single extreme bar, so a spike can swing it sharply until that bar leaves the window.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose asymmetry is measured.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many recent bars the moments are taken over, at least 3. A longer length gives a steadier reading.

faq.q: Is this exactly the textbook skewness?
faq.html: Close but not exact. Each deviation is measured against the mean on its own bar, and the window is not re-centred on the latest mean, which keeps the work per bar fixed at the cost of an approximation.

faq.q: Why does one bar change it so much?
faq.html: Skewness uses cubed deviations, so a single large move dominates the sum until it leaves the window.

faq.q: What does a reading of 0 mean?
faq.html: Either the recent values are balanced about their mean, or the window was flat and the standard deviation was effectively zero, in which case the study also reads 0.

related.title: Spearman Rank Correlation (SPEARMAN)
related.summary: Correlation between the ranks of two series of the chart's symbol over a window: whether they move together in order, regardless of size.

related.title: Quantile (QUANTILE)
related.summary: The requested quantile of the source over a rolling window, drawn on the price chart: 0.5 is the rolling median, 0 the low, 1 the high.

related.title: Standard Deviation (STDDEV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of the source over a rolling window, a direct measure of how widely recent values spread around their mean.

slope-linear-regression-slope.title: Slope, Linear Regression (SLOPE)
slope-linear-regression-slope.summary: Plots the slope of the least squares line fitted through the last N values, in price units per bar.
slope-linear-regression-slope.descriptionHtml:
Slope, Linear Regression (SLOPE) fits a straight line through the most recent period values of the source by least squares and plots how steep that line is. Each value is placed at its position in the window, from 0 for the oldest to period - 1 for the newest, and the slope is (n * sum(x * y) - sum(x) * sum(y)) / (n * sum(x * x) - sum(x) ^ 2), where n is the number of values present.

The result is in price units per bar: a slope of 25 means the fitted line rises 25 points from one bar to the next. On the first bars of the chart the window holds only the bars that exist so far, and a missing value is skipped while keeping its place in the window. With fewer than two values present nothing is drawn.
slope-linear-regression-slope.howToReadHtml:
Above zero the fitted trend over the window is rising, below zero it is falling, and near zero price is moving sideways. The further from zero, the steeper the trend. A slope that keeps its sign but shrinks toward zero shows a trend losing pace, and a cross of zero shows the fitted line turning.

Because the value is in price units, it is larger on higher-priced instruments and in more volatile markets, so compare it with its own history rather than across symbols. A short period follows turns quickly but is noisy; a long one is smooth but lags.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the line is fitted through. A longer period gives a smoother slope that turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series the line is fitted to, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: What unit is the slope in?
faq.html: Price units per bar. A value of 10 on an hourly chart means the fitted line climbs 10 points each hour.

faq.q: How is it different from momentum?
faq.html: Momentum compares two prices, the latest and one from period bars ago. The slope uses every bar in the window, so a single unusual bar at either end moves it less.

faq.q: Why does it start on the second bar?
faq.html: Two points are enough to fit a line, so the slope appears as soon as two values exist and uses the full window once period bars have passed.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots the square root of the chosen source, which compresses large values and stretches small ones onto a flatter scale.

related.title: Logistic Function (SIGMOID)
related.summary: Passes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the logistic curve, giving an oscillator bounded between 0 and 1.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots y equal to the square root of the source, compressing large readings far more than small ones and leaving gaps below zero.

simple-moving-average-sma.title: Simple Moving Average (SMA)
simple-moving-average-sma.summary: The plain average of the last N prices, with every bar in the window counted equally, drawn from the very first bar of the chart.
simple-moving-average-sma.descriptionHtml:
The Simple Moving Average adds up the source over the last period bars and divides by the number of bars. Every bar in the window counts the same, so the line is the centre of gravity of recent prices, and it trails behind them by roughly half the window.

This version keeps a running total rather than waiting for a full window. On the first bars of the chart it averages every bar seen so far, so the line starts on bar one and settles into the ordinary windowed average once period bars exist. A missing price is counted as zero.
simple-moving-average-sma.howToReadHtml:
Price above a rising average is the usual picture of an uptrend, and price below a falling one of a downtrend. A flat average with price weaving across it says the market has no direction over that window. Many traders watch for the close crossing the line, or for a short average crossing a long one, as a sign the trend may be turning.

The average reacts late by design: it only turns after enough new prices have outweighed the old ones. The first period - 1 bars use a shorter window and so move more than the settled line does.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars are averaged. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar instead of after the period?
faq.html: Until the window is full it averages all the bars seen so far, so the first values come from a shorter window. From bar period on it is the usual windowed mean.

faq.q: How far behind price does it lag?
faq.html: About half the period. A 10-bar average reflects prices centred roughly five bars ago, which is why it turns after the market has already turned.

faq.q: Why use it over a weighted or exponential average?
faq.html: It is the easiest to reason about: every bar counts equally and a bar leaves the average exactly period bars after it arrived. The cost is more lag than averages that weight recent bars more.

related.title: SP15: Spencer 15-Point Moving Average
related.summary: A fixed 15-bar weighted average of the close, with weights chosen so that cycles four and five bars long are removed rather than only damped.

related.title: Sine-weighted Moving Average (SINEMA)
related.summary: A moving average whose weights follow half a sine wave across the window, so the middle bars count most and the line runs smooth.

related.title: SWMA: Symmetric Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close with triangular weights, so the bars in the middle of the window count most and the ends count least.

symmetric-mean-absolute-error-smape.title: Symmetric Mean Absolute %Error (SMAPE)
symmetric-mean-absolute-error-smape.summary: The average symmetric percentage gap between price and its own exponential average, a bounded error score that treats overshoot and undershoot alike.
symmetric-mean-absolute-error-smape.descriptionHtml:
Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE) measures how far a source series runs from its own exponential moving average, in percent. The average uses Period as its length and starts from the simple average of its first Period values. On every bar the symmetric error is 200 times the absolute gap between the source and the average, divided by the sum of their absolute values. Dividing by both sides rather than by one keeps the score between 0 and 200 and makes a miss above count the same as a miss below.

While the average has no value yet, the error for that bar counts as zero, and those zeros do enter the average. The plotted value is the mean of the symmetric errors over the last Period bars, or over every bar so far while fewer than Period have passed. The exponential average itself is drawn on the price chart.
symmetric-mean-absolute-error-smape.howToReadHtml:
Read the pane as the typical percentage distance between price and its trend line. A reading of 1 means price has been about one percent from its exponential average on an average bar of the window. A rising line means price is stretching further from the average; a falling one means it is settling back toward it.

The early part of the line is pulled toward zero by the warmup bars, which count as zero error, so do not read the first Period or so bars as a quiet market. The score shows the size of the gap, not its direction.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series compared with its own exponential average.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average and of the window the symmetric errors are averaged over (the window is capped at 4000 bars).

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero and climb?
faq.html: Before the exponential average has a value each bar counts as zero error, and those zeros sit in the window. As real errors replace them, the line rises to its true level.

faq.q: Why is it called symmetric?
faq.html: The gap is divided by the sum of both magnitudes rather than by the actual value alone, so swapping price and the average gives the same score and the reading cannot exceed 200.

faq.q: What is the forecast here?
faq.html: The exponential moving average of the source with the same length as the window. The study treats the average as a forecast of price and scores how far price strays from it.

related.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
related.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.

related.title: R² Coefficient of Determination (RSQUARED)
related.summary: How much of price's variation around its rolling mean an exponential average explains: 1 is a perfect fit and below 0 is worse than flat.

related.title: Tukey's Biweight Loss (TukeyBiweight)
related.summary: A rolling average of the bisquare loss between an actual and a predicted series, a robust error score that caps the cost of any outlier.

stochastic-momentum-index-smi.title: Stochastic Momentum Index (SMI)
stochastic-momentum-index-smi.summary: Where the close sits relative to the midpoint of its recent high-low range, double smoothed and centred on zero, with a smoothed signal line.
stochastic-momentum-index-smi.descriptionHtml:
The Stochastic Momentum Index measures the distance from the source to the middle of the recent range rather than to its low. It finds the highest high and lowest low of the last %K Period bars, takes their midpoint and half their distance, and expresses the source's distance from the midpoint as a percentage of that half range. The result runs from about minus 100 at the low to plus 100 at the high.

With the Blau Method switch on, that ratio is smoothed twice with an exponential mean of length %K Smooth to give %K. With it off, the distance and the half range are each smoothed twice first and then divided, which weights wide-range bars more heavily. In both cases %D is an exponential mean of %K with length %D Smooth.

Every exponential stage starts at zero and, while any stage still owes weight to that start, is divided by the weight it has earned, so the lines answer from the first bar. Until %K Period bars exist, the range uses the bars seen so far.
stochastic-momentum-index-smi.howToReadHtml:
Above zero the source is in the upper half of its recent range, below zero in the lower half. Readings above 40 are often treated as overbought and below minus 40 as oversold, though the exact lines vary with the settings. A cross of %K above %D is a sign of improving momentum, and a cross below of weakening momentum; a cross of zero says price has moved to the other half of its range.

The double smoothing makes the SMI steadier than a plain stochastic but also later to turn. In a strong trend it can stay on one side of zero for a long time.

settings.label: %K Period
settings.html: How many bars the high-low range covers. A longer window gives a wider range and calmer readings.

settings.label: %K Smooth
settings.html: The length of both exponential smoothing passes that produce %K. Higher values give a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: %D Smooth
settings.html: The length of the exponential mean of %K that forms the %D signal line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series compared with the range midpoint, the close by default.

settings.label: Blau Method
settings.html: On: smooth the ratio itself. Off: smooth the distance and the half range separately and divide afterwards, so wide-range bars count for more.

faq.q: How is the SMI different from a stochastic?
faq.html: A stochastic measures from the low of the range, so it runs 0 to 100. The SMI measures from the midpoint, so it runs from about minus 100 to plus 100 and its sign tells you which half of the range price is in.

faq.q: What does the Blau Method switch change?
faq.html: Whether the ratio is smoothed (on) or the distance and the half range are smoothed apart and then divided (off). The second way gives bars with a wide range more say in the result.

faq.q: Why does it start without a blank warmup?
faq.html: Each smoothing stage is corrected for starting at zero, and the range uses the bars seen so far until the window fills, so both lines have values from the first bar.

related.title: Squeeze Momentum (SQUEEZE)
related.summary: Flags the quiet stretches where the Bollinger Bands sit inside the Keltner Channel, and draws a momentum histogram for the move that follows.

related.title: Relative Vigor Index (RVGI)
related.summary: Compares where bars close relative to their open with the size of their range, so it reads the conviction behind a move as a signed ratio.

related.title: Schaff Trend Cycle (STC)
related.summary: A MACD line put through two rounds of stochastic scaling, giving a 0 to 100 trend reading that turns faster than the MACD itself.

solar-cycle-solar.title: Solar Cycle (SOLAR)
solar-cycle-solar.summary: Plots the sine of the Sun's position along the ecliptic at each bar's time, a calendar wave from -1 at the winter solstice to +1 at the summer solstice.
solar-cycle-solar.descriptionHtml:
Solar Cycle is a pure calendar series: it never reads price or volume. For each bar it takes the bar's open time, converts it to a Julian date and then to Julian centuries since the J2000 epoch, and works out where the Sun sits on the ecliptic using the standard low precision solar formulas: the Sun's mean longitude, its mean anomaly, and the equation of centre that corrects one into the other.

The result is the sine of that apparent longitude. It reads 0 at the March and September equinoxes, rises to +1 at the June solstice and falls to -1 at the December solstice, so one full wave takes one year. On an hourly chart the line moves very slowly; it is meant to line seasonal studies up with the astronomical year rather than to move with the market.

The study also marks the four turning points. Peak Summer and Peak Winter are drawn on the curve on the bar where it turns after sitting beyond +0.985 or -0.985, and Spring Rise and Autumn Fall are drawn on the zero line on the bar where the curve crosses it upward or downward.
solar-cycle-solar.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the season, not as a signal. A value near +1 means the bars fall close to the June solstice, near -1 close to the December solstice, and a crossing of zero is an equinox. Put it beside a price study to see whether a market's behaviour lines up with the time of year, or use the marks as dates for comparing one year with the next.

It says nothing about price by itself, and any link between the solar year and a market is something you have to test on your own data. On an intraday chart a few weeks of bars cover only a small slice of the wave, so expect long stretches with no marks at all.

faq.q: Does this study use price at all?
faq.html: No. Every value comes from the bar's time alone, so two instruments on the same timeframe show exactly the same line.

faq.q: Why is the line so flat on an hourly chart?
faq.html: One full wave takes a year. A few weeks of hourly bars cover only a small part of it, so the line drifts slowly and the four marks appear only when the chart spans a solstice or an equinox.

faq.q: How accurate are the solstice and equinox marks?
faq.html: They use the low precision solar position formulas, which place the Sun to within about a hundredth of a degree. An equinox mark lands on the first bar at or past the zero crossing, and a solstice mark on the first bar after the curve turns, so on an hourly chart a mark can sit an hour or so away from the exact astronomical moment.

faq.q: Which hemisphere does it follow?
faq.html: The labels follow the northern hemisphere calendar: +1 is the June solstice. In the southern hemisphere the seasons are the other way round, but the astronomical events fall on the same bars.

related.title: SSF-Based Detrended Synthetic Price
related.summary: Subtracts a half-cycle Super Smoother filter from a quarter-cycle one, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that follows the market's dominant cycle.

related.title: Ehlers Sine Wave (SINE)
related.summary: The phase of the detrended price cycle as a wave between -1 and +1, from the in-phase value over its length with a quadrature partner.

related.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
related.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.

sp15-spencer-15-point-moving-average.title: SP15: Spencer 15-Point Moving Average
sp15-spencer-15-point-moving-average.summary: A fixed 15-bar weighted average of the close, with weights chosen so that cycles four and five bars long are removed rather than only damped.
sp15-spencer-15-point-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The 15-point average is a fixed weighted filter on the close. It multiplies the last 15 closes by the weights -3, -6, -5, 3, 21, 46, 67, 74, 67, 46, 21, 3, -5, -6, -3 (from the newest bar to the bar 14 bars back), adds them up and divides by 320, the sum of the weights.

The weights are symmetric around the bar seven bars back and include small negative values at both ends. That shape passes the slower trend almost unchanged while cancelling swings that repeat every four or five bars. The filter is drawn on the current bar with no offset, so it describes prices centred seven bars ago.
sp15-spencer-15-point-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a smooth trend line that ignores short repeating wiggles. Its direction shows the trend over the last 15 bars, and a change in slope marks a change in that trend. Because the negative end weights give a little overshoot, the line can briefly move past a sharp turn before settling.

It has no settings: the window is always 15 bars and the series is always the close. The line starts on the fifteenth bar and lags price by about seven bars.

faq.q: Why are some weights negative?
faq.html: They let the filter pass a curving trend unchanged: any straight, quadratic or cubic run of prices comes out exactly as it went in, measured at the centre of the window, while cycles of four and five bars are cancelled. A filter with only positive weights always flattens a curve.

faq.q: Why is there nothing to configure?
faq.html: The weights are a fixed set built for a 15-bar window. Changing the length would need a different set of weights.

faq.q: How much does it lag?
faq.html: The weights are centred seven bars back, so the line reflects the price of about seven bars ago.

related.title: SWMA: Symmetric Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close with triangular weights, so the bars in the middle of the window count most and the ends count least.

related.title: Simple Moving Average (SMA)
related.summary: The plain average of the last N prices, with every bar in the window counted equally, drawn from the very first bar of the chart.

related.title: Tillson T3 Moving Average (T3)
related.summary: Six chained exponential averages blended by a volume factor into a smooth line with much less lag than its smoothing would suggest.

ehlers-super-passband-filter-spbf.title: Ehlers Super Passband Filter (SPBF)
ehlers-super-passband-filter-spbf.summary: The difference of two fast exponential smoothings of price, a zero-centred passband line with a root-mean-square envelope above and below.
ehlers-super-passband-filter-spbf.descriptionHtml:
The Super Passband Filter subtracts a slow exponential smoothing of price from a faster one. Both use a smoothing factor of 5 / period rather than the usual 2 / (period + 1), so they react more quickly than standard exponential averages of the same length. Written as one formula, the difference becomes a two-pole recursion on the current and previous price and the filter's own last two values. The result, SuperPB, swings around zero as price moves between the two speeds.

The study also measures how large those swings have been. It squares the passband value on each bar, sums the squares over the last RMS Period bars, divides by RMS Period and takes the square root. That root-mean-square is drawn as +RMS above zero and -RMS below it.

Before a full RMS window exists the sum is still divided by the whole RMS Period, so the envelope grows in from zero over the first window.
ehlers-super-passband-filter-spbf.howToReadHtml:
Read SuperPB as a fast cycle oscillator: above zero the short smoothing is above the long one and price is pushing up, below zero it is pushing down. The RMS lines give the typical size of those swings. A move of the passband beyond +RMS or -RMS is a swing larger than usual and can be read as a cycle extreme forming; a cross back inside the envelope can be read as the first sign of a turn.

The values are in price units, not normalised. The envelope adapts to recent volatility but only over RMS Period bars, so a sudden regime change can leave the line outside the envelope for some time.

settings.label: Short Period
settings.html: The period of the fast smoothing; its factor is 5 divided by this value.

settings.label: Long Period
settings.html: The period of the slow smoothing; its factor is 5 divided by this value.

settings.label: RMS Period
settings.html: How many bars the root-mean-square envelope is averaged over.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter runs on, the close by default.

faq.q: Why 5 / period instead of the usual factor?
faq.html: A factor of 5 / period makes each smoothing much faster than a standard exponential average of the same period, which keeps the passband responsive.

faq.q: What do the RMS lines show?
faq.html: The root-mean-square of the passband over the last RMS Period bars, which is a measure of its typical swing size. They are mirrored above and below zero.

faq.q: Why are the RMS lines small at the start?
faq.html: The sum of squares is always divided by the full RMS Period, so until that many bars exist the envelope is smaller than it will be later.

related.title: Supersmooth Filter (SSF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass filter that removes short-term chop from price with much less lag than a moving average of the same length.

related.title: Savitzky-Golay Filter (SGF)
related.summary: A smoothing line built from a polynomial fitting kernel, which at the default order keeps the height of a swing better than a plain moving average of the same length.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF2)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive smoother that removes the fast wiggle a moving average of the same length still passes, with less lag.

spearman-rank-correlation-spearman.title: Spearman Rank Correlation (SPEARMAN)
spearman-rank-correlation-spearman.summary: Correlation between the ranks of two series of the chart's symbol over a window: whether they move together in order, regardless of size.
spearman-rank-correlation-spearman.descriptionHtml:
Spearman's rank correlation replaces each value in the window by its rank, then measures the Pearson correlation between the two rank series. Each value's rank is the count of smaller values in its window, plus half the number of other values equal to it, plus one, so tied values share the average of their ranks.

Because only order matters, the result is unmoved by outliers and by any rescaling that keeps the order of the values. It reads +1 when the two series rise and fall in perfect step, -1 when one rises exactly as the other falls, and 0 when their orderings are unrelated. When either series is flat over the window the study reads 0.

Both series come from the chart's own symbol, the close and the open by default. The study needs a full window of Lookback Period bars, and a bar is left blank when any value in the window is absent.
spearman-rank-correlation-spearman.howToReadHtml:
With the default inputs, a reading near +1 means the closes and opens have been ranked the same way, which happens in a steady trend; readings that fall toward zero show the two drifting apart within the window. The dashed lines at plus and minus 0.5 mark a moderate relationship, and the solid lines at plus and minus 1 are the bounds.

Rank correlation is less sensitive to a single extreme bar than Pearson correlation, but over a short window it still moves a lot by chance. The lookback is capped at 60 bars.

settings.label: Source 1
settings.html: The first series of the pair, the close by default.

settings.label: Source 2
settings.html: The second series of the pair, from the same symbol. It defaults to the open because a series compared with itself always reads +1.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars are ranked, from 2 to 60. A longer period gives a steadier reading.

faq.q: How does it differ from Pearson correlation?
faq.html: Pearson correlation uses the values themselves and measures a straight-line relationship, so one extreme bar can dominate it. Spearman uses only the order of the values, so it measures whether the two series rise and fall together in any steady way.

faq.q: Why is the lookback capped at 60?
faq.html: Ranking compares every value in the window with every other, so the work grows with the square of the window. The cap keeps the study fast.

faq.q: Why does it default to close against open?
faq.html: Both series come from the chart's own symbol, and comparing a series with itself reads +1 on every bar. The open is a different series of the same instrument.

related.title: Standard Deviation (STDDEV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of the source over a rolling window, a direct measure of how widely recent values spread around their mean.

related.title: Skewness (SKEW)
related.summary: A rolling measure of how lopsided the recent values are about their mean: positive when the long tail is above, negative when it is below.

related.title: Standard Error of Regression (STDERR)
related.summary: How far price scatters around its own least-squares trend line over a rolling window: low when price tracks the line, high when it wanders.

square-root-transformation-sqrt.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
square-root-transformation-sqrt.summary: Plots the square root of the chosen source, which compresses large values and stretches small ones onto a flatter scale.
square-root-transformation-sqrt.descriptionHtml:
Square Root Transformation (SQRT) replaces each value of the source with its square root. The transformation is applied bar by bar, with no lookback and no smoothing.

The square root grows more slowly than the value it is taken of. Going from 100 to 400 doubles the root from 10 to 20, while going from 10,000 to 40,000 also only doubles it, from 100 to 200. Large values are compressed far more than small ones, so a strongly skewed series, such as a price that has risen many times over, reads on a gentler scale. A negative value has no real square root and is left as a gap.
square-root-transformation-sqrt.howToReadHtml:
Read the shape of the line rather than its level. Moves look smaller at high prices than they do on the raw chart, so a long rise that seems to accelerate in price units can look steadier once transformed, and early moves at low prices become easier to see.

The values are not prices, so do not set orders against them. The transformation is a lens on the series, often used before comparing spans of very different price levels or as a step before further statistics.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series to transform, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: Why is part of the line missing?
faq.html: The source was negative on those bars. A negative number has no real square root, so those bars are left blank.

faq.q: How does it differ from a logarithmic scale?
faq.html: Both compress large values. The square root compresses less strongly than a logarithm, so it sits between the raw series and a log view.

faq.q: Does it change the direction of moves?
faq.html: No. The square root rises whenever the source rises and falls whenever it falls, so turns appear on the same bars; only the size of each move changes.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots y equal to the square root of the source, compressing large readings far more than small ones and leaving gaps below zero.

related.title: Slope, Linear Regression (SLOPE)
related.summary: Plots the slope of the least squares line fitted through the last N values, in price units per bar.

related.title: Standardization (Z-score)
related.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.

sqrttrans.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
sqrttrans.summary: Plots y equal to the square root of the source, compressing large readings far more than small ones and leaving gaps below zero.
sqrttrans.descriptionHtml:
This Square Root Transformation (SQRT) computes y = sqrt(x) for each value of the chosen source, one bar at a time, with no lookback and no smoothing.

The effect is a change of scale. Quadrupling the source only doubles the result, so large readings are pulled in much more than small ones and a series that spans a wide range is laid out on a flatter curve. Bars where the source is negative, or missing, have no real root and are drawn as gaps rather than as zero.
sqrttrans.howToReadHtml:
Look at the pattern of the line, not its number. Rises and falls happen on the same bars as on the raw source, but swings at high levels look smaller and swings at low levels look larger, which helps when comparing behaviour across very different price levels.

The output is not a price, so it is not a level to trade against. Treat it as a view of the series that tames large values, or as a preparation step for statistics that expect a less skewed input.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose square root is drawn, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: What happens when the source is below zero?
faq.html: Nothing is drawn on that bar. A negative number has no real square root, and the study leaves a gap rather than inventing a value.

faq.q: Why would I transform price at all?
faq.html: A series that has grown many times over is dominated on a plain chart by its latest, largest moves. The square root evens that out so earlier moves stay visible.

faq.q: Do turning points move?
faq.html: No. The square root keeps the order of values, so highs and lows fall on the same bars as in the source.

related.title: Standardization (Z-score)
related.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots the square root of the chosen source, which compresses large values and stretches small ones onto a flatter scale.

related.title: Hyperbolic Tangent (TANH)
related.summary: Squashes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the hyperbolic tangent, giving an oscillator between -1 and +1.

squeeze-momentum-squeeze.title: Squeeze Momentum (SQUEEZE)
squeeze-momentum-squeeze.summary: Flags the quiet stretches where the Bollinger Bands sit inside the Keltner Channel, and draws a momentum histogram for the move that follows.
squeeze-momentum-squeeze.descriptionHtml:
Squeeze Momentum combines a volatility test with a momentum reading. The test compares two envelopes of the same period. The Bollinger Bands are the simple mean of the source plus and minus BB Multiplier population standard deviations. The Keltner Channel is an exponential mean of the source plus and minus KC Multiplier times an average true range smoothed with weight 1 / period. The squeeze is on while the Bollinger Bands sit wholly inside the channel, which happens when the source has stayed in a tight cluster over the period compared with the size of the average bar range.

The momentum histogram is a least squares line fitted through the last period values of a distance: the source minus the average of two midpoints, the Donchian midpoint of the period's highest high and lowest low, and the simple mean. The histogram plots that line's value at the current bar.

Every window uses the bars seen so far until a full period exists, and both exponential means are corrected for their zero start, so the study answers from the first bar. The histogram is bright green while positive and rising, darker green while positive and falling, red while negative and falling, and maroon while negative and rising.
squeeze-momentum-squeeze.howToReadHtml:
The red line along zero marks bars in a squeeze, and the green line marks bars out of one. A squeeze says volatility has contracted; a quiet stretch like this is often followed by a wider move, though not always. When the squeeze ends, the histogram's side of zero suggests the direction of that move, and its colour shows whether momentum is still building or already fading.

The squeeze says nothing about when the release will come, and a release can fail and fold back. Some traders wait for the squeeze to end and the histogram to agree before acting, and take the change from bright to dark colour as the first sign a move is losing pace.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series used for the means, the deviation and the momentum, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window shared by the bands, the channel, the Donchian range and the regression. Longer periods give slower, steadier readings.

settings.label: BB Multiplier
settings.html: How many standard deviations the Bollinger Bands sit from their mean. A larger value makes a squeeze rarer.

settings.label: KC Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges the Keltner Channel sits from its mean. A larger value makes a squeeze more common.

faq.q: What are the two lines along zero?
faq.html: They show the squeeze state. The red line is drawn on bars where the Bollinger Bands are inside the Keltner Channel, and the green line on bars where they are not, so the colour along zero tells you which state each bar is in.

faq.q: What do the four histogram colours mean?
faq.html: Bright green: positive and higher than the bar before. Dark green: positive but lower. Red: negative and lower than the bar before. Maroon: negative but higher. The dark shades show momentum fading toward zero.

faq.q: How is the momentum value worked out?
faq.html: It fits a straight line through the last period values of the source minus the average of the Donchian midpoint and the simple mean, and reads that line at the current bar. This smooths the distance with less lag than a plain average of the same window.

squeeze-momentum-squeeze.deviation: The Squeeze On and Squeeze Off states are drawn as red and green line segments along zero rather than as separate dots, because a plot in this OpenScript version has no dots-only style.

related.title: Schaff Trend Cycle (STC)
related.summary: A MACD line put through two rounds of stochastic scaling, giving a 0 to 100 trend reading that turns faster than the MACD itself.

related.title: Stochastic Momentum Index (SMI)
related.summary: Where the close sits relative to the midpoint of its recent high-low range, double smoothed and centred on zero, with a smoothed signal line.

related.title: Stochastic Oscillator (STOCH)
related.summary: Places the close inside the high-low range of the last K bars as a 0 to 100 reading, with a simple average of it as the %D line.

supersmooth-filter-ssf.title: Supersmooth Filter (SSF)
supersmooth-filter-ssf.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass filter that removes short-term chop from price with much less lag than a moving average of the same length.
supersmooth-filter-ssf.descriptionHtml:
The Supersmooth Filter is a two-pole recursive lowpass filter. Each new value is a weighted blend of this bar's price and the filter's own two previous values. The weights come from the length setting: with arg = sqrt(2) * pi / length, the filter uses c2 = 2 * exp(-arg) * cos(arg), c3 = -exp(-2 * arg) and c1 = 1 - c2 - c3, and computes SSF = c1 * price + c2 * SSF[1] + c3 * SSF[2].

Because the three weights add up to one, a flat price passes through unchanged. Before the filter has two values of its own it reads the price in their place, so the first bar equals the price exactly and the line answers from the first bar.

The length sets the cutoff: cycles shorter than roughly the length are suppressed, and slower movements pass through. The two-pole design cuts short cycles much harder than a single exponential average, which is why the line looks so much smoother for the lag it carries.
supersmooth-filter-ssf.howToReadHtml:
Use the SSF as a smooth trend line on the price chart. When it turns up, the slower part of the move has turned up; when it turns down, it has turned down. Price crossing the line, or two SSF lines of different lengths crossing each other, are common ways to time a change in direction.

The filter can overshoot slightly after a sharp move, and like every smoother it still lags. It removes noise; it does not predict the next bar.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. A longer length removes slower swings and makes the line smoother but later to turn.

faq.q: How is this different from an exponential moving average?
faq.html: An exponential average has one pole and lets a fair amount of short-term chop through. This filter has two poles, so it suppresses short cycles much more strongly for a similar amount of lag.
