faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the filter has two earlier values of its own, it uses the price in their place. The weights sum to one, so the first value equals the price.

faq.q: Why does it sometimes run past price after a jump?
faq.html: A two-pole filter carries a little momentum. After a sudden move it can overshoot by a small amount before it settles.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF2)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive smoother that removes the fast wiggle a moving average of the same length still passes, with less lag.

related.title: Ehlers Super Passband Filter (SPBF)
related.summary: The difference of two fast exponential smoothings of price, a zero-centred passband line with a root-mean-square envelope above and below.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF3)
related.summary: A three-pole recursive smoother on price that removes short swings with little lag and almost no overshoot, answering from the first bar.

ehlers-2-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf2.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF2)
ehlers-2-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf2.summary: A two-pole recursive smoother that removes the fast wiggle a moving average of the same length still passes, with less lag.
ehlers-2-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf2.descriptionHtml:
The 2-Pole Super Smoother is a recursive lowpass filter. Each value blends the current price with the filter's two previous outputs, using coefficients chosen so that fast price noise is strongly damped while slower movement passes through.

From the length it sets arg = sqrt(2) pi / length and e = exp(-arg), then c2 = 2e cos(arg), c3 = -e squared and c1 = 1 - c2 - c3. On each bar the value is c1 times the price plus c2 times the previous output plus c3 times the output two bars back. Where an earlier output does not exist yet, the nearest price is used in its place, so on the first bar the filter returns the price itself and settles from there without a blank warmup. A missing price borrows the previous one.
ehlers-2-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf2.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a low-lag moving average. Price above a rising line points to upward short-term direction, and below a falling line to downward direction. Turns in the line, and crossings between price and the line, mark changes in the smoothed trend.

It stays smooth through choppy bars where a simple or exponential average of the same length would still twitch. A longer length gives a calmer line that turns later. It follows moves rather than anticipating them.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. A longer length removes more noise and turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from an exponential moving average?
faq.html: An exponential average has one pole and still passes much of the fastest noise. This filter has two poles, so its response falls off about twice as steeply past the cutoff and damps that noise far more.

faq.q: Why does it start on the first bar?
faq.html: Missing earlier values are filled with the nearest available price, so the first output equals the price and the recursion builds from there.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF3)
related.summary: A three-pole recursive smoother on price that removes short swings with little lag and almost no overshoot, answering from the first bar.

related.title: Supersmooth Filter (SSF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive lowpass filter that removes short-term chop from price with much less lag than a moving average of the same length.

related.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.

ehlers-3-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf3.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF3)
ehlers-3-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf3.summary: A three-pole recursive smoother on price that removes short swings with little lag and almost no overshoot, answering from the first bar.
ehlers-3-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf3.descriptionHtml:
The 3-Pole Super Smoother is a recursive lowpass filter. Each value is the current price times one coefficient plus the filter's own last three values times three more, so it needs no long window of past prices. The coefficients come from a pole radius of exp(-pi / Length) and an angle of sqrt(3) * pi / Length, and the price coefficient is chosen so all four add up to one, which keeps the line on top of a flat price.

Unlike the Butterworth design it feeds only the current price into the filter, not a weighted window of recent prices. The poles are placed so the filter's own ringing cancels out, which is why the line follows price smoothly without the wiggles a simple fast average shows.

Where a previous value does not exist yet, at the start of the chart, the newest available price stands in for it, so the line begins exactly at the first price and has no warm-up gap.
ehlers-3-pole-super-smoother-filter-ssf3.howToReadHtml:
Treat the line as the trend of price at the scale set by Length. A rising line means the smoothed price is going up, a falling line means it is going down, and a change in slope marks a change in the swing. Because the filter adds very little overshoot, a turn in the line is usually a real turn rather than ringing.

The line still lags price; a larger Length smooths more and lags more. On a sideways market it flattens out and its slope carries little information, so pair it with something that measures whether a trend is present.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Larger values remove longer swings and make the line smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it start on the very first bar?
faq.html: Missing earlier values are filled with the newest price that exists, so the recursion can start at once. The first bar's value equals the first price.

faq.q: How does it compare with a moving average of the same length?
faq.html: It lags less and is smoother, because it is a recursive filter tuned to cut short cycles rather than an equal-weight average of a window.

faq.q: What is the difference from the two-pole Super Smoother?
faq.html: The extra pole removes short swings more steeply. The line is a little smoother and a little slower for the same length.

related.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.

related.title: Ehlers 2-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF2)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive smoother that removes the fast wiggle a moving average of the same length still passes, with less lag.

related.title: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter (VOSS)
related.summary: A two-pole bandpass around one cycle length, with a feedback predictor line that runs a few bars ahead of it so cycle turns show earlier.

ssf-based-detrended-synthetic-price.title: SSF-Based Detrended Synthetic Price
ssf-based-detrended-synthetic-price.summary: Subtracts a half-cycle Super Smoother filter from a quarter-cycle one, leaving a zero-centred oscillator that follows the market's dominant cycle.
ssf-based-detrended-synthetic-price.descriptionHtml:
This study builds a synthetic price that keeps the cycle and drops the trend. It runs two Super Smoother filters over the same input. The fast one is tuned to a quarter of the dominant cycle period and the slow one to half of it (with floors of 2 and 3 bars). Each is a two-pole recursive filter whose coefficients come from the period through an exponential and a cosine, which gives a smooth line with little lag for its length.

The input to both filters is the average of this bar's source and the previous bar's, a light two-bar smoothing. Both filters start from that first value, so the output begins at zero. The plotted value is the fast filter minus the slow filter.

Because the slow filter follows the trend and the fast one follows the trend plus the cycle, their difference cancels most of the trend and leaves a wave centred on zero, swinging with the cycle length you set.
ssf-based-detrended-synthetic-price.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a cycle oscillator. A rise through the zero line marks the upswing of the cycle and a fall through it marks the downswing; the peaks and troughs of the wave tend to sit near the swing highs and lows of price when the cycle period matches the market.

It works best when the market really is cycling at roughly the period you set. In a strong trend the slow filter lags and the oscillator can stay on one side of zero for a long time. The swings have no fixed scale, so compare a peak with earlier peaks on the same chart rather than with a set number.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series both filters smooth. The default is the typical price, the average of high, low and close.

settings.label: Dominant Cycle Period
settings.html: The cycle length in bars. The fast filter uses a quarter of it and the slow filter half of it, so a longer period gives slower, wider swings.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: Both filters are seeded with the same first input, so on the first bar their difference is exactly zero. The oscillator then moves away from zero as the two filters respond at different speeds.

faq.q: How do I choose the cycle period?
faq.html: Set it to the typical distance in bars between two swing lows on your chart. If the waves look too choppy, raise it; if they lag the turns of price badly, lower it.

faq.q: Is a reading above zero bullish?
faq.html: It means the faster filter sits above the slower one, which is the rising half of the cycle. It is a timing tool for swings, not a statement about the longer trend.

related.title: Solar Cycle (SOLAR)
related.summary: Plots the sine of the Sun's position along the ecliptic at each bar's time, a calendar wave from -1 at the winter solstice to +1 at the summer solstice.

related.title: Ehlers Sine Wave (SINE)
related.summary: The phase of the detrended price cycle as a wave between -1 and +1, from the in-phase value over its length with a quadrature partner.

related.title: Ehlers Phasor Analysis (PHASOR)
related.summary: The phase angle of price against a reference cosine and sine of one Period, unwrapped and ratcheted, with an optional derived cycle period and trend state.

standardization-z-score.title: Standardization (Z-score)
standardization-z-score.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.
standardization-z-score.descriptionHtml:
Standardization rescales a series into z-scores. For each bar it takes the mean and the sample standard deviation of the source over the lookback window, then reports how far the current value is from that mean, measured in standard deviations. A reading of 2 means the value is two standard deviations above its recent average; -1 means one below.

The study keeps running sums of the values and of their squares over the window and derives the mean and variance from them. Until the window fills it uses the bars seen so far, so it starts on the second bar. A variance below 1e-10 counts as zero, and a window with no spread at all reads 0 when the value sits on its mean.
standardization-z-score.howToReadHtml:
Values near zero mean price is close to its recent average. Readings beyond plus or minus 2 are unusual for the window and often mark stretched moves, while a series that keeps returning to zero is mean reverting over that horizon. Because every series becomes unitless, you can compare the z-score of two instruments or two indicators directly.

The scale assumes a roughly bell-shaped spread. Trending markets can hold high or low z-scores for a long time, so an extreme reading describes how unusual the move is, not that it must reverse.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is standardized, the close by default.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars the mean and standard deviation cover. Longer windows give a steadier baseline that reacts more slowly.

faq.q: Why does it use the sample standard deviation?
faq.html: The variance is divided by the count minus one, the sample form, which is slightly larger than the population form on short windows. That is why the window must hold at least two values.

faq.q: What does a reading of 3 mean?
faq.html: The current value is three standard deviations above the window mean. On a normal spread that happens rarely, so it marks an unusually strong move relative to recent behaviour.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the second bar?
faq.html: A single value has no spread. From the second bar the study uses all the bars seen so far, and once the window is full it uses only the last Lookback Period bars.

related.title: Hyperbolic Tangent (TANH)
related.summary: Squashes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the hyperbolic tangent, giving an oscillator between -1 and +1.

related.title: Square Root Transformation (SQRT)
related.summary: Plots y equal to the square root of the source, compressing large readings far more than small ones and leaving gaps below zero.

related.title: Student's t-Distribution CDF (TDIST)
related.summary: Maps where price sits in its recent range onto a heavy-tailed probability scale from 0 to 1 using the Student's t cumulative distribution.

stoller-average-range-channel-starchanne.title: Stoller Average Range Channel (STARCHANNEL)
stoller-average-range-channel-starchanne.summary: A simple mean of the source as the centre line, with bands a multiple of an average true range above and below it.
stoller-average-range-channel-starchanne.descriptionHtml:
This channel combines a simple moving average with an average true range. The middle line is the simple mean of the source over the last Length bars, and until Length bars exist it is the mean of every bar so far, so the line starts on the first bar.

The width comes from true range: the largest of the bar's high minus low, the high minus the previous close, and the previous close minus the low. On the first bar the previous close is that bar's own close. True range is smoothed recursively, each bar keeping (Length - 1) / Length of the previous average and adding 1 / Length of the new true range. The average starts from zero, and the share of the starting weight that has not yet decayed is divided back out, so the average is unbiased from the first bar. The upper and lower bands sit that average true range, times the multiplier, above and below the middle line.
stoller-average-range-channel-starchanne.howToReadHtml:
Because the width follows true range rather than closing-price variance, the channel widens when bars get larger or gap and narrows in quiet trading. A close beyond a band is a move of more than the chosen number of average ranges from the mean. In a range the bands mark stretched prices; in a trend price can travel along one band, and the middle line acts as the level that marks a loss of momentum.

The width is measured in price units, so a multiplier that suits one timeframe may be too tight or too loose on another.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the middle line averages.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars both the middle line and the average true range cover. A longer length gives a smoother channel.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: Half-width of the channel as a multiple of the average true range. A larger value widens the bands.

faq.q: Why use true range instead of standard deviation?
faq.html: True range measures how far each bar actually travels, including gaps from the previous close. A channel built from it reacts to bigger bars even when closes barely change.

faq.q: Why are there values from the very first bar?
faq.html: The middle line averages however many bars exist, and the average true range divides out the weight of the history it has not seen yet, so neither needs a warmup.

faq.q: What is a typical multiplier?
faq.html: The default is 2. Smaller values hug price and are touched often; larger values are touched only on unusually large moves.

related.title: Super Trend Bands (STBANDS)
related.summary: Ratcheting upper and lower bands built from the bar midpoint plus and minus a multiple of the average true range, tightening until price breaks them.

related.title: Standard Deviation Channel (SDCHANNEL)
related.summary: A least-squares line through the lookback window with a channel a fixed multiple of the residual standard deviation on each side.

related.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
related.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.

super-trend-bands-stbands.title: Super Trend Bands (STBANDS)
super-trend-bands-stbands.summary: Ratcheting upper and lower bands built from the bar midpoint plus and minus a multiple of the average true range, tightening until price breaks them.
super-trend-bands-stbands.descriptionHtml:
Super Trend Bands starts from the midpoint of each bar, (high + low) / 2, and places a basic upper band above it and a basic lower band below it, each a multiple of the average true range away. True range here is the largest of the bar's high minus low and the distances from the high and the low to the previous source value. It is averaged with a simple mean over the ATR Period, and over however many bars exist until the period is filled, so the bands start on the first bar.

The drawn bands ratchet. The upper band only moves down: it takes the new basic upper band when that is lower, and otherwise holds its previous value, unless the previous source value closed above it, in which case it resets to the basic band. The lower band is the mirror image and only moves up until the previous source value closes below it.
super-trend-bands-stbands.howToReadHtml:
The two bands frame price from above and below and step toward it as a move matures, so they work as trailing levels. While price stays between them the trend is intact; a close through the upper band shows strength strong enough to reset resistance, and a close through the lower band does the same for support. Many traders trail a stop on the band on the far side of their position.

The reset is decided by the previous bar's close, so a band reacts one bar after the break. A larger multiplier keeps the bands farther from price and gives fewer resets.

settings.label: ATR Period
settings.html: How many bars the simple average of true range covers. A longer period gives steadier band distances.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose previous value decides when a band resets and anchors the true range. The close by default.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: Distance of each basic band from the bar midpoint as a multiple of the average true range. A larger value widens the bands.

faq.q: How does this differ from a single supertrend line?
faq.html: A supertrend line shows only the band on the active side of the trend. This study draws both ratcheting bands all the time, so you see support and resistance together.

faq.q: Is the average true range a recursively smoothed average here?
faq.html: No. It is a simple mean of the true range over the ATR Period, and over all bars so far until that many exist.

faq.q: Why does a band jump away from price?
faq.html: When the previous source value closes beyond a band, the band resets to the basic band computed from the current bar, which is usually much farther away.

related.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
related.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.

related.title: Stoller Average Range Channel (STARCHANNEL)
related.summary: A simple mean of the source as the centre line, with bands a multiple of an average true range above and below it.

related.title: Ultimate Channel (UCHANNEL)
related.summary: A two-pole ultra smooth filter of price as the centre line, with bands a multiple of a smoothed true range on each side.

schaff-trend-cycle-stc.title: Schaff Trend Cycle (STC)
schaff-trend-cycle-stc.summary: A MACD line put through two rounds of stochastic scaling, giving a 0 to 100 trend reading that turns faster than the MACD itself.
schaff-trend-cycle-stc.descriptionHtml:
The Schaff Trend Cycle starts with a MACD line: a fast exponential mean of the source minus a slow one. Each mean uses weight 2 / length, passes the first value straight through, and is corrected for its zero start until that correction no longer matters.

The MACD line is then scaled like a stochastic. The study finds its highest and lowest value over the last Cycle Length bars and places the current value in that range from 0 to 100, reading 0 until the window is full or when the range is flat. That result is smoothed with a three-bar exponential mean, and the same stochastic scaling is applied a second time.

The last step depends on the Smoothing setting. 0 shows the second stochastic as it is, 1 smooths it again with a three-bar exponential mean, 2 passes it through a sigmoid curve centred on 50, and 3 latches the line to 100 above 75 and to 0 below 25, holding the last value in between.
schaff-trend-cycle-stc.howToReadHtml:
The line spends most of its time near the top or the bottom of the scale and moves quickly between them. A rise from below 25 says the MACD has turned up relative to its recent range, an early sign of an upswing; a fall from above 75 says it has turned down. With the digital setting the line is simply on or off, which some traders use as a trend filter.

Because both stochastic steps stretch small changes in the MACD to the full scale, the line can flip on modest moves in a quiet market. Read its turns in the direction of the larger trend.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the MACD is built from, the close by default.

settings.label: Cycle Length
settings.html: The window for both stochastic steps. A shorter cycle makes the line faster and more prone to flipping.

settings.label: Fast Length
settings.html: The length of the fast exponential mean in the MACD. Shorter values make the MACD react sooner.

settings.label: Slow Length
settings.html: The length of the slow exponential mean in the MACD. Longer values make the MACD reflect a longer trend.

settings.label: Smoothing
settings.html: The final step: 0 none, 1 a three-bar exponential mean, 2 a sigmoid curve centred on 50, 3 a digital latch to 100 above 75 and 0 below 25.

faq.q: Why does the line flatten at the top and bottom?
faq.html: Each stochastic step places its input in that input's recent range, so a step reads 100 or 0 whenever its input is at a new high or low for the window, and the second step often stays there for several bars. The default sigmoid finish turns those ends into about 99.3 and 0.7 and compresses readings near them, while it steepens the middle of the scale.

faq.q: What does the digital setting do?
faq.html: It turns the line into a switch: 100 once the second stochastic rises above 75, 0 once it falls below 25, and the previous value in between. Before the first switch it has no value.

faq.q: How is it different from a MACD?
faq.html: It uses the same MACD line but rescales it twice to a 0 to 100 range, so it turns sooner and reads on a fixed scale, at the cost of more false turns in a quiet market.

related.title: Stochastic Oscillator (STOCH)
related.summary: Places the close inside the high-low range of the last K bars as a 0 to 100 reading, with a simple average of it as the %D line.

related.title: Squeeze Momentum (SQUEEZE)
related.summary: Flags the quiet stretches where the Bollinger Bands sit inside the Keltner Channel, and draws a momentum histogram for the move that follows.

related.title: Stochastic Fast (STOCHF)
related.summary: The raw stochastic: where the close sits in the high-low range of the last K bars, with a D-bar average of it as the signal line.

standard-deviation-stddev.title: Standard Deviation (STDDEV)
standard-deviation-stddev.summary: The population standard deviation of the source over a rolling window, a direct measure of how widely recent values spread around their mean.
standard-deviation-stddev.descriptionHtml:
The study measures the spread of the last Period values of the source around their mean. It keeps a running sum and a running sum of squares, removing the value that leaves the window before adding the new one, and computes the population standard deviation as the square root of the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

There is no warmup gap: until the window is full the deviation is taken over the values that exist, and a single value has a deviation of 0. An absent value counts as zero. Because it divides by the number of values rather than one less, this is the population form, slightly smaller than the sample form on a short window.
standard-deviation-stddev.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means recent values are spreading further from their mean, which is what volatility expansion looks like; a falling line means they are bunching together. A long stretch of low readings marks a quiet market; it says nothing about when the next larger move comes or which way it goes.

The value is in the same units as the source, so on price it is a distance in price. That makes it useful for sizing stops or bands, but it also means readings from instruments at very different prices are not comparable without scaling.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent values the deviation is taken over. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose spread is measured, the close by default.

faq.q: Is this the population or the sample standard deviation?
faq.html: The population form: it divides by the number of values, not by one less. On a long window the two are almost the same.

faq.q: Why does it start at zero?
faq.html: On the first bar there is only one value, and one value has no spread. After that the deviation is taken over the bars that exist until the window is full.

faq.q: How is it used in bands?
faq.html: Adding and subtracting a multiple of the standard deviation from a moving average gives volatility bands that widen in active markets and narrow in quiet ones.

related.title: Standard Error of Regression (STDERR)
related.summary: How far price scatters around its own least-squares trend line over a rolling window: low when price tracks the line, high when it wanders.

related.title: Spearman Rank Correlation (SPEARMAN)
related.summary: Correlation between the ranks of two series of the chart's symbol over a window: whether they move together in order, regardless of size.

related.title: Rolling Sum
related.summary: The total of the last N values of the source, kept with error compensation so the running total does not drift over a long history.

standard-error-of-regression-stderr.title: Standard Error of Regression (STDERR)
standard-error-of-regression-stderr.summary: How far price scatters around its own least-squares trend line over a rolling window: low when price tracks the line, high when it wanders.
standard-error-of-regression-stderr.descriptionHtml:
The study fits a straight line by least squares through the last Period values of the source, with the oldest value at x = 0 and the newest at the far end. It then measures each value's vertical distance from that line, squares the distances, adds them up, divides by the number of values minus two, and takes the square root. That is the standard error of the regression, the typical size of a residual around the fitted trend.

Until the window is full the regression runs over the values that exist, starting once there are at least three. An absent value counts as zero. The result is in the same units as the source.
standard-error-of-regression-stderr.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means price has been moving close to a straight line, an orderly trend or a quiet range. A high reading means it has been scattering away from its own trend, either because the trend is bending or because the market is choppy. A sharp rise after a calm stretch means price has moved away from the line it was tracking.

The standard error says nothing about direction or slope: a steep clean trend and a flat quiet range can read the same. Pair it with a regression line or a slope measure to see which way the trend runs.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent values the line is fitted through, at least 3. A longer period gives a steadier reading.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series the line is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from the standard deviation?
faq.html: The standard deviation measures spread around the mean, so a clean trend reads high. The standard error measures spread around the trend line, so a clean trend reads low.

faq.q: Why divide by the period minus two?
faq.html: Fitting a line uses up two degrees of freedom, its slope and its intercept, so the residuals are averaged over n - 2 rather than n.

faq.q: Why are the first two bars blank?
faq.html: A line through two points fits them exactly and has no residual to measure, so the study starts once the window holds three values.

related.title: Rolling Sum
related.summary: The total of the last N values of the source, kept with error compensation so the running total does not drift over a long history.

related.title: Standard Deviation (STDDEV)
related.summary: The population standard deviation of the source over a rolling window, a direct measure of how widely recent values spread around their mean.

related.title: Theil Index (THEIL)
related.summary: Measures how unevenly the last N values of a positive series are spread, from 0 when they are all equal upward as a few values dominate.

stochastic-oscillator-stoch.title: Stochastic Oscillator (STOCH)
stochastic-oscillator-stoch.summary: Places the close inside the high-low range of the last K bars as a 0 to 100 reading, with a simple average of it as the %D line.
stochastic-oscillator-stoch.descriptionHtml:
The Stochastic Oscillator asks where the close sits in its recent range. It finds the lowest low and highest high of the last K Length bars and works out how far up that range the close is, from 0 at the low to 100 at the high. That is the %K line. When the range is flat, %K reads 0. Until K Length bars exist, the range uses the bars seen so far.

The %D line is the simple mean of %K over the last D Smooth bars. On the first bar every slot of that average is filled with the first %K, and each later bar replaces the oldest slot, so %D answers from the first bar and settles into an ordinary moving average once the window has turned over.

A missing high or low is read as 0.
stochastic-oscillator-stoch.howToReadHtml:
A high reading means the close is near the top of its recent range and a low one near the bottom. Above 80 is usually read as overbought and below 20 as oversold, but in a trend the line can hold in those zones for many bars, and that persistence is itself a sign of strength. A cross of %K above %D is read as an early upturn, a cross below as an early downturn.

The raw %K line is quick and noisy, and in a sideways market the two lines cross often. Divergence, where price makes a new extreme that the oscillator does not, is a common way to read it.

settings.label: K Length
settings.html: How many bars the high-low range covers. A shorter window makes %K faster and noisier.

settings.label: D Smooth
settings.html: How many %K readings the %D line averages. A longer average gives a smoother, slower signal line.

faq.q: What do the two lines mean?
faq.html: %K is the close's position in its recent range. %D is a simple average of %K and acts as a signal line; crosses between the two are the usual signals.

faq.q: Why does %D start at the same value as %K?
faq.html: On the first bar every slot of the average holds the first %K, so %D equals it. As later bars arrive they replace the slots one at a time.

faq.q: Is a reading above 80 a sell signal?
faq.html: Not on its own. It says the close is near the top of its recent range, which is also what a strong uptrend looks like. Many traders wait for the line to fall back below 80 or for a cross of %D.

related.title: Stochastic Fast (STOCHF)
related.summary: The raw stochastic: where the close sits in the high-low range of the last K bars, with a D-bar average of it as the signal line.

related.title: Schaff Trend Cycle (STC)
related.summary: A MACD line put through two rounds of stochastic scaling, giving a 0 to 100 trend reading that turns faster than the MACD itself.

related.title: Stochastic RSI (STOCHRSI)
related.summary: A stochastic applied to the RSI: where the RSI sits inside its own recent range, smoothed into a %K line and a %D signal line.

stochastic-fast-stochf.title: Stochastic Fast (STOCHF)
stochastic-fast-stochf.summary: The raw stochastic: where the close sits in the high-low range of the last K bars, with a D-bar average of it as the signal line.
stochastic-fast-stochf.descriptionHtml:
The fast stochastic places the close inside the range of recent prices. It finds the lowest low and the highest high of the last K Length bars and works out how far up that range the close sits, from 0 at the low to 100 at the high. That raw reading is the Fast %K line, with no smoothing applied. When the range is flat the line reads 0.

The Fast %D line is the simple mean of %K over the last D Length bars.

Both windows use the bars seen so far until they are full, so the two lines answer from the first bar rather than waiting out a warmup. A missing high, low or close is read as 0.
stochastic-fast-stochf.howToReadHtml:
High readings mean the close is near the top of its recent range, low readings near the bottom. Above 80 is usually read as overbought and below 20 as oversold, but in a trend the line can stay in those zones for a long time. A cross of %K above %D is an early sign of an upturn, and a cross below of a downturn.

With no smoothing on %K the fast stochastic is jumpy and gives many crosses, most of them noise in a sideways market. Many traders prefer to read it alongside a trend tool, or to use the smoother stochastic for signals and the fast one for timing.

settings.label: K Length
settings.html: How many bars the high-low range covers. A shorter window makes %K more sensitive to every bar.

settings.label: D Length
settings.html: How many %K readings the signal line averages. A longer average gives a smoother, slower %D.

faq.q: How is this different from the slow stochastic?
faq.html: Here %K is the raw position of the close in its range, with no smoothing. The slow version smooths that reading first, so its lines move less and cross less often.

faq.q: Why does %K read 0 on some bars?
faq.html: When the highest high and the lowest low of the window are equal, which means every bar in it traded at one price, the range is zero and the position cannot be computed, so the line reads 0.

faq.q: Does it need a warmup?
faq.html: No. Until a full window exists, the range and the average use the bars seen so far, so both lines start on the first bar.

related.title: Stochastic RSI (STOCHRSI)
related.summary: A stochastic applied to the RSI: where the RSI sits inside its own recent range, smoothed into a %K line and a %D signal line.

related.title: Stochastic Oscillator (STOCH)
related.summary: Places the close inside the high-low range of the last K bars as a 0 to 100 reading, with a simple average of it as the %D line.

related.title: TD Sequential (TD_SEQ)
related.summary: Counts consecutive closes against the close a few bars back up to 9, then a slower countdown toward 13, to flag a move that may be exhausted.

stochastic-rsi-stochrsi.title: Stochastic RSI (STOCHRSI)
stochastic-rsi-stochrsi.summary: A stochastic applied to the RSI: where the RSI sits inside its own recent range, smoothed into a %K line and a %D signal line.
stochastic-rsi-stochrsi.descriptionHtml:
The Stochastic RSI first computes an RSI of the source. The up and down moves against the previous bar are smoothed with weight 1 / RSI Length; for the first RSI Length bars the smoothed move is simply that bar's move, so on those bars the RSI reads 100 when the source did not fall and 0 when it fell. The bar before the first one reads as 0, so the very first move is the whole source value.

It then finds the highest and lowest RSI over the last Stochastic Length bars and places the current RSI in that range from 0 to 100, reading 50 when the range is flat. That raw value is averaged over %K Smooth bars to give %K, and %K is averaged over %D Smooth bars to give %D.

Every window uses the bars seen so far until it is full, so both lines answer from the first bar.
stochastic-rsi-stochrsi.howToReadHtml:
The line shows whether the RSI is near the top or the bottom of its own recent range. It moves much faster than the RSI and spends a lot of time pinned near 0 or 100. Readings above 80 are usually read as overbought and below 20 as oversold; a cross of %K above %D from low readings is read as an upturn, and a cross below from high readings as a downturn.

Because it is a stochastic of an indicator rather than of price, small changes in the RSI can swing it across the full scale. Use it for timing inside a trend you have identified another way, not as a trend signal in itself. Ignore the start of the chart: for the first RSI Length bars the RSI is only ever 100 or 0, and those readings stay in the stochastic window for Stochastic Length bars after that.

settings.label: RSI Length
settings.html: The length of the RSI the stochastic is applied to. Shorter values make the RSI, and so the whole study, faster.

settings.label: Stochastic Length
settings.html: How many RSI readings the high-low range covers. A shorter window makes the line swing more.

settings.label: %K Smooth
settings.html: How many raw stochastic readings are averaged into %K. Higher values smooth out the jumps.

settings.label: %D Smooth
settings.html: How many %K readings are averaged into the %D signal line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the RSI is computed from, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it hit 0 and 100 so often?
faq.html: It measures the RSI against its own recent range, so every time the RSI makes a new high or low for the window the raw value is 100 or 0. Only the smoothing keeps %K and %D off the extremes.

faq.q: Why does it read 50 on some stretches?
faq.html: When the RSI has not changed across the whole window, its range is zero and the stochastic reads 50, the middle of the scale.

faq.q: Why do the first bars look odd?
faq.html: For the first RSI Length bars the smoothed up and down moves are just that bar's own move, so the RSI reads 100 on any bar that did not fall and 0 on a bar that fell, and the first bar compares the price with 0. The smoothing starts only after that, and the extreme readings stay in the stochastic window for another Stochastic Length bars, so the line settles after roughly RSI Length plus Stochastic Length bars.

related.title: TD Sequential (TD_SEQ)
related.summary: Counts consecutive closes against the close a few bars back up to 9, then a slower countdown toward 13, to flag a move that may be exhausted.

related.title: Stochastic Fast (STOCHF)
related.summary: The raw stochastic: where the close sits in the high-low range of the last K bars, with a D-bar average of it as the signal line.

related.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
related.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.

rolling-sum.title: Rolling Sum
rolling-sum.summary: The total of the last N values of the source, kept with error compensation so the running total does not drift over a long history.
rolling-sum.descriptionHtml:
The Rolling Sum study adds up the last Length values of the source. It keeps a running total, adding each new value as it arrives and subtracting the value that leaves the window, rather than adding the whole window again on every bar.

A running total built from many additions and subtractions slowly gathers rounding error. To stop that, the study carries two compensation terms that hold the part of each step lost to rounding and feed it back into the next one, a second-order compensated summation. The result stays accurate over thousands of bars.

The study answers from the first bar: before the window is full, the value is the total of however many values exist so far. An absent value counts as zero.
rolling-sum.howToReadHtml:
On a price source the rolling sum is the moving average multiplied by the length, so it has the same shape at a larger scale; its main use is as a building block, or on a series where the total itself means something. The Source menu offers only price series, so totalling volume or a series of changes means editing the script to sum that series instead.

The first Length bars climb steeply because the window is still filling, so ignore that stretch when reading the level.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many recent values are added together.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series being totalled, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

faq.q: Why does the line rise steeply at the start?
faq.html: Before the window is full the study totals however many values exist, so each early bar adds a value without removing one.

faq.q: What does the error compensation do?
faq.html: Adding and subtracting values over a long history leaves small rounding errors in the total. The study keeps track of what was lost on each step and adds it back, so the total stays within rounding of a fresh sum of the window.

faq.q: How is it related to a simple moving average?
faq.html: Once the window is full, the rolling sum divided by the length is the simple moving average of the same values.

related.title: Theil Index (THEIL)
related.summary: Measures how unevenly the last N values of a positive series are spread, from 0 when they are all equal upward as a few values dominate.

related.title: Standard Error of Regression (STDERR)
related.summary: How far price scatters around its own least-squares trend line over a rolling window: low when price tracks the line, high when it wanders.

related.title: TRIM: Trimmed Mean Moving Average
related.summary: Sorts the last N closes, drops a set percentage from each end and averages the middle, so single spikes cannot drag the line.

supertrend.title: SuperTrend
supertrend.summary: A trailing line set a multiple of average true range away from the bar midpoint, which flips sides when the close breaks through it.
supertrend.descriptionHtml:
SuperTrend builds two bands around the midpoint of each bar, the average of its high and low. Each band sits Multiplier times the average true range away from the midpoint. The average true range is a Wilder average of true range started from zero and scaled up by the factor that zero start leaves out, so it answers from the first bar. On the first bar the previous close is read as zero, which makes that bar's range very wide.

The bands only tighten toward price. The upper band moves down when the new basic band is lower, and the lower band moves up when the new basic band is higher; either one resets to the basic band when the previous close broke through it. The trend turns up when the close rises above the upper band and down when it falls below the lower band.

In an uptrend the line shows the lower band in green; in a downtrend it shows the upper band in red. A BUY label marks each turn up and a SELL label each turn down, and the first bar always carries one.
supertrend.howToReadHtml:
Green means the close has been holding above a trailing support, red that it has been holding below a trailing resistance. The line is often used as a trailing stop: it follows price in the direction of the trend and never moves against it until it flips. A BUY or SELL label marks the bar where the close crossed the line and the side changed.

In a sideways market the line flips often and each flip comes after the move, so the labels lag. A larger multiplier gives fewer and later flips, a smaller one more and earlier flips. The first stretch of bars is shaped by the very wide first range, so read the line once it has settled.

settings.label: ATR Period
settings.html: The length of the average true range that sizes the bands. A longer period gives steadier bands.

settings.label: Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges the bands sit from the bar midpoint. A larger value means fewer, later flips.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: Kept as a setting, but the bands are built from the high, low and close whatever it is set to.

faq.q: Why is there a BUY label on the first bar?
faq.html: The trend starts as up, and the direction on the first bar is compared with no previous direction, so it always counts as a change.

faq.q: Why does the Source setting change nothing?
faq.html: The calculation uses the bar's high, low and close directly. The setting is kept so the study's settings match its usual layout, but it is not read.

faq.q: Can the line move against the trend?
faq.html: No. While the trend holds, the support line can only rise and the resistance line can only fall. It only jumps when the trend flips or when the previous close broke through the band.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.

related.title: RAVI: Chande Range Action Verification Index
related.summary: The percentage gap between a fast and a slow simple average of the close, read against a threshold to separate trends from ranges.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A slope-coloured short exponential average with a faint ribbon whose width is the slope as a percentage, and triangles at each turn.

swing-high-low-detection.title: Swing High/Low Detection
swing-high-low-detection.summary: Finds bars whose high or low is the extreme of the bars on both sides and holds the latest swing high and swing low as two horizontal lines.
swing-high-low-detection.descriptionHtml:
A swing high is a bar whose value is not exceeded by any bar within Lookback Period bars on either side of it, and a swing low is a bar whose value is not undercut by any bar within that distance. A tie with a neighbour does not disqualify a bar. The high test reads Source High and the low test reads Source Low, which default to each bar's high and low.

A swing can only be confirmed once the bars after it have printed, so on each bar the study tests the bar that many bars back. When it qualifies, its value becomes the latest swing high or swing low. The two lines hold that value until a newer swing is confirmed, so they step to a new level on the bar that confirms it, not on the swing bar itself.
swing-high-low-detection.howToReadHtml:
The red line is the most recent confirmed swing high and the green line the most recent confirmed swing low. Together they frame the current swing structure: a close above the red line breaks the last swing high and a close below the green line breaks the last swing low, which many traders read as a change in the short-term trend.

Every swing is confirmed Lookback Period bars late, so the lines show where the market turned, not where it is turning. A larger lookback finds fewer, more significant swings and confirms them later.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars on each side a swing must stand above or below. A larger value finds fewer, bigger swings and confirms them later.

settings.label: Source High
settings.html: The price series tested for swing highs, normally the bar's high. Choose the close to find swings in closing prices only.

settings.label: Source Low
settings.html: The price series tested for swing lows, normally the bar's low. Choose the close to find swings in closing prices only.

settings.label: Show Swing High Lines
settings.html: Draw the line holding the latest confirmed swing high.

settings.label: Show Swing Low Lines
settings.html: Draw the line holding the latest confirmed swing low.

faq.q: Why does the line change several bars after the swing?
faq.html: A swing is only known once Lookback Period bars have printed after it. The study changes the line on the bar that confirms the swing, so nothing drawn earlier is ever revised.

faq.q: Why is there no line at the start of the chart?
faq.html: The first bar tested is the one Lookback Period bars after the start, and it can only be judged once the same number of bars have printed after it, so nothing is confirmed before bar number twice the lookback (counting from zero). The line then stays empty until the first swing is found.

faq.q: Can two bars at the same price both be swings?
faq.html: Yes. A neighbour equal to the candidate does not disqualify it, so two equal highs within the lookback can both count, and the later one sets the line.

related.title: TTM Scalper Alert
related.summary: Marks every three-bar pivot: a bar whose high tops both neighbours, or whose low sits under both, as short-term turning points.

related.title: Parabolic SAR
related.summary: A trailing stop and reverse line that accelerates toward price as a trend makes new extremes, and flips to the other side when price trades through it.

related.title: Pivot Points (Woodie)
related.summary: A pivot that weights the previous close twice, with three supports and three resistances built from the previous day, week or month.

swma-symmetric-weighted-moving-average.title: SWMA: Symmetric Weighted Moving Average
swma-symmetric-weighted-moving-average.summary: A moving average of the close with triangular weights, so the bars in the middle of the window count most and the ends count least.
swma-symmetric-weighted-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The Symmetric Weighted Moving Average averages the close over the last period bars with weights shaped like a triangle. With half = (period - 1) / 2, the bar k bars back weighs half + 1 - |k - half|: the middle bar weighs most, and the weights fall off evenly toward the newest and the oldest bar. The weighted sum is divided by the total of the weights.

A triangle of weights is what you get by smoothing with a simple average twice, so it removes more short-term noise than a single simple average of the same length. The line starts once period bars exist and always uses the close.
swma-symmetric-weighted-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a smooth trend line. It is calmer than a simple average of the same length, so a turn in the line is less likely to be a single noisy bar. Price holding above a rising line describes an uptrend, and below a falling line a downtrend.

The weights peak in the middle of the window, so the line describes prices centred about half bars ago and lags by that much. Shorter periods follow price closely; longer ones show only the broad swing.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the triangle spans. A longer period smooths more and lags more.

faq.q: Why are the middle bars weighted most?
faq.html: The triangle puts its peak at the centre of the window. That shape filters short noise better than equal weights, at the cost of a lag of about half the window.

faq.q: Can I choose a different price than the close?
faq.html: No. The calculation is fixed to the close, so there is no source setting.

faq.q: When does the line appear?
faq.html: Once period bars exist. Before that the oldest tap has no bar to read, so nothing is drawn.

related.title: Tillson T3 Moving Average (T3)
related.summary: Six chained exponential averages blended by a volume factor into a smooth line with much less lag than its smoothing would suggest.

related.title: SP15: Spencer 15-Point Moving Average
related.summary: A fixed 15-bar weighted average of the close, with weights chosen so that cycles four and five bars long are removed rather than only damped.

related.title: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA)
related.summary: Three chained exponential averages combined as 3 x EMA1 - 3 x EMA2 + EMA3, which removes most of the lag of a single EMA.

tillson-t3-moving-average-t3.title: Tillson T3 Moving Average (T3)
tillson-t3-moving-average-t3.summary: Six chained exponential averages blended by a volume factor into a smooth line with much less lag than its smoothing would suggest.
tillson-t3-moving-average-t3.descriptionHtml:
T3 runs the source through six exponential averages in a row, all with a smoothing factor of two over the period plus one. It then blends the last four stages with weights built from the volume factor v: -v^3 on the sixth, 3(v^2 + v^3) on the fifth, -3(2v^2 + v + v^3) on the fourth and 1 + 3v + 3v^2 + v^3 on the third. The weights add up to one, so the line stays on the price scale.

All six stages are seeded with the first source value, and that value is drawn on the first bar, so the line has no warmup gap. The volume factor controls the trade between smoothness and lag: at zero the output is the third stage alone, and as it rises toward one the blend pushes the line closer to price.
tillson-t3-moving-average-t3.howToReadHtml:
T3 is read as a smooth trend line that stays close to price. Price above a rising T3 describes an uptrend and price below a falling T3 a downtrend; the line's direction changes less often than a plain EMA of the same responsiveness, so its turns tend to be cleaner.

A higher volume factor makes the line faster and can make it overshoot after a sharp move; a lower one makes it smoother and slower. The six stages also mean the earliest bars still carry the seed value heavily, so give the line some bars before reading it.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing factor of all six stages. A larger period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Volume Factor
settings.html: Sets the blend of the last four stages, between 0 and 1. Higher values reduce lag and allow more overshoot.

faq.q: Does the volume factor use trading volume?
faq.html: No. It is only a weight between 0 and 1 that sets how the stages are blended. The study never reads volume.

faq.q: What does a volume factor of zero give?
faq.html: The weights collapse to one on the third stage, so the line is three chained exponential averages, smooth but slower.

faq.q: Why does the line start exactly at price?
faq.html: All six stages are seeded with the first source value, and that value is drawn on the first bar.

related.title: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA)
related.summary: Three chained exponential averages combined as 3 x EMA1 - 3 x EMA2 + EMA3, which removes most of the lag of a single EMA.

related.title: SWMA: Symmetric Weighted Moving Average
related.summary: A moving average of the close with triangular weights, so the bars in the middle of the window count most and the ends count least.

related.title: TRAMA: Trend Regularity Adaptive Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average that moves fast while new highs or new lows keep printing and slows to a halt when the range stops expanding.

hyperbolic-tangent-tanh.title: Hyperbolic Tangent (TANH)
hyperbolic-tangent-tanh.summary: Squashes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the hyperbolic tangent, giving an oscillator between -1 and +1.
hyperbolic-tangent-tanh.descriptionHtml:
The Hyperbolic Tangent study takes the distance between the source and its 200-bar simple moving average, multiplies it by a steepness factor k, and passes the result through the hyperbolic tangent. The output is tanh(k * (source - SMA200)), which is 0 when price sits on its average, approaches +1 when price is far above it and approaches -1 when price is far below it.

The tangent is computed in a form that cannot overflow: with e = exp(-2|y|), the magnitude is (1 - e) / (1 + e), signed like y. Far from the average this is exactly plus or minus one. The 200-bar average needs 200 bars of history, so the line starts on bar 200.
hyperbolic-tangent-tanh.howToReadHtml:
Read the zero line as price at its long average. Positive values mean price is above it and negative values mean below, with the size of the value showing how stretched it is. Near the middle the curve is almost straight, so small distances are shown in proportion, while large distances are compressed against the limits of -1 and +1.

The distance is in price units, so the useful steepness depends on the instrument's price level. If the line spends most of its time at -1 or +1, lower k. The midpoint is a slow 200-bar average, so the study shows where price stands against its long trend rather than short-term swings.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series compared with its own 200-bar simple moving average.

settings.label: Steepness (k)
settings.html: Multiplies the distance from the average before the tangent is applied. A higher value makes the curve steeper around the zero line, so it saturates sooner.

faq.q: How is this different from the logistic sigmoid?
faq.html: Both are S-shaped. The hyperbolic tangent runs from -1 to +1 with 0 at the average, while the logistic curve runs from 0 to 1 with 0.5 at the average. For the same input, tanh(y) equals 2 * sigmoid(2y) - 1.

faq.q: Why does the line start late?
faq.html: The inflection point is a 200-bar simple moving average, which has no value until 200 bars of history exist.

faq.q: Why is the line flat at +1 or -1?
faq.html: The distance from the average is large compared with 1 / k, so the curve is saturated. Lower the steepness to bring the line back into its working range.

related.title: Student's t-Distribution CDF (TDIST)
related.summary: Maps where price sits in its recent range onto a heavy-tailed probability scale from 0 to 1 using the Student's t cumulative distribution.

related.title: Standardization (Z-score)
related.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.

related.title: Weibull Distribution CDF (WEIBULLDIST)
related.summary: Places price within its recent high-low range and reads that position through the Weibull cumulative distribution, giving a value from 0 to 1.

td-sequential-td-seq.title: TD Sequential (TD_SEQ)
td-sequential-td-seq.summary: Counts consecutive closes against the close a few bars back up to 9, then a slower countdown toward 13, to flag a move that may be exhausted.
td-sequential-td-seq.descriptionHtml:
TD Sequential is a counting system in two phases. The setup compares each close with the close comparePeriod bars earlier. A close above it extends a positive count, a close below it extends a negative count, and an equal close resets the count to zero. A count that flips direction starts again from plus or minus 1, and the count is capped at plus or minus 9.

When the setup first reaches 9 or -9, a countdown opens in the same direction. Unlike the setup it does not need consecutive bars: it steps by one only on bars where the close is above the high of two bars earlier (for an up countdown) or below the low of two bars earlier (for a down countdown). It stops at plus or minus 13, and a completed setup in the opposite direction restarts it the other way. The setup is drawn as a histogram and the countdown as a line, with reference levels at 0, plus or minus 9 and plus or minus 13.
td-sequential-td-seq.howToReadHtml:
A setup bar reaching +9 means nine closes in a row above the close four bars earlier, a stretched advance; -9 is the same for a decline. Traders read a completed setup as a sign that the move is mature, not as an order to trade against it.

The countdown line then tracks whether the move keeps making progress. A countdown reaching +13 or -13 is the stronger exhaustion reading, and the line holds at that value until a new setup restarts it. Both counts describe how extended a move is; neither says where it will turn, and a strong trend can complete several setups in a row.

settings.label: Compare Period
settings.html: How many bars back each close is compared with during the setup. A shorter gap makes setups complete more often; a longer one demands a more sustained move.

faq.q: What resets the setup count?
faq.html: A close equal to the close comparePeriod bars earlier resets it to zero, and a close on the other side starts a new count from plus or minus 1 in the opposite direction.

faq.q: Why does the countdown move more slowly than the setup?
faq.html: It steps only on bars that close beyond the high or low of two bars earlier, and the bars in between do not have to qualify. A countdown can take many more bars than 13 to complete.

faq.q: Why does the countdown line stay flat at 13 or -13?
faq.html: Once it reaches 13 the countdown is complete and stops counting. The line keeps that value until a new setup in either direction starts a fresh countdown from zero.

related.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
related.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.

related.title: Stochastic RSI (STOCHRSI)
related.summary: A stochastic applied to the RSI: where the RSI sits inside its own recent range, smoothed into a %K line and a %D signal line.

related.title: TRIX
related.summary: The one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential moving average, a slow momentum line that crosses zero when the smoothed trend turns.

student-s-t-distribution-cdf-tdist.title: Student's t-Distribution CDF (TDIST)
student-s-t-distribution-cdf-tdist.summary: Maps where price sits in its recent range onto a heavy-tailed probability scale from 0 to 1 using the Student's t cumulative distribution.
student-s-t-distribution-cdf-tdist.descriptionHtml:
This study first finds where the source sits inside the highest and lowest values of the lookback window, as a fraction from 0 at the low to 1 at the high. A flat window counts as 0.5. That fraction is centred and stretched into a t-statistic running from -3 to 3, which is read through the cumulative distribution of Student's t with the chosen degrees of freedom. The output is a probability between 0 and 1.

The distribution is evaluated through the regularized incomplete beta function, computed with a continued fraction. That continued fraction starts at its first even term, so the result runs a few percent from the textbook value and is pushed slightly towards the extremes. Until a full window exists, the bars before the first one count as zero, which widens the early range to include zero.
student-s-t-distribution-cdf-tdist.howToReadHtml:
Readings near 0.5 put price in the middle of its recent range. Readings above the 0.95 line mean price is pressing the top of the range, and readings below 0.05 mean it is pressing the bottom. The degrees of freedom control how sharply the curve reacts: low values give heavy tails and a gentler response near the edges, high values approach the normal curve and saturate sooner.

The output describes position within a window, not momentum. In a strong trend it can stay near 1 or 0 for long stretches, so treat the extreme lines as context rather than reversal signals.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the highest and lowest values are taken over. A longer period gives a wider, slower range.

settings.label: Degrees of Freedom
settings.html: Tail weight of the distribution. Lower values give heavier tails and a softer curve; higher values approach the normal distribution.

faq.q: Why does the early part of the chart look different?
faq.html: Until a full window of bars exists, the bars before the first one count as zero, so the range is stretched down to zero and price reads near the top of it.

faq.q: What do the degrees of freedom change?
faq.html: They set how heavy the tails are. At 1 the curve is very flat in the tails, while large values make it behave like the normal curve and push readings towards 0 or 1 faster.

faq.q: Is the probability exact?
faq.html: Not quite. The continued fraction used here skips its leading term, so the result is a few percent away from the textbook value and slightly more extreme.

related.title: Weibull Distribution CDF (WEIBULLDIST)
related.summary: Places price within its recent high-low range and reads that position through the Weibull cumulative distribution, giving a value from 0 to 1.

related.title: Hyperbolic Tangent (TANH)
related.summary: Squashes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the hyperbolic tangent, giving an oscillator between -1 and +1.

related.title: Standardization (Z-score)
related.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.

triple-exponential-moving-average-tema.title: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA)
triple-exponential-moving-average-tema.summary: Three chained exponential averages combined as 3 x EMA1 - 3 x EMA2 + EMA3, which removes most of the lag of a single EMA.
triple-exponential-moving-average-tema.descriptionHtml:
TEMA reduces the lag of an exponential moving average by combining three of them. The first EMA smooths the source, the second smooths the first, and the third smooths the second, all with the same smoothing factor of two over the period plus one. The result is three times the first, minus three times the second, plus the third. The repeated smoothing cancels most of the delay a single EMA carries while keeping much of its smoothness.

Each stage starts at zero. During warmup every stage is divided by its own correction, one minus (1 - alpha) raised to the number of bars seen, so the line starts at the source on the first bar instead of rising slowly from zero. Once (1 - alpha) raised to the bars seen falls below 1e-10, the corrections are dropped and the stages run as plain recursions.
triple-exponential-moving-average-tema.howToReadHtml:
TEMA hugs price much more closely than an EMA of the same period, so it turns earlier at swing points which suits a reader who wants a fast but still smooth trend line. Price above a rising TEMA describes an uptrend, price below a falling one a downtrend.

The lag reduction has a cost. On sharp moves TEMA can overshoot price briefly, and in a choppy market it turns often. A longer period calms it, at the expense of some of the speed that is the reason to use it.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the smoothing factor shared by all three stages. A larger period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Is TEMA the same as an EMA applied three times?
faq.html: No. Three chained EMAs alone would lag even more. TEMA combines the three stages as 3 x EMA1 - 3 x EMA2 + EMA3, which cancels most of that lag.

faq.q: Why can TEMA move beyond price?
faq.html: The combination extrapolates the trend, so after a fast move it can briefly overshoot the latest price before the stages catch up.

faq.q: Why does the line appear from the first bar?
faq.html: Each stage is divided by a warmup correction that removes the effect of starting at zero, so the first value equals the source.

related.title: TRAMA: Trend Regularity Adaptive Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average that moves fast while new highs or new lows keep printing and slows to a halt when the range stops expanding.

related.title: Tillson T3 Moving Average (T3)
related.summary: Six chained exponential averages blended by a volume factor into a smooth line with much less lag than its smoothing would suggest.

related.title: Triangular Moving Average (TRIMA)
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights peak in the middle of the window, smoother than a simple average of the same length.

theil-index-theil.title: Theil Index (THEIL)
theil-index-theil.summary: Measures how unevenly the last N values of a positive series are spread, from 0 when they are all equal upward as a few values dominate.
theil-index-theil.descriptionHtml:
The Theil index is an entropy measure of inequality. Over the lookback window it takes the mean of the positive values, divides each value by that mean to get a ratio, and averages ratio * ln(ratio) across the window. When every value equals the mean, each ratio is 1, its logarithm is 0, and the index is 0. The further the window is from even, the higher the reading.

Only values above zero take part: a value that is absent, zero or negative is left out of both the mean and the count, which is why the source must be positive. The window grows from the first bar until it holds the full lookback, so the line answers from the start of the chart. On price, which moves only a small fraction of its level within a window, the readings are small numbers; on volume they are much larger, because volume is far less even from bar to bar.
theil-index-theil.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a measure of how lopsided the recent values are. A reading near zero means the window is calm and every value sits close to the average. A rise means a few values have pulled away from the rest, for example a sharp move in price or a burst of volume on one or two bars. A falling line means the window is evening out again.

The index has no direction: a spike up and a spike down both raise it. Multiplying the whole series by a constant leaves it unchanged, but it depends on how much the series varies relative to its own level, so compare readings on the same source and lookback.

settings.label: Source (must be positive values)
settings.html: The series whose spread is measured. Values at or below zero are skipped, so use a positive series such as a price or volume.

settings.label: Lookback Period
settings.html: How many bars the window holds. A longer window reacts more slowly and averages out single spikes.

faq.q: Why is the reading so small on price?
faq.html: Within a few bars price rarely moves more than a percent or two from its own average, so every ratio is close to 1 and ratio * ln(ratio) is tiny. The index is more expressive on uneven series such as volume.

faq.q: What happens to zero or negative values?
faq.html: They are skipped. The mean and the final average are taken over the positive values only, so a window with no positive value draws nothing.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is going up?
faq.html: No. The index measures unevenness, not direction. A sharp fall raises it just as a sharp rise does.

related.title: TRIM: Trimmed Mean Moving Average
related.summary: Sorts the last N closes, drops a set percentage from each end and averages the middle, so single spikes cannot drag the line.

related.title: Rolling Sum
related.summary: The total of the last N values of the source, kept with error compensation so the running total does not drift over a long history.

related.title: Variance, Dispersion or Spread (VARIANCE)
related.summary: The population variance of the source over the lookback, showing how widely price has been spread around its own mean.

theil-s-u-statistic-theilu.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
theil-s-u-statistic-theilu.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.
theil-s-u-statistic-theilu.descriptionHtml:
Theil's U Statistic compares a predicted series with an actual series over a rolling window and scales the error so the reading does not depend on the price level. On every bar it squares the forecast error (predicted minus actual), squares the actual value and squares the predicted value. Each of the three is totalled over the last Length bars.

The statistic is the square root of the error total divided by the square root of the actual total plus the predicted total. A window where both series are effectively zero has nothing to scale by and reads 0. An absent value on either side is read as zero before squaring.
theil-s-u-statistic-theilu.howToReadHtml:
Zero means the predicted series matched the actual one on every bar of the window. The further the reading climbs toward 1, the larger the misses are compared with the size of the series themselves. The dashed line at 1 marks a forecast that is no better than a naive one, and the line at 0 marks a perfect forecast.

On price series the two values are large and close together, so readings sit very near zero and the useful information is in the changes: a rising line means the predicted series is drifting further from the actual one. The line has no value until Length bars have passed.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the squared values are totalled over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: Why are the readings so close to zero on a price chart?
faq.html: The denominator is the size of the two series themselves. On an instrument trading in the thousands, a miss of a few points is tiny by comparison, so the ratio is small. Compare readings over time rather than against 1.

faq.q: Does the price level change the reading?
faq.html: No. Both the error and the scale are in the same units, so doubling every price leaves the statistic unchanged.

faq.q: What are the two dashed lines?
faq.html: The line at 0 is a perfect forecast and the line at 1 is the level of a naive forecast that adds no information.

related.title: Tukey's Biweight Loss (TukeyBiweight)
related.summary: A rolling average of the bisquare loss between an actual and a predicted series, a robust error score that caps the cost of any outlier.

related.title: Symmetric Mean Absolute %Error (SMAPE)
related.summary: The average symmetric percentage gap between price and its own exponential average, a bounded error score that treats overshoot and undershoot alike.

related.title: Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: Total absolute forecast error over a rolling window as a percentage of the total absolute actual value, steady where a plain percentage error is not.

true-range.title: True Range
true-range.summary: Measures each bar's full movement, the bar's own range widened to include any gap from the previous close.
true-range.descriptionHtml:
True range is the full size of a bar's move. The plain range, high minus low, misses the move that happened between bars: if a market closes at 100 and the next bar opens at 104 and trades between 104 and 106, the range is 2 but price actually travelled 6 from where it last stood.

The study takes the greatest of three distances on every bar: the high minus the low, the distance from the high to the previous close, and the distance from the low to the previous close. The first bar has no previous close, so its true range is simply its high minus its low.

It is the raw input to the average true range and to many stop and channel tools, shown here bar by bar without any smoothing.
true-range.howToReadHtml:
Each point is one bar's movement in price units. Tall spikes mark bars that moved far, often news bars or gaps; a run of low readings marks a quiet, compressed market.

Because it is not smoothed, the line is noisy. Read it for the size of individual bars, and compare a bar to its neighbours rather than to a fixed number, since the scale depends on the instrument's price.

faq.q: Why is true range different from high minus low?
faq.html: It also counts the gap from the previous close. On a bar that opens away from the last close, the move across the gap is included, so true range is never smaller than the plain range.

faq.q: What happens on the first bar?
faq.html: There is no previous close to compare with, so the first bar's true range is its high minus its low.

faq.q: How does it relate to the average true range?
faq.html: The average true range is a smoothed average of this series. This study shows the unsmoothed value of every bar.

related.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
related.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.

related.title: Relative Volatility Index (RVI)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator built on standard deviation, showing whether volatility is arriving on rising or falling bars.

related.title: Volatility of Volatility (VOV)
related.summary: The standard deviation of a rolling standard deviation, rising when the market's volatility is itself changing quickly.

trama-trend-regularity-adaptive-moving-a.title: TRAMA: Trend Regularity Adaptive Moving Average
trama-trend-regularity-adaptive-moving-a.summary: An adaptive average that moves fast while new highs or new lows keep printing and slows to a halt when the range stops expanding.
trama-trend-regularity-adaptive-moving-a.descriptionHtml:
TRAMA measures how regularly the market is making new extremes and uses that as its speed. On each bar it checks whether the highest high of the last period bars has risen or the lowest low has fallen. A bar where either happened counts as one, any other bar as zero. The simple average of those counts over the same period, squared, is the smoothing factor.

The average then steps toward the close by that factor: ama = ama[1] + tc x (close - ama[1]). When new extremes print on most bars the factor is near one and the line follows the close closely; when the range stops expanding the factor drops toward zero and the line flattens. Until the regularity measure has a full window there is no factor to step with: the line starts at the close on the first bar, has no value on the next, restarts at the close on the bar after that, and so on, so no continuous line appears until the window is full.
trama-trend-regularity-adaptive-moving-a.howToReadHtml:
A steep TRAMA that tracks price closely describes a market that keeps extending to new highs or lows, which is a regular trend. A flat TRAMA describes a market inside its recent range, where the line deliberately ignores the back and forth.

Price breaking away from a flat TRAMA suggests the range is expanding again; the line will start to follow once new extremes accumulate in the window. Because the factor is squared, the line reacts only weakly until a good share of recent bars set new extremes.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The window used for both the highest high and lowest low and for averaging how often they change. Longer periods react more slowly.

faq.q: Why is the regularity squared?
faq.html: Squaring keeps the factor small unless new extremes are frequent. A market setting new extremes on half the bars gets a factor of 0.25, not 0.5, so the line stays calm until the trend is clearly regular.

faq.q: Why is there no continuous line on the first bars?
