faq.html: The smoothing factor needs a full window of bars. Before that, a bar after a value has no value, and a bar after a gap restarts at the close, so the warmup alternates between the close and a gap. After the warmup the line is continuous.

faq.q: Which prices does it use?
faq.html: The high and low decide whether a new extreme was set, and the close is the value the average moves toward.

related.title: Triangular Moving Average (TRIMA)
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights peak in the middle of the window, smoother than a simple average of the same length.

related.title: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA)
related.summary: Three chained exponential averages combined as 3 x EMA1 - 3 x EMA2 + EMA3, which removes most of the lag of a single EMA.

related.title: Time Series Forecast
related.summary: Fits a straight line through recent prices and reads it at the newest bar or a set number of bars beyond it, so the line can run ahead of price.

ehlers-trendflex-indicator-trendflex.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
ehlers-trendflex-indicator-trendflex.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.
ehlers-trendflex-indicator-trendflex.descriptionHtml:
TRENDFLEX measures how strongly a smoothed price is moving in one direction. The source is first passed through a two-pole smoothing filter tuned to half the period. On the first two bars the filter passes the price straight through.

On each bar the study adds up the distance from the filtered value now to each of its last values over the period (fewer on the opening bars, while the history is still short) and divides by the period. When the filtered price has been rising, all those distances are positive and the sum is large; when it has been falling, the sum is large and negative.

That sum is then divided by the square root of an exponential mean of its own square, with a weight of 0.04, so the output reads in units of its own recent spread and the same levels mean the same thing on any instrument. A missing source value enters the filter as zero and is blanked on the plot.
ehlers-trendflex-indicator-trendflex.howToReadHtml:
Above zero the smoothed price sits above where it has been over the period, which is an uptrend; below zero it is a downtrend. The further from zero, the more one-sided the move compared with recent behaviour. A turn back toward zero shows the trend losing strength, and a crossing of zero shows it changing direction.

Because the output is scaled by its own recent spread, a long quiet spell can make a modest move read large. Use the period to match the length of trend you care about: short periods follow swings, long periods follow the broader move.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars the distances are measured over. The smoothing filter is tuned to half of it.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter reads. A missing value enters the filter as zero.

faq.q: How is this different from a cycle oscillator on the same filter?
faq.html: This one compares the filtered value with each past value directly, so a steady trend gives a steady positive or negative reading. A cycle oscillator compares it with a straight line through the window, which removes the trend.

faq.q: Why does the line open at zero and then near plus or minus 5?
faq.html: On the first bar there is no earlier filtered value, so the sum is zero. On the second bar the mean square, which starts from zero, holds only 0.04 times the first sum squared, so the sum divided by its square root is plus or minus 5. The opening bars are a settling stretch until the mean square has built up.

faq.q: Is there an overbought level?
faq.html: There is no fixed one. The output is scaled by its own recent spread, so readings beyond about plus or minus one are stronger than usual, but how far they can run depends on the market.

related.title: TRIX
related.summary: The one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential moving average, a slow momentum line that crosses zero when the smoothed trend turns.

related.title: TD Sequential (TD_SEQ)
related.summary: Counts consecutive closes against the close a few bars back up to 9, then a slower countdown toward 13, to flag a move that may be exhausted.

related.title: Ultimate Oscillator (ULTOSC)
related.summary: Buying pressure summed against true range over a fast, a medium and a slow window, blended by weight into one reading from 0 to 100.

trim-trimmed-mean-moving-average.title: TRIM: Trimmed Mean Moving Average
trim-trimmed-mean-moving-average.summary: Sorts the last N closes, drops a set percentage from each end and averages the middle, so single spikes cannot drag the line.
trim-trimmed-mean-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The trimmed mean takes the closes in the lookback window, sorts them from lowest to highest, discards the lowest and highest trim percent, and averages what is left. The number dropped from each end is the period times the trim percentage, rounded down, so with a period of 20 and a trim of 10 percent the two lowest and two highest closes are thrown away and the middle sixteen are averaged.

A trim of 0 keeps every value and gives a plain simple average. As the trim grows toward 49 percent, fewer middle values remain and the line moves toward the median. Closes before the start of the chart are read as zero, so the line is drawn from the first bar and climbs to price over the first period of bars; read it from the point where a full window of real closes is available.
trim-trimmed-mean-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read the line like a moving average that ignores outliers. A single wick or one wild close moves a simple average, but here it lands in the trimmed tail and is discarded, so the line holds its course. Price crossing the line, or the line turning, carries the same meaning as with any moving average, with fewer false turns caused by one bar.

The cost is that a genuine sharp move takes longer to register, because its first bars are treated as outliers. Ignore the first period of bars, where the zero padding pulls the line below price.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many closes the window holds. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Trim %
settings.html: The share of values dropped from each end of the sorted window. 0 gives a simple average; higher values move the line toward the median.

faq.q: Why does the line start near zero?
faq.html: Before a full window of closes exists, the missing values are read as zero and sorted into the low end of the window. Once no more zeros remain than the number trimmed from each end, they are all discarded and the line averages real closes only; with the defaults (period 20, trim 10) that is from the 18th bar.

faq.q: What trim makes it a median?
faq.html: As the trim approaches 49 percent only the central one or two values remain, which is close to the median of the window. The setting stops at 49 so at least one value is always kept.

faq.q: How is this different from the winsorized mean?
faq.html: The trimmed mean throws the extreme values away and averages fewer values. The winsorized mean keeps every slot but replaces the extremes with the boundary value, so it still averages the full window.

related.title: Variance, Dispersion or Spread (VARIANCE)
related.summary: The population variance of the source over the lookback, showing how widely price has been spread around its own mean.

related.title: Theil Index (THEIL)
related.summary: Measures how unevenly the last N values of a positive series are spread, from 0 when they are all equal upward as a few values dominate.

related.title: Weighted Average (WAVG)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average kept with running sums, with the newest bar weighted most and a value from the very first bar.

triangular-moving-average-trima.title: Triangular Moving Average (TRIMA)
triangular-moving-average-trima.summary: A weighted average whose weights peak in the middle of the window, smoother than a simple average of the same length.
triangular-moving-average-trima.descriptionHtml:
The Triangular Moving Average weights each bar in the window by its distance from the nearer edge. The newest and oldest bars carry a weight of 1, the next ones in carry 2, and so on up to the middle of the window, where the weight peaks. The weighted prices are added up and divided by the sum of the weights.

Because the middle of the window counts most, the average behaves like a simple average of a simple average: very smooth, but with more lag than a simple average of the same period. Over the first bars the window is simply the bars that exist, so the line is drawn from the very first bar and reaches its full length after Period bars.
triangular-moving-average-trima.howToReadHtml:
Use it as a slow, clean trend line. Price above a rising TRIMA describes an uptrend and price below a falling one a downtrend. Its smoothness makes its slope a steady read of direction, and crossings of price through it are less frequent than with a simple average.

The cost is lag. The weight is centred on the middle of the window, so the line reflects prices from about half a period ago and turns late after a sharp reversal. The first few bars use a shorter window and are less reliable.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the window. Longer is smoother and lags more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does it lag more than a simple moving average?
faq.html: The heaviest weights sit in the middle of the window rather than at the newest bar, so the line is centred about half a period back.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the very first bar?
faq.html: The window grows from one bar up to the full period, so early values are averages of the bars available so far rather than being left blank.

related.title: Time Series Forecast
related.summary: Fits a straight line through recent prices and reads it at the newest bar or a set number of bars beyond it, so the line can run ahead of price.

related.title: TRAMA: Trend Regularity Adaptive Moving Average
related.summary: An adaptive average that moves fast while new highs or new lows keep printing and slows to a halt when the range stops expanding.

related.title: TUKEY_W: Tukey (Tapered Cosine) Window MA
related.summary: An average of the close whose weights are flat through the middle of the window and taper off along a cosine curve at both ends.

trix.title: TRIX
trix.summary: The one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential moving average, a slow momentum line that crosses zero when the smoothed trend turns.
trix.descriptionHtml:
TRIX smooths the source three times with exponential moving averages of the same period, each one fed by the one before, and then reports the percentage change of the third average from one bar to the next. The triple smoothing removes most of the movement shorter than the period, so what is left is the slope of the underlying trend.

Each average starts from zero and is divided by a correction factor, one minus the decay raised to the number of bars seen, so all three read as the source from the first bar instead of climbing up from zero. The correction is dropped once it is smaller than one part in ten billion. On the first bar the previous value is the source itself, so the study reads zero.
trix.howToReadHtml:
TRIX above zero means the triple-smoothed price is rising, and below zero means it is falling. A cross of the zero line is the main reading: it marks a turn in the smoothed trend, and it comes later than a turn in price because of the smoothing.

The height of the line shows how fast the smoothed price is changing. A line that peaks and rolls over while still above zero shows the advance slowing. Because the values are small percentages, compare them on the same instrument and period rather than across different ones.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of each of the three exponential averages. A longer period removes more noise and turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is smoothed. The close is the default; a median or typical price includes more of each bar.

faq.q: Why smooth three times?
faq.html: Each pass removes more of the short swings. After three, little of the movement shorter than the period is left, so the rate of change reflects the slope of the smoothed trend rather than single bars. The cost is delay: each pass makes the line turn later.

faq.q: Why are the values so small?
faq.html: TRIX is a percentage change from one bar to the next of a heavily smoothed series. On an hourly chart that change is usually a small fraction of one percent.

faq.q: Does it have a warmup period?
faq.html: It answers from the first bar, because each average is corrected for its zero start. The earliest readings rest on very few bars, so give it a few multiples of the period before trusting a zero cross.

related.title: Ultimate Oscillator (ULTOSC)
related.summary: Buying pressure summed against true range over a fast, a medium and a slow window, blended by weight into one reading from 0 to 100.

related.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
related.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.

related.title: Williams %R (WILLR)
related.summary: Where the close sits inside the highest high and lowest low of the lookback window, on a scale from 0 at the top to -100 at the bottom.

time-series-forecast.title: Time Series Forecast
time-series-forecast.summary: Fits a straight line through recent prices and reads it at the newest bar or a set number of bars beyond it, so the line can run ahead of price.
time-series-forecast.descriptionHtml:
The Time Series Forecast fits a least squares straight line through the last Period values of the source. It then reads that line Forecast Periods - 1 bars past the newest bar of the window and plots the value it reaches there.

With the default forecast of 1 the plotted value is the end point of the fitted line at the newest bar, the same value a linear regression line gives. Each step above 1 reads the line one bar further ahead, so a forecast of 2 is where the fitted line puts the next bar. The first value appears once a full window of Period bars exists. The study also draws the source itself as a thin gray line, so the projection can be compared with the price it was fitted to.
time-series-forecast.howToReadHtml:
Read the gap between the forecast line and price. While price keeps pace with its recent slope the two stay close; when price falls behind the projection of an uptrend, or above the projection of a downtrend, the move is losing or gaining speed against its own recent pace. The slope of the forecast line itself shows the direction of the fitted trend.

The projection assumes the recent straight-line trend continues. At turning points it overshoots, because it keeps extending the old slope until enough new bars pull the fit round, and a longer forecast overshoots further.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the straight line is fitted through. Longer is steadier but slower to notice a change in slope.

settings.label: Forecast Periods
settings.html: Where the fitted line is read: 1 reads it at the newest bar, and each step above 1 reads it one bar further ahead. Larger values lead more and overshoot more at turns.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the line is fitted to, the close by default.

faq.q: How is this different from a linear regression line?
faq.html: Both fit the same least squares line, and both read it at the newest bar when the forecast is 1, so at the default the two lines are identical. With a forecast of k this study reads the line k - 1 bars further along, so it sits ahead of the regression value by the slope times k - 1.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot at tops and bottoms?
faq.html: The line is extended along the slope of the recent window. When price turns, the old slope still dominates the fit for a while, so the projection keeps going in the old direction.

faq.q: What is the gray line?
faq.html: It is the source the line was fitted to, drawn so the projection and the price it came from can be read side by side.

related.title: TUKEY_W: Tukey (Tapered Cosine) Window MA
related.summary: An average of the close whose weights are flat through the middle of the window and taper off along a cosine curve at both ends.

related.title: Triangular Moving Average (TRIMA)
related.summary: A weighted average whose weights peak in the middle of the window, smoother than a simple average of the same length.

related.title: Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (VAMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average whose length stretches when volatility is calm and shrinks when it expands, using two ATR readings.

true-strength-index-tsi.title: True Strength Index (TSI)
true-strength-index-tsi.summary: Double-smoothed price change over double-smoothed absolute price change, as a percentage from -100 to 100, with a signal line.
true-strength-index-tsi.descriptionHtml:
The True Strength Index measures how one-sided recent price changes have been. Each bar's change is the source minus the previous source, with a missing previous value read as zero. The change is smoothed by an exponential average of length longLen and then by one of length shortLen. The absolute size of the change is smoothed the same two ways. The TSI is 100 times the first result divided by the second, and it reads zero when the smoothed size is zero.

Every average here uses a weight of 2 / length. Each starts its accumulator at zero and passes its first value through unchanged; after that the accumulator is divided by (1 - e), where e is (1 - weight) raised to the number of updates, until e drops below 1e-10. The signal line is the same kind of average of the TSI over signalLen bars. Because the first bar's change is the whole price, the first reading is 100.
true-strength-index-tsi.howToReadHtml:
At lengths of 2 or more the TSI runs from -100 to 100. Near 100 nearly every recent change has been a rise, near -100 nearly every change a fall, and around zero rises and falls have balanced out. Above zero is the shape of upward momentum, below zero downward momentum.

Crosses of the TSI over its signal line are commonly read as momentum turning, and crosses of zero as the balance of changes flipping sides. The double smoothing keeps the line steady, which also means it turns after price does. Ignore the first bars: the first change is the whole price, and the averages need some bars to settle.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose bar-to-bar changes are measured. Close is the default.

settings.label: Long Length
settings.html: The length of the first smoothing of the change and of its size. Longer values make the line slower and smoother.

settings.label: Short Length
settings.html: The length of the second smoothing, applied to the output of the first.

settings.label: Signal Length
settings.html: The length of the average of the TSI that forms the signal line.

faq.q: Why does the line start at 100 or -100?
faq.html: The first bar has no previous value, which is read as zero, so its change is the whole price and fully one-sided. The averages then settle over the following bars.

faq.q: Why is the reading bounded between -100 and 100?
faq.html: With every length at 2 or more, each average weighs its inputs with positive weights, so the smoothed change can never be larger in size than the smoothed absolute change and their ratio stays between -1 and 1. A length of 1 gives a weight of 2, which overshoots, and the line can then run far outside that range.

faq.q: What happens on a bar with no price?
faq.html: Both lines hold their previous reading, or 50 if there is none yet, and the averages are left untouched.

related.title: Velocity (VEL)
related.summary: The change of price over a lookback, smoothed by an adaptive Jurik-style filter so the momentum reading turns with less lag than raw momentum.

related.title: SAM: Smoothed Adaptive Momentum
related.summary: Momentum over a lookback set by a measured price cycle, then smoothed by a two-pole filter, with a zero line for reference.

related.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.

ttm-trend.title: TTM Trend
ttm-trend.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.
ttm-trend.descriptionHtml:
TTM Trend draws a short exponential moving average of the source, the typical price by default, and colours it by the direction of its own slope: green while it rises, red while it falls and gray when it is flat. The average is seeded with the first bar's source, so it answers from the first bar, and that first bar has no slope.

Around the average sits an optional band. Its half width is the average multiplied by the strength, where the strength is the size of this bar's change in the average as a percentage of the previous value. A fast move therefore shows as a wide band and a quiet drift as a band that almost closes.

A small triangle marks each bar where the slope changes direction: an up triangle below the bar when it turns up, a down triangle above when it turns down.
ttm-trend.howToReadHtml:
Green says the short-term drift is up and red says it is down. The triangles mark the turns, and a run of bars with no new triangle is a run of bars moving one way. A widening band means the move is accelerating; a band that pinches in says it is slowing, which often comes before a turn.

The average is short, six bars by default, so it flips often in sideways markets and each flip on its own is a weak signal. Use it to time entries in the direction of a trend read from a slower tool rather than as a trend filter by itself.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average. A longer period turns less often and lags price more.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is computed from.

settings.label: Show Trend Strength %
settings.html: Draws or hides the band whose width follows the size of the slope. It does not change the line or the marks.

faq.q: How is the band width calculated?
faq.html: The change in the average on this bar, as a percentage of the previous value, is applied to the current average and drawn on both sides of it. A bigger step makes a wider band.

faq.q: Why is the first bar gray?
faq.html: The average is seeded with the first bar's own source, so it has no slope on that bar, and a flat slope is coloured gray.

faq.q: When does a triangle appear?
faq.html: On every bar where the direction of the slope differs from the previous bar's direction, as long as the new direction is up or down rather than flat.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A slope-coloured short exponential average with a faint ribbon whose width is the slope as a percentage, and triangles at each turn.

related.title: SuperTrend
related.summary: A trailing line set a multiple of average true range away from the bar midpoint, which flips sides when the close breaks through it.

related.title: VHF: Vertical Horizontal Filter
related.summary: The range of the closes over a window divided by the total distance they travelled, high in trends and low in ranges.

ttm-scalper-alert.title: TTM Scalper Alert
ttm-scalper-alert.summary: Marks every three-bar pivot: a bar whose high tops both neighbours, or whose low sits under both, as short-term turning points.
ttm-scalper-alert.descriptionHtml:
This study marks the smallest kind of turning point on a chart. A pivot high is a bar whose high is higher than the high of the bar before it and the bar after it. A pivot low is a bar whose low is lower than the lows of both neighbours. With Use Closes on, both tests read closing prices instead of highs and lows, which ignores wicks.

A pivot needs the bar after it, so it is known one bar after it forms. The study runs the test on that confirming bar and places the mark one bar back, at the pivot's own price on the bar it describes. Pivot highs are marked in red and pivot lows in green.
ttm-scalper-alert.howToReadHtml:
Each mark is a place where short-term momentum turned for at least one bar. A run of rising pivot lows shows buyers stepping in higher, and a run of falling pivot highs shows sellers pressing lower. Traders who scalp use the latest opposite pivot as a quick exit or stop reference.

Three-bar pivots are frequent, and most do not lead to a lasting turn. Treat a single mark as information about the last few bars and look for agreement with the wider trend before acting on it.

settings.label: Use Closes
settings.html: Test closing prices instead of highs and lows, so a long wick alone cannot create a pivot.

settings.label: Show Pivot Highs
settings.html: Draw the red marks at pivot highs, the bars that topped both neighbours.

settings.label: Show Pivot Lows
settings.html: Draw the green marks at pivot lows, the bars that sat under both neighbours.

faq.q: Why is the newest bar never marked?
faq.html: A pivot needs the bar after it to be confirmed. The newest bar has no bar after it yet, so it can only be marked once the next bar prints.

faq.q: Does a tie with a neighbour count?
faq.html: No. The middle bar must be strictly higher than both neighbours for a pivot high, or strictly lower for a pivot low.

faq.q: Can one bar carry both marks?
faq.html: Yes, while Use Closes is off. An outside bar whose high tops both neighbours and whose low sits under both is a pivot high and a pivot low at once. With Use Closes on, both tests read the same close, so a bar can be one or the other but not both.

related.title: Swing High/Low Detection
related.summary: Finds bars whose high or low is the extreme of the bars on both sides and holds the latest swing high and swing low as two horizontal lines.

related.title: Parabolic SAR
related.summary: A trailing stop and reverse line that accelerates toward price as a trend makes new extremes, and flips to the other side when price trades through it.

related.title: Pivot Points (Woodie)
related.summary: A pivot that weights the previous close twice, with three supports and three resistances built from the previous day, week or month.

ttmtrend.title: TTM Trend
ttmtrend.summary: A slope-coloured short exponential average with a faint ribbon whose width is the slope as a percentage, and triangles at each turn.
ttmtrend.descriptionHtml:
This version of TTM Trend draws a short exponential moving average of the source, the typical price by default, seeded with the first bar's source so it answers from the first bar. The line is green while the average rises, red while it falls and a faded gray when it is flat, which is always the case on the first bar.

The optional ribbon around it is built from the slope. On each bar the change in the average is taken as a percentage of the previous value, and the ribbon extends that percentage of the current average above and below it. The ribbon lines are drawn faint and the space between them lightly shaded, so an accelerating move reads as a widening ribbon without hiding the candles.

A small triangle is placed on each bar where the slope changes direction, below the bar for an upturn and above it for a downturn.
ttmtrend.howToReadHtml:
Follow the colour for the short-term drift and the triangles for the turns. A ribbon that widens over several bars shows a move gaining speed; one that narrows to almost nothing shows the move fading, which is often where the next triangle appears.

With a default length of six bars the line is quick, so in sideways markets it changes colour often and many triangles are noise. Its marks are most useful when they agree with a trend read from a slower measure, as a way to time entries rather than to decide direction.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The length of the exponential average. A longer period gives fewer colour changes and more lag.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average is computed from.

settings.label: Show Trend Strength %
settings.html: Draws or hides the ribbon around the line. The line and the triangles stay the same either way.

faq.q: How does this differ from the other TTM Trend entry?
faq.html: The calculation is the same. This one draws the ribbon fainter in a lighter blue and fades the gray of a flat slope, so it sits more quietly over the candles.

faq.q: What does a wide ribbon mean?
faq.html: The average moved a lot on that bar relative to its previous value. The ribbon width is that step, as a percentage, applied to the current average.

faq.q: Why does the line start gray?
faq.html: On the first bar the average equals the source, so it has no slope yet, and a flat slope is drawn in faded gray.

related.title: VHF: Vertical Horizontal Filter
related.summary: The range of the closes over a window divided by the total distance they travelled, high in trends and low in ranges.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.

related.title: Vortex Indicator
related.summary: Two lines, VI+ and VI-, that compare upward and downward bar-to-bar movement against true range to show which side is in control.

tukey-w-tukey-tapered-cosine-window-ma.title: TUKEY_W: Tukey (Tapered Cosine) Window MA
tukey-w-tukey-tapered-cosine-window-ma.summary: An average of the close whose weights are flat through the middle of the window and taper off along a cosine curve at both ends.
tukey-w-tukey-tapered-cosine-window-ma.descriptionHtml:
This study averages the last Period closes with a tapered cosine window. Bars in the middle of the window carry a weight of 1. Over a stretch at each end the weight falls along half a cosine curve, from 1 down to 0 at the very edge. The weighted closes are added up and divided by the sum of the weights.

The alpha setting decides how much of the window is tapered. At 0 there is no taper and the result is a simple moving average. At 1 the whole window is one cosine bell, which is a Hann window. At the default of 0.5, a quarter of the window at each end is tapered and the middle half is flat. The line starts once a full window of closes exists, and it always uses the close.
tukey-w-tukey-tapered-cosine-window-ma.howToReadHtml:
Read it like any trend average: price above a rising line describes an uptrend, price below a falling line a downtrend. The taper softens the moment a bar enters or leaves the window, so the line is smoother than a simple average of the same length and jumps less when an outlier bar drops out of the window.

Raising alpha makes the line smoother and gives the middle of the window more say, which adds lag; lowering it moves the line toward a simple average. Like every average built from a window, it turns only after price has turned.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of closes in the window. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: alpha
settings.html: The share of the window that is tapered, from 0 to 1. 0 gives a simple average, 1 a full cosine bell, 0.5 tapers a quarter at each end.

faq.q: What does alpha 0 give?
faq.html: Every weight is 1, so the study is a simple moving average of the close over the period.

faq.q: Why does it use the close and not a source setting?
faq.html: The calculation is defined on the close, and the study keeps that, so there is no source choice.

faq.q: Why are the first bars blank?
faq.html: The weights are fixed for a full window, so the line waits until Period closes exist before it draws.

related.title: Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (VAMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average whose length stretches when volatility is calm and shrinks when it expands, using two ATR readings.

related.title: Time Series Forecast
related.summary: Fits a straight line through recent prices and reads it at the newest bar or a set number of bars beyond it, so the line can run ahead of price.

related.title: Variable Index Dynamic Average (VIDYA)
related.summary: An exponential average that speeds up when short-term volatility rises against longer-term volatility and slows down when it falls.

tukey-s-biweight-loss-tukeybiweight.title: Tukey's Biweight Loss (TukeyBiweight)
tukey-s-biweight-loss-tukeybiweight.summary: A rolling average of the bisquare loss between an actual and a predicted series, a robust error score that caps the cost of any outlier.
tukey-s-biweight-loss-tukeybiweight.descriptionHtml:
Tukey's Biweight Loss scores the gap between an actual series and a predicted series with a loss that stops growing once the miss is large enough. On every bar the error is the actual value minus the predicted value. If the size of the error is larger than the threshold c, the bar costs a fixed c squared over six. Otherwise the error is divided by c, that ratio is squared and taken from one, the result is cubed and taken from one again, and the answer is multiplied by c squared over six.

The loss rises smoothly from zero for a perfect forecast and flattens out at its ceiling as the error approaches c, so every miss beyond the threshold counts the same. The study plots the simple average of this loss over the last Length bars. An absent value on either side is read as zero.
tukey-s-biweight-loss-tukeybiweight.howToReadHtml:
A lower line means more bars had small misses. Because each bar is capped, the line can never exceed c squared over six, and a reading near that ceiling says most bars in the window missed by more than c. A few extreme bars cannot push the line far, which is the point of the measure: it reports how often the forecast was close rather than how badly it failed at its worst.

The threshold has to be in the same price units as the error. With a threshold far below the size of a normal miss, almost every bar sits at the ceiling and the line goes flat. The line has no value for the first Length minus one bars.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the loss is averaged over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Threshold c
settings.html: The error size beyond which a miss stops costing more. A larger value lets bigger misses count in full and raises the ceiling of the line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: Why does the line go flat at a fixed value?
faq.html: Every bar whose error is larger than c costs exactly c squared over six. When all the bars in the window miss by more than c, the average sits at that ceiling. Raise c to bring the line back into its responsive range.

faq.q: Where does the default of 4.685 come from?
faq.html: It is the threshold commonly used for errors measured on a standardised scale. On raw price differences it is only a starting point; set c near the size of a typical miss on your chart.

faq.q: How is it different from the Pseudo-Huber Loss?
faq.html: The Pseudo-Huber Loss keeps growing for large errors, roughly in a straight line. The biweight loss stops growing entirely beyond c, so an outlier adds no more than any other large miss.

related.title: Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: Total absolute forecast error over a rolling window as a percentage of the total absolute actual value, steady where a plain percentage error is not.

related.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
related.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.

related.title: Weighted Root Mean Squared Error
related.summary: The root of the weighted mean squared gap between two price series over a rolling window, optionally weighting each bar by its volume.

trade-volume-index-tvi.title: Trade Volume Index (TVI)
trade-volume-index-tvi.summary: A running total of volume that adds while price ticks up by more than a minimum move and subtracts while it ticks down, holding direction through smaller moves.
trade-volume-index-tvi.descriptionHtml:
The Trade Volume Index keeps a running total of volume signed by the direction of price. On each bar the study compares the price with the previous bar's price. If it rose by more than the minimum move, the direction becomes up; if it fell by more than the minimum move, the direction becomes down; anything smaller leaves the direction as it was.

The bar's volume is then added to the total while the direction is up and subtracted while it is down. The direction starts as up, and the first bar compares its price with itself, so its volume is added. A missing price falls back to the close and a missing volume counts as zero.

The minimum move is what separates it from on-balance volume: small back-and-forth ticks inside the threshold do not flip the sign, so a quiet drift keeps accumulating in the direction of the last real move.
trade-volume-index-tvi.howToReadHtml:
Read the slope of the line. A rising TVI says volume has been flowing while price moves up, which is accumulation; a falling TVI says it flows while price moves down. Compare its swings with price: a new price high that TVI fails to confirm suggests the move is losing participation.

The level itself depends on where the chart starts, so it has no fixed meaning. Set the minimum move to suit the instrument: on a high-priced market a tiny threshold behaves almost exactly like on-balance volume, while a larger one makes the line hold its direction through noise.

settings.label: Price Field
settings.html: The price compared from bar to bar to decide the direction. The default is the close.

settings.label: Min. Move
settings.html: The smallest price change, in price units, that sets a new direction. Changes this size or smaller leave the last direction in place.

faq.q: How is TVI different from on-balance volume?
faq.html: On-balance volume flips sign on any change in the close. TVI flips only when the move exceeds the minimum, and on smaller or unchanged moves it keeps adding volume in the last direction.

faq.q: What minimum move should I use?
faq.html: Pick a value near the instrument's typical noise between bars. Too small and the line flips on every tick; too large and it rarely changes direction at all.

faq.q: Why does the first bar add its volume?
faq.html: The direction starts as up and the first bar has no earlier bar to compare with, so its change is zero and the starting direction carries.

related.title: Time Weighted Average Price (TWAP)
related.summary: The plain running average of price since the chosen period began, where every bar counts once regardless of how much traded in it.

related.title: Price Volume Trend (PVT)
related.summary: A running total of volume weighted by each bar's percentage price change, drawn with a moving average signal line and shaded by which of the two leads.

related.title: Volume Accumulation (VA)
related.summary: A running total of volume signed and scaled by how far each close sits above or below the middle of its own bar.

time-weighted-average-price-twap.title: Time Weighted Average Price (TWAP)
time-weighted-average-price-twap.summary: The plain running average of price since the chosen period began, where every bar counts once regardless of how much traded in it.
time-weighted-average-price-twap.descriptionHtml:
Time Weighted Average Price is the simple mean of the source over every bar since the current period started. Each bar's source value, the average of open, high, low and close by default, is added to a running sum, the bar count goes up by one, and the line is the sum divided by the count. When a new period begins both are cleared and the average starts again from that bar.

The period is set by the Session Reset menu. Intraday choices from one minute to four hours split each trading session into buckets counted from its first bar (the first bar of each calendar day where no session hours are known), 1D resets at each new calendar day, 1W at each Monday, and the monthly, quarterly, half-year and yearly choices at the start of each calendar period. Never keeps one average from the first bar of the chart. All boundaries are read in the chart's timezone.

Unlike a volume weighted average, a busy bar and a quiet bar carry exactly the same weight, so the line shows where price has spent its time rather than where most of the trading happened. A missing source value is counted as zero.
time-weighted-average-price-twap.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as the fair average price of the period so far. Price trading above it is higher than its average over the period so far; below it, lower. Execution desks use it as a benchmark: a buy filled below the TWAP of its period was a better than average fill.

Early in a period the line follows price closely because it averages only a few bars, and it becomes steadier as the period fills. Just after each reset it jumps to the new bar's price, so a crossing near a boundary says little.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price averaged on each bar. The default is the average of open, high, low and close.

settings.label: Session Reset
settings.html: When the running average starts again: an intraday bucket, a day, a week, a calendar month, quarter, half-year or year, or never.

faq.q: How does it differ from VWAP?
faq.html: VWAP weights each bar by its volume, so heavy bars pull the average towards them. TWAP gives every bar the same weight, so it reflects time spent at a price rather than volume traded there.

faq.q: Why does the line jump at certain bars?
faq.html: Those are the reset bars. When a new period starts, the average begins again from that bar's source value, so it lands right on the price and then settles as more bars arrive.

faq.q: What does an intraday reset shorter than the chart interval do?
faq.html: On an hourly chart a reset of one hour or less starts a new bucket on every bar, so the line simply equals each bar's source value.

related.title: Volume Accumulation (VA)
related.summary: A running total of volume signed and scaled by how far each close sits above or below the middle of its own bar.

related.title: Trade Volume Index (TVI)
related.summary: A running total of volume that adds while price ticks up by more than a minimum move and subtracts while it ticks down, holding direction through smaller moves.

related.title: Volume Force (VF)
related.summary: Each bar's price change multiplied by its volume, smoothed with an exponential average corrected so it reads accurately from the first bar.

typprice-typical-price.title: TYPPRICE: Typical Price
typprice-typical-price.summary: The plain average of each bar's high, low and close, a single price for where the bar traded, drawn on the price chart.
typprice-typical-price.descriptionHtml:
Typical Price is the average of three prices from each bar: the high, the low and the close, added together and divided by three. It leaves out the open and gives the close one third of the weight, so the value reflects both the range the bar covered and where it finished.

The study draws that value as a line over the price chart. There is no lookback window and no smoothing, so the line starts on the first bar and every point depends only on its own bar. It is the usual input for band and volume studies that want a price richer than the close.
typprice-typical-price.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as one representative price for each bar. A close above it means the bar ended near the top of its range; a close below it means the bar ended in its lower part.

On its own the line moves bar by bar and does not filter noise. Its main use is as a source for other studies: averages, deviation bands and money flow calculations built on the typical price react to the whole bar instead of only the last print.

faq.q: Why are only three prices used?
faq.html: The formula uses only the high, the low and the close: the high and the low describe the range, and the close describes where the bar settled.

faq.q: How is it different from Average Price?
faq.html: Average Price adds the open and divides by four. Typical Price leaves the open out and divides by three, so the close weighs a little more.

faq.q: Does it need any warmup?
faq.html: No. Each value uses only its own bar, so the line starts on the first bar of the chart.

related.title: WCLPRICE: Weighted Close Price
related.summary: A single-bar average that counts the close twice, so the close carries half the weight and the high and the low a quarter each.

related.title: MIDPRICE: Midpoint Price over Period
related.summary: The centre of the recent trading range: the highest high and the lowest low of the last N bars, averaged into one line.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

ehlers-ultimate-bands-ubands.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
ehlers-ultimate-bands-ubands.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.
ehlers-ultimate-bands-ubands.descriptionHtml:
The middle band is an ultrasmooth filter of the source. It is a two pole recursive filter whose coefficients come from the length: each output blends the current and two previous source values with the two previous outputs. The filter needs two earlier outputs, so on the first two bars it passes the source straight through.

The residual on each bar is the source minus the filter. The band width is the root mean square of those residuals over the last length bars, or over every bar so far while the window fills, multiplied by the RMS multiplier. The upper band adds that width to the filter and the lower band subtracts it.

Because the filter tracks price with little lag, the residual is small in a steady move and grows when price jumps away from it, which is when the bands open.
ehlers-ultimate-bands-ubands.howToReadHtml:
The middle band is a smooth estimate of price that turns early. Price above it is running ahead of the smooth path and price below it is lagging. The bands show how far price usually strays from that path, so a close beyond a band is a larger than usual departure.

Narrow bands mean price is following the filter closely; wide bands mean it is jumping around it. With a multiplier of one the bands are fairly tight, so touches are common and a close well beyond a band matters more than a touch.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is filtered and measured, the close by default.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The filter length and the number of bars in the root mean square window. Longer gives a smoother middle band.

settings.label: RMS Multiplier
settings.html: How many root mean square residuals the bands sit from the middle band. Larger values widen the channel.

faq.q: What is the residual?
faq.html: The source minus the filter on each bar. Its root mean square over the window sets the band width.

faq.q: Why does the middle band equal the source on the first two bars?
faq.html: The filter needs two earlier outputs. Until it has them it passes the source through unchanged.

faq.q: How is this different from a deviation band around an average?
faq.html: The spread is measured from a low lag filter rather than from a lagging average, so a trend by itself does not widen the bands as much.

related.title: Ultimate Channel (UCHANNEL)
related.summary: A two-pole ultra smooth filter of price as the centre line, with bands a multiple of a smoothed true range on each side.

related.title: Super Trend Bands (STBANDS)
related.summary: Ratcheting upper and lower bands built from the bar midpoint plus and minus a multiple of the average true range, tightening until price breaks them.

related.title: VWAP Bands (VWAPBANDS)
related.summary: A volume weighted average price that restarts each chosen period, with one and two volume weighted standard deviation bands around it.

ultimate-channel-uchannel.title: Ultimate Channel (UCHANNEL)
ultimate-channel-uchannel.summary: A two-pole ultra smooth filter of price as the centre line, with bands a multiple of a smoothed true range on each side.
ultimate-channel-uchannel.descriptionHtml:
Ultimate Channel runs the same two-pole ultra smooth filter twice. Applied to the centreline source with the Centerline Length, it gives the middle channel. Applied to a true range with the STR Length, it gives the smoothed true range that sets the width. The filter's coefficients depend only on its length, and it passes the raw value through on its first two bars, before it has outputs of its own to feed back.

The true range here is anchored on the previous value of the centreline source rather than on the previous close: the larger of this bar's high source and that value, minus the smaller of this bar's low source and that value. On the first bar it is simply the high minus the low. The upper and lower channels sit the smoothed true range, times the STR multiplier, above and below the middle channel.
ultimate-channel-uchannel.howToReadHtml:
The filter is designed to follow price with very little lag while removing most of the bar to bar noise, so the middle line turns close to where price turns. The bands widen as bars grow larger and narrow as they shrink. A close outside the channel is a move larger than the recent typical range; in a trend price tends to stay on one side of the middle line.

The smoothing reacts quickly, so the channel can follow a short spike more than a slow average would. Lengthen the two lengths for a calmer channel.

settings.label: Source for Centerline
settings.html: The series the middle channel smooths, and the anchor for the true range.

settings.label: Source for High
settings.html: The series used as the top of each bar's true range. The bar high by default.

settings.label: Source for Low
settings.html: The series used as the bottom of each bar's true range. The bar low by default.

settings.label: STR Length
settings.html: Lookback period for smoothing the true range. A longer length gives a steadier channel width.

settings.label: Centerline Length
settings.html: Lookback period for smoothing the centreline. A longer length gives a smoother, slower middle line.

settings.label: STR Multiplier
settings.html: Number of smoothed true ranges between the middle channel and each band. A larger value widens the channel.

faq.q: What is the ultra smooth filter?
faq.html: A two-pole recursive filter whose coefficients come from its length. Each output mixes the last three inputs with the previous two outputs, which keeps lag low while damping noise.

faq.q: Why is the true range anchored on the centreline source?
faq.html: The range runs from the lower of this bar's low and the previous source value to the higher of this bar's high and that value, so a gap from the previous source value widens the range just as a gap from the previous close does in a classic true range.

faq.q: Why do the first two bars equal price?
faq.html: The filter needs two previous outputs to feed back. Until it has them it passes the raw value through.

related.title: VWAP Bands (VWAPBANDS)
related.summary: A volume weighted average price that restarts each chosen period, with one and two volume weighted standard deviation bands around it.

related.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
related.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.

related.title: VWAP with Standard Deviation Bands
related.summary: A volume weighted average price anchored to a chosen reset period, with bands a number of volume weighted standard deviations away.

ulcer-index-ui.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
ulcer-index-ui.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.
ulcer-index-ui.descriptionHtml:
The Ulcer Index measures how deep and how long price has been below its recent high. Unlike most volatility measures it only counts falls: a market that rises steadily, however quickly, reads close to zero.

On each bar the study finds the highest source value over the last period bars (or over every bar so far while fewer exist) and the percentage drawdown of the source from that high. It squares the drawdown, averages the squares over the last period bars and takes the square root. Deep drawdowns weigh far more than shallow ones because they are squared, and long drawdowns weigh more because they fill more of the window.
ulcer-index-ui.howToReadHtml:
Zero means price has been at a new high on every bar of the window. Higher readings mean price has been sitting below its recent peak, further and for longer. The value is in percent, so it can be compared across instruments with very different prices.

Use it to judge how uncomfortable holding the instrument has been recently, or to compare the downside of two markets. It says nothing about direction going forward, and a sharp rally after a fall keeps the reading high until the old drawdown bars leave the window.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose drawdown from its recent high is measured.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the recent high and the average of squared drawdowns cover.

faq.q: Why does a strong uptrend read near zero?
faq.html: The index only measures how far price sits below its recent high. In a steady rise price keeps making new highs, so the drawdown on each bar is zero or small.

faq.q: What unit is the value in?
faq.html: Percent. A reading of 3 means the typical drawdown over the window, weighted toward the deeper ones, was about 3 percent below the recent high.

faq.q: Why are the first bars empty?
faq.html: The average of squared drawdowns needs a full window of period bars, so the line starts on the bar that completes the first window.

related.title: Volatility of Volatility (VOV)
related.summary: The standard deviation of a rolling standard deviation, rising when the market's volatility is itself changing quickly.

related.title: True Range
related.summary: Measures each bar's full movement, the bar's own range widened to include any gap from the previous close.

related.title: Volatility Ratio (VR)
related.summary: This bar's true range divided by an average true range, so values above 1 mark bars wider than the recent norm.

ultimate-oscillator-ultosc.title: Ultimate Oscillator (ULTOSC)
ultimate-oscillator-ultosc.summary: Buying pressure summed against true range over a fast, a medium and a slow window, blended by weight into one reading from 0 to 100.
ultimate-oscillator-ultosc.descriptionHtml:
The Ultimate Oscillator measures how much of each bar's true range was won by buyers. For every bar it takes the buying pressure, the close minus the true low (the lower of this bar's low and the previous close), and the true range, from the true low to the true high (the higher of this bar's high and the previous close).

It then sums both over three windows, the fast, medium and slow periods, and divides buying pressure by true range in each to get three ratios from 0 to 100. A window that is not yet full, or whose range sums to zero, contributes zero. The three ratios are blended with the fast, medium and slow weights and divided by the sum of the weights. Nothing is drawn until the slow window is full.
ultimate-oscillator-ultosc.howToReadHtml:
Readings above 70 show closes sitting near the top of their true ranges across all three windows, and readings below 30 show the opposite. A common way to read it is to look for a divergence: price makes a new low while the oscillator holds above its previous low, then the oscillator breaks upward.

Because the fast window carries the most weight by default, short bursts still move the line, but the slower windows keep a single bar from dominating. The line stays between 0 and 100 and can hold near an extreme throughout a strong trend.

settings.label: Fast Period
settings.html: Bars in the short window. A shorter window makes the fast ratio react to the latest few bars.

settings.label: Medium Period
settings.html: Bars in the middle window, which balances the fast and slow readings.

settings.label: Slow Period
settings.html: Bars in the long window. Nothing is drawn until this many bars have passed.

settings.label: Fast Weight
settings.html: How much the fast ratio counts in the blend. Raising it makes the oscillator more responsive.

settings.label: Medium Weight
settings.html: How much the medium ratio counts in the blend.

settings.label: Slow Weight
settings.html: How much the slow ratio counts in the blend. Raising it makes the oscillator steadier.

faq.q: Why three windows instead of one?
faq.html: A single window either reacts quickly and gives many false extremes or reacts slowly and turns late. Blending three windows lets short-term pressure show while the longer windows confirm it.

faq.q: What is buying pressure here?
faq.html: The distance from the true low up to the close. If the close finishes at the true high, the whole true range counts as buying pressure; if it finishes at the true low, none of it does.

faq.q: Why does the line start late?
faq.html: It waits until the slow window holds a full set of bars, so the first value appears on bar slowPeriod - 1.

related.title: Williams %R (WILLR)
related.summary: Where the close sits inside the highest high and lowest low of the lookback window, on a scale from 0 at the top to -100 at the bottom.

related.title: TRIX
related.summary: The one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential moving average, a slow momentum line that crosses zero when the smoothed trend turns.

related.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
related.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.

ultrasmooth-filter-usf.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
ultrasmooth-filter-usf.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.
ultrasmooth-filter-usf.descriptionHtml:
The Ultrasmooth Filter is a two-pole recursive filter that reads this bar's price, its two previous prices and its own two previous values. With arg = sqrt(2) * pi / length, it sets c2 = 2 * exp(-arg) * cos(arg), c3 = -exp(-2 * arg) and c1 = (1 + c2 - c3) / 4, then computes USF = (1 - c1) * price + (2 * c1 - c2) * price[1] - (c1 + c3) * price[2] + c2 * USF[1] + c3 * USF[2].

The extra terms on the earlier prices act as a momentum correction: they let the line keep up with a steady trend while the two-pole feedback removes short-term noise. Before the filter has two values of its own it uses the price in their place, so it answers from the first bar.

The length sets how slow a swing must be to pass through. Shorter swings are flattened; slower ones are followed closely.
ultrasmooth-filter-usf.howToReadHtml:
Read the USF as a smooth trend line that hugs price more tightly than a moving average of the same length. Its slope is the clearest signal: a line turning up marks the slower part of the market turning up, and a line turning down marks the reverse. Crossings of price, or of a second USF with a different length, can time those turns.

The momentum term means the line can overshoot after a sharp reversal. It still describes what price has done, and it lags a true turning point by at least a few bars.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: The cutoff period in bars. Larger values give a smoother line that turns later.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter smooths, the close by default.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Supersmooth Filter?
faq.html: Both share the same two-pole feedback. The Ultrasmooth Filter also feeds in the two previous prices through a momentum term, which tracks a steady trend more closely.

faq.q: Why can it overshoot price?
faq.html: The feedback and momentum terms carry the recent direction forward for a bar or two, so a sudden reversal leaves the line briefly beyond price.

faq.q: Does it repaint?
faq.html: No. Each value uses only this bar and earlier bars, so a value never changes once its bar has closed.

related.title: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter (VOSS)
related.summary: A two-pole bandpass around one cycle length, with a feedback predictor line that runs a few bars ahead of it so cycle turns show earlier.

related.title: Ehlers 3-Pole Super Smoother Filter (SSF3)
related.summary: A three-pole recursive smoother on price that removes short swings with little lag and almost no overshoot, answering from the first bar.

related.title: Wavelet Denoising Filter (WAVELET)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend and layers of detail, shrinks the small details as noise, and adds the rest back to give a denoised price line.

volume-accumulation-va.title: Volume Accumulation (VA)
volume-accumulation-va.summary: A running total of volume signed and scaled by how far each close sits above or below the middle of its own bar.
volume-accumulation-va.descriptionHtml:
Volume Accumulation measures where each bar closed within its own range and weights that by volume. For every bar the study finds the midpoint of the high and the low, takes the distance from that midpoint to the close, and multiplies it by the bar's volume. A close in the upper half gives a positive amount, a close in the lower half a negative one, and a close exactly in the middle gives nothing.

These amounts are added into a running total that starts at zero on the first bar. Because the distance is in price units rather than a fraction of the range, a wide bar that closes near its high counts for more than a narrow bar that does the same. A bar without volume adds nothing.

The idea is that buyers in control push the close towards the top of the bar and sellers push it towards the bottom, so the total tracks which side has been winning the bars, weighted by how much traded.
volume-accumulation-va.howToReadHtml:
Read the direction of the line. A rising VA means bars have been closing in their upper halves on meaningful volume, a sign of buying pressure; a falling VA means they have been closing low. A divergence, where price makes a new high while VA fails to, suggests the advance is being sold into within the bars.

The absolute level depends on where the chart starts and on the price scale of the instrument, so compare its swings rather than its value. It ignores gaps between bars, because it looks only inside each bar.

faq.q: How is it different from the accumulation/distribution line?
faq.html: The accumulation/distribution line uses the close's position as a fraction of the range, from -1 to +1. VA uses the raw distance from the midpoint in price units, so wider bars carry more weight.

faq.q: Why does a big gap not move the line?
faq.html: VA looks only at where the close sits inside the bar's own high and low. A gap between the previous close and this bar's range does not enter the calculation.

faq.q: Does it have any settings?
faq.html: No. It reads the high, low, close and volume of each bar directly, with nothing to tune.

related.title: Volume Force (VF)
related.summary: Each bar's price change multiplied by its volume, smoothed with an exponential average corrected so it reads accurately from the first bar.

related.title: Time Weighted Average Price (TWAP)
related.summary: The plain running average of price since the chosen period began, where every bar counts once regardless of how much traded in it.

related.title: Volume Oscillator (VO)
related.summary: The percentage gap between a short and a long average of volume, with its own averaged signal line, so volume expansion and contraction read around zero.

volatility-adjusted-moving-average-vama.title: Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (VAMA)
volatility-adjusted-moving-average-vama.summary: A simple moving average whose length stretches when volatility is calm and shrinks when it expands, using two ATR readings.
volatility-adjusted-moving-average-vama.descriptionHtml:
VAMA is a simple moving average with a window that changes every bar. It compares a long-term ATR with a short-term ATR: the base length is multiplied by long ATR divided by short ATR, held between the minimum and maximum length, and cut to a whole number of bars. The line is the mean of the newest values within that window.

Both ATRs smooth the true range with a factor of one over their period; they start at zero and are divided by a warmup correction, so they answer from the first bar. On the first bar the true range compares the bar's high and low with its own close. When short-term volatility runs above its longer average the ratio falls and the window shortens; when it runs below, the window lengthens. A minimum length set above the maximum is lowered to the maximum.
volatility-adjusted-moving-average-vama.howToReadHtml:
When the market turns volatile, VAMA shortens its window and follows price closely, so it reacts quickly to a fast move. When the market calms, it lengthens the window and smooths through small fluctuations. Price above a rising VAMA describes an uptrend and below a falling one a downtrend.

Because the window length changes, the line can step when the length jumps by several bars at once. The minimum and maximum length bound how fast and how slow it can become, so set them around the range of periods that makes sense for the timeframe.

settings.label: Base Length
settings.html: The window length when short and long ATR are equal. The volatility ratio scales it up or down.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

settings.label: Short ATR Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the ATR that measures current volatility.

settings.label: Long ATR Period
settings.html: The smoothing length of the ATR used as the reference volatility.

settings.label: Minimum Length
settings.html: The shortest window the average may use, however volatile the market is.

settings.label: Maximum Length
settings.html: The longest window the average may use, however calm the market is.

faq.q: Does the window get shorter or longer when volatility rises?
faq.html: Shorter. The length is the base length times long ATR over short ATR, so a jump in short-term volatility lowers the ratio and the average responds faster.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes step?
faq.html: The window is a whole number of bars and can change by several bars from one bar to the next, which shifts the mean in one move.

faq.q: What happens if the minimum length is above the maximum?
faq.html: The minimum is lowered to the maximum, so the window is fixed at the maximum length.

related.title: Variable Index Dynamic Average (VIDYA)
related.summary: An exponential average that speeds up when short-term volatility rises against longer-term volatility and slows down when it falls.

related.title: TUKEY_W: Tukey (Tapered Cosine) Window MA
related.summary: An average of the close whose weights are flat through the middle of the window and taper off along a cosine curve at both ends.

related.title: Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average in which the newest bar counts most and each older bar counts one step less.

variance-dispersion-or-spread-variance.title: Variance, Dispersion or Spread (VARIANCE)
variance-dispersion-or-spread-variance.summary: The population variance of the source over the lookback, showing how widely price has been spread around its own mean.
variance-dispersion-or-spread-variance.descriptionHtml:
Variance measures dispersion: the average squared distance of each value in the window from the window's mean. This study keeps a running sum and a running sum of squares over the last period values, and on each bar reports the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. That is the population variance, dividing by the number of values rather than one less.

Until the window fills, the average is taken over however many values have arrived, so the line starts on the first bar, where a single value reports 0. Because subtracting two large, nearly equal numbers can dip a hair below zero on a flat window, the result is clamped at zero. A missing source value counts as zero. The units are price squared, so the numbers are large on a high-priced instrument.
variance-dispersion-or-spread-variance.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a gauge of how spread out recent prices are, regardless of direction. A rising line means prices in the window are moving further from their average, which happens in expanding, volatile phases. A falling line means prices are bunching together in a quieter phase. Variance reacts strongly to large moves because the distances are squared.

The square root of variance is the standard deviation, which is in price units and easier to compare with a move on the chart. Compare variance on the same instrument over time rather than across instruments.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window holds. A longer period gives a steadier reading that responds later to a change in volatility.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series whose dispersion is measured, usually the close.

faq.q: Why are the numbers so large?
faq.html: Variance is in price squared. On an instrument priced in the tens of thousands, a typical move of a few hundred points becomes a variance in the tens of thousands or more. Take the square root for a figure in price units.

faq.q: Why does it start at 0?
faq.html: On the first bar the window holds one value, and one value has no spread. The window grows bar by bar until it holds the full period.

faq.q: Is this the sample or the population variance?
faq.html: The population variance: the sum of squared distances is divided by the number of values in the window, not by one less.

related.title: Weighted Average (WAVG)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average kept with running sums, with the newest bar weighted most and a value from the very first bar.

related.title: TRIM: Trimmed Mean Moving Average
related.summary: Sorts the last N closes, drops a set percentage from each end and averages the middle, so single spikes cannot drag the line.

related.title: WINS: Winsorized Mean Moving Average
related.summary: Averages the last N closes after pulling each tail in to its boundary value, so outliers lose their pull without shrinking the sample.

velocity-vel.title: Velocity (VEL)
velocity-vel.summary: The change of price over a lookback, smoothed by an adaptive Jurik-style filter so the momentum reading turns with less lag than raw momentum.
velocity-vel.descriptionHtml:
Velocity starts from plain momentum: the source minus the source Length bars ago. That raw difference is noisy, so it is passed through an adaptive smoothing filter of the Jurik family before it is plotted.

The filter tracks two bands around the momentum series and measures how far each new value breaks out of them. That volatility is averaged over ten bars and then over a longer exponential window, and the ratio of the current volatility to its average sets how fast the filter reacts: a sudden move gets a faster response, a quiet stretch a slower one. Two stages follow, a smoothed mean with a phase correction that pushes it ahead of the data and a final error-correcting stage, and their output is the plotted line. The phase is fixed at 100 and the power at 0.2, so the length is the only setting that shapes the filter.

The filter runs from the first bar, fed a zero change while the lookback does not exist yet, and the line starts once Length bars have passed.
velocity-vel.howToReadHtml:
Read it like a momentum oscillator. Above zero the source is higher than it was Length bars ago and the move is up; below zero it is lower. The slope of the line shows whether that momentum is building or fading, and a turn through zero marks the point where the lookback change flips sign.

The smoothing removes much of the jitter of raw momentum without the delay of a long average, but it is still a filter: it can overshoot after a sharp spike, and its values are in price units, so readings on different instruments are not comparable.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars back the change is measured, which also sets how strongly the filter smooths. A longer length gives a slower, smoother line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose change is measured, the close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from plain momentum?
faq.html: Plain momentum is the raw difference between the source and the source a set number of bars ago. Velocity takes that same difference and smooths it with an adaptive filter, so the line is cleaner and turns sooner than a simple moving average of momentum would.

faq.q: Why does the line start a few bars into the chart?
faq.html: The change over the lookback needs Length bars of history. The filter is already running before then, but the study draws nothing until the first real lookback difference exists.

faq.q: Can I change the phase or power of the filter?
faq.html: No. Both are fixed, at a phase of 100 and a power of 0.2. Only the length changes the filter.

related.title: True Strength Index (TSI)
related.summary: Double-smoothed price change over double-smoothed absolute price change, as a percentage from -100 to 100, with a signal line.

related.title: SAM: Smoothed Adaptive Momentum
related.summary: Momentum over a lookback set by a measured price cycle, then smoothed by a two-pole filter, with a zero line for reference.

related.title: Relative Strength Xtra (RSX)
related.summary: An RSI-style 0 to 100 oscillator whose up and down moves are smoothed by an adaptive filter, giving a much quieter line.

volume-force-vf.title: Volume Force (VF)
volume-force-vf.summary: Each bar's price change multiplied by its volume, smoothed with an exponential average corrected so it reads accurately from the first bar.
volume-force-vf.descriptionHtml:
Volume Force combines how far price moved with how much traded. On every bar the study takes the change in the close from the previous bar and multiplies it by the bar's volume. A large move on heavy volume gives a large force, a large move on thin volume a small one, and a bar with no volume no force at all. The first bar compares its close with itself and has no force.

The raw force is noisy, so it is smoothed with an exponential average whose weight is 2 / (period + 1). An exponential average that starts at zero is pulled towards zero for its first stretch of bars, so the study divides it by the share of weight gathered so far. That correction makes the first values a fair average of the bars seen rather than a fraction of one, and it switches off once the missing weight becomes negligible.

The pane shows the smoothed force with a dashed zero line, and is shaded green while the force is positive and red while it is zero or negative.
volume-force-vf.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, rising prices have been carrying more volume than falling ones over the smoothing window; below zero, the reverse. The green and red shading makes the side easy to see at a glance. A crossing of zero marks a change in which side is pushing harder.

Watch the size of the swings as well as the sign. A new price high made with a smaller positive force than the last one suggests the move is running on less conviction. Because price change is in price units, the scale depends on the instrument, so compare readings only within one chart.

settings.label: Smoothing Period
settings.html: The period of the exponential average that smooths the raw force. A longer period gives a calmer line that crosses zero less often.

faq.q: How is this related to the force index?
faq.html: It uses the same raw quantity, price change times volume, smoothed with an exponential average. The difference here is the warmup correction, which lets the line answer accurately from the first bar.

faq.q: Why does the line not start near zero?
faq.html: The early values are divided by the weight the average has gathered so far, which removes the pull towards the starting value of zero. The first bars therefore show a true average of the force seen so far.

faq.q: What does the shading mean?
faq.html: Green marks bars where the smoothed force is above zero and red where it is zero or below, so the side in control is visible without reading the scale.

related.title: Volume Oscillator (VO)
related.summary: The percentage gap between a short and a long average of volume, with its own averaged signal line, so volume expansion and contraction read around zero.

related.title: Volume Accumulation (VA)
related.summary: A running total of volume signed and scaled by how far each close sits above or below the middle of its own bar.

related.title: Volume Rate of Change (VROC)
related.summary: How much this bar's volume differs from the volume a fixed number of bars ago, shown as a raw difference or as a percentage.

vhf-vertical-horizontal-filter.title: VHF: Vertical Horizontal Filter
vhf-vertical-horizontal-filter.summary: The range of the closes over a window divided by the total distance they travelled, high in trends and low in ranges.
vhf-vertical-horizontal-filter.descriptionHtml:
The Vertical Horizontal Filter compares how far price got with how far it walked to get there. The vertical part is the highest close minus the lowest close over the last period plus one bars. The horizontal part is the sum of the absolute bar-to-bar changes in the close over the last period bars. The reading is the first divided by the second.

When price moves steadily in one direction, almost every step adds to the range, so the ratio is high. When price swings back and forth, the steps add up to a long path while the range stays narrow, so the ratio is low. If the closes have not moved at all over the window, nothing is drawn for that bar.

The line starts once a full period of changes is available. Two dashed levels mark the trend and range thresholds.
vhf-vertical-horizontal-filter.howToReadHtml:
Above the trend threshold, 0.4 by default, the closes have covered most of the path they walked, and the market is read as trending. Below the range threshold, 0.25 by default, most of the path was spent going back and forth, and the market is read as ranging. Between the two, the reading gives no clear verdict.

A rising line says the move is becoming more directional; a falling one says it is losing its shape. The filter has no direction, so it says nothing about whether the trend is up or down. Pair it with price or an average for that. The thresholds are fixed lines, and the level that separates the two states best differs between instruments and timeframes.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bar-to-bar changes the path sums over. A longer period gives a steadier reading that turns later.

settings.label: Trend Threshold
settings.html: Where the upper dashed line is drawn. It marks the level above which the market is read as trending and does not change the calculation.

settings.label: Range Threshold
