settings.html: Where the lower dashed line is drawn. It marks the level below which the market is read as ranging and does not change the calculation.

faq.q: Why can the value never exceed 1?
faq.html: The range of the closes can never be longer than the sum of the steps between them, so the ratio is at most 1, reached only when every step goes the same way.

faq.q: Can the line have gaps?
faq.html: Only where the closes did not move at all across the window. There is then nothing to divide by, so the study leaves that bar empty rather than inventing a value.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean prices are rising?
faq.html: No. A steady fall reads just as high as a steady rise. The filter measures how directional the move is, not its direction.

related.title: Vortex Indicator
related.summary: Two lines, VI+ and VI-, that compare upward and downward bar-to-bar movement against true range to show which side is in control.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A slope-coloured short exponential average with a faint ribbon whose width is the slope as a percentage, and triangles at each turn.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.

variable-index-dynamic-average-vidya.title: Variable Index Dynamic Average (VIDYA)
variable-index-dynamic-average-vidya.summary: An exponential average that speeds up when short-term volatility rises against longer-term volatility and slows down when it falls.
variable-index-dynamic-average-vidya.descriptionHtml:
VIDYA is an exponential moving average whose smoothing factor changes every bar. The base factor is two over the period plus one. It is multiplied by a volatility index: the population standard deviation of the last five source values divided by the population standard deviation over a slower window. The index is held between zero and one, so the line can only slow down from an ordinary EMA, never speed past it.

The slower window is the Std Dev Period, or the main period when that is zero. Both deviations are computed from sums of the values and their squares over the bars available, so the first bars use shorter windows. When the slower deviation is zero the index is one. The line is seeded with the first source value, and a missing source value leaves it where it was.
variable-index-dynamic-average-vidya.howToReadHtml:
When the last five bars are as volatile as the slower window or more, VIDYA moves like a normal EMA of the period. When recent bars are quiet against the longer window, the line nearly stops, so it stays flat through consolidation and resumes moving when price breaks out.

A flat VIDYA with price coiling around it describes a quiet market; a VIDYA that starts to slope again after a flat stretch shows that directional movement has returned. Because the index is capped at one, the line never reacts faster than the base EMA.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the base smoothing factor, and the slower deviation window when the Std Dev Period is zero.

settings.label: Std Dev Period (0=use Period)
settings.html: The window of the slower standard deviation. Zero uses the main period instead.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: Why is the fast window always five bars?
faq.html: The volatility index compares the deviation of the last five values with the deviation over the slower window. The five-bar window is fixed in the calculation; only the slower window can be set.

faq.q: Can VIDYA move faster than an EMA of the same period?
faq.html: No. The volatility index is held between zero and one, and it multiplies the EMA's smoothing factor, so VIDYA is at most as fast as that EMA.

faq.q: What does a flat VIDYA mean?
faq.html: Recent bars are much quieter than the slower window, so the smoothing factor is close to zero and the line barely moves.

related.title: Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average in which the newest bar counts most and each older bar counts one step less.

related.title: Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (VAMA)
related.summary: A simple moving average whose length stretches when volatility is calm and shrinks when it expands, using two ATR readings.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
related.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.

volume-oscillator-vo.title: Volume Oscillator (VO)
volume-oscillator-vo.summary: The percentage gap between a short and a long average of volume, with its own averaged signal line, so volume expansion and contraction read around zero.
volume-oscillator-vo.descriptionHtml:
The Volume Oscillator compares recent volume with longer-run volume. It takes a short average and a long average of each bar's volume and reports how far the short one sits above or below the long one, as a percentage of the long one. A reading of +20 means the last few bars traded 20% more than the longer window did on average.

Both averages are simple means over their periods, but they answer from the first bar: until a window has filled, each averages however many bars it has. Each bar's volume is read as at least 1, so a bar without volume never causes a division by zero.

A signal line, the same kind of mean of the oscillator over the signal period, is drawn alongside it to smooth out single spikes.
volume-oscillator-vo.howToReadHtml:
Above zero, volume is expanding: the recent bars are busier than the longer window. Below zero, it is contracting. Breakouts that come with the oscillator rising above zero have more participation behind them than those that come while it sits below zero, and a trend that continues while the oscillator falls is running on fading interest.

The oscillator says nothing about direction, only about activity, so read it beside price. Use the signal line to judge whether a rise is sustained or a one-bar spike, and expect the first bars of the chart to be rough because the averages are still filling.

settings.label: Short Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the fast volume average. A shorter period reacts sooner to a burst of volume.

settings.label: Long Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the slow volume average that the fast one is measured against.

settings.label: Signal Period
settings.html: The number of bars averaged to draw the signal line from the oscillator.

faq.q: Does a positive reading mean price will rise?
faq.html: No. It means recent volume is above its longer average. That can happen on a sharp fall as easily as on a rally, so read it with price direction.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: The averages divide by the number of bars available until the window fills, so they answer from the first bar instead of waiting out a warmup.

faq.q: What happens on bars with no volume?
faq.html: Volume is read as at least 1 on every bar, so the averages stay above zero and the percentage is always defined.

related.title: Volume Rate of Change (VROC)
related.summary: How much this bar's volume differs from the volume a fixed number of bars ago, shown as a raw difference or as a percentage.

related.title: Volume Force (VF)
related.summary: Each bar's price change multiplied by its volume, smoothed with an exponential average corrected so it reads accurately from the first bar.

related.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
related.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.

vortex-indicator.title: Vortex Indicator
vortex-indicator.summary: Two lines, VI+ and VI-, that compare upward and downward bar-to-bar movement against true range to show which side is in control.
vortex-indicator.descriptionHtml:
The Vortex Indicator measures upward and downward movement between neighbouring bars. Upward movement on a bar is the distance from the previous bar's low to this bar's high; downward movement is the distance from the previous bar's high to this bar's low. Each is summed over the period and divided by the sum of true range over the same bars, giving VI+ and VI-.

The sums start on the first bar and grow until they hold a full period of bars, after which the oldest bar drops out as each new one arrives, so both lines are drawn from the start of the chart. On the first bar, which has no previous bar, both movements take that bar's own range. If the summed true range is zero, both lines read zero.

A dashed reference line is drawn at 1.
vortex-indicator.howToReadHtml:
When VI+ is above VI-, upward movement has been covering more ground than downward movement over the window, and the trend leans up. When VI- is above VI+, the reverse holds. A crossing of the two lines marks the point where control changes hands, and the wider the gap between them, the more one-sided the move.

In a sideways market the lines tangle around each other and cross often, so many crossings are noise. A longer period gives fewer, later crossings. The first period bars are built from a shorter window and are less reliable.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the movements and the true range are summed over. A longer period gives smoother lines and fewer crossings.

faq.q: Why do the lines start on the first bar?
faq.html: The sums begin with the first bar and grow until they cover a full period. The early values are built from fewer bars, which is why they swing more.

faq.q: What does the line at 1 mean?
faq.html: It is a reference. Readings above 1 mean that side's movement exceeded the true range summed over the window, which happens in strong one-way moves.

faq.q: Can both lines rise together?
faq.html: Yes. In a period of wide, overlapping bars both movements grow relative to true range, so both lines can lift while neither side has clear control.

related.title: VHF: Vertical Horizontal Filter
related.summary: The range of the closes over a window divided by the total distance they travelled, high in trends and low in ranges.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A slope-coloured short exponential average with a faint ribbon whose width is the slope as a percentage, and triangles at each turn.

related.title: TTM Trend
related.summary: A short exponential average coloured by its slope, wrapped in a band as wide as that slope, with a mark where the slope turns.

ehlers-voss-predictive-filter-voss.title: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter (VOSS)
ehlers-voss-predictive-filter-voss.summary: A two-pole bandpass around one cycle length, with a feedback predictor line that runs a few bars ahead of it so cycle turns show earlier.
ehlers-voss-predictive-filter-voss.descriptionHtml:
The Voss Predictive Filter starts with a two-pole bandpass filter tuned to the cycle length in Period, with a width set by Bandwidth. The bandpass takes the change in price over two bars and keeps only the swings close to that cycle length, giving the red Bandpass line around zero. It is held at zero for the first six bars so the recursion is not started by a jump.

The blue Voss line is built from the bandpass with negative feedback. On each bar it takes the bandpass times (3 + order) / 2 and subtracts a weighted sum of its own last order values, where order is three times Predict and the oldest value carries the smallest weight. Values before the start of the chart count as zero.

The effect is a line that leads the bandpass by roughly Predict bars for a clean cycle, at the price of more noise.
ehlers-voss-predictive-filter-voss.howToReadHtml:
Read the two lines together. When the blue Voss line crosses above the red Bandpass line, the predicted cycle has turned up ahead of the filtered one; a cross below is the matching turn down. Both lines centre on zero, so their swings above and below zero are the cycle's highs and lows.

The lead only works while price is actually cycling near Period. In a strong trend or when the dominant cycle changes length, the prediction can turn too early or whipsaw. A larger Predict leads further but amplifies noise.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The cycle length in bars the bandpass is centred on.

settings.label: Predict
settings.html: How many bars ahead the Voss line aims to lead. It also sets how many past values the feedback uses.

settings.label: Bandwidth
settings.html: The width of the bandpass as a fraction of the period. Wider lets more cycle lengths through.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter runs on, the close by default.

faq.q: Does the Voss line really predict price?
faq.html: It leads the bandpass line for a steady cycle near the chosen period. It does not forecast price itself, and it loses its lead when the market stops cycling.

faq.q: Why are both lines flat at zero on the first bars?
faq.html: The bandpass is held at zero for the first six bars so the recursion is not started by an arbitrary jump.

faq.q: What is the usual signal?
faq.html: A crossing of the Voss line through the Bandpass line, read as an early turn of the cycle.

related.title: Wavelet Denoising Filter (WAVELET)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend and layers of detail, shrinks the small details as noise, and adds the rest back to give a denoised price line.

related.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.

related.title: Wiener Filter (WIENER)
related.summary: Blends price toward its own mean in proportion to how much of its recent variance looks like noise, smoothing quiet markets hard and trending ones lightly.

volatility-of-volatility-vov.title: Volatility of Volatility (VOV)
volatility-of-volatility-vov.summary: The standard deviation of a rolling standard deviation, rising when the market's volatility is itself changing quickly.
volatility-of-volatility-vov.descriptionHtml:
Volatility of volatility asks how stable the market's volatility is. A market can be very volatile in a steady way, or swing between calm and wild; this study separates the two.

First it computes a rolling population standard deviation of the source over the volatility period. Then it computes a second rolling population standard deviation, over the VOV period, of that volatility series. Both windows grow from the first bar until they are full, a missing value counts as zero, and a window holding a single value reads 0, so the line starts at zero on the first bar.
volatility-of-volatility-vov.howToReadHtml:
A low reading means volatility has been roughly constant over the recent window, whatever its level. A rising reading means volatility is shifting, for example as a quiet market breaks out or a busy one calms down.

The value is in the source's price units, so compare it with its own history on the same chart. The first bars rest on short windows and are less reliable until both windows have filled.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series whose volatility is measured.

settings.label: Volatility Period
settings.html: How many bars the first standard deviation, the volatility itself, covers.

settings.label: VOV Period
settings.html: How many bars the second standard deviation, of the volatility series, covers.

faq.q: How is this different from a plain volatility measure?
faq.html: A plain measure tells you how much price moves. This tells you how much that amount of movement is itself changing.

faq.q: Why does the line start at zero?
faq.html: Both standard deviations read 0 while their window holds a single value, so the first bar is 0 and the early bars use short windows.

faq.q: Which standard deviation does it use?
faq.html: The population form, dividing by the number of values in the window rather than one less.

related.title: Volatility Ratio (VR)
related.summary: This bar's true range divided by an average true range, so values above 1 mark bars wider than the recent norm.

related.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
related.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility (YZV)
related.summary: A volatility estimate combining the gap from the previous close, the open-to-close move and the intrabar range of every bar.

volatility-ratio-vr.title: Volatility Ratio (VR)
volatility-ratio-vr.summary: This bar's true range divided by an average true range, so values above 1 mark bars wider than the recent norm.
volatility-ratio-vr.descriptionHtml:
The volatility ratio compares the size of the current bar with the size of recent bars. The current bar is measured by its true range: the greatest of high minus low and the two distances from the high and the low to the previous close. The first bar uses high minus low.

The recent norm is a Wilder average of true range with weight 1 divided by the ATR period, set to the first bar's true range on the first bar. While a compensating weight, which starts at 1 and shrinks by the factor one minus 1 divided by the ATR period on every bar, is above a tiny threshold, the average is divided by one minus that weight. The ratio is the current true range divided by that average.

Because the average already starts from a real true range and is still divided by a small number at first, the early average is too large and the early ratio too small: on the first bar the ratio is exactly 1 divided by the ATR period. The effect fades as the compensating weight shrinks.
volatility-ratio-vr.howToReadHtml:
A reading of 1 means the bar is as wide as the recent average. Readings well above 1 mark expansion bars, often a breakout or a news move, and readings below 1 mark quiet bars inside a contraction. A cluster of high readings means volatility is expanding.

The first bars read low because of the start-up correction, so read the line once a few multiples of the ATR period have passed. The ratio carries no direction: a wide down bar and a wide up bar read the same.

settings.label: ATR Period
settings.html: How many bars the average true range in the denominator is smoothed over. A longer period makes the norm steadier.

faq.q: What does a value of 2 mean?
faq.html: The current bar's true range is twice the recent average true range: an unusually wide bar.

faq.q: Does it say which way price moved?
faq.html: No. True range is a size, so a strong up bar and a strong down bar give the same reading.

faq.q: Why are the early readings so low?
faq.html: The average starts from the first true range and is then divided by a number that is small at first, so it begins too large. The first reading is 1 divided by the ATR period, and the ratio climbs toward normal as that divisor approaches 1.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility (YZV)
related.summary: A volatility estimate combining the gap from the previous close, the open-to-close move and the intrabar range of every bar.

related.title: Volatility of Volatility (VOV)
related.summary: The standard deviation of a rolling standard deviation, rising when the market's volatility is itself changing quickly.

related.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
related.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.

volume-rate-of-change-vroc.title: Volume Rate of Change (VROC)
volume-rate-of-change-vroc.summary: How much this bar's volume differs from the volume a fixed number of bars ago, shown as a raw difference or as a percentage.
volume-rate-of-change-vroc.descriptionHtml:
Volume Rate of Change compares each bar's volume with the volume of the bar a set number of bars earlier. In Point mode it shows the plain difference, this volume minus that volume. In Percent mode it shows the difference as a percentage of the older volume, so +100 means this bar traded twice as much as the bar it is compared with.

The first bars of the chart have no bar that far back, so nothing is drawn until the period has passed. In Percent mode a bar whose comparison volume is zero is also left blank, because the percentage would be undefined.

No smoothing is applied: each value depends on exactly two bars, which makes the line responsive and also jumpy.
volume-rate-of-change-vroc.howToReadHtml:
Positive values mean volume is higher than it was a period ago and negative values mean it is lower. A run of large positive readings while price breaks out shows that the break is attracting fresh activity; a breakout on negative VROC is happening on less volume than before.

Because each reading compares only two single bars, one unusual bar at either end can produce a spike. Percent mode is easier to compare across instruments and over long histories, while Point mode shows the change in the instrument's own volume units.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars back the comparison bar is. A longer period compares against volume further in the past.

settings.label: Calculation Type
settings.html: Point shows the plain difference in volume; Percent shows it as a percentage of the older volume.

faq.q: Why are some bars blank in Percent mode?
faq.html: When the comparison bar traded no volume, the percentage cannot be computed, so that bar is left empty.

faq.q: Why does the line not start on the first bar?
faq.html: Each value needs the volume a full period earlier, which does not exist for the first period of bars.

faq.q: Which mode should I use?
faq.html: Percent mode makes readings comparable across instruments and over time. Point mode is useful when the absolute change in shares or contracts matters to you.

related.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
related.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.

related.title: Volume Oscillator (VO)
related.summary: The percentage gap between a short and a long average of volume, with its own averaged signal line, so volume expansion and contraction read around zero.

related.title: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
related.summary: The average price paid since the chosen period began, each bar weighted by its volume, so it shows where the traded value actually sits.

volume-weighted-accumulation-distributio.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
volume-weighted-accumulation-distributio.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.
volume-weighted-accumulation-distributio.descriptionHtml:
VWAD starts from the money flow multiplier used by the accumulation/distribution line: where the close sits in the bar's range, from -1 at the low to +1 at the high, worked out as ((close - low) - (high - close)) / (high - low). A bar whose high equals its low has a multiplier of zero.

The study then weights that multiplier twice by volume. It multiplies by the bar's own volume, as the classic line does, and again by that volume's share of the total volume over the last period bars. Until the window has filled, the total covers only the bars seen so far. The weighted amount is added to a running total that starts at zero on the first bar.

The second weighting makes the line far more sensitive to unusually busy bars: a bar that carries a large share of recent volume moves the total much more than a quiet bar with the same close position.
volume-weighted-accumulation-distributio.howToReadHtml:
A rising line means the heavy bars have been closing near their highs, which suggests buying is concentrated where most of the trading happens. A falling line means heavy bars close near their lows. Flat stretches mean either balanced closes or quiet volume.

Use it like the accumulation/distribution line, looking for divergences with price, but expect sharper steps on high-volume bars and less movement on ordinary ones. The level depends on where the chart starts and on the instrument's volume scale, so compare swings rather than values.

settings.label: Volume Weight Period
settings.html: The number of bars whose total volume each bar's volume is measured against. A shorter period makes a busy bar's share larger.

faq.q: How is it different from the accumulation/distribution line?
faq.html: Both use the same close-in-range multiplier and the bar's volume. VWAD multiplies once more by the bar's share of recent volume, so busy bars count for much more than quiet ones.

faq.q: What is the money flow multiplier?
faq.html: It is where the close sits in the bar: +1 when it closes on the high, -1 when it closes on the low, and 0 at the midpoint or when the bar has no range.

faq.q: Does the period change where the line starts?
faq.html: No. The line starts on the first bar either way. The period only sets how many bars of volume each bar is compared with.

related.title: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
related.summary: The average price paid since the chosen period began, each bar weighted by its volume, so it shows where the traded value actually sits.

related.title: Volume Rate of Change (VROC)
related.summary: How much this bar's volume differs from the volume a fixed number of bars ago, shown as a raw difference or as a percentage.

related.title: Volume Weighted Moving Average (VWMA)
related.summary: A moving average over a fixed window in which each bar is weighted by its volume, so the bars the market traded most pull the line towards them.

volume-weighted-average-price-vwap.title: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
volume-weighted-average-price-vwap.summary: The average price paid since the chosen period began, each bar weighted by its volume, so it shows where the traded value actually sits.
volume-weighted-average-price-vwap.descriptionHtml:
Volume Weighted Average Price is the running average of price since the start of the period, with each bar weighted by its volume. The study multiplies each bar's source price, the typical price of high, low and close by default, by its volume and adds it to a running sum, adds the volume to a second sum, and draws the first divided by the second. Bars with no volume add nothing, and until the period has seen any volume the line falls back to the source itself.

The Session Reset menu sets when the sums start again. Intraday choices from one minute to four hours split each trading session into buckets counted from its first bar (the first bar of each calendar day where no session hours are known), 1D resets at each new calendar day, 1W at each Monday, and the monthly, quarterly, half-year and yearly choices at the start of each calendar period. Never keeps one average from the first bar of the chart. All boundaries are read in the chart's timezone.

Because busy bars weigh more, the line sits where most of the trading in the period took place rather than at the middle of the prices seen.
volume-weighted-average-price-vwap.howToReadHtml:
Read VWAP as the average cost of everyone who traded in the period. Price above it means trades are now taking place above the period's volume weighted average; below it, the reverse. Many traders treat it as a level that intraday pullbacks test, and as a benchmark for judging their own fills.

Early in each period the line moves with every bar because few bars have been counted, and it becomes harder to move as volume accumulates. The reset makes it jump at period boundaries, so avoid reading crossings right at the reset bar.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price weighted by volume on each bar. The default is the typical price, the average of high, low and close.

settings.label: Session Reset
settings.html: When the running sums start again: an intraday bucket, a day, a week, a calendar month, quarter, half-year or year, or never.

faq.q: Why does VWAP jump at certain bars?
faq.html: Those are reset bars. When a new period begins the sums start again from that bar, so the line lands on its price and then settles as more volume arrives.

faq.q: What happens on a market without volume?
faq.html: Bars with no volume add nothing to the sums, and while the period has no volume at all the line simply follows the source price.

faq.q: Which reset should I use?
faq.html: The daily reset is the usual intraday benchmark. Weekly or monthly resets give a slower average cost that is useful for swing trading, and Never gives one average over the whole chart.

related.title: Volume Weighted Moving Average (VWMA)
related.summary: A moving average over a fixed window in which each bar is weighted by its volume, so the bars the market traded most pull the line towards them.

related.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
related.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.

related.title: Williams Accumulation/Distribution (WAD)
related.summary: A running total of each bar's move from its true range low on an up close, or from its true range high on a down close, weighted by volume.

vwap-bands-vwapbands.title: VWAP Bands (VWAPBANDS)
vwap-bands-vwapbands.summary: A volume weighted average price that restarts each chosen period, with one and two volume weighted standard deviation bands around it.
vwap-bands-vwapbands.descriptionHtml:
VWAP Bands accumulates three running sums from the start of each reset period: price times volume, volume, and price squared times volume. The VWAP is the first divided by the second. The variance of price about the VWAP is the third sum divided by the volume total minus the VWAP squared, floored at zero, and its square root is the volume weighted standard deviation. Bars with no volume add nothing, and the bands stay on the VWAP until the period holds at least two bars with volume.

The first bands sit the multiplier times that deviation above and below the VWAP, and the optional second bands twice as far. The reset period is chosen in the menu: from one minute up to four hours, counted from midnight, or a day, a week starting Monday, a month, a quarter, a half year or a year, all in the chart's timezone, or never. On an hourly chart every period of an hour or less restarts on every bar.
vwap-bands-vwapbands.howToReadHtml:
The VWAP is the average price paid for every unit traded since the period began, so price above it means the current price is higher than the average paid in the period and price below it means it is lower. The bands show how far price has stretched from that average relative to its own volume weighted scatter: the first bands contain ordinary moves, and the second bands mark extended ones.

Early in a period the sums hold few bars, so the bands are narrow and the VWAP moves easily. Choose a reset period longer than the chart interval; one equal to or shorter than it restarts on every bar and leaves the bands on the source.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price averaged by volume. The typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, by default.

settings.label: Session Reset
settings.html: When the running sums restart: an intraday period counted from midnight, a day, week, month, quarter, half year or year, or never.

settings.label: Standard Deviation Multiplier
settings.html: Distance of the first bands from the VWAP in volume weighted standard deviations. The second bands sit twice as far.

settings.label: Show 2nd Standard Deviation Bands
settings.html: Draw the outer pair of bands at twice the multiplier, or hide them.

faq.q: What happens when there is no volume?
faq.html: A bar with no volume adds nothing to the sums. If the period has no volume at all, the VWAP falls back to the source value and the bands collapse onto it.

faq.q: Why are the bands flat on the VWAP at the start of a day?
faq.html: The deviation needs at least two bars with volume in the period. On the first bar after a reset it is zero, so all the bands sit on the VWAP.

faq.q: Which timezone decides when a day or week begins?
faq.html: The chart's timezone. A day starts at midnight there, and a week starts at midnight on Monday.

related.title: VWAP with Standard Deviation Bands
related.summary: A volume weighted average price anchored to a chosen reset period, with bands a number of volume weighted standard deviations away.

related.title: Ultimate Channel (UCHANNEL)
related.summary: A two-pole ultra smooth filter of price as the centre line, with bands a multiple of a smoothed true range on each side.

related.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
related.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.

vwap-with-standard-deviation-bands.title: VWAP with Standard Deviation Bands
vwap-with-standard-deviation-bands.summary: A volume weighted average price anchored to a chosen reset period, with bands a number of volume weighted standard deviations away.
vwap-with-standard-deviation-bands.descriptionHtml:
This study builds the volume weighted average price from three running sums that restart at the beginning of each reset period: price times volume, volume, and price squared times volume. The VWAP is the first sum divided by the second. The variance is the third sum divided by the volume total minus the VWAP squared, floored at zero, and its square root is the volume weighted standard deviation of price around the VWAP.

The upper band is drawn in red and the lower band in green, each the chosen number of standard deviations from the VWAP, with the space between them shaded. The reset period is chosen in the menu: from one minute up to four hours counted from midnight, or a day, a week starting Monday, a month, a quarter, a half year or a year in the chart's timezone, or never. Bars with no volume add nothing to the sums.
vwap-with-standard-deviation-bands.howToReadHtml:
The VWAP shows the average price at which trade has actually been done since the period began, so it is a fair-value reference for the session. The bands show how far price has moved from it in units of its own volume weighted spread. A close near an outer band is a stretched price for the period, and a return to the VWAP after such a stretch is common in a range; in a strong trend price can hold near one band.

At the start of a period the sums hold few bars and the bands are narrow. A reset period equal to or shorter than the chart interval restarts on every bar and collapses the bands.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price averaged by volume. The typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, by default.

settings.label: Session Reset
settings.html: When the running sums restart: an intraday period counted from midnight, a day, week, month, quarter, half year or year, or never.

settings.label: Standard Deviations
settings.html: Number of volume weighted standard deviations between the VWAP and each band. A larger value widens the channel.

faq.q: How is the standard deviation weighted?
faq.html: By volume. Each bar's squared price counts in proportion to its volume, so the bands reflect where trade was done rather than every price equally.

faq.q: What if the instrument has no volume?
faq.html: Bars with no volume add nothing. With no volume in the period the VWAP falls back to the source value and the bands collapse onto it.

faq.q: When does a weekly reset happen?
faq.html: At the first bar of each week, with weeks starting at midnight on Monday in the chart's timezone.

related.title: VWAP Bands (VWAPBANDS)
related.summary: A volume weighted average price that restarts each chosen period, with one and two volume weighted standard deviation bands around it.

related.title: Ultimate Channel (UCHANNEL)
related.summary: A two-pole ultra smooth filter of price as the centre line, with bands a multiple of a smoothed true range on each side.

related.title: Ehlers Ultimate Bands (UBANDS)
related.summary: A low lag ultrasmooth filter of price with bands set a multiple of the root mean square of the residual away from it.

volume-weighted-moving-average-vwma.title: Volume Weighted Moving Average (VWMA)
volume-weighted-moving-average-vwma.summary: A moving average over a fixed window in which each bar is weighted by its volume, so the bars the market traded most pull the line towards them.
volume-weighted-moving-average-vwma.descriptionHtml:
The Volume Weighted Moving Average averages the source over the last period bars, weighting each bar by the volume traded on it. The study keeps two running sums over the window, price times volume and volume alone, and draws the first divided by the second. As a new bar enters the window, the bar that falls out of it is taken out of both sums.

Only bars with volume add to the sums: a bar with zero volume still takes a place in the window but contributes nothing. The line answers from the first bar, averaging however many bars it has until the window fills. If the window holds no volume at all, the line falls back to the source itself.

When every bar in the window trades the same volume, the result equals a simple moving average. The more uneven the volume, the further it moves towards the prices of the busy bars.
volume-weighted-moving-average-vwma.howToReadHtml:
Read it like a simple moving average: price above a rising VWMA is an uptrend, below a falling one a downtrend. The difference is in what it pays attention to. When a move happens on heavy volume, the VWMA follows it more closely than a simple average would, and when price drifts on thin volume, the VWMA barely moves.

Comparing it with a simple average of the same length is useful: VWMA above the simple average means the higher prices in the window came on heavier volume, which supports the move. The first bars of the chart average a partial window and are less reliable.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the window. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price averaged on each bar. The default is the close.

faq.q: How is VWMA different from VWAP?
faq.html: VWMA averages over a fixed window of recent bars that slides forward. VWAP accumulates from the start of a period, such as the day, and resets when the next period begins.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the window is full, the average uses only the bars seen so far, so it answers from the first bar rather than waiting out a warmup.

faq.q: When does it equal a simple moving average?
faq.html: When every bar in the window has the same volume. Uneven volume pulls it towards the prices of the busier bars.

related.title: Williams Accumulation/Distribution (WAD)
related.summary: A running total of each bar's move from its true range low on an up close, or from its true range high on a down close, weighted by volume.

related.title: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
related.summary: The average price paid since the chosen period began, each bar weighted by its volume, so it shows where the traded value actually sits.

related.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
related.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.

williams-accumulation-distribution-wad.title: Williams Accumulation/Distribution (WAD)
williams-accumulation-distribution-wad.summary: A running total of each bar's move from its true range low on an up close, or from its true range high on a down close, weighted by volume.
williams-accumulation-distribution-wad.descriptionHtml:
Williams Accumulation/Distribution measures each bar's move against the true range, which stretches the bar's range to include the previous close. On an up close, where the close is above the previous close, the move is the distance from the true range low (the lower of this bar's low and the previous close) up to the close. On a down close, the move is the distance from the true range high (the higher of this bar's high and the previous close) down to the close, which is negative. An unchanged close counts nothing.

The study multiplies each move by the bar's volume and adds it to a running total that starts at zero on the first bar. The first bar compares its close with itself, so it adds nothing, and a bar without volume adds nothing.

Using the true range means gaps count: a bar that gaps up and holds is credited with the gap as well as its own range.
williams-accumulation-distribution-wad.howToReadHtml:
Read the direction of the line and compare it with price. A rising WAD says up closes have been covering more ground on more volume than down closes, which is accumulation; a falling WAD says the reverse. The most common use is divergence: price making a new low while WAD makes a higher low suggests sellers are losing force.

The level depends on where the chart starts and on the instrument's price and volume scales, so it has no fixed meaning. Look at its swings and how they line up with price swings rather than at its value.

faq.q: What is the true range used here?
faq.html: It is this bar's high and low widened to include the previous close if that close lies outside them. It makes gaps between bars part of each bar's move.

faq.q: Why does an unchanged close add nothing?
faq.html: The move is only measured when the close differs from the previous close. A close equal to it is treated as neither accumulation nor distribution.

faq.q: Does it have any settings?
faq.html: No. It reads each bar's high, low, close, the previous close and the volume directly.

related.title: Volume Weighted Moving Average (VWMA)
related.summary: A moving average over a fixed window in which each bar is weighted by its volume, so the bars the market traded most pull the line towards them.

related.title: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
related.summary: The average price paid since the chosen period began, each bar weighted by its volume, so it shows where the traded value actually sits.

related.title: Volume Weighted Accumulation/Distribution (VWAD)
related.summary: An accumulation/distribution total weighted twice by volume, once by the bar's volume and again by its share of recent volume, so heavy bars dominate.

wavelet-denoising-filter-wavelet.title: Wavelet Denoising Filter (WAVELET)
wavelet-denoising-filter-wavelet.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend and layers of detail, shrinks the small details as noise, and adds the rest back to give a denoised price line.
wavelet-denoising-filter-wavelet.descriptionHtml:
This filter breaks the price into a coarse approximation plus several layers of detail, using a causal undecimated wavelet transform built from two-tap averages. Level 1 averages this bar with the previous bar; level 2 averages that result with its value 2 bars back; level 3 uses 4 bars back, and so on, doubling each time up to 128 bars at level 8. At every level the detail is what the averaging removed.

The noise level is estimated from the finest detail: the mean absolute level 1 detail over the last 2^levels bars, divided by 0.6745. The threshold is that estimate times sqrt(2 * ln(2^levels)), times the Threshold Multiplier. Each detail is then soft thresholded: a detail smaller than the threshold is dropped, and a larger one is shrunk toward zero by the threshold.

The output is the approximation at the chosen level plus all the shrunk details. Large, persistent moves survive almost untouched, while small, short-lived wiggles are removed. A multiplier of 0 removes nothing and returns the price itself.
wavelet-denoising-filter-wavelet.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as price with its small, noisy moves taken out. In a quiet market it flattens into steps; when price makes a decisive move larger than the noise threshold, the line follows it closely. A change of direction in the line is a move the filter judged larger than noise.

More levels and a higher multiplier give a smoother line that reacts later. The filter only uses bars that have closed, so it does not repaint, but it is a description of recent price rather than a forecast.

settings.label: Decomposition Levels
settings.html: How many layers of detail the price is split into. Each level doubles the span of the coarsest average, and the noise window is 2 to the power of this number.

settings.label: Threshold Multiplier
settings.html: Scales the noise threshold. 0 keeps every detail and returns the price; higher values remove larger moves as noise.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter cleans, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes look like steps?
faq.html: When every detail is smaller than the threshold, only the coarse approximation remains, and it moves slowly. A larger move pushes a detail past the threshold and the line jumps to follow.

faq.q: What does a Threshold Multiplier of 0 do?
faq.html: The threshold becomes zero, so no detail is shrunk, and the approximation plus all details rebuilds the source exactly.

faq.q: How far back does it look?
faq.html: The coarsest level reaches back up to 2 to the power of the level setting, and the noise estimate uses the same number of bars.

related.title: Wiener Filter (WIENER)
related.summary: Blends price toward its own mean in proportion to how much of its recent variance looks like noise, smoothing quiet markets hard and trending ones lightly.

related.title: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter (VOSS)
related.summary: A two-pole bandpass around one cycle length, with a feedback predictor line that runs a few bars ahead of it so cycle turns show earlier.

related.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.

weighted-average-wavg.title: Weighted Average (WAVG)
weighted-average-wavg.summary: A linearly weighted moving average kept with running sums, with the newest bar weighted most and a value from the very first bar.
weighted-average-wavg.descriptionHtml:
The weighted average gives each value in the window a weight by its age: the oldest carries weight 1, the next weight 2, and the newest carries a weight equal to the number of values in the window. The weighted sum is divided by the sum of the weights, count * (count + 1) / 2, so the result is an average that leans toward recent prices.

The study keeps the weighted sum and the plain sum as running totals. While the window is still filling it averages whatever has arrived, so the line starts on the first bar. Once the window is full, each new bar subtracts the plain sum from the weighted sum, which lowers every weight by one and removes the departing value, then adds the new value at the top weight. A missing source value counts as zero.
weighted-average-wavg.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a moving average that responds faster than a simple one of the same length, because the latest bars count most. Price above a rising line points to an uptrend and price below a falling line to a downtrend. A turn in the line arrives sooner than in a simple average, with a little more noise.

On the first bars the window is short and the line follows price closely; it settles into its full smoothing once a full period has passed.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being averaged, usually the close.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the window holds. A longer period gives a smoother line that lags more.

faq.q: How does it differ from a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple average weighs every bar in the window equally. Here the newest bar carries the most weight and the oldest the least, so the line reacts sooner to a change in price.

faq.q: Why is there a value on the first bar?
faq.html: While the window is filling the study averages the values that have arrived so far with weights 1 up to the count, rather than waiting for a full period.

related.title: WINS: Winsorized Mean Moving Average
related.summary: Averages the last N closes after pulling each tail in to its boundary value, so outliers lose their pull without shrinking the sample.

related.title: Variance, Dispersion or Spread (VARIANCE)
related.summary: The population variance of the source over the lookback, showing how widely price has been spread around its own mean.

related.title: Z-Score (ZSCORE)
related.summary: How far the current value sits from its rolling mean, measured in standard deviations of the lookback window.

wclprice-weighted-close-price.title: WCLPRICE: Weighted Close Price
wclprice-weighted-close-price.summary: A single-bar average that counts the close twice, so the close carries half the weight and the high and the low a quarter each.
wclprice-weighted-close-price.descriptionHtml:
Weighted Close Price blends three prices from each bar: the high, the low and the close, with the close counted twice. The sum is divided by four, so the close carries half the weight and the high and the low a quarter each. The open is not used.

The study draws that value as a line over the price chart. It has no lookback window and no smoothing, so it starts on the first bar and every point depends only on its own bar. It sits closer to the close than Typical Price does, while still reflecting the range the bar covered.
wclprice-weighted-close-price.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a price that respects the close but is pulled toward the middle of the bar's range. When the close is near the high, the line sits in the upper part of the candle; when the close is near the low, it sits in the lower part.

It is not a trend filter on its own. Use it as the source for averages, bands or oscillators when you want them to follow the close more than Typical Price does, without ignoring the bar's high and low.

faq.q: Why give the close double weight?
faq.html: The close is where the bar settled. Counting it twice keeps the line near the close while the high and the low still pull it toward the middle of the range.

faq.q: How does it compare with Typical Price?
faq.html: Typical Price weighs the high, low and close a third each. Weighted Close Price gives the close half and the high and low a quarter each, so it tracks the close more closely.

faq.q: Does it need any warmup?
faq.html: No. It answers from the first bar, because each value uses only its own bar.

related.title: TYPPRICE: Typical Price
related.summary: The plain average of each bar's high, low and close, a single price for where the bar traded, drawn on the price chart.

related.title: MIDPRICE: Midpoint Price over Period
related.summary: The centre of the recent trading range: the highest high and the lowest low of the last N bars, averaged into one line.

related.title: Midpoint (MIDPOINT)
related.summary: The centre of the source's rolling range: the average of its highest and lowest value over the lookback window.

weibull-distribution-cdf-weibulldist.title: Weibull Distribution CDF (WEIBULLDIST)
weibull-distribution-cdf-weibulldist.summary: Places price within its recent high-low range and reads that position through the Weibull cumulative distribution, giving a value from 0 to 1.
weibull-distribution-cdf-weibulldist.descriptionHtml:
This study scans the last Period bars of the source for their highest and lowest values and works out where the current value sits between them, from 0 at the low to 1 at the high. A flat window counts as 0.5. Bars before the first bar of data count as zero, and a period of 1 still compares the current bar with the previous one.

That position is fed through the Weibull cumulative distribution, 1 minus exp(-(x / lambda) raised to k). The shape k sets the form of the curve: below 1 it is concave, at 1 it is the exponential case, at 2 the Rayleigh case, and above 3 it becomes an S-curve. The scale lambda sets how quickly it rises towards 1.
weibull-distribution-cdf-weibulldist.howToReadHtml:
A reading near 1 means price is near the top of its recent range, and a reading near 0 means it is near the bottom. With the default shape of 2 and scale of 0.5 the curve rises quickly: the middle of the range reads about 0.63, three quarters of the way up reads about 0.89, and only the top eighth or so of the range passes 0.95. The 0.95 and 0.05 lines mark the extreme zones.

The study measures position, not direction. During a steady trend it can sit near one extreme for a long time, so it is best read alongside a trend measure, and the shape and scale should be set to the part of the range you want to resolve finely.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is placed within its range, the close by default.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the highest and lowest values are taken over. Longer periods give a wider and steadier range.

settings.label: Shape (k)
settings.html: The form of the curve: below 1 concave, 1 exponential, 2 Rayleigh, above 3 an S-curve.

settings.label: Scale (lambda)
settings.html: How quickly the curve rises. A larger scale keeps readings lower for longer; a smaller one pushes them to 1 sooner.

faq.q: Why does the line spend so much time near 1?
faq.html: With the default scale of 0.5, the middle of the range already reads about 0.63 and the top of the range about 0.98. Raise the scale to spread the upper part of the range out.

faq.q: What happens on the first bars?
faq.html: Bars before the start of the data count as zero, so early on the range reaches down to zero and the current price reads near the top of it.

faq.q: Can it go below 0 or above 1?
faq.html: No. It is a cumulative probability, so it always lies between 0 and 1.

related.title: Student's t-Distribution CDF (TDIST)
related.summary: Maps where price sits in its recent range onto a heavy-tailed probability scale from 0 to 1 using the Student's t cumulative distribution.

related.title: Hyperbolic Tangent (TANH)
related.summary: Squashes the distance between price and its 200-bar average through the hyperbolic tangent, giving an oscillator between -1 and +1.

related.title: Standardization (Z-score)
related.summary: Shows how many sample standard deviations the source sits above or below its own rolling mean, so different series share one scale.

wiener-filter-wiener.title: Wiener Filter (WIENER)
wiener-filter-wiener.summary: Blends price toward its own mean in proportion to how much of its recent variance looks like noise, smoothing quiet markets hard and trending ones lightly.
wiener-filter-wiener.descriptionHtml:
This filter estimates how much of recent price movement is signal and how much is noise, then pulls price toward its mean by the noise share. The noise variance comes from successive differences: the sum of the squared bar-to-bar changes over the last Length - 1 differences, divided by twice that count.

The total power comes from the Smoothing window. The mean is a simple average of the source over Smoothing bars, and the signal plus noise power is a simple average of the squared distance from that mean over the same number of bars. The signal variance is that power minus the noise variance, floored at zero.

The gain is the signal variance divided by the total of signal and noise variance, and the output is mean + gain * (price - mean). A gain near 1 leaves price almost untouched; a gain near 0 replaces it with the mean. When both variances are zero the gain is 0.
wiener-filter-wiener.howToReadHtml:
When the line sits on top of price, the filter judges the recent movement to be mostly signal, which usually happens in a clean trend. When the line flattens toward the mean and price wanders around it, the filter judges the movement to be mostly noise, which usually happens in a range.

The distance between price and the line is therefore a rough gauge of how noisy the market is. The line starts once both averages are filled, after about twice the Smoothing length, and it describes recent behaviour rather than predicting the next move.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bar-to-bar changes the noise estimate uses. A longer window gives a steadier noise estimate that adapts more slowly.

settings.label: Smoothing
settings.html: The window for the mean and for the total power. Larger values give a smoother mean and a slower start to the line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the filter works on, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line hug price in a trend and flatten in a range?
faq.html: In a trend, price moves far from its mean compared with its bar-to-bar noise, so the gain is high. In a range, those two are similar, so the gain falls and the line moves toward the mean.

faq.q: When does the line start?
faq.html: The mean needs Smoothing bars and the power average needs another Smoothing bars on top, so the first value appears after about twice the Smoothing length.

faq.q: Can the gain go above 1?
faq.html: No. The signal variance is floored at zero and divided by itself plus the noise variance, so the gain stays between 0 and 1.

related.title: Wavelet Denoising Filter (WAVELET)
related.summary: Splits price into a smooth trend and layers of detail, shrinks the small details as noise, and adds the rest back to give a denoised price line.

related.title: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter (VOSS)
related.summary: A two-pole bandpass around one cycle length, with a feedback predictor line that runs a few bars ahead of it so cycle turns show earlier.

related.title: Ultrasmooth Filter (USF)
related.summary: A two-pole recursive filter fed through a momentum term, giving a very smooth price line that turns with little lag.

williams-r-willr.title: Williams %R (WILLR)
williams-r-willr.summary: Where the close sits inside the highest high and lowest low of the lookback window, on a scale from 0 at the top to -100 at the bottom.
williams-r-willr.descriptionHtml:
Williams %R measures the close against the range of the last period bars. It takes the highest high and the lowest low of that window and reports how far the close sits below the top: -100 * (highest high - close) / (highest high - lowest low). A close at the top of the range reads 0, a close at the bottom reads -100, and a close in the middle reads -50.

The window starts from the first bar and grows until it holds period bars, so the line answers from bar 0 rather than waiting for a full window. When the range is zero, because every high and low in the window is equal, there is no top or bottom to measure from and the study reads -50.
williams-r-willr.howToReadHtml:
Readings near 0 mean the close is pressing against the top of its recent range, and readings near -100 mean it is pinned at the bottom. Many traders treat the band from 0 to -20 as overbought and from -80 to -100 as oversold, and watch for the line to leave those zones as a sign that the push has stalled.

In a strong trend the line can stay at an extreme for a long time, so an overbought reading is not by itself a reason to sell. The first bars of the chart use a shorter window and move more sharply than later ones.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the high and low range covers. A shorter period makes the line swing faster between 0 and -100; a longer one smooths it.

faq.q: Why is the scale negative?
faq.html: It measures the distance from the top of the range. A close at the top is 0 distance away, and a close at the bottom is the whole range away, written as -100.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: Until the window holds a full period bars, it uses every bar so far. The early readings are measured against a shorter range and swing more sharply.

faq.q: What does a reading of exactly -50 mean?
faq.html: Usually that the close is in the middle of its range. It is also what the study shows when the range is zero, since there is no top or bottom to measure from.

related.title: Ultimate Oscillator (ULTOSC)
related.summary: Buying pressure summed against true range over a fast, a medium and a slow window, blended by weight into one reading from 0 to 100.

related.title: TRIX
related.summary: The one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential moving average, a slow momentum line that crosses zero when the smoothed trend turns.

related.title: Ehlers Trendflex Indicator (TRENDFLEX)
related.summary: A trend gauge centred on zero: the average distance of smoothed price from its own recent values, scaled by its running root mean square.

wins-winsorized-mean-moving-average.title: WINS: Winsorized Mean Moving Average
wins-winsorized-mean-moving-average.summary: Averages the last N closes after pulling each tail in to its boundary value, so outliers lose their pull without shrinking the sample.
wins-winsorized-mean-moving-average.descriptionHtml:
The winsorized mean sorts the closes in the lookback window and replaces the most extreme values at each end with the value at the cut point. The number replaced at each end is the period times the winsorize percentage, rounded down. With a period of 20 and 10 percent, the two lowest closes are set equal to the third lowest and the two highest to the third highest, and then all twenty values are averaged.

Unlike a trimmed mean, nothing is thrown away: every slot still counts, but an extreme value can pull the average no further than the boundary. A setting of 0 replaces nothing and gives a simple average. The line is drawn once the window holds a full period of closes.
wins-winsorized-mean-moving-average.howToReadHtml:
Read the line as a moving average that is hard to knock off course with one spike. A single extreme close is pulled in to the boundary value, so its effect on the line is capped. Price crossings and turns read the same way as with any moving average.

Because the extremes are capped rather than removed, every close in the window still counts toward the average. A real breakout still moves it, but its first bars count only as much as the boundary value allows.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many closes the window holds. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Winsorize %
settings.html: The share of values at each end of the sorted window that are pulled in to the boundary. 0 gives a simple average.

faq.q: What is the difference from the trimmed mean?
faq.html: The trimmed mean drops the extreme values and averages fewer of them. The winsorized mean keeps every value but replaces the extremes with the boundary value, so the window size stays the same.

faq.q: Why does the line start late?
faq.html: It waits until the window holds a full period of closes, so the first bars of the chart carry no value.

related.title: Z-Score (ZSCORE)
related.summary: How far the current value sits from its rolling mean, measured in standard deviations of the lookback window.

related.title: Weighted Average (WAVG)
related.summary: A linearly weighted moving average kept with running sums, with the newest bar weighted most and a value from the very first bar.

related.title: One-Sample t-Test (ZTEST)
related.summary: A rolling t-statistic that asks whether the recent mean of the source sits significantly away from a hypothesized value, such as zero for returns.

weighted-moving-average-wma.title: Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
weighted-moving-average-wma.summary: A linearly weighted average in which the newest bar counts most and each older bar counts one step less.
weighted-moving-average-wma.descriptionHtml:
The Weighted Moving Average gives the newest value in the window a weight equal to Period, the one before it Period - 1, and so on down to a weight of 1 for the oldest. The weighted values are added up and divided by the sum of the weights, Period * (Period + 1) / 2.

The study keeps two running sums, the plain sum of the window and the weighted sum, and updates both as each bar arrives, so the cost does not grow with the period. While the window is still filling, the weights run from 1 up to the number of bars seen so far, which lets the line start on the very first bar. A missing value counts as zero.
weighted-moving-average-wma.howToReadHtml:
Because recent bars carry the most weight, the WMA follows price more closely than a simple average of the same period and turns sooner after a reversal. Price above a rising WMA describes an uptrend; price below a falling one a downtrend. A crossing of price through the line, or of a short WMA through a long one, is a common trigger for a trend change.

The faster response also means more false turns in a sideways market. During the first Period bars the window is still filling, so treat those early values with care.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: The number of bars in the window and the weight of the newest bar. Longer is smoother and slower.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series that is averaged, the close by default.

faq.q: How does it differ from a simple moving average?
faq.html: A simple average weights every bar equally. Here the newest bar counts Period times as much as the oldest, so the line reacts faster to recent prices.

faq.q: Why does the line start on the first bar?
faq.html: While the window fills, the average uses only the bars seen so far, weighted 1 up to their count, so it never waits for a full window.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
related.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.

related.title: Variable Index Dynamic Average (VIDYA)
related.summary: An exponential average that speeds up when short-term volatility rises against longer-term volatility and slows down when it falls.

related.title: Zero-Lag Double EMA (ZLDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average fed a de-lagged price, combining two kinds of lag reduction into a fast trend line.

weighted-mean-absolute-percentage-error.title: Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error
weighted-mean-absolute-percentage-error.summary: Total absolute forecast error over a rolling window as a percentage of the total absolute actual value, steady where a plain percentage error is not.
weighted-mean-absolute-percentage-error.descriptionHtml:
Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error (WMAPE) measures forecast error in percent without dividing bar by bar. On every bar it takes the absolute gap between the actual and the predicted series, and the absolute actual value. Both are totalled over the last Length bars, and the error total is divided by the actual total and multiplied by 100.

Because the division happens once on the window totals, a single bar with a tiny actual value cannot blow the reading up the way it can in a plain mean of percentage errors. Larger bars carry more weight, which is where the name comes from. A window whose actual values are all zero has no scale and reads 0. An absent value on either side is read as zero.
weighted-mean-absolute-percentage-error.howToReadHtml:
The reading is the share of the actual series that the forecast missed by, in percent. A value of 0.5 means the misses over the window added up to half a percent of the actual values. Lower is better, and the dashed line at 0 marks a perfect forecast. A rising line says the predicted series is drifting further from the actual one.

The line has no value until Length bars have passed. It shows the size of the miss, not its direction, so a forecast that is always too high and one that is always too low can score the same.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the errors and the actual values are totalled over. A longer window gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the truth. The total error is expressed as a percentage of this series.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series treated as the forecast that is scored against the actual one.

faq.q: How is it different from an ordinary percentage error?
faq.html: An ordinary percentage error divides each bar by its own actual value and then averages, so one bar with a small actual value can dominate. This one totals first and divides once, so each bar counts in proportion to its size.

faq.q: What does it show with the default settings?
faq.html: The actual series is the close and the predicted series is the open, so it reports the total open to close movement over the window as a percentage of the total close.

faq.q: Why is there no line on the first bars?
faq.html: The totals need a full window of Length bars before they are complete, so the first reading appears on the bar where that window fills.

related.title: Weighted Root Mean Squared Error
related.summary: The root of the weighted mean squared gap between two price series over a rolling window, optionally weighting each bar by its volume.

related.title: Tukey's Biweight Loss (TukeyBiweight)
related.summary: A rolling average of the bisquare loss between an actual and a predicted series, a robust error score that caps the cost of any outlier.

related.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
related.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.

weighted-root-mean-squared-error.title: Weighted Root Mean Squared Error
weighted-root-mean-squared-error.summary: The root of the weighted mean squared gap between two price series over a rolling window, optionally weighting each bar by its volume.
weighted-root-mean-squared-error.descriptionHtml:
Weighted Root Mean Squared Error measures how far one series sits from another, in the units of the data. On each bar it takes the gap between the Actual series (the close by default) and the Predicted series (the open by default), squares it and multiplies it by the bar's weight.

Over the last length bars it adds up those weighted squared gaps, divides by the sum of the weights and takes the square root. With every weight set to one this is the plain root mean squared error. With volume weighting switched on, each bar weighs as much as the volume it traded, so busy bars dominate the result and quiet bars barely count. A bar with no volume weighs one, a missing price counts as zero, and a window whose weights add up to nothing reads as zero.
weighted-root-mean-squared-error.howToReadHtml:
The line is always zero or above. Zero, marked by the dashed Perfect level, means the two series agreed exactly over the window. A higher value means a larger typical gap, and because the gaps are squared before they are averaged, a few large misses lift the line more than many small ones.

With the default inputs it reads as the typical size of the bar body, a gauge of how far price travels from open to close. Compare it with itself over time rather than across instruments, since it is measured in price units and scales with the price level.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the rolling window holds. A longer window gives a steadier line that reacts later.

settings.label: Use Volume as Weights
settings.html: Weight each bar's squared gap by its volume instead of giving every bar the same weight.

settings.label: Actual
settings.html: The series treated as the observed value. The close by default.

settings.label: Predicted
settings.html: The series compared against the actual one. The open by default.

faq.q: Why does the line start a few bars into the chart?
faq.html: It needs a full window of length bars before it can report a value, so the first length - 1 bars are left blank rather than drawn from a partial window.

faq.q: What changes when volume weighting is on?
faq.html: Bars that traded heavily count for more in the average and quiet bars for less, so the line follows the gaps that formed on busy bars. With it off every bar counts the same and the result is the ordinary root mean squared error.

faq.q: How is it different from mean absolute error?
faq.html: The gaps are squared before averaging and the root is taken afterwards, so large gaps weigh more than in an average of absolute gaps. The result is always at least as large as the mean absolute error over the same window.

related.title: Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error
related.summary: Total absolute forecast error over a rolling window as a percentage of the total absolute actual value, steady where a plain percentage error is not.

related.title: Tukey's Biweight Loss (TukeyBiweight)
related.summary: A rolling average of the bisquare loss between an actual and a predicted series, a robust error score that caps the cost of any outlier.

related.title: Theil's U Statistic (TheilU)
related.summary: Scores a predicted series against an actual one on a scale from 0 for a perfect match to about 1 for a forecast that adds nothing.

yang-zhang-volatility-yzv.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility (YZV)
yang-zhang-volatility-yzv.summary: A volatility estimate combining the gap from the previous close, the open-to-close move and the intrabar range of every bar.
yang-zhang-volatility-yzv.descriptionHtml:
Yang-Zhang volatility combines three views of a bar's movement into one variance estimate. The first is the gap: the log of the open over the previous close. The second is the body: the log of the close over the open. The third is the Rogers-Satchell term built from the high and low relative to the open and close, which measures movement inside the bar.

The squared gap is added to a weighted mix of the squared body and the Rogers-Satchell term, with a weight that depends on the length. That per-bar variance is smoothed with a Wilder average that is set to the first bar's estimate. While a compensating weight, which starts at 1 and shrinks by the factor one minus 1 divided by the length on every valid bar, is above a tiny threshold, the average is divided by one minus that weight. The square root of the result is the volatility. On the first bar the open stands in for the previous close, and a bar with a non-positive price gives no value and leaves the average unchanged.

Because the average starts from a real estimate and is still divided by a small number at first, the early values are too high: on the first bar the line is that bar's volatility times the square root of the length. The effect fades as the compensating weight shrinks.
yang-zhang-volatility-yzv.howToReadHtml:
The value is a volatility per bar as a fraction of price: 0.01 means bars typically move about 1 percent. A rising line means the market is becoming more volatile, counting both gaps between bars and movement within them; a falling line means it is calming.

Because it includes gaps, it reacts to markets that open away from the previous close, which range-only measures miss. It carries no direction, and it is a per-bar figure, not an annual one. The first bars read high because of the start-up correction, so judge the line once a few multiples of the length have passed.

settings.label: Length
settings.html: How many bars the Wilder average of the per-bar variance spans. It also sets the weight between the body and the intrabar term.

faq.q: Why combine three parts?
faq.html: Each misses something on its own. The gap catches moves between bars, the body catches the bar's net move, and the intrabar term catches swings within the bar.

faq.q: Is the value annualised?
faq.html: No. It is the volatility of a single bar. Multiply by the square root of the bars in a year if you need a yearly figure.

faq.q: What happens on the first bar?
faq.html: There is no previous close, so the open is used in its place and the gap term is zero.

related.title: Volatility Ratio (VR)
related.summary: This bar's true range divided by an average true range, so values above 1 mark bars wider than the recent norm.

related.title: Volatility of Volatility (VOV)
related.summary: The standard deviation of a rolling standard deviation, rising when the market's volatility is itself changing quickly.

related.title: Ulcer Index (UI)
related.summary: Measures downside risk as the root mean square of the percentage drawdown from the recent high, ignoring upside moves entirely.

yang-zhang-volatility-adjusted-moving-av.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
yang-zhang-volatility-adjusted-moving-av.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.
yang-zhang-volatility-adjusted-moving-av.descriptionHtml:
This study is a simple moving average whose length changes with volatility. Volatility is measured bar by bar from all four prices: the squared log jump from the previous close to this open, plus the squared log move from open to close weighted by k, plus a high-low term around the open weighted by 1 - k, where k = 0.34 / (1.34 + (n + 1) / (n - 1)) and n is the short period. That variance is smoothed with a running average of weight 1 / n, corrected for its zero start, and its square root is the short-term volatility.

The current volatility is ranked among the last percentileLookback readings, itself included, as the share it exceeds, from 0 to 100. A rank of 0 gives the maximum length and a rank of 100 the minimum, moving linearly in between and rounded down. The line is the plain mean of the newest that many source values, taken from the last maxLength bars.
yang-zhang-volatility-adjusted-moving-av.howToReadHtml:
When volatility is high compared with its recent history, the average shortens and tracks price closely, so it turns quickly in a fast market. When volatility is low, it lengthens and smooths out the noise of a quiet market. Read it like any moving average on price: price above a rising line describes an uptrend, below a falling line a downtrend.

Because the length can jump from one bar to the next, the line can step sharply when the volatility rank changes. It adapts to how volatile the market is, not to its direction, so a sharp sell-off shortens it just as a sharp rally does. The Long YZV Period setting is part of the indicator's settings but does not change the line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

settings.label: Short YZV Period
settings.html: The smoothing period of the short-term volatility that is ranked. A shorter period makes the length react to volatility changes faster.

settings.label: Long YZV Period
settings.html: Kept with the indicator's settings, but no part of the line reads it, so changing it does not change the average.

settings.label: Percentile Lookback
settings.html: How many past volatility readings the current one is ranked against. A longer lookback makes extreme ranks rarer.

settings.label: Minimum Length
settings.html: The shortest the average can become, used when volatility ranks at the top of its lookback. A value above the maximum is held at the maximum.

settings.label: Maximum Length
settings.html: The longest the average can become, used when volatility ranks at the bottom of its lookback. It is also how many bars of source are kept.

faq.q: Why does the line sometimes jump?
faq.html: The length is recalculated on every bar from the volatility rank. When the rank moves a lot, the number of bars averaged changes at once, and the mean steps to a new level.

faq.q: What does the Long YZV Period do?
faq.html: Nothing to the line. It is part of the settings, but no part of the calculation that produces the average reads it.

faq.q: Does high volatility make the line shorter or longer?
