faq.html: Shorter. A high volatility rank moves the length toward the minimum, so the average follows price more closely when the market is active.

related.title: Zero-Lag Double EMA (ZLDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average fed a de-lagged price, combining two kinds of lag reduction into a fast trend line.

related.title: Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
related.summary: A linearly weighted average in which the newest bar counts most and each older bar counts one step less.

related.title: Zero-Lag EMA (ZLEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average of a de-lagged price, the price plus its change over half the period, so it follows a trend with less delay.

zero-lag-double-ema-zldema.title: Zero-Lag Double EMA (ZLDEMA)
zero-lag-double-ema-zldema.summary: A double exponential average fed a de-lagged price, combining two kinds of lag reduction into a fast trend line.
zero-lag-double-ema-zldema.descriptionHtml:
Zero-Lag Double EMA stacks two ways of reducing lag. First the price is corrected: the de-lagged price is 2 * price - price lag bars ago, where the lag is half the period minus a half, rounded down, and at least one bar. Until that older price exists, the current price stands in for it.

The de-lagged price then passes through two exponential averages in a chain, each with weight 2 / (period + 1). Both start from zero, and while the zero start still carries weight e, each stage is multiplied by 1 / (1 - e) so the line starts on price instead of rising from zero. The result is the double average with its own lag subtracted once, 2 * first - second.
zero-lag-double-ema-zldema.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a fast moving average on price. Price above a rising line describes an uptrend, below a falling line a downtrend, and the slope turning is an early sign that the move is fading. It reacts faster than a plain exponential average of the same period and faster than a single zero-lag average, so it suits traders who want early turns and accept more false ones.

The double correction makes the line overshoot after sharp moves, and in a sideways market it wanders through price often. Pair it with a slower line or a trend filter rather than treating each cross as a signal on its own.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the weight of the two averages as 2 / (period + 1) and the lag of the correction as (period - 1) / 2, rounded down and at least 1. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

faq.q: How is it different from Zero-Lag EMA?
faq.html: Zero-Lag EMA applies one exponential average to the de-lagged price. This study applies two in a chain and subtracts the second from twice the first, which removes more lag and makes the line faster and more prone to overshoot.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot price?
faq.html: Both the price correction and the double average project the recent move forward. After a sharp reversal they keep pointing the old way for a few bars.

faq.q: Is the first part of the line reliable?
faq.html: It is drawn from the first bar because each stage is corrected for its zero start, but the early values rest on very few bars and are best treated as approximate.

related.title: Zero-Lag EMA (ZLEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average of a de-lagged price, the price plus its change over half the period, so it follows a trend with less delay.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
related.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.

related.title: Zero-Lag Triple EMA (ZLTEMA)
related.summary: A triple exponential average with progressively faster stages, fed a de-lagged price, for a very responsive trend line.

zero-lag-ema-zlema.title: Zero-Lag EMA (ZLEMA)
zero-lag-ema-zlema.summary: An exponential average of a de-lagged price, the price plus its change over half the period, so it follows a trend with less delay.
zero-lag-ema-zlema.descriptionHtml:
Zero-Lag EMA reduces the delay of an exponential average by feeding it a corrected price instead of the raw one. The correction lag is half the period minus a half, rounded down, and never less than one bar: 4 bars at the default period of 10. The de-lagged price is 2 * price - price lag bars ago, which is today's price plus the distance it travelled over that lag. While fewer than lag bars exist the older price is read as 0, so the first few de-lagged values are near twice the price.

That de-lagged price is averaged with weight 2 / (period + 1). The average starts from zero, and during warmup it is divided by 1 - e, where e is the weight the zero start still holds, so the line is not dragged toward zero over the first bars. Once that weight is negligible the plain average is used.
zero-lag-ema-zlema.howToReadHtml:
Read ZLEMA like any moving average drawn on price: price above a rising line describes an uptrend, price below a falling line a downtrend, and a cross of price through the line is an early sign of a turn. Compared with an ordinary exponential average of the same period it turns sooner, which gives earlier signals at the cost of more whipsaws in a sideways market.

The line can overshoot price after a sharp move, because the correction extends the most recent change. Disregard the first lag bars of the chart, where the older price is read as zero and the line starts well above price before settling.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the weight of the average as 2 / (period + 1) and the lag of the correction as (period - 1) / 2, rounded down and at least 1. A longer period gives a smoother, slower line.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

faq.q: Why does the line start far above price?
faq.html: Until lag bars exist the older price in the correction is read as zero, so the de-lagged price is about twice the actual price. The line settles onto price within those first few bars.

faq.q: How much lag does it remove?
faq.html: The correction adds the change over half the period to the price, which offsets most of the delay an exponential average of that period carries. It is not truly zero lag; it is much less lag.

faq.q: Why does it overshoot at turns?
faq.html: The correction projects the recent change forward. When price reverses sharply, the projected change is still pointing the old way for a few bars, so the line runs past price before turning.

related.title: Zero-Lag Triple EMA (ZLTEMA)
related.summary: A triple exponential average with progressively faster stages, fed a de-lagged price, for a very responsive trend line.

related.title: Zero-Lag Double EMA (ZLDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average fed a de-lagged price, combining two kinds of lag reduction into a fast trend line.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
related.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.

zero-lag-triple-ema-zltema.title: Zero-Lag Triple EMA (ZLTEMA)
zero-lag-triple-ema-zltema.summary: A triple exponential average with progressively faster stages, fed a de-lagged price, for a very responsive trend line.
zero-lag-triple-ema-zltema.descriptionHtml:
Zero-Lag Triple EMA corrects the price for lag and then smooths it through three exponential averages. The de-lagged price is 2 * price - price lag bars ago, with the lag half the period minus a half, rounded down, and at least one bar. Until lag bars exist, the first price of the chart stands in for the older one.

The first average has weight a1 = 2 / (period + 1). The second and third are faster: each weight is the one before multiplied by the cube root of 1 / a1, so the second is a1 ^ (2/3) and the third a1 ^ (1/3): about 0.18, 0.32 and 0.57 at the default period of 10. All three start from zero, and while the zero start still carries weight e each stage is multiplied by 1 / (1 - e). The line is 3 * first - 3 * second + third, the triple average combination that cancels most of the lag of the chain.
zero-lag-triple-ema-zltema.howToReadHtml:
Read it as a very fast moving average on price. A rising line with price above it describes an uptrend, a falling line with price below it a downtrend. Its turns come earlier than those of an exponential average of the same period, which is useful for timing but also means it reacts to noise that a slower line would ignore.

It overshoots price after sharp moves and can cross price many times in a range. It is most useful in trending conditions, or paired with a slower average that sets the direction.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: Sets the first stage's weight as 2 / (period + 1), from which the faster second and third weights follow, and the lag of the correction as (period - 1) / 2, rounded down and at least 1.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series the average follows, the close by default.

faq.q: Why are the second and third stages faster?
faq.html: Each weight is the one before multiplied by the cube root of 1 / a1, so the second stage uses a1 ^ (2/3) and the third a1 ^ (1/3), about 0.32 and 0.57 at the default period of 10. Heavier weights keep the extra stages from adding as much lag as two more averages of the first weight would.

faq.q: How does it compare with the double version?
faq.html: It adds a third average and combines the three as 3 times the first minus 3 times the second plus the third. That cancels more lag, at the cost of more overshoot.

faq.q: What stands in for the older price at the start?
faq.html: Until enough bars exist, the first price of the chart is used as the older price, so the correction starts small instead of jumping.

related.title: Zero-Lag EMA (ZLEMA)
related.summary: An exponential average of a de-lagged price, the price plus its change over half the period, so it follows a trend with less delay.

related.title: Zero-Lag Double EMA (ZLDEMA)
related.summary: A double exponential average fed a de-lagged price, combining two kinds of lag reduction into a fast trend line.

related.title: Yang-Zhang Volatility Adjusted Moving Average (YZVAMA)
related.summary: A simple average whose length shortens when short-term volatility ranks high and lengthens when it ranks low, so it hugs price in active markets.

z-score-zscore.title: Z-Score (ZSCORE)
z-score-zscore.summary: How far the current value sits from its rolling mean, measured in standard deviations of the lookback window.
z-score-zscore.descriptionHtml:
The Z-Score expresses the current value as a distance from the average of the lookback window, divided by the window's standard deviation. A reading of 2 means the value is two standard deviations above the mean; a reading of -1 means one below. The deviation is the population one, dividing by the number of values in the window.

The study keeps a running sum and sum of squares, so the window is partial until it fills and the first bar, with a single value, draws nothing. The variance is clamped at zero, and when the standard deviation is effectively zero (a flat window) the study reports 0 rather than dividing by it.
z-score-zscore.howToReadHtml:
Read the line against zero and against round levels. Near zero, price sits at its recent average. Readings beyond plus or minus 2 mean price has stretched unusually far from that average for the window, which mean reversion traders watch for a pullback and trend traders read as strength. A Z-Score that stays high while price keeps rising means the trend is outrunning its own recent range.

The score is relative to the window, so it adapts to quiet and volatile phases alike. It says nothing about direction ahead, and in a strong trend it can stay at an extreme for a long time.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The series being scored, usually the close.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many bars the mean and standard deviation cover. A short period scores against the very recent past; a long one against a broader average.

faq.q: Does a reading above 2 mean price will fall?
faq.html: No. It means price is unusually far above its recent average. In a sideways market some traders watch such a reading for a pullback, but in a strong trend the score can stay high for many bars.

faq.q: Why is it 0 on a flat stretch?
faq.html: When every value in the window is the same there is no spread to measure, and the study reports 0 rather than dividing by zero.

faq.q: Why do readings compare across quiet and busy periods?
faq.html: It divides by the window's own standard deviation, so it is measured in deviations rather than points, and a reading of 2 means the same stretch whatever the volatility.

one-sample-t-test-ztest.title: One-Sample t-Test (ZTEST)
one-sample-t-test-ztest.summary: A rolling t-statistic that asks whether the recent mean of the source sits significantly away from a hypothesized value, such as zero for returns.
one-sample-t-test-ztest.descriptionHtml:
The study tests the mean of the last Period values of the source against a hypothesized mean. It keeps running sums of the values and their squares, takes the sample mean, and builds a sample standard deviation with the usual n / (n - 1) correction. The standard error is that deviation divided by the square root of the number of values, and the t-statistic is the gap between the sample mean and the hypothesized mean divided by the standard error.

The test answers from the second bar, because two values are enough for a sample variance, and it uses all the bars held until the window is full. Absent values are left out of the window. When the standard error is effectively zero the bar is left blank.

The reading is most meaningful when the source is something centred near zero, such as a returns series, rather than raw price.
one-sample-t-test-ztest.howToReadHtml:
A value near zero means the recent mean is not distinguishable from the hypothesized mean. Readings beyond the dashed lines at plus or minus 2.04 and 2.75 correspond roughly to the 95 and 99 percent levels for a window of about 30 values. A sustained reading above them suggests the recent mean is reliably above the hypothesized value, and below them that it is reliably under it.

Applied to raw price the statistic will be very large, because price is far from zero, so either set the hypothesized mean near the price level or edit the script to test a change series, such as the close minus the previous close. The Source menu offers only price series. Overlapping windows are not independent, so treat the levels as a guide rather than a strict test.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: The price series being tested. The menu offers only price series, so a returns test needs a small edit to the script.

settings.label: Period
settings.html: How many recent values form the sample. A longer period gives a steadier statistic.

settings.label: Hypothesized Mean
settings.html: The value the sample mean is tested against. Use 0 when testing returns.

faq.q: Why are the readings so large on price?
faq.html: The statistic measures the distance from the hypothesized mean in units of standard error. With the default hypothesized mean of 0 and a price in the thousands, that distance is enormous. Set the hypothesized mean near the price, or edit the script so it tests a change series instead of price.

faq.q: What do the dashed lines mean?
faq.html: They mark plus and minus 2.04 and 2.75, roughly the two-sided 95 and 99 percent critical values for about 30 observations. A reading outside them is the kind a sample would rarely produce if the true mean equalled the hypothesized one.

faq.q: Why does it start on the second bar?
faq.html: A sample standard deviation needs at least two values, so the first bar has no reading. After that the window grows until it holds the full period.

displacement-candles-scanner.title: Displacement Candles Scanner
displacement-candles-scanner.summary: Counts runs of wide, one-directional candles, labels each run's length when it ends, and can flag the first pull-back to the run's Fibonacci level.
displacement-candles-scanner.descriptionHtml:
A displacement candle is a bar whose high-low range is at least a set percentage of the average high-low range of the last 14 bars and that closes in one direction: a bullish one closes above its open, a bearish one below. By default it must also close beyond the previous close, and it can be asked to close beyond the previous high or low, or to have a range wider than the ATR times a multiplier. For the first 13 bars, before the 14-bar average exists, the size test is skipped.

The study counts consecutive displacement candles on each side. A bullish candle restarts the bearish count and a bearish one restarts the bullish count. The study tracks each run's highest high and lowest low. Once a run reaches the minimum length it sets a Fibonacci level inside it: for a bullish run the high minus the range times the Fibonacci value, for a bearish run the low plus the range times the value. The level is held until the next qualifying run on the same side replaces it. When a run of at least the minimum length ends, its length is labelled on its last candle.

In Retracement mode the study then waits for price to come back into the newest run. The first bar whose low crosses down through a bullish run's level (or whose high crosses up through a bearish run's level), after a bar that sat beyond it, is flagged with a triangle, coloured, and joined to the first candle of the run by a dotted line. Each run gives at most one such signal. A small table on the newest bar shows the sum of the bar-to-bar percentage changes of the close since the day began, the day's running volume against the previous day's total, and both volumes in lakhs.
displacement-candles-scanner.howToReadHtml:
A green number above a candle closes a bullish run and says how many displacement candles it held; a red number below a candle closes a bearish run. A long run marks a stretch where one side moved price in wide candles without a pause.

In Retracement mode a green triangle under a candle marks the first pull-back into a bullish run's Fibonacci level, a red triangle over a candle the first rally into a bearish run's level, and the dotted line shows the level and where the run began. The signal fires on the bar that crosses the level and does not judge whether the pull-back holds, so read it as a place to look rather than an entry by itself. The time and date filters apply only to these retracement signals.

faq.q: Why is the run length labelled one bar late?
faq.html: A run is only known to have ended when a bar fails to extend it. The study sees that on the next bar and places the label back on the run's last candle, so a label never appears and then moves.

faq.q: Why do the first bars of the chart count as displacement candles so easily?
faq.html: The size test compares each candle with the 14-bar average range. Before 14 bars exist there is no average, the threshold is zero, and only the direction and close tests apply.

faq.q: Can one run give more than one retracement signal?
faq.html: No. In Retracement mode the first signal closes the run. A new signal needs a new run of at least the minimum length on either side.

faq.q: What does the volume in the table mean?
faq.html: Vol is the volume traded so far today and PD Vol the previous day's total, both in lakhs (hundred thousands). Vol %Chg compares the two, and %Chg adds up the bar-to-bar percentage changes of the close since the day began.

displacement-candles-indicator.title: Displacement Candles Indicator
displacement-candles-indicator.summary: Counts runs of large one-way candles, labels each run with its length, and can mark the first pullback to a Fibonacci level of the run.
displacement-candles-indicator.descriptionHtml:
A displacement is a fast, one-sided move made of long candles. This study tests every bar for it. A bar is a bullish displacement candle when it closes above its open, its high-low range is at least the Minimal Deviation percentage of the average high-low range of the last 14 bars, and (with the default filter) it closes above the previous close. A bearish candle is the mirror image. Until the 14-bar average exists the size threshold is zero, so the first bars only need the right direction. Optional filters also demand a close beyond the previous high or low, or a range larger than the ATR times a multiplier.

Consecutive candles of one side form a run, and any other bar ends it. When a run of at least Minimum Bars candles ends, its length is printed as a label on its last candle. While a run is long enough, the study keeps a level inside it: the run's highest high minus its height times the Fibonacci Value for a bullish run, and the lowest low plus the height times that value for a bearish one. At 0.5 that is the midpoint of the run.

With the Retracement method the study waits for price to come back to that level. The first bar whose low crosses down through a bullish run's level (or whose high crosses up through a bearish run's level), coming from the far side, is marked with a triangle, its candle is coloured, and a dotted line is drawn from the run's first candle to that bar. Each run produces at most one retracement signal, and a new run on either side replaces the one being watched. A small table on the newest bar shows the sum of the bar-to-bar percentage changes since the day began, the day's volume so far against the whole previous day's volume as a percentage change, and both volumes in lakhs (units of one hundred thousand). Days are calendar days in the chart's timezone.
displacement-candles-indicator.howToReadHtml:
A number label marks the end of a displacement run and says how many candles it held: light green above the candle for a bullish run, light red below it for a bearish run. A longer run is a longer stretch of consecutive large candles in one direction. On the Retracement setting, a light green triangle under a candle, with the candle painted the same colour, is the first pullback into a bullish run's Fibonacci level, a possible place to rejoin the move, and a light red triangle above a light red candle is the same for a bearish run. The dotted line shows which run and which level the signal belongs to.

A triangle is drawn once its bar has closed, and it is not a prediction: a pullback can continue straight through the level. The time and date filters read the bar's clock in the chart's timezone, so set them for the chart you use.

settings.html: Displacement shows only the run labels. Retracement also marks the first pullback to each run's Fibonacci level, with a triangle, a coloured candle and a dotted line.

settings.label: Apply Close Above/Below Prev High/Low

settings.html: Where the retracement level sits inside the run: 0 at the far end of the move, 1 at its start, 0.5 at the midpoint.

settings.label: Apply ATR Filter

faq.q: Why are the first few candles of the chart counted so easily?
faq.html: The size test compares each candle with the average range of the last 14 bars. Until 14 bars exist there is no average, so the threshold is zero and any candle in the right direction counts.

faq.q: Why do I see run labels but no triangles?
faq.html: Triangles, coloured candles and dotted lines appear only with the Scanning Method set to Retracement. On Displacement the study only labels the runs.

faq.html: No. A run is marked done on its first retracement signal and is watched again only if a new run reaches the minimum length. A new run on the other side also replaces it.

faq.html: Volume is shown in lakhs, one hundred thousand units, rounded to two decimals. On an instrument with small traded quantities, such as a crypto pair quoted in coins, the day's volume rounds to zero.

equal-highs-and-lows.title: Equal Highs and Lows
equal-highs-and-lows.summary: Boxes two consecutive swing highs, or two consecutive swing lows, that formed within a small percentage of each other.
equal-highs-and-lows.descriptionHtml:
Equal Highs and Lows looks for places where the market turned at almost the same price twice in a row. It finds swing points with a pivot test: a swing high is a bar whose high stands above the highs of the Left bars before it and the Right bars after it, and a swing low is the mirror image. With the Open/Close source the test reads the top and bottom of each candle's body instead of its wicks.

Each time a new swing point of one side is confirmed, the study compares it with the previous swing point of the same side. The distance between the two is taken as a percentage of the older one. When that percentage is below Equal HL %, the pair counts as equal: a box is drawn from the earlier pivot bar to the later one, spanning the two prices, and the later pivot bar is tagged with an x at its high or low. Equal highs are drawn in red and equal lows in green. Only the newest 50 boxes are kept on the chart.
equal-highs-and-lows.howToReadHtml:
Two highs at nearly the same price mark a ceiling that buyers failed to clear twice, and the stops of traders who are short usually sit just above it. Two equal lows mark a floor with stops resting just below it. Many traders watch these levels for a sweep: a quick move through the level that takes out those stops and then reverses, or for a clean break that turns the level into the start of a move.

A pivot needs Right bars after it to be confirmed, so each box and tag appears Right bars after the second pivot formed. With the default of 30 bars that is a long delay, and the study describes structure that has already formed rather than calling a turn as it happens. Smaller Left and Right values find more, smaller swings.

settings.label: Left
settings.html: How many bars before a candidate bar it must stand above (or below) to count as a swing point. Larger values keep only the more significant swings.

settings.label: Right
settings.html: How many bars after a candidate bar it must stand above (or below). This is also how many bars the study waits before a swing point, and any box built on it, can appear.

settings.label: Equal HL %
settings.html: The largest distance between two consecutive swing points, as a percentage of the older one, for the pair to count as equal. Lower values demand that the two prices sit closer together.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: High/Low finds swing points on the wicks of the candles. Open/Close finds them on the candle bodies, using the higher and lower of each bar's open and close. On a market that trades without gaps, where every bar opens at the previous close, neighbouring bodies always touch, so no body stands strictly above or below its neighbours and Open/Close finds no swing points.

faq.q: Why does a box appear so long after the second swing formed?
faq.html: A swing point is only confirmed once Right bars have closed after it without exceeding it. The box is drawn on the bar that confirms the second swing, but it is anchored back on the two pivot bars themselves.

faq.q: Are only consecutive swing points compared?
faq.html: Yes. Each new swing high is compared only with the swing high just before it, and each new swing low with the swing low just before it. Two equal highs separated by a different swing high in between are not paired.

faq.q: Why do older boxes disappear?
faq.html: The study keeps the newest 50 boxes, highs and lows together, and removes the oldest when a new one is drawn. The x tags on the pivot bars stay.

faq.q: What value of Equal HL % should I use?
faq.html: It depends on how much the instrument moves. On a market that moves a few percent a day, 0.05 percent keeps only very close matches; raise it to see looser pairs, or lower it on a quiet instrument.

equal-highs-and-lows-with-screener.title: Equal Highs and Lows with Screener
equal-highs-and-lows-with-screener.summary: Boxes pairs of consecutive swing highs or swing lows that print within a set percentage of each other, and lists the latest hits in a table.
equal-highs-and-lows-with-screener.descriptionHtml:
Equal highs and equal lows are two swing points of the same side that print at almost the same price. Resting orders tend to collect just beyond such a level, stops above a pair of equal highs and below a pair of equal lows, so the pair marks a place price may be drawn to and run through.

A swing high is a bar whose high (or candle body top, with the Open/Close source) is the highest of Left bars before it and Right bars after it; a swing low is the mirror image. Each swing is only known Right bars after it forms. The study keeps the two newest swings of each side and measures the gap between them as a percentage of the older one. When a new swing arrives and that gap is below Equal HL %, the pair is boxed from the earlier swing to the later one and the later swing bar is tagged EQH or EQL at its own high or low. Only the newest 50 boxes are kept.

The screener table lists the most recent hits on this chart, newest first, with the bar's time in Indian time (IST), H for an equal high or L for an equal low, and the close rounded to the instrument's tick. With the Equals method a hit is the bar that confirms the pair; with Equals Sweep a hit waits until the high crosses above the newest equal high, or the low crosses below the newest equal low, while the pair is still within the percentage.
equal-highs-and-lows-with-screener.howToReadHtml:
Read each box as a level where price has turned twice at nearly the same place. Many traders expect price to be drawn towards such a level and to run through it before a real move, so a box above the market marks a possible target for a rally and a box below marks one for a decline. A sweep hit in the table says that run through the level has just happened.

The swings are confirmed Right bars late, so a box and its tag appear well after the second swing formed. With the default 60 and 30 bars only large swings count, and on a fast chart pairs are rare; lower the lengths or raise the percentage to see more of them, at the cost of weaker levels.

settings.label: Screening Method
settings.html: Equals lists a pair on the bar that confirms it. Equals Sweep lists it only when price crosses through the newest equal level.

settings.label: Direction
settings.html: Both lists equal highs and equal lows. Bullish drops the equal lows from the table and Bearish drops the equal highs.

settings.label: Only Bullish
settings.html: When off, equal lows are left out of the table. The boxes and tags are drawn either way.

settings.label: Only Bearish
settings.html: When off, equal highs are left out of the table. The boxes and tags are drawn either way.

settings.label: Display Rows
settings.html: How many of the latest hits the table lists, newest first. Zero hides the table.

settings.label: Table Position
settings.html: Where the table sits. Each of the nine positions is drawn in its nearest corner of the chart.

settings.label: Table Size
settings.html: The text size asked for the table. Tables in this version draw at the chart's own text size, so changing it has no visible effect.

settings.label: Left
settings.html: Bars before a swing that it must stand above or below. Larger values keep only bigger swings.

settings.label: Right
settings.html: Bars after a swing that it must stand above or below. Larger values confirm swings later and keep only bigger ones.

settings.label: Equal HL %
settings.html: The largest gap, as a percentage of the older swing, for two swings to count as equal. Lower values demand closer prices.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: High/Low finds swings on the wicks. Open/Close finds them on the candle bodies, ignoring the wicks. A swing must stand strictly above or below its neighbours, so on a market where every bar opens at the previous close (one that trades round the clock) neighbouring bodies always share an edge and Open/Close finds no swings at all.

faq.q: Why does a box appear so long after the second swing?
faq.html: A swing is only confirmed once Right bars have closed after it without beating it. With the default of 30 bars the box is drawn 30 bars after the later swing formed, and nothing drawn changes after that.

faq.q: Why do the Only Bullish and Only Bearish switches seem reversed?
faq.html: The Direction menu calls an equal high bullish and an equal low bearish, but the two switches are wired the other way round: Only Bullish lists the equal lows and Only Bearish lists the equal highs. They change only the table, never the boxes or tags.

faq.q: Does the screener scan other symbols?
faq.html: No. It runs the same test on the chart's own instrument and lists the hits found in the bars loaded on the chart.

faq.q: Why are some old boxes missing?
faq.html: Only the newest 50 boxes are kept, to keep a long chart readable. The EQH and EQL tags stay on every pair.

external-range-liquidity-static-multi-ti.title: External Range Liquidity Static Multi-timeframe (Swing High and Low)
external-range-liquidity-static-multi-ti.summary: Draws higher timeframe swing highs and lows from three timeframes until price trades through them, and boxes equal highs and equal lows.
external-range-liquidity-static-multi-ti.descriptionHtml:
The study maps swing highs and swing lows, the prices beyond which resting stop orders are commonly assumed to sit, and shows which of them price has already traded through. For each of three timeframes, 15, 60 and 240 minutes by default, it folds the chart's bars into higher timeframe bars and finds pivot highs and pivot lows on them: a bar whose high is strictly above the Left bars before it and the Right bars after it, and the mirror image for lows. A pivot is read one completed higher timeframe bar later, unless the timeframe is no coarser than the chart, so a level never appears before the bars that confirm it.

Each level is drawn from the chart bar that actually made the swing, found by searching back for the bar whose high or low (or body top or bottom, with Open/Close) sits closest to the pivot price, and runs forward bar by bar until a bar's high is above it and its low below it. That bar traded through the level, and the line stops on the bar just before it. Only the newest levels are kept for each timeframe, highs and lows counted together, and an optional label shows the price.

A separate pass works on the chart's own bars with much wider pivots, 60 bars left and 30 right by default. When two consecutive swing highs, or two consecutive swing lows, differ by less than Equal HL % percent, the study boxes the pair and marks the newer swing with an x. The newest 50 boxes are kept. The Source setting switches every pivot between the wicks and the candle bodies.
external-range-liquidity-static-multi-ti.howToReadHtml:
Red lines are swing highs and green lines are swing lows. A line that is still running to the right is untouched: no bar since the swing has traded through it. A line that stops has been taken: the next bar after its end is the first one whose high was above the level and whose low was below it. Each timeframe uses the same colours, so set a different line style per timeframe to tell them apart.

Equal highs and equal lows, the shaded boxes, are two consecutive swings of the same kind within Equal HL % of each other, the box spanning from the older swing's bar and price to the newer one's. Because pivots need bars on both sides to confirm them, every level and box appears some bars after the swing that made it; the study never draws one sooner. The levels show where earlier swings turned, not whether price will reach them.

settings.label: Pivot High Low 1
settings.html: Draw the levels of the first timeframe.

settings.label: Pivot High Low 2
settings.html: Draw the levels of the second timeframe.

settings.label: Pivot High Low 3
settings.html: Draw the levels of the third timeframe.

settings.label: Equal Pivot High Low
settings.html: Draw the equal high and equal low boxes and their x marks.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: High/Low reads the wicks; Open/Close reads the candle bodies, so a long shadow does not set a swing.

settings.label: PHL 1 Timeframe
settings.html: The first timeframe: a number for minutes, or D, W or M; blank uses the chart's own bars.

settings.label: PHL 1 Left
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars before a pivot that must sit below a high or above a low.

settings.label: PHL 1 Right
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars after a pivot that confirm it; a larger value draws the level later.

settings.label: PHL 1 Show Last
settings.html: How many of the newest levels to keep, highs and lows counted together; 0 hides them.

settings.label: PHL 1 Line Extend
settings.html: Run every level to the newest bar instead of stopping it where price traded through.

settings.label: PHL 1 Line Style
settings.html: Solid, dashed or dotted lines for the first timeframe.

settings.label: PHL 1 Line Width
settings.html: Thickness of the first timeframe's lines.

settings.label: PHL 1 Label
settings.html: Write each level's price at its right end, or at its left end if it never extended.

settings.label: PHL 2 Timeframe
settings.html: The second timeframe, 60 minutes by default.

settings.label: PHL 2 Left
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars before a pivot of the second timeframe.

settings.label: PHL 2 Right
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars after a pivot of the second timeframe that confirm it.

settings.label: PHL 2 Show Last
settings.html: How many of the second timeframe's newest levels to keep.

settings.label: PHL 2 Line Extend
settings.html: Run the second timeframe's levels to the newest bar.

settings.label: PHL 2 Line Style
settings.html: Solid, dashed or dotted lines for the second timeframe.

settings.label: PHL 2 Line Width
settings.html: Thickness of the second timeframe's lines.

settings.label: PHL 2 Label
settings.html: Write the price of each of the second timeframe's levels.

settings.label: PHL 3 Timeframe
settings.html: The third timeframe, 240 minutes by default.

settings.label: PHL 3 Left
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars before a pivot of the third timeframe.

settings.label: PHL 3 Right
settings.html: Higher timeframe bars after a pivot of the third timeframe that confirm it.

settings.label: PHL 3 Show Last
settings.html: How many of the third timeframe's newest levels to keep.

settings.label: PHL 3 Line Extend
settings.html: Run the third timeframe's levels to the newest bar.

settings.label: PHL 3 Line Style
settings.html: Solid, dashed or dotted lines for the third timeframe.

settings.label: PHL 3 Line Width
settings.html: Thickness of the third timeframe's lines.

settings.label: PHL 3 Label
settings.html: Write the price of each of the third timeframe's levels.

settings.label: Equal Left
settings.html: Chart bars before a swing that it must stand above or below, for the equal high and low pass.

settings.label: Equal Right
settings.html: Chart bars after a swing that confirm it; the box appears this many bars after the newer swing.

settings.label: Equal HL %
settings.html: The largest gap between two swings, as a percentage of the older one, that still counts as equal.

settings.label: Transparency
settings.html: Transparency of the equal boxes and marks, from 0 (solid) to 100 (invisible).

faq.q: Why does a line stop where it does?
faq.html: A level runs forward until the first bar whose high is above it and whose low is below it. That bar traded through the level, so the line ends on the bar just before it. With Line Extend on, every level runs to the newest bar instead.

faq.q: Why does a level start before the bar where it appeared?
faq.html: The pivot is found on the folded higher timeframe bars, but the line is anchored to the chart bar whose high or low sits closest to the pivot price, which is the bar that actually made the swing. It only becomes known some bars later, once the pivot is confirmed.

faq.q: Why are there so few equal high and low boxes?
faq.html: The default needs two consecutive swings, each confirmed by 60 bars before and 30 after, within 0.05 percent of each other, which few pairs meet. Raise Equal HL % or shorten Equal Left and Equal Right to see more pairs.

faq.q: What does Open/Close change?
faq.html: Every pivot, on all three timeframes and in the equal pass, is read from the candle bodies instead of the wicks. A pivot must be strictly above (or below) its neighbours, so on a market where every bar opens exactly at the previous close no body can form one and nothing is drawn; that is the case on many continuously traded instruments. Open/Close is useful where bars open with gaps.

fair-value-gap-fvg-scanner-v2.title: Fair Value Gap (FVG) Scanner v2
fair-value-gap-fvg-scanner-v2.summary: Draws every three-bar fair value gap as a box that trails until price fills it, and marks the bar where a chosen stage of the fill completes.
fair-value-gap-fvg-scanner-v2.descriptionHtml:
A fair value gap is a three-bar imbalance. A down gap forms when this bar's high stays below the low of the bar two back, leaving a stretch of price that the middle bar crossed without any overlap; an up gap is the mirror image, with this bar's low above the high two bars back. A gap only counts when it is at least Minimal Deviation (%) of the 14-bar average high-low range, and while that average is still warming up every gap counts.

Each gap is drawn as a box from the first of its three bars and trailed to the right until price fills it. With Close FVG Partially on, every bar that trades into the gap freezes the current box and starts a smaller one over the part price has not yet reached, and the gap ends when price trades through its far edge. With it off, the first touch ends the gap. Max Bars can also end a gap after a fixed number of bars, and only the newest Max Number of FVG gaps are kept on the chart, each with all of its boxes.

The scanner follows the newest gap on each side through six stages. FVG % is the gap itself. First Touch is a later bar whose high crosses above the near edge of a down gap (or whose low crosses below the near edge of an up gap). Full Fill is a high crossing above the far edge of a down gap with the close still below that edge (or a low crossing below the far edge of an up gap with the close still above it). Reversal is a close that crosses beyond the far edge. The two Confirmed stages wait, after a touch or a full fill, for the close to cross back over the low (short) or high (long) of the bar that made it. Once a gap arms a stage, the stage fires once and then waits for the next gap. A small table on the newest bar shows the day's percentage change (each bar's change from the previous close, summed since the day began), the day's volume so far as a percentage change against the previous day's total, and the two volumes themselves in lakhs (units of 100,000).
fair-value-gap-fvg-scanner-v2.howToReadHtml:
Red boxes are down gaps sitting above price, and green boxes are up gaps sitting below it. A box that still runs to the newest bar is a gap price has not filled; the stack of smaller boxes shows how far each push into it reached. Markers and candle colours show where the chosen stage fired: a short-side touch or fill is marked with a light red triangle above the bar, a long-side one with a light green triangle below. Reversal is drawn the other way round, because a close beyond the top of a down gap is bullish: the short side is marked below the bar in light green and the long side above it in light red. On the two touch stages a short-side candle is painted light red and a long-side one light green; on the fill stages and Reversal the two colours swap.

The stages are a description of how price dealt with the newest gap, not a forecast. Each side follows only its newest gap, so an older gap still on the chart does not trigger signals. FVG % marks nothing on the chart; for that stage the boxes are the whole picture. The time and date filters hold back signals outside the window, in the chart's timezone. Volume in the table is shown in lakhs with two decimals, so a symbol that trades fewer than 500 units a day reads 0 L.

settings.label: Scanning Method
settings.html: The stage the markers and candle colours report: the gap itself, the first touch, a full fill, a reversal, or the confirmation of a touch or a fill.

settings.label: Long Signals
settings.html: Show markers and candle colours for the up gaps, the ones price falls back into.

settings.label: Short Signals
settings.html: Show markers and candle colours for the down gaps, the ones price rallies back into.

settings.label: Close FVG Partially
settings.html: On, each push into a gap starts a smaller box over the unfilled part, until price trades through the far edge. Off, the first touch ends the gap.

settings.label: Max Number of FVG
settings.html: How many gaps stay on the chart. When a new one forms past this count, the oldest gap is removed with all of its boxes.

settings.label: Minimal Deviation (%)
settings.html: The smallest gap that counts, as a percentage of the 14-bar average high-low range. Raise it to keep only the larger gaps.

settings.label: Max Bars
settings.html: End a gap once its newest box has run the given number of bars, whether or not price filled it.

settings.label: Max Gap Trail Length (bars)
settings.html: How many bars a gap's newest box may run before Max Bars ends it.

settings.label: Transp
settings.html: Transparency of the gap boxes, from 0 for solid to 100 for invisible. The border is 20 points more transparent than the fill.

settings.label: Apply Time Filter
settings.html: Only allow signals on bars that open inside the time window, in the chart's timezone.

settings.label: Time From (hour)
settings.html: The hour the time window opens.

settings.label: Time From (minute)
settings.html: The minute the time window opens. A bar opening at this minute is inside the window.

settings.label: Time To (hour)
settings.html: The hour the time window closes.

settings.label: Time To (minute)
settings.html: The minute the time window closes. A bar opening at this minute is already outside it.

settings.label: Apply Date Filter
settings.html: Only allow signals on bars of one calendar date, in the chart's timezone.

settings.label: Day
settings.html: The day of the month the date filter accepts.

settings.label: Month
settings.html: The month, 1 to 12, the date filter accepts.

settings.label: Year
settings.html: The year the date filter accepts.

settings.label: Display Table
settings.html: Show the panel with the day's change, the day's volume change, the day's volume and the previous day's volume.

settings.label: Position
settings.html: Where the panel sits. Panels pin to the four corners, so a top position goes to the top and a middle or bottom one to the bottom, on the left for a left position and on the right otherwise.

settings.label: Size
settings.html: The panel's text size. Tables in this version draw at the chart's own text size, so changing it has no visible effect.

faq.q: Why does a gap leave several boxes behind?
faq.html: With Close FVG Partially on, each bar that trades into the gap freezes the box it reached and starts a smaller one over the part price has not touched. The stack shows how far each push went. When price trades through the far edge, the last remnant is removed and the gap stops trailing.

faq.q: Why does an old box get a touch without a marker?
faq.html: The scanner follows only the newest gap on each side. Every gap on the chart keeps trailing and shrinking, but a touch, fill or reversal of an older gap does not fire a stage.

faq.q: What does the Confirmed stage wait for?
faq.html: After a short-side touch or full fill it records that bar's low, and fires when the close later crosses below it. On the long side it records the bar's high and waits for the close to cross above it. It turns a push into the gap into a rejection of it.

faq.q: Why does FVG % show no markers?
faq.html: That stage is meant for a screener across many symbols, where each new gap is the event. On a single chart the boxes already show every gap, so it adds no markers or candle colours.

liquidity-sweep-pattern-scanner.title: Liquidity Sweep Pattern Scanner
liquidity-sweep-pattern-scanner.summary: Tracks a zig zag of the last seven swings and flags the bar where the newest swing runs through an earlier swing level after a set shape has formed.
liquidity-sweep-pattern-scanner.descriptionHtml:
The study builds a zig zag from running highs and lows. A bar is a swing high when its high is the highest of the last Zig Zag Length bars, and a swing low when its low is the lowest. When the direction turns a new swing point is added; while the swing in progress keeps extending, its newest point moves with it. The seven newest swing points are kept, numbered from the newest (zz1) to the oldest (zz7).

A sweep needs two things. First, the six swings behind the newest one must sit in a fixed shape: for a short, a sequence of lower highs and lows that leaves the oldest swing above all the others, and the mirror image for a long. Second, the newest swing must cross the chosen earlier swing level: the 1st, 2nd or 3rd swing of the same side back, picked by Screening Method. A short fires when the newest swing crosses above that level, a long when it crosses below it. With the first method the long side is tested against the same shape as the short side, exactly as the calculation defines it.

On a signal the candle is tinted, a small triangle is drawn above or below it, and a line is drawn from the swept swing across to the signal bar at the swept price. A small table shows the day's running percentage change, the change in the day's volume against the previous day, the day's volume and the previous day's volume in lakhs, with days counted in the chart's own timezone.
liquidity-sweep-pattern-scanner.howToReadHtml:
A short signal marks a push above an earlier swing high that came after a falling swing structure: price has run the stops resting above that high. A long signal is the same idea below an earlier swing low. The horizontal line shows which level was taken and where it came from, so you can judge whether price is accepted beyond it or snaps back.

The swings are built from running highs and lows, so the newest swing point can still move while the swing in progress extends, and a signal depends on the shape at the time it fired. The blue zig zag line is drawn 60 bars behind the newest bar, once its legs have usually settled, so the most recent swings are read from the markers and level lines rather than from the line. Treat a signal as a level to watch rather than an order to trade.

settings.label: Screening Method
settings.html: Which earlier swing the newest swing has to sweep: the 1st, 2nd or 3rd swing of the same side back. A deeper swing gives fewer, larger sweeps.

settings.label: Long Signals
settings.html: Show the long sweeps, where the newest swing runs below an earlier swing low.

settings.label: Short Signals
settings.html: Show the short sweeps, where the newest swing runs above an earlier swing high.

settings.label: Display Zig Zag
settings.html: Draw the zig zag line joining the swing points. The signals are found the same way whether it is shown or not.

settings.label: Zig Zag Length
settings.html: How many bars a high or low must lead to count as a swing point. A longer length gives fewer, larger swings.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: Build the swings from the wicks (High/Low) or from the candle bodies (Open/Close).

settings.label: Swept Level Line Style
settings.html: Style of the line drawn from the swept swing across to the signal bar: solid, dashed or dotted.

settings.label: Display Table
settings.html: Show the table of the day's percentage change, volume change, volume and previous day volume.

settings.label: Position
settings.html: Where the table sits. Tables pin to a corner, so a centre column is drawn on the right and a middle row at the bottom.

settings.label: Size
settings.html: Kept for the text size of the table; the table is drawn at the chart's own text size in this version.

faq.q: Why does the zig zag line stop short of the newest bars?
faq.html: A leg of the zig zag is only known once the swing after it has formed, so the line is drawn 60 bars behind the newest bar, where its legs have usually settled. At the default length that holds; with a long Zig Zag Length one swing can take more than 60 bars to settle, and the line on those bars can then differ from the final swings. The swing points, signals and level lines are all computed on the newest bar and are not affected.

faq.q: What is the shape the six earlier swings must form?
faq.html: For a short, the swings behind the newest one step down from an oldest high that stands above all of them, with each comparison between them fixed. For a long it is the mirror image. Only when that shape holds does a cross of the chosen level count as a sweep.

faq.q: What does the line on a signal show?
faq.html: It starts at the swept swing point, at that swing's price, and runs across to the signal bar, so it shows which level the newest swing took and how far back it was set.

faq.q: Why does the first method behave differently on the long side?
faq.html: With Prev 1 Swing Sweep the long condition is tested against the same falling shape as the short condition rather than its mirror, so long signals with that method are rare. The other two methods test longs against the mirrored shape.

liquidity-sweep-pattern-scanner.deviation: The zig zag line is drawn 60 bars behind the newest bar because a plot cannot redraw bars it has already drawn, so the newest 60 bars show no zig zag line and, with a long Zig Zag Length where a swing takes more than 60 bars to settle, parts of the older line can differ from the final swings (signals, level lines and candle colours are unaffected); the table is drawn at the chart's own text size and in the nearest corner, because a table here has no size setting and pins only to a corner.

liquidity-void-fill-scanner.title: Liquidity Void Fill Scanner
liquidity-void-fill-scanner.summary: Finds wide, full-bodied displacement candles, plots the Fibonacci level inside each one and signals when price retraces back to that level.
liquidity-void-fill-scanner.descriptionHtml:
A displacement candle is a bar that moves price a long way in one direction with little wick. Price crossed that range so quickly that few orders were filled inside it, leaving what is often called a liquidity void, and traders watch for price to come back into part of it. This study finds those candles, plots the level inside each one that price has to reach, and signals the bar on which it does.

A candle qualifies when it passes every filter that is switched on. The ATR filter asks for a high to low range larger than the average true range times the multiplier. The body filter asks for the body to cover at least Body % Above of the range. The optional body size filter also asks for a range at least the multiplier times the previous bar's range. A qualifying bearish candle is recoloured light red and a bullish one light green, and it arms its side.

The level is Fib Value of the newest qualifying candle's range: down from the high of a bearish candle, up from the low of a bullish one. A short signal fires when the high crosses up through the bearish level of an armed side, and a long signal when the low crosses down through the bullish level. A signal disarms its side until the next displacement candle, and the optional time and date filters limit which bars may signal. A small table shows the day's percentage change (each bar's change in close added up since the day began, the first bar measured from the previous day's last close), the day's volume so far against the previous day's total, and both days' volume in lakhs.
liquidity-void-fill-scanner.howToReadHtml:
A recoloured candle says a strong one-sided move has just happened. While its side is armed, the Short Fill Level or Long Fill Level line shows the price that would fill the void. A triangle above a bar is a short signal: price has rallied back into a bearish void, where sellers may defend it. A triangle below a bar is a long signal: price has dipped back into a bullish void. The line ends on the signal bar.

If a newer displacement candle arrives before the fill, the line moves to the newer candle's level. A signal only says price has reached the level, not that it will turn there; in a strong trend price often runs straight through, so traders usually wait for a reaction at the level.

settings.label: Long Signals
settings.html: Show the bullish side: the light green candles, the long triangles and the Long Fill Level line.

settings.label: Short Signals
settings.html: Show the bearish side: the light red candles, the short triangles and the Short Fill Level line.

settings.label: Fib Value
settings.html: How far into the candle the level sits, from 0 at the start of the move to 1 at its far end. 0.5 is the midpoint.

settings.label: Apply ATR Filter
settings.html: Require a displacement candle's range to exceed the average true range times the multiplier.

settings.label: ATR Length
settings.html: Bars in the average true range used by the ATR filter. The filter blocks every candle until it has enough bars.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges a candle must span. Higher values keep only larger candles.

settings.label: Apply Body % Filter
settings.html: Require a displacement candle's body to cover at least the set share of its range.

settings.label: Body % Above
settings.html: The smallest body as a percentage of the candle's range. At 80 the wicks together may be at most a fifth of it.

settings.label: Apply Body Size Filter
settings.html: Also require a full body and a range at least the multiplier times the previous candle's range.

settings.label: Body Size Multiplier (x)
settings.html: How many times the previous candle's range a displacement candle must reach when the body size filter is on.

settings.label: Apply Time Filter
settings.html: Allow signals only on bars that open inside the window below, read on the chart's clock.

settings.label: Time From (hour)
settings.html: The hour the signal window opens, on a 24 hour clock.

settings.label: Time From (minute)
settings.html: The minute the signal window opens.

settings.label: Time To (hour)
settings.html: The hour the signal window closes. A bar opening at the closing time is outside it.

settings.label: Time To (minute)
settings.html: The minute the signal window closes.

settings.label: Apply Date Filter
settings.html: Allow signals only on bars of the single date below, read on the chart's calendar.

settings.label: Day
settings.html: Day of the month for the date filter.

settings.label: Month
settings.html: Month, 1 to 12, for the date filter.

settings.label: Year
settings.html: Four digit year for the date filter.

settings.label: Display Table
settings.html: Show the table of the day's percentage change and volume against the previous day.

faq.q: Why does the fill level line sometimes stop without a signal?
faq.html: It does not stop without one: the line runs while its side is armed and ends on the bar that fills the level. A line still running at the right edge of the chart is a void that has not been filled yet. Where the line changes level before a signal, a newer displacement candle replaced the level before the fill.

faq.q: What do the volume figures in the table mean?
faq.html: Vol is the volume traded so far today and PD Vol the previous day's total, both in lakhs (hundred thousands). Vol %Chg compares today's running volume with the previous day's total, so it starts each day near minus 100 percent and climbs as the day trades. The day boundary follows the chart's calendar.

faq.q: Does the scanner check other symbols?
faq.html: No. It runs on the chart's own instrument only and reports what it finds in the bars loaded on the chart.

liquidity-void-fill-scanner.deviation: The fill level lines are drawn on every bar while a side is armed, so they also show levels that a newer displacement candle replaced and levels that were never filled, whereas the original draws a level only from the newest displacement candle to the bar that fills it; whether a level will be filled is known only on the fill bar, and a study cannot go back and blank the bars it has already drawn. Every level shown agrees with the original.
liquidity-void-fill-scanner.credit: Original work (c) Arun K Bhaskar, MPL-2.0

liquidity-void-fill.title: Liquidity Void Fill
liquidity-void-fill.summary: Marks wide, full-bodied displacement candles and signals when price later retraces into the void they left, at a chosen Fibonacci depth of the candle.
liquidity-void-fill.descriptionHtml:
A displacement candle is a bar that moves price a long way in one direction with little wick: the market traded through that range so quickly that few orders were filled inside it. That thin stretch is often called a liquidity void, and traders watch for price to come back into part of it. This study finds those candles and marks the bar on which price returns into them.

A candle qualifies when it passes every filter that is switched on. The ATR filter asks for a high to low range larger than the average true range times the multiplier. The body filter asks for the body to cover at least Body % Above of the range. The optional body size filter also asks for a range at least the multiplier times the previous bar's range. A qualifying bearish candle is recoloured light red and a bullish one light green.

From the newest qualifying candle of each side the study measures a level at Fib Value of its range: down from the high of a bearish candle, up from the low of a bullish one. A short signal fires when the high crosses up through the bearish level after a bearish candle has armed it, and a long signal fires when the low crosses down through the bullish level. Each signal draws a line at the level from the candle to the signal bar, and the optional time and date filters limit which bars may signal.
liquidity-void-fill.howToReadHtml:
A recoloured candle says a strong one-sided move has just happened and arms that side. A triangle above a bar is a short signal: price has rallied back into a bearish void, where sellers who drove the move may defend it. A triangle below a bar is a long signal: price has dipped back into a bullish void. The line shows the level that was reached and the candle it came from.

A signal only says price has returned to the level, not that it will turn there. Strong trends often run straight through a void, so traders usually look for a reaction at the level or combine it with structure before acting. A Fib Value nearer 0 puts the level nearer the start of the move, so price has to retrace further and signals come fewer and later; nearer 1 the level sits by the end of the move and is reached sooner.

settings.label: Long Signals
settings.html: Show the bullish side: the light green candles, the long triangles and their lines.

settings.label: Short Signals
settings.html: Show the bearish side: the light red candles, the short triangles and their lines.

settings.label: Fib Value
settings.html: How far into the candle the level sits, from 0 at the start of the move to 1 at its far end. 0.5 is the midpoint.

settings.label: Line Style
settings.html: Draw the fill lines solid, dashed or dotted.

settings.label: Apply ATR Filter
settings.html: Require a displacement candle's range to exceed the average true range times the multiplier.

settings.label: ATR Length
settings.html: Bars in the average true range used by the ATR filter. The filter blocks every candle until it has enough bars.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: How many average true ranges a candle must span. Higher values keep only larger candles.

settings.label: Apply Body % Filter
settings.html: Require a displacement candle's body to cover at least the set share of its range.

settings.label: Body % Above
settings.html: The smallest body as a percentage of the candle's range. At 80 the wicks together may be at most a fifth of it.

settings.label: Apply Body Size Filter
settings.html: Also require a full body and a range at least the multiplier times the previous candle's range.

settings.label: Body Size Multiplier (x)
settings.html: How many times the previous candle's range a displacement candle must reach when the body size filter is on.

settings.label: Apply Time Filter
settings.html: Allow signals only on bars that open inside the window below, read on the chart's clock.

settings.label: Time From (hour)
settings.html: The hour the signal window opens, on a 24 hour clock.

settings.label: Time From (minute)
settings.html: The minute the signal window opens.

settings.label: Time To (hour)
settings.html: The hour the signal window closes. A bar opening at the closing time is outside it.

settings.label: Time To (minute)
settings.html: The minute the signal window closes.

settings.label: Apply Date Filter
settings.html: Allow signals only on bars of the single date below, read on the chart's calendar.

settings.label: Day
settings.html: Day of the month for the date filter.

settings.label: Month
settings.html: Month, 1 to 12, for the date filter.

settings.label: Year
settings.html: Four digit year for the date filter.

faq.q: Why did a recoloured candle produce no signal?
faq.html: A side fires once per arming. After a signal the side waits for a new displacement candle, and a candle that arrives while a side is already armed only moves the level to the newer candle. If price never returns to the level, there is no signal.

faq.q: Do the time and date filters change which candles qualify?
faq.html: No. They apply only to the retracement bar that signals. Displacement candles are found and recoloured on every bar.

faq.q: Why are there no signals at the start of the chart?
faq.html: With the ATR filter on, no candle can qualify until the average true range has enough bars, so the first signals appear after that warmup.

liquidity-void-multi-timeframe.title: Liquidity Void Multi-timeframe
liquidity-void-multi-timeframe.summary: Boxes the untraded price gaps between same-direction candles of a chosen timeframe, with a level line that runs right until price returns.
liquidity-void-multi-timeframe.descriptionHtml:
A liquidity void is a range of price that two candles of the same direction left untraded between them. A bearish void forms on a rising candle whose high is at or below the low of the previous rising candle. A bullish void is the mirror image: a falling candle whose low is at or above the high of the previous falling candle. Each void is drawn as a shaded box between the two candles, red for bearish and green for bullish, with a level line at the far edge, at the 0.79 retracement from the near edge, or at the midpoint.

The candles can come from a longer timeframe than the chart's. The study folds the chart's own bars into buckets of the chosen length (minutes, hours, days, weeks or months) and runs the test on those buckets, so a 4 hour void can be read on an hourly chart. Calendar days, weeks and months are counted in Indian time, and a week starts on Monday. The bucket that holds the newest bar is still forming, so it moves and clears drawings but never creates a void.

A height filter drops narrow voids: a void must be taller than the bucket timeframe's average true range times a multiplier, or taller than a percentage of its far edge. Each box and line stretches right with every bucket until a bucket's range reaches it, and is then frozen there. Only the newest Show Last voids of each side are kept.
liquidity-void-multi-timeframe.howToReadHtml:
Read a void as a stretch of price the market skipped on the chosen timeframe. A box or line that is still stretching to the newest bar marks a gap price has not returned to; a frozen one shows where price first came back. The level line, at the far edge, the 0.79 retracement or the midpoint depending on Source, is the price many traders watch for a reaction when price returns.

Voids from a longer timeframe are fewer and larger, and they are usually treated as more important than the chart's own. Because the test needs a finished bucket, a void appears only once the bucket that formed it has closed. With the default filter of four times the average true range, only very large gaps qualify; choose Percentage and set it to 0 to see every void.

settings.label: Timeframe
settings.html: The timeframe the voids are measured on. Leave it empty for the chart's own bars. A bare number is minutes (15, 60), and a suffix names the unit: 1h, 4h, D, 2D, W or M for months.

settings.label: Show Last
settings.html: How many of the most recent voids of each side keep their box and line on the chart. At 0 no voids are drawn.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: Where the level line sits inside each void: the far edge, the 0.79 retracement measured from the near edge, or the midpoint.

settings.label: Bearish
settings.html: Find and draw bearish voids, the gaps between two rising candles of the chosen timeframe.

settings.label: Bullish
settings.html: Find and draw bullish voids, the gaps between two falling candles of the chosen timeframe.

settings.label: Hide Crossed
settings.html: Remove a void's line as soon as a bucket's range reaches its level, and remove its box once a bucket's range reaches the box's far edge, rather than leaving them frozen on the chart.

settings.label: Filter Using
settings.html: How narrow voids are dropped: by comparing the void's height with the average true range of the chosen timeframe, or with a percentage of its far edge.

settings.label: ATR Period
settings.html: The number of buckets in the average true range the ATR filter reads. Used only when Filter Using is ATR.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: A void must be taller than the average true range times this number. Higher values keep only the larger voids.

settings.label: Percentage Above
settings.html: With the Percentage filter, a void must be taller than this percentage of its far edge. Set it to 0 to keep every void.

faq.q: Which timeframe codes does it read?
faq.html: A bare number is minutes, so 15 and 240 are 15 minutes and 4 hours. A suffix names the unit: s for seconds, m or min for minutes, h for hours, D for days, W for weeks and an upper-case M for months, with an optional number in front such as 2D. An empty or unreadable code uses the chart's own bars.

faq.q: Why does a new void appear only after the bucket has closed?
faq.html: A void is defined by a finished candle of the chosen timeframe. The bucket that holds the newest bar is still forming, so the study waits for it to close before it can create a void from it. It still freezes or clears existing drawings as that bucket trades.

faq.q: Why are there so few voids on my chart?
faq.html: The default filter keeps only voids taller than four times the average true range of the chosen timeframe. Lower the ATR Multiplier, or choose Percentage and set it to 0, to see more.

liquidity-void-screener.title: Liquidity Void Screener
liquidity-void-screener.summary: Boxes the untraded price gaps between candles of the same direction and marks the bars where price crosses back through the newest void level.
liquidity-void-screener.descriptionHtml:
A liquidity void here is a range of price that two candles of the same direction left untraded between them. A bearish void forms on a rising candle whose high is at or below the low of the previous rising candle, so price jumped down between them. A bullish void is the mirror image: a falling candle whose low is at or above the high of the previous falling candle. Each void is drawn as a shaded box between the two candles' near edges, red for bearish and green for bullish, with a level line drawn across it.

The level sits at the far edge of the void (High/Low), at the 0.79 retracement from the near edge (OTE 0.79%), or at the midpoint (50%). A height filter drops narrow voids: either the void must be taller than the average true range times a multiplier, or taller than a percentage of the far edge. Each box and line stretches right with every new bar until a bar's range reaches it, and is then frozen at that bar. Only the newest Show Last voids of each side are kept.

The study also watches the newest void level of each side. An H is marked above a bar whose high rises through the newest bearish level, and an L below a bar whose low falls through the newest bullish level.
liquidity-void-screener.howToReadHtml:
Read a void as a stretch of price the market skipped. Price may come back to such a range later, and a box that is still stretching to the right is a void price has not returned to yet. A frozen box or line shows where price first came back. The level line, at the far edge, the 0.79 retracement or the midpoint depending on Source, is the price many traders watch for a reaction when that return happens.

The H and L marks flag the bars where price crossed back through the newest void level, which can be read as the void being filled or tested. They are signals about the most recent void of each side only. The filter matters a great deal: with the default four times the average true range only very large gaps qualify, so on a calm market there may be few or no voids on the chart. Choose Percentage and set it to 0 to see every void.

settings.label: Show Last
settings.html: How many of the most recent voids of each side keep their box and line on the chart. At 0 no voids are drawn, though the signals still fire.

settings.label: Source
settings.html: Where the level line sits inside each void: the far edge, the 0.79 retracement measured from the near edge, or the midpoint. The signals use this level too.

settings.label: Bearish
settings.html: Find and draw bearish voids, the gaps between two rising candles. Turning it off also stops the H signals, which need a bearish level.

settings.label: Bullish
settings.html: Find and draw bullish voids, the gaps between two falling candles. Turning it off also stops the L signals, which need a bullish level.

settings.label: Hide Crossed
settings.html: Remove a void's line as soon as a bar's range reaches its level, and remove its box once a bar's range reaches the box's far edge, rather than leaving them frozen on the chart.

settings.label: Filter Using
settings.html: How narrow voids are dropped: by comparing the void's height with the average true range, or with a percentage of its far edge.

settings.label: ATR Period
settings.html: The length of the average true range the ATR filter reads. Used only when Filter Using is ATR.

settings.label: ATR Multiplier
settings.html: A void must be taller than the average true range times this number. Higher values keep only the larger voids.

settings.label: Percentage Above
settings.html: With the Percentage filter, a void must be taller than this percentage of its far edge. Set it to 0 to keep every void.

settings.label: Direction
settings.html: Both shows H and L signals. Bullish shows only the H signals, where price rises through a bearish level. Bearish shows only the L signals, where price falls through a bullish level.

settings.label: Only Bullish
settings.html: Show the L signals, the bars whose low falls back through the newest bullish void level.

settings.label: Only Bearish
settings.html: Show the H signals, the bars whose high rises back through the newest bearish void level.

faq.q: Why are there so few voids on my chart?
faq.html: The default filter keeps only voids taller than four times the 14-bar average true range, which is a large gap on most instruments. Lower the ATR Multiplier, or choose Percentage and set it to 0 to see every void.

faq.q: Which void does a signal refer to?
faq.html: Only the newest void of each side. When a new bullish void forms, its level replaces the previous one, and an L marks the next bar whose low falls through that new level. If an H and an L would fall on the same bar, only the L is marked.

faq.q: Why does a box stop stretching before price has filled it?
faq.html: A box is frozen as soon as a bar's range reaches its near edge, the side next to the candle that created it. Price may not have reached the far edge yet. With Hide Crossed on, the box is removed once price reaches the far edge too.
